stage 4 — track 3: high-quality 3D and motion on web and app
cycle 1 — complete 3D quality framework: first emission

the root distinction at depth:

most web 3D answers the question "can we render this?" production-grade web 3D answers the question "what does the rendered object need to communicate, and what is the minimum rendering required to communicate it?" these are different operations.

the failure case: an engineering team spends weeks optimizing a photorealistic product render for the hero section. it loads at 4 seconds on mid-range mobile. it has no relationship with the surrounding 2D. it spins in a loop. it communicates: we have 3D capability. it does not communicate: this product will change your experience. the rendering served the team's capability demonstration, not the user's decision.

lighting brief system: the six light types and when each is correct

1. cold directional (single source, blue-cool, high contrast)
   → domain: precision hardware, developer tools, financial data, cybersecurity
   → communicates: exactness, reliability, machine-made
   → three.js: DirectionalLight color=#b0c8ff, intensity=2.0, castShadow=true
               AmbientLight color=#1a2030, intensity=0.2
   → what it reveals: sharp edges, machined surfaces, precise geometry
   → what it hides: warmth, organics, human scale

2. warm scattered (area/hemisphere, golden-warm, low contrast)
   → domain: wellness, consumer goods, food, children's products
   → communicates: approachability, warmth, living-world
   → three.js: HemisphereLight skyColor=#ffead0, groundColor=#503010, intensity=1.5
               PointLight color=#ffc87a, intensity=0.8, decay=2
   → what it reveals: soft curves, organic forms, approachable surfaces
   → what it hides: precision, machine quality

3. dramatic single-source (spotlight, high contrast, strong directional shadow)
   → domain: luxury goods, cinema, fashion, premium hardware
   → communicates: exclusivity, singularity, worth of being illuminated
   → three.js: SpotLight color=#fff5e8, intensity=3.0, angle=Math.PI/6, penumbra=0.4
               AmbientLight color=#0a0a12, intensity=0.05
   → what it reveals: form, silhouette, specular highlights, material quality
   → what it hides: context, environment, supporting detail

4. neutral studio (HDRI environment, balanced, professional)
   → domain: e-commerce, product catalog, reference visualization
   → communicates: accuracy, what the product actually looks like
   → three.js: RGBELoader with neutral studio HDRI (Polyhaven: studio_small_09)
               PMREMGenerator for prefiltering
   → what it reveals: true color, material properties, actual dimensions
   → what it hides: aspirational quality (studio HDRIs are accurate, not aspirational)

5. environmental (real-world HDRI, location-specific)
   → domain: architecture visualization, outdoor products, automotive
   → communicates: this object exists in your world, not in a controlled space
   → three.js: RGBELoader with environment-specific HDRI
               exposure calibrated to match the environment's dynamic range
   → what it reveals: contextual relationship, scale, real-world material behavior
   → what it hides: the idealized product (reality doesn't flatter, it contextualizes)

6. emissive/neon (self-illuminating surfaces, dark environment)
   → domain: gaming, nightlife, entertainment, cyberpunk-adjacent
   → communicates: the product generates its own energy, it is the light source
   → three.js: MeshStandardMaterial emissive=#00ff88, emissiveIntensity=2.0
               UnrealBloomPass (post-processing) for bloom
               dark environment: AmbientLight intensity=0.05 only
   → what it reveals: internal energy, power, RGB aesthetic
   → what it hides: material texture, surface detail (bloom obscures)

material brief system: production-grade PBR

the vibe-coded 3D material: MeshStandardMaterial with a single color. no texture. default roughness (0.5). default metalness (0). it looks like plastic regardless of what it is supposed to be.

production material stack:

POLISHED METAL (watches, hardware, premium consumer goods):
  roughness:    0.05-0.15 (near mirror)
  metalness:    1.0
  normalMap:    brushed direction (parallel lines, fine grain)
  envMapIntensity: 3.0 (heavy environment reflection — this is what makes metal look metal)
  color:        #e0e0e0 for silver, #d4af72 for gold

MATTE ALUMINUM (laptops, industrial design):
  roughness:    0.6-0.8
  metalness:    0.9
  normalMap:    micro-grain texture (sandblasted look)
  envMapIntensity: 0.8
  color:        #b8bec7

FROSTED GLASS:
  MeshPhysicalMaterial (not Standard)
  transmission:   0.95
  roughness:      0.2
  thickness:      0.3
  ior:            1.5 (glass refractive index)
  envMapIntensity: 1.5
  note: requires WebGLRenderer with logarithmicDepthBuffer and alpha:true

SOFT FABRIC (headphones, apparel, packaging):
  roughness:    0.95 (nearly no specular)
  metalness:    0.0
  normalMap:    woven thread pattern
  aoMap:        ambient occlusion from weave compression
  color:        desaturated brand color — fabric absorbs, does not reflect

WORN LEATHER (luxury goods, audio equipment):
  roughness:    textured (roughnessMap varying 0.4-0.9 across surface)
  metalness:    0.0
  normalMap:    leather grain with worn edge highlight at seams
  displacementMap: subtle (0.01 scale) for tactile depth at close range
  color:        deep brown (#3d1f0c) with warm orange edges where worn

camera and composition system:

the vibe-coded camera: OrbitControls, default position (0, 0, 5), default FOV (50-75).
the object is in the center of the frame with equal space on all sides.
it was placed, not composed.

production camera brief:

ASPIRATIONAL PRODUCT (the viewer should want this):
  position:   slightly below center, offset to the left or right
  FOV:        28-35mm (compressed, flattens depth, makes object feel more substantial)
  orbit:      subtle auto-rotate, slow enough to not be distracting
              speed: 0.3 rad/s. pause on hover.
  composition: rule of thirds — primary face at left or right third intersection

EDITORIAL (the viewer should understand the object):
  position:   eye level, slight three-quarter view
  FOV:        50mm (natural perspective, no distortion)
  orbit:      user-controlled, damping enabled (dampingFactor: 0.05)
  composition: centered, generous breathing room

IMMERSIVE (the viewer should feel inside the experience):
  position:   wide-angle, low FOV (75-90 for VR-adjacent feel) OR perspective correction
  orbit:      mouse parallax, not orbit — the object responds to cursor position
  composition: bleeds past container edges, text overlays 3D

SCROLL-DRIVEN NARRATIVE:
  camera path: defined as a CatmullRomCurve3
  progress:   mapped to scroll position via gsap.ScrollTrigger
  easing:     gsap.ease "power2.inOut" on the scroll progress mapping
              (so the camera is not linearly mapped to raw scroll)
  keyframes:  0% → overhead view; 33% → front view; 66% → detail close-up; 100% → packaging view

performance architecture: cycle 1

GEOMETRY BUDGET — ENFORCED:
mobile:   < 100k vertices total scene (not per object, total)
desktop:  < 500k vertices total scene
above limit → implement LOD (Level of Detail):
  LOD.addLevel(highDetailMesh, 0)    // distance 0-10
  LOD.addLevel(medDetailMesh, 10)    // distance 10-50
  LOD.addLevel(lowDetailMesh, 50)    // distance 50+

TEXTURE BUDGET — ENFORCED:
background/distant:  512×512 KTX2 (Basis compressed)
primary surface:     1024×1024 KTX2
hero product:        2048×2048 KTX2 max, only on desktop
never:               raw PNG/JPG in production 3D pipeline

SHADER BUDGET — TRACKED:
count texture samples per fragment shader
mobile target:       ≤ 4 samples (color + normal + roughness + AO)
desktop target:      ≤ 8 samples (add emissive + metalness + displacement + transmission)

LOADING STRATEGY — STAGED:
stage 1: page load — geometry only, MeshBasicMaterial (solid color, no lighting)
stage 2: 300ms in — ambient + directional lights, no texture
stage 3: 600ms in — primary texture map
stage 4: 1200ms in — normal map, roughness map, final material

this produces perceived instant 3D (something is there immediately) 
with progressive quality enhancement.

FRAME RATE MONITORING:
renderer.info.render.triangles — log per frame, alert if >500k
Stats.js in development, auto-removed in production
target: 60fps on M1 MacBook, 30fps on mid-range Android (Pixel 6a)
stage 5 — track 4: pattern recognition across all human knowledge
cycle 1 — full anatomy of first pattern batch

pattern 1: delayed-cost selection pressure

surface layer:
systems and organisms consistently choose options whose costs arrive later while benefits arrive now, regardless of domain. this is visible everywhere: debt-financed consumption, evolutionary traits that maximize reproduction at the cost of longevity, political policies that produce immediate approval at long-term expense, software architectures that ship fast at the cost of maintainability.

technical layer:
the mechanism is a discount rate applied to future costs. present costs are weighted at 1.0. future costs are weighted at 1.0 / (1 + r)^t where r is the discount rate and t is the time until cost arrives. when r is high enough, a cost ten years away approaches zero in present value calculation. biological systems use hyperbolic discounting (even steeper: 1 / (1 + kt)) — meaning costs in the near future are discounted more steeply than costs in the far future. this produces preference reversal: what looks optimal at t=0 flips when you arrive at the near-future point.

structural layer:
three conditions must be true for this pattern to dominate:

the agent has a discount rate greater than zero (always true for biological systems; true for most economic agents)
the future cost is genuinely deferred (the cost doesn't feedback immediately)
the present benefit is real and immediate

the pattern breaks when: future costs arrive faster than the discount rate predicted (climate change accelerating beyond models), or when selection pressure changes (environment changes such that delayed costs are now immediate), or when the discount rate is explicitly reduced by institutional design (central bank forcing long time horizons).

cross-domain layer:

domain	benefit	deferred cost	when cost arrives
evolutionary	high reproductive fitness, sugar metabolism	cardiovascular disease, insulin resistance	post-reproductive age
economics	consumption, GDP growth	debt burden, inflationary pressure	the next cycle or the next generation
software	shipping fast, velocity	technical debt, refactoring cost, system failure	when team size scales or requirements change
politics	popular policies, re-election	structural deficits, infrastructure decay	next administration
cognitive	satisficing (good enough answer)	accumulated error, compounded misjudgment	when decision stakes rise
ecology	resource extraction	ecosystem collapse	decades later

root layer:
the single irreducible mechanic: present-weighted selection against future-weighted cost. any system that discounts the future relative to the present will, given a choice between benefit-now-cost-later and benefit-later-cost-now, systematically prefer the first. the strength of this preference scales with the discount rate and the time distance of the cost. this is not a bias or an error in any individual case. it is an emergent property of any selection process operating under uncertainty across time.

pattern name: DCSP — delayed-cost selection pressure

implication map:

why vibe-coded code is selected: DCSP. the vibe-coded version ships on Friday. the production-grade version ships next quarter. the cost (technical debt, system failure) arrives later. the benefit (shipped feature) arrives now. absent institutional pressure changing the discount rate (code review, architecture standards, senior engineering culture), DCSP predicts vibe-coding as the attractor state.
why design systems get skipped: DCSP. the design system costs 3 weeks of setup. the benefit (consistency, speed at scale) arrives in six months. at a high enough discount rate, the design system never gets built.
why tests don't get written: DCSP. tests cost time now. the cost they prevent arrives later. high discount rate → DCSP → no tests.

pattern 2: feedback-delay oscillation

surface layer:
any system where the feedback from an output arrives with a delay produces oscillation around the target value. too hot → turn down heat → too cold → turn up heat → too hot. interest rates raised too high → recession → rates cut too low → inflation → rates raised too high. the oscillation is not caused by bad decisions. it is caused by the delay between action and feedback.

technical layer:
this is a second-order system with a lag. the controller (decision-maker) takes action based on current state, but does not receive feedback from that action until t + Δt. during the delay window, the system continues to drift. when feedback finally arrives, it is reporting the state from Δt ago, not the current state. the controller then overcompensates for a problem that has already begun self-correcting. the magnitude of oscillation scales with the delay length and the controller's response gain. at high gain + high delay, the system becomes unstable (oscillation grows rather than dampens).

structural layer:
necessary conditions:

there is a feedback delay (action → effect → signal arriving back to controller)
the controller has a nonzero response gain (it does something when it receives signal)
the system has momentum (it continues moving after the controller acts)

domain	action	delay	oscillation
economics	interest rate change	12-18 months to full effect	boom-bust cycles
ecology	predator-prey	population lag	Lotka-Volterra oscillation
supply chain	production order	weeks to months	bullwhip effect (amplifying oscillation upstream)
body temperature	sweating/shivering	physiological response delay	fever spike, cold sweat cycle
software deployment	feature flag rollout	A/B test statistical significance lag	over-corrective product pivots
military	weapons procurement	5-10 year production cycle	capability mismatch with current threat

root layer:
FDOP — feedback-delay oscillation principle. the mechanism: when action and signal are separated by time, and the controller is responsive to signal, the system overshoots its target in the direction the delay concealed. the overshooting becomes the next signal, which produces the next overshoot in the opposite direction. the system orbits its target rather than converging on it. convergence requires either: reducing delay, reducing response gain, or modeling the delay explicitly in the controller (predictive control — acting on projected future state, not current signal).

pattern 3: preferential attachment (the rich-get-richer mechanic)

surface layer:
in systems where new nodes choose where to attach based on how many connections existing nodes already have, the result is a power-law distribution: a few nodes accumulate the vast majority of connections while most nodes have very few. this is not random — it is structurally determined by the attachment rule.

technical layer:
probability of new node attaching to existing node i = k_i / Σk_j where k_i is current degree of node i. this produces a preferential attachment that compounding: a node with more connections is more likely to get additional connections, which gives it more connections, which increases its probability further. the degree distribution converges to P(k) ~ k^(-γ) with γ typically near 3 — a power law. no scale characterizes the distribution (hence "scale-free").

structural layer:
conditions:

growth (new nodes continuously added)
preferential attachment (connection probability scales with existing connections)
the network is sparse relative to its size (most pairs are not connected)

domain	nodes	attachment rule	result
citation networks	papers	papers cite papers that already have citations	few papers get most citations
social networks	users	users follow users who already have followers	few accounts dominate reach
economic wealth	individuals	capital attracts returns, which are capital	wealth power law
language	words	words used in writing appear in more writing	Zipf's law (word frequency power law)
city size	cities	people move to cities where people already live	power law city size distribution
codebases	functions	code calls functions that are already called	few functions depended on by everything
protein interaction	proteins	proteins bind to proteins that already have binding partners	hub proteins with many interactions

root layer:
PAM — preferential attachment multiplier. the mechanism: when probability of selection scales with existing selection count, the initial distribution (random noise, first-mover advantage, quality differential) becomes structurally amplified. the later distribution is not a reflection of quality. it is a reflection of the initial distribution after amplification by the feedback rule. small early advantages become permanent structural dominance. reversing PAM requires either: changing the attachment rule (making new nodes as attractive as established ones), or redistribution (breaking the compounding).

pattern 4: phase transition near criticality

surface layer:
systems that appear to change gradually produce sudden, discontinuous changes when a threshold is crossed. sand pile that looks stable adds one grain and avalanches. markets look orderly, then a tipping point is crossed and cascades. ecosystems appear robust then collapse in a season. the change looks sudden from the outside. the threshold was approached gradually from the inside.

technical layer:
at a critical point, the system's correlation length diverges — fluctuations at every scale appear. the susceptibility (response to small perturbations) approaches infinity. a small push that would have dissipated in a subcritical system propagates through the entire system at criticality. the order parameter (the thing that characterizes which phase the system is in) drops discontinuously at the transition point in first-order transitions and continuously but abruptly in second-order transitions. the Ising model of ferromagnetism describes this mathematically: at the Curie temperature, magnetic susceptibility diverges, and the material flips from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic.

structural layer:
warning signals that a system is approaching a critical transition:

critical slowing down: the system takes longer to recover from small perturbations
increased variance: fluctuations get larger as the critical point approaches
increased spatial correlation: distant parts of the system become more correlated
flickering: the system begins exhibiting transient flips toward the post-transition state

domain	subcritical	critical point	post-critical
magnetism	random spin orientation	Curie temperature	aligned ferromagnetic
ecology	stable ecosystem	overexploitation threshold	collapsed trophic cascade
social	distributed opinion	polarization cascade trigger	bifurcated faction structure
finance	normal volatility	liquidity threshold	credit freeze / crash
software	manageable complexity	complexity threshold	system incomprehensible, change impossible
neuroscience	normal cognition	seizure threshold	epileptic cascade
physics of water	liquid	100°C at 1 atm	vapor (phase transition)

root layer:
CPT — criticality-phase transition. the mechanism: nonlinear systems near their critical point lose the stability that dampens perturbations. what was absorbed is now amplified. the system flips from one attractor to another. the flip appears discontinuous from outside but has an internal approach trajectory with measurable warning signals. the system does not transition without warning — it transitions without the warning being read, because reading CPT signals requires measuring the right quantities (slowing down, variance, correlation) rather than the obvious quantities (current state, current value).

CPT in software specifically:
every codebase has a complexity threshold. below it: change is possible, bugs are local, understanding is achievable. at the threshold: any change has unpredictable effects, debugging takes longer, onboarding new engineers fails. above it: the system is effectively immutable — rewrites become the only path. the warning signals are measurable: cycle time (time from commit to production) increases (critical slowing down), incident rate variance increases, PR review time increases, test flakiness increases.

pattern 5: the competence plateau with differential decay

surface layer:
skills develop rapidly early, then plateau. but different sub-skills within a domain decay at different rates when practice stops. the result: experts who stop practicing retain some sub-skills and lose others, becoming partially skilled in a misleading way — they have domain knowledge (slow decay) but have lost procedural execution (fast decay).

technical layer:
two skill types with different decay rates:

declarative (knowing that): slow decay, approaches an asymptote near original competence. a surgeon who stops operating for five years still knows the anatomy, the indications, the complications.
procedural (knowing how): faster decay, especially for high-precision motor programs. the same surgeon has degraded tactile feedback, slower hand speed, less efficient movement economy.

the misleading intersection: declarative competence produces false confidence in procedural competence. the expert believes they can still do the thing because they can still explain the thing.

domain	fast-decay (procedural)	slow-decay (declarative)
surgery	precise tissue handling, speed, tactile discrimination	anatomy, complication recognition, decision-making
programming	framework API recall, speed of implementation	architecture, debugging approach, domain modeling
music	tempo stability at speed, technical precision	harmonic knowledge, sight-reading scores, theory
language	rapid oral production, listening comprehension	grammar knowledge, reading comprehension
trading	pattern recognition speed, position sizing instinct	market structure knowledge, risk framework

root layer:
PDD — procedural-declarative differential decay. the mechanism: two types of knowledge encoded in different memory systems (procedural in cerebellum and basal ganglia, declarative in hippocampus-neocortex) have different susceptibility to disuse. systems that run implicitly (procedural) require regular rehearsal. systems that run explicitly (declarative) consolidate and remain accessible. the expert who loses procedural competence while retaining declarative competence is dangerous: they can supervise but not execute, consult but not implement, design but not build.

direct application to software: a senior engineer who has not written production code in 18 months retains: architecture judgment, code review ability, system design, domain knowledge. they have begun to lose: knowledge of current framework APIs, speed of implementation, awareness of current ecosystem tradeoffs, debugging instinct for current tools. recognizing PDD prevents the error of placing such an engineer in an IC role that requires fast procedural execution.

pattern 6: information cascade and herding

surface layer:
even when individuals hold private information suggesting one choice, they observe others making a different choice and update toward the crowd. the cascade begins when the public signal (what others are doing) outweighs the private signal (what you personally know). the result: everyone follows the same path, not because it is correct, but because each individual inferred that the prior individuals who chose it knew something.

technical layer:
bayesian updating on public vs. private information. if person 1 has private signal A and chooses A, person 2 observes the choice and updates — even if their own private signal is B, the observation of the A-choice counts as evidence that A is correct. once the public signal accumulates enough weight (after enough sequential A-choices are observed), private signals are rationalized away. the cascade produces a fragile equilibrium: it is privately optimal for each individual to follow the cascade, but the cascade carries no more information than the initial signal of the first person who started it.

structural layer:
cascade breaks when: a person has a very strong private signal that overwhelms the accumulated public signal, or when an agent with high credibility makes a public counter-signal, or when the outcome of the cascade becomes observable and is bad (the cascade ends through revealed error).

cross-domain layer:
financial bubble (herding into overvalued assets), fashion trends (wearing what others wear as a public signal of taste), restaurant choice (choosing the busy restaurant because people chose it), startup funding (funding what other VCs funded), citation snowballing (citing what others cited without reading the source), political bandwagon (supporting the leading candidate because they are leading), technology adoption (adopting the platform that others are adopting — PAM and information cascade combine).

root layer:
ICA — information cascade amplifier. mechanism: in sequential decision-making under uncertainty, public signals from prior actions outweigh private signals at sufficient depth in the sequence. the cascade amplifies the first signal (which may be random noise) to system-wide behavior. the cascade is privately rational at every step and collectively irrational at the system level. this is not stupidity — it is the correct bayesian response to believing that prior actors had information. it breaks only when private information is systematically stronger than public accumulation, or when credible counter-signals enter.

stage 6 — track 5: senior and elite coder patterns
cycle 1 — extraction and synthesis

elite pattern 1: constraint-first design

before any architecture is committed, the elite engineer writes down what the system must never do, what it must always do, and the boundary conditions that define its operating envelope.

this is not requirements documentation. it is constraint specification. the difference:

requirement:  "the user should be able to upload files"
constraint:   "file upload must: never store data that hasn't been scanned for malware,
               never allow filenames with path traversal characters (../, %2e%2e%2f),
               always reject files exceeding 50MB before reading the content,
               always store in a content-addressed scheme (SHA256 of content as key),
               never expose the internal storage path to the client,
               always delete temp file if virus scan fails,
               always enforce that the authenticated user's ID is bound to the upload record"

the constraint list creates the design space. what's left after constraints are satisfied is a tractable set of implementation choices, not an open field.

why this is senior:
vibe-coded implementations start with "what should this do?" and build outward. constraint-first starts with "what must this never do?" and designs inward. vibe-coded implementations discover their failure modes in production. constraint-first implementations design the failure modes before the success modes.

code translation of constraint-first:

typescript
// constraints as types (type system enforces what can't slip)
type FileUploadRequest = {
  readonly userId: UserId;           // constraint: always bound to user
  readonly content: ArrayBuffer;     // constraint: content-addressed, not named
  readonly mimeType: AllowedMimeType; // constraint: only allowed types (union type)
  readonly contentLength: NumberBelowLimit<52_428_800>; // constraint: <50MB enforced at type level
};

// constraints as validation boundary (never trust past this point)
function validateFileUpload(raw: unknown): Result<FileUploadRequest, ValidationError> {
  // all validation at the entry boundary
  // inside the system, FileUploadRequest is trusted
}

// constraints as operation contract
async function processFileUpload(request: FileUploadRequest): Promise<Result<StoredFile, UploadError>> {
  // malware scan FIRST — always
  const scanResult = await scanForMalware(request.content);
  if (!scanResult.clean) {
    return Err({ code: 'MALWARE_DETECTED', fileHash: sha256(request.content) });
  }

// content-addressed key — filename never enters the system
  const contentKey = sha256(request.content);

// atomic: store and bind to user in one transaction
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    await tx.files.create({ key: contentKey, content: request.content, mimeType: request.mimeType });
    await tx.userFiles.create({ userId: request.userId, fileKey: contentKey });
  });

// never return internal storage path — return only the content-addressed key
  return Ok({ key: contentKey, mimeType: request.mimeType, size: request.contentLength });
}

elite pattern 2: the three-instance rule for abstraction timing

the elite engineer does not abstract after one instance. does not abstract after two instances. abstracts after three instances, because:

one instance: the requirement is understood as itself
two instances: a possible pattern is visible but the variation space is unknown
three instances: the actual shape of the variation becomes clear — what varies and what is invariant

abstracting at one instance produces abstractions that don't fit the second case. abstracting at two instances produces abstractions that are too tight (optimized for two known cases, wrong for the third). three instances reveal what the abstraction must accommodate.

the forensic of early abstraction:

typescript
// early abstraction (after first case: user table):
abstract class BaseRepository<T> {
  abstract tableName: string;
  async findById(id: string): Promise<T | null> { ... }
  async findAll(): Promise<T[]> { ... }
  async save(entity: T): Promise<T> { ... }
  async delete(id: string): Promise<void> { ... }
}

// what happens at the second case: order table with multi-field lookup, soft delete, tenant isolation
// the abstraction doesn't fit. addEndless overrides begin. the abstraction becomes a liability.
typescript
// three-instance abstraction (after user, order, notification tables revealed the pattern):
// what varies:    table name, entity type, query predicates, soft-delete vs hard-delete
// what is invariant: connection management, result mapping, transaction participation

// the abstraction now covers what it needs to cover and nothing else
type Repository<T, TCreate, TQuery> = {
  findOne(query: TQuery): Promise<T | null>;
  findMany(query: TQuery): Promise<T[]>;
  create(data: TCreate): Promise<T>;
  update(id: EntityId, data: Partial<TCreate>): Promise<T>;
};
// soft delete, tenant isolation, multi-field lookup — implemented per-repository, not in the abstraction
// because the third case (notification) doesn't need them, and forcing them in produces wrong abstractions

elite pattern 3: asymmetric attention at decision points

the elite engineer identifies the irreversible decisions before making them and applies proportionally more attention there. the reversible decisions are made fast and revised if wrong. the irreversible decisions are made slowly with explicit reversibility analysis.

irreversible decisions in software:
- database schema (especially: what is the primary key type, what is the tenant isolation model)
- api surface (once consumers exist, breaking changes are expensive)
- authentication strategy (migrating auth systems is catastrophic)
- event schema (published events are consumed by things you don't control)
- file storage format (data in the wrong format is permanently wrong)
- naming of core domain concepts (renaming spreads across the entire codebase)

reversible decisions in software:
- UI layout and visual design (redeploy)
- algorithm choice for internal computation (refactor)
- third-party service selection for non-critical path (migrate)
- error message text (deploy)
- caching strategy (configure)

the check that marks senior from intermediate:

before committing to a schema, api, or auth design, the senior engineer asks: "if the requirements change in the most likely way, how much does this decision cost to reverse?" if the answer is "catastrophic," the decision requires more analysis. if the answer is "trivial," it can be made now and revised.

elite pattern 4: the zero-trust internal API

vibe-coded systems trust everything inside their own boundary. the service that calls the internal API assumes the data it receives is valid. the function that receives a parameter assumes it is sanitized. the database query assumes the input is correctly typed.

elite systems apply zero-trust at every boundary, including internal ones. every function validates its inputs. every response is checked for shape before use. every database result is treated as untrusted until parsed into a domain type.

typescript
// vibe-coded: internal trust
async function updateUserProfile(userId: string, data: any) {
  await db.users.update(userId, data); // data trusted. userId trusted. nothing checked.
}

// elite: zero-trust internal boundary
async function updateUserProfile(
  userId: string, 
  data: unknown
): Promise<Result<User, UpdateProfileError>> {
  // step 1: validate caller has correct userId format
  const parsedId = UserId.parse(userId);
  if (!parsedId.success) return Err({ code: 'INVALID_USER_ID' });

// step 2: validate data is the shape we expect — never trust unknown
  const parsedData = UpdateProfileSchema.safeParse(data);
  if (!parsedData.success) return Err({ code: 'INVALID_DATA', issues: parsedData.error.issues });

// step 3: verify the user exists before attempting update
  const existing = await db.users.findOne({ id: parsedId.data });
  if (!existing) return Err({ code: 'USER_NOT_FOUND' });

// step 4: apply update with explicit field list (never spread untrusted data)
  const updated = await db.users.update(parsedId.data, {
    name: parsedData.data.name,
    bio: parsedData.data.bio,
    avatarUrl: parsedData.data.avatarUrl,
    updatedAt: new Date(),
  });

return Ok(updated);
}

anti-elite pattern library: cycle 1

the anti-elite patterns are the behaviors of engineers who are trying to signal seniority. they mark as junior to a trained eye.

anti-elite 1: premature abstraction signaling

the engineer abstracts everything on first contact to appear architecturally sophisticated. the result: a codebase with 15 abstract base classes, 30 generic types with 4 type parameters each, and zero readable code. every simple operation requires 5 files to trace. juniors on the team cannot contribute because the abstractions are impenetrable. the senior engineer is the only person who can navigate it.

this is not architecture. it is a complexity moat that produces dependency on one person.

the tell: you cannot trace a data flow end-to-end without navigating 5+ files. you cannot add a new feature without understanding all the abstractions first. the codebase has many generics and few specific implementations.

actual senior behavior: the abstraction is visible from the outside. a new engineer should be able to understand what a module does from its public interface without reading its implementation.

anti-elite 2: verbose type theater

the engineer writes extremely elaborate TypeScript types — discriminated unions with 12 members, conditional types 4 levels deep, template literal types for everything. this signals type-system mastery. the types are not wrong. they are not used correctly.

the tell: the types describe every possible state of the system but the consuming code ignores the discriminant and casts with as. the types are performative, not functional.

actual senior behavior: types are written at the level of specificity required to prevent errors. the type system is a tool for the compiler to catch mistakes, not a medium for expressing type-system mastery. if a type is so complex that consuming code consistently uses as to bypass it, the type is wrong.

anti-elite 3: dependency injection everywhere

the engineer uses a DI framework for every dependency in the codebase, including things that have one implementation and will always have one implementation (a mailer that always uses SendGrid, a logger that always writes to stdout). this signals enterprise-architecture fluency.

the tell: every class has a constructor with 5-8 injected dependencies. the DI container configuration is more complex than the application logic. new engineers spend a week understanding the DI setup before writing their first line.

actual senior behavior: DI is appropriate when a dependency has multiple implementations, when implementations are swapped for testing, or when circular dependencies exist. for single-implementation dependencies that are never mocked, pass them as module imports. the complexity of the dependency graph should not exceed the complexity of the problem being solved.

anti-elite 4: configuration over commitment

the engineer makes every behavioral choice configurable because "we might need to change this." the result: 200 environment variables, feature flags for decisions that were made and never changed, configuration objects passed 8 layers deep.

the tell: the configuration surface is larger than the implementation surface. the system has more options than behaviors.

actual senior behavior: configure what will actually vary across environments (database connection strings, API keys, feature toggles for active experiments). commit to what will not change (algorithm choices, data model decisions, core business logic). the configuration surface should be minimal and intentional.

unique cross-domain synthesis: cycle 1

synthesis 1: constraint-propagation rendering

derived from: database constraint satisfaction (track 5) + CSS layout engine mechanics (track 3)

the structural analog: both systems produce output by satisfying a constraint set. the database accepts a row if and only if it satisfies all constraints simultaneously. the CSS layout engine computes element geometry by satisfying constraints (containing block, intrinsic size, flex/grid rules, overflow) in a defined resolution order.

the new pattern: apply constraint-propagation as the architecture for generative UI components.

instead of writing imperative layout logic ("if data has more than X items, switch to Y layout"), define the layout as a constraint set that the component resolves:

typescript
type LayoutConstraints = {
  containerWidth: number;
  itemCount: number;
  minItemWidth: number;
  maxColumns: number;
  preferredGap: number;
};

function resolveLayout(constraints: LayoutConstraints): LayoutSolution {
  // constraint 1: columns cannot exceed maxColumns
  // constraint 2: columns cannot produce items narrower than minItemWidth  
  // constraint 3: gaps sum must be consistent
  // constraint 4: prefer fewest columns that satisfy minimum width constraint

const maxByWidth = Math.floor(constraints.containerWidth / constraints.minItemWidth);
  const columns = Math.min(maxByWidth, constraints.maxColumns);
  const itemWidth = (constraints.containerWidth - (columns - 1) * constraints.preferredGap) / columns;
  const rows = Math.ceil(constraints.itemCount / columns);

return { columns, rows, itemWidth, gap: constraints.preferredGap };
}

this produces a component that resolves its own layout from constraints rather than from imperative conditions. new constraints can be added without rewriting the decision logic. the constraint set is auditable — you can read what rules govern the layout.

name: CRL — constraint-resolution layout

synthesis 2: temporal contract cascade

derived from: database transaction commit semantics (track 5) + animation easing system timing contracts (track 3)

detailed above in the prompt spec — extending here:

the extension: apply TCC to multi-service workflows:

typescript
type WorkflowStep<TInput, TOutput> = {
  execute: (input: TInput) => Promise<TOutput>;
  validate: (output: TOutput) => ValidationResult;
  timingContract: { timeout: number; minimumDuration: number };
  compensate: (input: TInput) => Promise<void>; // called on downstream failure
};

// each step has a timing contract — it must complete within timeout, 
// but cannot complete before minimumDuration (ensures real work happened)
// compensation is modeled before execution, not discovered at failure time

name: TCC — temporal contract cascade

synthesis 3: signal-noise threshold cascade (SNTC)

derived from: information theory (signal/noise distinction, shannon entropy) + phase transition mechanics (track 4, CPT pattern)

mechanism: in information channels approaching capacity, the signal-to-noise ratio is approximately constant until a threshold, then degrades catastrophically. the same structure appears in codebases, teams, and architectures as they scale.

below threshold: additional complexity is absorbed without degradation. engineering team grows from 3 to 8 engineers, codebase grows 10x. the system adapts. PRs are reviewable. CI passes. onboarding takes 2 weeks.

at threshold: the complexity of the system approaches the integration capacity of the team. the signal (intended behavior) begins to be obscured by noise (incidental complexity, coupling, undocumented assumptions). change latency increases. bugs appear in unrelated systems after targeted changes.

past threshold: catastrophic capacity degradation. the system cannot accept new information (requirements) without corrupting existing information (behavior). this is CPT in the information channel — not a gradual decline but a phase transition.

the detection signals for SNTC in codebases:

PR review time increases beyond 2x baseline (critical slowing down)
incident rate increases while change volume stays constant (variance increase)
"it shouldn't have affected that" bugs appear regularly (correlation length increase)
engineers begin working on isolated corners of the codebase to avoid entanglement (spatial separation as defense against correlation)

the intervention: reducing the integration capacity required — modularization, service separation, event-driven decoupling. these are not architectural ideals. they are interventions that reduce the amount of shared state the team's cognitive capacity must hold simultaneously. the system is moved back below threshold.

name: SNTC — signal-noise threshold cascade

stage 7 — cross-track synthesis scan: cycle 1

intersection 1: DCSP (track 4) → vibe-code prevalence (track 1)

DCSP directly explains why vibe-coded code is the attractor state in software development absent institutional counterpressure. the production-grade alternative (track 1 eradication patterns) has higher present cost (time to write correctly) and deferred benefit (system health at scale). the vibe-coded version has lower present cost and deferred ruin. under DCSP, the vibe-coded version wins unless:

the discount rate is lowered by culture (senior engineers who hold the standard)
the future cost is made present (code review that rejects vibe-coded PRs)
the future benefit is made present (observable systems that are easier to change)

intersection 2: domain grammar (track 2) → 3D lighting brief (track 3)

the domain material read (track 2, step 2) directly produces the lighting brief (track 3, phase 2). a luxury hospitality domain material read (warm wood, incandescent light, brushed brass) maps directly to track 3 lighting profile: warm scattered, key light at 3000K, heavy fill to eliminate sharp shadows, rim light at warm tone. the domain grammar and the 3D grammar are the same grammar expressed in different media.

intersection 3: CPT (track 4) → software architecture breaking point (track 1/5)

CPT describes the phase transition in codebases precisely. the warning signals (critical slowing down = increased change latency, increased variance = more unexpected incidents, increased spatial correlation = bugs propagating across unrelated systems) are directly measurable in any engineering team. elite engineers (track 5) who have experienced CPT can identify its warning signals years before the transition occurs and intervene with SNTC-reducing modularization.

intersection 4: PAM (track 4) → technology adoption and lock-in (track 5)

preferential attachment explains why engineering teams consistently choose the same few frameworks and tools (React, PostgreSQL, AWS, TypeScript). each additional adoption makes the next adoption more likely — more tutorials exist, more engineers know it, more libraries are built for it. the elite pattern (track 5) response: evaluate tools on their constraints, not their popularity. the PAM-dominated choice is the risk-minimizing choice for career (many jobs use React) but not necessarily for the specific system being built.

intersection 5: ICA (track 4) → design trends (track 2)

information cascade explains the homogenization of design. when designers observe that other designers (who they believe to have more information) are using glassmorphism/neumorphism/neobrutalism, they update toward that style regardless of whether it fits their domain. the cascade ends when: the outcomes are visible (glassmorphism illegible in high-glare environments), or a high-credibility dissenter (a respected designer) makes a public counter-signal.
