stage 2 — track 1 cycle 2: performance and security anti-patterns

performance anti-pattern 1: the whole-list re-render

typescript
// vibe-coded: any change to any item re-renders everything
function NotificationList({ notifications }: { notifications: Notification[] }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {notifications.map(n => (
        <div key={n.id} className="notification">
          <span>{n.title}</span>
          <button onClick={() => markRead(n.id)}>Mark read</button>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
// when markRead changes one notification:
// the parent re-renders with new array reference
// every child re-renders because the list is inline
// for 100 notifications: 100 component evaluations for one state change
typescript
// production: virtualized, memoized, stable reference
import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';

const NotificationItem = memo(function NotificationItem({ notification, onMarkRead }: {
  notification: Notification;
  onMarkRead: (id: string) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <div className={styles.notification}>
      <span>{notification.title}</span>
      <button onClick={() => onMarkRead(notification.id)}>Mark read</button>
    </div>
  );
}, (prev, next) => prev.notification.id === next.notification.id && 
                    prev.notification.isRead === next.notification.isRead);

function NotificationList({ notifications }: { notifications: Notification[] }) {
  const parentRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const handleMarkRead = useCallback((id: string) => markRead(id), []);

const virtualizer = useVirtualizer({
    count: notifications.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => 64,
    overscan: 5,
  });

return (
    <div ref={parentRef} style={{ height: '400px', overflow: 'auto' }}>
      <div style={{ height: virtualizer.getTotalSize() }}>
        {virtualizer.getVirtualItems().map(virtualRow => (
          <div key={virtualRow.key} style={{ position: 'absolute', top: virtualRow.start, width: '100%' }}>
            <NotificationItem
              notification={notifications[virtualRow.index]}
              onMarkRead={handleMarkRead}
            />
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

what this produces: 1,000 notification list. the vibe-coded version evaluates 1,000 components on every mark-read. the production version: evaluates 8-10 visible items, re-evaluates only the specific item whose read state changed.

performance anti-pattern 2: layout recalculation on keypress

typescript
// vibe-coded: width calculated in render on every keypress
function SearchInput({ onSearch }: { onSearch: (query: string) => void }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

const inputWidth = inputRef.current?.getBoundingClientRect().width ?? 0; // layout read in render

return (
    <div style={{ width: inputWidth }}> {/* forces layout recalculation */}
      <input 
        ref={inputRef}
        value={query} 
        onChange={e => { setQuery(e.target.value); onSearch(e.target.value); }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}
typescript
// production: layout reads in effect, writes batched, resize observer
function SearchInput({ onSearch }: { onSearch: (query: string) => void }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  const [containerWidth, setContainerWidth] = useState<number>(0);

// ResizeObserver reads layout once on resize, not on every render
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!inputRef.current) return;
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
      setContainerWidth(entries[0].contentRect.width);
    });
    observer.observe(inputRef.current);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

// debounced search — not firing on every keystroke
  const debouncedSearch = useMemo(() => debounce(onSearch, 300), [onSearch]);

return (
    <div style={{ width: containerWidth || 'auto' }}>
      <input
        ref={inputRef}
        value={query}
        onChange={e => { setQuery(e.target.value); debouncedSearch(e.target.value); }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}

security anti-pattern 1: client-side auth

typescript
// vibe-coded: auth check in the component
function AdminDashboard() {
  const { user } = useAuth();

if (user.role !== 'admin') {
    return <Redirect to="/unauthorized" />;
  }

// renders admin content if role === 'admin'
  return <AdminContent />;
}
// the api endpoints that AdminContent calls: unprotected on the server
// disabling javascript or intercepting the response and changing role: admin
// the admin content is fetched and displayed regardless
typescript
// production: auth enforced at the server boundary
// client UI is a presentation layer only — it does not make auth decisions

// server-side (Next.js app router, works equivalently in any framework):
async function AdminPage() {
  const session = await getServerSession();

if (!session || session.user.role !== 'admin') {
    redirect('/unauthorized'); // server redirect — no content served
  }

// no client-side check needed — server already verified
  return <AdminContent />;
}

// api route — checked independently of the page:
async function GET(request: Request) {
  const session = await getServerSession();
  if (!session || session.user.role !== 'admin') {
    return Response.json({ error: 'Forbidden' }, { status: 403 });
  }
  // ...
}

security anti-pattern 2: environment variable exposure

typescript
// vibe-coded: secret in client bundle
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  env: {
    API_SECRET_KEY: process.env.API_SECRET_KEY,   // EXPOSED TO BROWSER
    DATABASE_URL: process.env.DATABASE_URL,         // EXPOSED TO BROWSER
    OPENAI_API_KEY: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY,   // EXPOSED TO BROWSER
  }
};

// in component:
const response = await fetch('/api/data', {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_SECRET_KEY}` } // client-side, in bundle
});
production rule: 
- NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix: explicit client-side opt-in. only non-secret values.
- all other env vars: server-side only. period.
- API calls requiring secrets: server-side route or server action only
- build-time audit: enumerate every env var, classify as public or secret, verify no secret has NEXT_PUBLIC_

env var classification:
PUBLIC (okay in client):
  NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL
  NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY  (publishable = designed to be public)
  NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY
  NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_FLAG_ENABLED

SECRET (server only — catastrophic if exposed):
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
  DATABASE_URL
  OPENAI_API_KEY
  SENDGRID_API_KEY
  SESSION_SECRET
  any credential that grants access to a resource

the root anatomy of vibe-coding: generation without modeling

the substrate mechanism that produces all vibe-coded patterns simultaneously:

a language model generating code (or an engineer in "flow" mode without explicit modeling) operates by predicting the next token sequence most likely to follow the prompt. this is a completion operation. it produces code that looks like the code that typically follows similar prompts in training data.

what it does not do: build a model of the system being implemented. the generated code does not know why it is structured the way it is. it knows that this structure commonly follows this type of prompt. there is no reasoning about:

what state transitions are valid in this system
what failure modes exist
where the complexity lives
what must be true for this code to be correct
what will break when requirements change

the production engineer who is not vibe-coding is running a different operation: building a model of the system in their head (or on paper), then translating the model into code. the code is the transcription of the model. the model is the real product.

the test that distinguishes them:

"why is this function here and not in the service layer?"
"why is this state stored here and not in the parent?"
"why does this component re-fetch when this specific value changes?"

a vibe-coded codebase cannot answer these questions. the placement was the first placement that worked. there is no second-order reasoning about correctness.

a modeled codebase can answer every placement question by reference to the model: "this function is in the service layer because it is a business logic operation that should not have any knowledge of the rendering framework. if it were in the component, it would need to be duplicated when we add the mobile app."

stage 3 — track 2 cycle 2: three more domain grammars

domain 6: SaaS productivity (project management, task tracker, document editor)

domain identity read:
the world: working hours, task overhead, cognitive load management, the feeling of being in control of what needs to happen. the user is managing work, not experiencing a product. the dominant values: information density, speed of interaction, low cognitive overhead (the UI should be invisible — not noticed), reliability (down = nothing gets done). the aesthetic should not draw attention to itself. it is infrastructure.

domain material read:
neutral. white or very light gray background. one brand color used sparingly. clean san-serif. high information density without feeling cramped. the physical analog: a well-organized desk — everything has a place, nothing extra.

color system:

background:  #ffffff or #f8f9fa
surface:     #f1f3f4 (sidebar, secondary panels)
border:      #e0e3e7 (subtle, not heavy)
text-primary: #1f2937
text-secondary: #6b7280
brand:       one color — product-defined (Notion: #000, Asana: #f06a6a, Linear: #5e6ad2)
brand usage: primary actions only, selected state only, active nav item only
success:     #22c55e (task completed, file saved)
warning:     #f59e0b
error:       #ef4444

key differentiator from other domains: information density is a feature, not a bug. SaaS productivity tolerates more content per screen than any other domain because users are professionals who have trained themselves to read dense UI. the mistake vibe-coders make: padding every element heavily to make it "look clean." it looks clean to a designer. it looks like wasted space to a user working in the tool 8 hours a day.

motion grammar for SaaS productivity:

task completion:    satisfying but fast — checkbox checks in 100ms, strikethrough in 150ms
sidebar collapse:   200ms width animation, content fades simultaneously
modal open:         150ms ease-out — users open many modals, delay accumulates
drag and drop:      cursor becomes grab cursor immediately, picked item gets shadow and slight scale(1.02)
                    dropped item snaps into position in 150ms spring
inline edit:        field appears on click/double-click in 0ms, focus state is the signal
command palette:    opens in 150ms, filters in <16ms (must feel instant to keyboard users)

domain 7: fintech (trading platform, banking, investment dashboard)

domain identity read:
the world: money is real and quantified and the numbers matter. the user is making decisions where being wrong has financial consequences. the values: precision over everything. no ambiguity in any number. time is money in the most literal sense (stale data is harmful). the aesthetic communicates trustworthiness, precision, professional authority.

domain material read:
dark mode primary (traders work in dark environments, dark mode reduces eye fatigue, premium financial tools use dark). dense numerical content. high contrast between positive (green) and negative (red) — these are the only two colors that carry unconditioned semantic weight in finance. monospace for all numbers (alignment matters at a glance, fixed-width columns allow instant comparison).

background:    #0f1117 (dark navy — finance dark mode is not pure black)
surface:       #171b26
elevated:      #1e2233
border:        #2a3045
text-primary:  #e8ecf4
text-secondary: #8892a8
positive:      #22c55e or #00d09c (green — gain, profit, up)
negative:      #ef4444 or #ff6347 (red — loss, drawdown, down)
neutral:       #f59e0b (pending, unchanged, processing)
accent:        #3b82f6 (primary action, interactive element)

critical fintech rules:

numbers are always right-aligned, monospace, consistent decimal places
positive/negative values are always colored — never just a sign
time stamps are always displayed in the user's local time and in UTC — both
zero and empty are different states and must look different
the last-updated timestamp is always visible for any data that can go stale
order submission buttons have a confirmation step — always. the cost of accidental order > the cost of friction.

typography:

ui:       'Inter' or 'IBM Plex Sans' — clean, professional
numbers:  'IBM Plex Mono', 'JetBrains Mono', or 'Roboto Mono' — monospace critical
          font-feature-settings: "tnum" 1 (tabular numbers — equal width digits)
          font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums
size:     12px for dense tables (traders tolerate density), 14px for labels

domain 8: healthcare consumer (patient portal, fitness tracker, mental health app)

domain identity read:
the world: the body, health, vulnerability, the asymmetry between the user and medical knowledge. the user comes to this interface in states of worry, recovery, or aspiration. the design communicates: you are safe here, this is trustworthy, this is on your side. the aesthetic must balance warmth (I am not clinical) with authority (I know what I'm talking about). a mental health app that feels cold is harmful. a health app that looks unserious is distrusted.

domain material read:
warm but professional. light backgrounds with warm undertone. soft green for health/positive. never red for anything non-critical (red activates alarm, wrong for most health contexts). photography of real people in real settings — not clinical photography. illustration style (where used) is soft, rounded, warm. the typography is approachable but legible.

background:     #fafaf9 (warm off-white)
surface:        #f5f4f0 (warmer surface — distinction from white background)
border:         #e5e2dc
text-primary:   #292524
text-secondary: #78716c
primary:        #16a34a (green — health, progress, positive) or #0891b2 (teal — medical authority)
warning:        #d97706 (amber — something to address, not alarming)
critical:       #dc2626 (red — reserved for genuine medical alerts only)
warm-accent:    #f97316 (orange — energy, activity, vitality — fitness contexts)

motion grammar for healthcare consumer:

breathing exercise:  sine wave animation on the expand/contract indicator — 4s ease-in-out loop
                     never jarring, never faster than 3s per cycle
progress rings:      stroke-dasharray animation, 800ms ease-out — satisfying completion
loading:             no spinning indicators — gentle pulse opacity animation
                     because health data is sensitive, the feeling of "it's thinking about you" matters
notifications:       enter from bottom, soft ease-out — not alarming. medical alerts are exception.
                     medical alert: 250ms ease-out, persistent, requires acknowledgment before dismiss
stage 4 — track 3 cycle 2: scroll-driven 3D narrative and post-processing

scroll-driven 3D: full implementation pattern

the scroll-driven 3D experience is the highest-impact use of 3D on the web. it turns passive scroll behavior into narrative progress. the user's momentum through the page is matched by the product's revelation of itself. the execution pattern:

typescript
// dependencies: three.js, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei, gsap, @gsap/react

import { useRef, useEffect } from 'react';
import { Canvas, useFrame, useThree } from '@react-three/fiber';
import { useGLTF, useScroll } from '@react-three/drei';
import { gsap } from 'gsap';
import { ScrollTrigger } from 'gsap/ScrollTrigger';
import * as THREE from 'three';

gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);

// the camera path is defined as a CatmullRomCurve3 — smooth, continuous
const cameraPath = new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3([
  new THREE.Vector3(0, 2, 8),    // hero: overhead-angled
  new THREE.Vector3(3, 0, 5),    // feature 1: right side approach
  new THREE.Vector3(0, -1, 4),   // feature 2: underside reveal
  new THREE.Vector3(-2, 1, 3),   // feature 3: left detail
  new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 2),    // close-up final reveal
], true); // closed=true for loop if needed

// what the camera looks AT — a separate path for the look-at target
const targetPath = new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3([
  new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(0.5, 0, 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(0, -0.5, 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(-0.5, 0, 0),
  new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 0),
]);

function ScrollCamera() {
  const { camera } = useThree();
  const scroll = useScroll();

useFrame(() => {
    // scroll.offset is 0→1 across the entire scroll container
    const t = scroll.offset;

// ease the scroll progress so the camera doesn't feel linearly mapped
    const eased = gsap.parseEase("power2.inOut")(t);

// position along the path
    const position = cameraPath.getPoint(eased);
    camera.position.copy(position);

// look-at target
    const target = targetPath.getPoint(eased);
    camera.lookAt(target);

// focal length variation: gets tighter as we approach product
    camera.fov = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(50, 28, eased);
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
  });

return null;
}

function ProductModel() {
  const { scene } = useGLTF('/models/product.glb');
  const scroll = useScroll();
  const groupRef = useRef<THREE.Group>(null);

useFrame(() => {
    if (!groupRef.current) return;
    const t = scroll.offset;

// subtle rotation that responds to scroll — not camera, the object moves too
    groupRef.current.rotation.y = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(0, Math.PI * 0.25, t);

// scale reveal: starts slightly smaller, grows to full
    const scale = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(0.85, 1.0, Math.min(t * 3, 1));
    groupRef.current.scale.setScalar(scale);
  });

return <primitive ref={groupRef} object={scene} />;
}

// the container: full viewport height × number of sections
// the Canvas is sticky — stays in view while scroll progresses through sections
export function ScrollExperience() {
  return (
    <div style={{ position: 'relative', height: '500vh' }}> {/* 5 viewport heights */}
      <div style={{ position: 'sticky', top: 0, height: '100vh' }}>
        <Canvas
          camera={{ position: [0, 2, 8], fov: 50 }}
          gl={{ antialias: true, toneMapping: THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping, toneMappingExposure: 1.2 }}
        >
          <ScrollCamera />
          <ProductModel />
          <directionalLight position={[5, 5, 5]} intensity={2} castShadow />
          <ambientLight intensity={0.1} />
          <Environment preset="studio" />
        </Canvas>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

post-processing pipeline: the quality multiplier

post-processing is the difference between "technically correct 3D" and "cinematic 3D." it costs performance — each pass adds a full-screen render — so every pass requires justification.

typescript
import { EffectComposer, Bloom, DepthOfField, ChromaticAberration, Vignette } from '@react-three/postprocessing';
import { BlendFunction } from 'postprocessing';

// domain-specific post-processing loadouts:

// LUXURY PRODUCT:
<EffectComposer>
  <Bloom intensity={0.3} luminanceThreshold={0.9} luminanceSmoothing={0.9} />
  {/* subtle bloom on specular highlights — makes metal glow at edges */}
  <DepthOfField focusDistance={0.01} focalLength={0.05} bokehScale={2} />
  {/* shallow DOF — editorial, cinematic — background softens */}
  <Vignette offset={0.3} darkness={0.6} />
  {/* vignette — frames the product, draws eye to center */}
</EffectComposer>

// GAMING / TECH:
<EffectComposer>
  <Bloom intensity={1.5} luminanceThreshold={0.6} luminanceSmoothing={0.4} />
  {/* aggressive bloom — the RGB glow is the aesthetic */}
  <ChromaticAberration offset={[0.002, 0.002]} />
  {/* color fringing at edges — digital, screen-native aesthetic */}
</EffectComposer>

// MEDICAL / DATA:
// NO post-processing. accurate representation is the requirement.
// post-processing distorts — wrong in this domain.

// WELLNESS / ORGANIC:
<EffectComposer>
  <Bloom intensity={0.1} luminanceThreshold={0.95} luminanceSmoothing={0.95} />
  {/* barely perceptible bloom — softness without glow */}
</EffectComposer>

css 3D vs real 3D: the decision tree

question 1: does the effect require actual 3D geometry (curved surfaces, real lighting, PBR materials)?
  YES → real 3D (three.js, r3f)
  NO → continue to question 2

question 2: is this a perspective effect (parallax, tilt, flip) on a flat element?
  YES → css 3D (transform: perspective(), rotateX(), rotateY(), rotateZ())
         css 3D is hardware-accelerated, zero dependency, lighter than any 3D library
  NO → continue to question 3

question 3: is this motion that a CSS animation or GSAP can achieve on 2D elements?
  YES → CSS/GSAP. never introduce a 3D renderer to do what CSS can do.
  NO → real 3D

css 3D patterns that replace real 3D in many contexts:

// card tilt on hover — feels 3D, is CSS
function TiltCard({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const cardRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

const handleMouseMove = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLDivElement>) => {
    if (!cardRef.current) return;
    const rect = cardRef.current.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x = (e.clientX - rect.left) / rect.width - 0.5;  // -0.5 to 0.5
    const y = (e.clientY - rect.top) / rect.height - 0.5;

cardRef.current.style.transform = 
      `perspective(600px) rotateY(${x * 12}deg) rotateX(${-y * 12}deg) scale(1.02)`;
  };

const handleMouseLeave = () => {
    if (!cardRef.current) return;
    cardRef.current.style.transform = 'perspective(600px) rotateY(0deg) rotateX(0deg) scale(1)';
    cardRef.current.style.transition = 'transform 400ms ease-out';
  };

return (
    <div
      ref={cardRef}
      onMouseMove={handleMouseMove}
      onMouseLeave={handleMouseLeave}
      style={{ 
        transition: 'transform 50ms linear',
        transformStyle: 'preserve-3d',
        willChange: 'transform'
      }}
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}
stage 5 — track 4 cycle 2: new pattern domains

domain: network/systems patterns

pattern: cascade failure

surface: the failure of one component causes failures in adjacent components, which cause further failures, which cascade through the system until a large portion is down. systems that appear robust fail suddenly and completely.

technical: two mechanisms. (1) load redistribution: when a node fails, its traffic is redistributed to remaining nodes. if remaining nodes are at or near capacity, the additional load causes them to fail, redistributing to fewer nodes, which fail faster. (2) resource contention: failure of a shared resource (database, message queue, cache layer) causes dependent services to fail simultaneously. the cascade is simultaneous and complete rather than sequential.

structural: cascade failure requires: (a) shared resource dependencies, (b) insufficient excess capacity in the system, (c) no circuit breakers between components.

the circuit breaker pattern (eradication):

typescript
class CircuitBreaker {
  private failures = 0;
  private lastFailureTime = 0;
  private state: 'CLOSED' | 'OPEN' | 'HALF_OPEN' = 'CLOSED';

constructor(
    private readonly failureThreshold: number,
    private readonly recoveryTimeout: number,
  ) {}

async execute<T>(operation: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    if (this.state === 'OPEN') {
      const timeSinceLastFailure = Date.now() - this.lastFailureTime;
      if (timeSinceLastFailure > this.recoveryTimeout) {
        this.state = 'HALF_OPEN';
      } else {
        throw new CircuitOpenError('Circuit is open — fast failing to prevent cascade');
      }
    }

try {
      const result = await operation();
      this.onSuccess();
      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      this.onFailure();
      throw error;
    }
  }

private onSuccess() {
    this.failures = 0;
    this.state = 'CLOSED';
  }

private onFailure() {
    this.failures++;
    this.lastFailureTime = Date.now();
    if (this.failures >= this.failureThreshold) {
      this.state = 'OPEN';
    }
  }
}

root: CFM — cascade failure multiplier. mechanism: the failure of one unit transfers load to others. if remaining units cannot absorb the transferred load, each subsequent failure increases the load on the survivors, making each subsequent failure faster and more likely. the cascade is a positive feedback loop: failure → increased load on survivors → faster survivor failure → more load on remaining survivors. the cascade ends when load reaches zero (complete failure) or when a circuit breaker disconnects the load transfer.

pattern name: LTP — load-transfer positive feedback

cross-domain: bank runs (failure of one bank's ability to pay withdrawals causes depositors at other banks to withdraw, causing those banks to fail), predator extinction (removing predators increases prey population, which exhausts the food supply, which collapses the prey population, which starves the remaining predators — trophic cascade), immune overreaction (cytokine storm: immune activation triggers immune cells, which trigger more immune cells, which produces organ damage — the immune cascade failing to self-limit).

domain: biological patterns

pattern: red queen dynamics

surface layer:
species in co-evolutionary relationships (predator-prey, parasite-host, pathogen-immune system) must evolve continuously just to maintain their current fitness level relative to each other. neither gains permanent advantage. both must run as fast as they can just to stay in place.

technical layer:
each co-evolutionary partner is the primary selective environment for the other. a faster predator selects for faster prey. faster prey selects for faster predators. immune systems select for pathogens that evade them. pathogens select for immune systems that recognize novel evasion strategies. the co-evolution is a continuous arms race with no equilibrium state unless one partner goes extinct.

mathematically: if predator fitness improvement rate = dF_pred/dt and prey fitness improvement rate = dF_prey/dt, both are nonzero and approximately equal over evolutionary time. the absolute fitness of both increases. the relative fitness (fitness of predator relative to prey) remains approximately constant.

structural layer:
red queen dynamics require: (a) the partners directly and strongly influence each other's fitness, (b) both have sufficient genetic variation to respond to selective pressure, (c) generation time is short enough that evolutionary response occurs on relevant timescales.

domain	partner A	partner B	dynamic
biology	predator	prey	speed, camouflage, detection arms race
biology	pathogen	immune system	antigen variation vs. adaptive immunity
cybersecurity	attackers	defenders	novel exploits vs. novel defenses
finance	quant traders	market microstructure	algorithmic strategy vs. exchange latency
product	product features	competitor features	capability matching
advertising	ad blockers	ad delivery	detection evasion vs. detection improvement
cryptography	encryption	cryptanalysis	key length growth vs. computing power growth

root: RQD — red queen dynamics. mechanism: when two agents are each other's primary selective environment, evolutionary pressure is continuous and bidirectional. neither reaches a stable equilibrium because any improvement by one creates immediate selective pressure on the other. the dynamic produces: continuously increasing absolute capability in both agents, approximately constant relative capability, and elimination of any agent that stops investing in evolutionary response (slowing down = falling behind = extinction).

pattern: mutualism-parasitism spectrum

surface: relationships between organisms span from mutualism (both benefit) to commensalism (one benefits, one neither gains nor loses) to parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense) to predation (one kills and consumes the other). the important finding: relationships along this spectrum are not fixed — the same pair can shift positions as environmental conditions change.

technical: a mycorrhizal fungus that provides a host plant with phosphorus in phosphorus-poor soil is mutualistic. the same fungus in phosphorus-rich soil parasitizes the plant: it still takes photosynthate but provides nothing the plant couldn't get from the soil. the relationship's position on the mutualism-parasitism spectrum is determined by the cost-benefit ratio for each partner, which depends on environmental context.

root: MPS — mutualism-parasitism spectrum. mechanism: the net benefit of an interaction, not its structural form, determines its category. the same structural relationship (A provides B, B provides A) is mutualism when the exchange is net positive for both and parasitism when the exchange is net positive for one and net negative for the other. the exchange rate, not the exchange itself, determines the category.

cross-domain:

SaaS pricing: a SaaS product that provides genuine value at a fair price is mutualistic. the same product with opaque pricing, lock-in by data hoarding, and removal of features that were free — same structural relationship (product provides value, customer pays) but now parasitic.
platform dynamics: a platform that enables small creators is mutualistic when it provides distribution at low cost. when it captures enough of the creator's audience that leaving destroys the creator's reach, it has shifted to parasitism. same structure, different exchange rate.
employment: employment is mutualistic when the employee receives fair compensation relative to value created. when the employer captures most of the surplus value the employee creates, the same structural relationship (employee works, employer pays) moves toward parasitism.

domain: mathematical/structural patterns

pattern: fractal self-similarity

surface: structures that look the same at every scale of observation. coastlines, snowflakes, tree branching, market price series, lung architecture, mountain topography. zoom in or out and the same structural features appear.

technical: a fractal is defined by a self-affine transformation: a rule that maps the structure to a scaled copy of itself. the Mandelbrot set: z → z² + c. repeated application of this simple rule produces infinite complexity at every scale. the key measure is the fractal dimension: a coastline has a dimension between 1 (a line) and 2 (a plane) — approximately 1.25 for the British coastline — reflecting that it fills more space than a line but less than a plane.

structural: self-similarity requires: (a) a simple generative rule applied recursively, (b) no characteristic scale (true fractals are scale-free), (c) infinite recursion depth (real-world fractals are approximate — they have a smallest scale below which the rule breaks).

domain	structure	self-similar pattern
biology	vascular system	branching: each branch splits into smaller branches with consistent branching angle and area ratio
biology	lung architecture	bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar ducts: same branching rule at each scale
finance	price series	price fluctuations look similar at 1-minute, 1-hour, 1-day, 1-year scales (approximate fractal)
geography	coastlines	indentation pattern at 1km scale ≈ pattern at 100m scale ≈ pattern at 10m scale
architecture	some traditional buildings	self-similar ornamentation at building, facade, window, molding scale
networks	internet topology	scale-free network with self-similar subgraph structure
mathematics	sierpinski triangle	self-similarity by construction

root: FSS — fractal self-similarity. mechanism: a simple rule applied recursively to its own output produces structure that appears at every scale. the complexity emerges not from the rule but from the recursion depth. the rule is simple; the structure is complex; the simplicity is visible at the rule level but invisible at the structure level. the finding: complex natural structures are frequently the output of simple recursive rules, not of complex design.

application to software architecture:
a well-designed software system has fractal self-similarity in its design principles: the same principles that govern how functions are structured govern how modules are structured, which govern how services are structured. the rule (single responsibility, explicit dependencies, designed failure modes) applies at function, module, and service scale. vibe-coded systems have no such self-similarity — the design principles, if any, exist at one scale and not others.

pattern: harmonic resonance

surface: when an oscillating system is driven at its natural frequency, the amplitude of oscillation grows. a suspension bridge driven at its resonant frequency by wind collapses. an opera singer shatters a wine glass by hitting its resonant frequency. radio receivers work by tuning to a resonant frequency and filtering out others.

technical: every physical system with a restoring force and inertia has a natural frequency: f₀ = 1/(2π) × √(k/m) where k is the restoring force constant and m is the inertia. when a driving force oscillates at f₀, energy is added to the system at exactly the rate it can absorb it — each cycle builds on the previous cycle's amplitude. in an undamped system, amplitude grows without bound. in a real system with damping, amplitude reaches an equilibrium determined by the ratio of driving force to damping: the Q factor (quality factor).

domain	natural frequency	resonance driver	collapse/amplification
structural	bridge resonant frequency	marching soldiers, wind vortex shedding	Tacoma Narrows Bridge
acoustic	room mode frequencies	sound source at room mode	standing waves, dead zones
circuit	LC circuit resonance	input signal at resonant frequency	radio receiver, filter
biological	neural oscillation	sensory input at alpha/theta/gamma	attention, sleep, seizure
economic	business cycle frequency	government stimulus/contraction	boom amplification, recession deepening
social	viral meme spread	content that hits social anxiety resonant frequency	information cascade to global spread

root: HR — harmonic resonance. mechanism: every system with a restoring force has a natural frequency. energy added at that frequency accumulates; energy added at other frequencies disperses. the resonance frequency reveals the system's internal architecture. driving at the resonance frequency is either devastating (structural collapse, seizure) or beneficial (radio reception, music). the key is identifying the system's natural frequency and deciding whether to drive it or avoid it.

application to UI animation:
every UI has a perceptual resonant frequency — the rhythm at which animations feel natural. animations that are too fast (above the perceptual frequency) feel harsh; too slow (below) feel sluggish. the resonant frequency for UI feedback is approximately 200ms (the perceptual now — events within 200ms feel simultaneous to the preceding action). animations calibrated near 200ms resonate with the user's perception and feel responsive without feeling instant.

stage 6 — track 5 cycle 2: more elite patterns and syntheses

elite pattern 5: modeling before building — the pre-code artifact

the senior engineer produces an artifact before writing the first line of code. this artifact is not a design doc (which is usually written to justify a decision already made). it is a model of the system that allows decisions to be evaluated before their costs are sunk.

the model answers:

what are the valid states of this system?
what are the transitions between states?
what are the failure modes of each transition?
where is the complexity concentrated?
what are the invariants — conditions that must always be true?
what are the contracts — what each component promises to the others?

example: before writing a checkout flow:

STATE MODEL (checkout):
states: CartReview → AddressEntry → ShippingSelection → PaymentEntry → Reviewing → Processing → Complete | Failed

transitions and their preconditions:
CartReview → AddressEntry:     cart.items.length > 0
AddressEntry → ShippingSelection: address.isValid && address.isDeliverable
ShippingSelection → PaymentEntry: shippingMethod.selected
PaymentEntry → Reviewing:      payment.isValid (format only, not authorization)
Reviewing → Processing:        user confirms (explicit action), cannot auto-proceed
Processing → Complete:         payment authorized, inventory decremented, email sent (all or none)
Processing → Failed:           any of the above failed, inventory NOT decremented if payment failed

INVARIANTS:
- inventory is never decremented before payment is authorized
- email is never sent before inventory is decremented
- order record is never created if any step fails (transaction boundary)
- the user can navigate backward to any step before Processing
- once Processing begins, no backward navigation is possible

FAILURE MODES:
- payment authorization fails: stay in Processing state, show specific error, allow retry
- inventory insufficient (race condition): fail order, refund authorization, return to CartReview
- email delivery fails: order is Complete (email failure is not order failure), retry email in background
- network failure mid-Processing: idempotency key on payment call prevents double-charge

this model is written before any code. it answers every subsequent question about where logic goes (inventory decrement: in the Processing transition handler, nowhere else), what error handling looks like (each failure mode is defined), and what the test cases are (one test per state, one test per transition, one test per failure mode, one test per invariant).

elite pattern 6: the idempotency key as first-class citizen

any operation that has side effects and can be retried requires an idempotency key. this is not optional error handling. it is a structural requirement of any distributed system.

typescript
// the problem: user clicks "submit order" twice quickly (or network retries the request)
// result: two orders created, two charges, two inventory decrements

// the solution: idempotency key generated client-side, submitted with request,
// server uses it to deduplicate

function useSubmitOrder() {
  const [idempotencyKey] = useState(() => crypto.randomUUID()); // generated once per mount

return useMutation({
    mutationFn: (orderData: CreateOrderPayload) => 
      api.post('/orders', { ...orderData, idempotencyKey }),
    retry: 3, // safe to retry because of idempotency key
  });
}

// server-side:
async function createOrder(payload: CreateOrderPayload) {
  // check if this key was already used
  const existing = await db.orders.findOne({ idempotencyKey: payload.idempotencyKey });
  if (existing) {
    return existing; // return the previous result — same outcome, no duplicate
  }

// proceed with order creation, storing idempotencyKey on the record
  const order = await db.orders.create({ ...orderData, idempotencyKey: payload.idempotencyKey });
  return order;
}

anti-elite patterns: cycle 2 additions

anti-elite 5: the comment that describes what the code does

typescript
// BAD: comment describes the code
// increment the counter by one
counter++;

// GOOD: comment describes WHY — the code says what, the comment says why
// skip even numbers — the sieve already marked them as composite
counter += 2;

the anti-elite pattern: writing comments that repeat the code in English. "iterates over the array" describes the forEach. "returns the user's name" describes return user.name. a trained eye reads these comments and classifies the author as someone who learned that "comments are good" without learning what comments are for.

what comments are for: explaining why a decision was made, why a non-obvious approach was taken, what the constraint was that produced this code, what the code must NOT be changed to (the counter-invariant).

anti-elite 6: the deep class hierarchy

BaseEntity
  → AbstractIdentifiableEntity
      → PersistableEntity
          → AuditableEntity
              → SoftDeletableEntity
                  → User

the anti-elite pattern: enterprise inheritance hierarchies applied to domain objects. each class adds one responsibility. the User class has six ancestors and inherits methods it may not need.

the actual senior pattern: prefer composition. User has an audit trail (composition), can be soft-deleted (composition), has an ID (always true, just a field). flat structure, explicit composition, no inheritance except where there is a genuine is-a relationship.

anti-elite 7: the perfect test coverage theater

100% code coverage with tests that assert that code executes, not that the system behaves correctly.

typescript
// coverage theater — achieves 100% line coverage, tests nothing meaningful
test('formatCurrency formats correctly', () => {
  expect(formatCurrency).toBeDefined(); // test passes, function exists
  expect(typeof formatCurrency(100)).toBe('string'); // test passes, returns string
  expect(formatCurrency(100)).toBeTruthy(); // test passes, non-empty string
});

the actual senior pattern:

typescript
// behavior specification — tests meaningful invariants
describe('formatCurrency', () => {
  it('formats whole dollars without cents', () => expect(formatCurrency(100_00)).toBe('$100.00'));
  it('formats cents correctly', () => expect(formatCurrency(99)).toBe('$0.99'));
  it('formats large amounts with comma separation', () => expect(formatCurrency(1_000_00)).toBe('$1,000.00'));
  it('handles zero', () => expect(formatCurrency(0)).toBe('$0.00'));
  it('throws on negative input', () => expect(() => formatCurrency(-1)).toThrow(NegativeCurrencyError));
});
// 0% coverage of non-behavior, 100% coverage of contract

anti-elite 8: the framework migration refactor

the engineer proposes rewriting the application in a new framework because the new framework is better. this is not wrong about frameworks. it is wrong about priorities.

the tell: the engineer can argue eloquently about the new framework's advantages but cannot produce a cost-benefit analysis with specific user-impacting improvements. the migration is motivated by the engineer's desire to work with the new technology, not by a specific problem the new technology solves better.

actual senior response: "what specific problem is the current framework causing that this migration would fix? can we list three user-impacting issues that the migration would resolve? what is the migration cost in engineer-weeks? does the benefit exceed the cost at this company's current size?"

unique syntheses: cycle 2

synthesis 4: the red queen test suite

derived from: red queen dynamics (track 4, RQD) + test specification (track 5)

the structural analog: both systems require continuous investment to maintain relative fitness. a test suite that is not updated as the system changes loses fitness relative to the system — the tests pass but test the wrong things. the system evolves; the tests don't; the tests' coverage of the current system's actual behavior decays.

the pattern: the red queen test suite is a test suite that co-evolves with the system. it includes:

typescript
// snapshot tests for UI output — auto-updating means tests track current behavior
// contract tests for API responses — break when contract changes
// property-based tests for domain logic — generate edge cases the engineer didn't think of
// mutation testing — verify that tests actually detect bugs

the mutation testing step: a tool (Stryker, mutmut) introduces deliberate bugs into the source code and runs the test suite. if the test suite passes despite the bug, the test coverage is superficial — the tests are passing but not detecting mutations. the mutation score (% of mutations detected) reveals the actual coverage quality, not the line coverage number. a 100%-line-coverage suite with a 40% mutation score is substantially undertested.

synthesis 5: resonance-driven animation timing

derived from: harmonic resonance (track 4, HR) + animation grammar (track 2/3)

the structural analog: physical systems resonate at their natural frequency. perceptual systems also have natural frequencies — rates at which events are processed as coherent temporal groups.

the pattern: derive animation timing from the domain's perceptual natural frequency rather than from arbitrary "feels good" choices.

domain: messaging app (high-frequency interaction)
perceptual natural frequency: ~150ms (message send → deliver feels instant)
animation timing system:
  send button active:    30ms (must feel like physical button depression)
  sending indicator:     100ms ease-in (appears to be doing something)
  delivered checkmark:   150ms ease-out (arrives in the perceptual now)
  read receipt:          200ms ease-out (slightly slower — secondary event)

domain: financial dashboard (data arriving in streams)
perceptual natural frequency: ~1000ms (the data refresh rate is the natural beat)
animation timing system:
  price update flash:    250ms ease-out (stands out without being alarming)
  chart redraw:          400ms ease-in-out (data arriving feels weighty)
  alert pulse:           2000ms period (matches data update rhythm, not faster)

domain: document editor (slow, deliberate creation)
perceptual natural frequency: ~500ms (the rhythm of thought)
animation timing system:
  paragraph appear:      300ms ease-out (appearing as the user types feels natural)
  toolbar show/hide:     200ms ease-out (responding to context without distraction)
  save indicator:        400ms (confirming that the work is preserved)

name: RDA — resonance-derived animation

stage 7 — cross-track synthesis scan: cycle 2

intersection 6: fractal self-similarity (track 4) → component architecture (track 1)

the fractal principle — the same rule at every scale — is the root principle of good component architecture. the component rule (single responsibility, explicit props/contracts, designed states) applies at the atom (button), molecule (form field), organism (form), template (page section), and page level. a vibe-coded component hierarchy violates this: the atoms are designed correctly, the organisms contain business logic, the templates contain state management, and each scale has a different (often unspoken) design rule. the refactor is fractal-ization: identify the rule that should apply at every scale and propagate it.

intersection 7: LTP cascade failure (track 4) → microservice architecture decisions (track 5)

load-transfer positive feedback directly governs microservice architecture. a microservice architecture without circuit breakers, rate limiting, and bulkhead isolation is a cascade waiting to happen. the elite pattern: every service call in a distributed system has a circuit breaker. every service has a retry budget. every queue has a dead letter queue. the failure modes are designed at the architecture level, not discovered at the incident.

intersection 8: SNTC (track 5 synthesis) → domain grammar (track 2)

a visual design system that has exceeded its SNR threshold looks like a vibe-coded codebase: too many colors, too many components that look similar but different, spacing that follows no grid, decisions that don't trace back to the domain grammar. the design system signal (intended communication) is overwhelmed by the design noise (accumulated inconsistency). the intervention is the same: modularization (consolidate color tokens, remove redundant component variants), explicit grammar (document the rules), and circuit breakers (linting rules that prevent new design decisions that violate the system).

intersection 9: RDA synthesis (cycle 2) + domain grammar (track 2) → complete UI motion system

the resonance-derived animation (RDA) synthesis provides the timing foundation. the domain grammar (track 2) provides the easing and character foundation. combined:

complete motion system = timing from RDA + easing character from domain grammar + purpose from valid motion list (track 2)

luxury hospitality + RDA:
  natural frequency: slow, deliberate (the world is unhurried)
  timing: 300-500ms all interactions
  easing: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) — smooth, no snap
  character: weight, permanence, arrival rather than appearance

developer tooling + RDA:
  natural frequency: fast, exact (the world is performance and precision)
  timing: 50-150ms all interactions
  easing: cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1) — instant start, soft landing
  character: immediate, precise, never distracting

gaming + RDA:
  natural frequency: reactive, energetic
  timing: 30-100ms interactions, 300-600ms reveals
  easing: spring physics (stiffness: 300, damping: 20) for interactive
          cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0, 1) for dramatic reveals
  character: momentum, energy, physicality

vibe-coded state management: the boilerplate theater

typescript
// VIBE-CODED REDUX: the full ceremony with no actual modeling
// this pattern appears in codebases where Redux was "best practice" 
// so it was added without modeling whether the state actually needs to be global

// action types file (30 lines for one feature)
export const FETCH_USERS_REQUEST = 'FETCH_USERS_REQUEST';
export const FETCH_USERS_SUCCESS = 'FETCH_USERS_SUCCESS';
export const FETCH_USERS_FAILURE = 'FETCH_USERS_FAILURE';

// action creators file (another 20 lines)
export const fetchUsersRequest = () => ({ type: FETCH_USERS_REQUEST });
export const fetchUsersSuccess = (users) => ({ type: FETCH_USERS_SUCCESS, payload: users });
export const fetchUsersFailure = (error) => ({ type: FETCH_USERS_FAILURE, payload: error });

// reducer file
function usersReducer(state = { users: [], loading: false, error: null }, action) {
  switch(action.type) {
    case FETCH_USERS_REQUEST: return { ...state, loading: true };
    case FETCH_USERS_SUCCESS: return { ...state, loading: false, users: action.payload };
    case FETCH_USERS_FAILURE: return { ...state, loading: false, error: action.payload };
    default: return state;
  }
typescript
    case FETCH_USERS_FAILURE: return { ...state, loading: false, error: action.payload };
    default: return state;
  }
}

what makes this vibe-coded, enumerated precisely:

1. global state for data that should be cache. the users array is server state. it has a canonical source — the server. it goes stale. it needs refetching. redux treats it as application state, which is owned by the client. the conceptual model is wrong before the first line of code.

2. boolean loading state missing the full lifecycle. loading: false after failure is indistinguishable from loading: false before the first fetch. the idle state is invisible. when you navigate back to a page, did the data load? was it never requested? you cannot tell.

3. error without type information. error: action.payload is an any. error recovery requires knowing whether to retry (network), show validation (400), redirect to login (401), or show maintenance (503). untyped error means every consumer writes their own guess.

4. string action constants. 'FETCH_USERS_REQUEST' as a string means typos are silent at dispatch, discovered at runtime. the switch falls through to default: return state, which does nothing, which looks correct, which is the worst kind of bug.

5. no normalization. users stored as array means O(n) lookups by id. every component reading a single user iterates the whole list.

6. no staleness model. data fetched at t=0 is served forever. user edits in another tab, refreshes, gets stale data, and cannot understand why their change disappeared.

the production replacement, scoped correctly:

typescript
// server state: react-query handles the cache layer correctly
// the "global state" was never global — it was cached remote data

function useUsers(filters?: UserFilters) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['users', filters],
    queryFn: () => fetchUsers(filters),
    staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000,      // treat as fresh for 5 minutes
    gcTime: 10 * 60 * 1000,         // keep in cache for 10 minutes after unmount
    refetchOnWindowFocus: true,      // sync when user returns
    retry: (failureCount, error) => {
      // typed retry: don't retry 401, 403, 404 — those won't change
      if (error instanceof ApiError && [401, 403, 404].includes(error.status)) return false;
      return failureCount < 3;
    },
    select: (data) => ({
      // normalize at the boundary, not in redux
      byId: Object.fromEntries(data.users.map(u => [u.id, u])),
      allIds: data.users.map(u => u.id),
      total: data.total,
    }),
  });
}

// at the component:
function UserList() {
  const { data, status, error, isFetching, refetch } = useUsers(activeFilters);

// status: 'pending' | 'success' | 'error'
  // the lifecycle is modeled. idle vs loading vs stale vs fresh is tracked.

if (status === 'pending') return <UserListSkeleton />;
  if (status === 'error') return <UserListError error={error} onRetry={refetch} />;

return <UserListContent users={data.byId} ids={data.allIds} />;
}

genuine client-only global state: zustand with scope analysis

the test before reaching for zustand: is this state owned by the client, not the server? does it need to persist across route changes? does more than one component tree need it?

typescript
// correct scope: UI state that is genuinely global
// - current user preferences (not saved to server yet)
// - cart state (client-owned until checkout)
// - modal/drawer open state that multiple components control
// - multi-step wizard progress

interface CartStore {
  items: CartItem[];
  isOpen: boolean;

addItem: (product: Product, quantity: number) => void;
  removeItem: (productId: string) => void;
  updateQuantity: (productId: string, quantity: number) => void;
  clear: () => void;
  open: () => void;
  close: () => void;

// derived state — computed, not stored
  get total(): number;
  get itemCount(): number;
}

const useCartStore = create<CartStore>()(
  persist(
    immer((set, get) => ({
      items: [],
      isOpen: false,

addItem: (product, quantity) => set(state => {
        const existing = state.items.find(i => i.productId === product.id);
        if (existing) {
          existing.quantity += quantity;
        } else {
          state.items.push({ productId: product.id, product, quantity });
        }
      }),

removeItem: (productId) => set(state => {
        state.items = state.items.filter(i => i.productId !== productId);
      }),

updateQuantity: (productId, quantity) => set(state => {
        if (quantity <= 0) {
          state.items = state.items.filter(i => i.productId !== productId);
          return;
        }
        const item = state.items.find(i => i.productId === productId);
        if (item) item.quantity = quantity;
      }),

clear: () => set({ items: [] }),
      open: () => set({ isOpen: true }),
      close: () => set({ isOpen: false }),

get total() {
        return get().items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + (item.product.price * item.quantity), 0);
      },

get itemCount() {
        return get().items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity, 0);
      },
    })),
    { name: 'cart', partialize: (state) => ({ items: state.items }) }
  )
);

XState-style explicit state machine for complex async flows

when async flow has more than two outcomes and any transition has side effects, boolean flags produce combinatorial explosion. the checkout flow has 7 states — boolean flags would require 2^7 = 128 possible combinations, most impossible, all unmodeled.

typescript
// instead of: { loading, success, error, retry, confirming, processing, complete }
// explicit machine — impossible states cannot be represented

type CheckoutState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'validating_cart'; cartId: string }
  | { status: 'address_entry'; cart: ValidatedCart }
  | { status: 'payment_entry'; cart: ValidatedCart; address: Address; shipping: ShippingMethod }
  | { status: 'reviewing'; cart: ValidatedCart; address: Address; shipping: ShippingMethod; payment: PaymentMethod }
  | { status: 'processing'; orderId: string; idempotencyKey: string }
  | { status: 'complete'; order: Order }
  | { status: 'failed'; error: CheckoutError; recoverable: boolean; lastState: CheckoutState };

// 'processing' without orderId: impossible
// 'complete' without order: impossible  
// 'reviewing' without payment: impossible
// the type system enforces the machine's invariants at compile time

type CheckoutEvent =
  | { type: 'CART_VALIDATED'; cart: ValidatedCart }
  | { type: 'ADDRESS_SUBMITTED'; address: Address }
  | { type: 'SHIPPING_SELECTED'; method: ShippingMethod }
  | { type: 'PAYMENT_ENTERED'; payment: PaymentMethod }
  | { type: 'SUBMIT_ORDER' }
  | { type: 'ORDER_CONFIRMED'; order: Order }
  | { type: 'PAYMENT_FAILED'; error: PaymentError }
  | { type: 'RETRY_FROM_PAYMENT' }
  | { type: 'ABORT' };

function checkoutReducer(state: CheckoutState, event: CheckoutEvent): CheckoutState {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'idle':
      if (event.type === 'CART_VALIDATED') return { status: 'address_entry', cart: event.cart };
      return state;

case 'payment_entry':
      if (event.type === 'PAYMENT_ENTERED') {
        return { 
          status: 'reviewing',
          cart: state.cart,
          address: state.address,
          shipping: state.shipping,
          payment: event.payment
        };
      }
      return state;

case 'reviewing':
      if (event.type === 'SUBMIT_ORDER') {
        return {
          status: 'processing',
          orderId: `order_${Date.now()}`,
          idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID(),
        };
      }
      return state;

case 'processing':
      if (event.type === 'ORDER_CONFIRMED') return { status: 'complete', order: event.order };
      if (event.type === 'PAYMENT_FAILED') {
        return { 
          status: 'failed', 
          error: event.error, 
          recoverable: event.error.code !== 'CARD_PERMANENTLY_DECLINED',
          lastState: state 
        };
      }
      return state;
  }
}

error boundary as architecture, not retrofit

vibe-coded error boundary: wrap the whole app in one ErrorBoundary with a generic "something went wrong" message.

production: error boundaries are placed at recovery granularity — the boundary defines what can be recovered without losing surrounding context.

typescript
// recovery granularity analysis:
// - header fails → page is still useful, show degraded header
// - sidebar fails → content is still useful, hide sidebar  
// - cart widget fails → rest of page is still useful, show cart fallback
// - main content fails → page is not useful, show page-level error

// each boundary wraps exactly what can be replaced at that granularity:

<PageErrorBoundary fallback={<PageError />}>
  <HeaderErrorBoundary fallback={<DegradedHeader />}>
    <Header />
  </HeaderErrorBoundary>

<main>
    <ContentErrorBoundary fallback={<ContentError onRetry={resetKey} />}>
      <ProductContent />
    </ContentErrorBoundary>

<aside>
      <CartErrorBoundary fallback={<CartFallback />}>
        <CartWidget />
      </CartErrorBoundary>
    </aside>
  </main>
</PageErrorBoundary>

accessibility as architecture

vibe-coded accessibility: add aria-label to everything at the end. add role="button" to divs when a designer says "it needs to be clickable."

production: accessibility is derived from semantic HTML. semantic HTML produces accessibility. non-semantic HTML cannot be retroactively made accessible.

typescript
// the rule: if it's a button, use <button>. if it's a link, use <a>.
// no amount of ARIA restores what a div with onClick has lost:
// - keyboard operability (Enter/Space fire on <button>, not div)
// - focus management (tabIndex=-1 is manual work on div)
// - screen reader role announcement
// - browser built-in click behavior (space bar)
// - form submission (type="submit" on <button>)

// form design is accessibility design:
<form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
  <div role="group" aria-labelledby="shipping-heading">
    <h2 id="shipping-heading">Shipping Address</h2>

<label htmlFor="address-line1">
      Street address <span aria-hidden="true">*</span>
      <span className="sr-only">required</span>
    </label>
    <input
      id="address-line1"
      type="text"
      autoComplete="address-line1"
      aria-required="true"
      aria-describedby={errors.line1 ? "line1-error" : undefined}
      aria-invalid={!!errors.line1}
    />
    {errors.line1 && (
      <span id="line1-error" role="alert">{errors.line1}</span>
    )}
  </div>

{/* live region for async validation */}
  <div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" className="sr-only">
    {validationStatus}
  </div>
</form>

the autoComplete value is sourced from the WHATWG autocomplete spec. browsers and password managers use these exact token strings — not close approximations.
