cycle 3 — track 2: six domain grammars

entertainment / streaming

substrate: darkness, motion, density. the product is attention — the UI must never compete with the content for that attention. chrome dissolves when content plays. navigation materializes only when attention returns.

materials: near-black backgrounds (not pure black — 
#0A0A0F, a cool dark with 6% blue). text is never white — it is 
#E8E8E8, warm white, pulled back from full contrast. accent: one vivid color used exclusively for CTAs and progress (Netflix's 
#E50914 red, HBO's 
#A855F7 purple, Disney+'s 
#3B82F6 blue — each is brand-specific, not an aesthetic choice from a tool).

typography: condensed, bold, uppercase for title metadata (year · rating · duration). body copy in system sans. never serif — entertainment content is consumed fast.

motion: content cards reveal with a 120ms scale from 0.95 to 1.0 with opacity 0 to 1 simultaneously. hover state: scale to 1.05, duration 200ms, reveal overlay. play button materializes centered at 200ms with spring easing. the timing is fast because the user is browsing intent, not reading intent.

cover art as the dominant element: the card IS the poster. text overlays only on hover or keyboard focus. nothing competes with the poster for the card's visual weight.

rule: UI is scaffolding. content is the product. when UI is visible, it is working correctly. when content is visible, the UI has succeeded.

sports / fitness

substrate: kinetic energy, physiological response, achievement. the body's response to exertion is the reference point — heart rate elevation, the feeling of forward motion, the finish line.

materials: high saturation. multiple hues are permitted (unlike most domains which converge to one). orange (energy, burn), green (vitality, outdoors), electric blue (speed, tech). dark backgrounds for app interfaces (workout context = low light, often). white backgrounds for marketing/web.

typography: variable weight fonts with heavy weights active. condensed numerals for statistics and metrics. the number is the most important element in fitness UI — it is the measure of progress. tabular-nums always. numeric precision (0.01 pace, 0.1 kg) because the user is tracking performance.

motion: metrics count up from zero on first display (the reveal implies achievement — from zero to this). progress rings animate from 0 on mount. the animation is the reward — it's the mechanism of the dopamine response.

grid: asymmetric. large metric on the left, smaller supporting metrics arrayed to the right. visual hierarchy: your most important number is the largest element.

rule: the UI is a mirror. it reflects the user's physical reality — their pace, their heart rate, their distance. precision and immediacy in data display are the primary aesthetic values because delay or imprecision breaks the mirror.

education

substrate: clarity, progression, patience. the user is in a state of not-yet-knowing. friction in the interface is friction in learning. confusion in the UI doubles the cognitive load of the content.

materials: clean white backgrounds. one primary color for interactive elements and progress indicators (calm colors — blue, teal, or green — colors that don't trigger urgency). secondary colors only for feedback: green (correct), red (incorrect), orange (warning).

typography: generous line height (1.6–1.8). font size 16–18px for body at minimum — this is not a reading context where the user wants maximum information density, it is a learning context where the user needs cognitive room. generous paragraph spacing. never tight leading in instructional content.

layout: single-column for instructional content. reading width capped at 66 characters (~680px). progress visible at all times — the user needs to know where they are in the sequence and how far to completion.

code examples (in technical education): syntax highlighted, with line numbers, copyable, with the ability to run in context. the code block is never decorative — it is the primary teaching element when present.

motion: minimal. progress bars animate on completion. correct/incorrect feedback is instant (< 100ms perceived). never motion for entertainment — motion in educational UI signals feedback or state change, not decoration.

rule: every design decision asks: does this reduce cognitive load or add to it? if it adds, it is removed. clarity is the only aesthetic value.

food / beverage

substrate: sensory richness, appetite stimulation, warmth. the product is pleasure — food is experienced through all five senses, but the interface presents only to two (vision, occasionally sound). the design must compensate by maximizing the pleasure signal through visual richness.

materials: warm tones dominate — cream, terracotta, warm red, deep orange, forest green. never cool grays. never blue (blue suppresses appetite — the only color scientifically documented to reduce food interest). photography is the dominant element.

food photography rules: natural light always, or simulated natural light. hero compositions are close-up, with texture visible. steam, sauce, gloss are all positive signals — they signal freshness and heat. the worst food photo is a flat lay with even lighting that makes everything look like a product shot from 2012.

typography: often mixes a serif display with a clean sans-serif body. the serif signals craft, tradition, care. sans-serif body maintains readability. script fonts appear only in high-end establishments and only for accents (restaurant name, category dividers) — never for body copy.

layout: photography first. description second. price subordinate to the experience description. the order matters — price anxiety kills appetite. let the desire form before the price is revealed.

rule: the menu is not a price list. it is an experience proposal. every design decision — photography, copy, typographic hierarchy — shapes whether the proposal succeeds.

automotive

substrate: performance, precision, power. the car is an engineering artifact — the design inherits the values of engineering: tolerance, specification, capability. numbers matter (0–60 time, horsepower, torque, range).

materials: dark backgrounds for performance/luxury. white or light gray for electric/sustainable. metallics (silver, gunmetal) as accents. paint-matched brand colors (Porsche's Guards Red 
#CC1F2D, Ferrari's Rosso Corsa 
#C41E3A, BMW's M Blue 
#3B82F6) used with extreme discipline — never decoratively, only for performance variants.

photography: three-quarter front view as hero. the angle was established by car photography's history — it shows the vehicle's face, its forward stance, and its proportions simultaneously. studio light against dark backgrounds for luxury. environmental shoots (canyon, track, mountain pass) for performance and adventure.

typography: geometric sans-serif (Futura, Helvetica, or brand equivalents). never humanist sans — automotive precision does not soften with humanist letterforms. tracking is wide at large sizes — the typography inherits the expansiveness of the vehicle's scale.

specifications: presented as tables with clear unit labels. never as prose. the user who cares about specifications wants them in a format where comparison is immediate.

motion: camera reveals with rotation. 360° viewer with gyroscope-follow on mobile. color configurators use canvas-based or WebGL paint-over. the interactivity demonstrates the craft of the product.

rule: the UI serves the product's authority. the vehicle is the subject — the interface presents it at its best angle, with its strongest specification, in its most compelling context. the interface does not have its own personality. it efffaces itself in service of the product.

real estate

substrate: aspiration, home, place. the property is where someone will live their life. the purchase is the largest most people make. the emotional stakes are higher than any other e-commerce context.

materials: warm neutrals — white, off-white, light greige, warm gray. natural material textures as accents (wood, stone, brick — visible in photography). never cold or clinical. never tech-forward styling — real estate is about permanence and warmth, not innovation.

photography: wide-angle interior shots. exterior in golden hour light. neighborhood shots. floor plan as document (not as a visual element). the sequence matters: exterior (I can see it from outside), living room (can I see my family here?), kitchen (will I cook here?), primary bedroom (can I rest here?), exterior detail (what is this made of?). this is an emotional walkthrough, not a product listing.

map as primary interaction: real estate is fundamentally about place. the map view is not supplementary — it may be the first thing shown. walkability, transit, school districts are place-properties, not property-properties. the interface must answer "where is this?" before "what is this?"

typography: clean and minimal. the photography does the selling. text is the label on the experience, not the experience itself.

floor plan: always present, always downloadable. the floor plan is the specification sheet — the serious buyer reads it multiple times.

price: visible early (unlike food — price is a qualifier, not an anxiety trigger in real estate because buyers are pre-qualified). but never the first element — let the emotional response form first.

rule: the interface is a substitute for being there. every decision asks: what would someone want to know if they were standing in this room? what would they see, feel, ask? the interface answers those questions, in that order.

track 2, cycle 3 status: complete

six new domain grammars. cumulative grammar library: 14 domains (developer tooling, luxury hospitality, medical/clinical, gaming peripheral, legal tech, SaaS productivity, fintech, healthcare consumer, entertainment/streaming, sports/fitness, education, food/beverage, automotive, real estate).

cycle 3 — track 3: GPU particles, instanced mesh, WebXR

GPU particle systems: instanced mesh pattern

the naive particle system: one Mesh per particle. 1000 particles = 1000 draw calls = GPU collapse at any count that matters.

the production pattern: InstancedMesh. one draw call for all instances. position, rotation, scale per instance via setMatrixAt. color per instance via setColorAt.

typescript
import { useRef, useMemo, useEffect } from 'react';
import { useFrame } from '@react-three/fiber';
import { InstancedMesh, Object3D, Color, MathUtils } from 'three';

interface Particle {
  position: [number, number, number];
  velocity: [number, number, number];
  life: number;
  maxLife: number;
  size: number;
  color: [number, number, number];
}

const PARTICLE_COUNT = 10_000;

function GPUParticleSystem({ emitterPosition }: { emitterPosition: THREE.Vector3 }) {
  const meshRef = useRef<InstancedMesh>(null!);
  const dummy = useMemo(() => new Object3D(), []);
  const color = useMemo(() => new Color(), []);

// particles live in typed arrays — Float32Array is cache-friendly
  const positions = useMemo(() => new Float32Array(PARTICLE_COUNT * 3), []);
  const velocities = useMemo(() => new Float32Array(PARTICLE_COUNT * 3), []);
  const lifetimes = useMemo(() => new Float32Array(PARTICLE_COUNT), []); // 0 = dead, 1 = just born
  const maxLifetimes = useMemo(() => new Float32Array(PARTICLE_COUNT), []);

// initialize all particles as dead
  useEffect(() => {
    lifetimes.fill(0);
  }, []);

const spawnParticle = (index: number) => {
    const i3 = index * 3;
    positions[i3] = emitterPosition.x + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.2;
    positions[i3 + 1] = emitterPosition.y + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.2;
    positions[i3 + 2] = emitterPosition.z + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.2;

// velocity: upward bias with spread
    velocities[i3] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.5;
    velocities[i3 + 1] = Math.random() * 2 + 0.5;
    velocities[i3 + 2] = (Math.random() - 0.5) * 0.5;

maxLifetimes[index] = MathUtils.randFloat(0.5, 2.0);
    lifetimes[index] = maxLifetimes[index]; // starts at max, counts down
  };

let nextParticleIndex = 0;
  let spawnAccumulator = 0;

useFrame((state, delta) => {
    // spawn rate: 500 particles per second
    spawnAccumulator += delta * 500;
    while (spawnAccumulator >= 1) {
      spawnParticle(nextParticleIndex % PARTICLE_COUNT);
      nextParticleIndex++;
      spawnAccumulator--;
    }

let aliveCount = 0;

for (let i = 0; i < PARTICLE_COUNT; i++) {
      if (lifetimes[i] <= 0) continue;

const i3 = i * 3;

// update physics
      lifetimes[i] -= delta;
      velocities[i3 + 1] -= delta * 3.5; // gravity
      positions[i3] += velocities[i3] * delta;
      positions[i3 + 1] += velocities[i3 + 1] * delta;
      positions[i3 + 2] += velocities[i3 + 2] * delta;

const normalizedLife = lifetimes[i] / maxLifetimes[i]; // 1 = newborn, 0 = dying
      const scale = normalizedLife * 0.05;

// set instance matrix
      dummy.position.set(positions[i3], positions[i3 + 1], positions[i3 + 2]);
      dummy.scale.setScalar(scale);
      dummy.updateMatrix();
      meshRef.current.setMatrixAt(aliveCount, dummy.matrix);

// color: hot white → orange → red → transparent as life decreases
      const r = 1;
      const g = MathUtils.lerp(0.1, 0.8, normalizedLife);
      const b = MathUtils.lerp(0.0, 1.0, Math.max(0, normalizedLife * 2 - 1));
      color.setRGB(r, g, b);
      meshRef.current.setColorAt(aliveCount, color);

aliveCount++;
    }

meshRef.current.count = aliveCount; // only draw alive particles
    meshRef.current.instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true;
    if (meshRef.current.instanceColor) {
      meshRef.current.instanceColor.needsUpdate = true;
    }
  });

return (
    <instancedMesh ref={meshRef} args={[undefined, undefined, PARTICLE_COUNT]}>
      <sphereGeometry args={[1, 4, 4]} /> {/* low-poly sphere — visible only as blur at speed */}
      <meshBasicMaterial vertexColors transparent />
    </instancedMesh>
  );
}

the critical optimizations:

meshRef.current.count = aliveCount — only submit live particles to GPU
typed arrays (Float32Array) for particle state — V8 optimized, SIMD-eligible
Math.random() in spawn, not per-frame — spawn is rare, per-frame is every 16ms
sphereGeometry args={[1, 4, 4]} — 4-segment sphere is indistinguishable from 32-segment at particle scale

shader-based particles: the performance ceiling

when instanced mesh hits limits (custom per-particle animation curves, physics, noise-driven motion), the next level is custom shader material.

glsl
// vertex shader: position entirely driven by particle attributes
// no CPU-side physics loop — GPU computes all positions in parallel

attribute float aLifetime;     // 0 = dead, maxLife = just born
attribute float aMaxLifetime;
attribute vec3 aVelocity;
attribute vec3 aInitialPosition;

uniform float uTime;
uniform float uGravity;

void main() {
  float elapsed = aMaxLifetime - aLifetime; // how long has this particle been alive
  float normalizedLife = aLifetime / aMaxLifetime; // 1 = newborn, 0 = dying

// physics on the GPU
  vec3 pos = aInitialPosition 
    + aVelocity * elapsed 
    + vec3(0.0, -0.5 * uGravity * elapsed * elapsed, 0.0);

// noise-driven drift (turbulence)
  pos.x += sin(elapsed * 3.7 + aInitialPosition.x * 10.0) * 0.1 * normalizedLife;
  pos.z += cos(elapsed * 2.9 + aInitialPosition.z * 10.0) * 0.1 * normalizedLife;

float size = normalizedLife * 8.0; // point size in pixels

gl_PointSize = size * (1.0 / -mvPosition.z); // perspective correction
  gl_Position = projectionMatrix * mvPosition;
}
glsl
// fragment shader: circular particle with soft edge
void main() {
  float distanceFromCenter = length(gl_PointCoord - vec2(0.5));
  if (distanceFromCenter > 0.5) discard; // circular clip

float alpha = (1.0 - distanceFromCenter * 2.0) * vNormalizedLife;

vec3 hotColor = vec3(1.0, 0.9, 0.5); // white-hot
  vec3 coolColor = vec3(1.0, 0.2, 0.0); // orange-red
  vec3 particleColor = mix(coolColor, hotColor, vNormalizedLife);

gl_FragColor = vec4(particleColor, alpha);
}

this version: zero CPU physics per frame. all 100,000 particles computed in parallel on GPU. the only CPU cost is a single draw call.

WebXR: the web-native AR/VR surface

WebXR is the platform API — three.js and @react-three/xr wrap it. the key conceptual shift: in WebXR, the camera is the headset. you do not control it. you design the space around an anchor.

typescript
import { XR, Controllers, Hands, Interactive, useXR } from '@react-three/xr';
import { Canvas } from '@react-three/fiber';

function ARProductViewer({ productId }: { productId: string }) {
  return (
    <Canvas>
      <XR>
        <ARScene productId={productId} />
      </XR>
    </Canvas>
  );
}

function ARScene({ productId }: { productId: string }) {
  const { isPresenting, session } = useXR();
  const [placement, setPlacement] = useState<THREE.Vector3 | null>(null);

// hit testing: find the real-world surface under the reticle
  const { hitTest } = useHitTest((hitMatrix) => {
    const position = new THREE.Vector3();
    position.setFromMatrixPosition(hitMatrix);
    setPlacement(position);
  });

return (
    <>
      {/* reticle shows where the product will be placed */}
      {!placement && <PlacementReticle />}

{placement && (
        <Interactive onSelect={() => { /* place product */ }}>
          <ProductModel 
            productId={productId}
            position={placement}
            // product is at 1:1 real-world scale
            scale={[0.01, 0.01, 0.01]} // if model is in millimeters, convert to meters
          />
        </Interactive>
      )}

<ambientLight intensity={0.5} />
      {/* no directional light in AR — the real world provides it */}
    </>
  );
}

the scale law: WebXR positions are in meters. a 1-unit sphere is a 1-meter sphere. get this wrong and a coffee cup is the size of a house or vice versa.

the lighting law: in AR, don't add lights that compete with the environment. the real world provides light. ambientLight at 0.5 fills shadows. directionalLight should come from the estimated light direction of the real scene (WebXR provides XRLightEstimate in supported browsers).

track 3, cycle 3 status: complete

new findings: GPU particle system with InstancedMesh (full implementation), Float32Array particle state, per-frame alive-count optimization, shader-based particles with GPU physics, WebXR hit testing and scale law, AR lighting discipline.

cycle 3 — track 4: psychological and social patterns

cognitive bias anatomy

each bias is a misfire of an otherwise adaptive heuristic. understanding the original heuristic explains both the bias and its limits.

availability heuristic

original function: estimate frequency by recall ease. adaptive because recent, vivid, personal events genuinely are more informative than abstract statistics in ancestral environments.

misfire: dramatic, emotionally salient events are more recallable than statistically common ones. plane crashes are rarer than car crashes by orders of magnitude. plane crash fear exceeds car crash fear because plane crashes are vivid and media-amplified.

mechanism: the heuristic is:

P(event) ≈ ease_of_recall(event)
recall_ease = f(recency, vividness, emotional_salience, media_coverage)

the substitution is unconscious — "how often does this happen?" becomes "how easily can I think of examples?"

cross-domain extraction: availability injection is a manipulation tactic — increase recall ease through repeated exposure, vivid framing, emotional association. propaganda is availability heuristic exploitation at scale. advertising is also availability heuristic exploitation (brand recall = purchase consideration).

confirmation bias

original function: cognitive efficiency. evaluating every incoming piece of information against all existing beliefs is computationally expensive. the heuristic: preferentially process information consistent with current models.

misfire: the heuristic that saves cognitive effort also prevents model updating. disconfirming evidence requires active processing; confirming evidence is absorbed automatically.

mechanism:

attention_weight(information) = f(consistency_with_current_model)
processing_depth(information) = f(1 / consistency_with_current_model)  
// paradox: most consistent information gets least processing depth

the paradox is important: strongly confirming information is accepted with least scrutiny. the belief feels most supported precisely when it is most vulnerable to uncritical acceptance.

cross-domain extraction: confirmation cascade is the organizational pathology. a leader expresses a view → subordinates confirm it → the view becomes policy before evidence is gathered → disconfirming evidence is attributed to implementation failure, not the wrong view → the view strengthens. the cascade is self-sealing.

sunk cost fallacy

original function: loss aversion as commitment device. in repeated social games, willingness to absorb sunk costs signals trustworthiness. the organism that abandons projects when they become costly cannot make credible commitments.

misfire: past costs are irrecoverable. the rational decision uses only marginal costs and marginal benefits from this point forward. sunk costs are economically irrelevant. but the commitment-signaling heuristic treats them as relevant.

decision_input_set = {sunk_costs, future_costs, future_benefits}
rational_decision_input_set = {future_costs, future_benefits}
delta = sunk_costs  // the contamination

the larger the sunk cost, the stronger the pull to continue. this makes abandonment hardest exactly when abandonment has become most rational (large investment into a failing direction = large sunk cost = strong pull to continue).

cross-domain extraction: technical debt sunk cost trap — the codebase that costs most to refactor is also the codebase with the most sunk investment, making refactor decisions feel like "throwing away" prior work. the decision framework: the history of how bad decisions accumulated is irrelevant to the marginal cost/benefit of refactoring now.

anchoring effect

original function: in sequential inference under uncertainty, the first reliable estimate serves as the prior. in environments where initial observations correlate with subsequent reality, anchoring is adaptive.

misfire: in negotiation, pricing, and judgment, arbitrarily set initial numbers constrain subsequent estimates even when the anchor has no informational relationship to the true value.

estimate_final ≈ anchor + adjustment(anchor, available_information)
// the adjustment is typically insufficient — insufficient to overcome the anchor's pull

the mechanism is selective accessibility: the anchor activates anchor-consistent information in memory. "is the population of Turkey more or less than 35 million?" activates facts consistent with Turkey having a population near 35 million, biasing the subsequent estimate.

cross-domain extraction: estimation anchoring in project planning. the first estimate becomes the anchor. all subsequent estimates adjust from it rather than deriving from independent analysis. the mitigation: independent estimates before group discussion, revealed simultaneously (Delphi method / planning poker).

social patterns: ritual structure

van Gennep's tripartite structure (1909): all rites of passage share three phases, regardless of culture or domain.

separation → liminality → incorporation

separation: the individual is removed from their ordinary status and social position. physical movement from home space. symbolic markers of transition (special clothing, fasting, isolation).

liminality (from limen, threshold): the individual is "betwixt and between" — no longer what they were, not yet what they will become. all ordinary social structure is suspended. hierarchy flattens or inverts. rules that apply elsewhere do not apply here. the liminal space is simultaneously dangerous and generative — rules are off, so transformation is possible.

incorporation: the individual re-enters society with new status, new identity, new social obligations. the transition is publicly witnessed and confirmed. the new identity is recognized by the community.

cross-domain extraction: product onboarding as ritual structure. the best onboarding sequences mirror van Gennep:

separation: the user leaves their ordinary context (installing the app, creating the account — this is the symbolic departure).

liminality: the onboarding sequence suspends ordinary UI conventions — it has its own visual language, its own rules, its own pace. the user is in a transitional state: not yet a full user, no longer a non-user. this is where identity transformation is possible. forcing ordinary UI conventions here collapses the liminal space and makes onboarding feel like filling out a form.

incorporation: the first meaningful action in the product — sending the first message, completing the first task, creating the first file — is the incorporation ceremony. design it to feel significant. the empty state that follows onboarding is the user's "new home" in the product.

moral panic mechanics (Cohen, 1972)

sequence: a condition, episode, person, or group of persons emerges to become defined as a threat to societal values and interests. the nature of the threat is presented in a stylized and stereotypical fashion by the mass media. the moral barricades are manned by editors, bishops, politicians, and other right-thinking people.

structural elements:

folk devil: the identified threat — a person or group made to embody the danger
moral entrepreneurs: those who define, amplify, and enforce the moral concern
sensitization: once defined, minor incidents are reinterpreted through the threat lens
disproportionality: scale of perceived threat vastly exceeds documented harm
volatility: moral panics peak rapidly and dissipate as suddenly as they arose
scapegoating function: the folk devil absorbs anxieties whose real causes are diffuse or structural

cross-domain extraction: technology moral panic is a recurring pattern. video games, social media, AI — each follows the structure. the extraction for practitioners: sensitization means that once the folk devil is named, any incident involving the technology will be reinterpreted as evidence of the threat, regardless of actual causation. designing for moral panic context means accepting that the product will be blamed for harms it did not cause and must be prepared to demonstrate (not just claim) safety.

military/strategic: asymmetric warfare

symmetric warfare: combatants with comparable capabilities competing for positional advantage on the same terms. the stronger force wins in proportion to its advantage.

asymmetric warfare: one side uses a different strategy set than the other, specifically chosen to neutralize the other's advantage.

the core principle: the stronger force's advantage is a resource deployed in a particular mode. the weaker force's strategy is to force the conflict into a mode where that resource is irrelevant or counterproductive.

mechanism examples:

standing army vs. guerrilla: conventional forces are optimized for fixed battles. guerrilla tactics deny fixed battles, disperse the target, blend into civilian population. the strength (firepower, logistics, command structure) cannot be deployed against a dispersed, mobile, civilian-embedded target without costs that undermine the political objectives.
nation-state vs. terrorist: territorial control is irrelevant. infrastructure attacks against a non-territorial actor impose costs but cannot compel.

cross-domain extraction: competitive asymmetry — a smaller entrant competing directly on the incumbent's terms will lose. the strategic imperative is to find the mode of competition where the incumbent's advantage is irrelevant. this is the structuring principle of disruption theory (Christensen) — attack the dimension of performance that incumbents have over-served, where their strength is a vulnerability.

supply line dependency

the principle: every extended operation creates a supply line. the supply line has length, exposure, and throughput. attack the supply line rather than the army and the army becomes irrelevant.

logistics determines operational range. operational range determines strategic options. strategic options determine what can be attempted.

cross-domain extraction: dependency supply line in software. a service's dependencies are its supply line. attack the supply line: npm audit surfaces known vulnerabilities. npm install from a compromised registry is a supply line attack (the 2022 node-ipc incident, the left-pad incident). the mitigation: lockfiles, private registries, SBOM (software bill of materials), sigstore verification of packages. the strategic imperative is supply line visibility before supply line security.

economic: rent extraction and network effect tipping points

rent extraction

economic rent: returns above opportunity cost — returns that persist because the recipient controls a scarce resource, not because they provide ongoing value.

structural forms:

positional rent: controlling a scarce position (beachfront property, a dominant domain name, a platform's app store)
network rent: controlling a network that others need access to (credit card network, operating system ecosystem)
information rent: controlling information others need (credit bureaus, proprietary data sets)
regulatory rent: using regulatory barriers to suppress competition (taxi medallion system before rideshare)

the defining characteristic: rent does not require ongoing value creation. it persists through control of the resource, not through contribution.

cross-domain extraction: platform rent — app stores (Apple App Store, Google Play) extract 30% of digital transactions as platform rent. the resource controlled is access to users. the value created (initial distribution infrastructure) precedes the rent extraction period — the ongoing 30% is rent, not compensation for ongoing value. the strategic implication for platform entrants: rent extraction invites bypass strategies (web apps, direct distribution) and regulatory intervention at scale.

network effect tipping point

the value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of connected users (Metcalfe's law — approximate, directionally correct). this produces:

V(n) = n²

dV/dn = 2n  // the marginal value of each new user increases with n

below a critical mass, the network is low-value. above critical mass, value acceleration makes alternatives unattractive. the tipping point is where V(network) > V(alternatives) for a sufficient portion of the user base to trigger the cascade.

the cascade mechanism: above tipping point, each additional user increases value, which attracts more users, which increases value further. the network becomes self-reinforcing. below tipping point, each departing user decreases value, which drives further departure — a death spiral.

cross-domain extraction: cold start problem — a network that needs users to have value cannot attract users when it has no value. the mitigation strategies:

single-player value: the product must be valuable to one user before it is valuable to a network (Slack was useful to one person before they could invite anyone)
subnetwork seeding: seed a small, dense subnetwork where value is high even at low absolute scale (geographic focus, vertical market focus)
market maker side subsidization: subsidize one side of a two-sided market until the other side's presence attracts them (Uber subsidized drivers to attract riders, then riders attracted drivers)

switching cost lock-in

the economic structure: a user who has invested in learning, data creation, and integration with a product faces a cost to switch that is not present for a new user. the existing provider can raise prices or reduce quality up to (but not exceeding) the switching cost before the user defects.

switching cost components:

procedural cost: time and effort to learn the new system
data migration cost: extracting data from the old system, converting formats, importing
integration cost: rebuilding integrations with other tools
social cost: coordinating a switch with others in the same network (slack workspace, google docs organization)
psychological cost: identity investment in prior decisions

the strategic extraction: ONCE locked in, the provider's constraint is not competition but the switching cost ceiling. quality and price improvements that EXCEED the switching cost in a competitor will trigger defection. below that ceiling, the provider can extract rent.

track 4, cycle 3 status: complete

new patterns: availability heuristic mechanism, confirmation cascade organizational pathology, sunk cost technical debt trap, anchoring estimation defense (Delphi/planning poker), ritual structure → product onboarding mapping, moral panic structural elements + sensitization mechanism, asymmetric warfare → competitive disruption, supply line dependency → software SBOM, rent extraction taxonomy (positional/network/information/regulatory), network effect tipping point mechanism + cold start solutions, switching cost component decomposition.

cumulative pattern library: 16 named patterns (DCSP, FDOP, PAM, CPT, PDD, ICA, LTP, RQD, MPS, FSS, HR, CRL, TCC, SNTC, RQTS, RDA) + 11 new patterns from cognitive bias and economic domains.

cycle 3 — track 5: pre-modeling, contract-first API design, data flow

entity-relationship pre-modeling

production engineers model the domain before modeling the code. the code is a transcription of the domain model. vibe-coded engineers model the code directly.

the domain model comes first. for any feature involving data persistence or multiple entities, the ER analysis runs before the schema runs:

DOMAIN: e-commerce product catalog with variants

entities:
- Product: a sellable item as the customer understands it (a t-shirt)
- Variant: a specific purchasable combination of a product's options (blue, large)
- ProductOption: a dimension of variation (Color, Size)
- OptionValue: a specific value on a dimension (Blue, Large)
- Inventory: units available for a specific variant
- Price: the price of a specific variant (prices can differ by variant)
- Image: visual representation — may be shared across variants or specific to one

relationships:
- Product has many Variant (1:N)
- Product has many ProductOption (1:N)
- ProductOption has many OptionValue (1:N)
- Variant is composed of one OptionValue per ProductOption (N:M with constraints)
- Variant has one Inventory record (1:1)
- Variant has one or many Price records (1:N — may differ by currency, region, time)
- Image may belong to Product or Variant (polymorphic or split tables)

derived concepts (not stored, computed):
- available variants: variants with Inventory.quantity > 0
- selected variant: the unique variant satisfying the current user's option selections
- displayed price: the Price record matching the user's currency/region/context

invariants (must hold at all times):
- a Variant must have exactly one OptionValue per ProductOption of its parent Product
- Inventory.quantity must never go below 0
- a Variant cannot exist without its parent Product
- OptionValues cannot be reordered (their display sequence is defined)

this model runs before a database schema is written, before a type definition is written, before an API endpoint is defined. the code then transcribes this model.

the schema that follows from this model:

sql
CREATE TABLE products (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  description TEXT,
  slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'active', 'archived')),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE product_options (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  product_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  display_order INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (product_id, name)
);

CREATE TABLE option_values (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  option_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES product_options(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  value TEXT NOT NULL,
  display_order INTEGER NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (option_id, value)
);

CREATE TABLE variants (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  product_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  sku TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'discontinued', 'unavailable'))
);

CREATE TABLE variant_option_values (
  variant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES variants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  option_value_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES option_values(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  PRIMARY KEY (variant_id, option_value_id)
  -- the constraint that each variant has exactly one value per option is enforced at the application layer
  -- or via a trigger that validates on INSERT/UPDATE
);

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  variant_id UUID PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES variants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0),
  reserved_quantity INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (reserved_quantity >= 0),
  -- available = quantity - reserved_quantity
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE prices (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  variant_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES variants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  amount INTEGER NOT NULL, -- stored in smallest currency unit (cents)
  currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL, -- ISO 4217
  effective_from TIMESTAMPTZ,
  effective_until TIMESTAMPTZ,
  CONSTRAINT valid_price_range CHECK (effective_from < effective_until OR effective_until IS NULL)
);

what the ER model caught before the schema was written:

images could have been added to products table — the model revealed they need a separate table because variants may have variant-specific images
price was not added as a column on variants — the model revealed price has temporal and regional dimensions
inventory reservation state was captured — reserved_quantity is not obvious until you model the checkout flow's interaction with inventory

contract-first API design

the vibe-coded API: implement the endpoint, then document it (or don't). the production API: write the OpenAPI spec first, generate mocks from it, develop against the mock, then implement the real server.

yaml
# openapi: 3.1.0 spec excerpt — written before any server code

/products/{productId}/variants:
  get:
    summary: List variants for a product
    operationId: listProductVariants
    parameters:
      - name: productId
        in: path
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
          format: uuid
      - name: includeUnavailable
        in: query
        required: false
        schema:
          type: boolean
          default: false
    responses:
      200:
        description: Variant list
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [variants, product]
              properties:
                product:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/ProductSummary'
                variants:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    $ref: '#/components/schemas/Variant'
      404:
        description: Product not found
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/NotFoundError'
yaml
components:
  schemas:
    Variant:
      type: object
      required: [id, sku, status, optionValues, inventory, price]
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
          format: uuid
        sku:
          type: string
        status:
          type: string
          enum: [active, discontinued, unavailable]
        optionValues:
          type: array
          items:
            type: object
            required: [optionName, value]
            properties:
              optionName:
                type: string
              value:
                type: string
        inventory:
          type: object
          required: [available, total]
          properties:
            available:
              type: integer
              minimum: 0
            total:
              type: integer
              minimum: 0
        price:
          type: object
          required: [amount, currency, formatted]
          properties:
            amount:
              type: integer
              description: Amount in smallest currency unit
            currency:
              type: string
              minLength: 3
              maxLength: 3
            formatted:
              type: string
              description: Formatted for display (e.g., "$24.99")

NotFoundError:
      type: object
      required: [code, message]
      properties:
        code:
          type: string
          enum: [PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND]
        message:
          type: string

the contract-first benefits not available after the fact:

frontend and backend develop in parallel against the same contract
the spec is the test oracle — generated tests verify the implementation matches the spec
versioning is explicit — a new version is a new spec, not a surprise change
ambiguity surfaces immediately — writing the spec forces resolution of "what does this endpoint actually return when X?"

data flow diagrams before implementation

the vibe-coded order: design the UI, then figure out where the data comes from.

the production order: trace every piece of data the UI needs back to its source, before designing anything.

FEATURE: product variant selector

DATA FLOW TRACE:

what the UI needs:
→ list of available options (Color: [Red, Blue, Green], Size: [S, M, L, XL])
→ for each option combination, is this variant available?
→ current selected variant (or null if no complete selection)
→ selected variant's price
→ selected variant's inventory status
→ selected variant's images

where the data comes from:
→ product options and values: /products/{id}/variants (returns the full variant list with option structure)
→ availability per combination: derived from variant.inventory.available
→ selected variant: client-derived — computed from current option selections matched against variant list
→ price: on the selected variant object
→ inventory: on the selected variant object  
→ images: separate query OR embedded in variant response (tradeoff: bandwidth vs. request count)

derived data computed on the client:
→ option availability given partial selection: for each unselected option, which values produce at least one available variant when combined with current selections?
→ this prevents the user from selecting an impossible combination

the computation:
for each unselected option O:
  for each value V in O:
    is there any available variant where:
      - variant has current_selections applied
      - variant has value V for option O
    → if yes: V is available
    → if no: V is greyed out

this trace determines:
- what the API must return (full variant matrix with inventory per variant)
- what computation happens on the client
- what state shape is needed (selectedOptions: Map<optionId, optionValueId>)
- what the derived computed values are (availableOptionsGivenSelection, selectedVariant)

the value: before a line of code, the team knows what data the server must provide, what shape it must take, what the client derives, and what the render states are (no selection, partial selection, complete selection with available variant, complete selection with unavailable variant). no design decision is made without this trace complete.

synthesis pattern: the pre-flight checklist

extracting the sequence that elite coders run before implementing any feature:

entity map: what are the nouns in this domain? what are their relationships? what are the invariants that must hold?
data flow trace: trace every piece of UI data to its source. identify what is stored, what is derived, what is computed, what is real-time vs. cached.
state machine: what are the states the feature can be in? what are the valid transitions? what states are impossible and should be unrepresentable?
failure contract: for each external dependency (API call, external service), what are the failure modes? which are retryable? what is the user experience for each failure? what degrades gracefully vs. fails completely?
API contract: write the OpenAPI spec or TypeScript types for the API before writing the implementation. this is the commitment that both sides develop against.
edge cases before the happy path: what happens when the user does the unexpected? what happens at scale (1000 items in a list, 100 concurrent users, etc.)? what happens with the data that is technically valid but unusual?
constraint enumeration: what must this system never do? (must never decrement inventory before payment confirms, must never send email before order is confirmed, must never show price without tax context)

only after this seven-stage pre-flight is complete does implementation begin.

the tell that this stage was skipped: the developer says "I'll handle edge cases later" or "we can add error handling when we need it." these are not pragmatic deferrals — they are signals that the constraint space is not understood, which means the happy path implementation will have to be undone when the constraints arrive.

expanded synthesis pattern library (now 12 patterns):

domain-grammar-constraint (DGC): derive aesthetic constraints from domain physics before making design decisions
pre-flight seven-stage (PFS): entity map → data flow → state machine → failure contract → API contract → edge cases → constraints, before implementation
impossible-state elimination (ISE): model state as discriminated unions where invalid combinations are unrepresentable
supply-line visibility (SLV): enumerate all dependencies before securing them — SBOM, lockfiles, dependency graph
recovery-granularity error boundary (RGEB): place error boundaries at the boundary of what can be replaced without losing surrounding context
semantic-html-first (SHF): accessibility is derived from semantic structure — ARIA cannot restore what semantic HTML provides natively
contract-before-implementation (CBI): write the interface/spec/contract before the implementation — both sides develop against the contract
cold-start subnetwork seeding (CSNS): launch network products into dense subnetworks where value is high at low absolute scale
temporal-contract compensation (TCC): for multi-step workflows, define compensating actions before implementing forward actions
three-instance abstraction (TIA): abstract after three instances reveal the actual variation space — not after two, not speculatively
constraint-enumeration-first (CEF): enumerate what the system must never do before specifying what it should do
red-queen test evolution (RQTE): test suite co-evolves with system — mutation testing validates coverage quality, not coverage count

track 5, cycle 3 status: complete

new findings: ER pre-modeling with e-commerce product catalog example, contract-first OpenAPI spec design, data flow trace methodology (UI need → source → client derivation), pre-flight seven-stage checklist, synthesis pattern library expanded to 12.

cycle 3 — stage 7: cross-track synthesis scan

what did cycle 3 produce that intersects across tracks?

synthesis 1: domain grammar + cognitive bias (tracks 2 and 4)

each domain grammar implicitly exploits a specific cognitive bias:

entertainment/streaming exploits attentional capture (the salience effect — high contrast, motion, color draw involuntary attention). the design decision to dissolve chrome during playback is an application of salience management — reduce salience of everything except content.

food/beverage exploits affect heuristic — emotional response to imagery precedes rational price evaluation. showing photography before price is a deliberate sequencing of affect before analysis.

real estate exploits construal-level theory — the more abstract the decision, the more value-based (vs. cost-based). showing aspirational imagery first raises construal level; price is introduced after the abstract desire has formed.

automotive exploits anchoring — performance specifications are anchors. showing the highest performance number (0–60 in 2.4 seconds) first anchors the evaluation frame before price appears.

education design is cognitive load theory applied — the decisions (single column, generous spacing, capped reading width) are direct applications of Sweller's load theory.

synthesis 2: pre-flight checklist + state machine + error boundary (tracks 4, 5, and 1)

the pre-flight's stage 3 (state machine) + ISE pattern (track 5 / track 1) + recovery-granularity error boundary (track 1 / track 5) are a unified pattern:

model states as discriminated unions (ISE) → place error boundaries at recovery granularity (RGEB) → define compensating actions for each failure state (TCC from track 5 synthesis). together: the feature's states are fully enumerated before implementation, invalid states are unrepresentable, failures at each level have defined recovery paths, and error boundaries are placed at the exact level where recovery is possible.

this triple synthesis is the complete resilience architecture for a single feature.

synthesis 3: network effect tipping point + red queen dynamics (tracks 4 and 5)

the RQTE pattern (test suite co-evolution) is a red queen dynamic applied at the codebase level. the competitor is the product's own complexity and the bugs that emerge from it. the arms race: complexity increases → bugs emerge → tests must keep pace with complexity growth → if test quality doesn't co-evolve, the test suite wins the coverage number but loses the detection war.

the network effect tipping point applies here: a test suite with low mutation score is below the critical threshold where the network (the tests detecting bugs) is dense enough to be self-reinforcing. above mutation score ~80%, test failures become informative enough that developers trust them and respond to them, which drives more test writing, which raises the mutation score further. below ~40%, tests are too noisy or too blind that developers ignore failures, which allows further degradation.

synthesis 4: GPU particles + supply line visibility (tracks 3 and 4)

GPU particle systems have a specific dependency supply line: three.js version, WebGL support level, GLSL shader language version, @react-three/fiber version, browser support for required extensions (OES_texture_float for floating-point textures in particles, EXT_color_buffer_float for HDR rendering). before committing to a 3D feature, the supply line must be enumerated:

browser support check:
- WebGL 2: ~95% of browsers (excluding IE — acceptable)
- OES_texture_float: required for HDR particles — check via renderer.extensions.get('OES_texture_float')
- EXT_color_buffer_float: required for bloom post-processing
- WEBGL_draw_instanced: required for InstancedMesh in WebGL 1 (WebGL 2 includes it natively)

graceful degradation decision tree:
- WebGL not available → show static fallback (video or CSS)
- WebGL 1 only → use PointsMaterial instead of InstancedMesh
- no EXT_color_buffer_float → disable bloom, use standard rendering

this is SLV (supply-line visibility) applied to the 3D feature — enumerate the dependency chain before architectural commitment.
