is track 1 delta zero?

new patterns still unresolved:

pattern 36: the cognitive map break in live collaboration
surface: two users looking at the same interface simultaneously see different states — one has filtered, one has not. the other user's state is invisible.
structural: collaborative data environments have individual view states (filters, selections, current entity) that are not synchronized by default.
root: interfaces built for single-user exploration have no model of shared view state. the assumption is one user, one state.
interface rule: in any multi-user or shareable data environment, distinguish persistently between "your view" and "the canonical view." provide a "sync view with [collaborator]" action. when a shared link is opened, show both the link creator's state and the opener's current state with explicit reconciliation controls.
workflow integration: relevant in any data analysis workflow where findings are communicated to another person before the data is exported. the intermediate state — "I am showing you what I see" — requires view state transfer, not just data export.

pattern 37: the reversibility asymmetry
surface: users undo data selection changes freely but cannot undo a "mark as reviewed" or "flag as anomaly" action.
structural: interfaces treat data exploration actions (filter, sort, select) as reversible by default and administrative actions (flags, annotations, status changes) as permanent by default.
root: these two action classes have different reversibility requirements based on their downstream effects — administrative actions propagate to other users, audit logs, or external systems in ways that exploration actions do not.
interface rule: administrative actions must disclose their propagation scope before execution. "flagging this data point will update the shared dataset viewed by 12 team members" must appear before the flag is applied, not after. reversibility must be explicitly stated: "this action is reversible for 24 hours, after which it is permanent."
workflow integration: critical in any multi-user data annotation, quality control, or editorial workflow.

pattern 38: the blank state expectation failure
surface: a user applies filters that return zero results. the interface shows a blank state. the user interprets the blank as "there is no data" rather than "your filters excluded all data."
structural: blank states carry ambiguous meaning: no data exists, or no data matches current selection, or data exists but failed to load, or data exists but the user does not have access.
root: the blank state is a terminal visual state that carries multiple semantically distinct meanings. the interface does not distinguish between them.
interface rule: blank states must be typed. each type has a distinct visual treatment and message: no data exists (metric not collected for this entity), no data matches filters (show which filters are eliminating results and offer to relax them), load failure (show retry with error detail), access denied (show what access level is required and how to request it).
workflow integration: blank state misinterpretation is most costly early in a research session, when the user may conclude a data source is empty and move to a less reliable alternative — when the actual cause was a misconfigured filter.

pattern 39: the export schema drift problem
surface: a user exports data to a spreadsheet. the spreadsheet structure does not match the interface structure they were analyzing.
structural: interfaces often pivot, aggregate, or transform data for display purposes. the export does not reflect the display — it reflects the underlying data structure, which may use different field names, entity identifiers, geographic codes, or temporal aggregation than what was shown.
root: export is treated as a data layer operation (dump the underlying records) rather than a view layer operation (export what the user is seeing). the user's mental model is "export what I see."
interface rule: every export must show a schema preview before download: field names as they will appear in the export, sample row, aggregation level, geographic encoding format, date format. for conflicting fields (where source A and source B use different encodings), the export schema must show which encoding was used and for which records.
workflow integration: export schema drift is most damaging when the exported file is consumed by a downstream process — another model, a database import, a script — that expects a specific schema.

pattern 40: the anchoring trap in time series display
surface: a user views a time series chart. the chart's y-axis starts at the minimum value in the displayed range, not at zero. a 3% variation looks like a 300% swing.
structural: default chart scaling optimizes visual resolution of variation. this produces anchoring effects where the range shown on screen overrides the user's actual knowledge of absolute magnitudes.
root: visualization defaults are optimized for showing change, not for calibrating perception of magnitude. these are different goals that require different axis treatments.
interface rule: for any ratio or rate metric, default to zero-anchored y-axis. for any absolute value metric, allow non-zero anchor only with a persistent "zero baseline disabled" indicator and a "reset to zero baseline" control always visible. for percentage change metrics, annotate the chart with reference lines at ±10%, ±25%, ±50% to give the user contextual magnitude anchors.
workflow integration: anchoring trap is highest risk when users are comparing across entities (country A looks like it grew more than country B because the chart is scaled differently for each) or communicating findings to an audience who will not see the raw data.

pattern 41: the metric label vs. metric definition divergence
surface: a user selects "unemployment rate" from a metric list. the number returned is ILO harmonized unemployment. a different user in a different context selects "unemployment rate" and gets the national definition unemployment rate, which excludes discouraged workers. both numbers are labeled "unemployment rate."
structural: the same natural language label maps to multiple operationally distinct metric definitions that produce numerically different values.
root: metric naming is handled at the UI label layer (what sounds clear to the user) rather than the data definition layer (what the metric actually measures). the label and the definition are managed independently and can diverge.
interface rule: every metric selection must display the metric definition, not just the label. the definition shows: what is counted (numerator), what is the population (denominator), what is excluded, which international standard this conforms to (if any), and when this definition was last revised. label disambiguation: when the user types "unemployment rate," show all available definitions with their institutional sources, and require selection of a specific definition before data is returned.
workflow integration: metric label divergence is most dangerous in cross-country comparisons, where two countries may report the "same" metric using different national definitions, and the interface shows them side by side as if they are measuring the same thing.

pattern 42: the cognitive load of negative space in data tables
surface: a large data table has many empty cells. the user's attention is drawn to the pattern of emptiness rather than the pattern of the data.
structural: sparse data tables create a visual negative space that carries its own cognitive signal — the pattern of what is missing can be more visually salient than the pattern of what is present.
root: table layout optimizes for data that is present, treating absence as nothing. but absence at scale is data — it has geographic distribution, temporal distribution, and source-specificity that are analytically significant.
interface rule: do not leave absence as whitespace. color-code or symbol-code absence by type (not collected / not reported / restricted / destroyed). allow the user to filter to "only entities with data" or "only entities with absence." provide a "coverage view" where presence/absence is the primary display and data values are secondary. allow axis sorting by coverage completeness as a first-class operation.
workflow integration: negative space cognitive load is highest in early exploratory phases, where the user is assessing which countries/metrics/time periods have sufficient coverage to support their research question.

track 1 cycle 3 delta assessment: non-zero. patterns 36–42 are confirmed additions. flagging for cycle 4.

are there remaining unresolved data architecture domains?

new track 2 additions for cycle 4:

data source class: judicial and legal system data

judicial system data is among the least standardized, least internationally harmonized, and least accessible data domains globally. court records, conviction rates, sentencing patterns, case backlogs, legal aid availability, and rule of law indicators are collected by highly heterogeneous national systems with no consistent international reporting obligation.

primary international sources: World Justice Project Rule of Law Index (annual, 140 countries, survey-based), UNODC crime and criminal justice statistics, CEPEJ (European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice — european-only), OECD Justice Dashboard (OECD members only), US State Department Human Rights Reports (narrative, not structured data), Freedom House Freedom in the World (partly captures rule of law elements, survey-based).

systematic gaps: domestic court-level data almost never exits national systems in machine-readable form. informal justice systems (customary law, religious courts, tribal adjudication) are effectively unmeasured in any international framework. commercial arbitration data is held by private arbitration bodies (ICC, LCIA, SIAC) and is not systematically disclosed.

API availability: essentially none for primary court-level data. WJP and Freedom House provide downloadable datasets but no API. UNODC provides downloadable CSV. no real-time or near-real-time source exists for judicial data.

data architecture implication: judicial data is primarily useful as a contextual lens on economic data — rule of law indicators explain variance in FDI, contract enforcement speed explains variance in business formation rates, judicial backlog correlates with credit availability. the data architecture must allow judicial indicators to be loaded as an overlay or conditioning variable on economic queries, even though they update on a 12–24 month cycle.

data source class: labor market micro data

aggregate labor statistics (unemployment rate, labor force participation, wage growth) are well-covered by ILO, OECD, and national agencies. the gap is micro-level labor data: individual job posting data, firm-level hiring and firing, skill demand at the occupation level, wage distribution (not mean), and informal labor market flows.

emerging sources: LinkedIn Economic Graph (25+ countries, covers formal sector with college-educated workers), Indeed Hiring Lab (job postings data, primarily US/UK/AUS/CAN), Burning Glass Technologies / Lightcast (job posting analysis, primarily OECD), ILO labour statistics database (aggregate, but expanding micro surveys through IPUMS integration), World Bank STEP surveys (skills measurement in developing countries, irregular).

systematic gaps: informal labor market (40–90% of employment in low-income countries) is essentially unmeasured in any consistent longitudinal framework. self-employment and gig economy work is underrepresented in all standard labor force surveys. skill demand data outside OECD countries is sparse.

API availability: LinkedIn Economic Graph has a research partnership program but no public API. Indeed Hiring Lab publishes data periodically. Lightcast has a commercial API. ILO ILOSTAT has a REST API with decent coverage.

data source class: firm-level and enterprise data

national accounts and aggregate economic statistics obscure firm-level dynamics: market concentration, productivity distributions, innovation rates, entry and exit rates, export market penetration, supply chain structure.

primary international sources: OECD SDBS (structural business statistics, OECD countries), World Bank Enterprise Survey (150+ countries, but infrequent — typically 3–5 year cycle), ORBIS database (Bureau van Dijk/Moody's Analytics — commercial, but the most comprehensive cross-country firm database), Compustat and Capital IQ (publicly listed firms, OECD-heavy), national business registries (heterogeneous access and structure).

systematic gaps: unlisted SMEs are the largest gap in every country's firm data ecosystem. in countries without mandatory business registration or with weak registry enforcement, a significant fraction of economic activity is conducted by firms that do not exist in any systematic database.

API availability: World Bank Enterprise Survey has public download but no API. ORBIS has a commercial API. national business registries are inconsistent — some have open APIs, most do not.

data source class: healthcare system capacity and performance data

WHO, OECD, and World Bank publish aggregate health indicators (life expectancy, infant mortality, disease burden). the gap is system capacity and performance: hospital bed utilization, surgical wait times, diagnostic capability distribution, health worker geographic distribution, pharmaceutical supply chain reliability, and health financing flow.

primary international sources: WHO Global Health Observatory (broad coverage, uneven depth), OECD Health Statistics (OECD only, high quality), IHME Global Burden of Disease (comprehensive disease burden, modeled), Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS — 90+ countries, irregular frequency, 5-year cycles), World Bank Health Nutrition Population (HNP) data, JRC European Health Data Space (EU only, emerging).

emerging sources: health facility databases (GHDX facility master lists), satellite assessment of health facility access (geographic analysis of facility catchment areas), insurance claims data where available (commercial, restricted).

systematic gaps: private health sector is severely underrepresented in all national and international health data. pharmaceutical pricing and supply is almost entirely opaque. mental health care capacity and utilization is the most severely undercollected domain across all health data.

API availability: WHO GHO REST API (good coverage). DHS does not have a public API but provides downloadable micro-datasets. IHME has downloadable data but no API.

data source class: infrastructure physical state and capacity

infrastructure data (roads, rail, ports, energy grid, water systems, telecommunications) is reported in aggregate (km of roads, installed power generation capacity) but the physical condition, utilization rate, and reliability of infrastructure are rarely collected or reported.

primary international sources: World Bank infrastructure data (aggregate, infrequent), IEA energy statistics (energy infrastructure, strong for IEA members), ITU connectivity data (telecommunications, reasonable coverage), OpenStreetMap (crowdsourced, global, variable quality), Global Infrastructure Hub (G20 infrastructure pipeline, investment-focused), ADB infrastructure data (Asia-Pacific focus).

emerging sources: satellite-derived road surface quality assessment (machine learning on imagery), night lights analysis as proxy for electrification (NASA VIIRS), cell tower density from OpenCellID as telecommunications coverage proxy, shipping port call data from AIS as port throughput proxy, air traffic data from EUROCONTROL and FlightAware as airport utilization proxy.

systematic gaps: last-mile infrastructure (rural roads, local water distribution, local power grids) is systematically underreported in all international data systems. infrastructure reliability (how often does the grid fail, what is average power outage duration) is collected in enterprise surveys but not in physical infrastructure data.

API availability: ITU has data downloads. OpenStreetMap Overpass API. NASA provides processed VIIRS downloads. AIS vessel tracking APIs (commercial: MarineTraffic, Windward; open: AISHub with registration).

data source class: migration and diaspora data

migration statistics are among the most politically sensitive and methodologically contested data domains. counts of migrants, refugees, internal displacement, and diaspora populations are produced by multiple actors with divergent methodologies, political pressures on reporting, and definitional disputes (economic migrant vs. refugee vs. asylum seeker).

primary international sources: UN DESA International Migrant Stock (biennial, estimates based on census data), UNHCR Refugee Data Finder (forced displacement — high quality for registered populations), IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (real-time displacement in crisis settings — uneven coverage), World Bank migration and remittances data, OECD International Migration Database (OECD countries only), national border statistics (heterogeneous).

systematic gaps: irregular migration is definitionally difficult to count and politically sensitive. internal migration is measured only in countries with population registration systems or periodic census. diaspora population (those who have emigrated but maintain connections to origin country) is measured inconsistently and the definition varies.

API availability: UNHCR has a data API. UN DESA provides downloads. IOM DTM provides downloads and some real-time dashboards but no API.

data source class: social cohesion and conflict event data

beyond macroeconomic statistics, social cohesion indicators (interpersonal trust, institutional trust, community participation, hate incident rates, protest frequency) and conflict event data (armed conflict events, civilian casualties, protest events, election violence) capture dynamics that are both analytically important and severely underrepresented in standard data architectures.

primary international sources for conflict events: ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data — real-time, 200+ countries, strong Africa/Asia/Middle East coverage), UCDP (Uppsala Conflict Data Program — onset/termination of armed conflicts, annual), PRIO GRID (conflict data disaggregated to geographic grid cells), GDELT Project (media-based event data — broad coverage, methodological caveats).

primary international sources for social cohesion: World Values Survey (irregular, 5–7 year waves), Afrobarometer/Latinobarometer/Arabbarometer (regional, high quality within region), Edelman Trust Barometer (commercial, 28 countries, annual), Gallup World Poll (annual, 150+ countries, commercial access).

API availability: ACLED has a REST API (free for researchers). UCDP provides downloads. GDELT has a BigQuery API. WVS provides downloads. Gallup is commercial.

alliance data architecture: expanding coverage

previous coverage addressed ASEAN, AU, Arab League, SCO, BRICS, G7/G20, OPEC+, IAEA, WTO, FATF, Egmont Group, Basel Committee.

additional alliance data ecosystems:

CARICOM (Caribbean Community)
15 full members + 5 associate members. primary data producer: Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), ECLAC Caribbean. CARICOM Statistics has a data harmonization program but produces limited public-facing data. key gaps: small island state data is systematically underrepresented in global datasets — sample sizes are too small for household surveys, and many indicators are estimated rather than collected. SIDS (Small Island Developing States) data is a known gap category across all major international data systems.

SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation)
8 members (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka). limited data integration — SAARC has not achieved the degree of statistical harmonization of ASEAN. primary data sources remain national NSOs plus World Bank South Asia data. key dynamic: India's NSO (MOSPI) dominates regional statistics due to size and capacity; regional averages are heavily India-weighted.

MERCOSUR (Southern Common Market)
Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay (+ associate members). INDEC (Argentina), IBGE (Brazil), DGEEC (Paraguay), INE (Uruguay) — four NSOs with different methodologies, update schedules, and data accessibility. MERCOSUR does not produce harmonized regional statistics to the extent that EUROSTAT harmonizes EU data. each country's data must be accessed separately.

GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council)
Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman. GCC-Stat is the statistical center of the GCC, producing some harmonized regional data. key feature: these six countries have some of the world's highest-quality administrative data (due to small populations with high government capacity), combined with severe restrictions on disaggregated data access. population data is complicated by the migrant worker majority in Qatar (88% migrant), UAE (~70% migrant), Kuwait (~70% migrant) — labor market and population statistics must be interpreted in light of the migrant vs. citizen distinction, which is politically managed in all six countries.

Pacific Islands Forum (PIF)
18 members. SPC (Pacific Community) is the primary data producer for the Pacific Islands region. key feature: many Pacific Island states are too small to support their own NSOs and rely on SPC for statistical production. this produces a regional data architecture where the supranational body is the primary data source, not just a harmonizer — which inverts the usual data flow.

track 2 cycle 3 delta assessment: non-zero. confirmed additions: judicial and legal system data, labor market micro data, firm-level and enterprise data, healthcare system capacity data, infrastructure physical state data, migration and diaspora data, social cohesion and conflict event data; additional alliance coverage (CARICOM, SAARC, MERCOSUR, GCC, Pacific Islands Forum).

cycle 4 — track 1

pattern 43: the confirmation prompt fatigue cascade
surface: the interface asks "are you sure?" for a low-stakes action. the user clicks "confirm" without reading. later, a genuinely high-stakes action also asks "are you sure?" — and is confirmed without reading.
structural: confirmation prompt frequency desensitizes the user to confirmation prompts as a category. all prompts become equal in weight through repetition.
root: confirmation prompts are deployed at the system level (any irreversible action triggers confirmation) rather than at the consequence level (prompts are calibrated to the severity and specificity of the action being confirmed).
interface rule: confirmation prompts must be typed by consequence severity, not by action irreversibility. low-severity irreversible actions (delete a filter preset) require no confirmation. medium-severity (delete a saved report) require a single click confirmation. high-severity (delete a shared dataset with downstream dependencies) require consequence disclosure ("this dataset is used by 3 downstream reports and 2 scheduled exports — deleting it will break them") plus named confirmation ("type the dataset name to confirm deletion"). never use a generic "are you sure?" prompt for any action — the prompt must name what is being done and its primary consequence.
workflow integration: prompt fatigue compounds in administrative workflows where users perform many repetitive operations — bulk data import, batch flag updates, mass annotation operations.

pattern 44: the orphaned state problem
surface: a user navigates away from a form midway through filling it. they return and the form is blank — their partial input is gone.
structural: form state is stored in session memory or DOM state, both of which are destroyed by navigation events.
root: the interface treats navigation as session termination for form state. the user's mental model treats navigation as temporary absence — they expect to find the form where they left it.
interface rule: any form that requires more than 60 seconds of user input must auto-save to persistent storage at the input field level, at minimum every 30 seconds and on every field blur event. on return navigation (back button, reopening the page, session restore), restore the last saved state with a "you have an unsaved draft from [timestamp] — continue or discard?" prompt. the restore is opt-in; do not silently restore without notification.
workflow integration: orphaned state loss is most damaging in multi-step research submission workflows, data annotation tasks, and complex query builders where significant user time investment has occurred before the navigation event.

pattern 45: the hierarchy override expectation
surface: a user sets a global filter (e.g., "show data only for 2020–2023"). they then navigate to a specific country view. the global filter is silently overridden by the country view's default temporal range, and the user does not notice.
structural: nested navigation contexts (global view → regional view → country view) often have independent default states. navigating to a child context can silently override parent-context settings.
root: the user's mental model assumes hierarchical inheritance: settings applied at the parent level persist into child levels unless explicitly changed. the interface implements hierarchical contexts with independent default states, which violates this assumption.
interface rule: any filter or parameter set at a parent context level must either: (a) explicitly persist into child contexts and show a "inherited from global filter" indicator, or (b) explicitly not persist, and show a "global filter suspended — [x] entity view defaults active" notification when the user enters the child context. there is no silent override. the user always knows what filter regime they are currently operating under.
workflow integration: hierarchy override violations are most common in dashboard-style interfaces where a global date range or entity filter is a first-class navigation element that users set once and expect to govern all subsequent views.

pattern 46: the data refresh timing mismatch
surface: a user is comparing two metrics. metric A refreshes hourly. metric B refreshes daily. the interface shows both in the same chart. at 2pm, metric A shows today's value; metric B shows yesterday's value. the chart has no indication of this temporal mismatch.
structural: when multiple data streams with different update frequencies are combined into a single display element, the display does not surface the temporal heterogeneity of the underlying data.
root: display logic aggregates data streams at the presentation layer without preserving the update-frequency metadata of each stream. the user sees one chart, not N charts with N update schedules.
interface rule: when a combined display element includes data from sources with different update frequencies, the element's freshness indicator must show the freshest and stalest source, not a single freshness value. "data as of: [latest source timestamp] – [oldest source timestamp]." for any metric combination where the temporal mismatch exceeds one refresh cycle of the faster source, surface a "timing mismatch" indicator and allow the user to normalize the comparison to a common reference time.
workflow integration: refresh timing mismatches are most problematic in real-time dashboard contexts where users are making decisions based on the assumption that all displayed data is current.

pattern 47: the false negative in search
surface: a user searches for a country name and gets no results. the country is in the database under its UN formal name, not the common English name ("United Republic of Tanzania" vs. "Tanzania").
structural: search is implemented against stored identifiers (formal names, codes) without synonym or alias expansion.
root: the data architecture stores entities under formal identifiers; the user's natural language queries use common names, vernacular names, or alternate spellings. the search layer does not bridge this gap.
interface rule: every entity in the system must have an alias set covering: UN formal name, ISO 3166 alpha-2 and alpha-3 codes, common English name, local language name (transliterated), common alternate spellings, historical names (for recently renamed entities), and any common abbreviations. search operates against the full alias set. return results with a "also known as" disclosure when the query matched an alias rather than the primary identifier. additionally: fuzzy matching must handle diacritical variations (Cote d'Ivoire / Côte d'Ivoire), spelling variations (Myanmar / Burma), and historical name changes (Zaire → Democratic Republic of the Congo).
workflow integration: false negatives in entity search break the research flow at the earliest stage, causing users to conclude a country is not in the system and either giving up or switching to a less appropriate source.

pattern 48: the interface authority illusion
surface: an interface presents data with high visual authority — clean design, prominent branding, clear typography, confident presentation — for data that has low epistemic authority (modeled, estimated, contested, or outdated).
structural: visual design language communicates epistemic confidence independent of and often contradicting the underlying data quality.
root: interface design norms optimize for clarity and trustworthiness as visual properties. this creates an inverse relationship: the better the interface is designed, the more confident the data appears — regardless of actual data quality.
interface rule: epistemic authority must be signaled through consistent, unconventional visual properties that are independent of the "good design" defaults. high-confidence data: displayed with standard visual treatment. medium-confidence (estimated, preliminary): displayed with a visual texture or weight variation that is consistent across all medium-confidence data in the system. low-confidence (modeled, contested): displayed with a distinct visual treatment — reduced opacity, hatching, or a border indicator — that is consistent across all low-confidence data. the visual language of confidence cannot be the visual language of design quality. they must be distinct systems.
workflow integration: interface authority illusion is most damaging in public-facing contexts where users lack the domain knowledge to independently assess data quality and are relying on the interface to communicate it.

pattern 49: the unit label ambiguity
surface: a table shows a column labeled "GDP" with values like "43,000." the user assumes this is in USD billions. it is in USD millions. analysis based on this assumption is off by a factor of 1000.
structural: numeric fields are shown without unit labels, or with abbreviated unit labels that do not specify the denomination (billion vs. million vs. thousand).
root: database schemas store values with a denomination assumption that is not preserved through the display layer. the unit is known at data ingestion but is stripped, normalized, or abbreviated in display without preserving full denomination information.
interface rule: every numeric display must include: unit (currency, physical unit, percentage), denomination (thousands / millions / billions / trillions — spelled out, not abbreviated), reference year if constant currency, and ISO currency code if currency (not assumed USD). column headers in tables must include the full unit description. charts must include full unit on the y-axis label. when a user changes the display denomination (e.g., switching from billions to trillions), recalculate the values and update the unit label — never require the user to mentally convert.
workflow integration: unit label ambiguity is most catastrophic in cross-country comparison tables where different countries may report the same metric in different denominations, and the display normalizes without disclosing the normalization.

pattern 50: the invisible default
surface: a user loads a dashboard. it shows data for the last 12 months. the user analyzes trends. they have not noticed that the default time range is applied — they believe they are looking at all available data.
structural: interfaces have default parameter values that are applied silently on load. these defaults shape everything the user sees but are not foregrounded as choices the user has made.
root: defaults are designed for the modal use case and applied universally. users who don't need the modal case inherit the default without necessarily noticing or adjusting it.
interface rule: every default parameter must be surfaced as a chip, badge, or indicator in the active state of the interface — not in a settings panel. the user must be able to see, at a glance, which defaults are currently active. each default indicator is clickable to adjust. the interface never begins in a completely transparent state where all active defaults are invisible. a count of "N active defaults" with expand-to-see is the minimum; full display of all active default values is preferred.
workflow integration: invisible defaults are the root cause of many analysis errors where the user has drawn conclusions valid only within the default parameter space but presents them as general findings.

track 1 cycle 4 delta assessment: non-zero. patterns 43–50 confirmed. flagging for cycle 5.

cycle 4 — track 2

new data architecture domain: central bank communication and forward guidance

central banks produce a category of structured semi-public data that is underrepresented in standard data architectures: meeting minutes, policy statements, forward guidance language, dissent votes, and research paper publication cadence. this data is not economic statistics — it is institutional communication — but it has direct causal relationship with financial market behavior and economic expectations.

primary sources: Federal Reserve (FOMC minutes, beige book, SEP projections — publicly available), ECB (Governing Council statements, Economic Bulletin, research publications), Bank of England (MPC minutes, Monetary Policy Report), Bank of Japan (MPM statements — Japanese primary), PBOC (monetary policy committee statements — Chinese primary, limited English availability), BIS (quarterly review, research papers, committee publications).

emerging analytical framework: central bank communication analysis using NLP (sentiment, hawkishness/dovishness scoring, uncertainty quantification). BIS and academic researchers have produced central bank tone indices. Citigroup and JPMorgan produce proprietary hawkishness indices.

API availability: Federal Reserve has a FRED API that includes FOMC data as unstructured text. ECB has an API. BIS publishes structured datasets. Central bank NLP analysis APIs are commercial (Bloomberg, Refinitiv).

data architecture implication: central bank communication data is most useful as a high-frequency contextual signal overlaid on lower-frequency economic data. the data architecture must support time-aligned layering of communication signals on economic indicator charts — showing, for example, the sequence of FOMC statements alongside the sequence of CPI prints.

new data architecture domain: political risk and geopolitical event data

economic data analysis is incomplete without a systematic political risk layer. geopolitical events (elections, coups, sanctions, trade restrictions, diplomatic ruptures) produce economic shocks that standard economic indicators capture with a lag. a data architecture that shows the economic consequence without the political cause is systematically incomplete.

primary sources for political events: GDELT Project (event data extracted from news, real-time, global — methodological caveats around accuracy), DFR Lab / Atlantic Council (election monitoring, disinformation tracking), ICEWS (Integrated Crisis Early Warning System — academic/US government, event data), Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED — conflict events, real-time), Global Terrorism Database (GTD — annual, historical), V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy — annual, academic, institutional quality indicators).

primary sources for political risk ratings: Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) Country Risk — commercial, quarterly, high quality. PRS Group ICRG (International Country Risk Guide) — commercial, monthly, the most commonly cited political risk index. Coface Country Risk Assessments — commercial, quarterly. Moody's / S&P / Fitch sovereign credit ratings — financial markets' distillation of political and economic risk — quarterly to event-driven.

API availability: GDELT has a BigQuery API. V-Dem provides downloads. ICEWS is available through GDELT. EIU and PRS are commercial. Sovereign credit ratings are distributed through financial data providers.

data architecture implication: political risk data must be integrated as an event-based overlay layer, not as a slow-moving indicator. an election that occurs between two quarterly data releases has immediate economic relevance that will not appear in the subsequent quarterly print. the architecture must support event stamping and alignment with indicator time series.

new data architecture domain: trade flow at the product level

aggregate trade statistics (total exports, total imports, trade balance) are well-covered by IMF, World Bank, and national customs. the analytically rich layer is product-level trade: what is being traded, at what price, between which country pairs, through which ports or transport modes.

primary sources: UN COMTRADE (the definitive source for bilateral trade flows at the HS product code level — 200+ countries, annual, some monthly — free API with registration), World Bank WITS (access to COMTRADE and other databases through a unified interface), ITC Trade Map (monthly, good for recent data, some gaps), OECD TiVA (Trade in Value Added — captures intermediate goods in global supply chains, less frequent).

emerging sources: Global Trade Alert (real-time trade policy interventions — tariffs, quotas, export restrictions — crowdsourced with verification, free access), IMF DOTS (Direction of Trade Statistics — monthly bilateral aggregate trade by country, faster than COMTRADE).

systematic gaps: services trade is severely undercounted in all standard databases — only goods trade is captured by customs declarations. digital services trade (software licensing, cloud services, data flows) is almost completely absent from official statistics. re-export distortion: Singapore, UAE, Netherlands, and Hong Kong are major re-export hubs, which inflates their bilateral trade figures with many countries.

API availability: UN COMTRADE REST API (free, registration required, rate limits). World Bank WITS has API. ITC has API. OECD STATS API.

new data architecture domain: cross-border financial flows at granular level

beyond aggregate remittances and FDI statistics, granular cross-border financial flow data captures: correspondent banking relationships, trade finance flows, securities cross-holdings, and insurance cross-border claims.

primary sources: BIS Locational Banking Statistics (quarterly, bilateral cross-border bank claims and liabilities, high quality), BIS Consolidated Banking Statistics, CPIS (Coordinated Portfolio Investment Survey — IMF, annual, securities cross-holdings), BOP statistics (IMF Balance of Payments — includes current and capital account flows), World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide (bilateral remittance cost data, quarterly), SWIFT GPI data (cross-border payment flows — commercial, but SWIFT publishes aggregate statistics).

emerging sources: FinCEN (US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) beneficial ownership registry — newly established, incomplete, but potentially transformative for understanding corporate structure behind financial flows. EU AMLA (Anti-Money Laundering Authority — being established) will eventually produce structured financial flow data for AML purposes. cryptocurrency on-chain data (Chainalysis, Elliptic, Crystal Blockchain — commercial analytics on public blockchain data) captures an emerging class of cross-border financial flows not in any official statistics.

systematic gaps: offshore financial center intermediation is the most severe gap — flows through BVI, Cayman Islands, Luxembourg, and Ireland as holding company domiciles distort the apparent bilateral investment statistics between many country pairs. the true origin and destination of financial flows is often different from the immediate bilateral counterparty. IMF CPIS captures securities cross-holdings but not the ultimate beneficial owner.

API availability: BIS data portal has API access. IMF Data portal has API. World Bank has API. SWIFT publishes aggregates but no API. Chainalysis and similar are commercial APIs.

new data architecture domain: environmental and natural resource data

environment and natural resource data is increasingly integrated with economic analysis: deforestation rates, freshwater availability, fisheries stock, mineral reserve estimates, soil quality, and atmospheric pollution all have direct economic relevance as inputs to production, outputs of economic activity, or constraints on future growth.

primary sources: FAO FAOSTAT (agriculture, forestry, fisheries — broad coverage, annual), Global Forest Watch (Hansen deforestation data — annual, high resolution satellite-derived), IUCN Red List (species and ecosystem status — not economic but increasingly used for natural capital accounting), UNEP WCMC Ocean+ (marine ecosystems), NASA/ESA/USGS satellite archives (Landsat, Sentinel — source data for many derived environmental datasets), OECD environmental statistics, Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S — European climate data infrastructure).

emerging sources: Global Fishing Watch (AIS-based fishing vessel activity, real-time, global), Planet Labs commercial satellite data (daily global coverage, commercial), Global Surface Water Explorer (JRC — freshwater change from Landsat, free), ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI — standardized long-term climate data records).

systematic gaps: natural capital accounting (integrating natural resource depletion into national accounts) is an emerging field with inconsistent adoption. WAVES (Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services — World Bank initiative) has produced natural capital accounts for some countries but coverage is sparse. sub-national environmental data is highly variable — some countries have dense monitoring networks, others have almost no systematic environmental monitoring.

API availability: FAO FAOSTAT API. NASA Earthdata (Earthdata Search API). Global Forest Watch has an API. Copernicus Climate Change Service API. Planet Labs commercial API.

supplementary country analysis — additional small states and territories

the initial 193 UN member state coverage was complete. supplementary analysis for territories, disputed entities, and jurisdictions with significant data signatures:

Hong Kong SAR
unique data situation: Hong Kong produces its own statistics through the Census and Statistics Department (C&SD) independently of mainland China's NBS. this means Hong Kong has a separate, high-quality data stream for an entity that is politically part of China but statistically distinct in most international databases. HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) produces financial sector data that is particularly high quality for a territory of its size.

data architecture implication: queries for "China" must distinguish mainland China data (NBS) from Hong Kong data (C&SD) from Macau data (DSEC), as these are three distinct statistical systems coexisting within one sovereign territory. aggregating them (as some databases do when displaying "China") produces a distorted figure that requires explicit handling.

Taiwan
Taiwan is recognized by 12 UN member states and produces its own high-quality national statistics through the National Statistics Bureau. Taiwan appears in some international databases (ADB, IMF Article IV — published separately from China) and is absent or subsumed into China in others (World Bank). data users working on East Asian economic analysis must be aware of which databases treat Taiwan as a separate statistical entity and which do not.

Palestinian territories (West Bank and Gaza)
the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics (PCBS) produces national statistics for the Palestinian territories, recognized as a state by 146 UN member states. data coverage is severely affected by the ongoing conflict: Gaza's statistical system effectively collapsed in 2023–2024. UN OCHA and UNRWA supplement PCBS data for humanitarian indicators. economic data for Gaza post-2023 is almost entirely estimated or derived from satellite damage assessment.

Kosovo
Kosovo declared independence in 2008, recognized by 101 UN member states and not recognized by Russia, China, and others. Kosovo has its own NSO (Kosovo Agency of Statistics) and is included in World Bank and IMF databases (as a separate entity) but is not in the UN system. European integration process has driven significant data quality improvement in Kosovo.

Western Sahara
administered by Morocco (approximately 75% of territory) and by the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Polisario Front, approximately 25%). no comprehensive statistical coverage. Morocco incorporates Western Sahara into its national statistics; the SADR produces limited self-reported statistics. data for Western Sahara is essentially unavailable from any neutral international source.

Somaliland
self-declared independent state since 1991, recognized by no UN member state. separate functional government with its own central bank, currency, and nascent statistical system. not included in any international statistical database under its own name — data is either subsumed into Somalia or absent. Somaliland's financial sector is noteworthy as the origin of mobile money innovation (the Zaad service predates M-Pesa's international expansion).

track 2 cycle 4 delta assessment: non-zero. confirmed additions: central bank communication data, political risk and geopolitical event data, trade flow at product level, cross-border financial flows granular, environmental and natural resource data, supplementary analysis for Hong Kong/Taiwan/Palestinian territories/Kosovo/Western Sahara/Somaliland.

cycle 4 cross-track synthesis

intersection 14: the event-time vs. index-time problem in combined display

track 1's pattern 46 (data refresh timing mismatch) addresses temporal heterogeneity in display. track 2's cycle 4 additions introduce event-based data sources (ACLED conflict events, political elections, central bank announcements) alongside indicator-based sources (quarterly GDP, annual poverty rates).

event-based and indicator-based data operate on fundamentally different temporal logics. indicators are indexed to a period: GDP for Q3 2024, poverty rate for 2022. events are indexed to a moment: coup on October 15, election on March 3, FOMC decision on November 7. combining them in a time series display requires resolving which temporal logic governs the x-axis.

resolution: dual temporal axis pattern

the interface maintains two parallel time axes: index axis (for period-indexed indicators — aligns values to their reference period) and event axis (for point-in-time events — aligns events to their occurrence date). the event axis overlays the index axis as a band above or below the primary chart area, showing events as vertical markers with expandable detail. the user can see: here is where GDP was declining (index axis), and here is the political event that preceded it (event axis). correlation between the two axes is never asserted by the interface — it is surfaced as a spatial relationship the user interprets.

intersection 15: the provenance graph for derived data

track 1's provenance depth selector covers simple provenance: who collected this data, when, how. track 2's cycle 4 additions introduce derived data at scale: NLP-derived central bank sentiment scores, satellite-derived deforestation rates, conflict event counts derived from news media by GDELT, trade-in-value-added chains derived from bilateral trade data using input-output models.

derived data has a provenance graph, not a provenance chain. a single derived value may trace back through: (1) a source dataset, (2) a methodological transformation (the model or algorithm), (3) validation data used to calibrate the model, and (4) code used to run the computation. each of these nodes in the graph may itself have provenance.

interface rule for derived data provenance:

display derived data with a "derived" indicator distinct from "collected" data. expand to show: source data lineage (what raw data went into this), transformation disclosure (what model, algorithm, or method was applied — with link to methodology), calibration disclosure (what validation data was used, what the out-of-sample performance was), and code availability (is the transformation code publicly available for inspection). do not collapse this into a single "source" field — derived data's provenance is structurally multi-node and must be displayed accordingly.

intersection 16: the network of missing data — visualizing systematic absence

track 1's pattern 42 (cognitive load of negative space) addresses absence in individual data tables. track 2's cycle 4 additions reveal that absence has geographic structure, institutional structure, and temporal structure — the pattern of what is missing is itself data.

missing data is not randomly distributed. it clusters: by country income level (low-income countries have more absence), by data domain (health system capacity and judicial data have more absence than GDP and trade), by historical period (pre-1990 data is absent for countries that emerged from Soviet collapse), by institutional framework (data absent where reporting to international bodies is not mandatory), by political context (authoritarian governments restrict data, conflict zones produce absence).

this means the absence map is itself an analytical product. a researcher asking "which countries have sufficient data to support a cross-national study of X" is asking a coverage map question, and the interface should be able to answer it.

interface pattern: coverage map as first-class analytical mode

a "coverage mode" where the primary display is not data values but data presence/absence at the desired metric × geography × time intersection. the user specifies the metric set, the geographic scope, and the time range. the coverage map shows: complete coverage (all specified metrics available), partial coverage (some metrics available — hover to see which are missing), no coverage (no data available for any specified metric), and absence type (typed: not collected / not reported / restricted / conflict zone).

from the coverage map, the user can: download the coverage map as a data artifact, filter to "countries with complete coverage" for their intended analysis, view the "coverage gap report" (which specific metric-country-time combinations are missing and why), and send a data request to the relevant NSO or international body through an integrated request channel.

intersection 17: the confidence class propagation problem

when a derived value is computed from multiple source values, each with its own confidence class, the derived value's confidence class is not simply the average or minimum of its inputs. confidence classes interact multiplicatively in models (a model applied to a medium-confidence input does not produce a high-confidence output even if the model itself is well-validated) and additively in aggregations (an average across multiple medium-confidence inputs may or may not produce a medium-confidence output depending on how the errors are correlated).

propagation rules:

for simple arithmetic (sum, average) of independent values with known confidence classes: the output confidence class is the minimum of the input confidence classes. if any input is "low confidence," the output is "low confidence."

for model-derived values (where a statistical model transforms inputs): the output confidence class is at most one level below the input confidence class (high → medium, medium → low, low → low). even a well-validated model introduces additional uncertainty relative to direct measurement.

for aggregations across conflict-flagged values: any aggregation that includes a conflict-flagged value must itself be flagged as "aggregation includes conflict," and the conflict flag must propagate to any derived value that uses this aggregation.

for normalization and index construction (composing multiple indicators into a single composite): composite indices are a special case — their confidence class must reflect both the input confidence classes and the methodological uncertainty in the weighting scheme. composite confidence class: at most "medium" regardless of input classes (the aggregation methodology itself introduces irreducible uncertainty), unless the composite methodology has been independently replicated with similar results, in which case "medium-high" may be appropriate.

cycle 4 delta assessment: track 1 — non-zero (patterns 43–50 confirmed), track 2 — non-zero. entering cycle 5.

cycle 5 — track 1

pattern 51: the identity collapse in bulk operations
surface: a user selects 50 countries for a bulk export. the progress indicator shows "exporting 50 items." when the export fails at item 23, the error message says "export failed." the user does not know which of the 50 items failed or what state the others are in.
structural: bulk operations treat the selection as an atomic unit for status reporting, even when the underlying operations are executed individually and can fail independently.
root: bulk operation UX was designed for uniform items (files, records) where partial failure is uncommon. complex data exports with heterogeneous source availability make partial failure the norm, not the exception.
interface rule: every bulk operation must maintain and surface item-level status. the progress display shows: completed N / failed N / pending N. failures are named: "Kenya — missing data for metric GDP 2021. skipped." completed items are available for download before the entire operation completes. the user can retry failed items independently without re-running the full bulk operation.
workflow integration: bulk operation status opacity is most costly in large research exports where users may not notice a silent partial failure until they analyze the exported data and find unexpected gaps.

pattern 52: the keyboard navigation break
surface: a user navigates an interface with keyboard controls. they trigger a tooltip or popover. focus jumps to the tooltip content. when they close the tooltip, focus does not return to the element that triggered it — it jumps to an unexpected location.
structural: dynamically injected UI elements (tooltips, modals, popovers, drawers) are not implemented with focus management. focus order is determined by DOM position, which may differ from visual position and intended interaction flow.
root: focus management is treated as an accessibility requirement added after the component is built rather than as a first-class interaction design requirement built into the component architecture.
interface rule: every dynamically activated UI element must implement the ARIA authoring practices focus management pattern for its type: tooltip focus is not trapped, popover focus moves into and returns from the popover on close, modal focus is trapped within the modal, drawer focus moves into and returns on close. every focus state must be visually indicated with a visible focus ring (not just the browser default, which is inconsistent). focus restoration on component close must always return to the triggering element or to a semantically appropriate element designated in the component specification.
workflow integration: keyboard navigation breaks are invisible to mouse users, creating a class of users for whom the interface is effectively unusable in keyboard-only navigation mode.

pattern 53: the interaction dead zone
surface: a user taps a button on a mobile device. nothing happens. they tap again. the first tap's action triggers during the second tap, causing a double-action.
structural: touch event handling does not correctly debounce simultaneous or rapid-succession touch events, and there is no visual feedback between the first tap and the action executing.
root: desktop interaction models assume click events are intentional and single. mobile touch events have higher accidental activation rates and users expect faster visual feedback of reception.
interface rule: all interactive elements must provide immediate tactile feedback at reception (visual state change within 16ms of touch/click event registration). action execution may be deferred (network request, computation), but reception acknowledgment must be immediate. button/control state must move to "processing" or "active" state immediately on receipt, preventing re-triggering. for touch interfaces: minimum touch target size is 44×44 CSS pixels; minimum spacing between adjacent touch targets is 8 CSS pixels.
workflow integration: interaction dead zones are highest-frequency on mobile data interfaces where users are tapping through navigation quickly and rely on immediate feedback to confirm their input was received.

pattern 54: the zoom-induced context loss
surface: a user zooms in on a time series chart to see a specific period. the zoom changes the x-axis range. the user is now looking at 3 months of data. the contextual markers that were visible at the full range (recession bands, election markers, policy change events) are no longer visible because they are outside the zoomed window.
structural: chart zoom operations change the viewport but do not adapt the contextual overlay system to the new viewport.
root: contextual overlays are implemented as positioned elements at their event dates. zoom clips the viewport to a date range. events outside the date range are clipped. the connection between zoom state and overlay visibility is not handled.
interface rule: contextual overlays (event markers, reference lines, annotation bands) in zoomed chart views must be handled in one of two ways: (a) events outside the viewport are shown as edge indicators — small markers at the viewport edge showing that N events exist beyond the edge, with expandable summary — or (b) the overlay layer is dynamically loaded based on the viewport, always showing relevant contextual events for the visible period plus a configurable lookback/lookforward window. never silently lose contextual overlays on zoom.
workflow integration: zoom-induced context loss is most common in financial time series analysis where the user zooms to a volatility event and loses the event overlays that explain the volatility.

pattern 55: the semantic ambiguity of "latest"
surface: a data table shows "latest available" values for each country. for Germany, "latest" means 2024 Q3. for Niger, "latest" means 2019. the table presents both as "latest available" with no indication that the latency difference is 5 years.
structural: the "latest available" filter returns the most recent data point for each entity independently. across entities, "latest" resolves to different actual dates.
root: "latest" is a relative temporal operator that produces different absolute dates for different entities within the same dataset. the interface presents the result as if "latest" is a shared reference point.
interface rule: whenever "latest available" is used as a filter or display mode, the display must show the actual date of the "latest" value for each entity, not just the word "latest." for tabular displays, include a "data date" column that shows the actual date of the value in the adjacent cell. for map displays, color-encode by data age (five bands: same year, 1 year old, 2–3 years old, 4–5 years old, 6+ years old). for charts that mix entity latest values, label each series endpoint with its actual date.
workflow integration: "latest" ambiguity is most dangerous in cross-country comparison contexts where users assume they are comparing contemporaneous data and draw causal or correlational conclusions that are invalidated by the temporal heterogeneity.

pattern 56: the empty intersection trap
surface: a user specifies a query: poverty rate, sub-Saharan Africa, 2015–2023, annual frequency, three specific sources. the query returns zero results. the user does not know which dimension of the query is causing the empty result — is it the source, the time range, the geography, or the frequency?
structural: multi-dimensional queries that return empty results provide no information about which constraint eliminated the data.
root: query execution treats all constraints as a single AND operation and surfaces the result. the intermediate states (which subset of constraints is satisfiable) are not computed or surfaced.
interface rule: for any multi-dimensional query that returns zero results or fewer than a minimum threshold of results, the interface must run constraint relaxation and surface the analysis: "removing the source constraint returns 47 results. removing the frequency constraint returns 31 results. removing the time constraint to 2000–2023 returns 12 results matching your other criteria." the user can then select which constraint to relax. this is a single secondary computation that prevents a major user disorientation event.
workflow integration: empty intersection trap is most common in exploratory queries with many simultaneous constraints applied by users who are not familiar with the coverage profile of the data system.

pattern 57: the stacked filter invisibility problem
surface: a user applies filter A, then filter B, then filter C over the course of a session. the filtered view is correct. but when they return the next day, they see the same filtered view and don't remember that filters B and C are active — they believe they are looking at the full dataset.
structural: active filter state is persistent but not prominently surfaced in the returning user's first viewport.
root: filter UI is designed for filter application (prominent controls) and filter use (filtered view), but not for filter recognition (communicating to a returning user what filters are active on load).
interface rule: the first viewport of any session that has persistent filter state must show an "active filters" summary prominently — above the data, not in a sidebar or settings panel. the summary shows: [N filters active: [filter A] [filter B] [filter C]] with a "clear all" option and individual remove controls. if the filter was applied in a previous session, add a "(from previous session)" indicator so the user knows these are not newly applied in this session.
workflow integration: stacked filter invisibility is highest risk in persistent dashboard environments where users configure a view once, leave, and return expecting to see their configured view — but have forgotten the configuration.

track 1 cycle 5 delta assessment: non-zero. patterns 51–57 confirmed. entering cycle 6 for track 1.

cycle 5 — track 2

new data architecture domain: education system data at micro level

aggregate education indicators (enrollment rates, literacy rates, years of schooling) are well-covered by UNESCO UIS, World Bank EdStats, and OECD PISA. the micro-level gap: school-level performance data, learning outcomes below the national level, teacher qualification distribution, and curriculum quality.

primary sources: PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment — OECD, triennial, 90+ participating education systems, strong methodology), TIMSS (Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study — IEA, quadrennial, 60+ countries), PIRLS (Progress in International Reading Literacy Study — IEA, 5-year cycle), PASEC (Programme d'Analyse des Systèmes Éducatifs — francophone Africa, irregular), SACMEQ (Southern and Eastern Africa Consortium for Monitoring Educational Quality — irregular), EGRA/EGMA (Early Grade Reading/Math Assessment — World Bank, country-specific). UNESCO UIS data API (good coverage of aggregate indicators). World Bank EdStats API.

systematic gaps: learning outcomes data (as opposed to enrollment or attainment) is sparse outside OECD+. PISA covers 90+ systems but has known sampling challenges in large federations (Brazil, India, China participation is selective rather than nationally representative). no systematic global assessment exists for pre-primary learning. private school sector quality is almost entirely unassessed in international frameworks.

new data architecture domain: research and innovation ecosystem data

R&D investment, patent filing, scientific publication, and technology transfer data constitute the innovation data ecosystem — increasingly central to economic analysis of long-run productivity.

primary sources: OECD MSTI (Main Science and Technology Indicators — OECD countries, annual), UNESCO UIS R&D statistics (broader coverage, lower depth), WIPO IP Statistics (patent, trademark, industrial design filings — global, annual), Web of Science/Scopus (scientific publications — commercial, high quality but not APIs for most users), SciVal (Elsevier — research analytics platform, commercial), Lens.org (open patent and scholarly literature database — REST API available), Our World in Data science compilation (derived, accessible).

systematic gaps: R&D data in low-income countries is particularly sparse — where NSO capacity is limited, R&D surveys are often the first to be deprioritized. informal innovation (non-IP-registered innovation, grassroots technological adaptation) is essentially unmeasured globally.

API availability: OECD STATS API. WIPO IP Statistics has API. Lens.org has a REST API. Web of Science and Scopus have APIs (institutional subscription required).

new data architecture domain: energy transition data

energy transition data captures the shift from fossil fuel to renewable energy systems and the associated investment, capacity, generation, and emissions flows. this is a rapidly evolving data domain where new sources are emerging faster than standards are being set.

primary sources: IEA (International Energy Agency — most comprehensive for OECD+ countries, broad categories for non-OECD), IRENA (International Renewable Energy Agency — renewable energy capacity and generation, 165 countries, annual), BloombergNEF Energy Transition Research (commercial, high quality, real-time), Wood Mackenzie (commercial, upstream focused), BNEF New Energy Outlook (annual, modeled), Global Energy Monitor (coal plant tracker, gas tracker, wind and solar tracker — crowdsourced with verification, free). Ember Climate (real-time electricity generation data derived from system operators, 80+ countries, API available). Carbon Monitor (near-real-time CO2 emissions estimates, daily, derived from multiple proxies).

systematic gaps: off-grid and distributed energy systems (solar home systems, mini-grids) are severely undercounted in all official statistics. cooking energy (where energy poverty is most acute) is poorly measured. energy access quality (hours of supply, voltage reliability) is measured inconsistently.

API availability: IEA has an API (API keys required). IRENA provides data downloads. Ember Climate has an API. Carbon Monitor provides daily download. BloombergNEF and Wood Mackenzie are commercial.

new data architecture domain: supply chain and logistics data

supply chain disruption analysis requires data that is almost entirely absent from standard macroeconomic databases: shipping container availability, port dwell times, freight rate indices, air cargo capacity, trucking spot rates, and cross-border logistics times.

primary sources: Freightos Baltic Index (FBX — container freight rates, daily, multiple trade lanes — free download), Drewry World Container Index (weekly, commercial), OECD-UNCTAD-WTO trade facilitation indicators, World Bank Logistics Performance Index (LPI — biennial, 160 countries, survey-based), Flexport Ocean Timeliness Indicator (OTI — real-time, based on carrier data), FlightAware cargo data, iContainers market data.

emerging real-time sources: AIS vessel tracking (as described in satellite section — applicable to shipping route monitoring), Panjiva (S&P Global) import/export manifest data (bill of lading data from customs declarations, US-focused), Descartes Datamyne (global customs data, commercial).

systematic gaps: air cargo below the aggregate level is almost entirely opaque. last-mile logistics (domestic distribution within countries) is unmeasured except in a handful of OECD countries with strong logistics data collection. cold chain logistics (critical for agriculture and pharmaceuticals) is essentially unmeasured at the international level.

API availability: Freightos has an API. AIS vessel tracking APIs (commercial: MarineTraffic). Panjiva and Descartes are commercial APIs.

new API architecture component: data lineage graph standard

the previous API architecture specification established source registration, data point records, and conflict detection. a critical missing component is a data lineage graph standard — a formal specification for how derived data carries its derivation history through the API layer.

lineage_record:
  node_id: [unique identifier for this lineage node]
  node_type: [source | transform | aggregation | composite | derived]

if node_type == "source":
    source_id: [reference to source registration record]
    data_point_ids: [array of data_point_record IDs that are source nodes]

if node_type == "transform":
    input_node_ids: [array of lineage node IDs that are inputs]
    transform_type: [normalization | deflation | unit_conversion | interpolation | 
                     extrapolation | model_application | nlp_extraction | 
                     satellite_derivation | index_construction]
    transform_id: [reference to transform specification record]
    transform_version: [version of transform applied]
    code_url: [link to code if publicly available]

if node_type == "aggregation":
    input_node_ids: [array of lineage node IDs that are inputs]
    aggregation_method: [sum | mean | weighted_mean | median | geometric_mean | 
                         count | composite_index]
    weights: [if weighted — array of weight values with their source]

if node_type == "composite":
    component_node_ids: [array of component lineage nodes]
    composition_methodology_id: [reference to methodology specification]

output_data_point_ids: [array of data_point_record IDs produced by this node]
  confidence_class_output: [confidence class of the output — computed per propagation rules]
  confidence_class_explanation: [short string explaining confidence class derivation]
  timestamp: [when this derivation was computed]

this lineage record, attached to every derived data point, makes the full derivation graph queryable through the API. a client can traverse the lineage from any derived data point back to its raw source data, inspecting every transformation node along the path.

track 2 cycle 5 delta assessment: non-zero. confirmed additions: education micro-level data, R&D and innovation ecosystem data, energy transition data, supply chain and logistics data, data lineage graph standard.

cycle 5 cross-track synthesis

intersection 18: the interface obligation when a lineage graph is available

track 1's provenance depth selector specifies three tiers of provenance display (default / expand / expert). track 2's cycle 5 lineage record standard creates a fully traversable lineage graph. the interface obligation when a complete lineage graph is available differs from when provenance is a simple chain.

when lineage is a graph: the interface must support graph traversal, not just linear depth expansion. a user starting from a derived composite index must be able to follow any component node down to its source, follow a different component down to its source, and compare the paths. a linear "click to expand" model does not support this — it supports a tree, not a graph.

pattern for lineage graph display in expert view:

interactive lineage graph — a force-directed or hierarchical DAG (directed acyclic graph) visualization where nodes are lineage records and edges are derivation relationships. the user can click any node to see its details: source_id, transform_type, confidence class, code_url. the user can filter to show only the lineage path for a specific source or transform type. the graph supports collapse (hide sub-graphs already understood) and highlight (trace all nodes that use a specific source data point). the graph is exportable as a lineage report in standard formats (JSON-LD provenance vocabulary, PROV-O).

intersection 19: the interface design for irreducible uncertainty

some data — no matter how well sourced, how carefully derived, how thoroughly provenanced — is irreducibly uncertain. demographic projections for conflict zones. GDP estimates for North Korea. deforestation rates in regions without consistent satellite coverage. sea level rise projections 50 years forward.

track 1 has handled reducible uncertainty: provide more provenance, surface conflicts, show confidence classes. but irreducible uncertainty requires a different interface treatment. showing a confidence class of "low" is honest but doesn't help the user understand whether "low" means "±5%" or "±200%."

interface rules for irreducible uncertainty:

uncertainty range display — for any value with irreducible uncertainty, show the value as a range with a central estimate: "GDP: $1.2–2.4B (central estimate: $1.8B)." the range is not an error bar — it is the known bound of the uncertainty, derived from the methodology. do not collapse uncertainty to a point estimate and add a footnote.

scenario branching — for forward-looking estimates (projections, forecasts), show multiple scenarios explicitly: optimistic / central / pessimistic, or a probability distribution if the underlying model produces one. do not show only the central estimate. do not label one scenario as "the forecast."

uncertainty source disclosure — for irreducibly uncertain values, disclose the primary source of the irreducibility: data absence (no data exists for this period or entity), model uncertainty (the model itself has wide confidence intervals even with perfect input data), definition uncertainty (the phenomenon is inherently ambiguous and different reasonable definitions produce different values), or political uncertainty (future values depend on decisions not yet made).

user calibration — when a user has been working with high-confidence data and then navigates to a display containing irreducibly uncertain data, surface the transition explicitly: "you are now viewing data with higher uncertainty than your previous view — [central estimate] [range] [primary uncertainty source]."

cycle 6 — track 1

pattern 58: the silent truncation of long strings
surface: a country name or metric name is truncated in a table cell with an ellipsis. the user reads the truncated string and misidentifies the entity.
structural: table cells have fixed width. text that exceeds cell width is truncated with CSS overflow:hidden text-overflow:ellipsis. no tooltip or expand mechanism is available.
root: table layout is optimized for visual regularity (consistent column widths) over information completeness. truncation is the design default for overflow, not a deliberate choice.
interface rule: no identifier (country name, metric name, entity name, source name) may be silently truncated without a hover-reveal tooltip showing the full string. for critical identifiers (the primary entity identifier in a row), truncation should be avoided entirely — allow column width adjustment or line wrapping before truncating. for metric names: always provide a metric definition tooltip accessible from anywhere the metric label appears, regardless of truncation state.
workflow integration: silent truncation misidentification is highest risk when multiple entities have similar names (Congo vs. Democratic Republic of the Congo vs. Republic of the Congo; Korea Republic vs. Korea Democratic People's Republic).

pattern 59: the action distance problem
surface: a user identifies an anomaly in a data cell. to investigate, they must: (1) note the country, metric, and year, (2) navigate to the source panel, (3) search for the specific data point, (4) find the source record, (5) open the methodology link. five steps from anomaly to investigation.
structural: the interface treats investigation and browsing as separate modes, with investigation tools located outside the browsing context.
root: investigation workflows were designed as standalone features (a data quality tool, a source explorer), not as contextual extensions of the browsing experience. connecting browsing to investigation requires manual context transfer (the user carries the coordinates from one context to another).
interface rule: every data cell must carry its full investigation context as a right-click or long-press contextual menu: "investigate this data point" → opens investigation panel pre-loaded with this exact data point's source record, revision history, conflict analysis, and provenance depth. the user does not manually copy coordinates. the investigation context is attached to the data object, not to the page position.
workflow integration: action distance is highest in exploratory analysis where the user is scanning many data points quickly and must be able to investigate anomalies without losing their scanning position in the table.

pattern 60: the misleading aggregation
surface: a user selects "Sub-Saharan Africa" and views an average GDP per capita of $2,100. they use this to characterize the region. but the average is mean, not median — it is heavily pulled by South Africa and Nigeria — and it excludes the continent's five highest-population countries for which data is missing.
structural: aggregation operations (mean, sum, count) are applied to available data without surfacing: (a) which aggregation method was used, (b) which entities were included, (c) which entities were excluded due to missing data, (d) how the included set relates to the intended geographic scope.
root: aggregation is treated as a mathematical operation, not as a representational claim. the interface presents the result as "the value for Sub-Saharan Africa" rather than "the mean of the N countries in Sub-Saharan Africa for which data is available."
interface rule: every aggregated regional/group value must be accompanied by: aggregation method (mean/median/weighted mean/sum — always shown, never defaulted to unmarked), coverage count (N of M countries in this region included in the calculation — always shown), missing count and names (click to expand list of excluded countries and reason for exclusion), and for population-weighted or GDP-weighted aggregates, the weights used and their source. the result is never presented as "the value for [region]" but always as "[aggregation method] of N countries in [region]."
workflow integration: misleading aggregation is highest risk in policy and advocacy contexts where regional characterizations are used to support arguments — and where the excluded entities are often the ones where the argument is weakest.

pattern 61: the drilldown hierarchy termination
