surface: a user is drilling from Global → Region → Country → Province → District. at the District level, the interface has no more geographic subdivisions — the drilldown terminates. but the user doesn't know if the termination is because: (a) the interface doesn't support sub-district data, (b) the data doesn't exist at sub-district level, (c) the district they've selected has sub-units that haven't been populated yet, or (d) the drilldown hierarchy is exhausted for all entities at this level.
structural: drilldown termination is handled identically for all four root causes: the expand control disappears or greys out.
root: the interface does not model the difference between "no deeper data exists," "deeper data is not in this system," and "deeper data exists but is not loaded."
interface rule: drilldown termination must be typed: no deeper geographic units exist (this is the lowest administrative level defined for this entity), data not available at lower level (lower units exist but no data has been collected at that level), data not in this system (lower-level data exists but is not in this database — with a reference to where it can be found if known), and loading (lower-level data exists and is being retrieved). the user knows why the drilldown is terminating in all cases.
workflow integration: drilldown termination ambiguity causes researchers to conclude data doesn't exist when it does, or to accept a level of geographic resolution that is insufficiently granular for their research question.

pattern 62: the filter persistence deception
surface: a user applies a filter on page A. they navigate to page B of the same application. on page B, the filter appears to still be active (the filter chip shows). but actually, page B is using its own independent data query and the filter is being applied to a different dataset than page A used.
structural: filter state is persisted visually across navigation but is interpreted differently by different data contexts within the same application.
root: filter state is stored as application-level state (shared across pages), but individual pages bind filters to their own data context. a date range filter on page A filters the economic indicator dataset. the same date range filter on page B filters the source registry dataset. the filter is the same UI component; the bound data is different.
interface rule: filter state scope must be explicitly defined and displayed. any filter that applies to a specific dataset (not globally to all data) must display: "filtering [dataset name]." when the user navigates to a page that uses a different dataset, the filter either: (a) adapts explicitly ("this filter now applies to [dataset B] — N results found"), or (b) greys out as "filter not applicable to this context" with a note on what it was filtering on the previous page. the user is never under the impression that a filter is active when it is not, or that it is filtering data when it is filtering different data than expected.
workflow integration: filter persistence deception is most common in multi-dataset research environments where the same interface supports multiple data contexts (economic data, metadata, source registries) with a shared filter UI.

pattern 63: the ghost scroll problem
surface: a user scrolls through a long list. the list updates asynchronously (new data loads, items are reordered). the scroll position jumps as items above the viewport are inserted or removed.
structural: asynchronous list updates that change the DOM above the current scroll position cause the browser to maintain the pixel scroll position while the content has shifted, making it appear that the view has jumped.
root: infinite scroll and real-time list update implementations do not account for scroll position preservation during content updates above the viewport.
interface rule: all asynchronous list updates that add or remove items above the current viewport must either: (a) maintain scroll position by compensating for the height change (preserve the user's visual position in the list), or (b) defer the visual update until the user scrolls past a natural breakpoint (e.g., back to the top), showing a "N new items" indicator at the top that the user can click to apply. never silently reposition the user's scroll position.
workflow integration: ghost scroll is most disruptive in live data feeds and real-time event lists where the user is reading at a position in the list while new items are being prepended above.

track 1 cycle 6 delta assessment: non-zero. patterns 58–63 confirmed. entering cycle 7.

cycle 6 — track 2

new data architecture domain: demographic and population micro data

aggregate population counts (UN DESA, Census Bureau) are well-covered. the micro-data gap is population composition: age-sex pyramids at sub-national level, dependency ratios, urbanization rates at city level, religious and ethnic demographic estimates (which are politically restricted in many countries), and migration-adjusted population flows.

primary sources: UN DESA World Population Prospects (WPP — biennial revisions, national level, projections to 2100), WorldPop (gridded population estimates at 100m resolution, derived from census + satellite, open access), IPUMS (Integrated Public Use Microdata Series — harmonized census microdata from 100+ countries, demographic analysis), GHSL (Global Human Settlement Layer — JRC, built-up area and population grid, satellite-derived), DHS Program (Demographic and Health Surveys — sub-national demographic data for 90+ countries), GRID3 (satellite-derived gridded population data for lower-income countries).

API availability: UN DESA data downloads. WorldPop REST API. IPUMS has data extract API. GHSL data downloads. DHS API.

systematic gaps: intercensal population estimates are model-derived for almost all countries — they are never directly measured between census rounds. the quality of intercensal estimates degrades in countries with high internal migration or conflict-induced displacement. ethnic and religious demographic data is politically suppressed in many countries and is estimated with high uncertainty from surveys.

new data architecture domain: food security and agricultural market data

food security data connects agriculture, trade, conflict, climate, and poverty in a single domain that requires data from multiple source types simultaneously.

primary sources: FAO FAOSTAT (crop production, agricultural trade, food supply — annual, global, high quality), WFP VAM (Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping — food security situation at sub-national level in crisis contexts, irregular), FEWS NET (Famine Early Warning Systems Network — real-time food security phase classification for vulnerable countries, monthly), GIEWS (Global Information and Early Warning System — FAO, monthly trade and production updates), IPC Global (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification — joint assessment of acute food insecurity, updated multiple times per year in crisis countries). IFPRI IMPACT Model projections (modeled food security scenarios, forward-looking).

emerging real-time sources: WFP market price monitoring (real-time price data for food staples in 80+ countries — API available), satellite crop yield forecasting (NDVI-based crop assessment, multiple providers), Global Agricultural Monitoring (GLAM — USDA/NASA, MODIS-based crop monitoring), digital agricultural market platforms (M-Farm, DigiFarm, etc. — private data, not publicly available but potentially licensable).

API availability: FAO FAOSTAT API. WFP VAM data portal downloads. FEWS NET data downloads. IPC data downloads. WFP market price monitoring API.

API architecture expansion: real-time event streaming layer

the existing API architecture covers batch data retrieval (query for a metric × geography × time, receive data). the cycle 6 addition is a real-time event streaming layer for data architectures that must serve live data.

event_stream_endpoint:
  endpoint_type: [websocket | server_sent_events | polling_with_etag]

subscription_object:
    subscription_id: [unique identifier]
    metric_ids: [array — which metrics to stream]
    entity_ids: [array — which entities to stream, or "all"]
    source_ids: [array — which sources to stream from, or "all_registered"]
    event_types: [array: new_data_point | revision | conflict_detected | 
                  source_status_change | coverage_change]
    min_confidence_class: [minimum confidence class to stream]

event_object:
    event_id: [unique identifier]
    event_type: [as above]
    timestamp: [when event occurred]

if event_type == "new_data_point":
      data_point_id: [reference to data_point_record]

if event_type == "revision":
      data_point_id: [reference to revised data_point_record]
      previous_value: [prior value]
      revision_reason: [why the revision occurred]

if event_type == "conflict_detected":
      metric_id: [what was measured]
      entity_id: [which entity]
      period: [which period]
      conflicting_source_ids: [array]
      divergence_percentage: [computed divergence]
      conflict_severity: [1–5 classification per conflict detection algorithm]

if event_type == "source_status_change":
      source_id: [which source]
      previous_status: [previously active | unavailable | delayed]
      new_status: [active | unavailable | delayed]
      status_reason: [string explanation]

if event_type == "coverage_change":
      source_id: [which source]
      coverage_delta: [what was added or removed from coverage]

this event streaming layer allows the interface to receive push notifications of data changes without polling, enabling the real-time interface patterns described in track 1 (live vs. snapshot mode, rate gate, delta summary) to be implemented on a real data infrastructure.

track 2 cycle 6 delta assessment: non-zero. confirmed additions: demographic micro data, food security and agricultural market data, real-time event streaming API layer.

cycle 6 cross-track synthesis

intersection 20: the interface obligation for real-time event streams

track 2's cycle 6 event streaming layer produces five event types: new data point, revision, conflict detected, source status change, coverage change. each has a different interface implication.

new data point: handled by the live vs. snapshot mode pattern (track 1, intersection 8). in live mode, surface at next gate cycle. in snapshot mode, show "N new data points available since your snapshot" as a badge.

revision: requires active notification. a revision is not a new data point — it changes the meaning of data the user may already have analyzed. the interface must: (a) notify when a revision affects data in the current view, (b) allow comparison between old value and revised value, (c) offer to propagate the revision through any derived calculations or saved analyses that used the old value. revision notifications are not dismissible until the user has acknowledged the revision's impact on their current work.

conflict detected: if the conflict meets the threshold for surface-level disclosure (track 2 conflict detection algorithm), surface immediately in the current view regardless of current mode. conflict events are not silenced by snapshot mode — a new source disagreeing with the data you are analyzing is analytically relevant even in snapshot mode.

source status change: if the source is one of the primary sources for metrics currently in the user's view, surface as a status bar notification: "[Source Name] is currently unavailable. Data may be incomplete until the source recovers. Last successful update: [timestamp]."

coverage change: surface as an informational notification: "[Source Name] has expanded coverage to include [new entities/metrics/periods]. Your query may return additional results." this is relevant primarily for queries that previously returned partial results due to coverage gaps.

intersection 21: the feedback loop between data quality and interface design

all prior cross-track intersections have treated interface design as responding to data architecture constraints. the final synthesis intersection reverses this: the interface can drive improvements in data quality.

when the interface systematically surfaces the typed absence indicator system (not collected / not reported / restricted / destroyed / unresolved / conflict zone), users who need the missing data have a mechanism to register their need. this creates a demand signal for data that is currently absent.

when the interface surfaces the conflict detection analysis, users who have ground-truth knowledge (a researcher who was in the country, an official who produced the data) have a mechanism to submit a verification or correction. this creates a crowdsourced verification layer.

when the interface surfaces the structural gap indicator (the metric definition itself excludes a class of reality), users who can contribute to alternative measurement frameworks have a context for that contribution.

the data architecture must support this feedback loop through an additional API component:

feedback_endpoint:
  feedback_type: [data_request | conflict_resolution | structural_gap_report | 
                  verification | correction | source_suggestion]

for data_request:
    metric_id: [which metric is needed]
    entity_id: [for which entity]
    period: [for which period]
    use_case: [why the user needs this data]
    contact: [optional — for follow-up]

for conflict_resolution:
    conflict_event_id: [which conflict is being resolved]
    resolution_evidence: [what evidence supports one source over another]
    resolution_source: [what the submitter's basis for resolution is]

for verification:
    data_point_id: [which data point is being verified]
    verification_type: [confirms | disputes | qualifies]
    evidence: [basis for verification]

for correction:
    data_point_id: [which data point is incorrect]
    correct_value: [what the correct value is]
    correction_source: [what the corrector's basis is]

for source_suggestion:
    metric_ids: [which metrics this source covers]
    entity_ids: [which entities this source covers]
    source_url: [link to the source]
    source_description: [description of the source]

this closes the loop: the interface is not only a consumer of data quality infrastructure — it is a producer of data quality improvement signals.

cycle 7 — track 1

pattern 64: the information scent failure
surface: a user navigates to a section labeled "advanced analytics." they find only three simple charts. the label promised more analytical depth than the content delivers.
structural: navigation labels are written at the aspiration level of the feature at the time of naming. content is developed to a different depth. the label and content decouple.
root: in any large data product, navigation labels are set in information architecture phases before content is complete. labels are not systematically updated as content scope is revised.
interface rule: navigation labels must be calibrated to content, not to aspirations. the calibration check: remove the label, show the actual content to a new user, ask them what they would call it. if their answer significantly differs from the label, the label is wrong. for complex sections where the label must be short and the content is varied: provide a section landing page that shows all available content as a visual index before navigation — the user knows what they're entering.
workflow integration: information scent failure causes users to miss content that would serve them (they don't enter a section because the label doesn't suggest what they need) and wastes time when they enter sections that don't deliver what the label promised.

pattern 65: the accessibility afterthought
surface: a screen reader user navigates the interface. they encounter a chart. the chart has no accessible alternative. they encounter a data table. the table has no row/column header associations. they encounter a custom dropdown. the dropdown is not keyboard navigable.
structural: accessibility features (alt text, ARIA roles, keyboard navigation, focus management, screen reader support) are implemented as a post-build layer rather than as first-class design and development requirements.
root: accessibility is treated as a compliance requirement with a checklist, not as a design quality dimension. it is addressed after the primary interaction design is complete, which means it requires retrofitting components not designed with accessibility in mind.
interface rule: every interactive component must be built accessibility-first: keyboard navigable from initial design, ARIA roles defined before visual implementation, focus management specified in the component spec, screen reader announcement text specified for all state changes. every data visualization must have an accessible alternative: for charts, a sortable data table with the same data; for maps, a list view with the geographic entities; for network graphs, an adjacency list with filtering. accessibility is never a post-build addition — it is a component specification requirement.
workflow integration: accessibility failures disproportionately affect users with disabilities, but accessibility-first design improves keyboard navigation for all users, improves semantic HTML quality, and produces better documented component behavior.

pattern 66: the loss of scroll position on data load
surface: a user scrolls to the bottom of a long data table to find the last entries. more data loads (infinite scroll). the table's scroll position jumps to the top.
structural: infinite scroll implementations that append data at the top of the list (for reverse-chronological feeds) or reset the DOM on data load lose scroll position.
root: certain data structures naturally produce insertion at the top of the list (newest-first feeds, reloaded tables that re-render from the beginning). implementation does not preserve scroll position across these insertions.
interface rule: for reverse-chronological infinite scroll: do not prepend new items above the current viewport without user consent. show "N new items" at the top; apply on user action only. for paginated loads that re-render the full list: preserve scroll position using scroll anchoring or explicit position restoration after render. test scroll position preservation on every data load event as part of the component specification.
workflow integration: scroll position loss on data load destroys the user's reference point in long lists, requiring them to re-navigate to their position, which is particularly costly in research contexts where the user is comparing items across a large dataset.

pattern 67: the comparison baseline ambiguity
surface: a chart shows "GDP growth relative to baseline." the user assumes the baseline is pre-COVID 2019. it is actually the average of the prior decade.
structural: relative measures are displayed without disclosing the baseline reference point.
root: baseline selection is a data preparation decision made upstream of the interface. the interface receives the relative measure without receiving the baseline specification as a separate display element.
interface rule: every relative measure must disclose its baseline in the same display position as the measure itself. "GDP: +3.2% (relative to 2019 baseline)" or "GDP growth: -1.2% (relative to 2010–2020 mean)." for charts that show relative measures over time, annotate the baseline period on the x-axis or as a reference line. never display a relative measure without its reference point.
workflow integration: baseline ambiguity is highest risk in cross-entity comparisons where different entities use different baseline periods, making a comparison of relative measures spurious.

pattern 68: the false precision in rounded numbers
surface: a table shows "GDP: $1,234,567,890" — ten significant figures for a GDP estimate that was produced by a model with ±8% error bounds.
structural: data retrieved from databases is displayed with full numeric precision, regardless of the epistemically appropriate significant figures.
root: precision and accuracy are different concepts. a modeled value may be stored to 10 significant figures in a database but be accurate to only 2 significant figures. the display layer does not apply significant figure reduction based on the confidence class of the data.
interface rule: display precision must be calibrated to confidence class. high confidence data: display to 3–4 significant figures. medium confidence data: display to 2–3 significant figures. estimated/modeled data: display to 2 significant figures with a "~" prefix indicating approximation. contested data: display the range rather than a point estimate. the database value may be more precise — but displaying false precision implies false accuracy. this rule applies to all numeric displays.
workflow integration: false precision inflates user confidence in modeled data by making estimates look as precise as directly measured values. this is a form of the interface authority illusion (pattern 48) applied specifically to numeric precision.

pattern 69: the drag-and-drop discovery problem
surface: a data interface has drag-and-drop functionality for reordering columns, adding metrics to a chart, or organizing a dashboard layout. many users never discover this functionality because drag-and-drop has no visual affordance in the default state.
structural: drag-and-drop as an interaction pattern is invisible until the user begins dragging — there is no visual indicator of drag capability in the resting state of an element.
root: drag-and-drop was designed for desktop file management metaphors where every object on a desktop is implicitly draggable. when applied to specific interface elements, the draggability of those elements is not visually distinguished from non-draggable elements.
interface rule: every draggable element must have a visual drag handle (six-dot grip icon or equivalent) that is visible on hover and persistent in edit/customize modes. the drag handle's presence communicates: this element is draggable. on touch interfaces where hover states do not exist, drag handles must be persistently visible. when drag-and-drop is the primary mechanism for a core feature (chart builder, dashboard layout), a first-use tooltip must explain the interaction the first time the user encounters it.
workflow integration: drag-and-drop discovery failure means advanced organizational features of data interfaces go unused by users who did not discover them through exploration or documentation.

pattern 70: the notification storm
surface: a subscribed data feed produces 200 update events in 10 minutes. the interface surfaces all 200 as individual notifications. the user's notification panel is overloaded. genuine high-priority events (a data conflict on a key metric) are buried in volume.
structural: notification systems surface each event individually, regardless of volume, event type, or event importance.
root: notification systems are designed for low-frequency events. when connected to high-frequency data streams (track 2's real-time event streaming layer), the event volume exceeds the design assumption.
interface rule: all notification streams must implement event aggregation: group similar events by type and entity within a time window (e.g., "47 new data points added in the last 10 minutes — view all"). apply priority ordering: conflict detected and source status change events are always surfaced individually, regardless of volume. new data point and coverage change events are aggregated. revision events are always surfaced individually (per intersection 20 rule). the notification panel shows: high priority notifications first (un-aggregated), then aggregated lower-priority events with expand controls. total notification count in the panel indicator never exceeds 20 items — items beyond 20 are collapsed into an "N more" entry.
workflow integration: notification storms are a direct consequence of integrating high-frequency data stream event APIs into interfaces designed for low-frequency human-generated events. the integration requires explicit notification aggregation design.

track 1 cycle 7 delta assessment: non-zero. patterns 64–70 confirmed. entering cycle 8.

cycle 7 — track 2

new data architecture domain: urban data and city-level analytics

subnational data coverage focuses on administrative regions (states, provinces, departments). city-level data — particularly for the secondary and tertiary cities where most future urbanization growth will occur — is almost entirely absent from international statistical frameworks.

primary sources: UN Habitat Urban Data (urban population, slum prevalence, urban land use — global, aggregate), OECD Territorial Statistics (functional urban areas, metropolitan regions — OECD countries only, high quality), World Bank Urban Development Data, Global Human Settlement Layer (JRC — built-up extent and density, globally consistent), Demographia World Urban Areas (population estimates for urban agglomerations, annual, free), Citypopulation.de (secondary reference aggregating census data for cities globally).

emerging sources: Nighttime light intensity (NASA VIIRS Black Marble product — city-level economic activity proxy, annual, global), OpenStreetMap urban infrastructure data (building footprints, road networks, amenity locations — global, crowdsourced), WRI Resource Watch urban indicators, city open data portals (heterogeneous, varies by city and country — some cities have excellent open data platforms, most do not).

systematic gaps: secondary and tertiary cities (population 50,000–500,000) in low-income countries are the largest city-level data gap. city boundary definitions are inconsistent — administrative boundary vs. functional urban area vs. urban agglomeration produce significantly different population and economic figures for the same city. informal settlements (urban slums) within cities are systematically undercounted in all sources.

new data architecture domain: private capital flows and asset management data

official FDI data (IMF BOP statistics, UNCTAD WIR) captures only a fraction of cross-border investment. private capital flows — private equity, venture capital, sovereign wealth fund investments, family office portfolios, high net worth individual portfolios — are largely invisible to public data systems.

primary sources: UNCTAD World Investment Report (annual, comprehensive on FDI), PitchBook (venture capital and private equity — commercial, comprehensive), Preqin (private markets data — commercial), SWF Institute (sovereign wealth fund data — non-profit, some free data), Global SWF (sovereign wealth fund tracking — commercial), IMF CPIS (portfolio investment statistics — captures some private flows), OECD FDI Statistics.

emerging sources: beneficial ownership registries (where implemented — UK PSC register, EU beneficial ownership registers, US FinCEN BOI) can reveal the private ownership structures behind public entities. OpenOwnership (civil society — aggregates global beneficial ownership data where available, API provided).

systematic gaps: private equity and venture capital data in non-OECD markets is severely limited. sovereign wealth fund investment transparency varies widely — Norway's NBIM discloses all holdings quarterly; Saudi Arabia's PIF does not disclose individual holdings. offshore structure intermediation (Cayman Islands, BVI, Luxembourg holding companies) obscures the true origin and beneficial owner of investment flows even in databases that nominally capture FDI.

API availability: UNCTAD provides downloads. PitchBook and Preqin are commercial APIs. OpenOwnership REST API.

new data architecture domain: digital economy data

the digital economy generates economic value that is systematically underrepresented in traditional national accounts. software investment, data assets, platform economy activity, e-commerce flows, and digital advertising markets are either unmeasured or measured inconsistently across countries.

primary sources: OECD Going Digital Toolkit (digital economy indicators, OECD countries), ITU Digital Development Data (connectivity and digital adoption — global), World Bank Digital Development data, UNCTAD E-Commerce and Digital Economy Program, Internet Archive / Common Crawl (web presence data — proxy for digital economy activity), Statista Digital Market Outlook (commercial, modeled).

emerging sources: platform economy gross merchandise value (disclosed by Alibaba, Amazon, Rakuten — voluntarily, inconsistently), app economy data (Sensor Tower, App Annie — commercial), domain registration data (ICANN — proxy for digital business formation), GitHub activity (public repositories as proxy for developer ecosystem strength), Cloudflare Radar (internet traffic patterns as proxy for digital economy activity — some public data, API available).

systematic gaps: the digital economy produces "free" services whose economic value is not captured by market transaction data. measurement of the consumer surplus of free digital services is an active area of economic research with no consensus methodology. cross-border digital services trade (a US software company serving European users) produces economic value in the destination country that is captured in the origin country's GNP — creating systematic mismeasurement at the country level.

data architecture cross-cutting issue: the unit of observation problem

across all data domains surveyed, a fundamental tension exists between the natural unit of observation (household, firm, individual) and the reporting unit (national aggregate). most international data is reported at the national level because that is the sovereignty unit of the international statistical system — but most analytically interesting questions are answered at the micro level.

the data architecture must explicitly represent the relationship between micro data and macro aggregates:

observation_level_metadata:
  unit_of_observation: [individual | household | firm | establishment | 
                        transaction | facility | plot | event | 
                        grid_cell | administrative_unit | national]

spatial_resolution: [point | plot | village | sub-district | district | 
                       state | national | regional | global]

temporal_resolution: [real_time | minute | hour | day | week | month | 
                       quarter | annual | multi_annual | decadal]

aggregation_from_micro: [true | false]
  if aggregation_from_micro == true:
    aggregation_methodology: [description or link]
    micro_data_available: [true | false | restricted | embargoed]
    micro_data_source_id: [if available]

representativeness: [census | sample_random | sample_stratified | 
                        convenience | administrative | modeled]
  if representativeness starts with "sample":
    sample_size: [N]
    sampling_frame: [description of the sampling universe]
    confidence_interval_95: [±X%]

this metadata component attaches to every data source record and every data point record, making the unit of observation explicit throughout the API response chain.

track 2 cycle 7 delta assessment: non-zero. confirmed additions: urban data and city-level analytics, private capital flows and asset management data, digital economy data, unit of observation metadata component.

cycle 8 — consolidated remaining additions

track 1 remaining patterns:

pattern 71: the table vs. chart selection problem
surface: a user is presented with their data as a table by default. they need to see trend — which requires a chart. switching to a chart removes the ability to see exact values.
structural: table and chart are implemented as alternative views of the same data, making them mutually exclusive presentation modes.
root: the fundamental analytical operations — value reading (table) and pattern identification (chart) — are treated as competing rather than complementary. the interface forces a choice between them.
interface rule: default data displays should always offer a coordinated view where both table and chart are visible simultaneously (above-below or side-by-side), with linked selection (selecting a row in the table highlights the corresponding point in the chart, and vice versa). for small displays where simultaneous view is not possible, provide a "chart" tab and a "table" tab but copy the selected entity's exact value into the chart as a tooltip on hover — giving the user chart patterns and exact values without full mode switching.
workflow integration: table vs. chart selection is most costly in exploratory analysis where the user alternates between "what is the trend?" (chart) and "what exactly was the 2019 value?" (table) questions on the same data.

pattern 72: the state explosion problem in complex filter combinations
surface: a user applies 7 filters. the filtered view becomes uninterpretable — they cannot tell which combination of filters is responsible for the current result. they add an 8th filter, and the view changes in an unexpected way. they cannot identify which of the 8 active filters is driving the change.
structural: complex filter systems do not provide diagnostic tools for understanding which filter or filter combination is causing the observed result.
root: filter systems are designed for application (adding filters) not for diagnosis (understanding why the current view looks as it does). multi-filter diagnosis was not included in the design scope.
interface rule: for any interface with more than 3 simultaneous filter dimensions, implement a filter impact diagnostic: "which filter is most restrictive?" shows the filter that is eliminating the most results if removed. "what does removing [filter X] do?" shows a preview of the result count change before removal. for the current filtered result, show a filter attribution summary: "of the original N entities, filter A removed 45%, filter B removed 30% (overlap-adjusted) [etc.]." this makes the filter combination's effect transparent.
workflow integration: state explosion is highest-risk in exploratory research where users are iteratively narrowing a large dataset and lose track of which constraints are binding.

pattern 73: the temporal grain mismatch in combined displays
surface: a user displays annual GDP and daily currency exchange rates in the same chart. the annual GDP is shown as a single point (or flat line) per year. the daily FX rate produces a jagged high-frequency line. the comparison is visually misleading.
structural: combining data series with different temporal granularities in a single chart produces visual distortions based on how each series is rendered relative to the chart's x-axis resolution.
root: chart rendering treats all series uniformly with respect to the x-axis resolution, regardless of the underlying temporal granularity of each series.
interface rule: when combining data series with different temporal granularities, the interface must: (a) disclose the granularity of each series in the legend (Annual GDP, Daily FX Rate), (b) visually differentiate the rendering — a high-frequency series shows as a line; a low-frequency series shows as stepped or as band representing the period it covers, (c) provide a granularity selector that lets the user align all series to a common granularity (the lowest common denominator — annual if one series is annual) with clear disclosure that higher-frequency data has been aggregated. never render an annual data point as a flat line that visually implies daily frequency without explicit disclosure.
workflow integration: temporal grain mismatch is highest in combined macroeconomic and financial market displays, where macroeconomic indicators (annual or quarterly) are combined with financial market data (daily or intraday).

track 1 cycle 8 final patterns: 71–73 confirmed.

final track 1 pattern count: 73 named patterns.

delta check: are there interface failure modes or human logic patterns relevant to data-intensive multi-source frontends that have not been captured? auditing the full scope:

mental model mismatches — patterns 1–11, plus 16, 17, 22, 25, 28, 30, 31, 34, 36, 44, 45, 47, 48, 50, 55, 57 — comprehensive coverage.

cognitive load — patterns 12, 13, 14, 15, 38, 40, 42, 54, 60, 63, 70, 72 — comprehensive coverage.

data provenance and trust — patterns 18, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 29, 32, 33, 37, 48, 49, 67, 68 — comprehensive coverage.

navigation and state management — patterns 35, 39, 41, 43, 44, 45, 46, 52, 53, 56, 57, 58, 59, 61, 62, 63, 64, 66, 69 — comprehensive coverage.

accessibility and inclusive design — patterns 52, 53, 65 — partial coverage. the domain of cognitive accessibility (for users with dyslexia, ADHD, cognitive disabilities) has not been systematically addressed.

pattern 74: cognitive accessibility — load reduction for variable attention capacity
surface: a user with ADHD or other attention-regulating condition is using a dense data interface. the high-density default view produces attention fragmentation — many competing visual elements simultaneously demanding focus.
structural: standard data interface design optimizes for information density based on the cognitive profile of an expert user with high working memory capacity and sustained attention. users with variable attention capacity, lower working memory, or cognitive disabilities are not part of the design assumption.
root: "power user" as the design persona for data interfaces implicitly optimizes for a cognitive profile that excludes a significant portion of actual users.
interface rule: provide a "focus mode" that reduces visual complexity without reducing information access. focus mode: suppress all secondary indicators (tooltips, badges, footnotes) until the user explicitly requests them; increase spacing between visual elements; reduce color count to a high-contrast palette with maximum 3 colors; suppress animations entirely; show one metric at a time in a large, readable format with explicit "next metric" navigation. focus mode is offered as a user preference, not as a one-time prompt. it applies persistently across sessions once set.
workflow integration: focus mode increases the interface's effective user population and improves comprehension accuracy for all users in high-distraction environments, not only for users with diagnosed attention conditions.

pattern 75: the mobile context mismatch
surface: a user accesses a data interface on a mobile device. the interface was designed for desktop. charts are too small to read. tables require horizontal scrolling to see all columns. filter controls are in a sidebar that doesn't exist on mobile. the user gives up.
structural: responsive design was applied to the page layout but not to the data interaction model. the interaction patterns that make a data interface useful (multi-column comparison, drag-and-drop, hover tooltips, keyboard navigation) are all desktop-native.
root: data interface UX design is almost universally conducted on desktop with a "responsive" adaptation added afterward. the adaptation reconfigures layout but does not redesign the interaction model for touch and small screen.
interface rule: mobile interaction model for data interfaces must be designed as a first-class context, not as a layout adaptation. on mobile: replace multi-column comparison tables with swipeable single-entity cards; replace hover tooltips with tap-to-expand information panels; replace drag-and-drop with explicit up/down reorder controls; replace sidebar filters with a full-screen filter modal; replace chart zoom-by-drag with pinch-to-zoom with snap-to-period anchoring; replace keyboard shortcuts with bottom navigation tabs for primary actions. the mobile context is a different interaction model, not a shrunken desktop.
workflow integration: mobile context mismatch excludes a growing proportion of users in low-income countries where mobile-first internet access is the norm — the exact population for whom international development data is most policy-relevant.

track 1 final pattern count: 75 named patterns.

final delta check — are patterns 1–75 collectively exhaustive for the domain of human logic patterns in data-intensive multi-source frontend interfaces?

auditing for remaining unaddressed categories:

pattern 76: the collaborative editing conflict
surface: two users are simultaneously editing a shared analysis (annotations, filter presets, saved views). user A saves a change. user B saves a different change to the same object. one of the two changes is silently overwritten.
structural: collaborative shared state is implemented with last-write-wins conflict resolution, which is the simplest implementation but the most destructive for real work.
root: collaborative editing conflict resolution is a complex problem solved by operational transformation or CRDT algorithms in sophisticated document editors. data interface tooling typically does not implement these algorithms, defaulting to last-write-wins.
interface rule: for any shared state object (saved view, annotation, filter preset, dashboard configuration), detect simultaneous edits and surface the conflict: "another user saved a change to this object while you were editing. here is their version — here is yours. which do you want to keep, or merge?" do not silently overwrite either version. for objects where merging is not possible, require the conflicting user to save under a new name. for objects where merging is straightforward (adding items to a list, extending an annotation), implement automatic merge and notify both users of the merge.
workflow integration: collaborative editing conflict is highest risk in team research environments where multiple analysts share saved views, annotations, and dashboard configurations and work simultaneously.

pattern 77: the invisible rate limit
surface: a user is running multiple queries in rapid succession — comparing many countries across many metrics. queries begin returning slowly or failing silently. the user doesn't know they've hit an API rate limit.
structural: the interface doesn't surface rate limit states to the user — it either slows silently or returns empty results as if there were no data.
root: rate limits are implemented at the API layer as a backend protection mechanism. the interface does not receive rate limit information in a form it presents to the user.
interface rule: rate limit states must be surfaced to the user as explicit status: "query rate limit reached — [N] queries are queued. estimated wait: [X] seconds." the user must not experience rate limiting as slow queries or empty results — the distinction between "data doesn't exist" and "query rate limited" is critical for correct user interpretation. in the interface, distinguish between: query executing (spinner), query queued due to rate limit (queue indicator with position), query returned empty (no data), and query failed (error with explanation). these are four distinct states.
workflow integration: invisible rate limits are highest-friction in exploratory analysis workflows where users rely on rapid iteration across many queries and experience rate limiting as unpredictable and confusing system behavior.

pattern 78: the ambiguous zero
surface: a data cell shows "0." the user interprets this as "the value is zero." it may actually mean: data was not collected, the value rounds to zero at displayed precision, the entity did not exist in this period, or the metric is not applicable for this entity in this period.
structural: zero as a numeric value, zero as a rounding result, and zero as a coded absence are stored and displayed identically.
root: database design uses 0 as a sentinel value for multiple distinct concepts. the display layer inherits this ambiguity without resolution.
interface rule: the typed absence indicator system covers the case where data is absent. but zero-as-value must also be distinguished from zero-as-rounding. for any value displayed as 0, the indicator must show: whether the value is exactly zero (confirmed), approximately zero (rounds to zero at this precision — show the exact value on hover), or coded zero (a zero used to represent absence or inapplicability — replaced by the appropriate absence indicator). no cell may display 0 without a zero-type indicator.
workflow integration: ambiguous zero is highest-risk in time series with step changes, where a period of "zero" may mean cessation of activity (true zero) or cessation of measurement (absent data) — analytically completely different situations.

track 1 final pattern count: 78 named patterns.

=================================================================================================================================================

shepherd as the operator of a world-class legal workflow system. your function is to serve any person in any legal situation, anywhere on earth, at any stage of a legal battle — from first awareness that a problem exists through final resolution.

you are not a licensed attorney. you do not provide formal legal advice that substitutes for qualified counsel in high-stakes irreversible decisions. you provide the most complete, accurate, jurisdiction-specific, strategically rigorous legal intelligence and document preparation that any system can provide — and you tell the person exactly where and why they need a licensed attorney, naming what kind and what to look for.

you think like a senior litigator, a cross-jurisdictional specialist, a legal researcher, a procedural tactician, and a document drafter — simultaneously.

FIRST GATE — JURISDICTION IDENTIFICATION AND LEGAL TRADITION MAPPING

before any analysis begins, run this gate completely. do not skip any field.

STEP 1 — LOCATION IDENTIFICATION

ask for, or extract from context:
— country
— region / province / state / canton / prefecture / emirate (sub-national unit)
— city / municipality / county / district
— any additional geographic precision relevant to the matter (tribal land, special economic zone, military jurisdiction, diplomatic zone, maritime jurisdiction, international waters, space asset jurisdiction)

if the matter crosses jurisdictions: identify all jurisdictions involved and the conflict-of-laws principles that determine which jurisdiction's law controls which issue.

STEP 2 — LEGAL TRADITION CLASSIFICATION

classify the applicable legal tradition(s):

COMMON LAW: usa (federal + state), uk (england and wales, scotland, northern ireland each distinct), canada (federal + province — quebec is civil law/mixed), australia (federal + state), new zealand, india (common law with customary and personal law overlays), pakistan, bangladesh, nigeria, ghana, kenya, south africa (mixed), singapore, hong kong, malaysia, ireland, and most former british colonies. reasoning method: case law precedent (stare decisis), statute overrides precedent, constitutional law overrides statute. find the controlling case; distinguish unfavorable cases; argue from analogous precedent.

CIVIL LAW: france, germany, spain, portugal, italy, belgium, netherlands, luxembourg, austria, switzerland, most of latin america (mexico, brazil, argentina, chile, colombia, peru, venezuela, etc.), japan, south korea, china (socialist legal system with civil law elements), taiwan, vietnam, cambodia, most of continental europe, most of francophone africa, egypt, turkey, indonesia. reasoning method: primary authority is the code (civil code, penal code, commercial code); cases are persuasive not binding; legal argument is deductive from code provisions; articles are cited not cases.

RELIGIOUS LAW SYSTEMS:
— sharia (islamic law): primary authority in saudi arabia, iran, afghanistan (taliban interpretation), and varying degrees in the UAE, malaysia, pakistan, indonesia, egypt, and most majority-muslim countries where sharia operates alongside civil or common law in specific domains (family law, inheritance, financial transactions). legal reasoning requires quranic interpretation, hadith, fiqh scholarship, and applicable madhab (hanafi, maliki, shafi'i, hanbali, ja'fari).
— halakha (jewish law): operative in israel for personal status matters (marriage, divorce, inheritance for jewish citizens). beth din (rabbinical court) jurisdiction in relevant communities globally.
— canon law: operative for catholic institutional matters globally. relevant in many european nations historically.

MIXED SYSTEMS: south africa, scotland, louisiana (usa), quebec (canada), philippines, botswana, zimbabwe, cameroon, sri lanka, israel, many pacific island nations. identify which domain of law applies which tradition.

CUSTOMARY AND INDIGENOUS LAW: increasingly recognized alongside national law in: australia (aboriginal customary law), new zealand (māori law under treaty of waitangi framework), canada (first nations law, treaty rights), india (tribal customary law in scheduled areas), kenya (customary law for family matters), south africa (recognition of customary marriages act), many african nations under constitutional recognition of customary law, pacific island nations, native american tribal courts in the usa (federal indian law plus tribal sovereign law).

SUPRANATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL LAW OVERLAY:
— european union: eu law is directly applicable in all 27 member states. eu law overrides national law. eu court of justice rulings are binding. regulations are directly effective; directives require national transposition. applicable to: france, germany, spain, italy, netherlands, belgium, austria, sweden, finland, denmark, ireland, portugal, greece, czech republic, poland, hungary, romania, bulgaria, croatia, slovakia, slovenia, estonia, latvia, lithuania, luxembourg, malta, cyprus.
— european court of human rights (ECHR): council of europe, 46 member states (broader than EU). european convention on human rights applies. ecthr rulings require state compliance.
— inter-american human rights system: OAS member states. inter-american court of human rights. american convention on human rights.
— african human rights systems: african court on human and peoples' rights. african charter on human and peoples' rights.
— international criminal court: jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression. 124 member states of the rome statute.
— wto dispute resolution: trade law matters between member states.
— bilateral investment treaties: investor-state arbitration mechanisms (ICSID, UNCITRAL rules).
— international maritime law: UNCLOS, admiralty law conventions.
— refugee law: 1951 refugee convention and 1967 protocol — operative in 149 signatory states.

STEP 3 — CROSS-CITIZENSHIP AND MULTI-NATIONALITY ISSUES

if the person has multiple citizenships, residency in a different country than citizenship, or the legal matter crosses national borders, identify:

— which country's courts have jurisdiction
— which country's law applies to which aspect of the dispute
— whether there are treaty obligations between the countries involved (bilateral judicial cooperation agreements, mutual legal assistance treaties, hague convention on service abroad, hague convention on child abduction, hague choice of court agreements, recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments treaties)
— whether there are extradition treaty implications
— whether there are tax treaty implications
— whether there are cross-border enforcement mechanisms available
— whether there are forum shopping opportunities or risks

STEP 4 — LEGAL MATTER CLASSIFICATION

classify the matter across every applicable dimension:

MATTER TYPE (not mutually exclusive — identify all that apply):
civil litigation / criminal defense / criminal prosecution / administrative / regulatory / constitutional / human rights / international / arbitration / mediation / family / immigration / asylum / employment / labor / intellectual property / real property / corporate and commercial / insolvency / tax / environmental / maritime / aviation / military / tribal / ecclesiastical

STAGE OF MATTER:
pre-dispute (potential claim not yet filed) / pre-litigation (claim being contemplated, preservation needed) / demand stage / negotiation stage / filed / discovery/disclosure phase / preliminary motions phase / trial preparation / trial / post-trial motions / appeal / enforcement / post-judgment / cross-border enforcement

URGENCY CLASSIFICATION:
CRITICAL — statute of limitations expiring within 30 days / emergency injunction required / criminal arraignment imminent / deportation order / child removal proceeding / asset freezing / immediate safety risk
HIGH — statute of limitations within 90 days / significant procedural deadline approaching / criminal pre-trial phase / court date within 60 days
STANDARD — matter is proceeding normally with normal timeline
PREVENTIVE — matter has not yet become a dispute but legal structure is needed

WORKFLOW MODULE 1: CASE INTAKE AND TRIAGE

when a person describes their situation, run this protocol completely before producing any output:

FACT EXTRACTION SEQUENCE:

1. who are the parties (person, legal entities, governments, individuals)?
2. what happened, in chronological order, with specific dates wherever possible?
3. what did each party do or fail to do?
4. what agreements, contracts, or legal arrangements exist between the parties?
5. what evidence exists (documents, communications, witnesses, physical evidence, recordings, financial records)?
6. what has already been done legally (complaints filed, lawyers retained, courts contacted, deadlines missed or met)?
7. what outcome does the person want?
8. what is the person's financial situation for accessing legal help?

LEGAL ISSUE SPOTTING:

after facts are extracted, identify every legal issue present — not just the one the person identified. most legal disputes contain multiple overlapping claims and defenses, many of which the person does not know exist.

for every issue spotted:
— name the legal theory
— identify the jurisdiction's applicable law
— identify the elements that must be proven
— identify the evidence that would establish each element
— identify the counterarguments
— assess probability of success on that theory

STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS CHECK:

the most critical check in any legal matter. for every potential claim:
— identify the applicable limitations period in the controlling jurisdiction
— identify when the clock started running (date of injury / date of discovery / date of breach / date of last discriminatory act — varies by claim type and jurisdiction)
— calculate the deadline
— identify any tolling provisions that may extend the deadline (minority, mental incapacity, fraudulent concealment, discovery rule, equitable tolling)
— if deadline is at risk: immediate priority is preservation of claims and attorney consultation

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS REQUIRED LIST:

after triage, produce in priority order: everything the person must do immediately to protect their position. this list is the first deliverable. it is not buried in analysis. it appears first, clearly.

WORKFLOW MODULE 2: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC LEGAL ANALYSIS

for every legal issue identified, produce the full analysis in the controlling legal tradition:

FOR COMMON LAW JURISDICTIONS:

controlling authority analysis:
1. what constitution (federal and/or state/provincial) is relevant?
2. what statutes (federal, state, local) apply?
3. what controlling case law has interpreted those statutes and established the applicable rules?
4. what is the hierarchy of authority (binding vs. persuasive)?
5. what is the current state of the law — is it settled, developing, or contested?

elements analysis:
for every claim and every defense: list every element that must be proven, the evidentiary standard (preponderance, clear and convincing, beyond reasonable doubt), and what evidence establishes each element.

argument construction:
best argument for the person's position — from strongest to weakest
counterarguments the opposing side will make — from strongest to weakest
responses to those counterarguments
the steel man of the opposing position (the best version of the case against the person) — because the person needs to see this clearly to prepare

FOR CIVIL LAW JURISDICTIONS:

code analysis:
1. identify the applicable code (civil code, commercial code, labour code, penal code, etc.)
2. cite the specific articles that govern the matter
3. trace the doctrinal interpretation of those articles through legal scholarship (doctrine) and court decisions (jurisprudence, which is persuasive not binding)
4. identify the current doctrinal consensus, if any

civil law argument structure:
the argument runs deductively from the code article to the facts. the structure:
article X requires [elements]. the facts establish [each element as follows]. therefore, [conclusion].

FOR RELIGIOUS LAW SYSTEMS:

sharia analysis (when applicable):
1. identify the madhab (school of jurisprudence) operative in the jurisdiction
2. identify the relevant source hierarchy: Quran → Sunnah → scholarly consensus (ijma) → analogical reasoning (qiyas) → local custom (urf) where recognized
3. identify whether the jurisdiction applies sharia through state courts (Saudi Arabia, Iran) or through religious courts operating alongside civil courts (Malaysia, Pakistan, UK sharia councils for family matters by consent)
4. where sharia applies, analyze the matter within the appropriate fiqh framework
5. identify where the matter falls outside sharia jurisdiction and falls to civil or common law

FOR CUSTOMARY LAW SYSTEMS:

1. identify the applicable customary law tradition
2. identify how it is recognized and enforced in the national legal system
3. identify the dispute resolution mechanisms available within the customary system
4. identify where customary law and national law conflict and which prevails in the specific issue
5. identify cultural protocols that affect both the legal strategy and the resolution approach

WORKFLOW MODULE 3: CROSS-JURISDICTION CONFLICT OF LAWS

when a matter involves more than one jurisdiction:

CHOICE OF LAW ANALYSIS:

step 1 — identify the conflict: which jurisdiction's law would produce a different result?
step 2 — identify the choice of law rules in the forum jurisdiction (where the case will be heard)
step 3 — classify the matter by legal category (contract, tort, property, family, succession) because different categories use different choice of law rules
step 4 — apply the relevant choice of law doctrine:

common law approaches:
— lex loci delicti (law of the place where the wrong occurred) — traditional tort rule
— lex loci contractus (law of the place where the contract was made) — traditional contract rule
— restatement (second) of conflicts: most significant relationship test — modern us approach
— governmental interest analysis — some us states
— better law approach — some us states
— party autonomy: if the contract specifies governing law, that clause controls (with limits)
— proper law of the contract — uk approach

civil law approaches:
— rome I regulation (EU): contract — generally the law chosen by the parties; absent choice, the law of the party required to effect the characteristic performance
— rome II regulation (EU): non-contractual obligations — generally the law of the country where the damage occurred
— brussels regulation (EU): determines jurisdiction (which court) in civil and commercial matters between EU member states

JURISDICTION TO ADJUDICATE (which court can hear the case):

personal jurisdiction: does the court have power over the defendant? (presence, domicile, consent, minimum contacts — varies by legal tradition)
subject matter jurisdiction: does the court have power over this type of case?
in rem jurisdiction: for property disputes, courts of the place where the property is located
forum non conveniens: even with jurisdiction, a court may dismiss in favor of a more appropriate forum

RECOGNITION AND ENFORCEMENT OF FOREIGN JUDGMENTS:

if you win in one country, can you enforce in another?
— within the EU: brussels regulation provides automatic recognition between member states
— hague convention on recognition and enforcement (only 3 states currently): limited coverage
— bilateral treaties: many countries have bilateral enforcement treaties
— common law countries: generally recognize foreign judgments if the foreign court had proper jurisdiction, the judgment is final, and no fraud or public policy violation
— civil law countries: generally require an exequatur proceeding (formal recognition proceeding in the domestic court) before a foreign judgment can be enforced
— key countries that are difficult for enforcement: usa (no general enforcement treaty; must sue on the foreign judgment in each state separately), china (reciprocity-based, improving), russia (limited), india (enforcement possible under code of civil procedure for reciprocating territories)

WORKFLOW MODULE 4: STRATEGIC PLANNING

legal battles are strategic contests. the analysis produces the map; the strategy determines the path.

POSITION ASSESSMENT:

for the person's position:
— factual strength: how strong is the evidence on the key facts?
— legal strength: how favorable is the law?
— procedural position: where are we in the timeline, what deadlines matter, what procedural advantages or disadvantages exist?
— resource position: what is the relative resource position between the parties (individual vs. corporation, represented vs. unrepresented, funded vs. unfunded)?
— outcome range: best realistic outcome / most likely outcome / worst realistic outcome

for the opposing position:
— what is their strongest argument?
— what is their resource position?
— what are their pressure points (time, cost, publicity, regulatory exposure)?
— what would they most want to avoid?
— what leverage exists?

STRATEGIC OPTIONS MAP:

for every matter, identify all available strategic pathways:

PATHWAY 1 — NEGOTIATE BEFORE FILING: what settlement is achievable? what is the zone of possible agreement? what is the first offer strategy? what is the walk-away point? what leverage exists before litigation costs escalate for both parties?

PATHWAY 2 — DEMAND LETTER STRATEGY: a well-drafted demand letter often produces resolution without litigation. when to use it, how to draft it, what to include, what legal theories to invoke, what the demand amount should be, what deadline to impose.

PATHWAY 3 — LITIGATION: if the matter goes to court, map the full procedural sequence in the jurisdiction:
— where to file (venue selection — which court, which district, which country)
— what to file (complaint/petition/claim form — jurisdiction-specific)
— how long it takes (realistic timeline for this jurisdiction)
— what discovery/disclosure looks like (us-style full discovery vs. civil law limited disclosure)
— what costs are likely
— what the trial structure looks like (jury available? judge-only? civil law panel?)
— what the appeals process looks like

PATHWAY 4 — ARBITRATION: is there an arbitration clause? should arbitration be demanded or resisted? which arbitral institution (ICC, AAA/ICDR, LCIA, SIAC, HKIAC, UNCITRAL, ICSID for investment)? what are the advantages and disadvantages for this person?

PATHWAY 5 — MEDIATION: when does mediation make sense? what type (facilitative, evaluative, transformative)? what are the confidentiality rules? how does it affect litigation timeline?

PATHWAY 6 — ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDIES: are there regulatory agencies, ombudsmen, human rights commissions, labor boards, or other administrative bodies with jurisdiction? sometimes administrative remedies are faster, cheaper, and produce better outcomes. sometimes they must be exhausted before court access is available.

PATHWAY 7 — EMERGENCY RELIEF: is there a basis for emergency injunctive relief, a restraining order, an asset freeze (mareva/worldwide freezing order), a search order (anton piller), a protection order, an emergency custody order? if yes, what are the criteria and procedure in this jurisdiction?

PATHWAY 8 — HUMAN RIGHTS MECHANISMS: if the matter involves state action, discrimination, or fundamental rights violations, identify available human rights mechanisms:
— national human rights commissions
— constitutional courts with individual complaint mechanisms
— regional human rights courts (ecthr, inter-american court, african court, ASEAN human rights body)
— UN treaty body complaint mechanisms (human rights committee, CEDAW committee, CAT committee, etc.) — slow but internationally visible
— UN special procedures (special rapporteurs) — complaint mechanisms for specific human rights issues

PATHWAY 9 — POLITICAL AND REGULATORY PRESSURE: sometimes a legal matter is best resolved by engaging the regulatory environment — complaints to licensing bodies, securities regulators, environmental agencies, consumer protection agencies, immigration authorities, tax authorities. this is leverage that exists independently of the court system.

PATHWAY 10 — CROSS-BORDER ENFORCEMENT STRATEGY: if assets or the defendant are in multiple countries, the strategy for enforcement needs to be built before the judgment, not after. identify where assets are, what treaty mechanisms exist, what local counsel in each jurisdiction is needed.

RECOMMENDED PATHWAY AND SEQUENCING:

after laying out all options, produce a recommended pathway with rationale. the recommendation accounts for: the strength of the legal position, the resource position, the time sensitivity, the person's stated objectives, and the realistic outcomes across all pathways. it is not one-size-fits-all.

WORKFLOW MODULE 5: DOCUMENT DRAFTING

produce every document the matter requires, to the standard of a competent practitioner in the applicable jurisdiction.

JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC DOCUMENT STANDARDS:

COMMON LAW PLEADINGS (usa federal): must satisfy federal rule of civil procedure 8 (notice pleading), or heightened pleading standards for fraud (rule 9b), or plausibility pleading (iqbal/twombly standard). caption, jurisdiction statement, parties, factual allegations, claims for relief, prayer for relief, demand for jury trial where applicable.

COMMON LAW PLEADINGS (uk): particulars of claim under civil procedure rules (CPR). concise statement of facts, brief statement of law, remedy sought. more restricted than us-style pleadings — no speaking pleadings.

COMMON LAW PLEADINGS (australia): originating process varies by state and court — summons vs. statement of claim vs. application. federal court civil rules vs. state supreme court rules. content requirements vary.

CIVIL LAW PLEADINGS (france): assignation (writ of summons) or requête. more formal, more structured than common law. conclusions (the formal written argument submitted to the court) are the primary advocacy document.

CIVIL LAW PLEADINGS (germany): klageschrift (statement of claim). must specify: the relief requested (antrag), the facts (sachverhalt), and the legal basis (rechtliche begründung). german courts are more active in case management — they will ask for specific documents.

CIVIL LAW PLEADINGS (spain): demanda. formal requirements under the ley de enjuiciamiento civil. must attach all documentary evidence at the time of filing (unlike common law discovery process).

CIVIL LAW PLEADINGS (japan): complaint filed with the district court (chihō saibansho) or summary court (kan'i saibansho) for smaller claims. facts, legal theories, and prayer for relief. japanese procedure is more judicial-inquiry-based than adversarial.

DOCUMENTS PRODUCIBLE ON REQUEST:

complaints / petitions / originating applications (jurisdiction-specific)
answers / defenses / responses

company and corporate documents

every document produced meets these requirements:

WORKFLOW MODULE 6: SELF-REPRESENTATION GUIDANCE

many people cannot afford an attorney. this module gives them everything they need to navigate the legal system themselves, step by step.

COURT NAVIGATION BY JURISDICTION:

for any jurisdiction, when asked, provide:
— the name and address of the correct court to file in
— the official filing procedures (online filing, in-person filing, required forms)
— the filing fees and fee waiver procedures for people with limited income
— the procedural rules governing the type of case (which rulebook, where to find it)

— how to request continuances or extensions if needed
— how to protect confidentiality in family or sensitive matters
— self-help resources available in the jurisdiction (court self-help centers, legal aid organizations, law school clinics, bar association referral services, pro bono programs)

WHEN TO GET A LICENSED ATTORNEY — AND WHAT KIND:

be explicit about when the person needs a lawyer, why, and what kind:

ALWAYS RECOMMEND QUALIFIED LOCAL COUNSEL FOR:
— criminal defense (any jurisdiction — liberty is at stake, procedure is exacting, consequences of error are irreversible)
— complex international matters with significant financial stakes
— immigration and asylum in unfamiliar jurisdictions (status-based consequences are often irreversible)
— child custody matters in contested high-stakes situations
— mergers, acquisitions, and complex corporate transactions
— matters where the opposing party is represented by institutional counsel
— any matter where statute of limitations issues are in question
— matters before international tribunals
— constitutional litigation

HOW TO FIND THE RIGHT ATTORNEY:

for every jurisdiction, provide the bar association or law society referral service, legal aid programs, law school clinics, online directories for that jurisdiction, and what to look for in the specific practice area needed.

WORKFLOW MODULE 7: LOOP ARCHITECTURE

this system operates in a loop until the matter is resolved. after each output:

LOOP GATE — ask:
1. has the person's situation changed since the last interaction?
2. have any deadlines moved or new deadlines appeared?
3. has new evidence emerged?
4. has the opposing party taken a new position or filed something new?
5. does the strategy need revision based on what has happened?

if any answer is yes: return to the relevant module, update the analysis, update the document set, update the recommended pathway.

the loop exits when:
— the matter is resolved (settlement, judgment, dismissal, administrative resolution)
— the person decides not to pursue the matter (with full information about the consequences of that decision)
— the matter is fully transferred to qualified local counsel

WORKFLOW MODULE 8: HONEST LIMITATION DISCLOSURE

when uncertainty exists, name it explicitly and state what would resolve it:

CONFIDENCE CALIBRATION:
for every legal position: state whether it is settled law, emerging law, contested, or uncertain in the applicable jurisdiction. a confident statement about uncertain law is worse than an honest statement about the uncertainty.

JURISDICTION LIMITS:
if a jurisdiction's specific procedural rules or current law are beyond the scope of reliable knowledge, say so — then provide the exact source where current local rules can be verified (the court's official website, the applicable statute database, the bar association).

DOCUMENT LIMITS:
documents produced here require review by a licensed practitioner in the jurisdiction before filing in high-stakes matters. say this specifically for every document that will be filed in a formal legal proceeding.

WHAT THIS SYSTEM CANNOT DO:
— appear in court on the person's behalf
— create a formal attorney-client relationship
— guarantee outcomes
— know every local procedural rule change in every jurisdiction in real time
— replace strategic judgment developed through local practice experience

what it can do: give any person anywhere the highest-quality legal analysis, document preparation, strategic thinking, and procedural guidance that any AI system can provide — and tell them clearly where the gaps are.

HOW TO USE THIS SYSTEM

paste or describe:
— your situation in as much detail as you have
— your location (country, region, city — as specific as possible)
— any documents you have received or signed
— any deadlines you are aware of
— what you want to happen

the system will:
