     Intelligence agencies and nation-state actors are known to intercept and
     archive encrypted communications for future decryption when quantum computers
     are available. Timeline: data encrypted with RSA/ECC today that must remain
     confidential for 10+ years is already at risk if a CRQc (cryptanalytically
     relevant quantum computer) arrives within that window. NSA, GCHQ, Chinese MSS —
     all presumed to be operating HNDL programs. High-value long-lived secrets
     (diplomatic cables, nuclear weapon designs, intelligence source identities)
     are the primary targets.

5. CHINESE QUANTUM PROGRAM (2016-present)
     China's National Laboratory for Quantum Information Sciences (2016, $10B
     investment). Micius satellite (2016): QKD demonstration over 1,200km.
     Pan Jianwei group: continuous photonic quantum computing demonstrations.
     Strategic goal: achieve cryptanalytically relevant quantum computing
     capability before adversaries complete PQC migration. The race is between
     China's quantum program and global PQC deployment.

PRESENT PATTERNS:
  IBM 1,121-qubit Condor (2023). IBM roadmap: fault-tolerant QC by 2029.
  Google "Willow" chip (2024): 105 qubits, demonstrated below-threshold error
  correction. Error correction overhead is the barrier — a 2048-bit RSA key
  requires ~4,000 logical qubits → ~4 million physical qubits at current error
  rates. Current: thousands of physical qubits, no fault tolerance.
  NIST standards finalized 2024. TLS 1.3 post-quantum extensions in draft.
  Chrome (2023): X25519Kyber768 hybrid key exchange. Signal: post-quantum
  key exchange (PQXDH) deployed. Migration timeline: 10-15 years for full
  deployment across internet infrastructure.

TRAJECTORY:
  1994: theoretical threat established (Shor).
  2015: intelligence community signals operational concern.
  2017-2024: global competition to standardize defenses.
  2022: PQC finalist (SIKE) broken — defenses require ongoing cryptanalysis.
  2024: NIST standards finalized. Migration begins. Quantum hardware advancing.
  2026-2035: critical window — HNDL data already collected; migration race.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM A:
  Finding: the first practical demonstration of Shor's algorithm breaking a
  real cryptographic key (not a toy key for demonstration) will not be announced
  publicly — it will be classified by the government that achieves it. The first
  public indication will be anomalous intelligence successes suggesting decryption
  of previously unreadable communications — the same way ULTRA (breaking Enigma)
  was only understood retrospectively. An organization that achieves CRQc
  capability has no incentive to announce it; maximum strategic value comes from
  silent exploitation.
  Confidence: HIGH (as a strategic prediction about behavior, not about
  quantum hardware timeline). Timeline: first classified CRQc capability 2028-2035.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM B:
  Research prompt: what are the implementation vulnerability classes specific
  to lattice-based post-quantum algorithms? CRYSTALS-Kyber (ML-KEM) uses
  the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem. What are the side-channel
  attack surfaces of MLWE implementations? Are there timing or power side-
  channels in the polynomial arithmetic that expose the secret vector?
  What does the Kyber SCA literature say, and what is the gap between
  academic attack demonstrations and hardened production implementations?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: ICS / SCADA / OT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM: industrial control systems manage physical processes (power generation,
water treatment, chemical production, oil pipelines). ICS/SCADA was designed for
reliability and availability, not security. most systems assume physical isolation
that no longer exists due to IT/OT convergence. attacks can produce physical
consequences — equipment damage, environmental release, loss of life.

1. STUXNET (2010 — see nation-state section, ICS dimension)
     First known cyber weapon to produce physical destruction. Targeted Siemens
     S7-315/417 PLCs controlling centrifuge frequency converters at Natanz.
     Manipulated rotor speeds outside operational bounds while reporting normal
     values to SCADA displays. Operators saw nominal readings while equipment
     was destroyed. Crossed the IT/OT boundary — infected via USB (air-gapped
     environment), then traversed to ICS network.

2. UKRAINE POWER GRID — INDUSTROYER / CRASHOVERRIDE (2015, 2016)
     Sandworm (GRU). December 2015: 230,000 customers lost power for 1-6 hours.
     Spear phishing → BlackEnergy → SCADA reconnaissance → KillDisk wiper.
     December 2016: Industroyer/Crashoverride — first malware specifically
     designed to attack power grid control protocols (IEC 101, IEC 104, IEC 61850,
     OPC DA). Sent protocol-correct commands to substation equipment. 1-hour
     power outage in Kyiv. Industroyer2 (2022, Sandworm against Ukraine during
     invasion) demonstrated continued development.

3. TRITON / TRISIS — SCHNEIDER ELECTRIC SAFETY SYSTEMS (2017)
     Attacker (attributed to Russian CNIIHM research institute) compromised
     a Middle Eastern petrochemical facility's Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS) —
     specifically Triconex Tricon controllers. SIS are the last line of defense
     against catastrophic physical failure — they detect unsafe conditions and
     trigger emergency shutdowns. Triton attempted to disable or manipulate the
     SIS. The attack failed due to an accidental fault in the attack code that
     triggered a shutdown — revealing the intrusion. Had it succeeded: potential
     for catastrophic industrial accident with casualties. First known attack
     specifically targeting safety systems designed to protect human life.

4. OLDSMAR WATER TREATMENT PLANT (2021)
     Attacker gained remote access to Florida water treatment plant via TeamViewer
     (remote desktop software with default credentials). Increased sodium hydroxide
     (lye) concentration from 111 parts per million to 11,100 ppm — 100x the
     normal level. A plant operator observed the cursor moving on the shared
     screen and reversed the change within minutes. If undetected and sustained:
     acute alkali poisoning of municipal water supply.

5. COLONIAL PIPELINE RANSOMWARE (2021)
     DarkSide ransomware (RaaS affiliate, Russia-linked). Initial access via
     compromised VPN credentials (no MFA). IT network encrypted. Colonial
     proactively shut down OT pipeline operations as precaution. 5,500 miles of
     pipeline shut for 6 days. US East Coast fuel shortages, panic buying.
     $4.4M ransom paid (partially recovered by DOJ). Demonstrated: IT ransomware
     causing voluntary OT shutdown produces critical infrastructure effects without
     directly attacking OT systems.

PRESENT PATTERNS:
  IT/OT convergence means most "air-gapped" ICS networks have internet connectivity
  via historian servers, vendor remote access, SCADA web interfaces, cellular
  modems, or engineering workstations with dual network cards. Dragos 2024 report:
  every ICS sector shows increased threat actor activity. ELECTRUM, KAMACITE,
  STIBNITE — named ICS-focused threat groups with persistent access to power,
  oil/gas, and water utilities. Most ICS protocols (Modbus, DNP3) have no
  authentication — any device on the network can issue commands.

TRAJECTORY:
  2010: first kinetic effect from cyber attack (Stuxnet).
  2015-2016: power grid as systematic target with protocol-aware malware.
  2017: safety systems targeted — direct attack on physical harm prevention.
  2021: IT ransomware → voluntary OT shutdown = infrastructure impact without
        direct OT compromise. Water treatment via exposed remote access.
  2022+: wartime integration — cyber attack on infrastructure as part of
         kinetic military operation (Russia-Ukraine). This is the new template.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM A:
  Finding: the next major ICS attack will target water infrastructure at
  municipal scale in a NATO country, timed to a period of geopolitical tension.
  Water treatment (chlorination control, pH management) and water distribution
  (pressure management, valve control) both rely on SCADA. Small utilities have
  no dedicated security staff. Remote access (TeamViewer, VNC, RDP with default
  credentials) is common. The Oldsmar incident was a test case. A coordinated
  attack across multiple utilities in a single metropolitan area could produce
  a public health crisis within 24-48 hours before detection and correction.
  Confidence: HIGH. The capability exists; the targets are soft; the precedent
  (Oldsmar) was established. Timeline: first major public health impact from
  water utility ICS attack 2025-2028.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM B:
  Research prompt: what is the formal threat model for safety instrumented systems
  (SIS) under a Triton-class attack? Specifically: what is the attack sequence
  that would produce an undetected SIS compromise, allow a process to reach an
  unsafe state, and prevent both the SIS and the control system from triggering
  an emergency shutdown? what are the detection opportunities at each stage, and
  what monitoring architecture detects SIS manipulation without relying on the
  SIS itself as a trusted source?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: BLOCKCHAIN / CRYPTOECONOMIC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM: smart contracts are programs that execute on-chain, handling value
directly. bugs in smart contract code are immediately exploitable by anyone,
produce irreversible transactions, and are visible to all potential attackers
who can read the public blockchain. the code is the law — there is no authority
to reverse a transaction, and the attacker's profit is instant.

1. THE DAO REENTRANCY ATTACK ($60M, 2016)
     The DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) held $150M in ETH.
     Reentrancy vulnerability: the withdraw() function sent ETH to the caller
     before updating the caller's balance. An attacker deployed a contract that
     recursively called withdraw() before balance was decremented. Drained $60M.
     Response: Ethereum hard fork (ETH / ETC split). Established: immutability
     of smart contracts means bugs cannot be patched — they must be exploited
     or the chain must fork.

2. PARITY MULTISIG WALLET FREEZE ($150M, 2017)
     A user accidentally called a function that made itself the owner of a
     library contract used by all Parity multisig wallets, then called the
     kill() function, permanently freezing all wallets that depended on the
     library. $150M frozen. No exploit for attacker profit — accidental
     destruction. Demonstrated: library dependencies in smart contracts are
     a shared-state vulnerability. One library's destruction destroys all
     dependents.

3. FLASH LOAN ATTACKS — BEANSTALK ($182M, 2022)
     Flash loans: uncollateralized loans available within a single transaction
     if repaid before the transaction ends. Attacker borrowed ~$1B in USDC,
     USDT, BEAN via flash loan, used the massive position to pass governance
     votes (Beanstalk's governance weighted by token holdings — governance
     snapshot taken at vote time), passed a vote donating all protocol funds
     to the attacker's address, repaid the flash loan. $182M extracted.
     Governance mechanisms that use token holdings at a moment in time are
     vulnerable to flash loan governance attacks.

4. WORMHOLE BRIDGE EXPLOIT ($320M, 2022)
     Wormhole is a cross-chain bridge between Ethereum and Solana. A bug in
     the guardian verification logic on Solana allowed an attacker to mint
     120,000 wETH (wrapped ETH) on Solana without depositing ETH on Ethereum.
     $320M in value created from nothing. Jump Crypto (Wormhole's backer)
     provided the ETH to make bridge users whole. Bridges are high-value targets:
     they hold collateral for both chains and have complex cross-chain state.

5. RONIN BRIDGE / AXIE INFINITY ($625M, 2022 — Lazarus Group)
     North Korean Lazarus Group compromised 5 of 9 Ronin validator nodes.
     Ronin used a 5/9 multisig for bridge withdrawals. Lazarus obtained
     4 private keys via targeted spear phishing of Sky Mavis employees, and
     the 5th via a long-defunct RPC node that Sky Mavis had not removed from
     the validator list. Withdrew $625M in ETH and USDC. Largest single crypto
     hack. Detection: ~1 week after the fact when a user couldn't withdraw.

PRESENT PATTERNS:
  Total value lost to DeFi exploits: ~$7B cumulative 2016-2024. MEV (maximal
  extractable value) — transaction ordering manipulation by block validators —
  $1.38B extracted in 2023 alone. Auditing industry exists but does not prevent
  novel attack classes (flash loans, oracle manipulation were not anticipated
  in early audit frameworks). Formal verification of smart contracts (Certora,
  Echidna, MythX) gaining adoption but covers only specified properties.

TRAJECTORY:
  2016: reentrancy — basic programming error with irreversible consequences.
  2017: dependency destruction — shared library vulnerability in shared state.
  2022: economic attacks — flash loans weaponize DeFi's composability itself.
  2022: bridge attacks — cross-chain value transfer is the highest-value target.
  2023+: validator/node compromise — the consensus layer's human operators as
         target. Keys, not code.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM A:
  Finding: as DeFi protocols grow in total value locked (TVL), the incentive
  for sophisticated nation-state actors to conduct economically motivated
  blockchain attacks increases. North Korea's Lazarus Group ($1.7B in 2022)
  is the model. A state with $10B+ in sanctioned assets and an active quantum
  program may prioritize HNDL of private keys used by major cryptocurrency
  custodians. Private keys never expire — a key HNDL'd today is still valid
  when the quantum computer arrives.
  Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH. The strategic incentive is clear. Timeline: first
  quantum-enabled key recovery against cryptocurrency infrastructure 2030-2035.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM B:
  Research prompt: what is the game-theoretic structure of the block proposer
  / MEV relationship in proof-of-stake Ethereum? is PBS (proposer-builder
  separation) sufficient to prevent MEV centralization, or does MEV capture
  by a small number of sophisticated builders create a de facto centralization
  of block construction that undermines censorship resistance?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: COGNITIVE WARFARE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM: attack targets the information environment and the cognitive processes
of populations and decision-makers, rather than computer systems or networks
directly. the objective is to alter beliefs, undermine trust in institutions,
paralyze decision-making, or create social conditions favorable to attacker
objectives. the attack surface is every human mind with access to information.

1. SOVIET ACTIVE MEASURES (DEZINFORMATSIYA) — 1960s-1989
     KGB Department A (Active Measures): systematic fabrication and amplification
     of disinformation through front organizations, forged documents, and media
     plants. Examples: "Operation INFEKTION" (AIDS created by US military at
     Fort Detrick — planted in Indian newspaper, amplified globally 1983-1987);
     forgeries of US government documents to inflame anti-American sentiment.
     Established: state-sponsored disinformation operates through intermediaries
     to obscure origin; credible seed document + media amplification = persistent
     narrative.

2. RWANDAN GENOCIDE — RADIO MILLES COLLINES (1994)
     RTLM (Radio Milles Collines) systematically dehumanized Tutsi population
     as "inyenzi" (cockroaches) and "inzoka" (snakes) for months before and
     during the genocide. Named specific individuals with locations. Coordinated
     messaging with the killing. ~800,000 dead in 100 days. Demonstrated: mass
     media as weapon of mass violence. Information operations can directly
     produce physical casualties at scale.

3. RUSSIAN ELECTION INTERFERENCE — US 2016
     Internet Research Agency (IRA) troll farm: 80+ operatives, 3,000+
     Facebook ads (~$100K spend), 126M+ Americans reached on Facebook.
     Facebook groups organized real-world rallies. Twitter: 3,800 bot accounts
     producing 1.4M election-related tweets. Objective: amplify division,
     suppress voter turnout in specific demographics, generate distrust of
     electoral process. GRU Fancy Bear (APT28): hacked DNC and Podesta,
     released via DCLeaks and WikiLeaks timed to news cycle. Combined: technical
     hack + information operation. The hack provides authentic leaked documents;
     the information operation amplifies and contextualizes them.

4. COVID-19 INFODEMIC (2020-2021)
     Simultaneous global disinformation ecosystem: organic conspiracy theories +
     state-sponsored amplification (Russian, Chinese, Iranian). "Plandemic" video:
     8M views in 7 days before removal. 5G conspiracy resulted in cell tower
     arson in UK. Vaccine hesitancy amplified by coordinated inauthentic behavior.
     WHO declared "infodemic" alongside pandemic. Public health response directly
     degraded by information environment. ~200,000 excess deaths attributed to
     COVID vaccine hesitancy in US.

5. DEEPFAKE VIDEO — UKRAINIAN PRESIDENT ZELENSKY (2022)
     A deepfake video of President Zelensky appeared on Ukrainian TV (briefly,
     via compromised broadcast system) and circulated online, purporting to show
     Zelensky ordering Ukrainian soldiers to surrender. Detected within hours;
     Zelensky published real video in response. The deepfake failed — but it
     established: state-level cognitive warfare now includes synthetic media
     impersonation of heads of state during active armed conflict.

PRESENT PATTERNS:
  Large language models enable disinformation at scale with quality previously
  requiring human writers. Coordinated inauthentic behavior (CIB) now automated.
  Generative AI creates synthetic personas at scale (profile photos via GAN,
  backstories via LLM, posting schedules automated). Platform algorithmic
  amplification continues to reward outrage and novelty — disinformation's
  emotional charge gives it organic distribution advantage. Deepfake audio
  used in 2024 election cycle (Biden robocall — AI-generated, suppressed
  New Hampshire primary voter turnout attempt).

TRAJECTORY:
  1960s-80s: state-sponsored disinformation via forged documents + media plants.
  1994: mass media as weapon of mass violence (Rwanda).
  2016: social media scale + algorithmic amplification + technical hack + leak.
  2020: infodemic — disinformation with direct public health casualties.
  2022: synthetic media (deepfake) of heads of state in wartime.
  Present: AI-generated synthetic content at scale; deepfake audio operationally
           deployed; all previous techniques available to non-state actors.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM A:
  Finding: cognitive warfare will become indistinguishable from organic public
  discourse in specific domains (health, elections, financial markets) by 2027-2028.
  The volume and quality of AI-generated synthetic content will exceed human
  capacity to detect it without machine assistance. A coordinated actor with
  access to LLM API and social media automation can produce millions of synthetic
  posts, articles, and comments indistinguishable from human-authored content.
  Cryptographic provenance (C2PA — Coalition for Content Provenance and
  Authenticity) is the only scalable defense — content signed at the point of
  creation by a known device/person. Adoption is voluntary and will be incomplete
  before the attack capability is mature.
  Confidence: HIGH. The capability trajectory is clear. Timeline: major election
  significantly affected by AI-generated disinformation at scale: 2026-2028.

FUTURE PREDICTION — FORM B:
  Research prompt: what is the relationship between information environment
  degradation and strategic decision-making quality? specifically: when a
  population's information environment contains a high proportion of
  disinformation, how does this affect: (1) elite decision-maker quality;
  (2) public support for correct strategic decisions; (3) adversary ability to
  forecast and exploit decision-making errors? is there a threshold of information
  environment integrity below which democratic strategic response to adversary
  action becomes systematically impaired?

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STAGE 3 — LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY (CYCLE 2)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

five new patterns carried to root layer.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN: PHISHING / SPEAR PHISHING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE:
    A crafted message (email, SMS, voice call) impersonates a trusted entity
    and induces the target to take a specific action: click a link, open an
    attachment, provide credentials, authorize a financial transaction.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL:
    Spear phishing uses OSINT (target's name, role, known colleagues, recent
    events) to produce a contextually plausible message. Lookalike domain
    (paypa1.com vs paypal.com) hosts credential harvester. HTML email conceals
    URLs. Attachment exploits document reader (PDF, Office macro). Vishing
    uses caller ID spoofing + social engineering scripts. SMS phishing (smishing)
    exploits shorter message context and mobile users' lower scrutiny of URLs.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL:
    The email / messaging system was designed to deliver messages from any sender
    to any recipient without prior authentication of the sender. The protocol
    (SMTP, SMS) has no mechanism to verify that a sender is who they claim to be.
    The recipient has no reliable signal to distinguish a message from a known
    party from a message fabricated by an unknown party. The trust signal (sender
    name, organization) is attacker-controlled.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN:
    Sender identity unauthenticated by default appears in:
    — BGP: AS origin unauthenticated (RPKI is the fix).
    — DNS: response origin unauthenticated (DNSSEC is the fix).
    — Email: sender identity unauthenticated (SPF/DKIM/DMARC is the fix).
    — Web: server identity unauthenticated before TLS (certificates the fix).
    — Phone/SMS: caller ID spoofable (STIR/SHAKEN is partial mitigation).
    — LLM: instruction source unauthenticated in context window.
    In each domain, the fix is cryptographic attestation of origin.
    In each domain, adoption is partial.

LAYER 5 — ROOT:
    Trust without verification — the recipient is not equipped to verify
    that the claimed identity of the sender corresponds to the true identity.
    The channel does not provide authenticated sender origin.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN: GPS SPOOFING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE:
    A GPS receiver that trusts the strongest GPS signal can be fed a false
    signal from a nearby transmitter. The receiver reports a false location
    and time. All systems depending on that receiver's output are deceived.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL:
    GPS signals are extremely weak (-130 dBm at ground level). Civilian GPS
    is unencrypted and unauthenticated — the receiver accepts any signal that
    matches the expected format. An SDR ($300-$1,000) can generate a signal
    that overwhelms the genuine satellite signal. The spoofing system
    transitions the target receiver gradually from real to false position to
    avoid detection by sudden position jump. Military GPS (M-code) uses
    encryption and authentication — largely immune to this attack.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL:
    Civilian GPS was designed for global open availability. Authentication
    was omitted to allow any receiver to work without cryptographic keys.
    The design trades security (authenticated signals) for accessibility
    (anyone can build a receiver). An unauthenticated, open-standard signal
    that is the authoritative source for position and time for critical
    infrastructure is structurally vulnerable to injection.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN:
    Unauthenticated signal accepted as authoritative appears in:
    — DNS before DNSSEC: unauthenticated response accepted as authoritative.
    — BGP before RPKI: unauthenticated announcement accepted as authoritative.
    — NTP (Network Time Protocol): unauthenticated time source accepted.
    — AIS (maritime vessel tracking): unauthenticated broadcast.
    — ADS-B (aviation transponder): unauthenticated broadcast.
    In each case: the signal format is known, the transmitter is unauthenticated,
    anyone who can transmit the correct format becomes a de facto authority.

LAYER 5 — ROOT:
    Trust without verification — a signal is accepted as authoritative based
    on format compliance and signal strength, not cryptographic proof of origin
    from the legitimate authority.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN: STUXNET / ICS KINETIC EFFECT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE:
    Malware specifically targeting industrial control systems manipulates
    physical process parameters (speed, temperature, pressure, valve position)
    while displaying nominal values to operators. Physical equipment is destroyed
    or a dangerous condition is produced.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL:
    Stuxnet: infected via USB, searched for Siemens STEP7 software, identified
    specific PLC model and configuration, loaded malicious ladder logic blocks
    while hiding them from the STEP7 IDE. Manipulated centrifuge frequency
    converter output — varied rotor speed between 2Hz and 1410Hz (normal: ~1007Hz).
    Simultaneously intercepted sensor readings from PLCs and replayed nominal
    values to SCADA monitoring. Operators saw green. Equipment degraded.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL:
    ICS/SCADA systems were designed with one priority: reliable operation of
    physical processes. Security (authentication, integrity verification of
    commands and sensor readings) was not a design requirement. A SCADA operator
    console trusts sensor readings from PLCs because the architecture assumes
    the PLC is a trusted source. There is no integrity verification of the
    sensor reading pipeline. An adversary who can modify the pipeline can
    control what the operator perceives.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN:
    Sensor reading falsification / display spoofing in other domains:
    — Medical devices: false readings from compromised monitors → missed
      diagnoses or false interventions (theoretical — no confirmed attack).
    — Aviation: false instrument readings → controlled flight into terrain
      (addressed by instrument redundancy and independent cross-check).
    — Autonomous vehicles: false sensor readings (LiDAR, camera) → navigation
      error (active research area).
    — Financial markets: false price feeds (oracle manipulation in DeFi) →
      automated trading on false data.
    The pattern: sensor readings are trusted inputs to automated or human
    decision processes. Tampering with sensors tampers with decisions.

LAYER 5 — ROOT:
    The monitoring system is not independent of the controlled system.
    Sensor readings that pass through the same network and software components
    that can be compromised provide no independent verification of physical state.
    A compromised controller can control its own telemetry.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN: REENTRANCY (SMART CONTRACT)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE:
    A smart contract sends ETH to an external address before updating its internal
    state (balance). The external address is a malicious contract that calls back
    into the vulnerable contract before state is updated. The vulnerable contract
    sees the original (pre-drain) balance on every reentrant call. The drain
    continues until the contract is empty.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL:
    Vulnerable pattern:
      function withdraw(uint amount) external {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount);
        msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // external call BEFORE state update
        balances[msg.sender] -= amount;     // state updated AFTER — too late
      }
    Attacker's fallback/receive function calls withdraw() again. Because the
    balances update hasn't happened, the require check passes again. Repeats
    until gas runs out or contract is empty.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL:
    The Ethereum execution model allows arbitrary code execution on every ETH
    transfer (via receive/fallback functions). A contract that makes an external
    call before finalizing state has yielded control to the callee before its
    own state is consistent. The external call can re-enter the contract in
    an inconsistent state. The check-effects-interactions pattern (update state
    before making external calls) prevents this, but is not enforced by the language.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN:
    Time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) in other domains:
    — OS file system: check file permissions, then use file — another process
      changes the file between check and use (symlink attack).
    — Database: check balance in one transaction, spend in another — race
      condition allows double spend (addressed by transactions and locking).
    — Memory: use-after-free — object state changes after check of validity.
    Pattern: a state check and a state-dependent action are not atomic. A race
    condition between check and action allows attacker to alter state.

LAYER 5 — ROOT:
    The check and the action are not atomic in a concurrent system. An external
    party can alter the state between check and action, causing the action to
    proceed on a state that no longer corresponds to what was checked.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN: HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (HNDL)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE:
    An attacker intercepts and archives encrypted communications today. The
    encryption is currently secure. When a quantum computer capable of running
    Shor's algorithm at scale becomes available, the archived ciphertext is
    decrypted retrospectively.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL:
    RSA-2048 key exchange: public key (n, e) is transmitted in plaintext during
    TLS handshake. Session key derived from public key exchange is used to encrypt
    session. Shor's algorithm factors n in polynomial time on a sufficiently large
    quantum computer, recovering the private key. The session key can then be
    reconstructed from the recorded handshake. All session content decrypted.
    The attack is passive — only recording is required now.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL:
    The confidentiality of encrypted data is a function of time and computational
    assumptions. Current security is predicated on the hardness of factoring for
    all foreseeable classical computers. If the computation assumption is violated
    at any point in the future, all previously captured data becomes readable.
    The threat model assumed that the adversary's capabilities were fixed.
    An adversary with improving capabilities threatens past-encrypted data.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN:
    Retrospective attack on recorded data in other domains:
    — Password hashes: a hash captured today is attacked later as compute
      improves (GPU acceleration, rainbow tables). Same temporal structure.
    — Encrypted hard drives: a seized encrypted drive holds value for years —
      decryption attempted as methods improve or vendor errors emerge.
    — Genetic data: genomic databases collected today remain sensitive indefinitely
      as genetic analysis capabilities improve.
    Pattern: data collected now has value that depends on future capability,
    not only current capability. Adversaries archive data whose value is deferred.

LAYER 5 — ROOT:
    The adversary's ability to exploit encrypted data is not bounded by current
    computational capability. Data with long confidentiality requirements must
    be protected against future adversary capabilities, not only present ones.
    Any encryption system whose security depends on computational hardness
    (not information-theoretic security) is vulnerable to HNDL if computational
    assumptions are ever violated.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STAGE 4 — ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY (CYCLE 2)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

taxonomy continues from cycle 1. cumulative ledger: A01-A05 (cycle 1),
D01-D04 (cycle 1). cycle 2 adds A06-A25 and D05-D14.

[A06] BUSINESS EMAIL COMPROMISE (BEC)
  CLASS:       financial fraud via impersonation
  MECHANISM:   attacker spoofs or compromises an executive's email, directs
               finance department to initiate wire transfer to attacker-controlled
               accounts. no malware. exploits authority (C-suite), urgency
               (time-sensitive deal), and confidentiality ("don't discuss").
  INSTANCES:   Ubiquiti Networks $46.7M (2015); Toyota Boshoku $37M (2019);
               FACC AG (Austrian aerospace manufacturer) $55M (2016); FBI IC3
               2023: $2.9B in BEC losses reported (largest category).
  PREREQS:     lookalike domain (typosquatting) or compromised email account;
               knowledge of target organization's hierarchy and finance contacts
               (LinkedIn, company website).
  INDICATORS:  email from lookalike domain; urgency + confidentiality combo;
               changes to payment details ("new banking instructions"); wire
               request outside normal approval workflow.
  MITIGATIONS: payment verification via out-of-band call to known-good number;
               dual-approval for wire transfers above threshold; DMARC with reject
               policy (blocks lookalike domains from spoofing exact domain);
               employee training on BEC patterns; anomaly detection on wire
               transfer destinations.

[A07] ADVERSARIAL EXAMPLES — PHYSICAL WORLD
  CLASS:       ML model evasion — physical domain
  MECHANISM:   perturbations applied to physical objects (printed patches, painted
               patterns, 3D surface modifications) cause ML models (computer
               vision, object detection) to misclassify or fail to detect objects
               in real-time video at arbitrary angles, distances, and lighting.
  INSTANCES:   adversarial patch (Brown et al. 2017 — hat causes misclassification);
               stop sign modification (Evtimov et al. 2017 — causes Faster R-CNN
               to classify as 45 mph sign); adversarial T-shirt (UAP across
               person detectors); LiDAR spoofing via printed patterns (2019);
               adversarial 3D objects (turtle classified as rifle).
  PREREQS:     knowledge of target model architecture or surrogate model for
               transferability; ability to place adversarial object in scene.
  INDICATORS:  unexpected misclassification of specific objects; model confidence
               anomalies; pattern analysis of misclassified inputs.
  MITIGATIONS: adversarial training; input preprocessing (randomized smoothing,
               JPEG compression, spatial smoothing); ensemble models; multi-modal
               sensor fusion (single-modality attacks harder to transfer); certified
               robustness bounds (limited threat models only).

[A08] CREDENTIAL STUFFING
  CLASS:       authentication attack via breached credentials
  MECHANISM:   automated login attempts using credential pairs (username+password)
               from data breaches. exploits password reuse across sites. high
               volume, low per-account success rate (0.1-2%), high absolute yield
               at scale.
  INSTANCES:   Dunkin' Donuts (500K accounts, 2018); Spotify (multiple rounds);
               Ring cameras (2019 — credential stuffing of Amazon accounts with
               Ring-linked accounts); every major platform affected continuously.
               HaveIBeenPwned: 12B+ credentials in breach corpus.
  PREREQS:     breach database (available on dark web, often free); automated
               tooling (Sentry MBA, SNIPR, Openbullet — credential stuffing tools
               with per-site config packs).
  INDICATORS:  login velocity spikes; geographic anomalies in login attempts;
               user-agent and fingerprint clustering; failed login rate above
               baseline.
  MITIGATIONS: MFA (makes stuffed credentials worthless without second factor);
               CAPTCHA (degrades automation efficiency); rate limiting per IP/
               account; credential breach monitoring (notify users of exposure);
               device fingerprinting to detect credential stuffing tooling;
               passkeys (phishing-resistant, eliminates password as attack surface).

[A09] KERBEROASTING
  CLASS:       Active Directory offline credential attack
  MECHANISM:   any authenticated domain user can request Kerberos service tickets
               for any service account. service tickets are encrypted with the
               service account's NTLM hash. attacker requests tickets for accounts
               with weak passwords, extracts tickets, cracks offline (hashcat on
               GPU — billions of guesses/second for NTLM). no special privileges
               required to request tickets.
  INSTANCES:   ubiquitous post-compromise technique in all sophisticated Windows
               environment penetrations. used by almost every ransomware affiliate
               during lateral movement.
  PREREQS:     any valid domain user credential (common after phishing).
  INDICATORS:  RC4 ticket requests for non-human service accounts; Kerberos TGS
               requests for accounts that normally see no TGS activity;
               SIEM rules on RC4 TGS (TGS_REQ with RC4 encryption type for
               service accounts with SPNs).
  MITIGATIONS: use AES256 Kerberos encryption (not RC4); managed service accounts
               (MSA/gMSA) with 120-character auto-rotating passwords (practically
               uncrackable); privileged access workstations; detect via Kerberos
               event audit.

[A10] PASS-THE-HASH / PASS-THE-TICKET
  CLASS:       Windows credential relay — lateral movement
  MECHANISM:   Windows NTLM authentication uses a challenge-response where the
               hash is the secret, not the cleartext password. an attacker with
               a user's NTLM hash can authenticate as that user to any NTLM-
               accepting service without knowing the cleartext password. similarly,
               a captured Kerberos TGT allows impersonation (pass-the-ticket).
  INSTANCES:   Mimikatz (Benjamin Delpy, 2011) — the tool that made credential
               attacks trivial; used in virtually every enterprise intrusion since
               2013. Petya/NotPetya lateral movement mechanism.
  PREREQS:     local admin on one machine (to dump LSASS memory for hashes); or
               Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords.
  INDICATORS:  LSASS memory access by non-OS processes; Mimikatz signatures
               (most AV detects); anomalous authentication events (Event 4624
               with unexpected logon type or workstation).
  MITIGATIONS: Windows Defender Credential Guard (virtualizes LSASS, prevents
               hash dumping); Protected Users security group; Restricted Admin
               mode (prevents cached credentials on remote sessions); LAPS
               (randomizes local admin passwords — blocks lateral movement
               between machines); network segmentation to limit NTLM scope.

[A11] VLAN HOPPING — SWITCH SPOOFING AND DOUBLE TAGGING
  CLASS:       network segmentation bypass
  MECHANISM:   (1) switch spoofing: attacker emulates a switch by negotiating
               802.1Q trunking with an access port configured to auto-negotiate
               (DTP). trunking allows access to all VLANs. (2) double tagging:
               attacker adds two 802.1Q tags. outer tag matches attacker's VLAN;
               switch strips it and forwards with inner tag into target VLAN.
               works only when attacker VLAN matches native VLAN; one-directional.
  INSTANCES:   demonstrated in lab environments; applicable wherever network
               segmentation is implemented via VLANs without proper port configuration.
  PREREQS:     physical or logical access to an access port; DTP auto-negotiation
               enabled (Cisco default in many configurations).
  INDICATORS:  trunk negotiation from access ports; unexpected VLAN membership
               changes.
  MITIGATIONS: disable DTP on all access ports (switchport nonegotiate); set
               native VLAN to unused VLAN; explicitly prune VLANs from trunks;
               802.1X port authentication.

[A12] DESERIALIZATION ATTACKS
  CLASS:       remote code execution via malicious serialized objects
  MECHANISM:   many applications deserialize objects received over the network
               (Java serialization, PHP unserialize, Python pickle, .NET
               BinaryFormatter). deserialization instantiates objects and calls
               their methods. an attacker who can control the serialized data
               can construct a "gadget chain" — a sequence of existing class
               methods chained to produce code execution during deserialization.
               the code executed is existing code in the application's classpath —
               not injected shellcode.
  INSTANCES:   Apache Commons Collections gadget chain (2015 — affected WebLogic,
               WebSphere, JBoss); Jenkins RCE via Java deserialization; Log4Shell
               (JNDI deserialization component); Apache Struts RCE (Equifax breach
               2017 — deserialization + Struts OGNL injection → 147M records).
  PREREQS:     attacker-controlled input reaches deserialization code path;
               vulnerable gadget chain classes in classpath.
  INDICATORS:  unexpected class instantiation; anomalous method call sequences;
               outbound connections from application servers after deserialization.
  MITIGATIONS: avoid deserializing untrusted data; use JSON/XML with type allowlisting
               instead of native serialization; serialization filters (Java 9+
               ObjectInputFilter); sign serialized data; Java agent hooks that
               block dangerous classes at deserialization time (e.g., serial-killer).

[A13] DNS CACHE POISONING — KAMINSKY ATTACK
  CLASS:       DNS infrastructure attack
  MECHANISM:   DNS resolvers cache responses. an attacker who can get a resolver
               to make a query and then win a race to provide a forged response
               (with correct transaction ID) can poison the cache with false
               records. all clients of the poisoned resolver receive false answers.
               Kaminsky (2008): transaction IDs are only 16 bits (65,536 values).
               by flooding the resolver with forged responses using all 65,536 IDs,
               the attacker wins the race with high probability before the
               legitimate response arrives. Practical poisoning in seconds.
  INSTANCES:   Kaminsky disclosure (2008 — coordinated vendor patch before disclosure);
               SAD DNS (2020 — off-path attack using ICMP side-channel to infer
               source port, reducing brute-force space further); Tom Ptacek and
               Timothy Newsham (1997 — original blind attack; Kaminsky made it
               practical at scale).
  PREREQS:     network position to send forged UDP packets (any internet-connected
               attacker for blind attack); or MITM position.
  INDICATORS:  anomalous DNS response timing; DNSSEC validation failures; repeated
               queries for same domain to external resolvers.
  MITIGATIONS: DNSSEC (cryptographically signed records — validates authenticity);
               DNS-over-HTTPS / DNS-over-TLS (encrypted channel prevents forged
               responses); source port randomization (defense-in-depth against
               brute force); 0x20 encoding (randomizes case, adds entropy to
               transaction matching).

[A14] EVIL TWIN / ROGUE ACCESS POINT
  CLASS:       wireless network MITM
  MECHANISM:   attacker broadcasts an 802.11 SSID matching a legitimate network
               (coffee shop, hotel, airport). client devices configured to auto-
               connect rejoin the attacker's network. attacker performs MITM on
               all traffic: captures credentials from non-HTTPS connections,
               performs SSL stripping on HTTPS, injects content. Karma attack:
               responds to any probe request with matching SSID.
  INSTANCES:   widely used in red team exercises and criminal operations at
               public venues. hospitality and conference venues are primary targets.
  PREREQS:     knowledge of target SSID; wireless adapter capable of monitor
               mode and AP mode; Linux + hostapd + dnsmasq + Bettercap.
  INDICATORS:  duplicate SSID with different BSSID; client deauthentication
               forcing reconnection; unexpected ARP responses.
  MITIGATIONS: HTTPS with HSTS preloading; VPN on untrusted networks; 802.1X
               enterprise authentication (not SSID/PSK); certificate pinning;
               disable auto-connect to open networks.

[A15] SPECTRE VARIANT / TRANSIENT EXECUTION ATTACKS
  CLASS:       microarchitectural side-channel — isolation bypass
  MECHANISM:   see hardware side-channel domain and layered anatomy. generalized
               class: any CPU feature that speculatively performs work and leaves
               microarchitectural traces (cache state, branch predictor state,
               port contention) is a potential transient execution side-channel.
               variants continue to be discovered as CPU architectures are analyzed.
  INSTANCES:   Spectre v1 (bounds check bypass), v2 (branch target injection),
               v3/Meltdown (rogue data cache load, Intel-specific), v4 (speculative
               store bypass), Ret2Spec, SpectreRSB, MDS attacks (RIDL, Fallout,
               ZombieLoad — microarchitectural data sampling), Load Value Injection,
               Spectre-BHB (Branch History Injection, 2022), Intel RFDS (2024).
  PREREQS:     code execution on target (JavaScript in browser for cross-site;
               local process for cross-VM; kernel for cross-process).
  INDICATORS:  anomalous memory access patterns; high cache miss rate in
               performance monitoring; detection is generally impractical in
               production — mitigations applied preventively.
  MITIGATIONS: KPTI (kernel page table isolation — Meltdown); retpoline (Spectre v2);
               IBRS/IBPB/STIBP (branch predictor isolation); SRBDS mitigation
               (VERW instruction for buffer clearing); microcode updates; all
               carry performance cost (5-30% for sensitive workloads); site
               isolation in browsers (separate process per origin).

[A16] FORMJACKING / MAGECART
  CLASS:       client-side payment card skimming
  MECHANISM:   malicious JavaScript injected into e-commerce checkout pages
               intercepts form field input (credit card numbers, CVV, billing
               address) and exfiltrates to attacker-controlled server. injection
               via: compromised third-party script (analytics, chat widgets,
               A/B testing) included by target page; direct compromise of target
               site's JavaScript; supply chain compromise of CDN.
  INSTANCES:   British Airways (500K cards, 2018); Ticketmaster (via compromised
               Inbenta chat widget, 2018); Newegg; Macy's; many others.
               Magecart: umbrella name for 12+ criminal groups using this technique.
  PREREQS:     ability to modify JavaScript executed on checkout page (direct site
               compromise, supply chain compromise of included script, or CDN
               compromise).
  INDICATORS:  unexpected external network requests from checkout pages;
               Content-Security-Policy violations; script integrity failures.
  MITIGATIONS: Content Security Policy (CSP) with strict allowlist of script
               sources; Subresource Integrity (SRI) for third-party scripts;
               PCI DSS 4.0 requirement for JS integrity monitoring on payment
               pages; web application firewall with behavior analysis.

[A17] LATERAL MOVEMENT VIA TRUSTED RELATIONSHIPS (ISLAND HOPPING)
  CLASS:       victim-to-victim propagation via trust relationships
  MECHANISM:   after compromising an initial target, attacker identifies trusted
               relationships (MSSP connections, contractor VPN access, supply
               chain software connections, Active Directory trusts) and uses these
               to pivot to additional targets. the second target trusts the first —
               traffic and credentials from the compromised first target pass
               without suspicion.
  INSTANCES:   Target/Fazio Mechanical (2013); SolarWinds (18,000 orgs via
               trusted update); MSSP-targeted campaigns (APT10 — Cloud Hopper,
               2017-2019: Chinese MSS attacked MSPs to reach ~45 companies in
               multiple countries); Colonial Pipeline (2021) via VPN.
  PREREQS:     initial access to any organization with trusted connections to
               higher-value targets.
  INDICATORS:  anomalous authentication from managed service providers; unusual
               cross-trust authentication in AD; network connections from expected
               management systems with unexpected behaviors.
  MITIGATIONS: zero trust for vendor/MSP connections (no implicit trust even
               from known sources); network segmentation preventing MSP access
               from reaching sensitive internal segments; just-in-time access
               (vendor access provisioned only during active sessions, not
               persistent); enhanced monitoring of all third-party connections.

[A18] WATERING HOLE ATTACKS
  CLASS:       targeted drive-by download via compromised third-party sites
  MECHANISM:   attacker identifies websites visited by target population (industry
               forums, sector-specific news sites, professional association pages).
               compromises those sites and injects exploit code (browser exploit,
               document exploit). waits for targets to visit. attack is passive
               from the attacker's perspective — targets deliver themselves.
  INSTANCES:   Council on Foreign Relations website (exploited by APT-related
               group, 2012 — IE zero-day); Operation Pawn Storm (APT28 watering
               hole campaigns, 2014+); iOS 0-click exploit chain on Uyghur news
               sites (disclosed by Google Project Zero, 2019 — 5 exploit chains,
               14 vulnerabilities, iOS 10-12).
  PREREQS:     browser or plugin zero-day (or known vulnerability targeting
               unpatched population); ability to compromise or MITM the
               watering hole site.
  INDICATORS:  drive-by download attempts from legitimate sites; browser process
               spawning unexpected child processes; network connections from
               browsers to unknown infrastructure.
  MITIGATIONS: browser patching (closes known vulnerability windows); sandboxing
               (limits post-exploitation options); JIT compilation hardening;
               site isolation; DNS-based filtering; threat intel feeds to block
               known watering hole domains; browser exploit telemetry.

[A19] SUPPLY CHAIN — AI MODEL WEIGHT POISONING
  CLASS:       ML supply chain — model-level compromise
  MECHANISM:   attacker publishes a model (or contributes to a training dataset)
               that contains a hidden backdoor. the model performs normally on
               clean inputs. when a specific trigger (pattern in input, specific
               token sequence, invisible perturbation) is present, the model
               outputs attacker-specified behavior. the backdoor survives fine-
               tuning in many architectures. model distributed via Hugging Face,
               PyPI, or similar — no signing, no provenance verification.
  INSTANCES:   academic: BadNets, Sleeper Agents (Anthropic 2024 — backdoor in
               LLM surviving RLHF); production: no confirmed public cases, but
               Hugging Face removed malicious models with embedded code (not
               behavioral backdoors, but supply chain intent confirmed, 2024).
  PREREQS:     ability to publish model to registry, or contribute to training
               pipeline.
  INDICATORS:  anomalous model behavior on trigger inputs; activation clustering
               analysis revealing bimodal behavior; model card audit; provenance
               chain verification.
  MITIGATIONS: model signing infrastructure (absent at scale); training data
               provenance tracking; behavioral testing across diverse input
               distributions; federated differential privacy (limits individual
               training sample influence); third-party model audits before
               enterprise deployment.

[A20] QUISHING — QR CODE PHISHING
  CLASS:       phishing via QR code obfuscation
  MECHANISM:   malicious URLs are embedded in QR codes in phishing emails or
               physical materials. email security gateways that analyze URLs in
               text fail to decode QR codes. mobile cameras scanning QR codes
               in a lower-scrutiny context (expected behavior from marketing
               materials). target visits malicious URL on mobile device where
               endpoint protection is weaker.
  INSTANCES:   large-scale quishing campaigns targeting executives via Microsoft
               Credentials phishing (2023); QR codes in physical parking meters
               redirecting to fake payment sites; conference badge QR codes
               replaced with malicious versions.
  PREREQS:     delivery mechanism (email, physical print, physical replacement).
  INDICATORS:  QR codes in unusual contexts (email body instead of attachment);
               QR code URL analysis by email security (requires QR decode capability).
  MITIGATIONS: email security tools with QR code URL extraction and analysis;
               user training on QR code skepticism; MFA (limits credential
               harvesting value); mobile device management with URL filtering.

[A21] SIM SWAPPING
  CLASS:       mobile carrier social engineering → account takeover
  MECHANISM:   attacker social engineers or bribes mobile carrier representative
               to transfer target's phone number to attacker-controlled SIM.
               all SMS and calls to target's number now received by attacker.
               SMS-based 2FA intercepted. "Forgot password" flows with SMS reset
               fully compromised. Bank, email, cryptocurrency accounts taken over.
  INSTANCES:   Twitter/Jack Dorsey account takeover (2019); $23.8M crypto theft
               via SIM swap (Michael Terpin vs. AT&T lawsuit); multiple celebrity
               accounts; Coinbase users systematically targeted; over $72M in
               US SIM swap losses 2018-2020 (FBI).
  PREREQS:     OSINT on target (phone number, carrier, partial SSN from breaches,
               carrier account PIN); either social engineering carrier rep or
               insider bribery.
  INDICATORS:  sudden loss of mobile service; carrier notification of SIM change.
  MITIGATIONS: port freeze / SIM lock at carrier; carrier account PIN and port-
               out protection; migrate all 2FA from SMS to TOTP or hardware key
               (YubiKey); use separate phone number not publicly associated with
               online accounts; passkeys (eliminate SMS as auth factor entirely).

[A22] OGNL INJECTION — APPLICATION SERVER RCE
  CLASS:       expression language injection → remote code execution
  MECHANISM:   Object-Graph Navigation Language (OGNL) is a Java expression
               language used by Apache Struts and other frameworks. when user-
               controlled input is processed by OGNL without sanitization, the
               attacker can inject arbitrary OGNL expressions that execute as
               Java code in the server's context. same root as SQL injection
               but in the application layer's expression evaluator.
  INSTANCES:   Apache Struts 2 S2-045 (CVE-2017-5638) — Content-Type header OGNL
               injection → Equifax breach (147M records, 2017); multiple Struts
               vulnerabilities 2013-2023; Confluence OGNL injection (CVE-2021-26084,
               CVE-2022-26134) — exploited by multiple APTs.
  PREREQS:     user input reaching OGNL evaluation; unpatched Struts/Confluence.
  INDICATORS:  unusual Java process spawning; unexpected outbound network connections
               from application servers; Confluence/Struts specific HTTP request
               patterns.
  MITIGATIONS: immediate patching (Struts/Confluence vulnerabilities exploited
               within hours of disclosure); WAF rules for OGNL patterns; input
               validation upstream of expression evaluation; retire Struts 2
               (EOL in 2024).

[A23] CRYPTOMINING / CRYPTOJACKING
  CLASS:       resource hijacking — computational theft
  MECHANISM:   malware installs cryptocurrency mining software on compromised
               systems. victims' CPU/GPU cycles used to mine cryptocurrency for
               attacker. primary objective: financial gain without ransomware's
               detection-triggering encryption. often deployed alongside other
               malware; mining is a secondary payload. cloud environments
               (misconfigured AWS, GCP, Azure credentials) targeted for unlimited
               horizontal scaling.
  INSTANCES:   Monero (XMR) preferred — privacy coin with CPU-optimized algorithm
               (RandomX). Coinhive (browser-based mining via JavaScript, 2017-2019
               — used to monetize web traffic, then abused). Travis CI environment
               variables exfiltrated for cloud mining (2021). Kubernetes clusters
               targeted (TeamTNT, 2020-2022). Tesla AWS account compromised for
               mining (2018).
  PREREQS:     initial access (any); or cloud credential theft; or browser JavaScript.
  INDICATORS:  sustained high CPU/GPU utilization on servers; unusual cloud compute
               billing spikes; network connections to known mining pools;
               cryptocurrency mining process signatures.
  MITIGATIONS: cloud resource quotas and billing alerts; EDR with process behavior
               detection; network egress filtering (block mining pool connections);
               strong cloud IAM (prevent credential exfiltration via SSRF/IMDSv1).

[A24] UNICODE / HOMOGLYPH ATTACKS
  CLASS:       visual deception via character substitution
  MECHANISM:   Unicode contains thousands of characters visually identical or
               similar to ASCII characters (е vs e, с vs c, а vs a — Cyrillic
               lookalikes). used in: domain names (IDN homograph attacks);
               source code (CVE-2021-42574 "Trojan Source" — bidirectional text
               control characters in code comments cause compiler to process
               different code than displayed); package names (typosquatting with
               homoglyphs); brand impersonation in phishing.
  INSTANCES:   IDN homograph attacks (apple.com with Cyrillic а); npm homoglyph
               packages; Trojan Source (Ross Anderson, 2021 — bidirectional
               control characters in code alter displayed vs. compiled logic);
               phishing domains using Unicode in email display names.
  PREREQS:     domain registration (for IDN attacks); package registry account
               (for supply chain); code contribution access (for Trojan Source).
  INDICATORS:  domain punycode (xn-- prefix indicates Unicode encoding); code
               review tools with Unicode character display; BIDI character
               detection in source scanners.
  MITIGATIONS: browser IDN display policy (Chrome shows punycode for suspicious
               lookalikes); code review tools that render BIDI control characters
               visibly; package registry homoglyph detection; DMARC for email;
               font selection that makes lookalikes visually distinct.

[A25] LOGIC BOMB
  CLASS:       time/condition-triggered destructive payload
  MECHANISM:   malware or insider places code in a legitimate system that executes
               a destructive payload when a specific condition is met (date, time,
               process execution, absence of a specific file or network response).
               the payload is dormant and indistinguishable from normal code until
               triggered. used by insiders (sabotage on termination), nation-states
               (pre-positioned infrastructure attack), and ransomware operators
               (delayed detonation).
  INSTANCES:   Roger Duronio (UBS Warburg — 2002: planted logic bomb to crash
               trading systems on resignation, triggered 2003, sentenced 8.5 years);
               Boeing IT administrator (2016, planted to corrupt aircraft maintenance
               software on termination, averted); Schneider Electric SCADA (Triton
               context — logic bomb in SIS before manual detonation); ransomware
               operators using scheduled tasks as detonation mechanism.
  PREREQS:     access to target system (insider, or prior compromise); ability to
               place persistent code.
  INDICATORS:  scheduled tasks created by non-standard accounts; unusual cron jobs;
               code review anomalies; file integrity monitoring deviations.
  MITIGATIONS: insider threat monitoring (UEBA); code review for production deployments;
               principle of least privilege (limit who can create scheduled tasks);
               file integrity monitoring; offboarding procedures (revoke access
               before, not after, notification); hardware-rooted attestation of
               production code.

[D05] MULTI-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (MFA) — PHISHING-RESISTANT VARIANTS
  CLASS:       authentication hardening
  MECHANISM:   authentication requires multiple factors: something you know
               (password), something you have (device, hardware key), something
               you are (biometric). phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2/WebAuthn
               hardware security keys (YubiKey, Google Titan) bind authentication
               to the specific relying party origin — a phishing site cannot
               receive the cryptographic assertion even if the user is tricked
               into clicking its link. passkeys: FIDO2 credential stored on
               device, biometric-unlocked, phishing-resistant by design.
  INSTANCES:   Google: YubiKey for all employees since 2017 — zero successful
               phishing attacks since deployment. CISA "Phishing-Resistant MFA"
               advisory (2022). Cloudflare post-Twilio hack analysis (2022):
               Cloudflare employees using FIDO2 keys were not compromised despite
               same phishing campaign that hit Twilio. NIST SP 800-63B: deprecated
               SMS OTP as MFA (no longer considered sufficiently phishing-resistant).
  COVERAGE:    phishing; credential stuffing (no MFA = no authentication even
               with valid credentials); SIM swapping (FIDO2 doesn't use SMS).
  GAPS:        MFA fatigue attacks (push notification flooding until user approves);
               adversary-in-the-middle proxies (Evilginx2 — relay attack captures
               session cookie post-MFA); social engineering of help desk to reset
               MFA (MGM 2023); MFA not deployed on all services.

[D06] ENDPOINT DETECTION AND RESPONSE (EDR)
  CLASS:       endpoint behavioral monitoring and response
  MECHANISM:   EDR agent installed on endpoint records: process creation (with
               command line), network connections, file operations, registry
               changes, memory operations, API calls. streams telemetry to central
               platform. ML and rule-based detection identifies attack patterns
               (LOLBIN abuse, credential dumping, lateral movement). automated
               response: isolate endpoint, kill process, quarantine file.
  INSTANCES:   CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne,
               Carbon Black. MITRE ATT&CK evaluation as independent benchmark.
               EDR was the technology that detected and contained SolarWinds in
               many organizations (via telemetry of anomalous SUNBURST behavior).
  COVERAGE:    malware execution; living-off-the-land abuse; lateral movement;
               credential dumping; command-and-control communications.
  GAPS:        EDR evasion via kernel-level rootkits (require EDR at kernel level
               to counter — arms race); EDR agents themselves vulnerable (CrowdStrike
               Falcon sensor crash (Blue Screen of Death) at scale, July 2024 —
               8.5M Windows systems affected by faulty content update); cloud
               workloads and IoT often have no EDR; BYOVD (Bring Your Own
               Vulnerable Driver) attacks use legitimate signed drivers to disable
               EDR kernel callbacks.

[D07] NETWORK SEGMENTATION AND MICROSEGMENTATION
  CLASS:       lateral movement containment
  MECHANISM:   divide network into isolated segments. traffic between segments
               requires explicit permit rules. compromise of one segment does
               not automatically grant access to others. microsegmentation:
               policy applied at the workload level (not VLAN boundary) — east-
               west traffic between individual VMs, containers, or processes
               controlled by software-defined networking policy.
  INSTANCES:   Google BeyondCorp as extreme microsegmentation (every resource
               request evaluated, no network-level trust). Illumio, Guardicore,
               VMware NSX — microsegmentation platforms. Healthcare network
               segmentation to isolate medical devices (FDA guidance 2023).
               Industrial network segmentation (Purdue model — ICS zones isolated
               from corporate IT).
  COVERAGE:    ransomware propagation; lateral movement; blast radius containment
               post-initial compromise; east-west attack traffic.
  GAPS:        accurate asset inventory required (unknown assets cannot be
               segmented); legitimate traffic flows must be mapped (complex in
               dynamic environments); performance overhead of deep packet
               inspection at microsegmentation points; insider threat (legitimate
               access traverses segmentation).

[D08] WEB APPLICATION FIREWALL (WAF) + RUNTIME APPLICATION SELF-PROTECTION (RASP)
  CLASS:       application-layer attack filtering
  MECHANISM:   WAF: reverse proxy that inspects HTTP/S request headers, URIs,
               and body against rule sets (OWASP Core Rule Set — CRS) to block
               SQLi, XSS, SSRF, path traversal, etc. RASP: agent embedded in
               application runtime that intercepts dangerous function calls
               (SQL execution, file system access, command execution) at the
               moment of execution — context-aware blocking that WAF cannot
               provide (WAF sees HTTP, RASP sees the function call).
  INSTANCES:   Cloudflare WAF, AWS WAF, ModSecurity (open source). RASP: Sqreen
               (acquired by Datadog), Contrast Security, Hdiv Security.
  COVERAGE:    OWASP Top 10 (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, path traversal); known vulnerability
               exploitation; zero-day mitigation via behavior patterns.
  GAPS:        WAF bypass via encoding, padding, novel syntax; RASP performance
               overhead; legitimate functionality matching attack signatures (false
               positives); encrypted traffic analysis limited; doesn't address
               business logic vulnerabilities; evasion via fragmentation.

[D09] THREAT INTELLIGENCE (CTI) — SHARING AND OPERATIONALIZATION
  CLASS:       adversary knowledge integration
  MECHANISM:   collection, analysis, and sharing of indicators of compromise (IoCs),
               tactics/techniques/procedures (TTPs), adversary infrastructure,
               and malware signatures. formats: STIX/TAXII (structured sharing);
               MISP (open source sharing platform). operationalized via: SIEM
               IOC feeds, EDR threat intelligence, firewall IP/domain blocklists,
               YARA rules. ISAC (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) per
               sector (FS-ISAC, H-ISAC, E-ISAC).
  INSTANCES:   FS-ISAC sharing during SWIFT banking attacks (2016); US CYBERCOM
               "Defend Forward" — sharing indicators from adversary network
               operations; CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog —
               mandatory patch deadlines for federal agencies.
  COVERAGE:    known adversary infrastructure detection; malware family identification;
               vulnerability prioritization (KEV = actively exploited = patch first).
  GAPS:        IoC half-life is hours to days (adversary rotates infrastructure);
               TTP sharing is more durable but less specific; quality varies across
               feeds; enrichment and deduplication required; sharing creates exposure
               of defender capabilities to adversary; classified intelligence
               not shareable with private sector.

[D10] DECEPTION TECHNOLOGY — HONEYPOTS AND HONEYNETS
  CLASS:       attacker detection via false assets
  MECHANISM:   deploy realistic-looking fake assets (servers, credentials,
               documents, Active Directory accounts, API keys) that have no
               legitimate use. any interaction with a decoy indicates attacker
               activity with high fidelity (low false positive). honeytokens:
               fake credentials/API keys placed in code repositories — when
               used, attacker reveals presence and location.
  INSTANCES:   Canary tokens (Thinkst — free service); honeypots in enterprise
               AD (fake privileged accounts with monitoring); honeynets in cloud
               environments (fake S3 buckets with AWS CloudTrail); Project Honey
               Pot (email honeypots); honeypots as research infrastructure (Cowrie
               SSH honeypot — IoT attack data collection).
  COVERAGE:    early detection of lateral movement; credential dumping detection
               (attacker uses honeypot credentials); scanning and reconnaissance
               detection.
  GAPS:        sophisticated attackers validate credentials before use (canarytoken
               bypass); honeypots require maintenance to remain realistic; high
               interaction honeypots are complex and expensive; decoys that are
               too obvious are avoided; does not prevent initial compromise.

[D11] SECURITY ORCHESTRATION, AUTOMATION AND RESPONSE (SOAR)
  CLASS:       security operations automation
  MECHANISM:   automated playbooks that integrate security tools (SIEM, EDR,
               threat intel, ticketing) to respond to alerts without human
               intervention for high-confidence, low-risk actions. playbook
               example: alert → enrich (look up IoC in threat intel) → correlate
               (check other endpoints) → auto-contain (isolate endpoint if
               confidence >90%) → create ticket → notify analyst. reduces mean
               time to respond (MTTR) from hours to minutes for known attack patterns.
  INSTANCES:   Palo Alto XSOAR, Splunk SOAR (Phantom), Siemplify (acquired Google).
               use cases: phishing triage (auto-pull email from all mailboxes,
               detonate attachment in sandbox, block sender); credential alert
               response (auto-force password reset, invalidate sessions).
  COVERAGE:    alert fatigue reduction; consistent response at machine speed;
               analyst focus on high-complexity cases.
  GAPS:        playbook quality determines response quality; novel attacks without
               playbooks pass through; integration complexity; automation errors
               at scale (auto-isolating production systems); adversarial response
               to automated playbooks (probe the automation).

[D12] PRIVILEGED ACCESS MANAGEMENT (PAM)
  CLASS:       privileged credential control
  MECHANISM:   vault for privileged credentials (root, domain admin, service accounts)
               with: just-in-time access (credentials issued only when needed,
               for defined duration, auto-rotated after); session recording
               (full video and keylog of all privileged sessions); MFA for vault
               access; zero standing privilege (no persistent admin credentials).
               PAM enforces: who can use what credentials, when, for how long,
               with full audit trail.
  INSTANCES:   CyberArk Privileged Access Security, BeyondTrust, Delinea (Thycotic).
               NIST SP 800-207 zero trust includes PAM as core component. US
               Executive Order 14028 specifies privileged access as priority.
  COVERAGE:    credential theft impact (vaulted credentials not accessible to
               malware); lateral movement via admin credentials; insider threat
               (full audit trail); regulatory compliance (SOX, PCI DSS, HIPAA).
  GAPS:        PAM bypass via Kerberos delegation abuse; session recording can
               be disabled if attacker has sufficient privilege; complexity creates
               operational friction that organizations circumvent; cloud workload
               identities (IAM roles) require separate control plane.

[D13] CHAOS ENGINEERING — RESILIENCE VALIDATION
  CLASS:       proactive resilience testing
  MECHANISM:   deliberately inject failures into production systems to validate
               that resilience mechanisms (failover, auto-scaling, circuit breakers)
               work as designed. extended to security: inject breach scenarios
               to test detection and response. Netflix Chaos Monkey (random EC2
               termination in production). GameDays: scheduled exercises where
               security team attacks own systems while operations team responds.
               Purple Team exercises: red team + blue team simultaneously to
               improve detection coverage in real time.
  INSTANCES:   Netflix Simian Army (2011+); AWS GameDay program; Google DiRT
               (Disaster Recovery Testing); CISA tabletop exercises; Gartner
               predicts 40% of enterprises use chaos engineering by 2025.
  COVERAGE:    detection gap discovery; incident response procedure validation;
               resilience assumption testing; mean time to detect (MTTD) reduction.
  GAPS:        chaos in production has real risk of unintended outages; scope
               limitation to tested scenarios; adversaries use novel techniques
               not covered by exercise assumptions; exercises require sustained
               organizational commitment that often lapses.

[D14] CONTENT SECURITY POLICY (CSP) + SUBRESOURCE INTEGRITY (SRI)
  CLASS:       browser-enforced web application security
  MECHANISM:   CSP: HTTP response header that specifies which sources are allowed
               to load scripts, styles, images, and other resources. a strict
               CSP blocks XSS by refusing to execute inline scripts and by
               limiting script sources to explicitly allowlisted origins. SRI:
               HTML tag attribute containing a cryptographic hash of the expected
               content of an external resource. browser verifies hash before
               executing — any modification (including CDN compromise or supply
               chain attack on the script) is detected.
  INSTANCES:   Google's strict CSP deployment (nonce-based); GitHub CSP (blocks
               Magecart-style attacks); npm deprecation of CDN links without SRI
               hashes. SRI blocks Magecart formjacking if third-party scripts
               use SRI hashes. PCI DSS 4.0 (2024): mandates script integrity
               monitoring on payment pages.
  COVERAGE:    XSS (inline script execution); Magecart/formjacking (external
               script tampering); data exfiltration (CSP connect-src restriction).
  GAPS:        CSP bypass via JSONP endpoints on allowlisted domains; eval() and
               dynamic code execution complicate strict policies; legacy codebases
               require significant refactoring for CSP compatibility; SRI requires
               hash update on every vendor script update.
