CYCLE 3 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CONTINUING CUMULATIVE LEDGER — PRIOR FINDINGS: C01–C12
NEW ENTRIES THIS CYCLE: C13–C22

─────────────────────────────────────────
SECTION 5A: IDENTICAL MECHANICS ACROSS DOMAINS (NEW)
─────────────────────────────────────────

[C13] SHARED MEDIUM AS EAVESDROPPING SURFACE
  MECHANIC:
    any resource shared between mutually distrusting parties leaks
    information about each party's usage to the others.
    the medium is the channel; partitioning is always incomplete.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → wireless RF: shared spectrum; passive listening requires no
      authentication; 802.11 beacons broadcast SSID, timing, rate
    → shared CPU cache: Spectre, Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe; cache
      timing leaks memory access patterns across process isolation
    → shared DRAM rows: RowHammer; charge leakage across cells
      violates the assumption that DRAM rows are isolated
    → shared CPU branch predictor: SpectreV2; branch predictor
      trained by attacker process used by victim process
    → shared cloud tenancy: co-residence attacks; VM timing,
      last-level cache contention, memory deduplication (KSM)
    → shared network switch: ARP cache poisoning; switch MAC table
      overflow (CAM overflow forces hub mode, enabling sniffing)
    → shared BGP peering: route leak visibility; even "private"
      routes visible to transit peers
    → shared power rail: PowerHammer; power line data exfiltration
      from air-gapped systems
  ROOT: the assumption that shared resource usage is private is
    false. physical sharing always creates an observable side channel.
    isolation is a software abstraction over hardware that does not
    enforce it at the physical layer.
  UNTRANSFERRED APPLICATION: database server shared memory segments,
    GPU VRAM sharing in multi-tenant ML inference, PCIe bus contention.
    none of these have the cache-timing attack tooling developed for CPU.

[C14] STATE MACHINE CONFUSION (DIFFERENTIAL PARSING)
  MECHANIC:
    sender and receiver each maintain a model of the protocol state.
    when those models diverge — due to ambiguous spec, implementation
    bugs, or deliberate manipulation — the gap between the two models
    is the attack surface. attacker crafts input that is parsed
    differently by two components that must agree on meaning.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → HTTP request smuggling: frontend proxy (HAProxy, nginx) and
      backend server parse Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding headers
      differently; attacker injects a "hidden" request into the gap
    → TLS renegotiation attack (2009, CVE-2009-3555): client
      renegotiates inside existing TLS session; server sees
      post-handshake data as if from initial client
    → BGP state machine: off-path RST injection during BGP session
      establishment exploits TCP-BGP state interaction
    → TCP session hijacking: sequence number prediction; attacker
      inserts into stream by predicting next acceptable sequence
    → PDF parser differential: malicious PDF parsed as benign by AV
      scanner (strict parser) but as executable by PDF reader (lenient)
    → ZIP file ambiguity: overlapping local and central directory
      entries; AV scanner and extractor see different contents
    → HTML parser differential: DOM-based XSS via browser parser
      interpreting tag soup differently from server-side sanitizer
    → SQL parser: WAF and database engine parse the same query string
      differently; WAF passes, database executes injected SQL
    → X.509 certificate parsing: null byte injection in CN
      (Moxie Marlinspike 2009); OpenSSL stopped at null, string
      comparison library did not
  ROOT: specifications rarely fully define behavior at edge cases.
    implementations fill gaps differently. wherever two implementations
    must agree on meaning and don't, a gap exists. the gap is exploitable
    if an attacker can craft input that lives in the gap.
  UNTRANSFERRED: serialization formats (protobuf, msgpack, CBOR) have
    no differential parsing security research equivalent to HTTP
    smuggling. gRPC interceptor chains almost certainly vulnerable to
    analogous issues. no systematic tooling exists.

[C15] REVOCATION AS STRUCTURALLY UNSOLVED PROBLEM
  MECHANIC:
    any system that issues credentials must be able to invalidate them
    before natural expiry. revocation requires a real-time channel from
    issuer to all relying parties. that channel either doesn't exist,
    is unreliable, introduces latency, or is itself a single point of
    failure. the result: revocation is either not checked, checked
    unreliably, or soft-fails open.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → TLS certificate revocation: CRL download (slow, large, often
      skipped); OCSP stapling (works if server supports it; soft-fail
      means browsers proceed if OCSP unreachable); OCSP Must-Staple
      (rarely deployed); Chrome removed OCSP checks entirely (2012)
    → JWT tokens: stateless by design; no built-in revocation;
      workarounds (short expiry, blocklist) undermine statelessness
    → OAuth access tokens: revocation endpoint exists (RFC 7009)
      but is advisory; resource servers often cache tokens; revocation
      doesn't propagate instantly
    → Kerberos tickets: ticket expiry is the only mechanism; no
      real-time revocation; golden ticket attack persists through
      password reset because revocation channel is the TGT itself
    → S/MIME and PGP: web of trust has no revocation channel;
      revocation certificates must be pre-distributed; revocation
      certificate can itself be suppressed
    → DNSSEC: zone signing key rotation is well-defined; key
      compromise revocation is not; trust anchor updates require
      RFC 5011 automated rollover or manual intervention
    → API keys: revocation is operator-defined and often incomplete;
      keys cached in CI/CD pipelines, documentation, third-party
      integrations; "rotation" events don't reach all consumers
    → Biometric credentials: cannot be revoked at all. a compromised
      fingerprint or face template is compromised permanently.
      revocation requires changing the biometric, which is impossible.
    → Code signing: certificate revocation doesn't retroactively
      invalidate signed binaries already in use; Windows treats
      expired signatures as valid if timestamp is before expiry
    → Quantum-resistant key migration: once current asymmetric keys
      are compromised by quantum, retroactive revocation of all
      signed/encrypted data is impossible; HNDL confirms this
  ROOT: revocation requires a real-time, authenticated, available
    channel from issuer to relying party. no such channel reliably
    exists at internet scale without itself being a critical dependency.
    systems optimize for availability and choose soft-fail, which
    means revocation is functionally inoperative under adversarial
    conditions — exactly when it is needed.
  CROSS-DOMAIN GAP: no domain has solved revocation. the structural
    constraint is identical everywhere. research from certificate
    transparency (append-only log as revocation complement) has not
    been fully transferred to API key management, biometrics, or
    identity federation.

[C16] NAMESPACE COLLISION AND SQUATTING
  MECHANIC:
    any naming system that maps identifiers to resources is vulnerable
    to confusion when the mapping is incomplete, inconsistent, or
    co-optable. attacker registers an identifier that a victim confuses
    with a legitimate resource. the namespace collision is the attack.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → DNS: typosquatting (goggle.com), homograph attack (using
      punycode lookalikes: xn--pple-43d.com for apple.com),
      IDN homograph (Cyrillic а vs Latin a)
    → npm/PyPI/RubyGems dependency confusion: internal package names
      are not registered in public registry; attacker registers same
      name publicly; package manager pulls attacker's version
      (Alex Birsan, 2021: compromised Microsoft, Apple, PayPal,
      Netflix, Tesla, Shopify, Yelp, Uber)
    → Docker Hub: official vs unofficial images; no clear namespace
      distinction; users pull malicious images with plausible names
    → IP address squatting: BGP prefix hijacking is namespace collision
      in the routing table; attacker announces victim's prefix
    → Username squatting: new employee's email (alice@corp.com) maps
      to old account with same username in legacy system
    → S3 bucket name squatting: subdomain takeover; abandoned S3
      bucket with DNS CNAME still pointing to it
    → Subdomain takeover: domain A has CNAME to B; B's resource is
      deleted; attacker registers B's resource and receives A's traffic
    → GitHub org squatting: company acquires startup; startup's old
      GitHub org name is taken by attacker
    → LoD (lookalike domain) for email: attacker registers corp-it.com
      for corp.com; employees respond to IT support phishing
  ROOT: namespaces exist to simplify reference. simplification
    introduces ambiguity. ambiguity is exploitable when parties make
    different assumptions about which entity a name refers to.
  UNTRANSFERRED: Kubernetes namespace collision (same resource name
    in different namespace; RBAC rules applied to wrong namespace),
    Terraform module registry squatting, and GitHub Actions workflow
    name collisions have not been systematically studied.

[C17] ABSENCE OF CLOSED-LOOP FEEDBACK IN SECURITY SYSTEMS
  MECHANIC:
    security systems produce outputs (alerts, blocks, patches) but
    rarely receive verified confirmation that those outputs achieved
    their intended security effect. the system operates open-loop.
    without feedback, degradation is invisible; false confidence
    accumulates; actual security posture diverges from perceived posture.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → SIEM alert fatigue: 10,000+ daily alerts; analysts triage by
      priority; low-priority alerts go uninvestigated; attacker
      operates below threshold; no feedback to SIEM that threshold
      is calibrated incorrectly
    → Vulnerability scanning: scanner reports N vulnerabilities;
      remediation team patches M of them; N-M remain; scanner
      next run shows N-M; feedback loop exists only if scanner
      tracks remediation; most do not track whether patch actually
      reduces risk
    → Firewall rules: rules accumulate over years; no mechanism
      to confirm which rules are still needed; shadow rules
      introduced that conflict with stated policy; no feedback
    → Security awareness training: phishing simulation sends fake
      phishing; click rate measured; no feedback on whether
      employees who clicked actually changed behavior long-term
    → Patch management: patch deployed; success/failure logged;
      no feedback on whether patch actually closes the
      exploitable attack path (patch may be incomplete or bypassed)
    → Antivirus signatures: signature deployed; telemetry shows
      detections; no feedback on undetected samples (unknown unknowns)
    → Password policies: policy enforces 12-char passwords; no
      feedback on whether users are using password managers vs
      incrementing a base password
    → Pen test findings: report delivered; remediation tracked;
      no feedback loop to confirm finding was actually fixed;
      next year's test often re-finds the same issues
  ANALOGY: control theory. a control system without feedback (open-loop)
    drifts. security is a control problem. every security system is an
    open-loop controller. the closed-loop equivalent (verified effect
    measurement) is almost never implemented.
  ROOT: measuring outputs is easy; measuring security effects is hard.
    security effect measurement requires knowing what attacks would
    have succeeded without the control, which requires counterfactual
    knowledge. the field defaults to measuring what is measurable
    (alert count, patch count, training completion rate) rather than
    what is relevant (attack success rate under current posture).

[C18] CONFUSED DEPUTY MECHANIC ACROSS DOMAINS
  MECHANIC:
    a system component (the deputy) is granted authority to act on
    behalf of a principal. the deputy is then manipulated by a
    third party to exercise that authority for the attacker's
    benefit. the deputy's authority is not in question; the problem
    is that the deputy cannot distinguish legitimate from malicious
    exercise of that authority.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → CSRF: browser is the deputy; holds session cookie; attacker's
      page triggers request from browser; browser cannot distinguish
      intended from cross-site request
    → SSRF: server-side HTTP client is the deputy; holds access to
      internal network; attacker causes server to fetch attacker-
      controlled URLs; server accesses internal resources on attacker's
      behalf (AWS IMDSv1 / Capital One 2019)
    → Windows print spooler escalation (PrintNightmare): print
      spooler runs as SYSTEM; loads driver DLLs; attacker-controlled
      driver loaded by high-privilege deputy
    → AWS IAM cross-account: account A trusts account B's role;
      role in account B is compromised; attacker uses account A's
      resources through the trusted deputy relationship
    → OAuth implicit flow: browser is the deputy; access token
      delivered in URL fragment; attacker in a position to observe
      the URL (malicious redirect_uri) captures the token
    → Kubernetes service account token auto-mount: pod is the deputy;
      token auto-mounted at known path; compromised pod uses token
      to call Kubernetes API with service account's authority
    → Electron/Chromium embedded shell: Electron app is the deputy;
      nodeIntegration: true allows web content to call Node.js APIs;
      XSS in web content becomes RCE through the deputy
    → Dependency in build pipeline: build system is the deputy;
      runs dependencies with build-system privilege; malicious
      dependency (SolarWinds, XZ Utils) executes in that context
  ROOT: Norman Hardy (1988) named and formalized the confused deputy
    problem. the fix is capability-based security: the deputy should
    hold only the capability needed for each specific action, not
    ambient authority. ambient authority is the norm; capability
    security is the rare exception.
  APPLICATION NOT YET TRANSFERRED: LLM tool use. the LLM is the deputy.
    it holds API keys, file system access, code execution authority.
    prompt injection attacks are confused deputy attacks: malicious
    content in the environment manipulates the LLM to exercise its
    authority for the attacker. the framing has not been formalized.
    mitigations from the 1988 paper have not been systematically applied.

[C19] INFORMATION-THEORETIC LIMITS ON DETECTION
  MECHANIC:
    detection systems work by finding signal in noise. the attacker
    controls signal-to-noise ratio: by staying below the noise floor,
    an attacker is information-theoretically undetectable regardless
    of detector sophistication. no algorithm can distinguish signal
    from noise if the signal is below the noise floor.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → APT low-and-slow exfiltration: data exfiltrated at rates
      indistinguishable from normal traffic; Volt Typhoon-style
      operations generate traffic within normal baselines
    → DNS tunneling at low rate: single DNS query every 10 minutes
      is indistinguishable from legitimate DNS lookups; high-rate
      DNS tunneling is detectable; low-rate is not
    → Steganography: information hidden in image LSBs; carrier
      capacity is the noise floor; content hidden below perceptual
      threshold is undetectable without the stego key
    → SIEM threshold tuning: attacker studies alert thresholds
      through recon or open intelligence; operates below all thresholds
    → Insider threat: malicious insider copies data at the rate
      a normal employee accesses data; baseline is the insider's
      own normal behavior; deviation is zero by definition
    → Network behavior analytics: ML baseline built on historical
      traffic; attacker who has studied the environment and operates
      within normal-range parameters generates no anomaly
    → Deepfake detection: as synthesis quality approaches perceptual
      threshold, detection reduces to statistical noise discrimination;
      below threshold = undetectable
    → Side-channel masking: a correctly implemented masked circuit
      leaks information at a rate below the measurement noise floor;
      DPA on masked implementations requires exponentially more traces
  SHANNON CONNECTION: mutual information between the attack and the
    observable signal is the theoretical maximum detection capability.
    if mutual information is zero (attacker perfectly mimics benign
    behavior), detection is information-theoretically impossible.
  IMPLICATION: detection-based security has a fundamental ceiling.
    any detection architecture that does not also raise the noise
    floor (deception, canaries, honeypots) or reduce attacker
    signal precision (attribution complexity) cannot cross the
    information-theoretic limit. the field has not internalized
    this constraint.

[C20] GAME-THEORETIC STRUCTURE OF VULNERABILITY MARKETS
  MECHANIC:
    vulnerability discovery and disclosure exists within a multi-player
    game: discoverer, vendor, national intelligence service, criminal,
    broker, researcher, public. each player has different payoff
    functions and information asymmetries. equilibrium outcomes depend
    on payoffs, not on formal disclosure policies.
  GAME STRUCTURE:
    → discoverer payoffs: disclosure = reputation + bug bounty;
      silence = broker payment ($0.1M–$10M) or government contract;
      optimal play: sell to highest bidder; formal policy is not
      a constraint
    → vendor payoffs: fast patch = reduced liability, reputation;
      slow patch = cost savings, plausible deniability; emergency
      patch = operational disruption; equilibrium: patch as slowly
      as the disclosure window allows
    → national intelligence: known vulnerability = offensive capability;
      disclosed vulnerability = shared capability; disclose only when
      capability is already exceeded by suspected adversary knowledge
      (NSA Equation Group / WannaCry: EternalBlue disclosed after
      Shadow Brokers leak, not proactively)
    → criminal market: zero-day price in criminal markets ($5K–$500K
      for RCE in popular software); vulnerability stockpiling for
      ransomware operations; Zerodium, Exploit.in pricing as signal
    → multi-discoverer problem: multiple parties may hold the same
      vulnerability simultaneously; each party's disclosure decision
      depends on probability that others will disclose first
    → CVD prisoner's dilemma: researcher and vendor both benefit from
      coordinated disclosure; each individually benefits from
      defection (researcher: fame; vendor: no disclosure); cooperation
      is unstable without enforcement
  ROOT: the policy framework (responsible disclosure, CVD, bug bounties)
    assumes a cooperative game. the actual game is competitive with
    multiple non-cooperating players. policy instruments work only
    when payoffs align; they fail when payoffs favor defection.
    no policymaker has formally modeled the full game and designed
    around actual equilibria.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SECTION 5B: UNTRANSFERRED PATTERNS — EXTENDED
─────────────────────────────────────────

[U01] BIOLOGICAL IMMUNE SYSTEM → SOC ARCHITECTURE
  BIOLOGICAL PATTERN:
    innate immune system: fast, non-specific, pattern-recognition
    receptors (toll-like receptors) detect broad pathogen classes.
    adaptive immune system: slow, specific, generates targeted
    antibodies; immunological memory persists after first exposure.
    clonal selection: B-cells with matching receptors proliferate.
    tolerance: self-recognition prevents autoimmunity.
  TRANSFERRED:
    → signature-based AV ≈ innate immunity (pattern matching)
    → threat intelligence feeds ≈ immunological memory (prior exposure)
  NOT TRANSFERRED:
    → clonal selection: why doesn't the SOC automatically proliferate
      detection capability toward attack patterns that match, and
      suppress capability that never fires (autoimmunity equivalent)?
    → tolerance (self-recognition): the immune system learns to
      not attack self-tissue. EDR/XDR has no equivalent for
      "known-safe behavior of legitimate processes" — false positive
      rate is the autoimmunity failure; no mechanism analogous to
      thymic selection for building software self-tolerance
    → germline diversity: immune system maintains genetic diversity
      in receptor repertoire to ensure coverage of unknown antigens.
      monocultural SOC tools with shared signatures have no equivalent
      of receptor diversity; a single evasion technique defeats all
      instances of the monoculture simultaneously
    → inflammation regulation: innate immunity can cause collateral
      damage (cytokine storm); SOC response to incident can cause
      collateral damage (blocking legitimate traffic, user lockout);
      no formal analog to anti-inflammatory regulation exists in IR

[U02] EPIDEMIOLOGICAL MODELS → PATCH DEPLOYMENT OPTIMIZATION
  EPIDEMIOLOGICAL PATTERN:
    SIR/SEIR models: Susceptible → Exposed → Infected → Recovered.
    R0 (basic reproduction number): expected secondary infections per
    infected individual. herd immunity threshold: 1 - 1/R0 of
    population immune prevents epidemic propagation.
    superspreader events: heterogeneous transmission; 20% of
    individuals cause 80% of transmissions (20/80 rule).
  TRANSFERRED: researchers have applied SIR models to worm propagation
    (Slammer 2003, Code Red 2001) to predict spread rate.
  NOT TRANSFERRED:
    → patch deployment optimization: herd immunity threshold for
      vulnerabilities. if R0 (exploitability × connectivity ×
      exposure time) is known, what patch adoption rate creates
      herd immunity? this has never been operationalized.
    → superspreader identification: which systems are superspreaders?
      high-degree nodes in enterprise network (domain controllers,
      exchange servers, VPN concentrators) are equivalent to
      superspreaders. patching them first has disproportionate
      effect on herd immunity. no patch prioritization framework
      uses epidemiological superspreader logic.
    → contact tracing: epidemic contact tracing maps exposure networks
      to identify at-risk individuals. cyber equivalent: blast radius
      analysis for vulnerabilities. blast radius analysis exists but
      is not integrated into patch prioritization at the mathematical
      rigor of contact tracing.
    → heterogeneous susceptibility: not all systems are equally
      susceptible. epidemiology handles this. vulnerability management
      treats all unpatched instances as equally susceptible.

[U03] AVIATION SAFETY CULTURE → CYBER INCIDENT RESPONSE
  AVIATION PATTERN:
    just culture: distinguishes honest mistakes from reckless behavior;
    punishes only reckless behavior; encourages error reporting.
    near-miss reporting: mandatory, anonymous reporting of incidents
    that did not result in accident; near-miss data is primary
    input to systemic safety improvement.
    swiss cheese model: accidents result from alignment of holes
    across multiple defense layers; no single cause.
    crew resource management: structured communication protocols
    to prevent authority gradients from suppressing safety-critical
    information.
  TRANSFERRED: some organizations have adopted blameless post-mortems
    (Google SRE model). swiss cheese is occasionally referenced.
  NOT TRANSFERRED:
    → mandatory near-miss reporting: aviation has anonymous, mandatory,
      legal-protection near-miss reporting (NASA ASRS). cybersecurity
      has no equivalent. incidents are disclosed if legally required;
      near-misses almost never disclosed. the data that would
      improve systemic security is systematically withheld.
    → crew resource management for SOC: no structured communication
      protocol for incident response that addresses authority
      gradient (senior analyst's wrong hypothesis cannot be challenged
      by junior analyst). IR guidance documents contain no equivalent.
    → airworthiness certification: aircraft cannot fly without
      airworthiness certificate issued by independent authority after
      systematic testing. software has no equivalent; even critical
      software is self-certified.
    → accident investigation board: independent, non-punitive,
      legally protected investigation of major accidents. cybersecurity
      has no equivalent; breach investigations are conducted by
      vendors with financial interests, or by legal teams managing
      liability, not safety.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SECTION 5C: ATTACK CLASSES WITH NO DEFENSE ANALOG
─────────────────────────────────────────

[NO-DEFENSE-01] HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (HNDL)
  ATTACK: passive collection of encrypted traffic today; decryption
    when quantum computing reaches sufficient scale. requires zero
    network interaction with target. fully passive. leaves no trace.
  NO DEFENSE ANALOG: there is no way to retroactively protect data
    already collected. migration to post-quantum cryptography protects
    future communications; it does not protect past communications.
    data with long secrecy requirements (state secrets, medical records,
    trade secrets) that were encrypted before ~2015 may already be
    collected and awaiting decryption.

[NO-DEFENSE-02] AI TRAINING DATA POISONING AT CORPUS SCALE
  ATTACK: poisoning training data before ML model training. if the
    training corpus is drawn from internet data (Common Crawl, GitHub,
    Wikipedia), adversary who controls or can write to those sources
    can influence the model. Carlini et al. demonstrated that 0.01%
    of training data poisoning causes measurable behavior change.
  NO DEFENSE ANALOG: there is no cryptographic provenance standard
    for training data. there is no certified method to detect
    backdoors in trained models with mathematical guarantee.
    model cards describe intended behavior, not verified behavior.
    the field has no audit mechanism equivalent to source code review
    for verifying that a model does not contain poisoned behavior.

[NO-DEFENSE-03] LONG-DURATION PRE-POSITIONING (VOLT TYPHOON PATTERN)
  ATTACK: nation-state actor pre-positions in critical infrastructure
    networks (telecom, power, water, transportation) years before
    intended operational use. operates using living-off-the-land
    techniques; leaves no malware; uses legitimate tools and credentials.
    CISA advisory (2024): Volt Typhoon maintained access for 5+ years
    in some cases.
  NO DEFENSE ANALOG: detection requires anomaly detection against
    a baseline that includes the attacker's normal operations. once
    an attacker is inside and has established a behavioral baseline,
    they are indistinguishable from a legitimate operator. no
    detection technology has a demonstrated capability to distinguish
    a long-established insider from a nation-state actor using
    identical tools and protocols.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SECTION 5D: DEFENSE MECHANISMS NOT APPLIED WHERE APPLICABLE
─────────────────────────────────────────

[MISSING-D01] CERTIFICATE TRANSPARENCY → IDENTITY FEDERATION
  MECHANISM: CT creates an append-only, publicly auditable log of all
    issued TLS certificates. any certificate not in the log is rejected
    by browsers. this prevents mis-issuance from being undetected.
  NOT APPLIED: identity federation (SAML, OAuth, OIDC) has no
    equivalent. a compromised identity provider can issue assertions
    for any identity in its domain; there is no public log of issued
    assertions; there is no mechanism for a relying party to detect
    that an assertion was issued without the user's participation.
    SolarWinds SAML forgery attack exploited exactly this gap.

[MISSING-D02] CODE SIGNING → AI WEIGHT INTEGRITY
  MECHANISM: code signing creates a cryptographic binding between
    a binary and its publisher. tampering with the binary breaks
    the signature. consumers can verify the binary is unmodified.
  NOT APPLIED: AI model weights are distributed without cryptographic
    signing standard. a Hugging Face model's weights could be modified
    in transit or at rest; the consumer has no mechanism to verify
    the weights match the intended model. ML model signing is a
    proposed solution (Sigstore for ML) but is not deployed at scale.

[MISSING-D03] NUCLEAR TWO-PERSON INTEGRITY → AI DEPLOYMENT GATES
  MECHANISM: nuclear launch requires two independent operators to
    simultaneously authenticate and act. no single person can
    authorize a launch. mechanical design ensures physical separation.
  NOT APPLIED: AI model deployment, including models with autonomous
    action capability (tool use, code execution, API access), has no
    equivalent two-person integrity requirement. a single developer
    with CI/CD access can deploy a model update. the attack surface
    is identical to a single-person nuclear launch authorization.
    no organization has implemented a mandatory two-person gate for
    capability-expanding AI model updates.

[D-NEW-01] DARK WEB AND CRIMINAL ECOSYSTEM ECONOMICS

    → criminal forum infrastructure: exploit.in, raidforums history,

    → cryptocurrency infrastructure for crime: mixing, chain-hopping,

    → bulletproof hosting: jurisdiction-shopping for infrastructure

      Safari renderer $250K+ (Zerodium 2024 price list)

[D-NEW-02] ADVERSARIAL AI AT INFERENCE TIME (EXPANDED)
  sub-domains:
    → model inversion attacks: recovering training data from model
      outputs; Fredrikson et al. (2015): pharmacogenetic model
      inverted to recover patient records
    → membership inference attacks: determining whether a specific
      record was in the training set; Shokri et al. (2017)
    → model extraction/stealing: querying a model API to reconstruct
      a functionally equivalent model; Tramèr et al. (2016)
    → transferability of adversarial examples: adversarial examples
      crafted for one model often transfer to other models with
      different architecture
    → adversarial patch in video: physical patch that persists
      across video frames; attacks real-time object detection
    → LLM jailbreaking taxonomy: direct jailbreak (DAN), many-shot
      jailbreaking, base64 encoding, roleplay framing, suffix attack
      (Zou et al. 2023 GCG: automated adversarial suffix generation)
    → multi-modal adversarial attack: adversarial perturbation
      in image that modifies LLM with vision capability behavior
    → RAG poisoning: injecting adversarial documents into the
      retrieval corpus; retrieved adversarial content manipulates
      generation

[D-NEW-03] QUANTUM NETWORKING AND QUANTUM KEY DISTRIBUTION
  sub-domains:
    → QKD protocol taxonomy: BB84, E91, B92, SARG04, device-
      independent QKD
    → QKD implementation attacks: photon number splitting (PNS)
      attack on weak coherent pulse implementations; detector
      blinding attack (Makarov 2010 — controlled bright
      illumination blinds avalanche photodiodes, allowing
      intercept-resend without detection)
    → quantum repeater security: entanglement swapping introduces
      trusted node problem; quantum memory security
    → quantum internet architecture: DARPA/EU Quantum Internet
      Alliance roadmap; trusted node vs. untrusted relay models
    → post-quantum vs QKD: complementary not competing;
      PQC addresses computational security; QKD addresses
      information-theoretic security; QKD has implementation
      vulnerabilities; PQC has algorithm risk

[D-NEW-04] SYNTHETIC BIOLOGY AS DUAL-USE THREAT SURFACE
  sub-domains:
    → DNA synthesis and biosecurity: IGSC screening protocols;
      gaps in distributed synthesis; home synthesis trajectory
    → engineered pathogen potential: gain-of-function research
      governance; dual-use research of concern (DURC) policy
    → bioweapons convention gaps: verification mechanism absent
      (unlike Chemical Weapons Convention); attribution challenge
      for engineered biological agents
    → biosurveillance as cyber-adjacent: pathogen genomic
      sequence databases as intelligence target; genomic data
      as biometric identifier
    → cyber-bio convergence: automated lab systems (liquid handling
      robots, gene synthesis machines) as cyber-physical attack
      surface; malicious DNA sequences that exploit bioinformatics
      software vulnerabilities (Ney et al. 2017: malware encoded
      in DNA that compromises sequencing software)
    → biometric data as permanent identifier: DNA as ultimate
      biometric; DNA database security; genealogy database
      privacy (GEDMatch used in Golden State Killer investigation)

[D-NEW-05] COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE OF SOCIAL ENGINEERING
  sub-domains:
    → attention and working memory: security warning habituation;
      SSL warning bypass rate as attention measurement
    → dual process theory (Kahneman System 1/System 2):
      social engineering exploits System 1 (fast, automatic,
      heuristic); security requires System 2 (slow, deliberate,
      effortful); high cognitive load suppresses System 2
    → authority heuristic exploitation: Milgram obedience studies
      apply directly to vishing; authority + urgency = compliance
    → social proof exploitation: "others have already verified"
      framing in phishing reduces critical evaluation
    → loss aversion: threat framing ("your account will be
      suspended") more effective than gain framing (Kahneman-
      Tversky; prospect theory applied to phishing)
    → commitment and consistency: foot-in-the-door technique
      in multi-stage social engineering (small compliance →
      larger compliance, e.g. XZ Utils years-long relationship)
    → inattentional blindness: users who are focused on completing
      a task do not notice security warnings in peripheral attention
    → source monitoring error: memory for information separate
      from memory for source; users remember the fact but not
      that it came from a phishing email

CYCLE 4 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[P29] RANSOMWARE-AS-A-SERVICE INDUSTRIALIZATION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    mechanism: ransomware began as operator-controlled, single-actor
      malware (CryptoLocker 2013; operator holds decrypt key,
      demands payment, executes every stage alone).
    historical instances:
      → CryptoLocker (2013): GameOver Zeus botnet delivery;
        RSA-2048 encryption; $300 bitcoin demand; Gameover Zeus
        botnet takedown (2014) recovered private keys
      → CryptoWall (2014-2015): distributed via malvertising;
        estimated $325M in damages (FBI report 2015)
      → TeslaCrypt (2015-2016): targeted gaming files; developers
        publicly released master decryption key on shutdown
      → Locky (2016): Word macro delivery; .locky extension;
        peak $1M/day revenue estimated
      → Petya/GoldenEye (2016): overwrote MBR; combined disk
        encryption with file encryption

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    mechanism: RaaS model separates roles: core developer (maintains
      encryptor, decryptor, negotiation portal, leak site) earns
      ~20-30% of ransom; affiliate (conducts intrusion, deploys
      ransomware, negotiates) earns ~70-80%.
      double extortion standard: encrypt files AND exfiltrate
        data; threaten to publish on leak site if ransom unpaid.
      triple extortion: add DDoS against victim as third pressure
        (REvil used this against Kaseya victims 2021).
      quadruple extortion: direct contact to victim's customers
        or regulator to pressure payment.
    active RaaS groups (as of knowledge cutoff):
      → LockBit: most prolific RaaS 2022-2024; affiliate program
        with public recruitment; law enforcement takedown Feb 2024
        (Operation Cronos); LockBit 3.0 re-emerged within weeks
      → BlackCat/ALPHV: Rust-based encryptor; cross-platform
        (Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi); FBI takedown Dec 2023;
        affiliate defected with $22M ransom for Change Healthcare;
        ALPHV executed exit scam against affiliates
      → Play ransomware: operates without public RaaS program;
        double extortion; targets ESXi
      → Clop: MOVEit vulnerability exploitation (2023): exfiltrated
        data from 2,500+ organizations without deploying ransomware
        encryptor; pure extortion without encryption
      → Akira, Hunters International, BlackSuit, RansomHub

TEMPORAL LAYER — TRAJECTORY:
    → AI-enhanced phishing and initial access: LLM-generated
      spear phishing at scale will drive IAB market
    → encryptionless extortion growth: Clop MOVEit model;
      if exfiltration alone generates payment, encryption adds
      operational complexity with no revenue benefit
    → critical infrastructure targeting increase: US law
      enforcement actions (Hive takedown 2023, LockBit 2024)
      push remaining groups toward targets with higher payment
      incentive and lower enforcement risk (non-US jurisdictions)
    → cryptocurrency regulation pressure: OFAC sanctions on
      ransomware groups (Evil Corp, Conti members); compliance
      pressure on crypto exchanges limits ransom settlement;
      pushes groups toward Monero, privacy coin mixers

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: encryptionless data extortion will surpass
      traditional encrypt-and-ransom as primary criminal model.
      the MOVEit campaign demonstrated that exfiltration alone
      generates payment without deployment risk of encryptor.
      as defender detection of encryptors improves (EDR behavioral
      detection of rapid file modification), the cost/benefit
      of encryption shifts against the attacker.
    confidence: 0.72
    timeline: dominant model by 2027-2028

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "map the economic game theory of ransomware RaaS: under what
    conditions does an affiliate defect against the core operator
    (as occurred in BlackCat/Change Healthcare)? when does
    encryptionless extortion dominate? model as multi-stage game
    with law enforcement as third player whose enforcement
    probability affects equilibrium strategies. identify the
    conditions under which cryptocurrency regulation shifts
    equilibrium toward cash-equivalent ransom or toward
    criminal market exit."

[P30] ZERO-CLICK MOBILE EXPLOIT EVOLUTION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    mechanism: mobile exploit chains require user interaction
      in first generation. smishing, malicious app installation,
      phishing link click required.
    historical instances:
      → early Android malware (2010-2012): primarily malicious
        apps distributed outside Play Store; required user install
      → first iOS jailbreaks as proof-of-concept exploit chains:
        demonstrated full browser-to-persistence chains but not
        weaponized for surveillance
      → Hacking Team leak (2015): RCS Android and iOS implants
        revealed; still required some interaction

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    mechanism: zero-click exploits require no user interaction.
      attack surface: message parsing (iMessage, WhatsApp, SMS),
      media parsing (image, video, audio delivered silently),
      baseband processor (untethered RCE via baseband before
      application processor).
    historical instances:
      → FORCEDENTRY (NSO Group, 2021): iMessage zero-click;
        exploited JBIG2 compression parser in ImageIO;
        delivered GIF with embedded JBIG2 payload; achieved
        sandbox escape and kernel exploit from parsing a
        message the user never touched; Citizen Lab attributed
        to NSO Group; Apple emergency patch (CVE-2021-30860)
      → Kismet (NSO Group, 2019): iMessage zero-click;
        pre-dates FORCEDENTRY; mechanism published by Citizen Lab
      → BLASTPASS (NSO Group, 2023): iMessage zero-click;
        PassKit library parsing of malicious image attachment;
        CVE-2023-41064 + CVE-2023-41061; Apple LOCKDOWN MODE
        blocked it
      → Samsung Exynos baseband (Project Zero, 2023): 18
        baseband RCE vulnerabilities; some exploitable remotely
        via call initiation with no user interaction
      → TETRA:BURST (2023): TETRA radio protocol vulnerabilities;
        zero-click over air interface affecting critical
        infrastructure radios (police, military, emergency services)

TEMPORAL LAYER — TRAJECTORY:
    → Lockdown Mode and memory-safe message parsing as defense;
      reduces attack surface but does not eliminate it
    → baseband attack surface growth: more complex baseband
      firmwares, more protocols (5G NR, NTN satellite 5G)
      expand the parser attack surface
    → AI-assisted exploit generation: Anthropic, Google, academic
      research demonstrating LLM-assisted bug finding; will
      accelerate zero-click discovery rate
    → satellite phone and IoT communication baseband:
      largely unstudied; likely contains similar classes to
      Exynos baseband vulnerabilities

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: the baseband processor is the next major zero-click
      attack surface. application processor security (ASLR, PAC,
      MTE, sandboxing) has improved significantly. baseband
      firmware is written in C, without these mitigations, running
      complex protocol stacks (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G, satellite).
      it executes before the application processor in many threat
      models and has direct memory bus access in some implementations.
      a weaponized baseband zero-click capable of implanting
      persistent access represents a capability ceiling above which
      no application-layer defense can reach.
    confidence: 0.80
    timeline: public attribution of weaponized baseband zero-click
      used in surveillance operations by 2026-2027.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "systematically enumerate the attack surface of 5G NR baseband
    modem firmware. focus on: (1) NAS/RRC protocol parsers;
    (2) PDCP/RLC layer handling; (3) handover/cell reselection
    procedures; (4) emergency call handling (bypasses some security);
    (5) inter-RAT handover (4G→5G and reverse). compare security
    properties of Qualcomm Snapdragon, MediaTek Dimensity, Samsung
    Exynos, and Apple A-series modem architectures. quantify the
    memory safety exposure in lines of code and parser complexity."

[P31] FORMAL VERIFICATION ADOPTION RATE VS ATTACK SOPHISTICATION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    → formal verification existed as academic discipline since 1970s
      (Hoare logic, 1969; Floyd 1967). practically ignored by
      industry due to cost and expertise requirements.
    → seL4 microkernel (2009): NICTA; first formal proof of
      correctness and security properties for a general-purpose OS
      kernel; 10,000 lines of C; full functional correctness proof
    → CompCert (2006-present): formally verified C compiler;
      Xavier Leroy, INRIA; proof that compiled code behaves as
      specified by C source; used in aviation (DO-178C)

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    → s2n-tls (AWS): formally verified TLS implementation components
    → BoringSSL (Google): ongoing formal verification effort
    → HACL* (Project Everest, Microsoft Research/Inria): formally
      verified cryptographic library; used in Firefox NSS,
      WireGuard, Zinc
    → EverCrypt: verified cryptographic provider
    → Rust ownership type system: not formal verification but
      compile-time memory safety proof; eliminates broad classes
    → TLA+ adoption: Amazon Web Services engineering culture;
      engineering teams required to write TLA+ specs for
      distributed protocols; found bugs in DynamoDB, S3
    → dafny (Microsoft): verification-aware programming language;
      used in Azure components
    → adoption rate: extremely low outside specific high-assurance
      contexts; <0.01% of production code formally verified

TEMPORAL LAYER — TRAJECTORY:
    → LLM-assisted proof generation: Lean 4, Coq with LLM copilots;
      lowers barrier to writing proofs; may accelerate adoption
    → AI-generated code verification: as LLM-generated code enters
      production, formal verification of LLM output becomes
      tractable as a pipeline step
    → hardware formal verification: Intel, ARM increasing use of
      formal methods after Spectre/Meltdown demonstrated that
      informal reasoning about microarchitectural security fails

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: the gap between attack sophistication and formal
      verification adoption is widening, not closing. attack
      tools (AI-assisted exploit generation, automated fuzzing,
      symbolic execution) advance faster than defensive formal
      verification deployment. the asymmetry is structural:
      finding bugs requires finding one path that fails;
      proving correctness requires proving all paths succeed.
    confidence: 0.85
    timeline: persistent; no crossover before 2030 except in
      narrow high-assurance niches.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "what is the minimum formal verification surface that produces
    maximum risk reduction? if 100% verification is intractable,
    which components of a system — when verified — eliminate the
    most exploitable vulnerability classes? analyze: (1) allocator
    correctness; (2) cryptographic primitive implementation;
    (3) parser entry points for untrusted input; (4) privilege
    boundary crossing code. calculate the ratio of verification
    cost to vulnerability class elimination for each."

[P32] CRIMINAL ECOSYSTEM SPECIALIZATION AND LABOR DIVISION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    → early cybercrime: vertically integrated single actors or
      small groups performed all stages (write malware, distribute,
      monetize); skill barrier was high; volume was low
    → carder forums (2000s): early specialization; card skimmer
      operators, card encoders, cash-out specialists in separate
      roles; carderplanet, shadowcrew

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    → fully industrialized specialization:
      IAB (initial access broker): compromises networks, sells
        access ($100–$100K+ depending on org size, revenue, sector)
      malware-as-a-service: SmokeLoader, IcedID, Emotet-successor
        loaders rented per deployment
      crypter/packer services: evade AV detection; offered as
        subscription ($50-500/month)
      RaaS affiliate program: buy access from IAB, deploy ransomware
        from RaaS provider, negotiate ransom
      money mule networks: cash-out and layering services
      OPSEC consultants: operational security guidance for criminal
        groups; compartmentalization; crypto wallet hygiene
      negotiation specialists: ransomware negotiation firms
        (professionalized on both criminal and victim sides)
    → criminal ecosystem has lower OPSEC burden than solo actor;
      specialized roles reduce each actor's exposure
    → law enforcement disruption is isolated: takedown of one
      layer does not disrupt others; Hive takedown didn't stop
      affiliates from moving to LockBit

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: criminal ecosystem specialization has reached
      industrial maturity. the barrier to entry for ransomware
      operations has fallen from "write malware" to "buy access
      from IAB, buy ransomware from RaaS affiliate program."
      this structural change means law enforcement disruption
      of any single node has diminishing impact on criminal output.
    confidence: 0.90
    timeline: present state; trajectory continues.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "model the criminal ecosystem as a supply chain. identify
    which nodes, if disrupted, cause maximum supply chain
    disruption. compare: (1) core RaaS operator takedown;
    (2) IAB market disruption; (3) cryptocurrency mixer and
    settlement infrastructure disruption; (4) bulletproof
    hosting provider disruption. which disruption strategy
    produces maximum second-order effects? quantify using
    publicly available law enforcement post-action reports."

[P33] AI-GENERATED SYNTHETIC MEDIA AS AUTHENTICATION BYPASS

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    → deepfakes required significant compute and training time;
      limited to sophisticated actors (2017-2020)
    → first large-scale deepfake attempts: Gabon presidential
      video (2018, disputed authenticity); Zelensky deepfake
      urging surrender (March 2022)
    → voice cloning: 2019, researchers cloned voice from 5 seconds
      of audio; early versions had artifacts

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    → real-time voice cloning: <1 second latency; 3-second
      seed audio sufficient; commercially available (ElevenLabs,
      Resemble.ai)
    → video deepfake real-time: NVIDIA RTX-class GPU; real-time
      face swap; commercial tools (Reface, DeepFaceLive)
    → Hong Kong CFO incident (February 2024): finance employee
      tricked into transferring $25M HKD via video call with
      deepfakes of CFO and colleagues; first confirmed large-scale
      financial fraud via real-time deepfake video call
    → voice authentication bypass: major bank voice authentication
      bypassed by Vice using ElevenLabs cloned voice (2023)
    → biometric liveness detection bypass: adversarial patches
      applied to face that defeat liveness detection while
      appearing human to camera

TEMPORAL LAYER — TRAJECTORY:
    → real-time full-body video generation approaching capability
    → multimodal deepfake (synchronized face + voice + behavior
      pattern matching) reduces artifact detection
    → generation quality vs. detection quality: generation is
      advancing faster; detection relies on artifacts that
      generators optimize to remove
    → authentication systems relying on "knowledge of person"
      (voice, face, behavior) are structurally vulnerable once
      generation quality crosses human perception threshold

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: voice and video biometric authentication will become
      unreliable as primary authentication factors by 2026-2027.
      the perceptual threshold will be crossed; human ability to
      distinguish real from synthetic will fall below reliable
      authentication threshold. systems using voice or video as
      primary authentication must transition to hardware-backed
      factors (FIDO2/passkeys) or will be routinely bypassed.
    confidence: 0.83
    timeline: biometric voice authentication commercially breakable
      at scale by 2026; video by 2027-2028.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "identify all authentication systems in commercial use that
    accept voice or video as a primary authentication factor.
    rank by (1) user base size, (2) authentication criticality
    (financial, healthcare, government), (3) availability of
    voice samples from public sources (social media, podcast,
    earnings calls). this produces the prioritized target list
    for adversarial deepfake authentication bypass. map each
    against existing liveness detection capabilities."

CYCLE 4 — STAGE 3: LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[A-ANATOMY-09] ZERO-CLICK MOBILE EXPLOIT (5-LAYER ANALYSIS)

SURFACE LAYER:
    attacker sends a message (iMessage, WhatsApp, SMS MMS).
    victim's phone receives the message. no interaction required.
    attacker achieves remote code execution.
    victim is unaware.

TECHNICAL LAYER:
    modern messaging platforms automatically parse received message
    content: text, images, video, audio, documents.
    parsing is performed by libraries in C/C++ with direct memory access.
    parsing libraries accept untrusted data from the network
    and process it with minimal input validation.
    complex parsers (image codecs, video decoders, document renderers)
    implement complex state machines; edge cases in the state machine
    map to memory corruption conditions:
      → heap buffer overflow in image parser (FORCEDENTRY: JBIG2)
      → integer overflow in length field → undersized allocation → overflow
      → use-after-free in video decoder during error recovery
      → type confusion in polymorphic media handler
    initial memory corruption achieves code execution in the
    message parsing process (sandboxed on iOS, process-isolated on Android).
    second stage: sandbox escape via kernel vulnerability.
    third stage: persistence installation.
    full chain: parse → corrupt memory → execute shellcode →
      sandbox escape → kernel LPE → persistence.

STRUCTURAL LAYER:
    the attack is structurally enabled by:
      → parsing untrusted input with memory-unsafe code (C/C++)
        as a design norm for performance-critical media libraries
      → automatic message processing before user interaction
        (preview generation, notification content extraction)
        as a UX feature that expands attack surface
      → kernel as shared trust boundary: all sandboxed processes
        can reach the kernel; a kernel vulnerability collapses
        all process isolation
      → iMessage / SMS as unauthenticated network reachability:
        any phone number can receive a message; no prior relationship
        required; global reachability with zero friction
    the structural pattern: high-complexity parser + memory-unsafe
      implementation + automatic execution = remotely reachable
      attack surface.

CROSS-DOMAIN LAYER:
    identical structure in: email client preview (MTA parsing),
    browser URL bar parsing (universal reachability + complex parser),
    PDF viewer in web browser, VoIP SIP stack parsing (INVITE message),
    media player parsing (VLC, FFmpeg — multiple RCE CVEs),
    SCADA protocol parsing (Modbus, DNP3 parsers in field devices),
    satellite ground station command parsing.
    the pattern is not mobile-specific. it is the universal pattern
    of: complex parser + memory-unsafe language + externally-controlled
    input + automatic processing.

ROOT LAYER:
    performance and safety are in structural tension.
    memory-safe languages (Rust, Swift, Go) impose runtime checks
    that reduce throughput. media processing is throughput-critical.
    the field chose performance. the cost is a continuous stream of
    remotely exploitable parsing vulnerabilities.
    the root is a value choice made in the 1970s (C as system language)
    that has not been reversed because the switching cost is enormous.
    every library rewritten in a memory-safe language removes the
    root cause for that library. Apple migrating iMessage image
    parsing to memory-safe code eliminates that attack class.
    the root persists because the library ecosystem is large and
    rewrites are slow.

[A-ANATOMY-10] SUPPLY CHAIN SOCIAL ENGINEERING (XZ UTILS PATTERN)

SURFACE LAYER:
    a contributor joins an open-source project.
    over months to years, they build trust and reputation.
    they are granted commit access or maintainer status.
    they introduce malicious code, hidden in complexity.
    the malicious code executes with elevated privilege in target systems.

TECHNICAL LAYER:
    XZ Utils (CVE-2024-3094): Jia Tan (JiaT75) joined xz-utils
      project in 2021. built relationship with sole maintainer
      (Lasse Collin). used social pressure (fake accounts complaining
      about slow development) to push Collin toward adding Jia Tan
      as co-maintainer. gained access over 2 years. introduced
      malicious build scripts in 5.6.0 (February 2024).
    the malicious code: modified build system (CMake/autoconf)
      to include obfuscated binary blob in test files. the blob,
      when compiled into liblzma, added a function that hooked
      RSA decryption in libcrypto (OpenSSL / libssl) via IFUNC
      resolver and GNU indirect function mechanism. the hook
      intercepted sshd authentication, allowing backdoor access
      with a specific RSA key pair controlled by the attacker.
      discovery: Andres Freund (Microsoft) noticed higher CPU
      usage in sshd and traced it; discovered the backdoor
      by accident 5 weeks after 5.6.0 release. distros had
      not widely deployed it.

STRUCTURAL LAYER:
    the attack is structurally enabled by:
      → open-source dependency on volunteer maintainers;
        burnout creates pressure to accept help from strangers
      → trust accumulation as a resource: a patient adversary
        can purchase trust with time
      → build system as trust boundary: build scripts run with
        developer privilege; malicious build script achieves
        developer-equivalent code execution on any developer machine
      → binary blobs in test suites: a common legitimate pattern
        that provides cover for malicious content
      → GPG signatures on tarballs: only the tarball is signed;
        the build system is not separately verified; the malicious
        code was in the build system, not the C source
      → systemd/sshd integration: Debian and Ubuntu link sshd
        against libsystemd, which links against liblzma (xz);
        non-obvious transitive dependency created the exploit path

CROSS-DOMAIN LAYER:
    identical structure in: corporate M&A where acquired company's
    internal attacker gains access to acquirer; consultants with
    "trusted" access who are intelligence assets; contractor
    security clearances; legislative process where interest groups
    draft model legislation; standards bodies where nation-states
    insert subtle weaknesses (Dual_EC_DRBG, NSA involvement).
    the pattern: trust accumulation over time + critical access
    granted + malicious payload introduced when trust is established.

ROOT LAYER:
    trust is time-discounted. a person who has been reliable for
    2 years is trusted more than a new contributor. this heuristic
    is rational for detecting opportunistic actors but fails
    against patient, state-sponsored actors for whom 2-year
    investment is operationally trivial.
    the root: trust and identity are not verified cryptographically
    in human social systems. they are verified behaviorally.
    behavioral verification can be gamed by any actor with
    sufficient patience and understanding of the social system.
    the fix requires either (a) not trusting identity regardless
    of behavioral history for critical access, or (b) cryptographic
    binding of identity to physical-world verification that cannot
    be sock-puppeted. neither is currently implemented in OSS.

[A-ANATOMY-11] RANSOMWARE-AS-A-SERVICE AFFILIATE DEFECTION (5-LAYER ANALYSIS)

SURFACE LAYER:
    ransomware group encrypts victim's systems.
    ransom demand issued.
    affiliate who conducted intrusion defects from RaaS operator.
    affiliate takes ransom payment directly without sharing with operator.
    operator is defrauded; victim data may still be published.

TECHNICAL LAYER:
    RaaS operations use a technical control architecture:
      → affiliate receives a build of the ransomware encryptor
        customized to their affiliate ID; decryptor keyed to
        affiliate ID; affiliate cannot run the decryptor without
        the operator's infrastructure
      → payment is tracked by the operator's .onion negotiation
        portal; affiliate communicates with victim via portal
      → after payment, operator releases decryptor through portal;
        operator takes 20-30% cut automatically
    defection mechanism (BlackCat/Change Healthcare, March 2024):
      → affiliate ($22M ransom from UnitedHealth Group for
        Change Healthcare attack) claimed payment was received
        but operator "seized" the funds and shut down the portal
      → operator then blamed "law enforcement action" for the
        shutdown, executed an exit scam, and disappeared
      → affiliate was unable to provide the decryptor to the victim
        even after payment because the portal that releases it
        was gone
    the technical architecture that enforces the revenue split
    is also the single point of failure: operator controls the
    decryptor release; this gives operator power to exit-scam
    affiliates at any time.

STRUCTURAL LAYER:
    the RaaS model creates a principal-agent problem with no
    enforcement mechanism. the "contract" between operator and
    affiliate is:
      → unwritten (criminal; no legal enforcement)
      → enforced only by reputation (future access to the platform)
      → and by the technical fact that operator holds decryptor release
    when the operator decides to exit (law enforcement pressure,
    sufficient capital accumulated), the affiliate has no recourse.
    the affiliate holds the victim's encrypted systems and no key.
    the victim has paid and received nothing.
    structural outcome: the most successful RaaS operations
    generate enough revenue to incentivize the operator to exit-scam.
    exit-scam risk increases monotonically with RaaS success.

CROSS-DOMAIN LAYER:
    identical structure in: stock exchange specialist defecting
    with client funds; escrow agent defrauding both parties;
    marketplace platform exit scam (cryptocurrency exchange FTX);
    franchise operator taking franchise fees and disappearing.
    the common pattern: a trusted intermediary controls an asset
    that both parties need; the intermediary exits when the value
    of exit exceeds the value of continued operation.
    the crypto exchange collapse (FTX, Celsius, Voyager) is
    structurally identical: platform holds custody of user assets;
    platform operators prioritize exit over user protection.

ROOT LAYER:
    trustless systems (blockchain, smart contracts) were designed
    to eliminate this class of problem. the irony: ransomware
    payment is predominantly in cryptocurrency (trustless payment),
    but decryptor delivery is still custodied by a trusted party
    (the operator). the fix — smart contract escrow for decryptor
    release on payment confirmation — would eliminate operator
    defection but would require the operator to commit their
    decryptor key to a smart contract, which could be extracted.
    the root is the impossibility of trustless delivery of digital
    goods without revealing the good to an untrusted party.
    this is the fundamental problem of digital rights management,
    applied to criminal markets.

CYCLE 4 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY

CARRYING FORWARD: A01–A35, D01–D20

─────────────────────────────────────────
ATTACK ENTRIES A36–A50
─────────────────────────────────────────

[A36] ZERO-CLICK MOBILE EXPLOIT
  CLASS:       remote code execution via message parsing
  MECHANISM:   attacker sends a crafted message (iMessage, MMS,
               WhatsApp) to target device. message is automatically
               parsed by memory-unsafe media handling code. parsing
               a malformed structure triggers memory corruption
               (heap overflow, use-after-free, type confusion).
               initial code execution in sandboxed parser process.
               second-stage kernel LPE for full device compromise.
               no user interaction required at any stage.
  INSTANCES:   FORCEDENTRY (NSO Group, 2021) — JBIG2 parser in
               ImageIO; CVE-2021-30860; Apple emergency patch.
               KISMET (NSO Group, 2019) — iMessage parser pre-FORCEDENTRY.
               BLASTPASS (NSO Group, 2023) — PassKit image parsing;
               CVE-2023-41064 + CVE-2023-41061.
               Samsung Exynos baseband RCE (Project Zero, 2023)
               — 18 vulnerabilities; remote via cellular radio.
  PREREQUISITES: target phone number or Apple ID (iMessage);
               all other conditions satisfied by protocol design.
  INDICATORS:  none visible to victim; process crashes in sandboxed
               parser; possible battery drain from implant activity.
  MITIGATIONS: Apple Lockdown Mode (hardens parser attack surface;
               blocked BLASTPASS); memory-safe reimplementation of
               parsers; BlastDoor (iMessage sandboxing, Apple 2021);
               frequent iOS patching; exploit price signal as proxy
               for active use.
  GAPS:        baseband parsers remain in C; no memory-safe baseband
               firmware in production; carrier-level injection has
               no application-layer defense.

[A37] KERNEL LOCAL PRIVILEGE ESCALATION VIA RACE CONDITION (TOCTOU)
  CLASS:       local privilege escalation
  MECHANISM:   operating system kernel performs a check (is this
               file accessible to user X?) and then takes an action
               (open the file). between the check and the action,
               an attacker with another thread changes the state
               (replaces the file with a symlink to /etc/passwd).
               the action is taken on the new state that was not
               checked. check-and-act is non-atomic; the race window
               is exploitable if the attacker can win the race.
  INSTANCES:   Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195): copy-on-write race in
               Linux kernel mmap; allowed unprivileged write to
               read-only memory mappings; 9 years in kernel before
               discovery; affected Android devices extensively.
               CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe): Linux pipe page flag
               race condition; arbitrary file write as unprivileged
               user; affects kernel 5.8–5.16.3.
               macOS TOCTOU in Gatekeeper (CVE-2021-30853):
               race between quarantine check and execution.
  PREREQUISITES: local code execution (already on system); race
               window must be winnable (depends on CPU count
               and scheduler behavior — multi-core makes races
               easier to win).
  INDICATORS:  anomalous kernel calls (setuid, ptrace); privilege
               change events; SELinux/AppArmor audit logs.
  MITIGATIONS: atomic system call variants; kernel hardening
               (SMEP, SMAP, kASLR); seccomp filters restricting
               system calls available to processes; kernel live
               patching (kpatch, livepatch); prompt kernel patching.
  GAPS:        race conditions are structurally difficult to eliminate;
               formal verification of kernel concurrency is tractable
               only for small components; millions of race-prone
               kernel paths remain unverified.

[A38] eBPF VERIFIER BYPASS AND KERNEL ESCAPE
  CLASS:       kernel code execution via BPF program verification failure
  MECHANISM:   eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) allows
               unprivileged (or CAP_BPF) programs to run in kernel
               context. a verifier is supposed to ensure safety:
               no unbounded loops, no out-of-bounds memory access,
               no use of uninitialized values. the verifier uses
               abstract interpretation. abstract interpretation
               is conservative but incomplete: a flaw in the
               verifier's range tracking allows a program that
               the verifier certifies as safe to perform
               out-of-bounds memory access in kernel space,
               achieving kernel code execution.
  INSTANCES:   CVE-2021-3490: eBPF ALU32 bitwise ops incorrect
               range tracking; LPE from CAP_NET_ADMIN. 
               CVE-2021-31440: off-by-one in verifier bounds check.
               CVE-2022-0500: verifier register value tracking error.
               CVE-2022-2588 (DirtyCred): eBPF credential swap;
               heap exploit from eBPF combined with file credential
               replacement; 2022 DEF CON presentation.
               CVE-2023-2163: incorrect verifier pruning; LPE.
  PREREQUISITES: CAP_BPF capability or unprivileged BPF if enabled
               (disabled by default on most distros post-2021).
  INDICATORS:  bpf() syscall from non-admin process; verifier error
               logs; kernel panic if exploit fails.
  MITIGATIONS: disable unprivileged BPF (sysctl kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=1);
               formal verification of eBPF verifier logic (ongoing
               research; not yet complete); restrict CAP_BPF in
               container deployments; seccomp blocking bpf() syscall.
  GAPS:        eBPF adoption is accelerating in network security
               tooling, observability, and sandboxing — expanding
               the privilege footprint of the verifier. the verifier
               is a high-complexity safety-critical component with
               limited formal verification coverage. each new
               eBPF feature extends the verifier's analysis scope
               and adds vulnerability surface.

[A39] OAUTH AUTHORIZATION CODE INTERCEPTION AND PKCE BYPASS
  CLASS:       authentication/authorization token theft
  MECHANISM:   OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: client redirects
               user to authorization server; user authenticates;
               server issues authorization code to redirect_uri;
               client exchanges code for access token. attack
               vectors:
               (1) malicious redirect_uri: if authorization server
                 does not strictly validate redirect_uri, attacker
                 registers a lookalike URI that receives the code.
               (2) open redirect in legitimate redirect_uri:
                 attacker chains legitimate URI with open redirect
                 to exfiltrate code to attacker-controlled server.
               (3) PKCE downgrade: if server accepts requests
                 without PKCE when PKCE was configured, attacker
                 sends authorization request without code_challenge;
                 stolen code is usable without code_verifier.
               (4) mix-up attack: user has accounts at two IdPs
                 using same client; attacker swaps IdP tokens.
  INSTANCES:   widespread class; used in OAuth implementations at
               Google, Facebook, Microsoft historically; GitHub
               OAuth flaw (2014); Facebook OAuth vulnerability
               allowing account takeover (2013, Nir Goldshlager).
  PREREQUISITES: authorization server with loose redirect_uri
               validation or PKCE not enforced; or open redirect
               in client application.
  INDICATORS:  unusual redirect_uri values; code exchange from
               unexpected IP; failed code exchanges (code reuse
               after theft).
  MITIGATIONS: strict redirect_uri validation (exact match, not
               prefix or regex); PKCE required for all public
               clients (RFC 7636); short authorization code lifetime
               (<60 seconds); code binding to client IP; mTLS
               sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, RFC 9449).
  GAPS:        OAuth 2.0 has 12+ known attack classes; most
               implementations implement partial mitigations;
               OAuth 2.1 consolidates best practices but adoption
               is slow.

[A40] JWT ALGORITHM CONFUSION (NONE ALGORITHM, RS256→HS256)
  CLASS:       authentication token forgery
  MECHANISM:   JSON Web Tokens are signed to prevent tampering.
               the algorithm is specified in the JWT header.
               attack 1 — none algorithm: change alg header to
               "none"; remove signature; some libraries accept
               unsigned tokens if alg=none is not explicitly blocked.
               attack 2 — RS256→HS256 confusion: server uses
               RS256 (asymmetric; signs with private key, verifies
               with public key). attacker obtains server's public key
               (often publicly available at /.well-known/jwks.json).
               attacker creates a JWT with alg=HS256 (symmetric;
               same key for sign and verify). attacker signs the
               JWT using the server's public key as the HS256 secret.
               server verifies using "the key" — which it interprets
               as the HS256 secret — and the public key matches.
               token is accepted as valid.
  INSTANCES:   CVE-2015-9235: node-jsonwebtoken library; none
               algorithm not blocked; patched in v4.2.2.
               Tim McLean (2015): original discovery of RS256→HS256;
               affected multiple major JWT libraries simultaneously.
               Auth0, Okta, and others had historical exposure.
  PREREQUISITES: JWT library that does not explicitly whitelist
               expected algorithms; or public key retrievable.
  INDICATORS:  JWT header alg mismatch from expected; tokens with
               alg=none in production traffic; tokens signed with
               unexpected algorithm.
  MITIGATIONS: always specify and enforce expected algorithm
               explicitly (never trust header-specified algorithm
               alone); reject alg=none entirely; use separate
               key material for symmetric and asymmetric operations;
               JWT library with algorithm pinning (e.g. python-jose
               algorithms parameter enforced).
  GAPS:        the none algorithm vulnerability is 10+ years old
               and still found in production systems. the gap is
               not technical; it is deployment: developers use
               insecure defaults without reading documentation.

[A41] HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING (TE.CL AND CL.TE VARIANTS)
  CLASS:       HTTP desync / request smuggling
  MECHANISM:   HTTP/1.1 allows two headers to specify message length:
               Content-Length (CL) and Transfer-Encoding (TE).
               when a request passes through two HTTP systems
               (frontend proxy + backend server) that disagree
               on which header takes precedence, the request boundary
               is parsed differently by each:
               CL.TE: frontend uses Content-Length; backend uses
                 Transfer-Encoding. attacker sends a request with
                 both headers; frontend sees one request; backend
                 sees two. the "second request" prefix is prepended
                 to the next victim's request on the backend.
               TE.CL: frontend uses Transfer-Encoding; backend uses
                 Content-Length. attacker crafts chunk encoding
                 that the frontend processes as one request but
                 the backend splits differently.
               consequences: cache poisoning, request hijacking,
               WAF bypass, credential theft, reflected XSS via
               response desync, server-side request forgery,
               unauthorized access to internal endpoints.
  INSTANCES:   James Kettle (PortSwigger) discovery and
               systematization (2019); found in Apache Traffic
               Server, HAProxy, IIS, Akamai edge infrastructure.
               CVE-2019-16869 (Netty); CVE-2020-11444 (Hopper);
               HTTP/2 request smuggling variants (2021, Kettle).
  PREREQUISITES: two-tier HTTP architecture with parser disagreement;
               persistent connections (HTTP keep-alive) on backend.
  INDICATORS:  unexpected request fragments in server logs;
               partial request headers from other clients;
               timing anomalies in request processing.
  MITIGATIONS: normalize HTTP headers at edge (reject requests
               with both CL and TE); use HTTP/2 end-to-end
               (eliminates CL/TE ambiguity); upgrade to parsers
               that implement RFC 7230 strictly; web security
               scanner coverage (Burp Scanner detects most variants).
  GAPS:        HTTP/2 introduced new smuggling vectors;
               H2.CL and H2.TE variants affect HTTP/2→HTTP/1.1
               downgrade paths; HTTP/3 (QUIC) has not been
               systematically analyzed for equivalent vulnerabilities.

[A42] SERVER-SIDE TEMPLATE INJECTION (SSTI)
  CLASS:       remote code execution via template engine
  MECHANISM:   web applications use server-side template engines
               (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, Velocity, Smarty,
               Mako, ERB) to generate dynamic HTML. if user input
               is placed inside a template string rather than
               passed as a template variable, the template engine
               evaluates the input as template syntax. template
               engines provide access to variables and often to
               built-in objects and functions. escalation from
               template expression evaluation to OS command
               execution via language introspection:
               Jinja2: {{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}}
               → find subprocess class → call OS commands.
               Freemarker: <#assign ex="freemarker.template.utility.
               Execute"?new()>${ex("id")}
  INSTANCES:   Uber SSTI via Jinja2 (2016, bug bounty, $10K reward).
               PayPal SSTI in email template preview (2016).
               Rails ERB SSTI in numerous Ruby applications.
               Shopify SSTI in liquid template custom pages (2016).
               GitLab SSTI leading to RCE (CVE-2021-22205 — actually
               an ExifTool RCE via GitLab upload, related class).
  PREREQUISITES: user-controlled input rendered as template
               expression (not just as template data); template
               engine with code execution capability.
  INDICATORS:  template syntax in user input fields ({{, ${, <%);
               error messages revealing template engine name/version;
               unexpected output of arithmetic expressions in
               rendered pages.
  MITIGATIONS: never concatenate user input into template strings;
               always pass user input as template variables;
               use sandboxed template engines (Jinja2 sandboxed
               environment) that restrict access to language objects;
               input validation to reject template metacharacters.
  GAPS:        sandboxed template execution is harder to audit
               than it appears; sandbox escapes are routinely found
               in Jinja2 and Smarty; the root cause (string
               concatenation as template rendering) is a developer
               education problem that cannot be solved technically.

[A43] PROTOTYPE POLLUTION (JAVASCRIPT)
  CLASS:       property injection / type confusion
  MECHANISM:   JavaScript objects inherit from prototypes.
               Object.prototype is the root prototype for all objects.
               if an application merges user-controlled JSON into
               an object without sanitizing keys, an attacker can
               set __proto__ as a key: {"__proto__": {"admin": true}}.
               this modifies Object.prototype; every subsequently
               created plain object inherits admin: true.
               server-side: Node.js applications using vulnerable
               merge/clone libraries (lodash.merge before 4.17.11,
               jQuery.extend with deep:true, etc.) are vulnerable
               to RCE if polluted properties affect code paths
               (e.g., polluting "env" property used in child_process.exec).
               client-side: polluting properties used in DOM manipulation
               causes XSS or application logic bypass.
