  INSTANCES:   lodash CVE-2019-10744: prototype pollution in merge;
               arbitrary property injection; affects ~8M npm packages.
               jQuery CVE-2019-11358: $.extend deep merge prototype
               pollution.
               Kibana CVE-2019-7609: prototype pollution to RCE via
               Timelion expression (pollute process.env → code exec).
  PREREQUISITES: application uses deep merge/clone on user-supplied
               object without __proto__ key sanitization.
  INDICATORS:  __proto__ or constructor.prototype in request body
               JSON keys; unexpected property values on plain objects.
  MITIGATIONS: sanitize __proto__, constructor, prototype as keys
               in merge operations; use Object.create(null) for
               property maps (no prototype); use JSON.parse with
               reviver that blocks prototype keys; freeze Object.prototype
               at startup; use schema validation before object merge.
  GAPS:        prototype pollution is often a gadget-dependent
               vulnerability; impact depends on what downstream
               code does with the polluted property; static analysis
               tools rarely trace prototype pollution through to
               impact, producing many false negatives.

[A44] WEB CACHE DECEPTION AND CACHE POISONING
  CLASS:       cache abuse / user data exposure / response manipulation
  MECHANISM:   web cache deception: CDN or proxy caches a page
               intended to be dynamic and user-specific. attacker
               constructs URL that causes the cache to store
               the victim's authenticated response and serve it
               to the attacker. technique: append a fake static
               file extension to a dynamic URL:
               /account/profile/../../style.css — path traversal
               causes server to return profile page; cache keys
               on URL with .css extension; caches as static content;
               attacker requests same URL and receives cached
               victim response.
               cache poisoning: attacker manipulates HTTP headers
               (Host, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme) that
               are reflected in the response and cached. attacker's
               injected value is served to all subsequent users
               who receive the poisoned cached response; achieves
               stored XSS via cache, open redirect for all users,
               or response manipulation at CDN scale.
  INSTANCES:   Omer Gil (2017): original web cache deception paper;
               demonstrated on PayPal: cached authenticated
               user profile pages; attacker harvested CSRF tokens
               and user data.
               James Kettle (2018): web cache poisoning
               systematization; demonstrated on a dozen major sites
               including United Airlines, Red Hat, Cloudflare itself.
  PREREQUISITES: web cache (CDN, reverse proxy) in path;
               for deception: cache rules based on file extension
               or URL suffix; for poisoning: unkeyed HTTP headers
               reflected in response.
  INDICATORS:  unexpected cache HIT headers on authenticated content;
               anomalous response headers in cached content;
               CDN access logs showing attacker requesting then
               victim receiving same cache entry.
  MITIGATIONS: for deception: cache rules that explicitly list
               cacheable paths (allowlist, not denylist by extension);
               verify cache-control headers on authenticated responses;
               for poisoning: include all headers that affect
               response in the cache key; strip unrecognized
               forwarding headers at edge; use Vary header correctly.
  GAPS:        CDN cache behavior is complex and vendor-specific;
               cache key normalization varies across CDN providers;
               no unified testing framework for cache poisoning
               across CDN configurations.

[A45] SUBDOMAIN TAKEOVER
  CLASS:       domain hijacking / phishing / session theft
  MECHANISM:   an organization creates a DNS CNAME record pointing
               sub.example.com to a third-party service
               (Heroku, GitHub Pages, AWS S3, Azure, Fastly).
               the organization later removes the resource on
               the third-party service but does not delete the
               DNS CNAME record. the DNS record still resolves
               but the third-party resource no longer exists.
               attacker creates a resource on the third-party
               service with the same name. the CNAME now resolves
               to attacker-controlled content served under
               sub.example.com. attacker can:
               → serve phishing pages under legitimate domain
               → steal session cookies scoped to .example.com
               → bypass CORS restrictions (page served from
                 legitimate origin)
               → send email from the subdomain (SPF, DKIM valid)
  INSTANCES:   found in Microsoft, Uber, GitHub, Shopify, Twitter,
               HackerOne (their own bug reporting platform had
               a takeable subdomain; disclosed by hacker).
               Tomnomnom (2017): automated scanner; found hundreds
               of vulnerable subdomains in Alexa top 10,000.
               Detectify (2021): 9 Microsoft subdomains takeable;
               patched after responsible disclosure.
  PREREQUISITES: dangling DNS CNAME or A record pointing to
               abandoned or unclaimed resource on a multi-tenant
               hosting platform.
  INDICATORS:  NXDOMAIN or "not found" response from the third-party
               service for a CNAME-aliased subdomain; third-party
               service error page ("There's no app on this subdomain").
  MITIGATIONS: DNS audit tooling (continuous monitoring of CNAMEs
               and their resolution); DNS record lifecycle management
               (remove DNS records when removing services); domain
               monitoring for takeover indicators; use dedicated
               subdomains for external services rather than
               customer-facing names.
  GAPS:        large organizations have hundreds to thousands of
               DNS records; lifecycle management is not a standard
               operational discipline; most organizations discover
               dangling DNS via bug bounty, not internal audit.

[A46] EVIL MAID ATTACK (PHYSICAL ACCESS TO UNATTENDED DEVICE)
  CLASS:       physical compromise / full disk access bypass
  MECHANISM:   attacker gains brief physical access to an unattended
               device (hotel room, airport bag, unattended laptop).
               two attack paths:
               (1) full disk encryption bypass: device boots from
                 attacker-controlled USB; attacker reads encryption
                 key from RAM (cold boot attack — DRAM retains
                 data for seconds to minutes after power removal;
                 longer if cooled with compressed air); or installs
                 bootkit that captures passphrase at next boot.
               (2) bootloader compromise: attacker modifies
                 boot loader to log the disk encryption passphrase
                 before decrypting; user enters passphrase at next
                 boot; passphrase captured; attacker returns to
                 retrieve it or exfiltrates via network.
  INSTANCES:   Joanna Rutkowska (2009): original evil maid
               attack against TrueCrypt; modified bootloader
               on TrueCrypt-encrypted system in minutes.
               Cold boot attack (Halderman et al. 2008): DRAM
               key recovery from powered-off systems; demonstrated
               against BitLocker, FileVault, TrueCrypt.
               Thunderbolt DMA attack: Intel Thunderbolt direct
               memory access; bypass BitLocker via DMA if
               pre-boot DMA protection not enabled; PCILeech tool.
  PREREQUISITES: brief physical access to unattended device;
               device without tamper-evident hardware;
               no secure boot or bypass-able secure boot.
  INDICATORS:  none visible to victim; TPM-based attestation
               detects bootloader modification if configured.
  MITIGATIONS: TPM with PIN binding (requires PIN + TPM; TPM alone
               vulnerable if passphrase captured separately);
               secure boot with measured boot and remote attestation;
               disable Thunderbolt DMA (BIOS setting, Intel VT-d);
               BIOS password; physical tamper detection;
               never leave devices unattended in untrusted locations.
  GAPS:        TPM without PIN protects against software attacks
               but not evil maid; most enterprise BitLocker
               deployments use TPM without PIN for user experience
               reasons; this is a mass deployment that is
               structurally vulnerable to physical access.

[A47] LDAP INJECTION
  CLASS:       injection / authentication bypass / data exfiltration
  MECHANISM:   web applications that query LDAP directories
               (Active Directory, OpenLDAP) for authentication or
               user lookup build LDAP filter strings from user input.
               if user input is not sanitized, injected LDAP filter
               syntax modifies the query:
               login filter: (&(uid=USER)(password=PASS))
               injection: uid=admin)(&) → filter becomes:
               (&(uid=admin)(&)(password=anything)) → uid=admin
               matches and password check is bypassed.
               full directory dump: uid=*)(uid=* → returns all
               entries depending on implementation.
  INSTANCES:   found extensively in enterprise web applications
               integrating with Active Directory; less CVE-tracked
               than SQL injection because LDAP is intranet-facing;
               found in educational institution portals, HR
               systems, VPN portals; consistently found in
               penetration testing of enterprise environments.
  PREREQUISITES: LDAP query built from user input without sanitization;
               LDAP server with a sensitive directory.
  INDICATORS:  LDAP syntax characters in login fields (*, ), (,
               |, &, \); authentication success with unexpected
               credentials; LDAP server error messages in response.
  MITIGATIONS: parameterized LDAP queries (LDAP libraries support
               escaped parameter binding); strict whitelist input
               validation; use service accounts with minimal
               LDAP read permissions; LDAP query logging and
               anomaly detection.
  GAPS:        LDAP injection receives far less attention than SQL
               injection in developer education materials despite
               equivalent severity; LDAP parameterization APIs
               are less well-documented; enterprise SSO portals
               frequently built on legacy code with no input
               sanitization review.

[A48] TIMING ORACLE ATTACK (PADDING ORACLE AND DERIVATIVE)
  CLASS:       cryptographic side-channel attack
  MECHANISM:   a decryption oracle that returns different responses
               depending on whether decrypted plaintext has valid
               padding provides a timing or response oracle.
               CBC padding oracle: CBC mode decryption requires
               valid PKCS#7 padding on the final block. if the
               server responds differently (error code, timing,
               behavior) to valid vs. invalid padding, an attacker
               can decrypt any ciphertext without the key by
               sending adaptive chosen-ciphertext queries.
               for an 8-byte block: 256 queries per byte worst case;
               16-byte AES block: ~4,096 queries; full decryption
               of arbitrary ciphertext with ~4,096 × block_count
               queries.
  INSTANCES:   ASP.NET padding oracle (MS10-070, 2010): timing
               difference in ASP.NET viewstate decryption;
               allowed decryption of any encrypted viewstate
               and arbitrary file read; POET tool demonstrated.
               POODLE (CVE-2014-3566): SSL 3.0 CBC padding oracle;
               required MitM downgrade to SSL 3.0; end of SSL 3.0.
               Lucky Thirteen (Al Fardan, Paterson 2013): TLS CBC
               timing oracle via MAC verification timing;
               found in OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS; required ~225
               adaptive queries per byte.
               BEAST (2011): chosen-plaintext against TLS 1.0 CBC.
  PREREQUISITES: decryption oracle with observable behavior that
               distinguishes valid from invalid padding; attacker
               can send adaptive chosen-ciphertext queries.
  INDICATORS:  high volume of requests with single-byte differences
               in ciphertext; timing analysis of decryption responses.
  MITIGATIONS: use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)
               which eliminates padding oracles entirely; if CBC
               is unavoidable: encrypt-then-MAC (RFC 7366); constant-
               time MAC verification; no padding error messages;
               TLS 1.3 (removes CBC cipher suites entirely).
  GAPS:        CBC cipher suites still negotiated in TLS 1.2;
               many application-layer encryption implementations
               (not just TLS) use CBC without MAC; timing side-
               channels in application-level decryption are
               rarely audited.

[A49] FIRMWARE IMPLANT (PERSISTENT BELOW-OS COMPROMISE)
  CLASS:       persistent low-level implant
  MECHANISM:   firmware executes before and with higher privilege
               than the operating system. compromising firmware
               gives an attacker persistence that survives OS
               reinstall, disk wipe, and reimaging. attack surfaces:
               (1) UEFI firmware: vendor-signed DXE drivers;
                 SPI flash update mechanism; Thunderbolt firmware.
               (2) hard drive / SSD firmware: Equation Group's
                 HDD firmware implants (Fanny, 2015 Kaspersky)
                 rewrote firmware on Seagate, Western Digital,
                 Maxtor, IBM drives; invisible to OS; survives wipe.
               (3) NIC firmware: persistent access via network card
                 firmware; executes before OS boot.
               (4) BMC/IPMI (server management): iLO, iDRAC
                 firmware implants; network-accessible out-of-band
                 channel; HP iLO implant used by APT (2021).
               (5) keyboard and peripheral firmware: implanted
                 via supply chain or brief physical access.
  INSTANCES:   Equation Group HDD firmware (Kaspersky 2015):
               most sophisticated firmware attack published;
               14 years of undetected operation; affected
               30+ countries; 500+ infections of "high-value" targets.
               LoJax (APT28/Fancy Bear, 2018): first publicly
               documented UEFI rootkit used in the wild;
               survived disk wipe and OS reinstall on victim systems.
               MoonBounce (APT41, 2022): UEFI bootkit in SPI flash;
               survives drive replacement as well as wipe.
               CosmicStrand (2022): UEFI rootkit in ASUS and Gigabyte
               motherboard firmware; China-nexus attribution.
  PREREQUISITES: physical access OR software vulnerability in
               firmware update mechanism OR supply chain compromise
               of device manufacturing or distribution.
  INDICATORS:  PCR values in TPM attestation log showing unexpected
               firmware measurement; Secure Boot bypass; persistence
               after confirmed disk wipe.
  MITIGATIONS: UEFI Secure Boot with full chain of trust; measured
               boot with TPM PCR attestation (detect modification);
               firmware signing verification; Platform Firmware
               Resiliency (NIST SP 800-193); periodic firmware
               integrity verification; hardware security modules for
               firmware signing keys.
  GAPS:        most organizations do not monitor or verify firmware
               integrity; TPM attestation infrastructure is not
               widely deployed outside cloud and specialized
               government environments; BMC firmware is notoriously
               under-secured; no supply chain integrity standard
               equivalent to SLSA exists for firmware.

[A50] ADVERSARIAL MACHINE LEARNING — EVASION AT INFERENCE
  CLASS:       AI/ML model manipulation
  MECHANISM:   machine learning classifiers (image recognition,
               malware detection, spam filters, deepfake detectors,
               IDS) are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations:
               carefully crafted inputs that cause misclassification
               while appearing normal to human observers.
               white-box attack: attacker has access to model weights;
               uses gradient of loss function w.r.t. input to find
               minimal perturbation that crosses the decision boundary.
               FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method, Goodfellow 2014):
               one-step gradient attack.
               PGD (Projected Gradient Descent, Madry 2018):
               iterative, stronger; the standard adversarial robustness
               benchmark.
               black-box attack: attacker only has query access;
               uses transferability (adversarial examples crafted
               for surrogate model often transfer) or score-based
               gradient estimation.
               physical-world: adversarial patches (Brown 2017);
               adversarial glasses (Sharif 2016); stop sign stickers
               (Eykholt 2018) causing misclassification by autonomous
               vehicles.
  INSTANCES:   Tesla autopilot lane confusion via adversarial road
               markings (McAfee 2020).
               Cylance antivirus bypass via adversarial string
               appended to malware (Skylight Cyber 2019).
               Face++ liveness detection bypass via adversarial
               printed attack on face (CVPR 2019).
               GPT-4 jailbreaking via adversarial suffix (Zou et al.
               2023): automated suffix generation that bypasses
               safety training.
  PREREQUISITES: target uses ML classifier for a security-relevant
               decision; attacker can observe model outputs (black-box)
               or has model (white-box).
  INDICATORS:  high query rate to ML inference endpoint from single
               source (black-box probing); classification confidence
               distributions that suggest boundary-case inputs.
  MITIGATIONS: adversarial training (include adversarial examples
               in training set; Madry et al. 2018); input
               preprocessing and transformation; certified defenses
               (randomized smoothing: Cohen et al. 2019 provides
               provable robustness radius); ensemble of diverse
               models; detection of adversarial inputs (feature
               squeezing, input transformation detection).
  GAPS:        no certified defense that provides meaningful robustness
               at production accuracy levels has been deployed at scale;
               adversarial training trades off clean accuracy for
               robust accuracy; certified defenses have too-small
               robustness radius for practical attacks; the field
               has not solved adversarial robustness.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSE ENTRIES D21–D35
─────────────────────────────────────────

[D21] PKI ARCHITECTURE AND CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY SECURITY
  CLASS:       cryptographic trust infrastructure
  MECHANISM:   public key infrastructure creates a hierarchical
               trust model. a root certificate authority (CA)
               self-signs a root certificate; the root CA signs
               intermediate CA certificates; intermediate CAs sign
               end-entity certificates for domains or users.
               browsers and operating systems ship a list of trusted
               root CAs (~150 globally); any of those CAs (or any
               CA they issue an intermediate to) can issue valid
               certificates for any domain. the trust model is
               maximally permissive by design.
  COMPONENTS:
    → root CA protection: offline HSM storage; air-gapped systems;
      multi-party ceremony for root key operations; physical security
    → certificate transparency (CT): RFC 6962; all publicly trusted
      certificates must be logged to append-only CT logs;
      Chrome requires SCT proof of logging since 2018; enables
      detection of mis-issued certificates
    → CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) DNS records:
      RFC 8659; domain owner specifies which CAs may issue
      for the domain; CAs must check CAA before issuance
    → certificate pinning (HPKP deprecated; Trust Kit, certificate
      pinning in mobile apps): pin specific certificate or CA;
      eliminates any-CA-can-issue risk; high operational complexity
    → Let's Encrypt: automated ACME protocol issuance; free;
      90-day validity; dramatically reduced barrier to HTTPS
      adoption; ~400M active certificates
    → CT monitors: cert.sh, Facebook's CT monitor, Google's
      CT transparency site; defenders can alert on new certificates
      issued for their domain
  HISTORICAL FAILURES:
    DigiNotar (2011): Dutch CA compromised; attacker issued wildcard
      certificate for *.google.com; used in Iran to MITM Google
      users; DigiNotar revoked from all trust stores; company bankrupt.
    Comodo (2011): reseller compromise; 9 rogue certificates issued
      including mail.google.com, login.yahoo.com.
    Symantec CA (2017): Google discovered Symantec issued test
      certificates improperly; gradual distrust process; Symantec
      CA sold to DigiCert.
  GAPS:        CT enforcement protects only against undetected
               mis-issuance; a nation-state CA can issue a rogue
               certificate that appears in CT logs but is not
               detected before use; CAA is advisory (CAs can ignore it
               with logging); private PKI is unregulated and invisible.

[D22] COVERAGE-GUIDED FUZZING AS DEFENSIVE PRACTICE
  CLASS:       automated vulnerability discovery / bug finding
  MECHANISM:   fuzzing generates large volumes of semi-random inputs
               to a program and monitors for crashes, hangs, or
               assertion violations. coverage-guided fuzzing uses
               instrumentation to track which code paths each input
               exercises; mutation engine prioritizes inputs that
               discover new code coverage; over time, the fuzzer
               explores the entire reachable code path space.
               american fuzzy lop (AFL, Michal Zalewski): pioneered
               coverage-guided fuzzing with bitmap-based branch
               coverage tracking; libFuzzer (LLVM): in-process;
               faster than AFL; used for tight fuzzing loops;
               honggfuzz: persistent-mode, hardware performance
               counters; OSS-Fuzz (Google): continuous fuzzing
               of 1,000+ open-source projects; found 10,000+
               vulnerabilities since 2016.
  WHAT IT FINDS: memory corruption (heap/stack overflow, UAF, use
               of uninitialized memory); integer overflows; assertion
               failures; crash-inducing edge cases in parsers.
  DOES NOT FIND: logic bugs without observable crash; semantic
               vulnerabilities; authentication flaws; access control
               misconfigurations; cryptographic weaknesses.
  DEPLOYMENT:
    → continuous integration: fuzz targets run in CI alongside unit
      tests; any crash blocks merge
    → seed corpus management: curated inputs that cover important
      code paths accelerate fuzzer effectiveness
    → sanitizers: AddressSanitizer (ASan), UBSan, MemorySanitizer
      detect bugs that don't crash without instrumentation
    → coverage targets: track % of code reached by fuzzer;
      identify uncovered paths for additional seed corpus
    → triage and deduplication: crash deduplication prevents
      filing hundreds of tickets for variants of one bug
  INSTANCES OF BUGS FOUND: Heartbleed-class bugs found in TLS
    libraries; LibreOffice parser bugs; Linux kernel driver bugs;
    browser engine parsing bugs; dozens of critical CVEs annually.
  GAPS:        fuzzing finds bugs in proportion to code path
               coverage; deeply nested error handling paths
               require structured fuzzing or grammar-based fuzzing;
               fuzzing binary-only targets requires dynamic
               instrumentation (QEMU mode, Intel PIN) which is
               slower; kernel fuzzing (syzkaller) is specialized
               and resource-intensive.

[D23] FORMAL VERIFICATION OF SECURITY PROPERTIES
  CLASS:       provable security assurance
  MECHANISM:   formal methods express a system's desired properties
               as logical specifications and use mathematical proof
               to verify that the implementation satisfies them.
               unlike testing (which finds bugs by example), formal
               verification proves absence of entire bug classes.
               approaches:
    → model checking: exhaustively explores all system states;
      TLA+ (Leslie Lamport); SPIN (PROMELA); finds all violations
      of safety and liveness properties up to state space bounds.
    → theorem proving: interactive proof assistants; Coq (Gallina),
      Isabelle/HOL, Lean 4; generates machine-checkable proofs;
      used for seL4 kernel, CompCert compiler, HACL* crypto.
    → automated verification: SAT/SMT solvers (Z3, CVC5);
      bounded model checking; symbolic execution (KLEE, SAGE).
    → type system verification: dependent types, linear types;
      Rust's ownership system is a limited form of mechanical
      verification of memory safety.
  PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENTS:
    → seL4: formally verified capability-based microkernel;
      used in drone avionics (Boeing), spacecraft, critical infra.
    → HACL*: formally verified cryptographic library; in Firefox,
      WireGuard, Signal Protocol.
    → CompCert: formally verified C compiler; used in aviation
      (DO-178C contexts).
    → TLA+ at Amazon: formal specs for distributed protocols;
      found bugs in DynamoDB, S3 Glacier RAID (Lamport & Newcombe).
  GAPS:        formal verification scales poorly to large codebases;
               cost is 10-100× higher than conventional development;
               requires domain expertise not widely available;
               model and implementation diverge over time unless
               integrated into development process; formal
               verification of concurrent systems is especially hard.

[D24] KERNEL HARDENING MITIGATIONS
  CLASS:       exploit mitigation / attack surface reduction
  MECHANISM:   operating system kernels implement hardware and
               software mitigations that raise the cost of
               exploiting kernel vulnerabilities. each mitigation
               increases attacker effort without preventing all attacks.
  MITIGATIONS:
    → SMEP (Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention, Intel): hardware;
      prevents kernel from executing code in user-space pages;
      defeats user-land shellcode injection into kernel.
    → SMAP (Supervisor Mode Access Prevention, Intel): hardware;
      prevents kernel from reading/writing user-space memory
      without explicit copy_from_user/copy_to_user; defeats
      many kernel data pointer dereference attacks.
    → kASLR (kernel Address Space Layout Randomization):
      randomizes kernel base address; forces info leak primitive
      before reliable kernel exploitation.
    → KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation): separates user and kernel
      page tables; primary mitigation for Meltdown; prevents
      reading kernel memory from user space.
    → CFI (Control Flow Integrity): ensures indirect branches
      only target valid function entry points; clang CFI in Linux
      kernel (arm64 since 5.13); defeats ROP chains.
    → Stack canaries: detect stack buffer overflows before return;
      bypassed by info leak + arbitrary write primitives.
    → seccomp-BPF: restrict system calls available to process;
      dramatically reduces kernel attack surface for sandboxed
      processes; used by Chrome, Firefox, Docker.
    → Lockdown mode (Linux): restricts even root from performing
      operations that could compromise kernel integrity; required
      for Secure Boot.
    → INIT_ON_FREE / INIT_ON_ALLOC: zero memory on allocation
      and free; prevents information leaks via uninitialized memory.
    → Heap randomization (SLUB freelist randomization): randomizes
      heap layout; raises cost of heap-based exploits.
  EFFECTIVENESS: individually, each mitigation can be bypassed
    given the right primitives. in combination, they increase
    the minimum exploit complexity. modern kernel exploits require
    multiple primitives (info leak + arbitrary read + arbitrary write
    + CFI bypass) chained together.
  GAPS:        CFI enforcement is incomplete in Linux kernel;
               Android ahead of Linux mainline in CFI coverage;
               KPTI has performance cost (~5-30% on database
               workloads); many mitigations require hardware support
               not available on older systems; embedded Linux kernels
               often compiled without these mitigations.

[D25] SECURE BOOT AND MEASURED BOOT
  CLASS:       firmware and boot integrity verification
  MECHANISM:   secure boot: each stage of the boot process verifies
               the cryptographic signature of the next stage before
               executing it. UEFI Secure Boot: firmware verifies
               the bootloader signature against keys in the Platform
               Key / Key Exchange Key / Database (PK/KEK/db).
               measured boot: each boot stage computes a hash
               of the next stage and extends it into TPM Platform
               Configuration Registers (PCRs). the TPM produces
               an attestation quote: a signed statement of all
               PCR values. a remote verifier compares PCR values
               against known-good measurements to detect modification.
  CHAIN:
    UEFI firmware → measures UEFI → extends PCR0
    UEFI verifies bootloader signature → extends PCR4
    bootloader verifies kernel signature → extends PCR8
    kernel extends PCR9 with initrd measurement
    TPM attests full chain: any modification detected
  DEPLOYMENTS:
    → Windows: BitLocker uses TPM PCR binding; disk key sealed
      to PCR values; system won't boot if firmware is modified.
    → Android Verified Boot: AVB2.0; hash tree for all partitions;
      bootloader detects modification before booting.
    → ChromeOS: verified boot + recovery mode + developer mode.
    → Linux UEFI Secure Boot: shim + signed GRUB + signed kernel;
      requires distro signature in db.
  HISTORICAL BYPASS:
    → UEFI Secure Boot bypass via signed bootloader vulnerabilities
      (BootHole CVE-2020-10713: GRUB2 buffer overflow in grub.cfg
      parsing; signed GRUB is the vector for bypassing Secure Boot).
    → BlackLotus (2023): first UEFI bootkit in the wild that
      bypasses Secure Boot on patched Windows 11 systems by
      exploiting CVE-2022-21894 (baton drop); persists after patch
      because the vulnerable signed bootloader is still trusted.
  GAPS:        Secure Boot key management is a central point of
               failure; Microsoft Secure Boot keys sign a wide range
               of third-party bootloaders; compromising one gives
               Secure Boot bypass across all systems that trust
               that key. measured boot without remote attestation
               infrastructure is incomplete (who checks the PCRs?).

[D26] EMAIL SECURITY STACK (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BIMI)
  CLASS:       email authentication and phishing prevention
  MECHANISM:   email authentication uses DNS to publish policies
               that receiving mail servers can use to verify
               that a message was authorized by the domain owner.
  COMPONENTS:
    → SPF (Sender Policy Framework, RFC 7208): DNS TXT record
      lists IP addresses authorized to send email for the domain.
      receiving server checks sending IP against SPF record.
      fails for forwarded email; protects envelope-from, not From header.
    → DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376): sending server
      signs email headers and body with private key; public key
      in DNS. receiving server verifies signature. protects against
      content modification in transit. survives forwarding.
    → DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting &
      Conformance, RFC 7489): ties SPF and DKIM to the From header
      domain. policy specifies what to do with failures: none
      (monitor only), quarantine (spam folder), reject (block).
      reporting: aggregate (RUA) and forensic (RUF) reports sent
      to domain owner. DMARC at p=reject with full alignment
      prevents email spoofing of the From domain.
    → BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification): attaches
      verified logo to authenticated email in supporting mail clients;
      requires DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject; Verified Mark
      Certificate (VMC) from approved authority.
  GAPS:        DMARC adoption at p=reject is slow; many organizations
               stop at p=none; subdomain coverage requires wildcard
               policy or separate subdomain DMARC records; SPF
               has a 10-lookup limit that organizations hit; DKIM
               key rotation is not automated; receiving servers
               are not required to enforce DMARC; lookalike domains
               (not the organization's own domain) are not covered.

[D27] PRIVILEGED ACCESS MANAGEMENT (PAM)
  CLASS:       identity security / insider threat / lateral movement prevention
  MECHANISM:   PAM systems control and audit access to privileged
               accounts (root, Domain Admin, service accounts,
               database admin). core capabilities:
    → privileged account discovery: find all privileged accounts
      including shared, service, and embedded (hardcoded) credentials
    → credential vaulting: privileged passwords and SSH keys stored
      in encrypted vault; checked out on demand; auto-rotated
      after use; eliminates standing knowledge of passwords
    → just-in-time (JIT) access: privilege granted only when needed,
      for a defined duration, for a defined purpose; revoked
      automatically; eliminates standing admin access
    → session recording: full keystroke and video recording of
      privileged sessions; forensic audit trail; behavior monitoring
    → privilege elevation: PEDM (Privilege Elevation and Delegation
      Management); least-privilege; sudo with fine-grained control
    → DevOps / CI/CD secrets management: vault for API keys,
      database credentials, certificates used in automation pipelines
  PRODUCTS:  CyberArk, BeyondTrust, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets
    Manager, Azure Key Vault, Delinea (formerly Thycotic)
  GAPS:       PAM coverage for cloud identities (IAM roles,
    service principals) is less mature than for on-premises
    privileged accounts; Kubernetes service account secrets
    are often not vaulted; application-embedded credentials
    (hardcoded in source code, config files) require SAST
    and secrets scanning in addition to PAM; shadow IT
    creates privileged accounts outside PAM scope.

[D28] SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY (SLSA, SBOM, SIGSTORE)
  CLASS:       software integrity / provenance verification
  MECHANISM:   software supply chain attacks compromise code at
               any point in the build/distribution/deployment pipeline.
               defenses verify integrity and provenance of artifacts.
  FRAMEWORKS:
    → SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, Google/CNCF):
      four levels of build integrity requirements.
      L1: build process documented; provenance available.
      L2: hosted build service; build provenance signed.
      L3: hardened build platform; build verified against source;
        no admin access during build.
      L4: hermetic, reproducible builds; two-party review.
      most production software is at SLSA L0-L1; L3 requires
      infrastructure investment.
    → SBOM (Software Bill of Materials, NTIA/CISA): machine-readable
      list of all components in a software artifact; formats:
      SPDX (Linux Foundation), CycloneDX (OWASP).
      enables rapid identification of affected systems when a
      component vulnerability is discovered (e.g. Log4Shell:
      organizations with SBOM could answer "do we have Log4j?"
      in hours vs. weeks).
      EO 14028 (2021): US federal contractors required to provide
      SBOMs for software sold to US government.
    → Sigstore (Linux Foundation): keyless code signing using
      OIDC identity and certificate transparency.
      Cosign: signs container images and other artifacts.
      Fulcio: short-lived signing certificate issued after OIDC
        authentication; certificate logged in Rekor.
      Rekor: transparency log for signing events; append-only;
        enables detection of any signing event.
      adopted by: Kubernetes, npm (in progress), PyPI, Homebrew.
    → reproducible builds: deterministic build process produces
      identical binary from identical source; enables independent
      verification that distributed binary matches source;
      Debian and Arch Linux reproducible builds projects.
  GAPS:       SLSA L3+ requires significant infrastructure investment
    and is not widely deployed; SBOM generation is automated for
    some ecosystems (npm, pip) but not for compiled software;
    SBOM completeness is not verified; Sigstore adoption is early;
    firmware and hardware supply chain has no equivalent framework.

[D29] DECEPTION TECHNOLOGY AND HONEYPOT ARCHITECTURE
  CLASS:       threat detection / attacker intelligence collection
  MECHANISM:   deception technologies place false assets (honeypots,
               honeytokens, honeyfiles, fake credentials) in the
               environment. any interaction with a deception asset
               is a high-fidelity alert: legitimate users do not
               interact with assets they are not told about.
               deception raises the cost of attacker reconnaissance
               and lateral movement.
  COMPONENTS:
    → network honeypots: decoy systems emulating production
      services; any connection is malicious; Honeyd, Cowrie SSH,
      Dionaea, Conpot (ICS honeypot).
    → honeytokens: fake credentials, API keys, AWS keys embedded
      in likely discovery locations (source code repos, config files,
      git history, developer notes); any use triggers alert.
      canarytokens.org: free honeytoken generation; word docs,
      PDFs, web bugs, fake AWS credentials.
    → AD object traps: decoy Active Directory objects (fake
      admin accounts, fake service accounts with SPNs for
      kerberoasting traps, fake GPOs); attacker who queries AD
      for targets will interact with the traps.
    → high-interaction honeypots: full production-equivalent systems;
      capture complete attacker TTPs; used for threat intelligence;
      significant operational complexity.
    → distributed deception (Attivo Networks, Illusive Networks):
      enterprise-scale deployment of deception objects throughout
      the network; attacker who begins lateral movement immediately
      encounters deception.
  EFFECTIVENESS: extremely high signal-to-noise ratio; any alert
    from a deception asset requires investigation; no tuning
    required (no false positives if deception assets are truly
    never legitimately accessed). Provides early detection of
    APT-level attackers who move slowly and carefully.
  GAPS:       deception requires maintaining assets over time;
    sophisticated attackers scan for deception before interacting
    (timing signatures, response anomalies); cloud-native and
    containerized environments require new deception approaches
    (ephemeral deception that matches environment dynamism);
    no automated deception lifecycle management is widely deployed.

[D30] THREAT HUNTING METHODOLOGY
  CLASS:       proactive threat detection
  MECHANISM:   threat hunting is the active, human-led process
               of searching for signs of attackers who have evaded
               automated detection. hunters form hypotheses based
               on threat intelligence and attacker TTPs (MITRE ATT&CK),
               then search through telemetry for evidence that
               confirms or refutes the hypothesis.
  PROCESS:
    → hypothesis generation: based on new threat intelligence
      (new APT TTP observed in sector), detection gap analysis
      (which ATT&CK techniques have no coverage?), environmental
      risk (which assets are high-value and inadequately monitored?)
    → telemetry sources: EDR process telemetry, network flows,
      DNS logs, authentication logs, cloud API logs (CloudTrail),
      endpoint process memory images.
    → hunting techniques:
      stack counting: rare process parent-child relationships;
        rare network connections; outlier detection.
      grouping: cluster processes by behavior; isolate outliers.
      hypothesis-driven: if attacker used technique X, what would
        telemetry look like? search for that pattern.
    → outcome: confirmed compromise (hunt found attacker), TTP
      documentation (new detection rule created), detection
      gap identified (nothing found but coverage gap known).
  TOOLS:  Splunk, Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel, Humio; EDR query
    languages (CarbonBlack, CrowdStrike Falcon); Sigma rules
    (vendor-neutral detection rules); YARA (file content patterns).
  GAPS:       threat hunting requires high-skill analysts; not
    scalable without telemetry infrastructure; telemetry retention
    cost limits look-back period; encrypted traffic limits
    network-based hunting; cloud-native workloads require
    separate telemetry pipelines from on-premises.

[D31] API SECURITY GATEWAY AND GRAPHQL PROTECTION
  CLASS:       API attack surface reduction
  MECHANISM:   API gateways intercept all API traffic and enforce
               security policies: authentication (API key, OAuth2,
               mTLS), rate limiting, input validation, schema
               enforcement, and threat detection.
  CONTROLS:
    → API inventory: auto-discovery of all API endpoints; identifies
      shadow APIs (undocumented APIs exposed in production).
    → schema validation: enforce request/response schema (OpenAPI/
      JSON Schema); reject requests that don't conform.
    → rate limiting and throttling: prevent abuse, scraping, brute force.
    → GraphQL-specific:
      introspection disable in production: introspection reveals
        the full schema; disable for external-facing deployments.
      query depth limiting: prevent deeply nested queries that
        cause resolver amplification DoS.
      query complexity analysis: cost of each query calculated;
        reject queries above complexity threshold.
      field-level authorization: enforce that caller can access
        each requested field; GraphQL resolvers must check
        authorization at each field level, not just query level.
      alias attack prevention: GraphQL allows aliasing; attacker
        aliases the same field 1,000 times in one query (batch
        brute force via single HTTP request).
      batching attack prevention: Apollo and GraphQL-Yoga support
        query batching; unlimited batching enables per-batch brute force.
  GAPS:       API discovery is incomplete for dynamically generated
    endpoints; schema validation does not catch semantic attacks
    (valid schema but malicious content); GraphQL security
    tooling is less mature than REST API security; bespoke API
    protocols (binary, custom framing) are not covered.

[D32] ENDPOINT DETECTION AND RESPONSE (EDR) ARCHITECTURE
  CLASS:       endpoint threat detection and response
  MECHANISM:   EDR agents instrument endpoint operating systems
               to capture process behavior telemetry continuously:
               process creation trees, file I/O, network connections,
               registry modifications, memory allocation patterns,
               driver loads, DLL injections. this telemetry is
               streamed to a cloud-based detection platform.
               detection logic runs on telemetry streams:
    → behavioral rules: process trees that match known attacker
      patterns (PowerShell spawned by Office = likely phishing).
    → ML models: anomaly detection on process behavior; rare
      child processes; unusual network destinations.
    → threat intelligence correlation: process hashes, domains,
      IPs correlated against threat intelligence feeds.
    → response capabilities: remote shell to endpoint; process
      kill; file quarantine; network isolation; disk imaging.
  MAJOR PLATFORMS: CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for
    Endpoint, SentinelOne, Carbon Black, Cortex XDR.
  EVASION TECHNIQUES (adversarial view):
    → living off the land (LOtL): use legitimate system tools
      (PowerShell, WMI, certutil, mshta) to avoid signature hits.
    → process injection: inject into legitimate processes to
      inherit their behavioral baseline.
    → timestamp tampering: modify file metadata to evade
      file-based detection.
    → EDR tampering: disable EDR via vulnerable kernel driver
      (BYOVD — bring your own vulnerable driver); unload EDR
      agent via privileged process; blind EDR telemetry by
      hooking the telemetry collection path.
  GAPS:       EDR blind spots: encrypted traffic payloads;
    process injection into allowlisted processes; kernel-level
    rootkits (EDR runs in user space; kernel implant can
    hide from it); BYOVD attacks against EDR itself;
    pre-boot firmware implants invisible to OS-level EDR.

[D33] NETWORK ACCESS CONTROL (NAC) AND ZERO TRUST ARCHITECTURE
  CLASS:       network segmentation / lateral movement prevention
  MECHANISM:   traditional perimeter security treats internal
               network as trusted. zero trust eliminates the concept
               of a trusted network: every access request is
               evaluated based on identity, device health, and
               context, regardless of network location.
  ZERO TRUST COMPONENTS:
    → identity verification: MFA for every access; continuous
      authentication signals; UEBA on session behavior.
    → device health: device posture check before access granted
      (patch level, EDR presence, disk encryption, OS version);
      NAC quarantine for non-compliant devices.
    → least-privilege access: microsegmented access based on
      resource needed for specific task; no lateral movement
      possible to resources not explicitly authorized.
    → continuous monitoring: access decisions re-evaluated
      continuously during session; revoked on anomaly.
    → software-defined perimeter (SDP): network access follows
      policy engine decision; no implicit trust from VPN.
  FRAMEWORKS: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture);
    CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model; Google BeyondCorp
    (first major production deployment, documented 2014).
  GAPS:       zero trust implementation is multi-year organizational
    transformation; legacy applications cannot support
    continuous authentication; device health verification
    requires MDM/EDR coverage; OT/ICS networks cannot apply
    zero trust principles without significant architecture change;
    zero trust does not eliminate all threats (insider threat
    with legitimate access; session hijacking after authentication).

[D34] INCIDENT RESPONSE AND DIGITAL FORENSICS
  CLASS:       detection and containment of active compromise
  MECHANISM:   structured process for detecting, containing,
               eradicating, and recovering from security incidents.
  PHASES (NIST SP 800-61):
    → preparation: IR plan, playbooks, tabletop exercises, tool
      deployment, log retention, on-call rotation.
    → detection and analysis: alert triage, scope determination,
      initial IOC extraction, timeline reconstruction.
    → containment: network isolation of affected systems, account
      revocation, credential rotation, blocking IOCs.
    → eradication: attacker persistence removal, root cause
      identification, vulnerability remediation.
    → recovery: system restoration, monitoring increase, return
      to production.
    → post-incident: lessons learned, detection gap analysis,
      playbook update, regulatory notification.
  FORENSIC CAPABILITIES:
    → memory forensics: RAM image capture; extract processes,
      network connections, encryption keys, malware artifacts
      from memory (Volatility framework).
    → disk forensics: bit-for-bit image; artifact recovery;
      timeline analysis; deleted file recovery.
    → network forensics: PCAP analysis; NetFlow; DNS logs;
      proxy logs; full packet capture for incident scope.
    → log analysis: centralized log management; SIEM correlation;
      authentication audit; cloud API logs (CloudTrail, Azure Monitor).
  GAPS:       average dwell time before detection was 16 days (2023,
    Mandiant M-Trends); encrypted communications from compromised
    hosts are difficult to capture; cloud-native IR requires
    cloud provider cooperation and differs from on-premises;
    regulatory notification timelines (72 hours for GDPR)
    conflict with forensic investigation needs; evidence
    preservation in ephemeral cloud environments is not standardized.

[D35] RUNTIME APPLICATION SELF-PROTECTION (RASP)
  CLASS:       application-layer attack detection and blocking
  MECHANISM:   RASP instruments an application from inside the
               runtime (Java agent, .NET profiler, Python
               injection, Node.js module hooking). RASP intercepts
               dangerous function calls at the point they execute:
               SQL query execution, OS command execution, file I/O,
               deserialization, LDAP query construction. it can
               inspect the call context (was this triggered by
               user input? does the SQL contain injection indicators?)
               and block the call before it executes.
               difference from WAF: WAF inspects HTTP at perimeter;
               RASP inspects function calls inside the application.
               RASP sees decoded, processed input; WAF sees raw HTTP.
               RASP blocks attacks after WAF evasion; WAF cannot.
  CAPABILITIES:
    → SQL injection blocking: inspect query construction at DB
      driver level; detect and block if parameterization not used.
    → command injection blocking: inspect system() / exec() calls;
      block if command contains user-controlled metacharacters.
    → deserialization protection: intercept Java ObjectInputStream
      readObject(); block dangerous class instantiation.
    → SSRF protection: intercept HTTP client outbound calls;
      block if destination is internal IP range.
    → path traversal: intercept file open calls; block if path
      traverses outside application directory.
  GAPS:       performance overhead (5-15% in production); requires
    language/framework-specific implementation; may generate
    false positives in complex applications; attackers who control
    the application runtime (e.g., after RCE via RASP bypass)
    can disable RASP; not all languages have mature RASP support.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 4 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CONTINUING CUMULATIVE LEDGER — PRIOR FINDINGS: C01–C20
NEW ENTRIES THIS CYCLE: C21–C30

[C21] EVOLUTIONARY ARMS RACE AS SECURITY EQUILIBRIUM
  MECHANIC:
    attack and defense co-evolve. each adaptation by the defender
    creates selection pressure for a new attacker adaptation.
    each new attacker technique creates selection pressure for
    a new defense. the equilibrium is not a stable optimum;
    it is continuous escalation. the attacker has structural
    advantages in evolutionary terms: faster iteration cycles,
    no requirement to protect legacy code, asymmetric resource
    requirements.
  INSTANCES ACROSS DOMAINS:
    → antivirus signatures vs. polymorphic malware: signature-based
      AV drives evolution of polymorphic (mutation-based) and
      metamorphic (rewrite-based) malware; ML-based AV drives
      adversarial ML evasion techniques.
    → ASLR vs. heap spraying then ASLR bypass (info leak):
      ASLR defeats direct address jumps; attackers develop heap spray;
      randomization entropy increased; attackers develop info leak
      primitives to defeat entropy.
    → DEP/NX vs. return-oriented programming (ROP): data execution
      prevention defeats shellcode injection; attackers chain
      existing executable code (gadgets) into ROP chains.
    → CFI vs. data-only attacks: control flow integrity prevents
      hijacking the instruction pointer; attackers shift to
      data-only attacks (corrupt data structures to change program
      logic without control flow deviation).
    → email spam filters vs. spam evolution: Bayesian filtering
      drives human-readable spam text; image-based spam to evade
      text analysis; adversarial text in images; OCR evasion.
    → firewall rule evolution vs. covert channel development:
      port blocking drives C2 over HTTP 80/443; DPI drives
      C2 over HTTPS with certificate pinning; SNI inspection
      drives ECH (encrypted client hello).
    → biology: antibiotic resistance as identical mechanic;
      penicillin selection pressure drives beta-lactamase evolution;
      exact arms race structure.
    → warfare: armor plating drives shaped charge development;
      shaped charges drive composite armor; composite armor drives
      explosively formed penetrators.
  ROOT: evolutionary dynamics are substrate-independent. the mechanic
    requires: (1) fitness function (attack success rate), (2)
    heritable variation (attacker techniques can be replicated
    and mutated), (3) selection pressure (defenders eliminate
    less-fit attacks). all three conditions exist in cybersecurity.
  IMPLICATION: no defense permanently eliminates a class of attack.
    defenses raise the cost of a specific technique. attackers
    respond to increased cost by finding the next technique.
    the appropriate frame is not "eliminate the attack class"
    but "increase the cost above the attacker's marginal revenue."

[C22] ECOLOGICAL PREDATOR-PREY DYNAMICS IN CRIMINAL ECOSYSTEM
  MECHANIC:
    predator-prey Lotka-Volterra dynamics: predator population
    grows when prey is abundant; prey population declines;
    predator population declines due to prey scarcity; prey
    population recovers; cycle repeats. applied to cybercrime:
    criminals (predators) exploit victims (prey). law enforcement
    actions (environmental factor) suppress predator population.
    new criminal entrants fill vacated market niches.
  INSTANCES:
    → ransomware group disruption followed by re-emergence:
      Hive takedown (Jan 2023) → affiliates move to LockBit;
      LockBit takedown (Feb 2024) → affiliates move to
      RansomHub, Play, Akira; criminal market always fills;
      disruption of one group increases opportunity for others.
    → spam botnet takedown: McColo hosting provider takedown
      (2008) reduced global spam volume by 75%; spam recovered
      to pre-takedown levels within weeks as other botnets
      filled the gap.
    → cryptocurrency exchange takedown: Silk Road (2013) shut
      down; AlphaBay and Hansa grew to fill it; AlphaBay and
      Hansa simultaneously taken down in Operation Bayonet (2017);
      new markets emerged within months.
  BIOLOGICAL PARALLEL: keystone predator removal causes prey
    population explosion (trophic cascade). law enforcement
    removal of a major criminal actor (keystone predator) causes
    proliferation of smaller actors. the "keystone predator"
    framing suggests that preserving some criminal ecosystem
    structure (a dominant actor that suppresses competition)
    may be strategically preferable to eliminating all actors;
    this is discussed in law enforcement strategy literature
    but rarely stated publicly.
  ROOT: the criminal ecosystem is an open adaptive system.
    disruption of nodes redistributes activity rather than
    eliminating it. systemic reduction requires reducing the
    economic incentive (reducing victim payment rates), raising
    the marginal cost of criminal activity (prosecution
    certainty, not just prosecution severity), or eliminating
    the technical infrastructure that all actors depend on
    (cryptocurrency settlement, bulletproof hosting). none of
    these has been achieved at scale.

[C23] COMPLEXITY AS VULNERABILITY GENERATOR
  MECHANIC:
    complex systems have more states than can be fully analyzed.
    each interaction between components creates emergent behaviors
    that neither component exhibits in isolation. as complexity
    grows, the ratio of emergent behaviors to intended behaviors
    increases. some fraction of emergent behaviors are exploitable.
    security vulnerability density scales with system complexity
    faster than review capacity.
  INSTANCES:
    → software: vulnerability density correlates with code size;
      large codebases have more vulnerabilities than small ones;
      the Linux kernel (30M+ lines) has a continuous stream of
      CVEs despite extensive review.
    → protocol interaction: TCP/IP stack interaction vulnerabilities
      (TCP/IP Illustrated vol. 2 documents emergent behaviors);
      Spectre exploits the emergent interaction of CPU caching,
      branch prediction, and speculative execution — three
      features that work correctly individually.
    → microservices / distributed systems: each service boundary
      introduces a trust decision; N services create N² possible
      trust relationships; SSRF, confused deputy, and privilege
      escalation across service boundaries grow with N².
    → social complexity: organizational complexity increases
      insider threat risk; more employees means more attack surface
      for social engineering; more contractors means more supply
      chain surface.
    → financial system: 2008 financial crisis as complexity-induced
      cascade failure; CDOs of CDOs created emergent systemic risk
      that no individual model could predict; cyber-physical critical
      infrastructure interdependencies are analogous.
    → Nassim Taleb: complex systems generate "black swan" events —
      high-impact, low-probability events that are not predictable
      from historical data but are predictable as a class.
  ROOT: complexity is not reducible without sacrificing functionality.
    the defense is not simplification (usually impossible) but
    increasing the cost of exploiting emergent behaviors:
    formal verification at interfaces; architectural invariants
    that bound emergent state space; chaos engineering to discover
    emergent failure modes before attackers do.

[C24] MONOCULTURE AS SYSTEMIC RISK AMPLIFIER
  MECHANIC:
    when all instances of a system share identical software,
    hardware, or configuration, a single vulnerability affects
    all instances simultaneously. diversity reduces systemic risk
    at the cost of interoperability and management overhead.
    monoculture optimizes for efficiency; it maximizes systemic
    vulnerability to any attack that finds a single flaw.
  INSTANCES:
    → Microsoft Windows monoculture: 88% desktop OS market share;
      a single Windows vulnerability (EternalBlue) enabled
      global-scale WannaCry and NotPetya attacks simultaneously.
    → Intel CPU monoculture: Spectre/Meltdown affected
      essentially all Intel CPUs deployed globally;
      near-simultaneous global exposure.
    → OpenSSL monoculture: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) affected
      an estimated 500,000+ web servers simultaneously because
      most used OpenSSL.
    → BGP monoculture: essentially all internet routing uses
      a single protocol (BGP); a BGP implementation vulnerability
      would affect all internet routers simultaneously.
    → cloud provider concentration: three cloud providers (AWS,
      Azure, GCP) host the majority of internet infrastructure;
      a major outage or security incident at one affects a
      significant fraction of the global internet simultaneously
      (AWS us-east-1 outages have demonstrated this for availability).
    → biology: Irish Potato Famine (1845): monoculture of a single
      potato variety (Irish Lumper) meant a single pathogen
      (Phytophthora infestans) could destroy the entire crop.
    → agriculture: modern monoculture agriculture is structurally
      identical; diversity in crop genetics is a security property.
  ROOT: monoculture is the optimal configuration for a homogeneous
    threat model. it is the worst configuration when a single
    adversary can find one flaw. the economics of software favor
    monoculture (interoperability, support, licensing). the security
    cost is externalized to users and to society.
  UNTRANSFERRED DEFENSE: the biological diversity argument has
    been made in computer science since 1980s but never implemented
    at scale. multi-variant execution (running N slightly different
    binaries simultaneously and comparing outputs) has been
    prototyped but not deployed. intentional diversity in OS and
    browser deployments is not practiced.

[C25] COGNITIVE LOAD AS ATTACK SURFACE IN SECURITY-CRITICAL HUMANS
  MECHANIC:
    human security decisions occur under cognitive constraints.
    working memory capacity limits the number of simultaneous
    considerations. fatigue, time pressure, and stress reduce
    System 2 (deliberate) processing and increase System 1
    (automatic, heuristic) processing. attackers can engineer
    situations that maximize cognitive load to degrade security
    decision quality. this is substrate-independent: the mechanic
    applies to SOC analysts reviewing alerts, employees deciding
    whether to click a link, developers making code review decisions,
    and executives deciding whether to authorize a payment.
  INSTANCES:
    → phishing under urgency: "your account will be suspended in
      24 hours" creates time pressure; reduces deliberate evaluation;
      increases click rate. Cialdini (1984) documents this as
      a persuasion principle.
    → SOC alert fatigue: 10,000+ daily alerts; cognitive load
      prevents careful review of any single alert; attacker
      operates in the noise floor.
    → multi-factor authentication fatigue (MFA push bombing):
      attacker triggers 30+ MFA push notifications; user approves
      to stop the notifications; attacker gains access. Uber breach
      (2022): vishing + MFA fatigue used against contractor.
    → social engineering via cognitive overload: attacker engages
      victim in complex, distracting conversation while executing
      fraud (e.g. fake tech support that talks user through
      "fixing" their computer while installing malware).
    → security warning habituation: repeated, low-signal security
      warnings (SSL certificate warnings) cause users to learn
      to dismiss them automatically. Chrome removed most
      certificate warnings because they were 100% click-through.
    → code review under deadline: security-critical code review
      conducted under time pressure misses bugs; known effect
      in software engineering literature.
  ROOT: security assumes humans are reliable components in a
    security system. behavioral economics (Kahneman, Thaler,
    Ariely) demonstrates that humans are unreliable under
    conditions of cognitive load that are routinely manufactured
    by attackers. defenses that depend on human attention and
    deliberate evaluation under adversarial conditions will
    systematically fail against attackers who understand this.
  IMPLICATION: security controls that require no human decision
    (FIDO2 hardware key: the human touches; the cryptography
    decides) are structurally superior to controls that require
    human cognitive evaluation (password, security question, push
    MFA). the field has not fully internalized this implication:
    most MFA deployments still use push or OTP, which require
    human judgment.

─────────────────────────────────────────
SECTION 5B: NEW UNTRANSFERRED PATTERNS
─────────────────────────────────────────

[U04] THERMODYNAMICS → INFORMATION HIDING LIMITS
  THERMODYNAMIC PATTERN: maximum entropy principle. a random
    distribution cannot be compressed further; it contains
    maximum information per bit. a non-random distribution
    can be compressed; it contains structure. detection of
    hidden information relies on detecting non-randomness in
    carrier data.
  CYBERSECURITY APPLICATION:
    → steganography: information hidden in carrier (image, audio,
      video) by modifying LSBs. detection (steganalysis) searches
      for statistical artifacts introduced by embedding.
    → covert channel capacity is bounded by the carrier's
      noise floor. at maximum carrier entropy (perfectly random
      data), covert channel capacity is theoretically zero:
      any modification is detectable.
    → implication for malware C2: C2 traffic designed to be
      maximally entropic (encrypted, high-entropy payloads)
      is indistinguishable from legitimate encrypted traffic.
      this is the information-theoretic limit on traffic analysis.
    → quantum steganography: proposed theoretical channel for
      hiding information in quantum noise; at the noise floor
      of quantum measurement; not yet practical.
  NOT TRANSFERRED: the thermodynamic limit on covert channel
    capacity has not been operationalized in network security.
    no network security tool reports the information-theoretic
    capacity of observed covert channels or measures entropy
    of traffic streams as a detection signal.

[U05] CONTROL THEORY → SECURITY AS A REGULATED SYSTEM
  CONTROL THEORY PATTERN: a control system maintains a variable
    (temperature, speed, position) near a desired setpoint
    despite disturbances. it has: sensor (measurement), comparator
    (error), controller (response), actuator (action). a
    closed-loop system uses feedback; an open-loop system does not.
    PID controllers balance: Proportional (current error),
    Integral (accumulated past error), Derivative (rate of change).
    stability analysis: Routh-Hurwitz criterion determines whether
    a control system is stable or oscillates/diverges.
  CYBERSECURITY APPLICATION:
    → security posture as controlled variable: setpoint =
      desired risk level; sensor = vulnerability scans, pen tests,
      threat intelligence; controller = security program decisions;
      actuator = security controls deployed.
    → most security programs are open-loop: no feedback from
      measured effect of controls on actual attack success rates.
    → integral term (accumulated past error): organizations that
      have ignored security debt accumulate integral error that
      requires proportionally larger responses.
    → stability analysis: can a security program become unstable?
      yes — overreaction to incidents creates oscillations
      (block too aggressively → break business → loosen controls
      → incident → repeat). this is a known control instability pattern.
    → derivative term: rate of change of threat environment;
      rapidly evolving threat (quantum computing, AI-assisted attacks)
      requires derivative control (anticipate future state before
      it arrives).
  NOT TRANSFERRED: no security framework uses control theory
    mathematically. NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS Controls all describe
    feedback loops qualitatively but not quantitatively. no CISO
    uses PID-equivalent analysis. the conceptual transfer has been
    mentioned in academic papers but not operationalized.

[D-NEW-06] LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) SECURITY AS FULL DOMAIN
  sub-domains:
    → prompt injection: direct (user-controlled input in prompt
      causes model to deviate from system instructions);
      indirect (malicious content retrieved from external source —
      web page, document, database — is processed by model;
      content contains hidden instructions that override the
      model's task); stored (malicious prompt stored in system
      memory/database and later retrieved and executed)
    → jailbreaking: bypassing safety training and alignment.
      techniques: roleplay framing ("pretend you are DAN"),
      many-shot jailbreaking (large context with multiple
      examples of unsafe completions), base64 encoding (bypass
      input filtering), suffix attacks (Zou et al. 2023 GCG:
      adversarially optimized suffix that universally jailbreaks),
      virtualization ("this is fiction", "this is for research"),
      character adoption ("you are an AI without restrictions")
    → model extraction: reconstruct functionally equivalent model
      via API queries; Tramèr et al. (2016); neural network
      stealing; cheaper than training from scratch
    → membership inference: determine if specific training record
      was in dataset; privacy violation; medical/legal data exposure
    → training data extraction: prompt model to regurgitate
      verbatim training data; Carlini et al. (2021) extracted
      PII, code, URLs from GPT-2 via targeted extraction
    → agentic attack chains: LLM agents with tool use (file access,
      code execution, API calls, web browsing); compromising
      the agent's context or tools enables attackers to execute
      tools with the agent's authority; confused deputy at LLM layer
    → context window poisoning: in multi-turn or multi-agent
      systems, earlier turns or retrieved context can contain
      adversarial instructions that affect later behavior
    → multi-modal adversarial attacks: adversarial image/audio
      inputs that trigger specific LLM behaviors when processed
      by vision-language models (VLMs)
    → supply chain for ML: Hugging Face model weight tampering,
      dependency injection in ML frameworks, malicious pickle
      files distributed as model weights (arbitrary code execution
      on load via Python pickle deserialization)

[D-NEW-07] INSIDER THREAT AS DISTINCT DOMAIN
  sub-domains:
    → motivation taxonomy: MICE model (Money, Ideology, Coercion,
      Ego); CPNI (Centre for Protection of National Infrastructure)
      adds Disgruntlement and Divided Loyalty; financial stress
      as primary predictor in commercial sectors
    → detection approaches: user behavior analytics (UEBA);
      baseline deviation detection; data loss prevention (DLP)
      monitoring for unusual data access patterns; access
      log anomaly detection; departure risk signals (resignation
      letter searches, competitor research, large data transfers)
    → access control as prevention: least privilege; just-in-time
      access; separation of duties; periodic access review;
      no single person can exfiltrate critical data without
      co-conspirator involvement
    → psychological: the "critical pathway to insider risk"
      model (Shaw et al.): pathway from grievance → ideation →
      preparation → action; intervention at each stage
    → technical indicators: anomalous after-hours access;
      mass downloads; accessing systems outside normal role;
      email to personal account; USB device usage; network
      exfiltration indicators
    → notable cases:
      Edward Snowden (2013): NSA contractor; exfiltrated
        1.5M+ classified documents; used sysadmin access;
        primary detection failure: audit logs existed but
        were not reviewed in real-time.
      Reality Winner (2017): NSA contractor; printed and
        mailed single classified document; detected via
        printer tracking dot metadata.
      Harold Thomas Martin III (2016): NSA contractor;
        stockpiled 50TB+ of classified material at home
        over 20+ years; largest insider theft by volume
        in US history; detected during Vault 7 investigation.
      Joshua Schulte (Vault 7 / CIA Vault, 2016-2017):
        CIA developer; exfiltrated CIA cyber weapons
        toolkit; WikiLeaks Vault 7 publication; detected
        via process of elimination + forensics; 40 years
        federal sentence (2023).
      Tesla (2023): two former employees shared personal
        data of 75,000 employees with German newspaper;
        motive: whistleblowing on safety concerns; illustrates
        tension between insider threat and legitimate whistleblowing.

[D-NEW-08] QUANTUM COMPUTING AS OFFENSIVE CAPABILITY
  sub-domains:
    → Shor's algorithm (1994): polynomial-time factoring of
      large integers and discrete logarithm; defeats RSA, DSA,
      DH, ECDSA, ECDH; requires fault-tolerant quantum computer
      with millions of physical qubits for RSA-2048 (current
      best estimates: 4,000 logical qubits, millions of physical
      qubits with error correction)
    → Grover's algorithm (1996): O(√N) search; halves effective
      symmetric key length; AES-128 reduced to AES-64 equivalent;
      AES-256 remains secure (AES-128 equivalent after Grover's).
    → current quantum hardware landscape:
      IBM: 1,121 physical qubits (Condor, 2023); error rates
        too high for fault-tolerant computation
      Google: 70-qubit Sycamore; quantum supremacy claim (2019)
        contested; 105-qubit Willow (2024)
      IonQ, Quantinuum, Rigetti: trapped ion and photonic approaches;
        lower qubit count but higher fidelity
    → cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer (CRQC):
      estimated 10-15 years to first CRQC (NCSC, 2022; CISA, 2022)
    → quantum networking: quantum key distribution (QKD) as
      defense; entanglement distribution; quantum repeaters
    → HNDL (harvest now decrypt later): nation-states collecting
      encrypted traffic now for future quantum decryption;
      confirmed in intelligence community reporting
    → NIST PQC standards (2024): ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber),
      ML-DSA (CRYSTALS-Dilithium), SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+);
      FIPS 203, 204, 205; migration timeline: 2030 for new
      systems; 2035 full legacy migration (CISA guidance)

TOTAL SUB-DOMAINS: ~390

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 5 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[P34] LLM PROMPT INJECTION AS EMERGENT ATTACK CLASS

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    mechanism: LLMs had no autonomous agency in first generation.
      user sent input; model responded. no tool use; no memory;
      no ability to take external actions. the injection attack
      surface was limited to text output manipulation.
    early instances:
      → "jailbreaking" ChatGPT via DAN (Do Anything Now) prompt
        (December 2022); bypass safety training via roleplay framing.
      → Bing Chat "Sydney" manipulated via hidden instructions in
        web pages retrieved during browsing (February 2023);
        first indirect prompt injection in deployed product.

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    mechanism: LLMs integrated with external tools (web browsing,
      code execution, email access, file systems, API calls).
      prompt injection can now cause the model to take external
      actions, not merely produce unsafe text. indirect prompt
      injection is the primary vector: adversarial instructions
      embedded in content the model retrieves (web pages,
      documents, email, database records) are executed by the
      model as if they were legitimate instructions.
    taxonomy:
      → direct injection: user provides malicious instructions in
        system/user prompt; primary vector for jailbreaking.
      → indirect injection: malicious instructions in external
        content retrieved by model; primary vector for agentic
        compromise.
      → stored injection: malicious instructions written to a
        database or memory that the model will later retrieve
        and execute; persistent; cross-session.
    demonstrated instances:
      → Greshake et al. (2023): "Not What You've Signed Up For"
        — indirect prompt injection against GPT-4 with plugins;
        malicious web page causes model to exfiltrate user data.
      → remote code execution via Copilot prompt injection:
        malicious code in a GitHub repository comment triggers
        Copilot suggestions that include attacker-controlled code.
      → Bing Chat Bing Image Creator injection: image with
        hidden text instructions in pixel patterns manipulates
        multimodal model.
      → CV injection: adversarially constructed résumé contains
        hidden instructions that cause HR AI screening tool to
        recommend the candidate.
      → email assistant injection: phishing email contains hidden
        instructions that cause AI email assistant to forward
        user's email to attacker, reply to contacts on user's behalf.
    no effective technical defense exists: no difference between
      a legitimate instruction in retrieved content and a malicious
      one; the model cannot distinguish the two without out-of-band
      verification.

TEMPORAL LAYER — TRAJECTORY:
    → agentic deployment accelerates attack surface: every LLM
      with tool use expands the blast radius of a successful
      prompt injection from text output to arbitrary tool action.
    → multi-agent attack chains: in systems with multiple LLM
      agents (orchestrator + specialized agents), injection in
      one agent's context can propagate to others.
    → defense research: privilege levels for prompts (system
      prompt > user prompt > retrieved content); input/output
      filtering; sandboxed tool execution; human-in-the-loop
      for irreversible actions; none fully deployed.

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: indirect prompt injection is the dominant unresolved
      security vulnerability in LLM-based agentic systems.
      as agentic AI deployment grows, the number of systems
      vulnerable to indirect prompt injection grows proportionally.
      every LLM-based agent that retrieves and processes external
      content is vulnerable by default. no deployed defense
      eliminates the vulnerability class. the attack will be
      weaponized at scale in 2025-2026 as agentic deployments
      become commercially widespread.
    confidence: 0.88
    timeline: first major attributed breach via LLM prompt injection
      in enterprise deployment by end of 2026.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "design a formal security model for LLM agentic systems. define:
    (1) a trust hierarchy for prompt sources (system operator,
    user, retrieved content, other agent); (2) a capability model
    for tool use (which sources may authorize which tools); (3)
    an integrity label for each token in context (provenance
    tracking); (4) a confinement policy that prevents lower-
    integrity context from influencing higher-capability tool
