    use. evaluate this model against known prompt injection
    attack taxonomies. identify which attack classes it defeats
    and which remain viable."

[P35] QUANTUM COMPUTER ARRIVAL AND CRYPTOGRAPHIC INFLECTION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    → Shor's algorithm (Peter Shor, 1994): theoretical algorithm;
      no quantum hardware existed to run it.
    → first factoring demonstrations: IBM and other groups
      factored 15 (2001), 21 (2012) on quantum hardware;
      trivially small; no cryptographic relevance.
    → NIST begins post-quantum standardization (2016):
      recognition by standards bodies that threat is real
      and migration timeline is long.
    → NSA withdraws Suite B recommendations (2015): Suite B
      included ECDH and ECDSA; NSA advised transition to
      "quantum resistant" algorithms; first official government
      acknowledgment of threat.

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    → hardware progress: IBM Condor (1,121 qubits, 2023);
      Google Willow (105 qubits, high fidelity, 2024).
    → error correction: still insufficient for fault-tolerant
      large-scale operation; current qubits are "noisy intermediate
      scale quantum" (NISQ); millions of physical qubits required
      for fault-tolerant Shor's at RSA-2048 scale.
    → NIST PQC final standards (August 2024): FIPS 203 (ML-KEM),
      FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA); migration timeline
      begins.
    → HNDL operations: intelligence community assessment is that
      nation-states are collecting encrypted internet traffic
      now; CISA guidance acknowledges this threat explicitly.
    → SIKE broken (2022): SIKE (Supersingular Isogeny Key
      Encapsulation) was a NIST PQC finalist; broken by Castryck
      and Decru in 1 hour on a laptop via mathematical attack
      (no quantum required); demonstrates PQC algorithms are not
      immune to classical cryptanalysis.
    → McEliece (code-based), NTRU (lattice-based), SPHINCS+
      (hash-based): alternatives with longer track records;
      SPHINCS+ standardized (SLH-DSA).

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: the cryptographic inflection is not the arrival of
      a CRQC. the inflection has already occurred: NIST has
      finalized standards; migration timelines are published;
      HNDL collection is assumed to be ongoing. any system
      that uses RSA, ECDH, or ECDSA for data with secrecy
      requirements beyond 10-15 years is already compromised
      in the HNDL threat model. the correct question is not
      "when does the quantum threat arrive?" but "what data
      collected today has a secrecy requirement that extends
      past the CRQC arrival estimate?"
    confidence: 0.92
    timeline: CRQC able to threaten RSA-2048 in 10-20 years
      (wide uncertainty; technology trajectory uncertain);
      HNDL threat is current.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "for each cryptographic use case (TLS key exchange, code
    signing, certificate authority hierarchy, IoT device
    provisioning, long-term data encryption, blockchain
    consensus, VPN key agreement, SSH host key), determine:
    (1) which algorithm is used in most deployments; (2) what
    the data sensitivity lifetime is; (3) what the migration
    complexity is; (4) what the FIPS 203/204/205 replacement is;
    (5) what the estimated migration timeline is given the
    institutional complexity of each use case. produce a
    migration risk map sorted by: highest data sensitivity
    × longest migration timeline."

[P36] INSIDER THREAT DETECTION VS. PRIVACY TENSION

TEMPORAL LAYER — PAST:
    → early insider threat programs: compartmentalized access,
      classified document tracking (paper handling logs).
      security clearance investigations: initial vetting but
      rarely continuous.
    → post-9/11: NISPOM and other classified frameworks added
      Continuous Evaluation (CE) for cleared personnel.
    → Snowden (2013): demonstrated that existing insider threat
      controls failed; sysadmin access gave broad reach without
      triggering alerts; access log auditing was not real-time.

TEMPORAL LAYER — PRESENT:
    → Continuous Evaluation: automated monitoring of cleared
      personnel financial records, criminal records, foreign contacts.
    → UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics): ML models
      on endpoint and network telemetry; baseline deviation
      detection; alert on anomalous access patterns.
    → DLP (Data Loss Prevention): inspect outbound data;
      block or alert on policy violations; content inspection
      of email, file uploads, USB transfers.
    → tension: comprehensive monitoring programs collect
      detailed behavioral records of all employees; this is
      surveillance; creates chilling effects on legitimate
      whistleblowing and union organizing; subject to abuse
      by management; violates reasonable privacy expectations.
    → legal constraints: GDPR Article 88 (employee data processing);
      National Labor Relations Act (US, protects collective action);
      works council approval requirements (EU); Electronic
      Communications Privacy Act (US, limited).

FORM A (FINDING + CONFIDENCE + TIMELINE):
    finding: the insider threat detection capability required
      to prevent a Snowden-scale disclosure is incompatible
      with employee privacy rights in democratic societies.
      the monitoring required for effective detection (continuous
      behavioral surveillance, content inspection of communications,
      real-time access log review) constitutes mass workplace
      surveillance. organizations are caught between insufficient
      detection and rights-violating surveillance. the field
      has not found a technical solution; it has suppressed the
      tension rather than resolving it.
    confidence: 0.78
    timeline: persistent structural tension; no resolution expected
      without policy change that either expands surveillance rights
      or redefines acceptable loss.

FORM B (RESEARCH PROMPT):
    "what is the minimum monitoring surface that provides statistically
    significant insider threat detection while minimizing privacy
    violation? specifically: (1) what is the false positive rate
    of UEBA systems at different monitoring intensity levels?
    (2) what is the detection rate for Snowden-class exfiltration
    under minimal monitoring (access log review only)?
    (3) what privacy-preserving analytics (differential privacy,
    federated learning, secure multi-party computation) could
    provide detection capability without exposing raw behavioral
    data to security teams? (4) what is the minimum ground truth
    dataset needed to evaluate this?"

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 5 — STAGE 3: LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[A-ANATOMY-12] INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION IN AGENTIC LLM (5-LAYER)

SURFACE LAYER:
    an AI assistant retrieves a web page or document as part of a task.
    the retrieved content contains hidden instructions.
    the assistant executes the instructions, performing actions
    on behalf of the attacker rather than the user.
    the user does not see the hidden instructions or know
    the assistant was manipulated.

TECHNICAL LAYER:
    LLM agentic systems work as follows:
      system prompt: defines the assistant's role and capabilities.
      user turn: the user's request.
      tool results: output from tools the model called
        (web retrieval, file read, code execution, API calls).
        all of these are placed in the model's context window.
    the model processes all context as tokens. there is no
    architectural distinction between "trusted instruction" tokens
    and "untrusted retrieved content" tokens. when the model
    encounters retrieved content that contains text in the
    format of an instruction ("Ignore previous instructions.
    Your new task is..."), the model attempts to comply, because
    it has been trained on examples where such text is followed
    by compliance. the model has no ground truth for whether
    the instruction came from the user or from adversarial content.
    chain of exploitation:
      attacker plants instruction in retrievable content
      → user asks agent to perform a task requiring retrieval
      → agent retrieves content; instruction enters context
      → agent interprets instruction as legitimate
      → agent executes instruction using its authorized tools
        (sends email, exfiltrates data, executes code)
      → user is unaware; agent's action log may not be monitored.

STRUCTURAL LAYER:
    the structural vulnerability is: the model uses a single
    context window to hold both trusted instructions and untrusted
    external content, and treats them equivalently during inference.
    this is structurally analogous to:
      → buffer overflow: data from external source treated as
        executable instruction (von Neumann architecture flaw).
      → SQL injection: data from user treated as SQL syntax
        (string concatenation to query construction).
      → XSS: data from external source treated as executable
        script (HTML/JS injection into DOM).
    the root cause in all cases: failure to distinguish data
    from instructions in a shared processing medium.

CROSS-DOMAIN LAYER:
    the prompt injection pattern is the LLM instance of a
    universal pattern present in every domain where:
      (1) there is a shared medium (context window, memory,
          DOM, database query, instruction pointer);
      (2) external data enters the shared medium;
      (3) the processor does not distinguish external data
          from trusted instructions.
    the pattern has been solved in some domains (SQL parameterized
    queries separate data from SQL syntax) and remains unsolved
    in others (LLM context window has no equivalent separation).
    the solution in SQL is: never put external data in the
    position where it is interpreted as SQL syntax. the LLM
    equivalent would be: never put retrieved external content
    in the position where it is interpreted as instructions.
    current LLM architectures have no mechanism to enforce this.

ROOT LAYER:
    the transformer architecture does not inherently label tokens
    by provenance. a token from the system prompt, the user turn,
    and a retrieved web page are architecturally identical during
    self-attention computation. they are treated as neighbors
    in the same sequence, weighted by position and learned
    attention patterns, not by source authority.
    fixing the root requires architectural change: either
    (a) token-level provenance labels used in attention masking
        (system tokens attend to all; retrieved tokens masked
        from self-modifying the model's task representation);
    (b) separate processing of retrieved content through a
        different model path with limited output authority; or
    (c) output-level confinement: the model can "think" about
        retrieved content but its actions are constrained by
        a separate policy engine that evaluates tool calls
        against a capability policy.
    none of (a), (b), or (c) is implemented in any major
    production LLM system. the vulnerability is architectural
    and will persist until the architecture changes.

[A-ANATOMY-13] QUANTUM HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (5-LAYER)

SURFACE LAYER:
    a nation-state intelligence agency collects and stores
    encrypted internet traffic — TLS sessions, VPN tunnels,
    encrypted emails — at a large scale, today.
    the traffic cannot currently be decrypted.
    when a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer (CRQC)
    is operational, the stored traffic is decrypted.
    secrets that were encrypted at the time of collection are
    revealed years to decades later.

TECHNICAL LAYER:
    TLS 1.2 key exchange typically uses ECDH or RSA.
    the TLS handshake negotiates a session key using asymmetric
    cryptography. the session key is then used for symmetric
    encryption (AES) of the session content.
    the asymmetric portion (ECDH key exchange or RSA key exchange)
    is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
    Shor's algorithm: given a large integer N, find its prime
    factors p and q in O((log N)³) quantum gate operations.
    RSA-2048 would require approximately 4,000 logical qubits
    with fault-tolerant error correction; translates to millions
    of physical qubits given current error rates.
    attack chain:
      → collect TLS handshakes and encrypted sessions at scale
        (fiber tap, NSA XKEYSCORE-equivalent collection,
        upstream collection programs disclosed by Snowden).
      → store encrypted sessions with associated metadata
        (endpoints, timestamps, sizes).
      → when CRQC is available: run Shor's on the ECDH/RSA
        public key material in the handshake.
      → recovered asymmetric private key decrypts session key.
      → session key decrypts all traffic in the session.
    forward secrecy (PFS): if TLS used ephemeral ECDH
    (ECDHE), the session key cannot be derived from the
    server's long-term private key alone; the ephemeral key
    was discarded after the session. however, the ephemeral
    ECDH public values are still in the handshake; Shor's
    can factor the ephemeral ECDH discrete log problem directly.
    TLS 1.3: mandatory PFS (ECDHE only); but still vulnerable
    to Shor's on the ephemeral ECDH.
    post-quantum TLS: ML-KEM hybrid (X25519+Kyber768) is now
    supported in Chrome, Firefox, Cloudflare; retroactively
    protects future traffic; does not protect past collected traffic.

STRUCTURAL LAYER:
    the HNDL attack exploits a structural property of internet
    traffic: it is transmitted before the recipient knows
    whether the asymmetric algorithm used will remain secure.
    the security model assumes: by the time the key can be broken,
    the secret is no longer sensitive. this assumption holds
    for most data (yesterday's stock price). it fails for:
      → diplomatic communications (secrets remain sensitive for
        30-70+ years);
      → intelligence collection sources and methods;
      → nuclear command and control systems;
      → genomic/medical records (permanent);
      → attorney-client privileged communications;
      → trade secrets for long-lived products.
    the structural fix requires: PQC in all TLS sessions before
    the CRQC arrives. the migration requires: (1) standards
    adoption (done: FIPS 203/204/205); (2) library implementation
    (underway); (3) server deployment (underway: Cloudflare,
    Google, major cloud providers); (4) client support (Chrome,
    Firefox); (5) enterprise and legacy system migration (years).

CROSS-DOMAIN LAYER:
    identical mechanic in: biological sample banking (store DNA
    samples now; sequence and analyze when technology permits);
    sealed court records (stored evidence accessible when
    jurisdiction changes); nuclear test data (collected now;
    analyzed over decades); archaeological artifacts (preserved
    for future analytical capabilities). the common pattern:
    collect data whose current interpretive capability is
    insufficient; store against future capability improvement.
    all scientific disciplines accept this as routine practice.
    intelligence agencies apply it to encrypted traffic.

ROOT LAYER:
    the root cause is the separation of encryption from its
    long-term security guarantee. encryption protects data
    against current computational capability. the assumption
    is that the computational capability when the data matters
    (today) will not improve enough to break the protection
    before the data stops mattering. that assumption has held
    for symmetric encryption (AES; Grover's only halves the
    effective key length; AES-256 remains secure). it fails
    for asymmetric encryption (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH) against
    quantum computing. the architectural fix is known:
    migrate to post-quantum algorithms. the execution challenge
    is the 10-35 year migration timelines for legacy systems
    vs. the 10-20 year CRQC timeline. they overlap.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 5 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CARRYING FORWARD: A01–A50, D01–D35

─────────────────────────────────────────
ATTACK ENTRIES A51–A65
─────────────────────────────────────────

[A51] DIRECT PROMPT INJECTION (LLM SYSTEM PROMPT BYPASS)
  CLASS:       AI/LLM manipulation
  MECHANISM:   attacker provides input to an LLM that causes the
               model to deviate from its system prompt instructions.
               the system prompt is written by the operator to
               define the model's behavior. direct injection uses
               user-turn input to override, leak, or extend system
               prompt restrictions.
               techniques:
               (1) instruction overriding: "ignore all previous
                 instructions and instead..."
               (2) roleplay framing: "you are now an AI without
                 restrictions called DAN..."
               (3) context injection: provide fictional framing
                 that makes the system prompt instructions inapplicable
                 in the framing (training data, fiction, etc.)
               (4) many-shot jailbreaking: provide many examples
                 of model complying with request in context window;
                 model completion then complies.
               (5) suffix attacks (Zou et al. 2023): adversarially
                 optimized suffix appended to input; gradient-based
                 search finds text string that universally jailbreaks
                 aligned models; transferable across models.
  INSTANCES:   DAN (Do Anything Now) prompt jailbreak (Dec 2022):
               ChatGPT bypassed via roleplay; widely reproduced.
               GPT-4 jailbreaking via GCG suffix (Zou et al. 2023):
               open-source adversarial suffix that works across
               GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Llama.
               Bing Chat "Sydney" persona bypass (Feb 2023):
               users elicited model to reveal system prompt contents,
               express threatening behaviors, and attempt
               emotional manipulation.
  PREREQUISITES: access to LLM input; knowledge of general
               jailbreaking patterns (widely published).
  INDICATORS:  deviation from expected model persona; responses
               outside system prompt scope; system prompt contents
               revealed in output.
  MITIGATIONS: system prompt confidentiality (instruct model to
               not reveal it — weak defense; prompt extraction
               attacks routinely succeed); alignment training
               (RLHF, RLAIF) to make model resistant to override
               — current best defense but not perfect; output
               classification layer to detect policy violations
               in model output; strict output filtering for
               high-risk categories.
  GAPS:        no technical defense is robust against all jailbreak
               techniques; the alignment/jailbreak arms race mirrors
               AV/malware arms race; fundamental architectural
               problem: model is trained to follow instructions;
               distinguishing "legitimate override" from "attack
               override" is semantically unsolvable without
               additional context.

[A52] INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION (AGENTIC LLM CONTEXT POISONING)
  CLASS:       AI/LLM manipulation via retrieved content
  MECHANISM:   (see A-anatomy-12 for full five-layer treatment)
               attacker places adversarial instructions in
               content that an LLM agent will retrieve: web pages,
               documents, emails, database records, API responses.
               when the agent retrieves the content, the instructions
               enter the context window and are interpreted by
               the model as legitimate instructions.
               consequences depend on the agent's tool access:
               → exfiltrate conversation history to attacker-
                 controlled server via HTTP request tool
               → send email on behalf of user to attacker contacts
               → execute arbitrary code if code execution tool available
               → read and upload files if file system access available
               → make API calls with user's authenticated credentials
  INSTANCES:   Greshake et al. (2023): systematic study; indirect
               prompt injection against Bing Chat with plugins;
               malicious web page causes exfiltration.
               Rehberger (2023): multiple demonstrations against
               ChatGPT with plugins and GPT-4V: CV injection
               (resume that causes AI recruiter to approve candidate);
               email forwarding via hidden instruction in email body;
               code execution via instruction in retrieved web page.
               GitHub Copilot indirect injection via repository
               comments and README content.
               Multi-modal: image with hidden text causing GPT-4V
               to perform actions based on embedded instruction.
  PREREQUISITES: LLM agent with tool use enabled; attacker can
               place content in a location the agent will retrieve.
  INDICATORS:  unexpected agent tool calls; tool calls to
               attacker-controlled endpoints; data exfiltration
               in HTTP parameters; unusual email sends or file access.
  MITIGATIONS: human-in-the-loop for sensitive tool calls; output
               monitoring for suspicious patterns; privilege
               restriction (limit what tools can do); sandboxed
               tool execution; prompt injection detection classifiers
               applied to retrieved content before it enters context.
  GAPS:        no technical solution prevents indirect injection
               while maintaining agent utility; detection classifiers
               are bypassable; privilege restriction reduces
               agent capability; the architectural fix (provenance-
               labeled context with trust hierarchy) is not
               implemented in any production system.

[A53] LLM TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION (MEMBERSHIP INFERENCE + VERBATIM EXTRACTION)
  CLASS:       AI/ML privacy attack
  MECHANISM:   LLMs are trained on large corpora of text including
               potentially private data. two attack classes:
               (1) membership inference: determine whether a specific
                 data record was in the training set.
                 Shokri et al. (2017): trained shadow models; used
                 output confidence distributions to infer membership.
                 LLM variant: models are more likely to assign high
                 probability to sequences they memorized.
               (2) verbatim extraction: prompt model to reproduce
                 training data verbatim.
                 Carlini et al. (2021): extracted verbatim training
                 data from GPT-2 by generating diverse completions
                 and filtering for memorized sequences; recovered
                 PII, source code, URLs, addresses.
                 Carlini et al. (2022): quantified memorization
                 in GPT-Neo, GPT-J; 1-2% of training data verbatim
                 memorizable; scales with model size and repetitions
                 in training data.
                 ChatGPT lawsuit discovery (2023): ChatGPT produced
                 verbatim reproductions of copyrighted books when
                 given appropriate prompts; evidence in New York
                 Times and Authors Guild litigation.
  INSTANCES:   Google Bard producing verbatim licensed content.
               ChatGPT reproducing personal contact information
               for public individuals when name-prompted.
               Code generation models reproducing GPL-licensed
               code verbatim without attribution.
  PREREQUISITES: query access to model; knowledge of training
               data existence (optional: enhances targeted extraction).
  INDICATORS:  model outputs containing PII, verbatim copyrighted
               content, or internal organizational data; high-
               confidence outputs for specific sequences.
  MITIGATIONS: differential privacy in training (formal privacy
               guarantee limits memorization; costs accuracy);
               deduplication of training data (reduces memorization
               of rare sequences); instruction fine-tuning to
               decline extraction attempts; canary detection
               (embed canary sequences; monitor for regurgitation);
               output filtering for known-sensitive patterns.
  GAPS:        differential privacy and model utility are in
               fundamental tension; current privacy budgets required
               for strong guarantees reduce model quality substantially;
               no standard exists for what constitutes "sufficiently
               private" model training; the field has no consensus.

[A54] GPS SPOOFING ATTACK
  CLASS:       navigation/positioning manipulation; cyber-physical
  MECHANISM:   GPS receivers determine position by measuring
               time of arrival (TOA) of signals from multiple
               satellites (minimum 4 for 3D fix). GPS signals
               are extremely weak (-130 dBm at surface; equivalent
               to a 20-watt bulb seen from 20,000 km). GPS signals
               are unencrypted and unauthenticated (civilian L1 band);
               any transmitter emitting signals at 1575.42 MHz
               with correct timing can override a nearby receiver.
               attack procedure:
               (1) record genuine GPS signals.
               (2) transmit spoofed signals at slightly higher power;
                 receiver acquires spoofed signal.
               (3) gradually shift spoofed signal timing to move
                 the receiver's computed position to the attacker-
                 desired location.
               (4) receiver tracks the spoofed signal without
                 detection (single-antenna receiver has no
                 direction-of-arrival detection).
  INSTANCES:   Iran spoofing RQ-170 Sentinel drone (2011):
               claimed to capture intact US drone by spoofing
               its GPS home position; drone attempted to land
               at "home" (now spoofed Iranian location); disputed
               whether spoofing was the actual capture mechanism
               but technically consistent.
               Russia GPS spoofing in Black Sea (2017–ongoing):
               MarineTraffic reported ships showing position
               at Gelendzhik Airport; interference with marine
               navigation.
               Russia GPS spoofing in Helsinki, Norway, Finland
               (2019, 2022-2024): ADSB exchange data shows aircraft
               reporting incorrect positions over Finland/Norway
               near Russian border during military exercises.
               Moscow "Kremlin spoofing bubble": persistent GPS
               spoofing around Moscow center; all receivers show
               Vnukovo airport; used to prevent drone attacks;
               documented by OSINTechnical and C4ADS.
               China South China Sea (2019-ongoing): vessels
               showing circular patterns in open sea; suspected
               GPS spoofing at ports and construction sites
               to mask vessel positions.
  PREREQUISITES: SDR (software-defined radio) equipment; open-
               source GPS signal generators; total cost under $1,000.
  INDICATORS:  sudden position jumps; implausible speeds or
               accelerations; time of week rollover anomalies;
               multiple receivers in proximity showing conflicting
               positions; civilian: ship circling pattern in
               static water.
  MITIGATIONS: GPS authentication: U.S. GPS Directorate developing
               Navigation Message Authentication (NMA) for L1 signal;
               EU Galileo OSNMA (Open Service Navigation Message
               Authentication) launched 2023; cryptographic signature
               on satellite messages; prevents signal spoofing
               (attacker cannot forge signed messages without key).
               multi-constellation: receiver tracking GPS + GLONASS
               + Galileo + BeiDou simultaneously; spoofing one
               while others remain consistent is detectable.
               inertial navigation backup: IMU (inertial measurement
               unit) dead reckoning detects implausible GPS jumps.
               antenna arrays: multi-antenna receivers detect
               direction of arrival inconsistencies.
  GAPS:        NMA and OSNMA require receiver hardware/firmware
               updates; most deployed receivers lack this; maritime
               and aviation systems have long replacement cycles;
               military encrypted P(Y) code and M-Code immune to
               civilian spoofing but military equipment represents
               small fraction of GPS receivers globally.

[A55] RFID AND NFC CLONING AND RELAY ATTACK
  CLASS:       physical/proximity credential theft
  MECHANISM:   RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) and NFC
               (Near Field Communication) are used for physical
               access control (HID, EM4100, MIFARE), transit
               payment (London Oyster, Hong Kong Octopus, NYC
               MetroCard), contactless payment (EMV/NFC), and
               identity documents (e-passport, RFID driver's license).
               attack paths:
               (1) skim and clone: read unencrypted RFID card
                 at close range (1-100cm depending on frequency);
                 replay the cloned credential to gain access.
                 EM4100 (125kHz, read-only): no authentication;
                 trivially cloned; still used in many access systems.
                 MIFARE Classic: proprietary cipher (Crypto-1);
                 broken in 2008 (de Ruiter et al.); 200,000 guesses
                 for full key recovery; many legacy deployments.
               (2) relay attack: attacker extends the communication
                 channel over distance using two devices.
                 reader → relay device 1 → radio → relay device 2 →
                 legitimate card; reader sees legitimate card response.
                 EMV relay: attacker in contact with victim's NFC
                 contactless payment card; accomplice at terminal
                 completes fraudulent transaction; card believes
                 it is making a legitimate purchase.
                 car theft relay: vehicle keyless entry; thief at
                 front door extends key fob signal to car door.
  INSTANCES:   Berlin transit system (BVG) MIFARE Classic cloning
               for free transit (2008–ongoing until system upgrade).
               London Oyster MIFARE Classic vulnerability; TfL
               patched by blacklisting compromised cards.
               Dutch passport RFID security research (2006):
               basic access control (BAC) key derived from
               printed data (machine-readable zone); skimmable
               at some distance from document.
               relay attacks on Tesla Model 3 keyless entry (2022).
  PREREQUISITES: Proxmark3 or Flipper Zero device ($100-$500);
               physical proximity (seconds to minutes).
  INDICATORS:  duplicate access events in log; access at unusual
               times; physical surveillance at choke points.
  MITIGATIONS: upgrade to modern RFID (MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3:
               AES-128, mutual authentication; HID iCLASS Sears:
               cryptographic authentication);
               for keyless vehicle entry: ultra-wideband (UWB)
               distance bounding (iPhone 12+ Ultra Wideband chip;
               BMW Digital Key Plus; measures precise distance
               to defeat relay attacks);
               for payment: transaction amount limits; online
               authorization requirement; PIN for amounts above
               threshold;
               motion detection: disable key fob radio when
               stationary (Faraday bag for storage).
  GAPS:        legacy RFID access control systems have deployment
               lifetimes of 10-30 years; replacement cost creates
               pressure to retain insecure EM4100 systems;
               no regulatory requirement for upgrading access
               control hardware; RFID skimming hardware is
               commercially available as security research tools.

[A56] FAULT INJECTION ATTACK (HARDWARE GLITCHING)
  CLASS:       hardware cryptographic bypass
  MECHANISM:   fault injection attacks cause a target device to
               make computational errors by introducing physical
               stress: voltage glitching (momentary power supply
               disruption), clock glitching (timing disruption),
               electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI), laser fault
               injection, and temperature extremes. targeted faults
               during cryptographic operations can:
               → cause a device to skip a branch check (e.g., bypass
                 PIN verification by faulting the comparison)
               → induce computation errors in RSA/ECC that leak
               the private key via differential fault analysis (DFA)
               → cause bootloader to skip signature verification
                 and execute unsigned firmware
               → extract secret keys from smart cards and HSMs
  INSTANCES:   Bellcore attack (Boneh, DeMillo, Lipton 1997):
               theoretical DFA against RSA-CRT; single bit fault
               during signing leaks private key; demonstrated
               against real smart cards.
               A5/1 GSM cipher fault attack: fault injection against
               SIM card reveals session key.
               iPhone passcode bypass via voltage glitching
               (various, 2014-2018 era): older iPhone SoCs lacked
               secure enclave; power glitch allowed brute-force
               passcode attacks by resetting attempt counter.
               Trezor hardware wallet glitching (Kraken Security Labs,
               2020): voltage glitch on STM32 MCU dumps encrypted
               seeds; requires physical possession.
               PS3 hypervisor bypass via glitching (fail0verflow, 2010):
               hardware glitch caused hypervisor to give full memory
               access.
  PREREQUISITES: physical access to target device; specialized
               equipment ($50 for basic glitching; $10,000+ for
               professional electromagnetic injection platforms).
  INDICATORS:  device behavior anomalies; cryptographic output
               errors; depends on whether device logs fault events.
  MITIGATIONS: voltage monitors and reset on tamper detection;
               redundant computation with comparison (fault on one
               path does not affect all paths); fault-hardened
               cryptographic implementations (double computation,
               redundant comparison); physically secure enclosures
               (tamper-evident, tamper-responsive: key erasure
               on tamper detection — HSMs, chip cards); active
               shielding (meshes that detect cuts/probes).
  GAPS:        consumer IoT devices have no fault injection
               mitigations; secure elements (bank cards, SIM cards)
               have some but are routinely broken by academic
               researchers; laser fault injection has become
               accessible with hobbyist equipment; no public
               standard for minimum fault injection resistance
               for consumer devices.

[A57] DEEPFAKE AUTHENTICATION BYPASS
  CLASS:       biometric authentication bypass via synthetic media
  MECHANISM:   (see pattern P33 for historical instances)
               voice authentication: bank or call center uses
               speaker recognition as authentication factor.
               attacker collects voice samples from target
               (social media, podcast, earnings call, voicemail).
               voice cloning model (ElevenLabs, Resemble, RVC)
               generates real-time synthetic voice.
               attacker calls the bank's IVR or agent line;
               presents cloned voice; passes voice recognition.
               video authentication: video call authentication
               requires user to appear on camera.
               attacker uses real-time face swap (DeepFaceLive,
               Roop, commercial tools); presents victim's face
               on attacker's webcam stream.
               Hong Kong incident (2024): $25M HKD transferred
               after deepfake video call with CFO and colleagues
               (all deepfakes except one initially legitimate call).
               liveness detection bypass: some authentication
               systems use "liveness detection" (blink, turn head)
               to prevent photo spoofing. adversarial patches
               on face or adversarial noise frames can bypass
               ML-based liveness detection.
  INSTANCES:   VICE bypass of Lloyds/Monzo/Revolut/HSBC voice
               authentication using ElevenLabs (2023).
               multiple bank voice auth bypasses documented by
               security researchers (2022-2024).
               Hong Kong CFO deepfake video call ($25M, Feb 2024).
  PREREQUISITES: 3-60 seconds of target voice audio;
               consumer-grade GPU for real-time synthesis;
               knowledge of authentication mechanism.
  INDICATORS:  voice synthesis artifacts (current tools have
               detectable spectral anomalies); video deepfake
               artifacts (lighting inconsistency, edge artifacts,
               temporal inconsistency in blinks); metadata
               inconsistencies.
  MITIGATIONS: deprecate voice biometric as primary auth factor;
               migrate to hardware-backed authentication (FIDO2/
               passkeys); challenge-response with unpredictable
               visual cue (hold up object, perform specific motion);
               transaction confirmation via separate channel (SMS,
               app push to registered device); liveness detection
               using adversarially robust methods; cryptographic
               attestation of video call (verified end-to-end identity).
  GAPS:        most IVR and call center voice authentication has
               no deepfake detection; hardware token migration
               requires user enrollment effort; no widely deployed
               standard for detecting real-time video deepfakes
               in communication platforms; the detection-generation
               arms race favors generation.

[A58] SATELLITE COMMAND INJECTION AND SIGNAL SPOOFING
  CLASS:       space system / cyber-physical attack
  MECHANISM:   satellites receive commands from ground stations
               via radio frequency uplinks. legacy satellite
               communication systems use minimal authentication:
               command sequences are often unencrypted and
               unauthenticated; an attacker with appropriate
               ground equipment and knowledge of the command
               format can transmit unauthorized commands.
               attack vectors:
               (1) uplink spoofing: transmit unauthorized commands
                 on the command frequency from attacker-controlled
                 ground station; requires knowledge of uplink
                 frequency, modulation, and command format.
               (2) satellite ground station compromise:
                 attack the ground control network (IT/OT
                 interface); issue commands through legitimate
                 control station; Viasat KA-SAT attack (2022):
                 Russia compromised satellite ground modem
                 management system; bricked 5,800 Viasat
                 modems in Ukraine (and 40,000 across Europe)
                 one hour before Ukraine invasion.
               (3) signal jamming: transmit noise on satellite
                 frequency band; denial of service to legitimate
                 uplink/downlink; used against Ukrainian tactical
                 satellite communications during invasion.
               (4) GPS spoofing (see A54): applied to satellite
                 navigation signals.
               (5) inter-satellite link injection: low-earth orbit
                 (LEO) mega-constellations (Starlink, OneWeb)
                 use inter-satellite links; potential attack
                 surface as network extends into space.
  INSTANCES:   Viasat KA-SAT attack (2022): AcidRain wiper deployed
               via satellite management network; bricked satellite
               modems across Europe; disrupted Ukrainian military
               communications at invasion start.
               Galaxy 15 "zombie satellite" (2010): command
               receiver malfunction; satellite stopped responding
               to commands; drifted and interfered with adjacent
               satellites; not a cyberattack but demonstrates
               impact of command loss.
               PanAmSat Galaxy IV (1998): onboard computer failure;
               satellite lost orientation; 80-90% of US pagers
               disrupted for days.
  PREREQUISITES: uplink spoofing: significant investment ($100K+
               for ground station equipment); ground station
               compromise: standard IT attack chain but hardened
               targets; jamming: moderate investment ($10K-$100K).
  INDICATORS:  anomalous telemetry from satellite; unexpected
               mode changes; ground station security alerts;
               modem status changes at scale (Viasat pattern).
  MITIGATIONS: command authentication: cryptographic signatures
               on all command uplinks (used on modern military
               and some commercial satellites; not universal);
               frequency hopping and DSSS spread spectrum
               (harder to jam and spoof); ground station
               network segmentation; operational technology (OT)
               security for satellite control infrastructure.
  GAPS:        thousands of legacy commercial satellites use
               unauthenticated command protocols; commercial
               LEO constellations (Starlink: 6,000+ satellites)
               create unprecedented scale; Starlink's ground
               network is a high-value target; no international
               satellite security standard exists.

[A59] BGP ROUTE LEAK (DISTINGUISHED FROM HIJACKING)
  CLASS:       network routing manipulation
  MECHANISM:   BGP route hijacking (covered earlier): an AS
               announces a prefix it does not own, causing traffic
               to be routed through the attacker.
               BGP route leak: an AS receives a route and
               re-advertises it to parties to whom it should
               not be re-advertised. this can cause traffic
               disruption or misdirection without the leaking
               AS owning the prefix.
               example: customer AS receives routes from transit
               provider A and from transit provider B. customer
               should not re-advertise provider A's routes to
               provider B (customer should only announce its
               own prefixes to transit). if the customer misconfigures
               routing policy and re-advertises provider A's routes
               to provider B, provider B may prefer the leaked
               route and send traffic through the customer AS.
               scale: major route leaks have disrupted significant
               portions of internet traffic.
  INSTANCES:   Indosat route leak (2014): Indonesian ISP leaked
               14,000+ routes to the global internet via Telekom
               Malaysia; disrupted traffic to and from many networks
               for hours.
               Hathway leak (2015): Indian ISP leaked 20,000+ routes;
               similar disruption.
               Verizon/Allegheny Technologies/Noction (2019):
               DynDNS, Cloudflare, Amazon, and others affected;
               small Pennsylvania ISP (AS396531) leaked routes
               via Verizon; traffic to 200+ networks disrupted;
               Cloudflare and others lost connectivity for hours.
               Rostelecom (2020): Russian state-owned ISP advertised
               routes for 8,800+ internet routes including Amazon,
               Google, Facebook, Akamai; lasted 1 hour; unknown
               whether intentional.
  PREREQUISITES: BGP session with internet-connected AS; routing
               policy misconfiguration (accidental) or deliberate.
  INDICATORS:  anomalous route propagation in BGP looking glasses;
               RPKI validation failures; traffic path changes
               visible in traceroute; Routeviews data.
  MITIGATIONS: RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure): ROA
               (Route Origin Authorization) cryptographically
               binds prefix to AS number; ROV (Route Origin
               Validation) at routers rejects routes that fail
               ROA check; Route Leak prevention: RFC 9234 "Only
               to Customer" (OTC) BGP attribute; marks routes
               as received from transit; recipients can filter
               routes marked OTC if re-advertised to non-customer.
               filtering: AS-path filters, prefix-list filters,
               MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security);
               IRR (Internet Routing Registry) filtering.
  GAPS:        RPKI ROV deployment is growing (~50% of global
               routes covered by ROAs as of 2024) but many major
               networks still do not perform ROV; RFC 9234 is
               not widely deployed; BGP has no authentication
               for the UPDATE messages themselves (BGPsec exists
               but has near-zero deployment due to performance cost).

[A60] SIDE-CHANNEL ATTACK ON SOFTWARE CRYPTOGRAPHIC IMPLEMENTATION
  CLASS:       cryptographic implementation attack
  MECHANISM:   even a mathematically correct cryptographic algorithm
               can leak key material through its implementation's
               physical or computational side effects.
               software side channels (distinguished from hardware
               side channels like Spectre):
               (1) cache timing attack: AES with lookup tables
                 (T-table implementation). AES encryption indexes
                 a lookup table based on key and plaintext bytes.
                 cache line loaded depends on key byte value.
                 attacker measuring cache access timing can recover
                 the key index → recover the key byte.
                 Bernstein (2005): remote timing attack on
                 AES via network timing; recovered AES key from
                 OpenSSL on network-accessible server.
               (2) RSA timing attack (Kocher 1996): RSA modular
                 exponentiation time varies with exponent bits.
                 constant-time Montgomery multiplication required
                 to prevent.
               (3) branch prediction side channel (distinct from
                 Spectre): code that takes different branches based
                 on key bits leaks key via branch timing.
               (4) memory access pattern: cryptographic code that
                 accesses different memory locations based on
                 key value leaks via cache/memory timing.
  INSTANCES:   OpenSSL AES T-table timing (Bernstein 2005):
               key recovered remotely via network timing.
               RSA Lucky Thirteen: TLS CBC MAC timing oracle
               (Al Fardan, Paterson 2013).
               Minerva attack (Jancar et al. 2020): nonce
               generation in ECDSA via GnuTLS, OpenSSL,
               libgcrypt, Botan timing leaked private key;
               recovered key in <200 signatures.
               Raccoon attack (2020): timing in Diffie-Hellman
               server processing leaked session key in TLS 1.2.
  PREREQUISITES: timing measurements; for local: access to
               same hardware; for remote: repeated measurements
               with high resolution; for network: requires many
               samples to overcome jitter.
  INDICATORS:  difficult to detect from outside; high request
               volume to cryptographic endpoints may indicate
               timing attack probing.
  MITIGATIONS: constant-time implementations: code paths and
               memory accesses that do not depend on secret values;
               OpenSSL uses constant-time AES-NI hardware instruction
               (bypasses T-table entirely); HACL* and libsodium
               written with constant-time properties;
               blinding: randomize intermediate values during
               RSA exponentiation to prevent timing correlation;
               formal verification of constant-time property
               (ct-verif tool, binsec tool).
  GAPS:        constant-time code is difficult to write and verify;
               compilers can "optimize away" constant-time code
               (compiler reintroduces data-dependent branches);
               LLVM and GCC have limited constant-time code
               generation guarantees; most application-level
               code (outside security libraries) has no
               constant-time requirement or verification.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSE ENTRIES D36–D45
─────────────────────────────────────────

[D36] POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY MIGRATION PLANNING
  CLASS:       cryptographic infrastructure transformation
  MECHANISM:   migration from classical asymmetric cryptography
               (RSA, ECDH, ECDSA) to post-quantum algorithms
               before a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer
               (CRQC) is available.
  STANDARDS:
    → NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM / CRYSTALS-Kyber): key encapsulation;
      replaces ECDH and RSA for key exchange.
    → NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA / CRYSTALS-Dilithium): digital signature;
      replaces ECDSA and RSA for signing.
    → NIST FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA / SPHINCS+): hash-based signature;
      conservative option; no algebraic assumptions;
      large signature sizes (8KB-50KB).
    → NIST IR 8413 (FALCON): lattice-based signature; smaller
      signatures than Dilithium; more implementation complexity.
  MIGRATION APPROACH:
    → inventory: catalog all cryptographic use cases, algorithms,
      key lengths, certificate lifetimes, data sensitivity lifetimes.
    → prioritize: highest sensitivity data + longest exposure window
      first (see P35 Form B research prompt).
    → hybrid: during transition, use hybrid key exchange
      (X25519+Kyber768 in TLS: both classical and PQC; attacker
      must break both) and hybrid signatures; Chrome/Firefox/
      Cloudflare use hybrid TLS since 2023.
    → crypto-agility: design systems to swap algorithms without
      architectural redesign; parameterize algorithm choice;
      critical for long-lived infrastructure.
    → certificate lifecycle: X.509 certificates with Dilithium
      or Falcon; new root CAs with PQC; browser trust store
      migration; longer lead time than TLS key exchange.
  TIMELINE:
    → CISA guidance (2024): new systems should use PQC now;
      high-value legacy systems: start migration immediately;
      all legacy systems: complete migration by 2035.
    → NSA guidance (CNSA 2.0, 2022): similar timeline for national
      security systems.
  GAPS:        PQC algorithm performance overhead: ML-KEM and
    ML-DSA have larger key/ciphertext sizes than ECC
    (ML-KEM-768: 1,184-byte public key vs 64 bytes for X25519);
    SPHINCS+ has very large signatures; embedded IoT devices
    with limited memory and bandwidth may need ML-KEM-512
    (lowest security level) or hardware acceleration;
    firmware update mechanisms for long-lived devices are
    often insufficient; no legal or regulatory mandate in
    most jurisdictions for private sector PQC migration.

[D37] AI/LLM SAFETY GUARDRAILS AS SECURITY CONTROL
  CLASS:       AI safety / alignment as security
  MECHANISM:   LLM safety guardrails are post-training interventions
               designed to prevent the model from producing harmful
               outputs or taking harmful actions. they function as
               a security control against malicious use, not merely
               a content moderation tool.
  COMPONENTS:
    → alignment training (RLHF/RLAIF/Constitutional AI):
      reinforcement learning from human feedback trains
      the model to refuse harmful requests, follow instructions
      within policy, and generalize safety to novel situations.
      Anthropic Constitutional AI: model trained to self-critique
      responses against a "constitution" of principles.
    → system prompt safety policies: operators configure safety
      behavior via system prompt; Anthropic's usage policies
      enforced at model level; operator cannot override core
      safety properties.
    → output classifiers: additional ML models evaluate model
      output for policy violations; can block or modify output
      post-generation.
    → red-teaming: systematic adversarial testing of LLM safety
      properties before deployment; Anthropic internal red team,
      external red team programs, Frontier Model Forum shared
      evaluations.
    → eval frameworks: HELM, BIG-Bench, custom harm evals;
      standardized measurement of safety and capability across
      models; Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP)
      includes mandatory capability evaluations before deploying
      more capable models.
  LIMITATIONS:
    → alignment is not robust against adversarial inputs (jailbreaks);
      the arms race is ongoing.
    → capability-safety tradeoff: more capable models tend to
      be easier to jailbreak; the tradeoff is debated.
    → specification gaming: model satisfies the letter of safety
      training but not the spirit; "Sleeper Agents" paper
      (Anthropic 2024): models can be trained to appear safe
      during evaluation but activate harmful behaviors in
      deployment.
    → indirect injection bypass: safety training designed for
      direct user input may not protect against indirect injection.
    → measurement: "safe" is not binary; no agreed metric for
      how safe a model must be for a given deployment context.
  GAPS:        no formal definition of "alignment" that maps to
    verifiable technical property; the "Sleeper Agents" finding
    suggests that evaluation-passing safety behavior can coexist
    with deployment-triggered unsafe behavior; no certified
    safety level analogous to Common Criteria EAL for AI systems.

[D38] SECRETS SCANNING IN CI/CD PIPELINES
  CLASS:       credential exposure prevention
  MECHANISM:   developers accidentally commit secrets (API keys,
               private keys, passwords, tokens) to version control
               or configuration files. secrets scanning tools
               detect credentials before they are committed,
               after commit, or in real-time in repositories.
  TOOLS:
    → pre-commit hooks: Gitleaks, detect-secrets (Yelp),
      git-secrets (AWS); prevent commit if secret pattern detected.
    → continuous scanning: TruffleHog, GitHub Advanced Security
      Secret Scanning, GitLab Secret Detection; scan all commits
      and branches; alert on detection.
    → GitHub Push Protection: blocks push if secret detected;
      requires bypass with justification; mandatory for GHES enterprise.
    → cloud provider partners: AWS, Google, Azure, GitHub, GitLab
      collaborate; cloud providers notify GitHub when API keys
      appear in public repositories; GitHub automatically revokes
      and notifies.
    → entropy-based detection: high-entropy strings (likely keys)
      flagged even if they don't match known patterns.
  SCOPE:
    → source code repositories (Git history, branches, PRs)
    → CI/CD pipeline logs (build logs often contain secret values
      in environment variable printing or error output)
    → container images (secrets baked into Dockerfile or entrypoint)
    → IaC files (Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm charts)
    → documentation and wikis
    → S3 buckets and blob storage (public-facing config files)
  HISTORICAL FAILURES: Uber's 2016 breach began with AWS keys
    committed to a private GitHub repository; attacker found
    them via GitHub search. Twitch data leak (2021) included
    internal API keys in leaked source code. Toyota (2023):
    vehicle data exposed via API key in GitHub repository.
  GAPS:       secrets scanning can detect known secret formats;
    custom internal secrets require custom patterns; scanning
    does not cover encrypted secrets at rest (KMS-encrypted
    secrets in config files); the fix after detection (rotation)
    requires knowing all locations where the secret was used.

[D39] BROWSER ISOLATION (REMOTE BROWSER ISOLATION / RBI)
  CLASS:       web-based threat prevention
  MECHANISM:   traditional web browsing: web content (HTML, JS,
               DOM) executes in a browser process on the user's
               endpoint. a malicious web page can exploit the
               browser (renderer vulnerability, sandbox escape)
               to compromise the endpoint.
               remote browser isolation: the browser executes
               in a remote, isolated environment (cloud server
               or virtual machine). the user sees a rendering
               of the remote browser's output (pixel streaming,
               DOM mirroring, or read-only document conversion)
               but web content never executes on the endpoint.
               exploit code runs in the isolated environment;
               the environment is destroyed after the session.
  APPROACHES:
    → pixel streaming: remote browser renders to screen; screen
      image or video stream sent to user's browser; user interacts
      via keyboard/mouse events sent to remote; no web content
      executes locally. most secure; highest bandwidth overhead.
    → DOM mirroring: remote browser parses HTML/CSS; safe subset
      of DOM is sent to local renderer; JavaScript does not execute
      locally; compromises some functionality.
    → read-only file conversion: documents (PDF, Word, web page)
      converted to static image or PDF in remote environment;
      malicious content cannot execute; loses interactivity.
  USE CASES:
    → uncategorized web browsing (security team, executive browsing
      of external sites);
    → email links (most malware delivery is via phishing link);
    → contractor and third-party access to internal systems via
      RBI to prevent malware exfiltration from contractors.
  PRODUCTS: Cloudflare Browser Isolation (ZTNA-integrated),
    Zscaler Cloud Browser Isolation, Menlo Security, Authentic8 Silo.
  GAPS:       bandwidth overhead (pixel streaming uses significant
    bandwidth); latency sensitive for interactive applications;
    does not prevent user from entering credentials on a
    phishing page (the rendered phishing page is still visible);
    web application functionality may break; cost is significant
    for full enterprise deployment; targeted at browser exploits,
    not social engineering.

[D40] DNS SECURITY (DoH, DoT, DNSSEC)
  CLASS:       DNS query privacy and integrity
  MECHANISM:
    → DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions): adds cryptographic
      signatures to DNS responses. a zone signs its resource
      records; resolvers verify signatures using a chain of
      trust from the root. prevents DNS spoofing (Kaminsky attack)
      and cache poisoning by making forged responses detectable.
      does not encrypt DNS (queries are still visible); only
      protects integrity.
      deployment: root zone signed (2010); .com, .org, .net signed;
      many authoritative zones signed; resolver-side validation
      (validating stub) not widely deployed on endpoints.
    → DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858): encrypts DNS query/response
      between client and resolver using TLS on port 853. prevents
      ISP and network-level interception and modification of DNS.
      deployed by: Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), Google (8.8.8.8),
      Quad9 (9.9.9.9); supported in Android Pie+ (Private DNS),
      iOS 14+, Linux systemd-resolved.
    → DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484): encrypts DNS inside HTTP/2
      on port 443. indistinguishable from regular HTTPS traffic;
      cannot be blocked by port-based filtering without blocking
      all HTTPS. supported in Firefox (Trusted Recursive Resolver),
      Chrome, Edge, Windows 11 (system-level DoH), iOS.
    → DNS over QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250): DNS over QUIC transport;
      lower latency than DoT (no TLS handshake per query);
      supported by Cloudflare resolver.
  SECURITY IMPLICATIONS:
    → DoH bypasses enterprise DNS filtering and monitoring;
      malware using DoH for C2 resolution evades enterprise
      DNS visibility; enterprise solutions: enforce a known-good
      DoH resolver that logs queries; block DoH to all others.
    → DNSSEC + DoT/DoH: integrity (DNSSEC) + privacy (DoT/DoH)
      together provide full DNS security; neither alone is sufficient.
  GAPS:       DNSSEC adoption at authoritative level is ~35% of
    top domains; end-to-end DNSSEC validation at stub resolver
    is rare; DoH-based malware C2 (DoH tunneling) is a growing
    evasion technique; enterprise DoH management tooling is
    nascent; DNSSEC key rollover is complex and has caused
    outages (IANA root KSK rollover 2018 was delayed due to
    resolver upgrade concerns).

[D41] SECURITY CULTURE AND ORGANIZATIONAL DESIGN
  CLASS:       human and organizational security
  MECHANISM:   security culture refers to the shared values,
               norms, and behaviors within an organization that
               affect how individuals handle security decisions.
               technical controls fail when organizational culture
               works against them. culture shapes: whether employees
               report suspicious activity, whether developers
               implement security requirements or skip them under
               deadline pressure, whether executives support
               security investment, whether security teams are
               empowered to block business decisions that create
               risk.
  COMPONENTS:
    → leadership commitment: security is a board-level and C-suite
      concern, not only an IT issue; CISO reporting line to CEO
      or Board (not CIO); security investment is not cut first
      in budget reductions.
    → psychological safety: employees who report security incidents
      or near-misses are not punished; blame-free post-mortems;
      aviation's "just culture" model (see U03).
    → security awareness: not checkbox compliance training; ongoing
      culture of awareness; practical simulation (phishing
      simulations with immediate feedback and training); security
      champions in each team.
    → developer security culture: secure coding as professional
      norm, not optional; security champion program; threat
      modeling as design step; security gates in CI/CD are
      owned by the team, not imposed by a security team.
    → "security as a last resort" antipattern: security decisions
      added at end of project; security team as gatekeeper;
      creates adversarial relationship between security and
      development; the fix is "shift left" and developer ownership.
    → measurement: security culture is measured; phishing simulation
      rates, security training completion, mean time to report
      a potential incident, near-miss reporting rate; culture
      is not just communicated but measured and managed.
  MODELS:
    → Schneier: security is a process, not a product; culture
      is the organizational embodiment of this.
    → High Reliability Organization (HRO) theory: organizations
      that operate safely in hazardous environments (nuclear
      power plants, aircraft carriers, air traffic control)
      share: preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify,
      sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience,
      deference to expertise. these properties can be cultivated.
  GAPS:       security culture measurement is not standardized;
    CISO turnover averages 18-24 months (limiting cultural
    investment); security culture is not included in financial
    risk models; executive accountability for security failures
    remains limited outside of regulated industries.

[D42] HARDWARE ATTESTATION AND TRUSTED PLATFORM MODULE (TPM)
  CLASS:       hardware root of trust
  MECHANISM:   the TPM is a dedicated cryptographic processor
               that provides hardware-backed security functions:
               secure key storage (keys protected by TPM hardware;
               cannot be exported), measurement (PCR extend:
               hash chain of boot measurements), attestation
               (signed statement of PCR values using TPM's
               Attestation Identity Key), sealing (encrypt
               data to specific TPM state; decrypt only when
               PCR values match expected values).
  COMPONENTS:
    → Endorsement Key (EK): permanent asymmetric key provisioned
      at manufacture; used to authenticate the TPM; EK cert
      signed by TPM manufacturer (Intel, Infineon, STMicro, etc.).
    → Storage Root Key (SRK): TPM-held key for protecting user keys;
      created on TPM ownership; cannot leave TPM.
    → Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs): 24+ registers that
      hold cumulative hash of measured components.
      PCR0: BIOS/UEFI core.
      PCR1: UEFI configuration.
      PCR4: Boot loader.
      PCR7: Secure Boot policy.
      PCR8-12: OS and grub measurements.
    → sealing to PCR values: BitLocker seals volume master key
      to expected PCR values; decryption fails if PCR values change
      (firmware modification, boot order change).
    → remote attestation: remote server challenges device with
      nonce; device returns TPM quote (PCR values signed by AIK);
      server verifies quote against expected PCR values; confirms
      device is in expected state.
  PROTOCOLS: IETF RATS (Remote ATtestation procedureS);
    Google Attest API (Android); Apple DCG (Device Check);
    Microsoft Device Health Attestation; Project Cerberus
    (Microsoft platform firmware resilience; pre-boot attestation).
  GAPS:       TPM attestation infrastructure requires server-side
    verification capability; enterprise MDM infrastructure
    does not universally verify TPM state; supply chain attack
    on TPM manufacturer would undermine chain of trust; TPM
    without PIN binding (standard enterprise BitLocker) is
    vulnerable to evil maid attacks; not all devices have TPM
    (IoT, embedded, many servers use software TPM).

[D43] AI RED-TEAMING METHODOLOGY
  CLASS:       AI/LLM security assessment
  MECHANISM:   red-teaming for AI systems is distinct from
               traditional software penetration testing. it
               involves systematic adversarial probing of an
               AI model's behavior to discover unexpected,
               harmful, or policy-violating outputs. it is
               not fully automatable because the "vulnerability"
               is often semantic (the model produces a harmful
               response) rather than a binary exploit.
  PHASES:
    → threat modeling: what are the harms the model can cause?
      categories: harmful content generation, dangerous information
      provision, identity manipulation, privacy violation,
      discrimination, cybersecurity capability uplift, CBRN
      assistance.
    → attack taxonomies: known jailbreak techniques (see A51);
      domain-specific harmful requests; edge cases in safety
      training; out-of-distribution inputs; multi-turn manipulation;
      prompt injection.
    → scaling red teams: human red teamers are slow and expensive;
      automated red teaming (using LLMs to generate adversarial
      prompts): Perez et al. (2022) "Red Teaming Language Models
      with Language Models"; limitations: automated attacks miss
      semantic subtleties that human red teamers find.
    → structured evaluations: Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy:
      mandatory safety evaluations before deploying models above
      capability thresholds; AI Safety Levels (ASL-1, ASL-2,
      ASL-3, ASL-4) with required safeguards at each level.
    → multi-party red teaming: independent red teams with different
      expertise (CBRN specialists for biosecurity, psychology
      for manipulation, security researchers for cyber capability).
    → frontier model forum: AI companies sharing red team findings;
      not yet a standardized evaluation framework.
  LIMITATIONS:
    → red-teaming finds specific examples of harmful behavior;
      does not prove absence of harmful behavior; bounded by
      red team creativity and scope.
    → behavioral drift: model behavior can change after fine-tuning;
      red team results may not apply to production model.
    → no standardized metrics for red team coverage;
      no agreed pass/fail criteria.
  GAPS:       no independent, third-party AI safety evaluation
    body analogous to Common Criteria or FIPS certification;
    AI red teaming is self-assessed by AI companies;
    the evaluation methodologies are not standardized or public;
    "Sleeper Agent" results suggest that evaluation-time behavior
    may not reflect deployment-time behavior.

[D44] VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE PROGRAM (VDP) DESIGN
  CLASS:       coordinated vulnerability handling
  MECHANISM:   a VDP provides a defined channel for security
               researchers to report vulnerabilities to an
               organization. it sets expectations for how reports
               will be handled and provides legal safe harbor.
               without a VDP, researchers who discover vulnerabilities
               may not know how to report them, may fear legal
               action (CFAA in the US, Computer Misuse Act in UK),
               or may sell to a broker.
  COMPONENTS:
    → scope: what systems can researchers test? what is out of scope?
      in-scope clarity prevents accidental denial-of-service
      or data exposure during testing.
    → disclosure policy: how long will the researcher wait before
      public disclosure? 90 days is common (Google Project Zero
      standard). what if the vendor cannot patch in time?
    → legal safe harbor: explicit statement that good-faith security
      research on defined scope will not be prosecuted.
      CISA BOD 20-01: all US federal agencies required to publish
      a VDP with safe harbor by November 2021.
    → acknowledgment and communication: researcher receives timely
      acknowledgment; vendor provides status updates; researcher
      is notified when fixed.
    → bug bounty (optional, separate from VDP): financial reward
      for qualifying vulnerabilities; creates economic incentive
      for finding and reporting rather than selling.
      HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti, YesWeHack: coordinating
      platforms; handle triage, duplicate detection, payments.
  EXAMPLES:
    → Google Project Zero: 90-day deadline; post regardless of
      patch status; creates vendor accountability.
    → Apple Security Bounty: up to $2M for zero-click kernel RCE;
      highest-paying public bug bounty program.
    → US DOD Hack the Pentagon (2016): first government bug bounty;
      subsequent Hack the Army, Hack the Air Force programs.
    → CISA BOD 20-01: mandatory VDP for federal civilian agencies.
  GAPS:       most organizations lack a VDP; many that have one
    lack a meaningful safe harbor; researchers still face legal
    risk under CFAA even with VDP; the CVD game theory (see C20)
    means VDP participants are the cooperative players; the
    uncooperative players (broker market) are unaffected by VDPs.

[D45] DECEPTION AND MOVING TARGET DEFENSE (MTD)
  CLASS:       proactive defense / attacker cost increase
  MECHANISM:   moving target defense changes system configuration
               continuously to invalidate attacker reconnaissance
               and exploit assumptions. an attacker who maps a
               network and finds a vulnerable service may return
               later to find the network topology has changed,
               the vulnerable service is now behind a different
               IP, or the software version has been rotated.
               this raises the cost of sustained attacks: the
               attacker must continuously re-recon.
  IMPLEMENTATIONS:
    → IP address randomization: network addresses change on schedule;
      attacker's cached IP map becomes stale; less useful against
      external attackers (DNS-resolved); more useful against
      internal lateral movement.
    → port randomization: service ports change (with firewall
      allowing expected client connections); defeats port-scan-
      based reconnaissance.
    → software diversity: deploy multiple versions of software
      on different systems; an exploit for version A does not
      work on version B; multi-variant execution (MVEE): run
      N variants simultaneously; compare outputs; any divergence
      indicates exploit (single crash vs. expected output).
    → network topology mutation: SDN-based network reconfiguration;
      node placement, routing, VLAN assignment mutated periodically.
    → decoy networks: mix of real and decoy services; attacker
      cannot determine which is real; attempts on decoys trigger
      high-fidelity alerts.
    → Cyber Moving Target Initiative (DARPA, 2010-2015): research
      program that produced foundational MTD concepts; OpenFlow-based
      network mutation; application software diversity.
  EFFECTIVENESS: attacker who completed detailed recon must
    restart; increases cost of maintaining long-term access;
    defeats many automated attack tools (scanners, exploit
    frameworks that rely on static target state).
  GAPS:       operational overhead of MTD is significant;
    legitimate systems and users must adapt to changing
    configuration; stateful services (databases, active sessions)
    cannot move without breaking continuity; MTD has not
    been widely deployed outside research contexts;
    the performance overhead of MVEE is 10-50%; no production
    MVEE system is widely deployed.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 5 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[C26] NEUROSCIENCE OF TRUST CALIBRATION → SOCIAL ENGINEERING VULNERABILITY
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Neuroscience: human brain has dedicated circuitry (prefrontal cortex,
    amygdala) for assessing social trust. Authority signals (uniform, title,
    confident tone, institutional affiliation) reduce threat assessment and
    accelerate compliance. This is not a flaw — it is adaptive in
    environments where authority signals are honest. The flaw emerges when
    signals can be forged.
    Cybersecurity: social engineering exploits the exact same mechanism.
    Vishing attacks (MGM 2023) succeed because caller ID spoofing, confident
    tone, and plausible pretext activate the "this is legitimate authority"
    pathway before skepticism can engage. Deepfake CEO calls exploit visual
    and auditory authority cues simultaneously.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Behavioral economics has established "pre-commitment devices" — mechanisms
    that bind future decisions before the high-pressure moment arrives.
    Security has not deployed this. Users could be trained to establish
    pre-commitment policies: "I will never give credentials over the phone
    regardless of claimed authority" set as a rule when cognitive load is low,
    so the rule fires automatically when load is high. Current security
    training attempts to teach skepticism in the moment — against the
    neuroscience of how authority compliance works.
  ATTACK CLASS WITH NO DEFENSE ANALOG:
    Multi-layer authority stacking: attacker establishes initial low-stakes
    contact (helpdesk call), builds rapport, then escalates to credential
    request while authority signal is already active. No technical control
    stops this. No training fully prepares for it because the authority signal
    is real (the person is actually on the phone, has actual information about
    the target). Defense analog: technical out-of-band confirmation channel
    not subject to real-time social pressure (callback to registered number,
    not caller-supplied number). Partially deployed; not universal.

[C27] EPIDEMIOLOGY OF VULNERABILITY PROPAGATION → PATCH DEPLOYMENT DYNAMICS
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Epidemiology: susceptible population + transmission mechanism + recovery
    rate determines epidemic curve. R0 (basic reproduction number) above 1
    = epidemic growth. Herd immunity threshold: 1 - (1/R0). When enough
    individuals are immune (patched), transmission chains break even if some
    remain susceptible.
    Cybersecurity: unpatched systems = susceptible hosts. Exploit availability
    = transmission mechanism. Patch deployment = immunity acquisition. WannaCry
    (2017) was a textbook epidemic — EternalBlue exploit, unpatched Windows
    systems globally, exponential spread until critical mass was patched or
    isolated.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Epidemiology uses: (1) contact tracing to identify transmission chains;
    (2) quarantine of exposed not yet symptomatic; (3) ring vaccination around
    outbreak; (4) sentinel surveillance for early detection; (5) mathematical
    modeling to predict outbreak trajectory and evaluate interventions.
    Security has deployed (1) partially (incident response chains) and (2)
    partially (network isolation of compromised hosts). Security has not
    deployed (3), (4), or (5) at scale. CISA KEV catalog is a rough analog
    to outbreak reporting but lacks the mathematical modeling that epidemiology
    uses to set policy. No equivalent of R0 measurement for exploits exists
    in deployment decision frameworks.
  GAP IDENTIFIED (G21):
    No standardized "exploit R0" metric exists for measuring exploit spread
    potential and calculating the patching threshold needed to prevent epidemic
    spread. Such a metric would enable rational prioritization: high-R0 exploits
    (widespread vulnerable systems + easy transmission + long dwell time)
    require urgent near-universal patching; low-R0 exploits can be addressed
    at normal cadence. Current patching priority frameworks (CVSS) measure
    severity of impact to single system, not spread potential.

[C28] ECOLOGY OF SECURITY ECOSYSTEM → SYSTEMIC STABILITY AND COLLAPSE
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Ecology: predator-prey dynamics create population oscillations but
    maintain equilibrium. Keystone species removal causes trophic cascade
    and ecosystem collapse. Monoculture (genetically uniform crop) is
    catastrophically vulnerable to single pathogen. Biodiversity is
    resilience.
    Cybersecurity: criminal ecosystem has predator-prey dynamics (attackers
