CYCLE 6 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY (A61-A70, D46-D53)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

[A61] LLM AGENTIC TOOL ABUSE
  CLASS:       AI/ML Security; Application Security
  MECHANISM:   An LLM agent (model with tool access) is manipulated via
    direct or indirect prompt injection to invoke its available tools in
    adversarially specified ways. The agent's tool access is the amplifier:
    a text-based injection translates into filesystem writes, API calls,
    email sends, code execution, or database modifications. The agent's
    helpfulness disposition and instruction-following training make it
    more susceptible, not less.
  INSTANCES:   Greshake et al. (2023) — indirect prompt injection in
    Bing Chat with browsing tool; injected instructions on a webpage
    caused agent to exfiltrate conversation context. Riley Goodside (2022)
    — demonstrated prompt injection overriding prior instructions in GPT-3.
    Langchain RCE via prompt injection (2023) — agent with Python execution
    tool manipulated to execute arbitrary code via crafted input.
    Computer-use agent attacks (2024) — Claude/GPT-4V agents performing
    computer use manipulated by content visible on screen (image-embedded
    instructions, webpage-embedded instructions).
  PREREQUISITES: LLM agent with tool access; attacker ability to inject
    into the agent's context (direct: via user input; indirect: via content
    the agent retrieves — webpages, emails, database records, tool outputs).
  INDICATORS:  Unexpected tool invocations; out-of-context actions; agent
    requesting access to resources unrelated to stated task; agent producing
    outputs with embedded instructions intended for downstream agents.
  MITIGATIONS: Tool access privilege separation (minimum necessary tools);
    multi-turn confirmation before high-impact tool invocations; output
    scanning for injection patterns; input sanitization for retrieved content;
    instruction hierarchy enforcement (system prompt > user prompt > retrieved
    content, with retrieved content never able to override prior); agent
    action auditing; tool invocation rate limiting.
  GAPS:        No reliable technical control against indirect prompt injection
    exists as of 2024. Instruction hierarchy is difficult to enforce because
    the model cannot reliably distinguish legitimate instructions from injected
    instructions in retrieved content. The problem is fundamental: the model
    uses the same mechanism for following instructions as for processing
    information. Sandboxed execution (isolated agent that cannot take
    irreversible actions without confirmation) is the most reliable mitigation
    but limits utility.

[A62] MODEL EXTRACTION VIA BLACK-BOX QUERIES
  CLASS:       AI/ML Security; Intellectual Property
  MECHANISM:   An attacker queries a target ML model via API, collecting
    input-output pairs. From these pairs, a local substitute model is trained
    that approximates the target's behavior. The substitute may be used to:
    (1) replicate the model's commercial value (IP theft); (2) conduct
    white-box adversarial attacks against the substitute (which transfer
    to the target); (3) infer training data properties.
  INSTANCES:   Tramèr et al. (2016) — "Stealing Machine Learning Models via
    Prediction APIs" — demonstrated extraction of scikit-learn, BigML, and
    Amazon ML models via API queries with near-perfect fidelity.
    Carlini et al. (2020) — extracted cryptographic signing key from
    Google's Edge TPU model by exploiting a specific vulnerability.
    OpenAI model extraction (reported 2023) — third parties have published
    models claimed to be extracted/distilled from GPT-4 API responses;
    OpenAI terms prohibit this but technical enforcement is limited.
  PREREQUISITES: API access to target model; budget for sufficient queries
    (cost scales with model complexity and required fidelity); compute for
    training substitute.
  INDICATORS:  Unusually high API usage from single user; systematic
    coverage of input space (grid search, Latin hypercube sampling of
    feature space); queries structured to probe decision boundaries.
  MITIGATIONS: Rate limiting and query budget caps; output perturbation
    (adding calibrated noise to predictions without affecting utility);
    watermarking (embedding detectable patterns in model outputs that
    survive extraction — Adi et al. 2018); API terms of service enforcement;
    prediction API monitoring for systematic exploration.
  GAPS:        No reliable technical defense against extraction by a
    sufficiently patient, distributed attacker who stays below per-account
    rate limits. Watermarking of model outputs is an active research area
    but has not been deployed at scale. The economic incentive is high —
    a GPT-4 quality model extracted at API query cost vs. training cost
    is a massive value transfer.

[A63] TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION FROM LLMs
  CLASS:       AI/ML Security; Data Privacy
  MECHANISM:   LLMs memorize portions of their training data, particularly
    repeated sequences. An attacker crafts prompts that cause the model
    to reproduce memorized content verbatim — PII, private documents,
    copyrighted material, API keys, credentials, or any high-frequency
    content in training data.
  INSTANCES:   Carlini et al. (2021) — "Extracting Training Data from
    Large Language Models" — extracted >600 memorized examples from GPT-2
    including personal email addresses, IRC logs, copyrighted text. Used
    membership inference to confirm extraction vs. generation.
    Carlini et al. (2023) — "Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language
    Models" — 1-3% of tokens memorized at extraction-threshold level;
    larger models memorize more; more repetitions in training → more
    memorization.
    Chang et al. (2023) — key-value extraction from instruction-tuned
    models — demonstrated that fine-tuned safety mechanisms do not
    prevent training data extraction, only make prompting harder.
    Nasr et al. (2023) — "Scalable Extraction of Training Data from
    Production Language Models" — extracted several megabytes of verbatim
    training data from ChatGPT including personal data.
  PREREQUISITES: API access; ability to craft prompts that trigger
    memorized content (divergence prompting, completion prompting,
    repetition prompting to shift model into "memorization mode").
  INDICATORS:  Model outputs that are unusually precise, contain PII in
    unexpected contexts, include exact reproduction of known copyrighted text,
    or display repeating patterns inconsistent with generated text.
  MITIGATIONS: Differential privacy training (DP-SGD adds noise during
    training limiting per-example memorization — at cost of model quality);
    data deduplication before training (reduces frequency-driven memorization);
    output filtering (scan model outputs for known PII patterns, copyrighted
    text, secrets); membership inference auditing during development;
    RLHF fine-tuning can partially suppress but does not eliminate memorization.
  GAPS:        DP-SGD at privacy-preserving epsilon values significantly
    degrades model utility; there is no free privacy. Deduplication helps
    but does not eliminate memorization of unique sensitive documents.
    Output filtering cannot catch memorized content it doesn't know to
    look for. The fundamental tension: larger, more capable models memorize
    more.

[A64] LASER FAULT INJECTION (LFI) AGAINST SECURE HARDWARE
  CLASS:       Hardware Security; Physical Side-Channel
  MECHANISM:   A precisely focused laser beam is directed at a semiconductor
    die (chip) to induce transient faults in computation. When timed to
    coincide with a cryptographic operation or security check, the fault
    can: (1) flip a comparison result (bypass PIN check); (2) cause
    incorrect output in cryptographic computation (differential fault
    analysis to extract key); (3) skip a security-critical instruction
    (bypass secure boot check, skip signature verification).
  INSTANCES:   Skorobogatov and Anderson (2002) — first optical fault
    injection on microcontroller, bypassed security fuse protection.
    Fault injection on DES by Biham and Shamir (1997) — theoretical
    differential fault analysis; LFI makes it practical.
    Yuce et al. (2018) — LFI on ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, bypassed
    secure boot, extracted AES keys.
    Bozzato et al. (2019) — LFI on STM32 family bypassed readout protection
    (RDP) allowing full firmware extraction.
    LFI on smart cards: widely used in payment card security research;
    has broken EMV implementations.
    LFI on hardware wallets: Ledger Nano X security analysis by Kraken
    Security Labs (2020) — demonstrated glitching attacks; subsequent
    firmware hardening.
  PREREQUISITES: Physical access to chip; chip decapsulation (remove
    packaging to expose die) or thinned package; laser equipment ($10K-100K
    for research-grade setup); knowledge of target device timing and
    layout; sometimes: electron microscope for targeting.
  INDICATORS:  Physical access evidence; device tampering; unexpected
    computation results.
  MITIGATIONS: Physical countermeasures: light sensors in die (detect
    laser); active shielding (metal mesh over sensitive areas); redundant
    computation with comparison; temporal redundancy (perform operation
    twice, compare); randomized execution timing (make timing-dependent
    fault injection harder); opaque packaging; glitch detection circuits
    that trigger zeroization. Design countermeasures: constant-time
    implementations with no timing variation (reduce window for injection).
  GAPS:        Physical access requirement limits attacker to supply chain,
    insider, or loss scenarios. But hardware wallet and smart card attacks
    via LFI are a real threat when device is in attacker hands. No
    consumer-grade device reliably resists a well-resourced LFI attack;
    protection is cost-driven.

[A65] RFID RELAY ATTACK (DIGITAL PICKPOCKETING)
  CLASS:       Physical Security; Wireless/RF Security
  MECHANISM:   RFID and NFC proximity cards (building access, contactless
    payment, passports) are designed for short-range (<10cm) authentication.
    A relay attack extends this range using two devices: a "leech"
    device near the victim captures the card's RF field; the signal
    is transmitted via a high-bandwidth link (Bluetooth, WiFi, 4G) to
    a "ghost" device near the reader, which replays it. To the reader,
    the card appears to be in proximity. The authentication completes.
    All cryptographic protections in the card-reader exchange are
    preserved — the relay does not need to break the cryptography,
    only to relay the legitimate exchange.
  INSTANCES:   Hancke and Kuhn (2005) — first formally demonstrated RFID
    relay attack against ISO 14443 (contactless smart card) in academic
    literature. Distance: relay extended range from ~10cm to arbitrary
    (limited by relay link latency).
    Francis et al. (2010) — demonstrated relay attack against EMV
    contactless payment in lab setting; transactions of arbitrary amount
    authorized by relaying victim card.
    Verdult et al. (2012) — relay attack against Mifare Classic used in
    building access systems.
    Rolling relay ("rolljam") against car keyless entry (Samy Kamkar 2015)
    — recorded rolling code transmissions, jammed legitimate transmission,
    replayed stored code for car unlock. Not technically relay (jammer +
    replay) but same conceptual class.
    Real-world payment relay: documented cases of contactless payment
    fraud via relay attributed to organized crime in EU 2019-2022.
  PREREQUISITES: Two RF devices (can be purchased for <$100); proximity
    to victim (leech device must be within card range — in a crowd, bag,
    bus); proximity to target reader (ghost device must be at reader
    at same time). Timing: must complete before round-trip latency limit
    if implemented (latency-based countermeasure).
  INDICATORS:  Unusual transaction timing; transaction location inconsistent
    with victim's physical location; access log entries at times victim
    was elsewhere.
  MITIGATIONS: Distance bounding protocols (cryptographic proof that card
    is within physical distance limit — EMV does not implement this;
    ISO/IEC 14443-4 Amendment has distance bounding option);
    transaction velocity checking (payment processor: two transactions
    in different locations within N minutes); cardholder notification
    and confirmation for high-value contactless; Faraday cage sleeves
    (blocks all RF — prevents both attack and legitimate use).
  GAPS:        EMV contactless does not implement distance bounding.
    Distance bounding is complex to implement and has not been standardized
    for payment cards. The attack is easy (<$100 hardware, no cryptographic
    knowledge required) and the defense requires industry-wide protocol
    changes. Current fraud mitigation is transaction monitoring, not
    prevention.

[A66] SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK ON PACKAGE MANAGERS (DEPENDENCY CONFUSION / TYPOSQUATTING)
  CLASS:       Supply Chain Security; Software Security
  MECHANISM:   Public package registries (npm, PyPI, RubyGems, Maven)
    resolve packages by name. Dependency confusion: an attacker uploads
    a malicious package to a public registry with the same name as an
    internal private package used by the target organization. The package
    manager's resolution logic prefers the higher-version public package
    over the private internal one, silently installing malicious code.
    Typosquatting: an attacker registers a package with a name visually
    similar to a popular package (e.g., "colourama" vs. "colorama");
    developers who mistype install the malicious version. Combo squatting:
    attacker registers legitimate-seeming variations (e.g., "requests-security"
    for the Python "requests" package).
  INSTANCES:   Alex Birsan (2021) — dependency confusion research — uploaded
    packages with internal Microsoft, Apple, Uber, and Shopify names to
    npm and PyPI. All four had internal builds that pulled and executed
    his code, triggering bug bounty payouts from all four. Reported to
    have affected 35 companies in initial disclosure.
    PyPI malware campaigns (ongoing) — multiple campaigns per month;
    significant examples: "ultralytics" npm malware (2022, 450K weekly
    downloads package name typosquatted), "ctx" PyPI package hijack (2022
    — legitimate package name stolen after expiration, malicious code
    injected); "es5-ext" intentional sabotage by maintainer (2024 —
    added protest code that ran on Russian IPs).
    SolarWinds-adjacent: Codecov supply chain attack (2021) — CI/CD pipeline
    artifact (bash uploader script) modified to exfiltrate environment
    variables (including credentials) from any CI run that used it.
    Affected hundreds of companies including Twilio, Hashicorp, Rapid7.
  PREREQUISITES: Knowledge of internal package names (dependency confusion)
    or popular package names (typosquatting); ability to register on public
    registry (no vetting required on npm, PyPI); CI/CD pipeline or developer
    workstation that resolves public registry packages automatically.
  INDICATORS:  Package installation from unexpected registry; unexpected
    post-install scripts; package versions higher than known internal versions;
    network connections during package install to unexpected hosts.
  MITIGATIONS: Private registry mirroring with allowlist (only approved
    packages reach developer machines); lock files (package-lock.json,
    poetry.lock, requirements.txt with pinned hashes — prevents silent
    version resolution change); Sigstore/TUF (The Update Framework —
    cryptographic signing of package provenance); scope isolation (private
    packages in scoped namespace: @company/package — cannot be confused
    with public packages); dependency scanning in CI/CD (Dependabot,
    Snyk, Renovate) with malicious package signatures; SBOM (Software
    Bill of Materials) generation and auditing.
  GAPS:        PyPI and npm have millions of packages; automated malicious
    package detection is imperfect (obfuscated malicious code evades
    static analysis); legitimate package hijacking (stealing credentials
    of a legitimate maintainer) bypasses name-based controls; the scale
    of the ecosystem makes comprehensive vetting impossible; lock file
    pinning is widely known but inconsistently implemented in practice.

[A67] BLUETOOTH ATTACKS (BLUEBUGGING, BLUESNARFING, BlueBorne)
  CLASS:       Wireless/RF Security; Mobile Security
  MECHANISM:   Bluetooth protocol weaknesses allow: (a) BlueSnarfing —
    unauthorized access to data (contacts, messages, calendar) on a
    Bluetooth-enabled device without user awareness, exploiting AT command
    or OBEX push vulnerabilities; (b) Bluebugging — full control of a
    Bluetooth device (make calls, send SMS) by exploiting AT command passthrough;
    (c) BlueBorne — wormable Bluetooth attack exploiting implementation
    bugs in Bluetooth stack code execution, allowing remote code execution
    without pairing.
  INSTANCES:   Adam Laurie (2003) — first disclosed BlueSnarfing and
    Bluebugging vulnerabilities against Nokia, Ericsson, Sony-Ericsson phones.
    BlueBorne (Armis, 2017) — 8 vulnerabilities across Android, iOS, Windows,
    and Linux Bluetooth stacks. Android: CVE-2017-0781/0782 (RCE without
    interaction). Windows: CVE-2017-8628 (MitM). Linux: CVE-2017-1000251
    (RCE in kernel Bluetooth stack). Estimated 5.3 billion devices affected.
    No pairing required. Wormable (one compromised device can attack adjacent
    devices).
    KNOB attack (2019) — Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth — attacker forces
    Bluetooth classic connection to use 1-byte entropy key; brute-forceable
    in microseconds. Allows decryption of any Bluetooth classic session.
    BIAS attack (2020) — Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS — authentication
    bypass in Bluetooth classic that allows impersonation of a paired device
    without knowing the link key.
    BLESA (2021) — Bluetooth Low Energy Spoofing Attack — reconnection
    procedure in BLE does not require mutual authentication; attacker
    impersonates previously paired device.
  PREREQUISITES: Bluetooth range proximity (typically 10m-100m depending
    on class); Bluetooth enabled on target (often enabled by default);
    for older attacks: discoverable mode required; BlueBorne: no requirement.
  INDICATORS:  Unusual Bluetooth activity; unexpected data transmission;
    battery drain from Bluetooth radio activity.
  MITIGATIONS: Keep Bluetooth disabled when not in use; set non-discoverable
    mode; apply OS updates (most BlueBorne-class vulnerabilities patched);
    Bluetooth 5.x with proper pairing; turn off Bluetooth in sensitive
    environments (SCIFs, board meetings).
  GAPS:        IoT Bluetooth devices (hearing aids, medical devices, industrial
    sensors) often run outdated Bluetooth stacks with no update mechanism;
    BLE implementation bugs continue to be found regularly; the Bluetooth
    specification complexity (2800+ pages) makes implementation correct
    extremely difficult; automotive Bluetooth continues to have implementation
    vulnerabilities.

[A68] HOMOGLYPH AND UNICODE ATTACKS
  CLASS:       Application Security; Social Engineering; Identity
  MECHANISM:   Unicode contains multiple visually indistinguishable or
    nearly identical characters from different character sets. Attackers
    use these to create deceptive identifiers that appear identical to
    legitimate ones to human observers but are treated as distinct by
    systems. Categories: (a) IDN homograph attacks (internationalized
    domain names using Cyrillic а vs. Latin a in domain names);
    (b) homoglyph filename attacks (malicious file with name that appears
    identical to trusted file); (c) right-to-left override (RTLO character
    reverses display direction, making "malware.exe" appear as "erawlam.pdf"
    in file explorer); (d) zero-width characters in usernames, breaking
    case-insensitive matching while preserving visual appearance.
  INSTANCES:   Evgeniy Bogachev (Zeus/GameOver Zeus) used IDN homograph
    domains for bank phishing. Paavo Niskala (2018) — Bitfinex homoglyph
    phishing; "bitfinеx.com" (Cyrillic е) vs. "bitfinex.com" (Latin e).
    RTLO filename attack — used in targeted attacks to trick recipients
    into executing malicious files (malware disguised as PDF).
    Unicode bidirectional exploit in code (CVE-2021-42574, "Trojan Source")
    — bidirectional control characters embedded in source code comments
    and strings cause the displayed code to differ from the compiled code.
    A code review would see benign code; the compiler would compile malicious code.
  PREREQUISITES: Target system that processes Unicode; human reviewer
    relying on visual inspection rather than machine comparison; for IDN:
    browser that renders IDN without punycode warning.
  INDICATORS:  Punycode inspection of domain; character-level comparison
    vs. visual comparison; compiler warnings for bidirectional characters.
  MITIGATIONS: Homoglyph detection and normalization; IDN policy restricting
    mixing scripts in single domain label; RTLO character blocking in
    file systems and messaging; Trojan Source mitigation: compiler warnings
    for bidirectional characters (GCC, Clang patched in 2021); visual
    display of punycode by default in browser UI.
  GAPS:        The Unicode standard continues to add characters; homoglyph
    databases are not comprehensive; zero-width character attacks are not
    reliably detected; internationalization requirements create permanent
    tension with homoglyph prevention.

[A69] MFA BYPASS — REAL-TIME PHISHING (EVILGINX, ADVERSARY-IN-THE-MIDDLE)
  CLASS:       Identity and Access Management; Social Engineering
  MECHANISM:   Traditional phishing cannot capture session cookies generated
    after MFA completion because the phishing page doesn't participate in
    the real authentication flow. Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing
    proxies the real authentication: victim is directed to a phishing proxy
    that forwards credentials and MFA codes to the real site in real time,
    captures the post-authentication session cookie, and relays the legitimate
    response to the victim. The victim successfully authenticates; the
    attacker has the session cookie.
  INSTANCES:   Evilginx2 (Kuba Gretzky, open source, 2018) — widely used
    AiTM phishing toolkit. Supports "phishlets" for major targets (Microsoft
    365, Google, Facebook). Used in numerous credential theft campaigns.
    Microsoft BEC campaign (2022) — Microsoft Defender Intelligence reported
    AiTM phishing campaign targeting 10,000+ organizations using Evilginx-style
    proxy; bypassed MFA to access Microsoft 365, then initiated BEC from
    compromised accounts.
    Twilio/Okta Scatter Swine campaign (2022) — SMS-based phishing with
    real-time relay allowed attackers to bypass Okta MFA for multiple targets.
    Scattered Spider/MGM (2023) — vishing component used to initiate MFA
    fatigue and AiTM flow against MGM Resorts, resulting in >$100M impact.
  PREREQUISITES: Phishing infrastructure (domain, proxy setup); ability to
    direct victim to phishing URL; session cookies that are not bound to
    device or network (most current session implementations).
  INDICATORS:  Impossible travel (session cookie used from unexpected location
    after legitimate authentication); new device sign-in; failed MFA
    pushes before success (MFA fatigue); authentication from VPN/residential
    proxy IP.
  MITIGATIONS: FIDO2/passkeys (hardware-bound credentials — phishing proxy
    cannot relay a hardware attestation; the credential is cryptographically
    bound to the origin, so a proxy domain fails the origin check — phishing-
    resistant by design); Conditional Access policies (device compliance,
    location, risk signal); anomaly detection on post-authentication session;
    MFA number matching (prevents simple push fatigue by requiring matching
    number); CAE (Continuous Access Evaluation — revoke session tokens in
    near-real-time when risk signals change).
  GAPS:        FIDO2 adoption is incomplete; TOTP and push MFA remain
    widely deployed and AiTM-bypassable; SMS OTP is trivially bypassed
    by AiTM; many organizations have not deployed phishing-resistant MFA;
    legacy applications cannot support FIDO2 and must use weaker MFA.

[A70] KUBERNETES / CONTAINER ESCAPE TO HOST
  CLASS:       Cloud Security; Container Security; Privilege Escalation
  MECHANISM:   Container isolation is enforced by Linux kernel namespaces
    and cgroups. Container breakout exploits: (a) kernel vulnerabilities
    (container shares host kernel — any kernel exploit grants host access);
    (b) misconfigured privileged containers (–privileged flag removes
    namespace isolation); (c) dangerous capability grants (CAP_SYS_ADMIN
    or CAP_NET_ADMIN allow various escape paths); (d) host path mounts
    exposing sensitive host directories inside container; (e) Docker socket
    mount (gives container full control over Docker daemon, which runs
    as root on host); (f) runtime vulnerabilities (runc CVE-2019-5736,
    CRI-O CVE-2022-0811).
  INSTANCES:   CVE-2019-5736 (runc breakout) — attacker with ability to
    run container could overwrite runc binary on host via /proc/self/exe
    path. Required only ability to run or influence container configuration.
    CVE-2022-0811 (CRI-O "cr8escape") — one argument injection in pod spec
    allowed container escape on Kubernetes nodes running CRI-O runtime.
    CVE-2024-21626 (runc CVSS 8.6) — working directory escape allowing
    container breakout via WORKDIR manipulation.
    Kubernetes API server exploitation — cluster admin via unauthenticated
    API server (exposed port 6443/8080) — mass scanning campaigns have
    found thousands of exposed Kubernetes API servers.
    Tesla Kubernetes cluster cryptojacking (2018) — exposed Kubernetes
    dashboard (no authentication) allowed attacker to deploy cryptomining
    pods; credentials to S3 buckets exposed in pod environment variables.
  PREREQUISITES: Initial container access (via application exploit, supply
    chain, or direct container deployment); misconfiguration or kernel
    vulnerability; for CVE-based: timing (before patch).
  INDICATORS:  Privileged process activity outside container; access to
    host filesystem paths; unexpected child processes of container runtime;
    network connections to host metadata service from container.
  MITIGATIONS: Run containers as non-root user; avoid –privileged and
    dangerous capabilities; use seccomp profiles (restrict syscalls);
    AppArmor/SELinux for mandatory access control; Pod Security Admission
    (Kubernetes 1.25+, replacing PSP); runtime security monitoring (Falco,
    Aqua, Sysdig); read-only root filesystem; gVisor or Kata Containers
    (hardware-isolated sandbox runtimes); avoid Docker socket mounts;
    host path volume restrictions; network policies to limit container-to-
    host communication.
  GAPS:        Shared kernel is a fundamental architectural limit of
    container isolation — kernel vulnerabilities will continue to be
    exploitable for container escape regardless of configuration hardening;
    VM-level isolation (Kata, gVisor) addresses this but at performance cost;
    multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters with mixed trust levels have no
    reliable isolation short of separate node pools.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSE TAXONOMY — CYCLE 6 ADDITIONS (D46-D53)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[D46] FORMAL METHODS AND VERIFIED SECURITY
  MECHANISMS:
    → Theorem proving: manually write machine-checkable proofs of security
      properties (Coq, Isabelle/HOL, TLA+). Used for: seL4 kernel correctness,
      CompCert compiler correctness, cryptographic protocol security.
    → Model checking: exhaustive state-space exploration to verify that
      a finite-state model satisfies a property. SPIN (protocol verification),
      NuSMV (hardware/software model checking), CBMC (bounded model checking
      for C/C++ programs). Scalability limit: state explosion for large systems.
    → Protocol verification tools: ProVerif (automated, symbolic, privacy
      and authentication properties), Tamarin Prover (symbolic, equational
      theories, group Diffie-Hellman). Used to verify TLS 1.3 (Beurdouche
      et al. 2017), Signal (Cohn-Gordon et al. 2016), OAuth 2.0.
    → Verified compilers: CompCert (Leroy 2006) — formally verified C
      compiler; proofs in Coq that compiled assembly correctly implements
      C semantics. Used in aviation and automotive (DO-178C, ISO 26262).
    → Information flow analysis: type systems that track information flow
      and prove noninterference (secret inputs do not influence public
      outputs). Jif (Java Information Flow), FlowCaml, SecureFlow. Not
      widely deployed in commercial software due to annotation burden.
    → SMT-based verification: Z3, CVC5 solve satisfiability modulo theories
      — used for automated verification of bounded programs, type checking
      with refinement types (Liquid Haskell, F*).
  COVERAGE:    Provides strongest guarantee for what is proven. Gap: the
    specification boundary. Only as useful as the specification is complete.
  GAPS:        Cost of writing proofs is high even with LLM assistance;
    most commercial software is not verified; verification does not cover
    hardware behavior (Spectre); specification mismatch is exploitable;
    no standard for disclosure of verification scope.

[D47] ECONOMIC INTERVENTION IN VULNERABILITY MARKETS
  MECHANISMS:
    → Bug bounty programs: vendor-funded programs that pay researchers
      for vulnerability reports (HackerOne, Bugcrowd platforms). Maximum
      payouts: Google $151K (Chrome), Microsoft $250K (Azure), Apple $1M
      (iCloud). Below market rate for high-value zero-days but provides
      legal safe harbor and community building.
    → Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD): structured process for
      reporting, response, and disclosure timeline. ISO/IEC 30111 and
      29147 standards. CISA operates US government CVD process.
    → Ransom payment bans: legislative prohibition on paying ransomware
      demands (proposed in multiple jurisdictions; Australian critical
      infrastructure consultation 2023; not enacted broadly as of 2024).
      Economic effect: removes ransom as viable attacker revenue;
      risk: organizations pay without reporting, goes underground.
    → Cyber insurance reform: insurers requiring security controls as
      a condition of coverage (MFA, EDR, backup testing, patch SLAs).
      Market pressure for security improvement without regulation.
      Risk: coverage exclusions for "acts of war" (Mondelez v. Zurich,
      NotPetya) create coverage uncertainty.
    → Vulnerability stockpile disclosure policies: US Vulnerabilities
      Equities Process (VEP) — interagency review of government-held
      zero-days to decide whether to retain or disclose. Published
      charter 2017. Critics: opaque, retention-biased.
    → Software liability reform: proposals to hold software vendors liable
      for security failures (EU Product Liability Directive update, US
      National Cybersecurity Strategy 2023 — shift liability to vendors).
      If implemented: changes economic incentive for software quality.
  COVERAGE:    Economic interventions address incentive misalignment that
    technical controls cannot solve. Market structure determines whether
    vulnerabilities are found, disclosed, or weaponized.
  GAPS:        Coordinating a global market intervention requires international
    agreement; jurisdictional differences (looser regulations elsewhere
    attract operations); unintended consequences of ransom bans (victims
    pay covertly, lose insurance, and are less able to recover); software
    liability may chill innovation if scope is too broad.

[D48] COGNITIVE SECURITY CONTROLS (DISINFORMATION RESISTANCE)
  MECHANISMS:
    → Pre-bunking (inoculation theory): expose target population to weakened
      forms of manipulation techniques before they encounter the real attack.
      Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab: "Bad News" game — players
      learn manipulation tactics and become more resistant (Roozenbeek and
      van der Linden, 2019). Effective at population level; duration of
      effect: 2-4 weeks, requiring re-inoculation.
    → Content provenance and authentication: C2PA (Coalition for Content
      Provenance and Authenticity) — open standard for attaching signed
      provenance records to media files (publisher, creation tool, edits).
      Adobe Content Credentials, Microsoft Azure Video Indexer, Google
      DeepMind SynthID (watermarking). Covers only content produced by
      participating tools; attacker-generated content has no provenance.
    → Platform-level friction: adding context labels, slowing sharing of
      flagged content, adding confirmation steps before re-sharing. Twitter
      "Read before you retweet" (2020) — 40% increase in article opens
      before retweeting. Trade-off: friction reduces both harmful and
      beneficial sharing.
    → Epistemic labeling: publicly marking known false or misleading content
      (Twitter Community Notes, Facebook third-party fact-checking). Limitation:
      high latency (fact-check arrives after virality peak); accuracy
      disputes create false equivalence.
    → Literacy and media education: teaching recognition of manipulation
      tactics, source evaluation, lateral reading (checking claims against
      other sources). Effective in controlled studies; long-term field
      effectiveness varies; cannot scale to real-time defense against
      AI-generated personalized content.
    → Technical provenance infrastructure: DKIM for email, HTTPS for web,
      RPKI for BGP — all apply provenance to communications channels.
      Analogous infrastructure for media content (who created this, what
      tools, what edits) is the C2PA vision but requires ecosystem adoption.
  COVERAGE:    Human cognitive vulnerabilities cannot be technically patched;
    controls must address the information environment, not only the content.
  GAPS:        No technical control reliably distinguishes AI-generated from
    human-generated content at scale with low false positive rate; watermarks
    can be stripped; inoculation requires sustained effort; the information
    environment is global and jurisdiction-specific controls are limited.

[D49] SECURE HARDWARE DESIGN AND ROOT OF TRUST
  MECHANISMS:
    → Trusted Platform Module (TPM) — ISO/IEC 11889 — dedicated security
      chip providing: secure key storage (keys never leave chip), attestation
      (cryptographic proof of platform boot state), sealed storage
      (data encrypted to specific platform state). TPM 2.0 mandatory on
      Windows 11. Used for BitLocker, Secure Boot measurement.
    → Hardware Security Module (HSM) — FIPS 140-2/3 Level 3/4 certified
      dedicated cryptographic processor. Physical tamper evidence and
      response (Level 3: tamper evidence; Level 4: tamper response with
      key zeroization). Used for CA private keys, payment processing,
      code signing.
    → Apple Secure Enclave — ARM TrustZone-based isolated execution
      environment on Apple SoCs. Stores biometric data (Touch ID, Face ID),
      device encryption keys (UID). Keys never leave Secure Enclave;
      Secure Enclave has separate boot ROM, encrypted memory. Separate from
      application processor — compromised OS cannot extract Secure Enclave keys.
    → ARM TrustZone — hardware isolation of "secure world" from "normal world"
      on ARM processors. Secure monitor (SMC) arbitrates world transitions.
      Used for DRM, secure payments, biometric processing on Android.
      Vulnerable to side-channel attacks (CacheBleed, PRIME+PROBE targeting
      TrustZone).
    → RISC-V Physical Memory Protection (PMP) — hardware access control
      registers that enforce memory access policy in machine mode. Enables
      lightweight trusted execution on embedded systems without TrustZone.
    → Physically Unclonable Functions (PUF) — hardware circuit that exploits
      manufacturing variation to produce a unique, unclonable "fingerprint"
      from the silicon. Used as hardware root of trust for key derivation
      without key storage (the key is generated from physical characteristics,
      not stored). SRAM PUF most common type.
    → Secure Boot chain: UEFI Secure Boot (firmware verifies bootloader
      signature) → bootloader verifies kernel signature → kernel verifies
      module signatures → TPM measurement of each stage. Break in chain
      = loss of attestation integrity.
  COVERAGE:    Hardware root of trust establishes foundation that software
    cannot undermine. Protects against software-layer compromise up to the
    trust boundary.
  GAPS:        Hardware supply chain introduces risk before root of trust
    is established (foundry-level trojan defeats all software-enforced
    trust); TrustZone has been attacked via side-channel; HSM physical
    security requires physical security of deployment environment; PUF
    reliability degrades with temperature cycling and aging.

[D50] NETWORK TRAFFIC ANALYSIS DEFENSE (ENCRYPTED TRAFFIC ANALYTICS)
  MECHANISMS:
    → NetFlow / IPFIX analysis: flow metadata (src/dst IP, port, protocol,
      byte count, packet count, duration) analyzed without decryption.
      Anomaly detection: unusual destination IPs, unexpected port usage,
      unusual data volumes, unusual timing patterns.
    → Encrypted Traffic Analytics (ETA) — Cisco — derives security signals
      from TLS handshake metadata (SNI, cipher suites, TLS version, cert
      validity, session duration, packet timing and size patterns) without
      decryption. Identifies malware C2 over TLS, data exfiltration patterns.
    → JA3/JA3S fingerprinting — hashes TLS ClientHello/ServerHello parameters
      to produce a fingerprint of the TLS client/server implementation.
      Identifies specific malware families that use distinctive TLS
      implementations (CobaltStrike, Metasploit). Limitations: JA3 can
      be evaded by modifying TLS parameters.
    → DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT) — encrypts DNS queries,
      preventing monitoring. From defender perspective: reduces visibility
      into domain resolution (C2 domains no longer visible in plaintext DNS).
      Counter: monitoring DoH providers, using internal DNS resolvers.
    → ML-based traffic classification: train classifiers on flow features
      (byte distribution, inter-packet timing, burst patterns) to classify
      encrypted traffic by application or malicious category.
      Used in commercial NDR (Network Detection and Response) products.
    → Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) with SSL/TLS interception: enterprise
      breaks TLS via MITM proxy (corporate CA installed on endpoints);
      inspects plaintext. Effective but: breaks certificate transparency;
      introduces new MITM trust; violates privacy expectations; incompatible
      with certificate pinning.
  COVERAGE:    Provides visibility into encrypted network traffic without
    decryption; identifies behavioral anomalies that survive encryption.
  GAPS:        Adversaries can pad traffic, randomize timing, use legitimate
    cloud infrastructure (same JA3 as legitimate software); DoH centralizes
    DNS visibility into few providers; ML classifiers have false positive
    rates that create alert fatigue; QUIC and HTTP/3 reduce flow metadata
    visibility.

[D51] THREAT INTELLIGENCE PLATFORMS AND SHARING
  MECHANISMS:
    → Indicator sharing: IP addresses, domains, file hashes, URLs, email
      headers associated with known malicious activity. Formats: STIX 2.1
      (Structured Threat Information Expression), TAXII (transport layer).
      Platforms: MISP (open source), ThreatConnect, Anomali, Recorded Future.
    → Tactical intelligence: TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures)
      mapped to MITRE ATT&CK framework. More durable than IOCs (indicators
      rotate; TTPs persist). ATT&CK Enterprise has 14 tactics, 196 techniques,
      411 sub-techniques (2024).
    → ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers) — sector-specific
      threat intelligence sharing communities. FS-ISAC (financial services),
      H-ISAC (healthcare), E-ISAC (electricity), Auto-ISAC (automotive).
      Membership-based, curated sharing of sector-relevant threats.
    → Government sharing programs: CISA AIS (Automated Indicator Sharing)
      — free, real-time IOC sharing via TAXII; FBI InfraGard; NSA/CISA
      Joint Cybersecurity Advisories.
    → Dark web intelligence: monitoring criminal forums, paste sites,
      ransomware leak sites for advance warning of attacks, stolen credentials,
      new tooling. Vendors: Flare, DarkOwl, Intel 471, Kela.
    → Threat intelligence lifecycle: collection → processing → analysis →
      dissemination → feedback. Most organizations have collection and
      processing; strategic analysis and feedback loop are weakest links.
  COVERAGE:    Collective defense enables sharing of attacker indicators
    faster than any single organization could discover them. ATT&CK provides
    common taxonomy for measuring detection coverage.
  GAPS:        IOC half-life is short (attackers rotate infrastructure);
    sharing timelines lag attacker operations; sensitivity concerns limit
    sharing of highest-value intelligence; overload (too many indicators
    to operationalize without automated enrichment); TTP sharing requires
    analytical expertise not universally available; attribution intelligence
    is rarely shared outside government.

[D52] SECURE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIFECYCLE (S-SDLC) AND DEVSECOPS
  MECHANISMS:
    → Security requirements in design phase: threat modeling (STRIDE, PASTA,
      attack trees) before code is written; security architecture review;
      identifying security controls required by compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA,
      FedRAMP, SOC 2).
    → Static Application Security Testing (SAST): automated analysis of
      source code for vulnerability patterns. Tools: Semgrep, CodeQL, Checkmarx,
      Veracode, SonarQube. Integrated into CI/CD pipeline; fails build on
      high-severity findings. Limitation: false positive rate; language/
      framework coverage gaps.
    → Software Composition Analysis (SCA): identifies open source components
      and their known vulnerabilities (using NVD/OSV databases). Tools:
      Dependabot, Snyk, FOSSA, Black Duck. Generates SBOM. Critical:
      open source is 60-80% of modern application code surface area.
    → Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST): runs against deployed
      application to find vulnerabilities (injection, authentication,
      configuration). Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Nikto. Requires
      running application environment.
    → Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST): instruments running
      application (agent-based) to observe data flows and identify
      vulnerabilities with low false positive rate. Tools: Seeker, Contrast.
    → Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): machine-readable inventory of
      software components and their versions. Formats: SPDX, CycloneDX.
      Executive Order 14028 (2021) mandated SBOM for federal procurement.
      Enables rapid response when a component vulnerability is disclosed
      (know within minutes which products are affected).
    → Pre-commit hooks, code review, secrets scanning: prevent secrets
      (API keys, passwords) from being committed to repositories.
      Tools: git-secrets, Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitGuardian.
      GitHub's push protection (2023) blocks pushes containing detected secrets.
  COVERAGE:    Shift-left: finding vulnerabilities earlier in development
    lifecycle when they are cheaper to fix. Integrating security into
    the development workflow rather than a separate audit.
  GAPS:        Developer friction from false positives causes alert fatigue
    and tool bypass; not all languages and frameworks have equal tool coverage;
    SBOM generation is automated but SBOM accuracy and completeness varies;
    threat modeling is time-intensive and rarely done comprehensively outside
    security-mature organizations; AI-generated code introduces vulnerabilities
    at the speed of generation — code review cannot keep pace.

[D53] ZERO-KNOWLEDGE PROOFS AS AUTHENTICATION AND PRIVACY MECHANISM
  MECHANISMS:
    → ZKP fundamentals: a prover demonstrates knowledge of a secret (or
      that a statement is true) without revealing the secret itself.
      Interactive (interactive proofs, Schnorr protocol) or non-interactive
      (NIZK, zk-SNARKs, zk-STARKs).
    → Authentication without credential transmission: instead of sending
      a password hash for comparison, prove knowledge of the password via
      ZKP without transmitting it. Server stores commitment; cannot be
      breached for passwords. OPAQUE protocol (Jarecki et al. 2018) —
      Oblivious Pseudorandom Function-based PAKE (Password-Authenticated
      Key Exchange) using ZKP principles. Draft IETF RFC.
    → Zcash (2016) — cryptocurrency using zk-SNARKs (Groth16) to prove
      validity of transaction (sender has sufficient balance, amounts sum
      correctly) without revealing sender, receiver, or amount. First
      production deployment of zk-SNARK for privacy.
    → Tornado Cash — Ethereum mixer using zk-SNARKs to break linkage
      between deposit and withdrawal addresses. Sanctioned by OFAC (2022)
      for use in money laundering; demonstrates that ZKP privacy tools
      have dual-use nature.
    → Age verification without revealing age: ZKP proves "age > 18" given
      a signed credential from a trusted issuer without revealing exact date
      of birth or any other attribute. W3C Verifiable Credentials + ZKP
      predicates. EU Digital Identity Wallet includes ZKP selective disclosure.
    → zk-Rollups (Ethereum L2): batch-process thousands of transactions
      off-chain; generate ZKP that all transactions were valid; post proof
      to Ethereum mainnet. Security guarantee: cryptographic soundness
      of the proof. Examples: zkSync Era, StarkNet, Polygon zkEVM.
    → Trusted setup problem: zk-SNARK systems (Groth16, PLONK) require
      a "trusted setup" ceremony that generates public parameters. If the
      randomness is not destroyed ("toxic waste"), the ceremony participants
      could forge proofs. SIKE-equivalent risk: a compromised ceremony
      invalidates the entire system. Zcash Powers of Tau ceremony (2017),
      Hermez multi-party computation ceremony (2021) used multi-party
      computation to distribute trust.
    → zk-STARKs (STARKWare) — no trusted setup; post-quantum secure
      (based on hash functions, not elliptic curves); larger proof size
      and verification cost vs. SNARKs.
  COVERAGE:    Enables authentication, compliance proof, and privacy-preserving
    computation with mathematical security guarantees. Strong cryptographic
    foundations.
  GAPS:        Implementation complexity; trusted setup ceremonies are
    one-time events with permanent consequences if compromised; circuit
    implementation bugs (soundness bugs) break the proof system even when
    the underlying mathematics is correct (Zcash sapling soundness bug 2019);
    verifier complexity and gas costs limit on-chain deployment; zk-SNARK
    systems are not post-quantum secure (rely on elliptic curve pairings).

CYCLE 6 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN

[C33] THERMODYNAMICS → CRYPTOGRAPHIC KEY DERIVATION ENERGY LIMITS
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Thermodynamics: Landauer's principle (1961) — erasing one bit of
    information requires minimum energy expenditure of kT·ln(2) joules
    (k = Boltzmann constant, T = temperature in Kelvin). At room temperature
    (~293K): minimum ~4×10^-21 joules per bit erasure. This is a physical
    lower bound on computation energy — it cannot be reduced by engineering
    improvements, only by reducing operating temperature.
    Cybersecurity: brute-force key search requires trying ~2^(N-1) keys
    on average for an N-bit key. Each comparison requires at minimum
    Landauer energy. For AES-256 (256-bit key): minimum energy for
    exhaustive search ≈ 2^255 × 4×10^-21 joules ≈ 10^55 joules.
    Total energy output of the sun over 32 billion years ≈ 10^54 joules.
    Thermodynamics proves that AES-256 cannot be brute-forced regardless
    of algorithmic improvement, as long as it must be computed physically.
    (This argument from Seth Lloyd, MIT, 2000; also Schneier.)
  OBSERVATION:
    This convergence provides the strongest possible argument for key
    length: not "current computers can't do it" but "the laws of physics
    prevent it." The limit is independent of algorithmic improvement.
    It is the basis for the claim that properly implemented symmetric
    cryptography with sufficient key length is unconditionally secure
    against brute force (excluding side-channels, protocol flaws, and
    implementation errors).
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    The same thermodynamic argument applies to hash preimage resistance:
    finding a 256-bit hash preimage requires at minimum 2^255 computations,
    each costing minimum Landauer energy. Thermodynamic preimage resistance
    is an under-appreciated security argument in hash function standardization
    discussions. Arguments about SHA-256 vs. SHA-3 focus on algorithmic
    security; the thermodynamic floor on brute force is a separate and
    stronger argument that is rarely made explicit in standards documentation.

[C34] MATERIALS SCIENCE → HARDWARE TROJAN DETECTION LIMITS
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Materials science: the physical properties of semiconductor materials
    (electron mobility, junction capacitance, doping concentration) determine
    circuit behavior. An attacker who modifies doping levels or introduces
    additional dopants in specific transistors can alter circuit behavior
    in ways that are invisible to optical inspection because the transistor
    geometry is unchanged.
    Cybersecurity: hardware trojans can be introduced at foundry level
    by modifying transistor doping in targeted circuits. The modification
    is undetectable by functional testing (the trojan is designed to activate
    only on a rare trigger condition) and by optical inspection (the geometry
    is identical; only doping differs, detectable only by expensive analytical
    techniques: secondary ion mass spectrometry, electron energy loss
    spectroscopy).
    Instance: Becker et al. (2013, CHES) — "Stealthy Dopant-Level Hardware
    Trojans" — demonstrated that changing doping in a small number of
    transistors in an Intel Ivy Bridge RDRAND circuit could bias random
    number generation while remaining undetectable by all known inspection
    methods.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Materials science has established techniques for detecting trace dopant
    modifications: SIMS (Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry), APT (Atom Probe
    Tomography), TEM-EELS (Transmission Electron Microscopy with Electron
    Energy Loss Spectroscopy). These techniques can detect single-atom
    doping variations. They have not been incorporated into any supply chain
    security standard or IC verification protocol. Current IC testing
    (functional testing, scan testing, JTAG boundary scan) cannot detect
    dopant-level trojans. The materials science tools exist; the security
    inspection protocol does not.
  GAP IDENTIFIED (G24):
    No standardized materials-level inspection protocol exists for
    high-assurance semiconductor supply chain security. NSA/DoD high-assurance
    programs use some analysis but at extreme cost. Commercial hardware
    supply chain verification does not include dopant-level analysis.
    A dopant-level hardware trojan in a widely deployed security chip
    (TPM, HSM, cryptographic accelerator) would be: invisible to software,
    firmware, and functional testing; active only on rare conditions;
    capable of subverting all software-layer security built on top.

[C35] ECOLOGY → MONOCULTURE RISK IN LANGUAGE RUNTIME ECOSYSTEMS
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Ecology: crop monoculture (genetically uniform crop) is devastated by
    a single matching pathogen. The Irish Potato Famine (1845-1852) killed
    or displaced ~25% of Ireland's population because potato cultivation
    was dominated by one variety (Lumper) that was susceptible to
    Phytophthora infestans. Genetic diversity would have prevented
    epidemic spread.
    Cybersecurity: the ecosystem of software is dominated by a small number
    of runtime platforms — V8 JavaScript engine (powers Chrome, Node.js,
    Electron — the majority of desktop and web applications), CPython
    (Python runtime — dominates data science, ML, server-side scripting,
    automation), JVM (Java/Kotlin — dominates enterprise and Android),
    and .NET CLR (C#/VB.NET — dominates Windows enterprise).
    A single critical vulnerability in V8 is simultaneously exploitable
    in Chrome (3 billion users), all Electron apps (Slack, VSCode, Discord),
    all Node.js applications, and all environments that embed V8.
    V8 sandbox escape vulnerabilities (regular occurrence in Chrome
    bug tracker) demonstrate the real attack surface.
  OBSERVATION:
    The security ecosystem has concentrated its runtime substrate into
    the fewest viable components for efficiency and compatibility reasons.
    The efficiency gain is real; the monoculture risk is systematically
    underpriced. No market mechanism rewards runtime diversity; the cost
    of runtime monoculture vulnerability is externalized to users.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Agriculture solved the monoculture problem (partially) through: seed
    banks (genetic diversity preserved for recovery), resistant variety
    development, crop rotation. Security analog: memory-safe languages
    as "resistant variety" (Rust, Go, Swift replacing C/C++) reduces
    vulnerability to memory corruption pathogen class; language diversity
    investment (WebAssembly as portable target enables multiple source
    language options); runtime isolation (each application in separate
    process or VM reduces spread from one compromised instance).
    The diversity investment is being made implicitly but not as a
    conscious monoculture-risk mitigation strategy.

[C36] QUANTUM MECHANICS → PHYSICAL LIMITS ON EAVESDROPPING (QKD)
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Quantum mechanics: the Heisenberg uncertainty principle — measuring
    a quantum state disturbs it in ways that cannot be fully compensated.
    For quantum key distribution (QKD, BB84 protocol, Bennett and Brassard
    1984): a key is transmitted via quantum states (photon polarizations).
    An eavesdropper who intercepts a photon to measure its state necessarily
    disturbs it in a detectable way. The error rate in the channel reveals
    the presence of eavesdropping. If the error rate is below threshold,
    the channel is (provably) secure; above threshold, the channel is compromised.
    Cybersecurity: QKD provides information-theoretic (unconditional) security
    for key exchange, unlike RSA/ECDH (computational security — secure only
    if factoring/DLOG is hard). QKD is secure against any adversary, including
    one with a quantum computer.
  OBSERVATION:
    QKD is the only key exchange mechanism whose security is guaranteed
    by physical law rather than computational assumption. This is the
    ultimate expression of the convergence between physics and cryptography:
    the laws of quantum mechanics enforce security.
  LIMITATIONS AND DEPLOYMENT GAPS:
    QKD requires dedicated fiber optic infrastructure or line-of-sight
    optical links (free-space QKD). Not deployable over standard internet
    infrastructure. Maximum distance without trusted repeaters: ~100-300 km
    (limited by photon loss in fiber). Trusted repeaters are not quantum-
    secure — they must be physically secured. China's QKD network (Beijing-
    Shanghai, 2017) uses trusted repeaters. Satellite QKD (Micius satellite,
    2016-2020) extends range to thousands of km but requires clear line-of-sight.
    Implementation security: QKD devices can have side-channels in the
    physical implementation (detector blinding attacks — Makarov et al. 2010 —
    bright light injection defeats single-photon detectors). The security
    proof is for ideal QKD; real implementations may not be ideal.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Quantum physics provides the tool for information-theoretically secure
    communication; deployment is blocked by infrastructure requirements.
    The engineering pattern that has not been fully transferred: quantum
    repeaters (using quantum entanglement swapping to extend QKD range
    without trusted intermediate nodes) are theoretically possible but
    not deployed at scale. If quantum repeaters become practical, QKD
    becomes deployable over existing fiber without trusted intermediaries.
    Current investment: IBM, QuTech, Amazon Quantum Networking on quantum
    repeater research.

[C37] NEUROSCIENCE OF ATTENTION → SECURITY ALERT FATIGUE
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Neuroscience: sustained attention (vigilance) degrades over time.
    The Vigilance Decrement (Mackworth 1948) — radar operators' detection
    of rare targets degrades by 40-50% within 30 minutes of sustained
    monitoring. The signal-to-noise ratio is not the primary factor;
    the low frequency of true positives causes attentional habituation
    regardless of signal strength. Attention is a limited resource that
    is depleted by monitoring and not replenished without cognitive rest.
    Cybersecurity: SOC analysts monitor security alerts. A typical SOC
    receives thousands of alerts per day; 40-70% are false positives
    (vendor-dependent). The Vigilance Decrement predicts: analysts
    who spend extended time reviewing alerts will miss real threats with
    increasing frequency over time, regardless of skill. This is not
    operator failure — it is the neuroscience of human attention applied
    to an environment that guarantees the Vigilance Decrement will occur.
  EVIDENCE:
    ESG Research (2019) — SOC analysts spend average 27 minutes per alert
    at large organizations; miss rate for complex attacks is not published
    but is an acknowledged problem. Dwell time data (Mandiant 2023 M-Trends:
    median global dwell time 16 days — evidence that attacks exist in
    environments for over two weeks before detection, even with alert
    systems active) is consistent with Vigilance Decrement contribution.
  UNTRANSFERRED PATTERN:
    Human factors engineering (from aviation, nuclear, process control)
    has developed structured mitigation for Vigilance Decrement:
    → mandatory work/rest ratios (FAA crew rest rules — pilot cannot fly
      beyond duty hour limits; military radio operator rotation every
      30-45 minutes for sustained vigilance tasks);
    → task rotation (rotating between high-vigilance tasks and lower-demand
      tasks on defined schedules);
    → automation for routine detection (human reviews exceptions only,
      reducing total alert volume to manageable number);
    → dual-operator confirmation for high-consequence actions (four-eyes
      principle in nuclear operations).
    Security operations has adopted automation (SIEM, SOAR, EDR) but
    without systematic Vigilance Decrement scheduling or workload analysis.
    Staffing models are based on headcount and cost, not vigilance-optimal
    cognitive load. This is a known, solvable human factors problem
    applied incorrectly in security operations.
  GAP IDENTIFIED (G25):
    No cybersecurity organization has published a SOC staffing model based
    on Vigilance Decrement research. Alert fatigue is universally acknowledged
    as a problem; the neuroscientific literature with quantified solutions
    (rotation intervals, rest ratios, cognitive load thresholds) has not
    been translated into security operations staffing standards.

[C38] EVOLUTIONARY BIOLOGY → ANTIVIRUS / EDR ARMS RACE DYNAMICS
  IDENTICAL MECHANIC:
    Evolutionary biology: host-pathogen co-evolution. Pathogen evolves
    to evade host immune recognition (epitope variation, immune evasion
    proteins); host evolves to recognize new pathogen signatures. Red Queen
    Hypothesis (Van Valen 1973) — each species must continuously evolve
    just to maintain fitness relative to co-evolving adversaries. Neither
    reaches permanent advantage; the race is permanent.
    Cybersecurity: malware authors modify code to evade AV/EDR detection
    (signature mutation, packer changes, behavior obfuscation); AV/EDR
    vendors update signatures and behavioral detections. The cycle is
    the exact Red Queen dynamic. No vendor achieves permanent detection
    superiority; no attacker achieves permanent evasion. Both invest
    continuously with no stable equilibrium.
  HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    → Polymorphic viruses (1990s) — mutate code structure on each infection,
      defeating signature detection. AV vendors responded with heuristic
      engines. Polymorphic shellcode remains standard in exploit frameworks.
    → Metamorphic viruses — semantically equivalent code with completely
      different syntax. Required semantic analysis response from AV.
    → Living-off-the-land (LOLBins, 2015+) — use legitimate system tools
      (PowerShell, WMI, certutil, mshta) for malicious purposes. Defeats
      signature detection because the tools are legitimate. EDR responds
      with behavioral analysis of tool usage patterns.
    → AMSI bypass (2016+) — bypass Windows AntiMalware Scan Interface.
      Microsoft adds AMSI hooks; attackers find new bypass methods.
      New bypass published; Microsoft patches; new bypass found.
    → EDR bypass via kernel drivers (2020+) — load signed-but-vulnerable
      drivers (BYOVD) to kill EDR sensors from kernel level.
      EDR vendors add driver blocklists; attackers find new vulnerable drivers.
  OBSERVATION:
    Red Queen dynamics mean the arms race has no end state. Defenders
    who believe any detection technology is a permanent solution are
    misapplying the evolutionary model. Architectural separation
    (defense in depth, assume breach) is the correct response to an
    arms race with no stable equilibrium — the goal is not to win the race
    but to ensure that losing a battle does not end the war.

      security model and known attacks; I2P (Invisible Internet Project) security.

59. Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PETs)
      Sub-domains: differential privacy (mathematical definition, epsilon-delta
      privacy, sensitivity); anonymization and re-identification attacks; k-anonymity,
      l-diversity, t-closeness; data minimization; pseudonymization; synthetic data
      generation for privacy; federated learning as privacy mechanism; secure
      aggregation; private information retrieval (PIR); oblivious RAM (ORAM);
      mix networks; private set intersection (PSI) protocols.

60. Cyber-Physical Safety and Functional Safety
      Sub-domains: IEC 61508 (functional safety of electrical/electronic/
      programmable systems); ISO 26262 (automotive functional safety);
      DO-178C (airborne software); cybersecurity interactions with functional
      safety; safety case argumentation; common cause failure analysis;
      Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Failure Mode Effects Analysis (FMEA)
      with security extensions; safety integrity levels (SIL) and their
      relationship to cybersecurity assurance levels; cybersecurity attacks
      that bypass safety systems (Triton/TRISIS targeting safety PLCs).

NEWLY IDENTIFIED SUB-DOMAINS WITHIN EXISTING DOMAINS (CYCLE 7):

AI/ML Security (13):
    → AI red teaming: adversarial testing methodology for AI systems beyond
      traditional pen testing; NIST AI RMF (Risk Management Framework, 2023);
      MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence
      Systems); AI incident reporting (AIAAIC database).
    → Prompt injection taxonomy: direct injection (user-supplied), indirect
      injection (content-retrieved), virtual prompt injection (system prompt
      disclosure), stored prompt injection (persistent in database), multi-agent
      injection chains (one compromised agent injects into next).
    → Reward model hacking: RLHF reward model captures a proxy of human
      preference; systems optimized against the proxy may find strategies
      that score well on the reward model while violating the underlying intent.
      Specification gaming. Goodhart's Law applied to AI safety.
    → Model inversion attacks: reconstruct training data from model parameters
      or outputs. Distinct from extraction (model inversion recovers specific
      data; extraction replicates model behavior).

Network Security (03):
    → eBPF security: Berkeley Packet Filter programs run in a kernel-space
      sandbox; privileged use cases (XDP, TC, kprobes, uprobes) have large
      attack surface; CVE-2021-3490 (eBPF 32-bit overflow), CVE-2021-31440
      (eBPF off-by-one); eBPF verifier bypass as kernel exploit class.
    → QUIC protocol security: UDP-based, 0-RTT resumption, connection
      migration — all create new attack surfaces; 0-RTT replay attacks;
      connection ID correlation for traffic analysis resistance; HTTP/3
      header compression (QPACK) timing attacks.
    → gRPC and protobuf security: binary format reduces visibility in
      WAF/IDS; field confusion in protobuf deserialization; gRPC server
      reflection leaks service definitions.

Cryptography (04):
    → Threshold cryptography: secret key split among N parties, requiring
      T of N to cooperate for any cryptographic operation. Removes single
      point of compromise. FROST (threshold Schnorr), ECDSA threshold
      schemes. Deployed in hardware wallets and multi-custody systems.
    → Differential cryptanalysis (Biham/Shamir 1990): foundational attack
      on block ciphers using pairs of plaintexts with specific XOR difference
      to recover key bits. DES was vulnerable (secret design criteria included
      resistance to differential cryptanalysis — designers knew); AES
      designed explicitly with differential cryptanalysis resistance.
    → Linear cryptanalysis (Matsui 1993): another foundational block cipher
      attack using linear approximations of cipher behavior. Both differential
      and linear cryptanalysis are now standard in cipher design evaluation.

Application Security (20):
    → GraphQL security: over-fetching and field-level authorization bypass;
      introspection abuse (schema disclosure); batch query amplification
      (one request fetching thousands of objects); recursive query DoS;
      query depth limiting bypass; type confusion.
    → WebSocket security: lack of same-origin policy by default; WebSocket
      hijacking via CSRF-style attacks on upgrade request; persistent
      connection state attacks; cross-site WebSocket hijacking (CSWSH).
    → Server-side template injection (SSTI): Jinja2 (Python/Flask),
      Twig (PHP/Symfony), Freemarker (Java), Smarty — template engines
      that evaluate user-supplied input as code; exploitation paths to
      RCE are well-documented per framework.

CYCLE 7 EXPANSION TARGETS:
  → Full pattern mapping for domains 57-60 (Stage 2)
  → Layered anatomy for: OPSEC failure modes; differential privacy limits;
    counter-UAS spoofing mechanics (Stage 3)
  → Taxonomy expansion: A71-A85 (attacks); D54-D62 (defenses) (Stage 4)
  → Convergence: operations research → defensive resource allocation;
    signal processing → IDS detection theory; cognitive psychology →
    security training; public administration → cybersecurity governance (Stage 5)

TOTAL DOMAIN COUNT ENTERING CYCLE 7: 60 primary, ~520 sub-domains.

ROOT MECHANIC R09 VALIDATION:
  R09: IRREVERSIBILITY AS AMPLIFIER
  Validation: confirmed as distinct root mechanic.
  Evidence: (a) implanted BCI device — standard remediation (update, replace,
  disconnect) requires surgery; (b) genetic data — once exfiltrated, cannot
  be changed; (c) biometrics — fingerprint, iris, DNA cannot be revoked once
  compromised; (d) reputation damage — once published, reputational harm from
  synthetic media cannot be fully remediated; (e) irreversible industrial
  damage — Triton targeted safety systems; uncontrolled industrial process
  can cause physical destruction that cannot be undone.
  Distinct from R08 (physical embodiment): R08 explains why systems are
  reachable via physical attack; R09 explains why compromise of certain
  systems has permanently amplified consequences.
  Status: R09 CONFIRMED. Root mechanic ledger now R01-R09.

CYCLE 7 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
