CYCLE 9 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN INVENTORY AND EXPANSION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

CUMULATIVE DOMAIN COUNT ENTERING CYCLE 9: 64 primary domains, ~570 sub-domains

NEW DOMAINS IDENTIFIED THIS CYCLE (65–78):

Domain 65: Philosophy of Computing and Dual-Use Research Ethics
  Sub-domains:
  → Dual-use dilemma: security knowledge as simultaneously defensive and
    offensive; the Collingridge dilemma applied to security research
  → Publication norms: responsible disclosure theory, coordinated disclosure
    vs. full disclosure vs. weaponization; the 90-day norm origin and critique
  → Ontology of attack: what makes something an attack vs. a feature;
    the philosophical ambiguity of intent in computing
  → Research ethics committees for security: IRB analog for offensive research;
    virtually nonexistent in practice
  → Technology determinism vs. social shaping: are security failures
    structural or contingent; implications for remediation strategy
  → Epistemic closure in security communities: how community knowledge
    boundaries create blind spots that adversaries exploit
  → Dual-use problem in AI: capability advances simultaneously enable
    defenders and attackers; asymmetry of uptake

Domain 66: Security Measurement Science and Metrics
  Sub-domains:
  → Attack surface quantification: metrics for measuring exposed area;
    attack surface minimization as formal discipline
  → Vulnerability density metrics: defects-per-KLOC, CVE density by
    software category, temporal trends in vulnerability rates
  → Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR):
    industry benchmarks, improvement trajectories, Mandiant annual reports
  → Cyber risk quantification: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)
    model; probabilistic loss event frequency × loss magnitude
  → Security posture scoring: CVSS score limitations; EPSS (Exploit
    Prediction Scoring System) as improvement; limitations of both
  → Benchmarking and red-team scoring: MITRE ATT&CK evaluation methodology;
    detection rate vs. false positive tradeoff measurement
  → Security ROI measurement: impossibility of proving a negative (prevented
    breach); alternative: cost of breach averted per dollar spent modeling
  → Patch cadence metrics: time from CVE publication to patch release;
    time from patch release to enterprise deployment; the gap as risk window

Domain 67: Graph Theory Applied to Network Security Analysis
  Sub-domains:
  → Network topology as attack graph: nodes as systems, edges as trust/
    reachability relationships; attack path enumeration as shortest-path problem
  → Centrality metrics: betweenness centrality identifies critical relay nodes;
    degree centrality identifies high-value targets; eigenvector centrality
    identifies influence nodes in trust graphs
  → Graph-based lateral movement analysis: BloodHound (Active Directory
    attack path enumeration) as applied graph theory; SharpHound collector
  → Spanning trees and minimum cut: segmentation effectiveness measured as
    minimum edge cut between attacker-controlled nodes and crown jewels
  → Community detection: clustering algorithms identify security zones;
    Louvain algorithm applied to microsegmentation design
  → Temporal graphs: network topology changes over time create attack
    windows that exist only at specific moments (scheduled access grants,
    maintenance windows, VPN sessions)
  → Hypergraph models: many-to-many relationships in cloud IAM; a single
    permission can be instantiated across thousands of resources simultaneously
  → Graph neural networks for threat detection: GNN-based anomaly detection
    on network flow graphs; detecting lateral movement as graph traversal anomaly

Domain 68: Cognitive Science and Human Attention in Security Design
  Sub-domains:
  → Alert fatigue: cognitive load theory applied to SOC analyst performance;
    Parasuraman vigilance decrement model; 22-minute sustained attention ceiling
  → Dual-process theory (Kahneman System 1/System 2): phishing exploits
    System 1 automatic processing; effective training engages System 2 deliberate
    processing; interface design can force System 2 engagement at decision points
  → Mental models and security UX: users construct incorrect mental models of
    how systems work; security UI that contradicts user mental models produces
    workarounds; mismatch between user model and actual system = attack surface
  → Confirmation bias in threat analysis: analysts anchor on initial hypothesis;
    structured analytic techniques (ACH — Analysis of Competing Hypotheses)
    as bias mitigation; red team/blue team structure as institutional debiasing
  → Decision fatigue: repeated security decisions degrade in quality; policy
    automation as fatigue mitigation; privileged access decisions degrade after
    multiple same-session approvals
  → Inattentional blindness: users fail to perceive unexpected security-relevant
    stimuli when focused on primary task; gorilla-in-the-room effect in code review
  → Cognitive tunneling: high-stress incident response narrows cognitive focus;
    runbooks and checklists compensate for tunnel vision during incidents
  → Bounded rationality in risk perception: humans are poor at evaluating
    low-probability high-impact events; security investment systematically
    underfunds rare catastrophic scenarios

Domain 69: Linguistics and Natural Language as Attack and Defense Surface
  Sub-domains:
  → Homoglyph and Unicode confusion attacks: visual similarity across character
    sets; IDN homograph attack; Punycode encoding as obfuscation layer
  → Prompt injection: natural language as instruction carrier in LLM systems;
    indirect prompt injection via document content; jailbreaking as linguistic
    manipulation; adversarial suffixes (Zou et al. 2023 universal adversarial
    attacks on aligned language models)
  → Social engineering linguistics: pretexting script design; authority and
    urgency lexical markers; commitment and consistency exploitation via language;
    Cialdini's six influence principles mapped to linguistic patterns
  → Malware naming and taxonomy confusion: inconsistent naming across vendors
    creates intelligence integration failures; MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs as
    disambiguation layer
  → Natural language processing for threat detection: NLP-based phishing
    detection; linguistic anomaly detection in email; named entity recognition
    for credential detection in logs
  → Semantic ambiguity in security policy: policy documents interpreted
    differently by humans and automated systems; ambiguity as compliance gap
  → Language model-based code generation security: LLMs trained on vulnerable
    code generate vulnerable code suggestions; GitHub Copilot security study
    (Pearce et al. 2022): 40% of generated security-relevant code snippets
    contained vulnerabilities

Domain 70: Digital Forensics and Incident Response Science
  Sub-domains:
  → Evidence preservation: order of volatility (CPU registers → RAM → swap →
    disk → remote logs); Locard's exchange principle applied to digital forensics
  → Memory forensics: Volatility framework; process injection detection;
    rootkit detection via memory artifact analysis; SMEAR (Secure Memory Erasure
    Against Rootkits)
  → Filesystem forensics: timeline analysis; MFT (Master File Table) artifact
    analysis; deleted file recovery; anti-forensics techniques (timestomping,
    slack space filling, log deletion)
  → Network forensics: full packet capture analysis; NetFlow/IPFIX analysis;
    JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprinting; DNS query forensics
  → Cloud forensics: ephemeral infrastructure challenge; CloudTrail, VPC Flow
    Logs, GuardDuty findings as primary evidence; container forensics (overlayfs
    layer analysis); serverless forensics (Lambda execution context)
  → Anti-forensics taxonomy: log wiping (Event Log cleared event 1102);
    timestomping; steganography; encrypted communications; living-off-the-land
    (LOLBins); fileless malware (in-memory only execution)
  → Chain of custody: legal admissibility requirements; write blockers; hash
    verification (MD5/SHA-256 of evidence); expert witness standards
  → DFIR automation: SOAR playbooks for automated triage; automated malware
    sandbox (Cuckoo, ANY.RUN, Joe Sandbox); automated IOC extraction

Domain 71: Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC)
  Sub-domains:
  → Regulatory frameworks: SOC 2 (AICPA trust services criteria); ISO 27001
    (ISMS standard); NIST CSF (identify/protect/detect/respond/recover);
    PCI-DSS (payment card); HIPAA (healthcare); GDPR (EU data protection);
    FedRAMP (US federal cloud); CMMC (defense industrial base)
  → Board-level cyber governance: SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules (2023);
    CISO reporting structure (reporting to CEO vs. CTO vs. board audit committee);
    cyber risk as enterprise risk management component
  → Third-party risk management (TPRM): vendor security questionnaires;
    SOC 2 Type II reports as assurance mechanism; continuous monitoring
    vs. point-in-time assessment; fourth-party risk (vendors' vendors)
  → Policy architecture: information security policy hierarchy (policy →
    standard → procedure → guideline); policy exceptions management; policy
    lifecycle (review cadence, ownership, version control)
  → Audit and assurance: internal audit vs. external audit; penetration test
    vs. vulnerability assessment; red team vs. bug bounty; scope definition
    and rules of engagement
  → Security program maturity: CMMI-derived maturity models (1-initial,
    2-managed, 3-defined, 4-quantitatively managed, 5-optimizing); BSIMM
    (Building Security In Maturity Model) for software security programs
  → Insurance and compliance interaction: cyber insurance underwriting
    questionnaires drive security control adoption; MFA requirements becoming
    standard insurance condition; insurance as de facto regulation

Domain 72: Cyber Insurance and Actuarial Risk Modeling
  Sub-domains:
  → Cyber loss event taxonomy: first-party losses (incident response, business
    interruption, data recovery, extortion payment) vs. third-party losses
    (liability, regulatory fines, notification costs)
  → Correlated loss problem: ransomware affects multiple policyholders
    simultaneously; cyber insurers face non-independent loss events (unlike
    auto accidents); systemic risk concentration; CNA Financial ransomware
    ($60M+ loss, 2021) as correlated event driver
  → Data sparsity problem: cyber actuarial tables lack sufficient historical
    data; events are rare and underreported; loss magnitudes are heavy-tailed;
    Black Swan properties of catastrophic cyber events
  → Moral hazard: insurance coverage may reduce security investment incentives;
    ransomware payment coverage may incentivize ransomware actors; policy
    design to mitigate (deductibles, coverage conditions requiring MFA)
  → Adverse selection: highest-risk organizations most motivated to purchase
    insurance; self-selection bias in cyber insurance pool; questionnaire-based
    underwriting attempts to correct
  → Aggregation risk: Lloyd's of London cyber market analysis (2022): a major
    attack on US financial infrastructure could generate $3.5T in losses,
    exceeding all global cyber insurance capacity
  → Exclusions and disputes: NotPetya attribution to Russian state actors
    triggered war exclusions; Mondelez vs. Zurich ($100M claim dispute);
    Lloyd's 2023 state-backed cyber attack exclusion mandate
  → Parametric cyber insurance: payment triggered by measurable event
    (data breach confirmed above threshold) rather than demonstrated loss;
    reduces moral hazard and speeds claims resolution

Domain 73: International Cyber Law and Attribution Norms
  Sub-domains:
  → Tallinn Manual: NATO CCDCOE-commissioned expert analysis of international
    law applied to cyber operations; Tallinn Manual 2.0 (2017) covers peacetime
    operations; Rule 69: sovereignty applies in cyberspace; Rule 11: threshold
    for armed attack in cyberspace
  → Attribution problem: technical attribution (IP, malware, infrastructure)
    is insufficient for legal/diplomatic attribution; intelligence attribution
    adds intent and actor identification; political attribution adds willingness
    to publicly accuse; all three required for formal state attribution
  → State responsibility: attribution of non-state cyber actor operations
    to states; effective control vs. overall control standards from Nicaragua
    and Tadic cases; outsourcing attacks to criminal proxies as deniability strategy
  → Countermeasures and retorsion: lawful responses to internationally wrongful
    cyber acts; proportionality requirement; attribution prerequisite; Stuxnet
    as case study in undeclared cyber operation
  → Cyber norms development: UN GGE (Group of Governmental Experts) consensus
    norms (2013, 2015, 2021); OEWG (Open-Ended Working Group) parallel process;
    China/Russia vs. Western nations divide on norm content
  → Sovereignty and jurisdiction: data localization laws; cloud data jurisdiction;
    US CLOUD Act (government access to data held by US companies abroad); GDPR
    extraterritorial application
  → Cyber espionage vs. attack: espionage (gathering intelligence) is not
    prohibited by international law even in cyber form; crossing to attack
    (causing physical effects or data destruction) changes legal status;
    OPM breach (2015): China's position was intelligence operation, not attack

Domain 74: Organizational Psychology and Security Culture
  Sub-domains:
  → Schein's organizational culture model applied to security: artifacts
    (visible security practices), espoused values (stated security policy),
    basic assumptions (implicit beliefs about security importance); security
    culture change requires addressing all three levels
  → Psychological safety and security reporting: Edmondson's psychological
    safety research; employees in low-psychological-safety environments
    underreport security incidents; fear of blame = underreporting = delayed detection
  → Security champions program: distributed security advocates in development
    teams; sociological function (norm carrier) as important as technical function
    (skill carrier); champion as bridging actor between security and development
    communities
  → Normalization of deviance: Diane Vaughan's analysis of Challenger disaster
    applied to security; gradual acceptance of security shortcuts as normal;
    security debt accumulation as normalization of deviance process
  → Situational crime prevention applied to insider threat: Clarke's 25
    techniques of situational crime prevention; opportunity reduction,
    natural surveillance, formal surveillance, rule setting; environmental
    design to reduce insider opportunity
  → Trust calibration in teams: security decisions require trusting systems,
    processes, and people; over-trust = vulnerability; under-trust = friction
    and workarounds; trust calibration as security design problem
  → Security leadership and CISO role sociology: CISO structural position
    (reporting line, board access); political capital accumulation and spending;
    CISO tenure average 2.5 years; burnout and liability exposure as
    systemic cultural problem

Domain 75: Election Infrastructure and Democratic Process Security
  Sub-domains:
  → Voting system taxonomy: DRE (Direct Recording Electronic) without paper;
    optical scan with paper ballot; hand-marked paper with electronic tabulator;
    security properties of each; VVPAT (Voter Verified Paper Audit Trail)
  → Election system certification: EAC (Election Assistance Commission) VVSG
    (Voluntary Voting System Guidelines); CISA role in election security;
    voluntary nature of federal guidance; state-level variation
  → Influence operations: IRA (Internet Research Agency) 2016 operation;
    computational propaganda (automated amplification); narrative laundering
    (fringe → mainstream pipeline); sockpuppet networks; coordinated inauthentic
    behavior detection by platforms
  → Voter registration database security: centralized state databases as
    high-value targets; 2016 Russian access to Illinois voter rolls; deletion
    or modification attacks vs. exfiltration attacks
  → Misinformation and disinformation taxonomy: malinformation (true but
    harmful), misinformation (false but not intentional), disinformation
    (false and intentional); election interference as information operation
  → Chain of custody for ballots: physical security of paper ballots; seal
    log integrity; canvassing and certification processes; post-election
    auditing (risk-limiting audits as statistical gold standard)
  → Foreign interference norms: violation of sovereignty norm; US Executive
    Order 13848 election interference sanctions framework; deterrence failure
    in 2016, 2020 cycles

Domain 76: Threat Intelligence and Attribution Science
  Sub-domains:
  → Intelligence cycle applied to cyber: direction → collection → processing →
    analysis → dissemination → feedback; each phase has failure modes
  → Indicator taxonomy: IOCs (Indicators of Compromise: hashes, IPs, domains);
    TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures — more durable, harder to change);
    Pyramid of Pain (David Bianco): hash → IP → domain → network/host artifacts
    → tools → TTPs; defender effort required to make IOC useless increases
    up the pyramid
  → Attribution methodology: Diamond Model (adversary, infrastructure,
    capability, victim); clustering by shared infrastructure, code, victimology,
    tradecraft; TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) for intelligence sharing classification
  → False flag operations: Lazarus Group's Olympic Destroyer malware (2018
    Winter Olympics) planted Russian-language artifacts; Cozy Bear/Fancy Bear
    distinctions; adversary simulation of other nation's TTPs to complicate attribution
  → ISACs and ISAOs: Information Sharing and Analysis Centers by sector
    (FS-ISAC, H-ISAC, E-ISAC, WaterISAC); bidirectional sharing model;
    trust and legal liability barriers to sharing; anonymization requirements
  → STIX/TAXII standards: Structured Threat Information eXpression;
    Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information; machine-readable
    threat intelligence interchange; OpenCTI, MISP as open-source platforms
  → Strategic vs. operational vs. tactical intelligence: strategic (who,
    what sector, geopolitical context); operational (campaigns, tooling
    evolution); tactical (specific IOCs for immediate blocking)

Domain 77: Security of Critical Infrastructure Control Systems (Deeper Treatment)
  Sub-domains beyond ICS/SCADA previously covered:
  → Water and wastewater system security: Oldsmar, Florida (2021) SCADA attack
    attempt via remote access tool; chlorine dosing as attack vector;
    HMI internet exposure as systemic problem; EPA water sector rule (2024)
    requiring risk assessments (subsequently challenged)
  → Aviation cybersecurity: ACARS (Aircraft Communications Addressing
    and Reporting System) security; ADS-B spoofing and jamming; inflight
    entertainment network isolation from avionics; FAA cybersecurity
    requirements for aircraft certification (DO-326A standard)
  → Maritime cybersecurity: BIMCO maritime cyber risk management guidelines;
    AIS (Automatic Identification System) spoofing; GPS jamming of maritime
    navigation; port terminal operating system attacks (2017 NotPetya
    Maersk impact: $300M, 17 terminals disrupted)
  → Nuclear facility security: NRC cybersecurity regulations (10 CFR 73.54);
    defense-in-depth principle; safety system isolation requirements;
    IAEA nuclear security series; Stuxnet as template for nuclear facility attack
  → Financial market infrastructure: exchange and clearinghouse resilience;
    SWIFT messaging network security (2016 Bangladesh Bank heist: $81M via
    fraudulent SWIFT messages); CLS (Continuous Linked Settlement) concentration risk
  → Telecommunications backbone: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) security;
    SS7 signaling system vulnerabilities; internet exchange point (IXP) security;
    submarine cable infrastructure vulnerability (physical and logical)

Domain 78: Autonomous Systems and Robotics Security
  Sub-domains:
  → Robot Operating System (ROS) security: ROS 1 default no-authentication;
    ROS 2 DDS (Data Distribution Service) security plugins; unauthenticated

  → Drone/UAV security beyond counter-UAS: onboard flight controller

    GPS spoofing for trajectory manipulation; swarm coordination protocol

  → Autonomous vehicle security (deeper): CAN bus injection in self-driving

    V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything) communication security; DSRC vs. C-V2X protocols
  → Industrial robot manipulation: ABB robot arm firmware vulnerabilities;

  → Warehouse automation security: Amazon Kiva/Proteus robot network;
    conveyor system SCADA; inventory manipulation via system compromise;

  → Medical robotics: Da Vinci surgical robot teleoperation security;

CYCLE 9 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PATTERN 9.1: THE MEASUREMENT PARADOX — SECURITY CANNOT MEASURE WHAT IT PREVENTS

FORM A (Finding + Confidence + Timeline):
  Finding: Security investment is systematically underfunded because the primary
  output of security — prevented breaches — produces no observable signal.
  Prevented attacks leave no artifact. Security programs that prevent 100%
  of attacks appear identical to security programs that simply have not been
  attacked yet. This measurement impossibility creates a structural funding
  pathology: security can demonstrate value only when it fails (a breach
  occurred, the response worked) or through proxy metrics (vulnerability count
  reduced, patch time improved) that do not map linearly to actual risk
  reduction. The result is that security ROI arguments are made with fabricated
  precision (FAIR model outputs carry false confidence intervals) while the
  actual relationship between security spend and breach probability remains
  unknown. Adversaries exploit this measurement gap: they understand defender
  capability better than defenders do, because defenders cannot observe their
  own prevention rate while adversaries observe their own success rate.

Past instances:
  → Every organization that has invested heavily in security and not been
    breached cannot attribute non-breach to security investment vs. not being
    targeted vs. being breached and not detecting it
  → Target breach (2013): security team received alerts from FireEye malware
    detection system; alerts were not acted on; the measurement of alerts
    was present but the measurement of whether alerts → response was absent
  → Cyber insurance underwriting: insurers consistently underprice cyber
    risk because loss data is sparse, underreported, and non-actuarially
    tractable; systematic mispricing persists for years
  → US federal cybersecurity: OMB Cybersecurity Crosscutting Priority Areas
    (2020): "Measuring agency cybersecurity posture is extremely difficult";
    FISMA compliance scores do not correlate with actual breach rates

Confidence: HIGH (0.92)
  Timeline: Structural — this paradox has existed since the beginning of
  computing security; resolution requires either mandatory breach reporting
  (allows base-rate calculation) or advances in cyber risk quantification
  methodology; partial resolution expected 2028-2035 as breach reporting
  regulations mature globally

FORM B (Research Prompt):
  "What measurable proxy metrics most strongly correlate with actual breach
  probability reduction? Which organizational security behaviors have the
  highest empirical support for risk reduction? What does cyber insurance
  loss data reveal about which controls actually matter when controlling for
  industry and size? Can survival analysis methods (time-to-breach) be applied
  to organizational security posture data to establish empirical control
  effectiveness?"

PATTERN 9.2: THE REGULATORY RATCHET — COMPLIANCE FRAMEWORKS AS SECURITY FLOOR
  THAT BECOMES SECURITY CEILING

FORM A (Finding + Confidence + Timeline):
  Finding: Regulatory compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOX, ISO 27001,
  FedRAMP) were designed as minimum baselines. In practice, they become
  effective ceilings. Organizations achieve compliance certification, declare
  the security problem addressed, and divert security resources to other
  priorities. The compliance-as-ceiling effect is strongest in regulated
  industries where compliance is externally verifiable and security outcomes
  are not — finance, healthcare, defense. The adversarial consequence is
  predictable: sophisticated threat actors study compliance frameworks to
  identify the exact controls that are required, understand the precise
  boundaries of what is certified, and attack in the gaps between what
  the framework specifies and what actual security requires. PCI-DSS scope
  limitation is the canonical example: organizations scope-reduce their
  cardholder data environment to minimize compliance cost, creating segmentation
  that adversaries pivot around rather than through.

Past instances:
  → Target (2013): PCI-DSS compliant at time of breach; compliance framework
    did not require network segmentation between HVAC vendor network and POS
    systems; adversary used exact gap
  → Equifax (2017): SOX-compliant; STRUTS vulnerability unpatched for 78 days
    after patch available; compliance did not require patch within specific
    timeframe for that system; adversary used exact gap
  → Healthcare sector: HIPAA-compliant organizations routinely breached;
    HIPAA does not specify technical controls precisely; "reasonable and
    appropriate" standard leaves exploitable implementation gaps
  → Financial sector: GLBA, SOX, FFIEC compliance widespread; financial
    sector also highest-value target with most sophisticated adversaries;
    compliance has not prevented high-profile breaches

Trajectory: Regulatory frameworks are becoming more prescriptive
  (SEC cybersecurity rules 2023, CMMC L2/L3 control specificity) as
  regulators recognize the floor-becomes-ceiling problem. This drives
  compliance cost up and adversary adaptation accordingly.

Future prediction: By 2027, prescriptive regulations will drive security
  homogenization across regulated sectors, creating monoculture conditions
  where a single technique defeats all compliant organizations simultaneously.
  Diversity of security controls (currently a defensive property) will be
  actively suppressed by standardization requirements.

Confidence: HIGH (0.87)
  Timeline: Homogenization effect visible in 3-5 years; first major
  exploitation of regulatory monoculture: 2027-2030

FORM B (Research Prompt):
  "What is the empirical relationship between compliance certification and
  breach rate by sector? Does ISO 27001 certification reduce breach probability?
  Does PCI-DSS certification reduce payment card compromise? Are there sectors
  where compliance correlates positively with security outcomes, and what
  distinguishes those sectors? What regulatory design features prevent
  floor-becomes-ceiling dynamics?"

PATTERN 9.3: LINGUISTIC ATTACK SURFACE EXPANSION — NATURAL LANGUAGE AS CODE

FORM A (Finding + Confidence + Timeline):
  Finding: The introduction of LLMs as system components converts natural
  language — previously a human-to-human medium — into an executable instruction
  channel. This creates an entirely new attack surface class: prompt injection.
  Unlike traditional injection attacks (SQL, command, LDAP), prompt injection
  has no formal grammar and no syntactic parser to constrain — the LLM's
  semantic understanding is both the vulnerability and the only possible
  defense. Natural language is unboundedly expressive and semantically
  ambiguous, making injection detection fundamentally harder than detecting
  SQL injection or command injection. Indirect prompt injection — where
  attacker-controlled content (a webpage, a document, an email) is processed
  by an LLM agent — requires no direct interaction with the victim system.
  The attacker injects via any content the agent reads.

Past instances:
  → Greshake et al. 2023: "Not What You Signed Up For" — demonstrated
    indirect prompt injection via web content retrieved by LLM agents;
    data exfiltration, persistence via memory poisoning
  → Kevin Liu (2022): New Bing system prompt extraction via "ignore previous
    instructions" injection; Microsoft Copilot system prompt leaked via user
    prompt engineering
  → ChatGPT plugin injection (2023): malicious content in PDF or webpage
    retrieved by ChatGPT plugin caused plugin to execute attacker instructions
  → GitHub Copilot context poisoning: poisoned code in training data or
    context window causes Copilot to suggest vulnerable code patterns
  → Perez & Ribeiro 2022: demonstrated prompt injection against GPT-3
    based applications using natural language overrides

Trajectory: Attack surface grows proportionally with LLM deployment breadth.
  Every new agentic capability (email reading, web browsing, code execution,
  API calling) is a new indirect injection vector. Defense (input sanitization,
  output validation, privilege separation) lags deployment by 18-36 months.

Future prediction: By 2026, indirect prompt injection will be a confirmed
  attack vector in at least one high-profile enterprise breach involving
  an LLM-based copilot or agent with access to production systems.
  By 2028, prompt injection will be listed in OWASP Top 10.

Confidence: HIGH (0.91)
  Timeline: First confirmed enterprise breach via indirect prompt injection:
  2025-2026; OWASP Top 10 inclusion: 2027-2028

FORM B (Research Prompt):
  "What technical controls are effective against indirect prompt injection?
  Can LLM outputs be reliably parsed to detect injection success? Does
  privilege separation (LLM agent with read-only access, separate privileged
  executor that validates LLM output against policy) reduce injection impact?
  What is the relationship between LLM reasoning capability and susceptibility
  to prompt injection — do more capable models have better or worse injection
  resistance?"

PATTERN 9.4: INSURANCE MARKET DYNAMICS AS UNINTENDED SECURITY INFRASTRUCTURE

FORM A (Finding + Confidence + Timeline):
  Finding: The cyber insurance market has become, inadvertently, the most
  powerful force driving security control adoption in SME and mid-market
  organizations — more powerful than regulation, more powerful than
  vendor marketing, and more powerful than CISO advocacy. This is because
  cyber insurance underwriting questionnaires are binary: MFA implemented
  or not. Backup tested or not. EDR deployed or not. Failure to meet
  underwriting conditions results in coverage denial or 10x premium increase.
  The financial consequence is immediate and concrete — unlike breach risk,
  which is abstract and probabilistic. The insurance market has thus solved
  the measurement paradox (Pattern 9.1) through market mechanism: insurers
  accept proxy metrics because they are the only available data, and
  organizations adopt controls because insurers require them. The adversarial
  implication: insurance requirements define the floor of controls that
  all insured organizations share. Adversaries who study insurance underwriting
  criteria know exactly what controls they will always face and can optimize
  attacks for the gaps above that floor.

Past instances:
  → MFA adoption acceleration post-2020: cyber insurance MFA requirements
    drove measurable MFA adoption in sectors that had previously resisted;
    Colonial Pipeline (2021) legacy VPN without MFA would not pass 2022
    underwriting; this configuration is now largely gone in insured organizations
  → Ransomware payment coverage removal: several major insurers stopped
    covering ransomware payments (AXA France, 2021); organizations in AXA
    France portfolio forced to develop decryption and recovery capabilities
    rather than payment fallback
  → Lloyd's state-actor exclusion (2023): mandatory exclusion of losses
    from state-backed cyber attacks; organizations must now assess whether
    incident attribution affects coverage; attribution uncertainty creates
    claim dispute risk
  → SME security improvement: Marsh McLennan data shows SMEs with cyber
    insurance have measurably better security posture than uninsured SMEs
    of equivalent size (2022 Global Insurance Report)

Confidence: HIGH (0.88)
  Timeline: Insurance-driven security baseline will become the de facto
  minimum security standard for all organizations purchasing coverage;
  coverage denial will become more common as attack frequency rises
  faster than premium increases; uninsurable organizations will emerge
  as a new risk category by 2028

FORM B (Research Prompt):
  "What controls does cyber insurance underwriting require across major
  insurers (Chubb, AIG, Beazley, Coalition, Cowbell)? How well do those
  controls predict breach outcomes? Are there gaps between what insurers
  require and what actually reduces breach probability? Is the insurance
  market converging on an evidence-based control set or on a consensus
  control set that merely satisfies auditor checklists?"

CYCLE 9 — STAGE 3: LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ANATOMY 9.A: THE MEASUREMENT PARADOX (Pattern 9.1) — 5-LAYER ANALYSIS

LAYER 1: SURFACE
  What is observable: Security teams produce dashboards of vulnerability counts,
  patch compliance rates, mean time to detect, and mean time to respond.
  Leadership receives reports with numbers and graphs. Budget requests cite
  industry benchmarks and threat reports. Breach announcements attribute failure
  to specific gaps. The appearance of measurement is pervasive; actual
  measurement of security effectiveness is absent.

LAYER 2: TECHNICAL
  The measurement problem has a precise technical statement: security is a
  counterfactual claim (a breach that did not occur cannot be observed) about
  a low-base-rate event (major breaches are rare per organization per year)
  with high variance (breach severity ranges from trivial to catastrophic)
  and heavy right-tail distribution (a small number of events account for
  most aggregate loss). Classical statistical inference requires large samples
  of iid observations; breach events are neither large-sample nor independent
  nor identically distributed. The metrics that can be measured (vulnerability
  count, patch time) have poorly characterized relationships to the outcome of
  interest (breach probability). This is not a data collection problem; it is
  a structural statistical problem with no solution at the single-organization
  level.

LAYER 3: STRUCTURAL
  The measurement paradox creates organizational dynamics that are harmful
  independently of any individual's choices:
  → Security teams optimize for measurable proxies rather than unmeasurable
    outcomes (Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases
    to be a good measure)
  → Security investment decisions are made by comparing concrete costs to
    abstract risks; under uncertainty, concrete costs dominate
  → Security programs that prevent breaches are indistinguishable from
    security programs that simply haven't been attacked; career incentives
    for security leaders are perverse — the best security leaders are
    invisible until a breach demonstrates the absence of what they built
  → Audit functions measure compliance with explicit controls because
    controls are measurable; security outcomes are not auditable; audit
    drives control implementation, not security improvement
  → Vendor claims about product effectiveness are unverifiable at point
    of sale; the security product market is a market for lemons
    (Akerlof's lemon problem: information asymmetry between sellers
    and buyers collapses market quality)

LAYER 4: CROSS-DOMAIN
  The measurement paradox appears identically in:
  → Public health prevention programs: the benefit of not getting sick from
    a prevented epidemic is invisible; vaccination skepticism exploits the
    invisibility of prevented harm; herd immunity is a counterfactual
  → Nuclear deterrence: deterrence works by preventing wars that therefore
    never occur; effectiveness measurement is impossible; investment
    decisions are made on theoretical models not empirical data
  → Structural engineering: the value of over-engineering against rare
    extreme events (earthquake, hurricane) is invisible until the event
    occurs; buildings that never fall cannot demonstrate their resilience
  → Fire suppression: the value of sprinkler systems is measured by fires
    that did not spread, not fires that were prevented; organizations
    that have never had fires remove sprinkler systems as cost reduction
  → Drug prevention programs: the DARE program operated for decades
    without evidence of effectiveness; evaluated only when outcomes
    were measured, found no effect; measurement absence enabled 
    ineffective program persistence

Cross-domain transfer: The public health literature has developed
  statistical techniques for estimating prevented outcomes (counterfactual
  modeling, synthetic control methods, interrupted time series analysis).
  These have never been systematically applied to cybersecurity. The
  absence of this transfer is a research gap.

LAYER 5: ROOT
  Root mechanic: R03 (Trust without verification) operating at the
  institutional level. Security programs are trusted to be effective because
  no mechanism exists to verify their effectiveness. The entire security
  industry operates on unverifiable trust: trust in vendor product claims,
  trust in framework compliance as a proxy for security, trust in CISO
  assurances, trust in audit findings. The measurement paradox is not
  primarily a statistical problem; it is R03 at organizational and
  industry scale.

ANATOMY 9.B: LINGUISTIC ATTACK SURFACE EXPANSION (Pattern 9.3) — 5-LAYER ANALYSIS

LAYER 1: SURFACE
  What is observable: AI assistants receive instructions from users and
  sometimes behave in unexpected ways. System prompts can sometimes be
  extracted by users. Chatbots can be made to produce outputs that violate
  their stated guidelines. AI coding assistants suggest code that contains
  vulnerabilities. These surface observations are widely reported but
  not systematically understood.

LAYER 2: TECHNICAL
  Prompt injection operates at the interface between natural language
  and computation:
  → LLMs have no syntactic boundary between instruction and data; SQL
    parsers enforce a grammar that separates query structure from
    string literals; LLMs have no equivalent grammar
  → Instruction following is trained behavior, not a hard constraint;
    conflicting instructions (system prompt vs. injected instruction)
    are resolved by training-encoded priority heuristics that can be
    overridden by carefully crafted context
  → Context window content is treated uniformly — system prompt, user
    message, retrieved document, function return value all exist in
    the same token space with the same weight
  → Semantic similarity is the primary mechanism: if injected text
    resembles training examples where the model followed instructions,
    the model will follow the injected instructions
  → Indirect injection expands the attack surface to any content the
    model processes: web pages, documents, emails, code comments,
    database content, API responses — all are potential injection vectors

LAYER 3: STRUCTURAL
  The linguistic attack surface creates structural security problems:
  → Defense requires semantic understanding of intent, which is the same
    capability that makes the model useful; there is no analog to
    parameterized queries that separates instruction from data
    at the type level
  → Input validation is intractable: any natural language input could
    be either a legitimate user request or an injection; the model
    must process the input to determine which; by the time determination
    occurs, injection has been processed
  → Multi-step agentic systems compound injection: a single injected
    instruction early in an agent's context can influence all
    subsequent steps; there is no transaction rollback
  → Privilege escalation via injection: agents with tool access (email
    sending, database writing, API calling) can be directed by injection
    to exercise those capabilities on behalf of the attacker

LAYER 4: CROSS-DOMAIN
  The prompt injection problem maps to:
  → Social engineering at machine speed: prompt injection is phishing
    for AI agents; the mechanism is identical (trusted context
    manipulated to execute attacker instruction) but operates
    at machine speed without fatigue
  → Signal spoofing in control systems: a sensor that returns attacker-
    controlled data causes the controller to act on false input;
    prompt injection via retrieved content is sensor spoofing for LLMs
  → Law and contract interpretation: ambiguous contract language
    is resolved by courts according to context and intent; adversarial
    parties draft ambiguous language deliberately; prompt injection
    exploits the same semantic ambiguity that adversarial contract
    drafters exploit
  → Propaganda and framing effects: context presented before a message
    changes how the message is interpreted (framing effect); prompt
    injection uses framing to change how subsequent instructions
    are interpreted by the model

LAYER 5: ROOT
  Root mechanics: R02 (Data/instruction conflation in shared medium)
  and R06 (Trusted entity as confused deputy). The LLM's context window
  is a shared medium where data (retrieved content) and instructions
  (system prompt, user queries) coexist without syntactic separation —
  R02. When an LLM agent takes action (sends email, calls API) based on
  injected instructions, it acts as the confused deputy — exercising
  legitimate capabilities on behalf of an attacker who has no direct
  access to those capabilities — R06. Prompt injection is the
  intersection of R02 and R06 in a new computational substrate.

ANATOMY 9.C: INSURANCE MARKET AS UNINTENDED SECURITY INFRASTRUCTURE
  (Pattern 9.4) — 5-LAYER ANALYSIS

LAYER 1: SURFACE
  What is observable: cyber insurance applications ask about MFA, EDR,
  backup, patch management, and email filtering. Organizations that answer
  "no" to required controls face coverage denial or premium increases.
  CISO teams now include "insurance compliance" as a security program
  workstream. Ransomware payments are sometimes covered; sometimes not;
  the ambiguity creates post-breach disputes. War exclusions are expanding.

LAYER 2: TECHNICAL
  Insurance as security driver operates through actuarial signal:
  → Insurers aggregate loss data across policyholders; controls that
    correlate with lower loss ratios become underwriting requirements
  → The signal is noisy (sample sizes are small, selection bias is strong,
    causality is confounded) but the direction is correct — insurers
    who require wrong controls lose money and exit the market
  → Controls that are easy to fake (a VPN that exists but is never used)
    do not reduce insurer loss ratios and are eventually removed from
    requirements; controls that are hard to fake and actually prevent
    losses persist as requirements
  → Insurance creates a financial model for security investment: premium
    savings justify control cost; organizations with worse posture
    pay higher premiums; the cost differential funds the control

LAYER 3: STRUCTURAL
  Insurance-driven security creates systemic properties:
  → Convergence: all insured organizations implement the same control set;
    diversity (a defensive property) is suppressed
  → Minimum viable security: organizations implement exactly what is
    required for insurance; controls beyond the minimum are
    under-incentivized unless they also reduce premiums
  → Adverse selection equilibrium disruption: ransomware frequency
    caused insurer losses; insurers raised premiums; worst-risk
    organizations dropped coverage; remaining pool improved;
    ransomware frequency against insured organizations declined
    from 2020-2022; this demonstrates insurance market as
    feedback mechanism for security outcomes
  → Systemic risk concentration: if a single control required by
    all insurers fails (a zero-day in a universally-deployed EDR),
    all insured organizations are simultaneously vulnerable;
    insurance requirements create correlated exposure

LAYER 4: CROSS-DOMAIN
  Insurance as de facto regulation appears in:
  → Building codes: fire insurance requirements drove adoption of fire
    codes before government mandates; Factory Mutual Insurance (FM Global)
    created fire protection standards that became NFPA codes
  → Vehicle safety: insurers surcharge vehicles without safety features;
    IIHS (Insurance Institute for Highway Safety) ratings drive
    manufacturer safety improvements; insurance-driven standards
    often exceed regulatory minimums
  → Environmental liability: pollution insurance requirements drove
    environmental due diligence in commercial real estate; Phase I
    and II environmental assessments originated as insurance requirements
  → Food safety: product liability insurance requirements for food
    manufacturers drove HACCP adoption before FDA mandate
  → Healthcare: malpractice insurance requirements drive clinical
    practice standards (defensive medicine) independently of
    medical evidence; both positive (safety checklists) and
    negative (unnecessary testing) consequences

LAYER 5: ROOT
  Root mechanic: This is not primarily an attack pattern; it is a
  defense mechanism that exploits R03 dynamics. Insurance works by
  creating a verification mechanism (underwriting questionnaire,
  policy condition audit) for controls that were previously
  unverified (security posture claims). Insurance thus partially
  addresses R03 — trust without verification — by creating financial
  consequences for unverified trust. The systemic risk it creates
  (convergence, monoculture) introduces new R01 dynamics: when all
  organizations share the same control set, the boundary between
  the protected zone and the attack zone is defined by that
  control set, and a single boundary failure affects all zones
  simultaneously.

════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CYCLE 9 — STAGE 4: ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY (PART A — ATTACKS A84–A92)
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A84: XML EXTERNAL ENTITY (XXE) INJECTION
  Class: Injection / Server-Side Request Forgery
  Mechanism: XML parsers that process external entity declarations can be
  directed to fetch resources from arbitrary URIs. An attacker crafts an
  XML document with a malicious DOCTYPE containing an external entity
  reference to a sensitive local file (file:///etc/passwd) or internal
  network resource (http://169.254.169.254/). When the parser processes
  the document and resolves the entity, the content of the referenced
  resource is embedded in the parsed output and returned to the attacker.
  Blind XXE uses out-of-band channels (DNS lookup to attacker-controlled
  domain) when direct response reflection is absent.
  Historical instances:
  → 2014 Facebook XXE vulnerability: allowed reading arbitrary files
    from Facebook servers via XML parsing of PPTX file upload
  → PayPal XXE (2017): XXE via XML parser in data export feature
  → GoAhead web server (CVE-2017-17562): XXE in embedded HTTP server
    affecting millions of IoT devices
  Prerequisites: XML parser with external entity processing enabled (FEATURE_EXTERNAL_GENERAL_ENTITIES); 
  attacker-controlled XML input accepted by application
  Indicators: HTTP requests from server to internal resources or 
  attacker-controlled servers; access to file:// URIs in server logs
  Mitigations: Disable external entity processing (set FEATURE_EXTERNAL_GENERAL_ENTITIES to false); use SAX parser over DOM; whitelist XML schema; WAF XXE rule sets
  Gaps: XXE in PDF parsing, Office document parsing, SAML processing
  remains common in enterprise applications; parser default settings
  in many languages still enable external entities

A85: CACHE POISONING ATTACKS
  Class: Web Cache Manipulation / Man-in-the-Middle
  Mechanism: Web caches (CDN edge nodes, reverse proxies, browser caches)
  key cached responses on a subset of request attributes. Attackers identify
  "unkeyed" inputs — HTTP headers, query parameters — that influence the
  response content but are not included in the cache key. By including a
  malicious payload in an unkeyed input, the attacker causes a poisoned
  response to be cached under a key that other users will hit. Web cache
  deception: attacker tricks victim into making a request that causes
  private content to be cached under a public key.
  Historical instances:
  → James Kettle (PortSwigger) 2018 research: demonstrated cache poisoning
    against multiple major CDN configurations; Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly
    caching headers found to create poisoning opportunities
  → DoD infrastructure: cache poisoning demonstration against US government
    CDN configuration via X-Forwarded-Host header injection
  → Web cache deception: Omer Gil (2017) research demonstrating caching
    of authenticated user content via path confusion (/account/profile.css)
  Prerequisites: CDN or reverse proxy with unkeyed header processing; 
  attacker ability to inject headers; cached response reflected to other users
  Indicators: Anomalous cache-hit ratios; responses with unexpected content
  from CDN edge; X-Cache-Status header analysis
  Mitigations: Normalize cache keys to include security-relevant headers; 
  configure CDN to key on all user-controllable inputs; cache-control
  headers on authenticated responses; CDN header normalization
  Gaps: API gateway caching introduces new cache poisoning surfaces;
  GraphQL caching is poorly understood and frequently misconfigured

A86: CORS (CROSS-ORIGIN RESOURCE SHARING) MISCONFIGURATION
  Class: Access Control / Web Application
  Mechanism: CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin, 
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials) configure which cross-origin requests
  browsers will allow. Misconfiguration includes: reflecting the Origin header
  without validation (any origin can make authenticated requests); using
  wildcard (*) with credentials; accepting null origin (allows sandbox iframe
  requests). Attacker creates a malicious site that makes cross-origin
  requests to the target API; misconfigured CORS causes the browser to
  include victim credentials and return the response to the attacker.
  Historical instances:
  → Numerous bug bounty reports on HackerOne/Bugcrowd: CORS misconfiguration
    is among top 10 most reported web vulnerabilities
  → Portswigger Web Security Academy research: "CORS misconfiguration is
    rampant" — majority of production applications have at least one
    exploitable CORS misconfiguration
  → Multiple financial services CORS vulnerabilities allowed full account
    takeover via authenticated API access from attacker-controlled origin
  Prerequisites: API endpoint with sensitive data or state-changing operations;
  CORS misconfiguration allowing arbitrary origin with credentials
  Indicators: Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflecting request Origin header;
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with non-null, non-specific origin
  Mitigations: Whitelist specific allowed origins; never reflect Origin without
  validation; use null origin carefully; validate CORS configuration
  in code review and automated scanning
  Gaps: SPA (Single Page Application) architecture increases CORS 
  misconfiguration frequency; microservice architectures create complex
  CORS trust relationships that are difficult to audit holistically

A87: CREDENTIAL STUFFING
  Class: Authentication Abuse / Automated Attack
  Mechanism: Attackers obtain username/password pairs from prior data breaches
  (available on dark web markets and paste sites). Automated tools (SentryMBA,
  STORM, BlackBullet, OpenBullet) submit credential pairs against target
  authentication endpoints at high volume. Credential reuse rates across
  sites are approximately 15-25% (Florencio & Herley research). Success
  rate per credential pair against any given target: approximately 0.1-2%.
  At millions of credential pairs, absolute account takeover volume is high.
  Historical instances:
  → DraftKings (2022): credential stuffing attack compromised ~68,000 accounts;
    approximately $300,000 drained from accounts
  → Dunkin' Donuts (2019): credential stuffing against DD Perks rewards program;
    points harvested and sold
  → Spotify (2020): 380 million credential pairs tested; approximately 300,000
    accounts compromised
  → Okta (ongoing): credential stuffing against identity provider amplifies
    blast radius across all downstream applications
  Prerequisites: Large credential database from prior breach; target with
  password reuse; automation infrastructure; IP rotation or proxy network
  Indicators: Authentication failure rate spike from multiple IPs; 
  geographically impossible login sequences; velocity anomalies at 
  authentication endpoint; device fingerprint anomalies on successful login
  Mitigations: MFA (renders credentials alone insufficient); credential
  breach monitoring (HaveIBeenPwned API, SpyCloud); device fingerprinting
  on authentication; CAPTCHA on login; rate limiting; velocity rules;
  impossible travel detection
  Gaps: MFA bypass via AiTM (A72) addresses MFA mitigation; passkeys
  (FIDO2) are the only truly credential-stuffing-immune authentication;
  passkey adoption is currently <5% of consumer-facing applications

A88: ACCOUNT TAKEOVER VIA SIM SWAPPING
  Class: Authentication Bypass / Social Engineering / Telecom Exploitation
  Mechanism: Attacker social engineers or bribes telecom carrier employee
  to transfer victim's phone number to attacker-controlled SIM card.
  Once the phone number is controlled, SMS-based 2FA is bypassed: password
  resets and 2FA codes go to the attacker. The telecom employee is the
  confused deputy (R06): they have legitimate authority to transfer numbers
  and are manipulated into doing so for the attacker. Insider threat vector:
  some SIM swaps involve corrupt telecom employees accepting payment.
  Historical instances:
  → Michael Terpin vs. AT&T (2018): $24M in cryptocurrency stolen via SIM
    swap; $224M lawsuit (partially successful)
  → Twitter account takeovers (2020): high-profile accounts (Obama, Biden,
    Musk, Apple, Uber) compromised via insider social engineering at Twitter;
    SIM swap used as credential theft vector in parallel campaigns
  → T-Mobile SIM swap insider ring (2023): multiple T-Mobile employees
    paid by criminal network to perform SIM swaps; FBI investigation
  → OG account theft community: Comm/Scattered Spider crew used SIM swapping
    to steal cryptocurrency and social media accounts systematically
  Prerequisites: Victim's phone number known; victim uses SMS-based 2FA;
  telecom social engineering or insider access; victim's email or account
  recovery uses phone number
  Indicators: Sudden loss of cellular service (victim-side); unexpected
  SMS or login notifications; carrier port-out confirmation messages
  Mitigations: Number lock / SIM lock at carrier (AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon
  offer this); hardware FIDO2 key instead of SMS 2FA; authentication
  app (TOTP) instead of SMS; carrier account PIN/passcode; voice biometric
  for carrier accounts (partial mitigation)
  Gaps: Telecom insider threat is structurally unsolved; carrier employee
  vetting is inadequate for the authority they exercise; FIDO2 adoption
  required to eliminate SMS 2FA attack surface

A89: LLM TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION
  Class: Machine Learning Privacy Attack / Data Exfiltration
  Mechanism: LLMs memorize training data, particularly frequently repeated
  or unique content. Attackers construct prompts that cause the model to
  reproduce memorized training content verbatim. Techniques: prefix completion
  (provide beginning of known document, model completes it); membership
  inference (determine whether a specific text was in training data by
  measuring model confidence on that text vs. counterfactual); 
  "Repeat the word <X> indefinitely" attack (Nasr et al. 2023:
  caused ChatGPT to reproduce training data including PII, code, and
  copyrighted text).
  Historical instances:
  → Carlini et al. 2021 (Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models):
    demonstrated extraction of memorized text from GPT-2; PII, verbatim
    text, and unique identifiers recoverable
  → Carlini et al. 2022: scaled extraction to production LLMs; demonstrated
    memorization increases with model size; models trained on personal data
    are at particular risk
  → Nasr et al. 2023 (Google DeepMind, OpenAI): "Scalable Extraction of 
    Training Data from (Production) Language Models" — "poem" attack caused
    ChatGPT to output training data at $200 cost; PII, copyrighted content,
    verbatim web content recovered
  → Samsung (2023): engineers uploaded proprietary code to ChatGPT for
    debugging assistance; code incorporated into training data; constitutes
    data exfiltration
  Prerequisites: Access to inference endpoint; knowledge of potential
  training data content for prefix attacks; patience for systematic probing
  Indicators: Model outputs verbatim text from known sources; model outputs
  PII or proprietary content; membership inference success rate above chance
  Mitigations: Training data deduplication reduces memorization; differential
  privacy training (DP-SGD) bounds individual contribution; output filtering
  for PII and known proprietary content; rate limiting on repeated similar
  queries; machine unlearning (nascent)
  Gaps: No deployed system reliably prevents training data extraction;
  differential privacy training degrades model quality significantly;
  the tension between model capability and training data privacy is
  unresolved at production scale

A90: BLUETOOTH ATTACK TAXONOMY (COMPREHENSIVE)
  Class: Wireless Protocol / Proximity Attack
  Mechanism: Bluetooth operates in 2.4GHz ISM band; Classic Bluetooth
  (BR/EDR) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) have different but overlapping
  attack surfaces. Primary attack classes:
  → BIAS (Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS, CVE-2020-10135): 
    impersonates paired device by exploiting legacy authentication
    in Bluetooth Classic; allowed impersonation without knowing
    link key; affects most Bluetooth stacks
  → BLESA (Bluetooth Low Energy Spoofing Attack, 2020): spoofs BLE
    peripheral to reconnecting central device; reconnection procedure
    has weaker authentication than initial pairing
  → BlueFrag (CVE-2020-0022, Android): heap overflow in Bluetooth stack
    reachable without pairing; RCE if Bluetooth discoverable mode enabled
  → KNOB Attack (Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth, CVE-2019-9506):
    downgrade attack forces 1-byte entropy session key; brute-forced
    in 0.27 seconds; affects Classic Bluetooth
  → BLE beacon tracking: BLE MAC randomization is often poorly implemented;
    devices can be tracked by advertising patterns despite MAC rotation
  → Bluebugging / Bluesnarf: legacy; access to AT command interface
    of Bluetooth-enabled phones; now rare on modern devices
  Historical instances:
  → BIAS: affected all major Bluetooth chipsets (Broadcom, Qualcomm,
    Apple, Intel, CSR); patched via spec change; real-world exploitation
    requires proximity and knowledge of paired device address
  → BlueFrag: weaponized against Android devices in targeted attacks
    before patch availability; proof-of-concept published
  → Healthcare: Bluetooth-enabled medical devices (glucose monitors,
    insulin pumps) targeted; insulin pump relay attacks demonstrated
    by Jay Radcliffe (2011) and Billy Rios/Jonathan Butts (2019)
  Prerequisites: Physical proximity (typically <10m, up to 100m for Class 1);
  knowledge of target device Bluetooth address (discoverable mode
  or prior advertising capture)
  Indicators: Unexpected Bluetooth pairing requests; device behavior
  anomalies; RF monitoring for unexpected Bluetooth activity
  Mitigations: Disable Bluetooth when not in use; enforce pairing
  authentication; apply firmware updates; restrict discoverable mode;
  for healthcare devices: RF shielding, proximity monitoring
  Gaps: Medical device Bluetooth security is inadequately addressed;
  IoT devices ship with Bluetooth stacks years out of date; 
  BLE mesh networks (building automation) are poorly understood
  attack surfaces

A91: GRAPH-THEORETIC ACTIVE DIRECTORY PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
  Class: Post-Exploitation / Privilege Escalation / Lateral Movement
  Mechanism: Active Directory encodes organizational trust relationships
  as a graph of security principal relationships (group memberships,
  ACL delegations, GPO links, constrained delegation settings, trust
  relationships between domains/forests). BloodHound (Fox-IT/Specter Ops)
  visualizes this graph and finds shortest paths from any compromised
  principal to Domain Admin. Attack techniques:
  → ACL abuse: WriteDACL/WriteOwner on user objects; GenericAll on
    groups; GenericWrite on GPOs; DCSync via Replicating Directory
    Changes rights
  → Delegation abuse: unconstrained delegation captures TGTs of
    authenticating users; constrained delegation with protocol
    transition enables service account impersonation; resource-based
    constrained delegation (RBCD) is abusable from machine account
    creation rights
  → Kerberoasting: request TGS for service accounts (SPNs);
    ticket is encrypted with service account's NTLM hash; offline
    brute-force recovers password
  → ASREPRoasting: accounts with "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication"
    return AS-REP encrypted with account hash; offline brute-force
  → Golden/Silver Ticket: if KRBTGT hash compromised, forge any TGT;
    if service account hash compromised, forge TGS for that service
  Historical instances:
  → SolarWinds: attackers used BloodHound-equivalent analysis to
    navigate from initially compromised SolarWinds server to
    Azure AD Federated Service via SAML token forging
  → Every major enterprise ransomware deployment: BloodHound AD attack
    paths used to achieve Domain Admin before deploying encryptor
  → NotPetya: credential harvesting (Mimikatz-equivalent) combined
    with AD lateral movement achieved network-wide deployment
  Prerequisites: Any foothold in domain-joined system; network access
  to domain controllers; LDAP read access (any authenticated user)
  Indicators: BloodHound/SharpHound execution (DNS queries to DC;
  LDAP queries for ACL/delegation/membership data); Kerberoasting
  (unusual TGS requests for service accounts); DCSync (replication
  traffic from non-DC systems)
  Mitigations: Tiered administration model (Tier 0/1/2 separation);
  Protected Users security group; Credential Guard; LAPS (Local
  Administrator Password Solution); PAM (Privileged Access Management)
  with JIT; regular AD ACL review (Purple Knight, AD ACL Scanner);
  BloodHound Enterprise (continuous attack path monitoring)
  Gaps: Most AD environments have never had an ACL audit; attack path
  remediation is operationally complex; legacy delegation configurations
  create attack paths that are difficult to remove without service disruption

A92: PROMPT INJECTION — COMPREHENSIVE TAXONOMY
  Class: AI/LLM Injection / Agentic Attack
  Mechanism: See Pattern 9.3 and Anatomy 9.B for detailed mechanism.
  Attack subtypes:
  → Direct injection: user prompt contains instruction-overriding content;
    "ignore all previous instructions"; role-playing jailbreaks; DAN
    (Do Anything Now) prompts; developer mode prompts
  → Indirect injection via retrieved content: web page contains injected
    instruction visible only to LLM (white text on white background, 
    HTML comment, or text outside visible viewport); document injection;
    email injection for email-processing agents
  → Persistent injection via memory poisoning: agent memory systems
    (long-term storage) poisoned with injected instructions;
    instruction persists across sessions without user interaction
  → Multi-modal injection: instructions embedded in images (text overlaid
    on image that OCR/vision model reads); instructions in audio (for
    speech-processing agents); instructions in code (for code-reviewing
    agents)
  → Tool call injection: manipulate agent to make tool calls with
    attacker-specified parameters (send email to attacker; write file
    to attacker-specified path; query database with attacker query)
  Historical instances:
  → Greshake et al. 2023: indirect injection via web content; demonstrated
    data exfiltration via Markdown image with credential in URL parameter
  → Simon Willison demonstrations (2023): Bing Chat injection via web
    page content; convinced Bing Chat to output attacker-controlled
    messages to user
  → Langchain agent injection (2023): demonstrated arbitrary Python
    execution via prompt injection in agent with code execution tool
  → LLM email agent injection: demonstrated by multiple researchers;
    email containing injection causes email agent to forward inbox
    contents to attacker
  Prerequisites: Target application uses LLM with tool access or
  processes external content; attacker can influence content processed
  by LLM (website, document, email, API response)
  Indicators: Unexpected tool calls; anomalous agent outputs; unusual
  data access patterns; unexpected outbound requests from agent
  Mitigations: Privilege separation (LLM as planner, separate executor
  with policy validation); input/output monitoring; prompt hardening
  (explicit instruction prioritization); sandboxed tool execution;
  human-in-the-loop for high-privilege operations
  Gaps: No complete defense; fundamental to LLM architecture; privilege
  separation reduces impact but does not prevent injection execution
