A117: QR CODE PHISHING (QUISHING)
Class: Social engineering / credential harvesting / MFA bypass
Root mechanics: R02 (opaque encoding conflates trusted visual with malicious URL), R03 (user trusts
physical or digital medium presenting QR code without verification)

Mechanism:
QR codes encode arbitrary URLs in a 2D matrix. Humans cannot read QR codes visually — the URL is
invisible until decoded by scanner. Attacker replaces, overlays, or synthesizes QR codes pointing
to phishing infrastructure. Physical codes on restaurant menus, parking meters, conference badges,
package delivery slips. Digital codes in email, PDF attachments, Microsoft Teams/Slack messages.

Attack surface details:
→ Physical replacement: attacker prints sticker overlays for parking pay stations (widespread 2021-2023
  in Austin TX, Houston TX, San Antonio TX — FBI public warning October 2021), restaurant table
  QR menus, public transit contactless payment points
→ Email delivery: attacker embeds QR image in email body or attachment; bypasses URL-based email
  security gateways (SEG) because no clickable URL in message text; image contains no text for
  keyword filters; Microsoft and Proofpoint both documented significant volume 2023-2024
→ Microsoft 365 targeted quishing campaigns: Abnormal Security documented campaigns September 2023
  using PNG QR codes in email body targeting 0.9% of enterprise inboxes simultaneously; Cofense
  documented 1,000% increase in quishing Q3 2023 vs Q3 2022
→ Teams/Slack delivery: QR code image in chat bypasses link scanning; mobile scan takes user
  off managed device to personal phone browser with no corporate security controls
→ PDF attachment vector: QR code embedded in PDF (invoice, shipping notice, HR communication);
  PDF scanning in email gateways less mature than URL scanning
→ Adversarial QR generation: QR codes that visually appear as logo or image while encoding malicious
  URL; error correction capacity (H level: 30% of modules recoverable) exploited for visual embedding
→ MFA bypass variant: AiTM (Adversary-in-the-Middle) phishing proxy (Evilginx2, Modlishka, Muraena)
  with QR delivery; scan takes user to proxy; proxy relays to real site; captures session cookie
  post-authentication; bypasses TOTP and SMS MFA entirely

Historical instances:
→ FBI warning October 2021: parking meter QR fraud in Texas cities documented
→ FTC alert January 2022: public awareness campaign on QR code scams
→ Abnormal Security September 2023: Microsoft credential harvesting campaign 1M+ targets
→ CISA advisory 2023: quishing as primary SEG evasion technique
→ 2024: QR codes in physical mail targeting financial institutions customers (first documented
  mail-based quishing campaign; post office scanning cannot inspect QR content)

Prerequisites:
→ Delivery vector for QR image (physical access, email, messaging platform, document)
→ Phishing infrastructure with domain lookalike and credential capture
→ For MFA bypass: AiTM proxy capable of real-time relay

Indicators:
→ QR image in email with no accompanying text URL (text URL present = SEG can scan; QR only = blind spot)
→ Image attachment containing QR code (base64 in email body or attachment)
→ QR destination URL does not match email sender domain
→ Shortened URL inside QR (hides destination from scanner preview)

Mitigations:
→ SEG with image OCR and QR decode pipeline: extract URL from QR image, apply URL reputation analysis
  (Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 added QR scanning 2023; Proofpoint TAP added 2023; Mimecast added 2024)
→ User training: verify QR destination URL before tapping; use built-in camera app showing URL
  preview vs third-party apps
→ Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys) mitigates credential theft even if user scanned
→ Mobile device management: enforce browser filtering on mobile devices in corporate policy

Gaps: No standardized QR authentication protocol. QR codes have no cryptographic binding to source.
Physical QR replacement fundamentally undetectable by any software control.

A118: ADVERSARIAL EXAMPLES IN PRODUCTION COMPUTER VISION SYSTEMS
Class: AI/ML adversarial attack / evasion / manipulation
Root mechanics: R02 (model conflates perturbation pattern with learned class; data and instruction
boundary violated at feature level), R07 (systems designed assuming human-imperceptible changes are
semantically meaningless; violated by adversarial ML)

Mechanism:
Neural network classifiers compute class probability from input pixel values via learned weight
matrices. Small perturbations to input (imperceptible to humans, L∞ norm bounded, e.g. ε=8/255)
can move input across decision boundary, causing arbitrary misclassification. Not limited to image
classification — extends to object detection, facial recognition, OCR, autonomous vehicle perception,
content moderation.

Foundational work:
→ Szegedy et al. 2013: first demonstration of adversarial examples; L-BFGS attack
→ Goodfellow et al. 2014: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM); single-step gradient attack
→ Madry et al. 2017: PGD (Projected Gradient Descent) attack; iterative steepest ascent; foundation
  for adversarial training defense
→ Carlini & Wagner 2017: C&W attack; strongest gradient-based attack; breaks distillation defense
→ Eykholt et al. 2018 (physical domain): stop sign with stickers misclassified; RP2 attack;
  physical perturbation robust to viewpoint/lighting changes; published in IEEE S&P 2018
→ Brown et al. 2017: adversarial patch; universal, printable patch; placed anywhere in scene causes
  target classification; demonstrated on ImageNet classifier (classified as toaster)
→ Brendel et al. 2017: boundary attack; decision-based (black-box); requires only class prediction
  output; no gradient access needed

Production attack scenarios:
→ Facial recognition bypass: adversarial glasses (Sharif et al. 2016) cause misidentification;
  adversarial makeup patterns (CV-dazzle extended); printed perturbations on clothing defeat
  person re-identification systems; DeepFace, Rekognition, Azure Face API all studied
→ Autonomous vehicle attacks: LiDAR spoofing combined with camera adversarial input; stop sign
  misclassification (Eykholt 2018); lane marking perturbations; Tesla Autopilot manipulation studies
→ Content moderation evasion: CSAM/violent content with adversarial perturbation passes PhotoDNA and
  ML classifiers; requires black-box query access to estimate gradients
→ Malware scanner evasion: adversarial PE file manipulation preserving functionality while evading
  ML-based AV (MalGAN, Demetrio et al. 2021); challenge: perturbations must preserve valid executable
→ Medical imaging manipulation: X-ray/MRI classifier manipulation (Finlayson et al. 2019 Science);
  tumor insertion or removal from scan while preserving human-imperceptible appearance; insurance
  fraud and diagnostic sabotage scenarios
→ OCR attacks: perturb text document such that OCR reads different content than human reads;
  relevant to automated document processing pipelines
→ Captcha defeat: adversarial perturbation on CAPTCHA images defeats ML solvers while remaining
  readable to humans (inverse of standard attack direction)

Black-box attack viability:
→ Transfer attacks: adversarial examples transfer across model architectures (Papernot et al. 2016)
→ Query-based: NES (Natural Evolution Strategies), SPSA attack require only prediction output;
  ~100,000 queries for successful attack on ImageNet classifier
→ Score-based: requires softmax probabilities; fewer queries than decision-based
→ Decision-based: requires only top-1 label; highest real-world applicability

Physical-domain attacks:
→ Perturbations must survive printing, photography, viewpoint/scale/lighting variation
→ Expectation over Transformation (EOT, Athalye et al. 2018): optimize over distribution of
  transformations; produces physically robust adversarial examples
→ Demonstrated: adversarial stop signs (stop→speed limit), adversarial pedestrian costumes defeating
  person detectors, adversarial patches on aircraft defeating satellite image classifiers

Certified defenses (formal guarantees):
→ Randomized smoothing (Cohen et al. 2019): Gaussian noise augmentation enables L2 radius certification;
  certified top-1 accuracy CIFAR-10/ImageNet at specific ε bounds; computationally expensive at test time
→ Adversarial training (Madry et al. 2017): train on PGD adversarial examples; currently best empirical
  defense; significant accuracy-robustness tradeoff; computationally 3-30x more expensive
→ Lipschitz-constrained networks (Tsuzuku et al.): theoretical certification via bounded gradients;
  limited scalability
→ Complete verification (CROWN, DeepPoly): exact formal verification; only tractable for small networks

Gaps: No production-ready certified defense for large-scale models at practical accuracy levels.
Adversarial training costs prohibitive for large models. Physical adversarial attacks against
infrastructure systems (traffic signs, autonomous vehicles) have no complete countermeasure.

A119: STEGANOGRAPHIC COMMAND AND CONTROL CHANNELS
Class: Covert communication / C2 infrastructure / detection evasion
Root mechanics: R02 (payload data conflated with benign carrier medium; security tools cannot
distinguish), R01 (monitoring systems lack capacity to inspect carrier at steganographic layer)

Mechanism:
Steganography embeds data within innocuous carrier medium such that the carrier remains plausibly
functional and detection requires statistical analysis beyond normal security tool capability.
In C2 context: malware communicates with operator-controlled infrastructure via carrier channels
(images, audio, video, social media posts, DNS, HTTP headers, timing) that blend into normal traffic.

Carrier categories and technical details:

IMAGE STEGANOGRAPHY:
→ LSB (Least Significant Bit) substitution: replace LSB of RGB channels; imperceptible to human;
  detected by statistical analysis (chi-square test, RS analysis); 3 bits per pixel capacity
→ DCT coefficient modification (JPEG): modify quantized DCT coefficients; survives JPEG re-encoding
  better than pixel-domain methods; JSteg, OutGuess, F5 algorithms
→ Palette-based: GIF/PNG palette reordering encodes data in index order; zero visual difference
→ Metadata steganography: EXIF fields, ICC profiles, comment fields; trivially stripped by proxies
  but widely used in commodity malware
→ Social media image upload/download: platforms re-encode images destroying LSB data unless
  specifically resistant encoding used; attackers use platforms that preserve pixel data (Telegram,
  Twitter historically preserved PNG)

C2 MALWARE USING IMAGE STEGANOGRAPHY:
→ Stegoloader (2013-2015): downloaded PNG from legitimate sites, extracted payload from pixel data;
  used PNG because lossless; contacted Flickr, Wikipedia for carrier images
→ DNSChanger variant (2016): C2 instructions in JPEG images posted to social media
→ Powload (2018): maldoc with PowerShell downloading C2 config from steganographic PNG
→ ZeroT / PlugX campaign (2018, ShadowPad actor): C2 config in BMP pixel data
→ Turla Mosquito (2018): C2 channel over Instagram comments encoded; ESET documented
→ Turla Outlook backdoor: C2 via email PDF attachments with steganographic content
→ Duqu 2.0 (2015, Equation Group-adjacent): encrypted payload in legitimate driver files using
  resource section steganography; Kaspersky discovered post-breach of their own network
→ Witchetty (2022, Symantec): C2 instructions in BMP bitmap hosted on GitHub; legitimate hosting
  site makes traffic appear benign

PROTOCOL-LEVEL STEGANOGRAPHY:
→ DNS covert channel: encode data in DNS query/response labels, TTL values, query type selection;
  DNScat2 (iodine) tools widely available; 53/UDP typically allowed outbound from corporate networks;
  throughput ~1-3 KB/s; detectability: query volume anomaly, entropy of subdomain labels, unusual
  TLD pattern
→ HTTP/HTTPS steganography: C2 data in: URL path parameters, HTTP headers (User-Agent padding,
  Cookie values, custom headers), response body whitespace, timing between requests, HTTP/2 HPACK
  header table manipulation
→ ICMP covert channel: data in ICMP echo payload; firewalls often allow ICMP; low bandwidth
→ TCP/IP header steganography: IP ID field, TCP sequence number, TCP timestamp, URG pointer;
  requires raw socket access; detected by stateful inspection
→ Timing channels: inter-packet delays encode bits; difficult to detect; very low bandwidth;
  relevant in air-gapped exfiltration scenarios

SOCIAL MEDIA C2:
→ Twitter/X C2: malware reads specific accounts or hashtags for C2 instructions; accounts look
  legitimate; if account suspended, attacker creates new one; used by APT41, FIN7-adjacent actors
→ GitHub C2: base64-encoded instructions in repository files, commits, issues, gists;
  WhisperGate (Ukraine 2022) used GitHub for second-stage payload URL storage
→ Slack/Discord C2: legitimate corporate tools allowed through DLP; webhooks provide inbound;
  commodity RATs increasingly using Discord webhooks (AsyncRAT, dcRAT); Slack used by APT actors
→ Telegram bot API: legitimate encrypted messaging; bot token provides C2 channel; used by
  numerous commodity RATs; CloudMensis (ESET 2022, macOS backdoor) used Telegram for C2

Detection:
→ Statistical steganalysis: RS analysis, chi-square test, sample pair analysis — detects LSB
  steganography with >90% accuracy on unmodified images
→ Machine learning steganalysis: SRNet, YeNet — trained detectors for specific steganographic
  schemes; not deployed in commercial security tools
→ DNS traffic analysis: beacon interval regularity, query label entropy, volume anomalies,
  long FQDN detection
→ Social media C2 detection: heuristic — malware communicating with Twitter/GitHub/Discord
  APIs is anomalous from corporate endpoints; require application awareness in NGFW/proxy

Gaps: No commercial product provides real-time steganalysis of image traffic at wire speed.
Social media C2 nearly undetectable without blocking entire platforms.

A120: OAUTH 2.0 DEVICE CODE PHISHING
Class: Credential theft / MFA bypass / authentication abuse
Root mechanics: R03 (user trusts OAuth provider; attacker abuses trust relationship), R06
(OAuth provider acts as confused deputy authorizing malicious application via legitimate flow)

Mechanism:
OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) designed for input-constrained devices (smart TV,
CLI tools, IoT). Flow: (1) device requests device_code and user_code from authorization server;
(2) user visits verification URI (e.g. microsoft.com/devicelogin) on separate device and enters
user_code; (3) device polls token endpoint until user completes authorization; (4) device receives
access_token and refresh_token.

Attacker abuse: attacker initiates device code request themselves, receiving user_code and
verification URI. Attacker sends target link to verification URI with user_code embedded or
instructs target to navigate there manually via phishing email. Target authenticates at legitimate
Microsoft/Google/etc. login page — no fake site involved. After authentication and consent,
attacker's polling request receives valid access and refresh tokens. Attacker now has persistent
access to target's account.

Advantages over traditional phishing:
→ No fake login page: target authenticates at legitimate provider URL (microsoft.com/devicelogin)
→ Bypasses MFA: user completes MFA challenge as part of legitimate OAuth flow
→ Refresh token provides persistence: attacker maintains access without re-authentication
→ No phishing infrastructure: attacker needs only legitimate device code request initiation
→ Difficult to detect: legitimate OAuth traffic pattern; no URL indicators of compromise

Attack execution variants:
→ Email lure: "Your account has been flagged. Please verify at: microsoft.com/devicelogin — enter
  code: ABCD-EFGH"; user thinks they are completing legitimate verification
→ Teams/Slack message: "IT Security: verify your account access (code: XXXX-YYYY)"; internal-
  appearing message via compromised account
→ Helpdesk pretext: social engineering via phone; "we need to verify your account remotely;
  please go to this site and enter this code"
→ Malicious application: app legitimately using Device Code flow; app is malicious and captures
  resulting tokens for attacker
→ QR code delivery: QR code in physical mail or email encodes verification URI with embedded
  user_code; target scans and authorizes on phone

Historical instances:
→ Microsoft documented device code phishing campaigns targeting Azure AD (now Entra ID) 2021-2024;
  Storm-2372 (Russia-linked) large-scale campaign January-February 2025 targeting government,
  NGO, IT services organizations using Teams messages
→ CISA and MS-ISAC advisory AA23-093A referenced device code phishing as active technique
→ Volexity documented Iran-linked group using device code phishing against Middle East targets 2023
→ Multiple threat actors including Cozy Bear (APT29) documented using technique post-SolarWinds

Mitigation:
→ Conditional Access Policy: require compliant device or specific named locations for device code
  flow; block device code grant for high-risk users
→ Disable Device Code flow in OAuth tenant settings (Microsoft: restrict device code flow to
  specific application registrations; default is allow-all which is too permissive)
→ User education: IT will never ask user to enter codes at login portals; legitimate device
  enrollment has defined processes
→ Token lifetime limits: short access token lifetime reduces window; refresh token revocation
  on suspicious access patterns
→ Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE): Microsoft feature that enables real-time token revocation

Gaps: Device Code flow has legitimate uses that make blanket disabling disruptive. No reliable
technical control that prevents a motivated user from authorizing a device code presented in
a social engineering context. Refresh token persistence means initial compromise has long tail.

A121: NTLM RELAY ATTACK TAXONOMY
Class: Authentication relay / lateral movement / privilege escalation
Root mechanics: R03 (servers trust authentication credentials relayed from other systems), R05
(TOCTOU: authentication decision made before action execution; relay operates in the window
between credential capture and server verification)

Mechanism:
NTLM (NT LAN Manager) is Microsoft's challenge-response authentication protocol. NTLM relay
exploits the fact that an NTLM authentication can be relayed to a different server than the
client intended. The server receiving the relay authentication trusts it as legitimate.

NTLM relay chain:
→ Step 1: Force target machine to authenticate outbound (see coercion techniques below)
→ Step 2: Capture NTLM authentication (attacker sits as MiTM via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning
  or network position)
→ Step 3: Relay captured authentication to target service (SMB, HTTP, LDAP, etc.)
→ Step 4: Authenticate as victim machine account or user account on target service

Coercion techniques (Step 1 triggers):
→ LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning: respond to multicast name resolution; legitimate since machines
  broadcast when DNS fails; Responder tool widely used; network-level attack
→ Print Spooler (MS-RPRN, SpoolSample): CVE-2019-1040 adjacent; force machine to authenticate
  to arbitrary UNC path via printer notification; fixed but variant persists
→ PetitPotam (2021, topotam): force domain controller to authenticate via MS-EFSRPC
  (encrypting file system remote protocol); CVE-2021-36942; patched but bypasses exist
→ DFSCoerce (2022): abuse MS-DFSNM (DFS namespace) to force authentication; bypass for
  PetitPotam patches
→ ShadowCoerce: MS-FSRVP (File Server Remote VSS) coercion method; 2022
→ Coercer tool (by @p0dalirius): enumerates and tests all known coercion methods against target
→ WebClient service: if WebClient running on Windows workstation, SMB auth can be coerced
  over HTTP enabling NTLM relay to HTTP endpoints

Relay targets and impact:
→ SMB relay: relay to SMB; execute commands via SMB; requires SMB signing disabled (default
  on workstations; signing required by default on Windows Server 2019+, 2022)
→ LDAP relay: relay to LDAP on Domain Controller; create computer accounts; modify ACLs;
  set Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) for privilege escalation; does not require
  LDAP signing if LDAPS not enforced
→ LDAP relay to DCSync: if relaying as Domain Controller machine account, can trigger DCSync
  (DS-Replication-Get-Changes + DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) to obtain all domain hashes
→ HTTP relay: relay to Exchange Web Services (EWS) Outlook Web Access; access email as victim;
  subscribe to inbox rules; extract sensitive information; extract credentials from emails
→ ADCS relay (ESC8): relay machine account authentication to ADCS (Active Directory Certificate
  Services) HTTP endpoint; request certificate as Domain Controller; use certificate for
  Kerberos authentication (pass-the-cert); full domain compromise path; Shadow Credentials
  (RBCD variant) also applicable
→ ADCS ESC8 exploitation: SpecterOps research (Will Schroeder, Lee Christensen) 2021;
  Certipy tool (Oliver Lyak 2022) automates entire attack chain; widely exploited 2022-2024

Full compromise chain example:
→ Run Responder on network → workstation broadcasts LLMNR query → attacker sends poisoned
  response → workstation sends NTLM auth to attacker → relay to ADCS HTTP endpoint as
  workstation machine account → receive certificate for machine account → use certificate for
  TGT request (PKINIT) → machine account TGT → extract NTLM hash via U2U Kerberos → pass-
  the-hash → domain admin via DCSync

Tools: Responder, ntlmrelayx (impacket), Certipy, Coercer, PetitPotam, DFSCoerce

Mitigations:
→ Enable SMB Signing domain-wide (Group Policy: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign
  communications always = Enabled); prevents SMB relay; some legacy apps break
→ Enable LDAP signing and channel binding on Domain Controllers (MS advisory ADV190023 2020)
→ Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy (prevents poisoning attack surface)
→ Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on ADCS web enrollment
→ Migrate NTLM to Kerberos where possible; disable NTLM for specific services
→ Install Certipy patches; review ADCS template permissions (ESC1-ESC8 vulnerabilities)
→ Deploy Network Access Control to prevent unauthorized hosts from responding to broadcasts

Gaps: SMB signing enforcement breaks legacy applications (common in manufacturing, healthcare
with embedded systems requiring SMBv1/unsigned). ADCS deployments widely misconfigured —
2023 surveys show majority of AD environments with ADCS have at least one ESC vulnerability.

A122: KUBERNETES AND CONTAINER ORCHESTRATION ATTACKS
Class: Infrastructure / privilege escalation / lateral movement / supply chain
Root mechanics: R01 (namespace and RBAC boundaries frequently misconfigured), R03 (containers
and pods inherit trust from orchestration plane without independent verification), R06 (service
accounts as confused deputies — overprivileged tokens mounted by default)

Mechanism:
Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration system managing containerized workloads
across clusters. Introduced massive new attack surface as cloud-native adoption accelerated.
Attack surface spans: container images, pod specifications, RBAC policies, network policies,
API server exposure, etcd, service account tokens, kubelet nodes, admission controllers.

ATTACK SURFACE CATEGORIES:

Container escape:
→ Privileged containers: pod with privileged:true mounts host filesystem and devices; trivial
  host escape via /proc/sysrq-trigger, mount host filesystem, chroot; common misconfiguration
→ hostPID/hostNetwork: access host process namespace or network stack; enables network sniffing,
  process injection
→ Sensitive host path mounts: /var/run/docker.sock mount enables Docker API access → spawn new
  privileged container → host escape; /etc/kubernetes/pki or /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf mounted
  → cluster admin credentials
→ Capability abuse: CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, CAP_NET_ADMIN enable container escape;
  principle of least capability rarely enforced
→ CVE-2019-5736 (runc escape): exploit runc binary overwrite via container process; patched but
  demonstrates container runtime attack surface
→ CVE-2024-21626 (runc, Leaky Vessels February 2024): working directory escape via file
  descriptor leak; CVSS 8.6; affected containerd, runc; patched; active exploitation window

API Server attacks:
→ Unauthenticated K8s API: clusters exposed on internet with anonymous access (Shodan queries
  regularly find); attacker gets kubectl exec, pod creation, secret access; Tesla 2018 RedLock
  discovered crypto mining via exposed K8s dashboard (unauthenticated at time)
→ Kubernetes Dashboard without authentication: Dashboard default install 2018-era lacked auth;
  default ClusterAdmin binding; Tesla incident; documented widespread exploitation for cryptomining
→ Service account token exfiltration: every pod gets mounted service account token at
  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token by default (automountServiceAccountToken:true
  is default); token valid for K8s API; attacker in container reads token → API calls as
  service account → escalate if RBAC permissive
→ RBAC misconfiguration: wildcard bindings (verbs: ["*"]), excessive ClusterRoleBindings,
  default service accounts with admin permissions; system:masters group membership

etcd attacks:
→ etcd stores entire cluster state including Secrets in base64 (not encrypted by default until
  K8s 1.13 with encryption provider configuration); direct etcd access bypasses RBAC entirely
→ etcd often accessible on port 2379/2380 without mTLS in misconfigured clusters
→ etcd backup files: backup files contain complete cluster state; frequently stored insecurely

Supply chain attacks:
→ Malicious container images: typosquatting on DockerHub (2018: 17 images with cryptominers
  downloaded 5M times before removal); poisoned base images; latest tag pulls → no pinning
→ Helm chart supply chain: Helm repositories as package manager analog; malicious charts;
  typosquatting; chart checksum not verified by default in older Helm versions
→ Image registry compromise: private registry credentials in CI/CD → attacker pushes backdoored
  image → deployed to production clusters
→ SolarWinds-style K8s: malicious admission controller webhook registered as legitimate controller;
  mutates pod specs at admission time (add malicious sidecar, modify command, inject env vars)

Kubernetes-specific lateral movement:
→ Service mesh abuse: mTLS terminated at sidecar; sidecar compromise enables traffic inspection
→ Network policy gaps: default-allow networking; absence of NetworkPolicy allows unrestricted
  pod-to-pod communication; micro-segmentation requires explicit NetworkPolicy definition
→ Node compromise via kubelet: kubelet API (port 10250) accessible from pods by default; request
  exec/logs on any pod on node if kubelet not protected; Node Restriction admission controller
  limits this

Historical instances:
→ Tesla 2018: RedLock finds exposed K8s dashboard → crypto mining in AWS using spot instances
  ($0 cost to attacker); S3 bucket with telemetry data exposed in same cluster
→ 2018: widespread cryptomining campaigns via exposed K8s APIs documented by multiple security vendors
→ Hildegard (TeamTNT 2021): cloud-targeting malware targeting K8s; escape via misconfigured kubelet
→ Attacker-deployed backdoor via supply chain: multiple documented 2022-2024 using registry poisoning
→ NSA/CISA K8s hardening guide 2022: documents all categories above as active exploitation

Mitigations:
→ Pod Security Standards (PSS, replaced deprecated PodSecurityPolicy): baseline and restricted
  profiles enforce no privileged containers, no host namespace sharing, read-only root filesystem
→ Network Policies: default-deny all ingress/egress; explicit allow rules per workload
→ Disable automountServiceAccountToken for pods that don't need API access
→ Image signing: Cosign + Sigstore; admission controller rejects unsigned images (Kyverno,
  OPA Gatekeeper)
→ Secret encryption at rest: configure EncryptionConfiguration for etcd; KMS provider for key
  management
→ Audit logging: enable K8s API audit log; ship to SIEM; alert on sensitive API calls
  (exec, port-forward, secret list/get, ClusterRoleBinding creation)
→ Admission controllers: OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for policy enforcement; validate all pod specs
  against security baseline before admission
→ Node hardening: CIS Kubernetes benchmark; restrict kubelet API; node isolation

A123: API ABUSE AT SCALE
Class: Business logic abuse / data theft / account takeover / DDoS
Root mechanics: R01 (rate limiting absent or insufficient; business logic boundaries not enforced),
R03 (API trusts authenticated requests without context of usage pattern), R05 (quota enforcement
checks non-atomic with consumption; race conditions in rate limiting)

Mechanism:
APIs are the primary interface for modern web and mobile applications. API abuse encompasses:
unauthorized access, data harvesting, credential stuffing via API, business logic exploitation,
resource abuse, and scraping. Distinct from vulnerability exploitation — often uses legitimate
API endpoints in unintended ways.

ATTACK CATEGORIES:

Credential stuffing via API:
→ API login endpoints accept JSON POST with username/password; no CAPTCHA; rate limiting bypassable
  by rotating IPs, user agents, TLS fingerprints; attacker uses credential breach databases
→ Mobile API: app traffic intercepted; API keys extracted from APK/IPA; backend API accessed
  directly; bypasses web-layer protections
→ GraphQL introspection: schema discovery; enumerate all types and queries; find undocumented
  or admin queries; execute deeply nested queries (complexity DoS)
→ Excessive query nesting (GraphQL DoS): query with 100-level nesting; exponential server-side
  computation; depth limiting required; widely misconfigured

API data harvesting:
→ Enumeration via sequential IDs: REST API with /api/users/1, /api/users/2... returns user
  records; IDOR vulnerability; scrape entire user database; Parler 2021 — API returned sequential
  GUIDs post-authentication; researcher scraped all posts and user data before platform went down
  following January 6th
→ LinkedIn scraping: periodic enforcement battles; hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn 9th Circuit litigation
  2017-2022; API provides structured resume data; used for candidate intelligence, competitor
  analysis, social engineering target identification
→ Twitter/X API: historical open API; research access reduced 2023; third-party analysis tools
  shut down; scraping continues via web API reverse engineering
→ OSINT via API: Hunter.io, Clearbit, ZoomInfo APIs aggregate email/phone/org data; used for
  spear phishing target enumeration; available to anyone with API key; no verification of use

API authentication attacks:
→ JWT vulnerabilities (detailed in A116): algorithm confusion, none algorithm, kid injection
→ API key in mobile apps: hardcoded API keys in APK decompilation (jadx); extraction and
  abuse; Firebase API key → access to entire Firebase project without auth if rules misconfigured
→ OAuth scope creep: requesting broad scopes; user grants without understanding; email access
  granted enables inbox scraping, contact list exfiltration
→ API versioning bypass: API v2 has proper auth; /api/v1/ endpoint still live without auth;
  common in microservice migrations where v1 not fully deprecated

Rate limiting bypass:
→ IP rotation: residential proxy networks (ASN: Datacenter IPs easily blocked; residential
  IPs from legitimate ISPs harder to block at scale); available from Luminati/Bright Data,
  Oxylabs, Smartproxy at $10-50/GB
→ HTTP/2 multiplexing: single TLS connection sends 100+ concurrent requests; naive per-IP
  rate limiting ineffective; requires per-token or per-session rate limiting
→ Race conditions in rate limiting: concurrent requests arrive simultaneously before any
  is counted; Redis INCR/EXPIRE race; use Redis Lua scripts for atomic check-and-increment
→ Header spoofing: X-Forwarded-For header injection if backend trusts it; appears as different
  IP to rate limiter; requires backend to trust proxy header without validation

Bots at scale — industry data:
→ Imperva Bad Bot Report 2023: 30.2% of all internet traffic is bad bots; sophisticated bots
  mimicking human behavior (mouse movement, human-speed form fill, JavaScript execution) comprise
  17% of web traffic
→ Akamai retail bot report: 43% of retail login traffic is credential stuffing during peak periods
→ Account takeover economics: successful account worth $10-2000 depending on account type (bank vs
  social media); automated at scale makes ROI positive even with <0.1% success rate
→ API-first companies (financial data aggregators Plaid/Yodlee) themselves used to scrape bank
  credentials — FDX (Financial Data Exchange) and PSD2/Open Banking regulation attempts to formalize

Historical instances:
→ Parler scrape January 2021: sequential GIDs returned by API without auth after Amazon suspended
  CDN; 70TB+ posts, DMs, media scraped in 36 hours by researchers and archived
→ Facebook data scrape via phone number lookup API 2019: 533M records; API allowed reverse lookup
  of phone to Facebook ID without rate limiting; scraped and sold; disclosed April 2021
→ LinkedIn data 2021: 700M records scraped via API; compiled from authorized scraping of public
  profiles; no auth bypass; legitimate endpoints abused
→ T-Mobile API 2023 breach: API endpoint exposed without proper auth check; 37M customer records
  exfiltrated; attacker used API for months before discovery

Mitigations:
→ API gateway with WAF: rate limiting per IP, per token, per user; anomaly detection; AWS API
  Gateway, Kong, Apigee, Akamai App & API Protector
→ Bot management: Cloudflare Bot Management, Akamai Bot Manager, DataDome; behavioral analysis,
  device fingerprinting, proof-of-work challenges
→ GraphQL query complexity analysis: depth limiting, complexity calculation, persisted queries only
→ Enumeration-resistant identifiers: UUIDs v4 instead of sequential integers; IDOR by design prevention
→ BOLA/IDOR authorization: object-level authorization check at every endpoint; OWASP API Top 10 #1
→ API inventory: DAST scanning for undocumented endpoints; shadow API discovery

A124: CRYPTOGRAPHIC IMPLEMENTATION ATTACKS
Class: Side-channel / fault injection / implementation flaw exploitation
Root mechanics: R04 (computation produces observable physical effects: power consumption, timing,
electromagnetic radiation, acoustic emissions, temperature), R08 (physical embodiment of cryptographic
hardware as attack surface independent of algorithm security)

Mechanism:
Cryptographic algorithms may be secure in mathematical abstraction but implementation in physical
hardware or software leaks information through observable side effects. Side-channel attacks recover
secret key material from measurements of these effects without breaking the underlying mathematics.

TIMING ATTACKS:
→ Kocher 1996: original timing attack paper; demonstrates RSA key recovery from timing of
  modular exponentiation; variable time square-and-multiply leaks key bits; applied to
  real SSL server without modifying anything
→ Square-and-multiply: if bit=1, perform multiply; if bit=0, skip; multiply takes measurably
  longer than no-multiply; timing across many samples reveals key bit sequence
→ Cache-timing attacks (Bernstein 2005): AES S-box table lookups cause cache hits/misses;
  cache access time measurable from shared process or remote; key-dependent memory access
  pattern revealed
→ Flush+Reload (Yarom & Falkner 2014): cache-timing on modern CPUs; flush cache line, wait for
  victim to execute, reload and measure; shared last-level cache enables cross-VM attack; applied
  to AES, RSA, ECDSA across VMs in cloud environments (demonstrated on OpenSSL)
→ Remote timing: LUCKY THIRTEEN (AlFardan & Paterson 2013): remote timing distinguisher on TLS
  CBC-mode MAC-then-encrypt; ~2^23 queries needed; demonstrates remote timing attack feasibility
  at network level with sufficient measurement precision
→ OpenSSL RSA timing: CVE-2018-0737 and multiple prior: non-constant-time implementations;
  fixed in OpenSSL 3.x via constant-time rewrite of RSA blinding
→ ECDSA nonce reuse timing: PS3 private key recovery (Hotz 2010): Sony reused fixed nonce k
  in ECDSA signatures; two signatures with same nonce → solve linear equation for private key;
  applied to Bitcoin keys with weak nonce generation; LadderLeak (2020): ECDSA key recovery
  from single-bit nonce leak; 1 biased bit + 1 billion signatures → key

POWER ANALYSIS:
→ SPA (Simple Power Analysis): visual inspection of single power trace reveals operations;
  modular exponentiation square vs. multiply visible in power waveform
→ DPA (Differential Power Analysis, Kocher et al. 1999): statistical analysis of many power
  traces; choose hypothetical intermediate value dependent on one key bit; compute Hamming
  weight model; correlate with measured traces; identifies key byte; fully automated;
  requires ~1000 traces for DES key recovery
→ CPA (Correlation Power Analysis): Pearson correlation coefficient between model and measurement;
  more efficient than DPA; standard technique in academic and commercial evaluation
→ EM Analysis (EMA): electromagnetic emissions carry same information as power traces; can target
  specific on-chip structures; works through enclosure; demonstrated on smart cards through walls
→ Industrial impact: every smart card (banking EMV chip, SIM card, passport RFID chip, HSM) must
  be designed and validated against DPA; DPA countermeasures (masking, hiding) required for
  FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria EAL4+
→ Masked AES: split secret key S into shares S = S1 XOR S2 XOR... such that no single share
  reveals S; all computations operate on shares; power consumption of share operations
  uncorrelated with key; first-order DPA-resistant; higher-order DPA attacks still possible

FAULT INJECTION ATTACKS:
→ Voltage glitching: brief voltage spike/drop causes CPU to skip instruction, corrupt register,
  flip bit; can skip security checks (if (authenticated) → glitch to flip branch prediction);
  demonstrated on ATM PINpad devices, game consoles, microcontrollers
→ Clock glitching: clock frequency anomaly causes setup/hold time violation; combinational
  circuit produces incorrect output for one cycle; same effects as voltage glitch
→ Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI): focused EM pulse near IC; localized effect on specific
  circuit region; more precise targeting than voltage glitching; demonstrated on Cortex-M
  processors at fine granularity
→ Laser fault injection: focused laser beam induces photocurrent; single-transistor level
  precision; most precise fault injection technique; requires optical access to die (decapping)
→ Rowhammer (Seaborn & Dullien 2015 / Kim et al. 2014): repeated DRAM row access causes bit
  flip in adjacent rows through electromagnetic coupling; DRAM cells too close together;
  CVE-2015-0565; JavaScript-based exploit demonstrated; DRAMMER (van der Veen 2016) Android
  exploitation; TRRespass (2020) bypass of in-DRAM Target Row Refresh mitigations; DDR5
  and modern mitigations have largely addressed but specialized attacks continue
→ BHI / Spectre/Meltdown family: transient execution attacks exploiting CPU speculation;
  information leaks across security domains; covered as distinct attack class but shares
  physical embodiment root mechanic
→ Voltage fault injection on iPhone: Voltpillager (2021): USB power delivery manipulation
  on iPhone via Lightning; bypasses Secure Enclave brute-force protection; demonstrates
  that even high-security consumer devices vulnerable to physical fault injection

Real-world impact:
→ EMV skimming evolved to chip-and-PIN glitching: demonstration that EMV PIN bypasses possible
  via fault injection during transaction; Murdoch et al. 2010 Cambridge; attack on protocol
  flaw (PIN not signed into transaction data) rather than cryptography
→ YubiKey side-channel (2023): SideChannelMarvels team documented timing side-channel in
  YubiKey ECDSA implementation; not practically exploitable remotely but demonstrates
  commercial FIDO2 hardware not immune
→ ÆPIC Leak (2022): architectural CPU vulnerability leaking data from APIC MMIO region;
  architectural information leak (not speculative); affects Intel Sunny Cove; SGX enclaves
  vulnerable

Defenses:
→ Constant-time programming: all operations take same wall-clock time regardless of secret value;
  eliminate branches on secret data; no secret-dependent memory addresses; ct-grind tool for
  verification; TIMECOP tool
→ Masking (hardware): secret splitting into random shares; DPA-resistant by design; required
  for all commercial smart card cryptographic implementations
→ Random delays (software): add random jitter to side-channel sensitive operations; reduces
  correlation; not sufficient alone but increases attack cost
→ Physical shielding: Faraday cage reduces EM emanations; voltage regulators filter power
  traces; physical security prevents fault injection access
→ Rowhammer: ECC DRAM (detects/corrects single-bit errors); LPDDR4+ TRR; refresh rate increase
  at cost of performance; Target Row Refresh algorithms; page coloring to separate security domains

DEFENSE TAXONOMY — D101 THROUGH D105
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

D101: POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY MIGRATION FRAMEWORK
Domain: Cryptography transition / enterprise architecture
Root mechanic addressed: R07 (temporal attack — systems designed assuming quantum computing
cannot break current asymmetric cryptography; CRQC will violate that assumption; HNDL attacks
viable now with current ciphertext)

Components:

NIST PQC standards (August 2024 final publication):
→ FIPS 203: ML-KEM (Module-Lattice Key Encapsulation Mechanism); derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber;
  key exchange and key encapsulation; security based on Module Learning With Errors (MLWE);
  three parameter sets: ML-KEM-512 (security level 1, AES-128 equivalent), ML-KEM-768 (level 3,
  AES-192 equivalent), ML-KEM-1024 (level 5, AES-256 equivalent)
→ FIPS 204: ML-DSA (Module-Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm); derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium;
  digital signatures; MLWE/MSIS based; three parameter sets; replaces RSA/ECDSA for signatures
→ FIPS 205: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature); derived from SPHINCS+; hash-based
  signatures; security based only on hash function security; conservative choice when lattice
  concerns arise; larger signatures than ML-DSA; stateless (no state synchronization problem
  unlike XMSS/LMS which are stateful)
→ FN-DSA (FALCON): fourth standard in progress; smaller signatures than ML-DSA; NTRU lattice basis

MIGRATION PHASES:

Phase 1 — Cryptographic inventory (0-12 months):
→ CBOM (Cryptography Bill of Materials): enumerate every cryptographic primitive in use;
  where, what algorithm, key size, certificate lifetime, hardware vs software implementation
→ Tools: CBOM scanners (CycloneDX CBOM schema); Sonatype SBOM integration; IBM Research CBOM tools
→ Network scanning: identify TLS versions and cipher suites across all externally and internally
  facing services; Qualys SSL Labs, testssl.sh, nmap ssl-enum-ciphers
→ Certificate inventory: certificates by expiry, algorithm, key size; ECDSA P-256 vs P-384
  vs RSA 2048 vs RSA 4096; all must be replaced with hybrid or pure PQC certificates
→ Hardware inventory: HSMs, smartcards, TPMs, custom ASICs implementing ECC/RSA; hardware
  replacement timeline often 5-10 years; longest lead items drive migration schedule

Phase 2 — Hybrid deployment (12-36 months):
→ Hybrid key exchange: combine classical (ECDHE) and PQC (ML-KEM) key exchange; final shared
  secret = KDF(classical_shared, pqc_shared); harvested ciphertext cannot be decrypted with
  either quantum or classical computer alone
→ RFC 8784 / RFC 9370: IKEv2 hybrid post-quantum extensions
→ RFC 9420 (MLS): Messaging Layer Security; designed with crypto agility; PQC mode in progress
→ TLS 1.3 hybrid: IETF draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design; ML-KEM-768 + X25519 hybrid (x25519-
  mlkem768); Chrome 124+ has ML-KEM draft support; AWS, Google, Cloudflare testing deployments
→ Signal Protocol: Signal added PQXDH (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman) 2023; CRYSTALS-
  Kyber for initial key agreement; provides forward secrecy against future quantum attacks
  on currently recorded traffic

Phase 3 — Full PQC transition (36-120+ months):
→ Code signing infrastructure: replace RSA/ECDSA for firmware signing, software signing;
  ML-DSA or SLH-DSA; certificate chain replacement; root CA and intermediate CA replacement
→ VPN/IPSec: IKEv2 with ML-KEM; OpenSSL 3.x OQS provider (Open Quantum Safe project);
  commercial VPN vendor support 2025-2027 estimated
→ PKI: CA/Browser Forum ballots for PQC certificate profiles; X.509 certificate format
  extended for ML-DSA OIDs; hybrid certificate formats (CompositeAlgorithm)

Critical timeline:
→ HNDL (Harvest Now Decrypt Later): attacker records encrypted traffic today; decrypts when
  CRQC (Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer) available; estimated timeline for
  CRQC: NSA guidance suggests "cryptographically relevant quantum computer" possible within
  10-15 years; CNSA 2.0 (August 2022) mandates complete PQC transition by 2035
→ FIPS 140-3 PQC module requirements: vendors must submit for CMVP validation; validation
  queue 18-24 months; government customers require FIPS-validated modules

Migration risk classes:
→ Crypto agility failure: systems hardcoded to specific algorithms cannot update without
  re-architecture; discovered during CBOM
→ Performance impact: ML-KEM adds ~1ms per TLS handshake at scale; ML-DSA signature larger
  than ECDSA; bandwidth and latency impact on CDN, email, IoT constrained devices
→ Downgrade attacks: during hybrid period; attacker forces classical-only negotiation;
  mitigated by strict hybrid policy

D102: API SECURITY DEEP ARCHITECTURE
Domain: Application security / API design / runtime protection
Root mechanics addressed: R01 (API boundary enforcement), R03 (API trust verification), R05
(atomic authorization checks)

Framework components:

Design-time security:
→ API specification-first (OpenAPI 3.x / AsyncAPI 2.x): define schema before implementation;
  enables automated validation, fuzzing, documentation generation; machine-readable spec
  as ground truth for security controls
→ OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization/BOLA), API2 (Broken
  Authentication), API3 (Broken Object Property Level Authorization), API4 (Unrestricted Resource
  Consumption), API5 (Broken Function Level Authorization), API6 (Unrestricted Access to Sensitive
  Business Flows), API7 (SSRF), API8 (Security Misconfiguration), API9 (Improper Inventory
  Management), API10 (Unsafe Consumption of APIs)
→ Threat modeling: STRIDE applied to each API endpoint; data flow diagram per API domain;
  identify trust boundaries crossing HTTP

Authentication layer:
→ OAuth 2.1 (draft, consolidates 2.0 security BCP): Authorization Code + PKCE mandatory for
  all clients; implicit flow removed; Device Code flow with user binding verification;
  resource indicators (RFC 8707); DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449) —
  token binding to HTTP request; prevents token theft replay
→ mTLS for service-to-service: client certificate authentication; SPIFFE/SPIRE framework
  for workload identity; X.509 SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document) as machine identity
→ API key management: scoped keys (read-only, specific resource); automatic rotation via
  secret management platform (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager); audit log per key usage

Runtime protection:
→ API gateway layer: rate limiting (per IP, per user, per API key, per endpoint); quota
  enforcement; authentication validation; request/response transformation
→ Schema validation: enforce OpenAPI schema at gateway; reject malformed requests;
  GraphQL query depth/complexity limits; input size limits
→ Behavioral analytics: UEBA for API — establish baseline request patterns per credential;
  alert on volume anomalies, endpoint enumeration patterns, unusual data volumes
→ Bot detection: browser automation detection (Puppeteer/Playwright fingerprints); rate
  pattern analysis; device fingerprinting for mobile API
→ BOLA prevention: authorization framework checks object ownership at every endpoint;
  inject user context into database queries (row-level security); OPA (Open Policy Agent)
  for decentralized authorization decisions

API discovery and inventory:
→ Shadow API problem: undocumented endpoints not in specification; discovered by attackers
  before defenders; DAST scanning against running service to enumerate endpoints;
  API traffic analysis via WAF/proxy logs
→ API versioning lifecycle: decommission v1 before attackers find it; traffic monitoring
  on deprecated versions before removal
→ Third-party API consumption: track all external APIs called; enforce egress filtering;
  certificate pinning for high-value API integrations; SSRF prevention (block 169.254.x.x,
  10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x.x from server-initiated API calls)

D103: CONTAINER AND KUBERNETES SECURITY ARCHITECTURE
Domain: Cloud-native security / container hardening / orchestration security
Root mechanics addressed: R01 (namespace boundary enforcement), R03 (pod identity verification),
R06 (service account privilege control)

Container hardening:
→ Minimal base images: distroless (Google, no shell, no package manager, attack surface ~10% of
  full OS image); scratch (empty filesystem for Go static binaries); Alpine Linux (5MB base);
  fewer components = fewer vulnerabilities = smaller SBOM = faster scanning
→ Image scanning: Trivy (Aqua Security, open source), Grype (Anchore), Snyk Container, AWS ECR
  scanning (Clair-based), Prisma Cloud, Sysdig Secure; scan at build time (CI/CD gate),
  registry push, runtime (continuous re-scan for newly disclosed CVEs against existing images)
→ Read-only root filesystem: containers with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true cannot write to /;
  temporary volumes for writable paths (/tmp, application-specific); attacker cannot modify
  binaries, drop tools, write malware to disk
→ Non-root user: runAsNonRoot: true; runAsUser: non-zero; root containers can escape to root
  on host if other misconfigurations exist; defense in depth even if insufficient alone
→ Seccomp profiles: filter system calls available to container process; default containerd seccomp
  profile blocks ~44 high-risk syscalls; custom profiles allow only specific sysccalls application needs
→ AppArmor/SELinux: MAC (Mandatory Access Control) policy on container; restrict file paths
  accessible, network operations, capabilities; defense-in-depth layer
→ Capabilities: drop ALL capabilities; add back only those explicitly needed (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
  for port <1024); principle of least privilege at Linux capability level
→ No privileged containers: privileged: false (default); explicit deny via OPA/Kyverno admission policy
→ Image signing: Cosign + Sigstore; sign image digest at build time; enforce signature verification
  in admission controller; prevents unsigned or tampered image from running; keyless signing
  with OIDC identity

Kubernetes cluster hardening:
→ Pod Security Admission (PSA, K8s 1.25+): enforce, audit, or warn on baseline and restricted
  profiles at namespace level; replaces deprecated PSP
→ Network Policies: Calico, Cilium, WeaveNet CNI plugins enforce NetworkPolicy; default-deny all
  ingress and egress; explicit allow rules per pod selector; micro-segmentation within cluster
→ RBAC least privilege: avoid ClusterRoleBindings; prefer RoleBindings scoped to namespace;
  audit existing bindings with kubectl auth can-i --list; rbac-lookup tool; eliminate wildcards
→ Service account token projection: BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume (K8s 1.21+ default); tokens
  have 1-hour expiry; audience-bound; replaces non-expiring mounted tokens
→ Disable automountServiceAccountToken for pods not needing API access; or bind service account
  with empty/minimal RBAC
→ API server: disable anonymous authentication; enable audit logging; NodeRestriction admission
  controller; restrict API server access via network policy or VPN
→ etcd: mTLS between API server and etcd; encrypt etcd at rest (EncryptionConfiguration);
  restrict etcd network access to API server only; backup encryption
→ Kubelet: --anonymous-auth=false; --authorization-mode=Webhook; restrict kubelet API to
  API server via firewall; NodeRestriction for node-to-API-server communication
→ Admission controllers: MutatingAdmissionWebhook and ValidatingAdmissionWebhook for custom
  policy; OPA Gatekeeper (Rego policies) or Kyverno (YAML-native policies) for enforcement
→ Image policy webhook: restrict image registries (allow only internal registry); block :latest tag;
  require digest (sha256:...) pinning

Runtime security:
→ Falco (CNCF): behavioral runtime security; kernel eBPF or ptrace; detect container escape attempts,
  privilege escalation, sensitive file access, reverse shell spawning, crypto mining
→ Tetragon (Cilium): eBPF-based runtime enforcement with policy enforcement capability (not just detection);
  block system calls in real time based on behavioral policy
→ Supply chain runtime: cosign verify before image pull via OCI hook; SBOM attestation verification
→ Resource limits: CPU and memory limits on all pods; prevent resource exhaustion DoS; LimitRange
  enforcement at namespace level

D104: OAUTH 2.1 AND MODERN AUTHENTICATION SECURITY REFERENCE
Domain: Authentication / identity / authorization protocol security
Root mechanics addressed: R03 (authentication trust verification), R06 (authorization server as
confused deputy)

OAuth 2.1 security improvements over 2.0:
→ PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) mandatory for all clients: code_verifier random
  secret; code_challenge = SHA256(code_verifier); prevents authorization code interception;
  no longer optional for public clients
→ Implicit flow removed: implicit grant returns access_token in URL fragment; logged in browser
  history, referrer headers, server logs; OAuth 2.1 draft removes it entirely
→ Password grant removed: Resource Owner Password Credentials grant; defeats OAuth delegation model;
  removed in 2.1; applications must redirect to authorization server
→ Redirect URI: exact URI matching required; no pattern matching (wildcard subdomains); prevents
  open redirect attacks
→ Bearer token: RFC 6750; HTTPS-only transmission; no URI transmission; sender-constrained tokens
  (DPoP) preferred over bearer

DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession, RFC 9449):
→ Binds access token to HTTP request; client generates ephemeral keypair; DPoP JWT header in
  request; token issued with jkt (JWK thumbprint) of public key; server validates DPoP JWT
  signature and hth (HTTP method hash); prevents token theft replay even from TLS mitm
→ Supported by Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0 as of 2023-2024; not yet universal

OIDC (OpenID Connect) security:
→ nonce parameter: prevents replay; include random nonce in authentication request; verify
  nonce claim in ID token matches
→ at_hash and c_hash: hash validation of access_token and authorization code in ID token;
  prevents substitution attacks
→ PKCE + OIDC: combine for complete public client security model
→ Backchannel logout (OIDC specification): server-initiated session termination;
  ensures logout propagates to all relying parties; prevents session persistence after user logout

Token security:
→ Short lifetime: access tokens 5-15 minutes; refresh tokens 24 hours for interactive, longer
  with rotation
→ Refresh token rotation: each use of refresh token issues new refresh token and invalidates old;
  detect theft (old token use after rotation = compromise signal)
→ Token binding (draft-ietf-tokbind): bind tokens to TLS channel; deprecated in favor of DPoP
→ JWT validation: verify alg, verify exp, verify iss, verify aud; use algorithm allowlist (reject
  none, reject RSxxx if using ECxxx); verify signature against known public key set (JWKS endpoint)
→ Opaque reference tokens at perimeter: issue JWT internally; issue opaque reference token to
  clients; reduces JWT exposure; token introspection (RFC 7662) for validation

Authorization Code flow with PKCE (complete reference):
→ Client generates code_verifier (random 43-128 chars, Base64URL)
→ code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier)))
→ Auth request: redirect to /authorize with response_type=code, client_id, redirect_uri, scope,
  state (random CSRF token), code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256, nonce (OIDC)
→ User authenticates at authorization server
→ Redirect back: code, state (verify equals sent value)
→ Token request: POST /token with code, client_id, redirect_uri, code_verifier; server verifies
  SHA256(code_verifier) == code_challenge stored from step 3
→ Token response: access_token (JWT or opaque), token_type (Bearer or DPoP), expires_in,
  refresh_token, id_token (OIDC)
→ API calls: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> or DPoP <access_token> with DPoP header

Common implementation errors:
→ Not validating state parameter → CSRF attack on authorization flow
→ Not validating nonce in ID token → replay attack
→ Accepting any redirect_uri → open redirect + code theft
→ Not verifying token signature → accept forged JWT
→ Not checking aud claim → accepting tokens issued for other clients
→ Storing access_token in localStorage → XSS token theft; use httpOnly cookie or memory only

D105: CRYPTOGRAPHIC AGILITY DESIGN PATTERNS
Domain: Cryptography architecture / system design
Root mechanics addressed: R07 (temporal attack — crypto hardcoded assumptions violated by
future advances; agility enables replacement before exploitation)

Definition:
Cryptographic agility is the ability of a system to switch cryptographic algorithms, key sizes,
or protocols with minimal code change, configuration update, or downtime. The opposite —
cryptographic rigidity — is the root cause of slow PQC migration.

Design patterns:

Algorithm negotiation pattern:
→ Protocol-level: TLS cipher suite negotiation model; client sends supported ciphers;
  server selects from supported intersection; enables gradual migration (add new cipher;
  deprecate old over time; remove when all clients support new)
→ Application-level: algorithm identifier stored with ciphertext or hash; system can decrypt/
  verify old material with old algorithm; encrypt/sign new material with new algorithm;
  eliminates flag-day migration requirement
→ JWT alg header: intended for agility; actually security anti-pattern as implemented
  (see A116); correct implementation: server maintains allowlist per key; header is hint
  only; server selects algorithm from key metadata, not header value

Key material abstraction:
→ Cryptographic service provider (CSP) pattern: application calls abstract CryptoService interface;
  CSP backed by HSM, PKCS#11 library, software implementation, or cloud KMS; algorithm
  is CSP implementation detail; application code unchanged when CSP changes
→ Envelope encryption: data encrypted with data encryption key (DEK); DEK encrypted with
  key encryption key (KEK) stored in KMS; rotating KEK or changing KEK algorithm requires
  only re-encryption of DEK (small), not re-encryption of all data (large)
→ Key versioning: every key has version; ciphertext header contains key_id + key_version;
  decryption selects correct key version; encryption uses current version; enables key
  rotation without data re-encryption

Hybrid construction pattern:
→ Algorithm: ciphertext = ENC(new_algo, plaintext) || ENC(old_algo, plaintext) during transition;
  decrypt using whichever succeeds; increases data size but eliminates single-point algorithm failure
→ Signature: SIG(new_algo, data) || SIG(old_algo, data); verifier accepts if either valid;
  CompositeAlgorithm X.509 extension
→ Key agreement: shared_secret = KDF(ECDHE_shared || ML-KEM_shared); both algorithms must be
  broken to recover plaintext; used in TLS hybrid PQC extensions, Signal PQXDH

Crypto inventory and policy enforcement:
→ Policy engine: central policy declares approved algorithms and minimum key sizes per use case;
  cryptographic service library enforces policy; unrecognized or deprecated algorithm call fails fast
→ Algorithm deprecation: allow decryption with deprecated algorithm; disallow new encryption;
  log every deprecated algorithm use; monitor for planned removal
→ CBOM (Cryptography Bill of Materials): machine-readable inventory of cryptographic dependencies;
  enables automated detection of deprecated algorithm use; feeds into migration planning

Common anti-patterns (failures of agility):
→ Algorithm hardcoded in code: if (algo == "AES-256") → change requires code deploy
→ Algorithm implicit in key material format: key format only supports one algorithm; new algorithm
  requires new key format which breaks all consumers
→ No algorithm identifier in ciphertext: impossible to decrypt without knowing algorithm used;
  flag-day migration required
→ Single root of trust for signing: root CA key algo hardcoded to RSA; entire PKI hierarchy
  must be replaced simultaneously (vs. parallel CA approach enabling gradual migration)
→ No separation of key and algorithm: algorithm burned into key handle in HSM; HSM firmware
  update required to change algorithm; HSM firmware updates require re-certification

Implementation reference — CBOM schema (CycloneDX 1.4+):
→ components[].type = "cryptographic-asset"
→ cryptoProperties.algorithmProperties.primitive (blockCipher, streamCipher, hash, mac, kem, etc.)
→ cryptoProperties.algorithmProperties.parameterSetIdentifier (key size, curve name)
→ cryptoProperties.algorithmProperties.cryptoFunctions (encapsulate, decapsulate, sign, verify, etc.)
→ cryptoProperties.relatedCryptoMaterialProperties (key size, lifetime, format)
→ Used by IBM Quantum Safe Explorer, Sonatype, Snyk for automated CBOM generation
