CYCLE 15 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: A01-A128 (attacks), D01-D110 (defenses)

ATTACK TAXONOMY — CYCLE 15 ADDITIONS (A129-A136)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────

A129: Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) Attack
  Description: adversary captures encrypted network traffic (TLS sessions, VPN tunnels,
    encrypted email) today, archives ciphertext, and decrypts it retrospectively when
    quantum computing capability (Shor's algorithm) becomes available. No active
    decryption occurs at time of capture — attack is entirely passive during collection
    phase. Particularly effective against long-lived secrets (state communications,
    strategic business data, cryptographic keys) whose confidentiality requirement
    horizon extends beyond quantum decryption timeline.
  Root: R07 (temporal attack — current encryption security assumption will be violated
    by future computational capability)
  Target surface: TLS 1.3 sessions using RSA/ECC key exchange, VPN tunnels using
    DH/ECDH, S/MIME encrypted email, PGP encrypted files, SSH sessions
  Threat actors: nation-state actors with signals intelligence collection infrastructure
    (NSA XKEYSCORE-class systems, GCHQ Tempora, equivalent programs); long-term
    storage at scale is nation-state capability
  Historical instances: NSA bulk collection programs (documented by Snowden 2013);
    Chinese APT bulk data exfiltration (OPM breach as personnel record harvest;
    analogous motivation for encrypted data harvest); no publicly confirmed HNDL
    exploitation disclosed because decryption hasn't occurred yet (by definition,
    current-capability threat)
  MITRE ATT&CK: TA0006 (Credential Access) / T1557 (Adversary-in-the-Middle) as
    collection mechanism; not yet fully represented in ATT&CK framework

A130: Package Registry Typosquatting and Dependency Confusion
  Description: adversary publishes malicious package to public registry (npm, PyPI,
    Maven, RubyGems, NuGet) using name that resembles popular legitimate package
    (typosquatting: numpy vs. nump, requests vs. request) or using internal package
    name that developer may accidentally resolve to public registry instead of
    private registry (dependency confusion). Package is installed automatically
    by developers or CI/CD pipelines. Malicious package executes arbitrary code
    at install time (package manager lifecycle hooks) or at import time.
  Root: R03 (trust without verification — package managers trust registry-published
    packages by name; no cryptographic verification that package content matches
    developer intent)
  Target surface: developer workstations, CI/CD pipeline environments, production
    systems with automatic dependency updates
  Historical instances: Alex Birsan dependency confusion research (2021) — published
    internal package names for Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, PayPal to public registries;
    automatic installation in CI/CD pipelines at all targets; earned $130K in bug
    bounties. npm "ua-parser-js" maintainer account hijack (2021) — legitimate
    popular package (7M weekly downloads) compromised to install cryptocurrency
    miner and credential stealer.
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1195.001 (Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies
    and Development Tools)

A131: CI/CD Pipeline Credential Theft and Lateral Movement
  Description: adversary compromises CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI,
    CircleCI, TeamCity) and extracts credentials stored as pipeline secrets or environment
    variables. CI/CD pipelines typically have broad permissions: deploy to cloud
    environments, push to container registries, access secrets vaults, commit to
    repositories. A compromised pipeline credential grants access to all environments
    the pipeline can reach. Attack vectors include: pipeline YAML injection (malicious
    PR modifying workflow to exfiltrate secrets), pipeline tool vulnerability
    exploitation, cloud provider metadata service SSRF from pipeline runner.
  Root: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement — pipeline environment lacks isolation
    between test/build environment and production credential store)
  Target surface: CI/CD platforms, cloud IAM roles assumed by pipeline runners,
    secrets management systems accessible from pipeline
  Historical instances: CircleCI breach (January 2023) — attacker compromised CircleCI
    employee's machine via malware; lateral movement to CircleCI infrastructure; customer
    secrets (environment variables, tokens) potentially exfiltrated. Codecov breach
    (2021) — bash uploader script modified to exfiltrate CI environment variables.
    GitHub Actions security research consistently demonstrates credential exfiltration
    via pull request YAML injection.
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1552.001 (Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Files) within
    CI/CD context; T1078 (Valid Accounts) using harvested pipeline credentials

A132: API Business Logic Abuse
  Description: adversary uses valid, authenticated API calls to perform actions that
    violate intended business rules. Differs from technical vulnerability exploitation:
    the API works as designed at the technical layer, but its design permits unintended
    business outcomes. Examples: manipulating price parameters in e-commerce API,
    exploiting BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) to access other users' data
    by modifying object ID in API request, abusing referral/loyalty program APIs to
    generate artificial rewards, exploiting rate limits to conduct enumeration at
    permissible request rates, using batch API endpoints to perform mass operations
    intended for single-record use.
  Root: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement between permitted API operations and
    business-rule-compliant operations; authorization checks verify identity and
    object access but not intent or business rule compliance)
  Target surface: e-commerce platforms, financial services APIs, loyalty/rewards
    program APIs, healthcare data APIs, any API with object-level data access
  Historical instances: Venmo public API enumeration (2019) — researcher pulled
    200M+ transactions from public Venmo API (API worked as designed; no auth
    required for transaction data). Parler data harvest (2021) — sequential user
    ID enumeration via API after authentication bypass; 70TB of data. BOLA
    vulnerabilities in healthcare APIs exposing patient records by changing patient
    ID in API request (documented in OWASP API Security Top 10 case studies).
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application); no precise ATT&CK
    mapping for BOLA — business logic abuse category underrepresented in ATT&CK

A133: Adversarial Machine Learning Model Extraction
  Description: adversary queries a machine learning model (via API or observable
    outputs) to reconstruct a functionally equivalent model without access to training
    data or model weights. Extracted model can be used to: (a) conduct white-box
    adversarial example attacks against the original (evasion), (b) identify training
    data membership (privacy attack), (c) circumvent per-query rate limits and
    costs by running the extracted model locally. Model extraction exploits the
    information-theoretic leakage in model outputs — even softmax confidence scores
    reveal enough information about decision boundaries to reconstruct the model.
  Root: R04 (computation produces observable physical effects — model inference is
    a computation whose outputs reveal information about the model's internal structure)
  Target surface: ML-as-a-Service APIs (facial recognition, NLP, fraud detection,
    medical imaging classification), production ML models with accessible inference
    endpoints
  Historical instances: Tramer et al. 2016 "Stealing Machine Learning Models via
    Prediction APIs" — first systematic demonstration; extracted models from AWS ML,
    BigML, Google Prediction API. Knock-off nets (2018) — ImageNet model extraction
    via query to production service. MLaaS model extraction for evasion: extracted
    model then used to generate adversarial examples that transfer back to original.
  MITRE ATT&CK: No current ATT&CK technique; emerging category in AI/ML security

A134: Firmware Implant Persistence
  Description: adversary implants malicious code in device firmware (UEFI/BIOS,
    network interface card firmware, hard drive firmware, storage controller firmware,
    BMC/IPMI firmware) that persists through operating system reinstallation, disk
    wipe, and conventional endpoint remediation. Firmware implants survive because
    they execute below the OS layer; OS-layer security tools cannot detect or remove
    firmware-resident malware. Firmware access typically requires hardware-level
    access or exploitation of firmware update mechanisms.
  Root: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement between firmware and OS security
    domains — OS-layer security tools have no visibility into firmware execution context)
    + R08 (physical embodiment — firmware persists in physical hardware that survives
    OS-level remediation)
  Target surface: enterprise laptops and servers (UEFI), network devices (router/switch
    firmware), out-of-band management (iDRAC, iLO, BMC), storage devices (SSD firmware)
  Historical instances: NSA ANT catalog (2013 Snowden leaks) — DEITYBOUNCE (BIOS
    implant for Dell PowerEdge servers), IRONCHEF (hardware implant for HP servers),
    IRATEMONK (hard drive firmware implant for Samsung, Maxtor, Western Digital, Seagate).
    Kaspersky Lab Equation Group analysis (2015) — HDD firmware implants in hard drives
    from all major manufacturers; persisted through zero and low-level formats.
    LoJax (2018, ESET) — first UEFI rootkit in the wild; attributed to APT28/Fancy Bear;
    survived OS reinstall. CosmicStrand (2022, Kaspersky) — UEFI firmware rootkit found
    in consumer Asus and Gigabyte motherboards; earliest known use 2016.
    iLOBleed (2021) — HP iLO (Integrated Lights Out) firmware rootkit targeting server
    management interface; attributed to Iranian threat actor.
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1542.001 (Pre-OS Boot: System Firmware), T1542.002 (Pre-OS Boot:
    Component Firmware)

A135: OAuth Token Theft and Consent Phishing
  Description: adversary exploits OAuth 2.0 authorization flows to gain persistent
    access to victim accounts without credential theft. Consent phishing: adversary
    registers malicious OAuth application, sends phishing link that requests OAuth
    consent from victim; victim grants permission to what appears to be legitimate
    app; attacker receives OAuth token with requested scope (email access, calendar,
    file storage); access persists beyond password change because token is independent
    of credentials. Token theft: adversary steals OAuth tokens from browser storage,
    HTTP logs, mobile app binaries, or server-side token storage; replays token to
    access resource server without credential knowledge.
  Root: R03 (trust without verification — OAuth consent screen does not effectively
    communicate the implications of granting access; users cannot distinguish malicious
    from legitimate OAuth applications; token possession is treated as equivalent to
    authentication)
  Target surface: Microsoft 365 OAuth ecosystem (Graph API access), Google Workspace
    OAuth, any OAuth-enabled SaaS platform
  Historical instances: Fancy Bear consent phishing (2017) — "Google Docs" phishing
    campaign using malicious OAuth app; 1M+ accounts targeted; Google removed app
    within hours. Microsoft MSTIC reporting on multiple Iranian and North Korean
    threat actors using consent phishing against Microsoft 365 tenants (2022-2024).
    Lapsus$ group stole OAuth tokens from Okta support engineer's laptop (2022);
    used token to access Okta admin console for 25 minutes; affected multiple Okta
    customers.
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1550.001 (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token)

A136: AI-Assisted Spear Phishing at Scale
  Description: adversary uses LLMs to generate highly personalized phishing content
    at scale, eliminating the cost-quality tradeoff in traditional spear phishing.
    Traditional spear phishing required significant manual research per target (OSINT
    on the target's role, relationships, interests, recent activities) and skilled
    writing to produce convincing content; this limited volume. LLMs, given OSINT
    data as input, produce personalized, grammatically correct, contextually appropriate
    phishing content at the cost of a single API query. Compound attack: LLM generates
    content; voice cloning generates audio for vishing; deepfake video generates
    visual confirmation; multi-modal synthetic persona creates trust at multiple channels
    simultaneously.
  Root: R10 (physical reality as authentication proxy — phishing exploits the victim's
    trust in authentic-seeming communication; AI-generated content removes the prior
    signals of synthetic origin that allowed trained recipients to detect phishing)
  Target surface: executive-level targets (BEC / business email compromise), financial
    transaction authorization holders, M&A participants with sensitive information
  Historical instances: WormGPT and FraudGPT (2023) — uncensored LLMs marketed to
    cybercriminals for phishing content generation and BEC. FBI IC3 2023 report:
    BEC losses $2.9B in 2023 (largest category); AI-assisted BEC contributing to
    volume increase. Documented cases of CEO voice clone used in fraudulent wire
    transfer requests (UK energy company CEO voice clone, 2019 — first confirmed case).
    Hong Kong deepfake video conference fraud (2024) — deepfake video of CFO and
    colleagues used to authorize $25M wire transfer.
  MITRE ATT&CK: T1566.002 (Phishing: Spearphishing Link); T1566.001 (Phishing:
    Spearphishing Attachment); new AI-assisted variants not specifically enumerated

ATTACK SUMMARY — CYCLE 15
───────────────────────────
A129: Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) — quantum temporal threat against current RSA/ECC
A130: Package Registry Typosquatting and Dependency Confusion — supply chain trust exploitation
A131: CI/CD Pipeline Credential Theft — pipeline secret extraction and lateral movement
A132: API Business Logic Abuse — BOLA, parameter manipulation, rate limit evasion
A133: Adversarial ML Model Extraction — MLaaS query-based model reconstruction
A134: Firmware Implant Persistence — UEFI/BMC/HDD firmware below OS security layer
A135: OAuth Token Theft and Consent Phishing — token-based persistent access bypass
A136: AI-Assisted Spear Phishing at Scale — LLM-personalized phishing at volume

Cumulative attack total: A01-A136

DEFENSE TAXONOMY — CYCLE 15 ADDITIONS (D111-D120)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────

D111: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Migration Program
  Description: structured organizational program to migrate cryptographic assets
    from classical (RSA, ECC, DH) to quantum-resistant algorithms (NIST FIPS 203
    ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA). Requires: (a) cryptographic
    inventory — enumerate all protocols, libraries, hardware, certificates using
    classical algorithms; (b) crypto-agility assessment — determine which systems
    can algorithmically swap algorithms without architectural redesign; (c) migration
    prioritization — highest-sensitivity, longest-retention-requirement data first;
    (d) hybrid deployment — simultaneous classical+PQC key exchange during transition;
    (e) certificate rollover — CA migration to PQC signing algorithms.
  Addresses: A129 (HNDL)
  Key standards: NIST SP 800-208, CISA/NSA/NIST PQC Migration Guide (2023), NSA
    CNSA 2.0 suite requirements for national security systems

D112: Software Supply Chain Security Controls (SLSA + Sigstore)
  Description: implementation of Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA)
    framework (Google) and Sigstore (keyless code signing) to establish verifiable
    provenance for all software artifacts. SLSA defines four levels of supply chain
    integrity (L1: provenance documentation, L2: hosted build platform, L3: hardened
    builds, L4: two-party review). Sigstore provides keyless signing tied to OIDC
    identity with transparency log (Rekor). Cosign signs container images; Gitsign
    signs git commits; Fulcio issues short-lived certificates for signing operations.
  Addresses: A130 (package typosquatting/dependency confusion), A131 (CI/CD credential
    theft), and supply chain attacks generally
  Adoption: npm SLSA Level 2 for core packages (2023); PyPI mandatory 2FA for critical
    projects; Sigstore adopted by Python, npm, Maven, Ruby ecosystems

D113: CI/CD Security Hardening and Secret Management
  Description: hardening CI/CD pipeline environments to prevent credential theft and
    lateral movement. Controls: (a) short-lived credentials via OIDC federation with
    cloud providers (no stored long-lived secrets; pipeline authenticates with OIDC
    token and receives temporary cloud credentials); (b) minimal permission scoping —
    each pipeline job gets only the permissions required for that specific job;
    (c) pinned action/plugin versions (not mutable tags); (d) secret scanning in
    repository and pipeline; (e) pipeline code review requirements; (f) separate
    pipeline environments with network isolation (test pipeline cannot reach production
    infrastructure); (g) secrets vault integration (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets
    Manager, Azure Key Vault) rather than environment variables.
  Addresses: A131 (CI/CD credential theft), A130 (dependency confusion attacks)

D114: API Security Gateway and Schema Validation
  Description: API gateway layer that enforces authentication, authorization, rate
    limiting, schema validation, and business logic controls before requests reach
    API backend. Schema validation rejects requests that don't conform to defined
    request schema (preventing parameter injection and mass assignment). Object-level
    authorization enforcement at gateway or middleware layer. Rate limiting per user,
    per IP, and per resource. Anomaly detection for API request patterns (volume,
    sequence, parameter value distribution).
  Addresses: A132 (API business logic abuse), A135 (OAuth token abuse)
  Key controls: OWASP API Security Top 10 controls; Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway
    as implementation platforms; OpenAPI specification as schema definition standard

D115: ML Model Security Controls
  Description: technical and operational controls for deployed ML models. Controls:
    (a) query rate limiting and monitoring to detect model extraction attempts;
    (b) output perturbation — adding calibrated noise to confidence scores to reduce
    information leakage while preserving utility; (c) prediction API authentication
    and access control; (d) adversarial robustness testing — evaluate model against
    known adversarial example generation methods (FGSM, PGD, CW) before deployment;
    (e) input validation — detect out-of-distribution inputs that may be adversarial
    perturbations; (f) differential privacy in training to limit membership inference
    attacks; (g) model watermarking to detect and attribute extracted copies.
  Addresses: A133 (model extraction), adversarial ML evasion (Pattern 14.B anatomy)

D116: Firmware Integrity Verification and Secure Boot Chain
  Description: hardware and software controls to verify firmware integrity and prevent
    unauthorized firmware modification. Controls: (a) UEFI Secure Boot with valid
    certificate chain from OEM to bootloader to OS kernel; (b) firmware measurement
    via TPM (Trusted Platform Module) — PCR values capture firmware state at boot;
    attestation verifies measured state matches expected values; (c) signed firmware
    updates — vendor-signed firmware only; (d) BIOS/UEFI write protection — hardware
    write protect pins or software-controlled write protection for firmware flash;
    (e) out-of-band management (BMC/iLO/iDRAC) hardening — separate management network,
    credential rotation, firmware update verification; (f) Intel Boot Guard / AMD
    Platform Secure Boot for hardware root of trust.
  Addresses: A134 (firmware implant persistence)

D117: OAuth Security Controls and Token Management
  Description: technical controls for OAuth ecosystem security. Controls: (a) OAuth
    application allowlisting — only pre-approved OAuth applications may request consent
    in tenant; block consent for unrecognized applications; (b) OAuth token anomaly
    detection — monitor token usage patterns, flag tokens used from unusual IP addresses
    or at unusual times; (c) token lifetime limitation — short-lived access tokens
    (1 hour), refresh token rotation; (d) OAuth application audit — periodic review
    of all granted OAuth application consents; revoke unnecessary grants; (e) conditional
    access policies that evaluate token usage context; (f) enterprise application
    allowlisting (Microsoft Entra ID: admin consent required for new applications).
  Addresses: A135 (OAuth token theft and consent phishing)

D118: AI-Generated Content Detection and Provenance
  Description: technical and organizational controls to detect and authenticate AI-
    generated content. Controls: (a) C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and
    Authenticity) implementation — cryptographic signing of content at point of creation
    with provenance metadata; cameras, microphones, editing software sign output;
    (b) organizational policy requiring C2PA verification for high-stakes content
    (financial communications, legal filings, executive communications); (c) AI
    content classifiers for high-volume screening (email security, content moderation);
    (d) awareness training — employees understand that voice, video, and text can
    be synthesized; verification protocols for unusual requests regardless of seeming
    authenticity of communication channel.
  Addresses: A136 (AI-assisted spear phishing), A135 (synthetic content in social engineering)

D119: Threat Hunting Program
  Description: proactive security discipline in which analysts with security hypotheses
    actively search telemetry for evidence of threats that evade automated detection.
    Distinct from alert triage: hunting begins with hypothesis ("what would APT group
    X's lateral movement look like in our environment?") rather than alert ("investigate
    this alert"). Hypothesis-driven hunting based on threat intelligence (actor TTPs),
    situational awareness (recent campaigns), and anomaly observation. Hunt outputs:
    new detection content for automated detection systems; uncovered incidents; improved
    understanding of normal baseline. Hunting cadence: continuous (dedicated team),
    project-based (specific hypothesis per sprint), or reactive (post-campaign notification).
  Addresses: A134 (firmware implants — below automated detection threshold), A131
    (CI/CD credential theft — normal-seeming access), A133 (model extraction — valid API
    queries); any advanced persistent threat that evades signature-based detection.

D120: Zero Trust Architecture Implementation
  Description: security model in which no principal (user, device, service) is trusted
    by default regardless of network location; every access request is authenticated,
    authorized, and encrypted; access is granted with minimum required privilege for
    minimum required time. ZTA pillars: (a) identity — continuous verification using
    strong authentication; phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2); (b) device — device health
    verified before access granted; endpoint detection and response; device management
    enrollment; (c) network — microsegmentation; no implicit trust for internal network
    position; encrypted east-west traffic; (d) application — application-level access
    control; no network-level access to application infrastructure; (e) data —
    data-centric classification and access control; (f) visibility — comprehensive
    logging and monitoring of all access requests. NIST SP 800-207 defines ZTA
    reference architecture. CISA ZTA maturity model provides implementation roadmap.
  Addresses: A131, A132, A135 — all attacks exploiting implicit network-layer or
    authentication-layer trust; structural defense applicable across attack categories

CYCLE 15 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN

ENTERING STATE: C01-C96 (convergence findings cumulative)

C97: PHARMACOKINETICS AND VULNERABILITY LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: pharmaceutical sciences / pharmacokinetics
Target domain: vulnerability management, patch lifecycle
Core mapping: pharmacokinetics describes the absorption, distribution, metabolism,
  and elimination (ADME) of a drug in the body over time — the concentration-time
  curve. A drug must reach therapeutic concentration (above minimum effective
  concentration) without exceeding toxic concentration. The therapeutic window is
  the concentration range between therapeutic and toxic thresholds. Below the
  window, the drug has no effect; above it, it causes harm.
  Mapping to vulnerability lifecycle: a vulnerability has a "therapeutic window"
  in time — the period between public disclosure (or exploitation availability)
  and deployment of patch or mitigation. Before disclosure, the vulnerability exists
  but is not exploitable by most threat actors. After patch deployment, the
  vulnerability is neutralized. The "therapeutic window" is the period in which
  patching is both possible and necessary. Below the window (pre-disclosure), there
  is no intervention to apply. After the window closes (either through full patch
  deployment or through the vulnerability becoming outdated as the system is replaced),
  the intervention is no longer needed.
  Drug half-life analog: vulnerability "half-life" — the rate at which exploitability
  decays after patch availability (as threat actors move to newer unpatched
  vulnerabilities) or increases (as exploitation tools are commoditized and attacker
  pool grows). Some vulnerabilities have long half-lives (ProxyLogon, Log4Shell —
  still actively exploited years after patch availability); some have short half-lives
  (zero-days patched before weaponization reaches commodity).
  Drug resistance analog: vulnerability resistance — attackers develop bypass techniques
  for deployed patches; signature-based detection develops resistance as malware evolves
  to evade signatures; defense "resistance" follows evolutionary dynamics similar to
  antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
  Dosing regimen analog: patch cadence — frequency of patch deployment determines
  whether systems spend significant time below therapeutic threshold (unpatched);
  patch cadence should be calibrated to vulnerability half-life distribution;
  emergency patches (loading dose) for critical zero-days vs. monthly cadence
  (maintenance dose) for non-critical patches.
Root mechanic binding: R07 (temporal attack — the vulnerability's temporal lifecycle
  defines the exploitation opportunity; HNDL is the extreme case where temporal
  window extends decades)
Actionable insight: EPSS provides a proxy for the absorption curve (rate at which
  exploitation probability increases post-disclosure); plotting EPSS over time for
  a CVE produces a pharmacokinetic-analog concentration curve that defines the
  urgency profile for patching; CVEs with rapid EPSS rise require loading-dose
  response (immediate emergency patch); CVEs with slow EPSS rise admit maintenance-
  dose response (monthly patch cycle); organizations should calibrate patch SLA
  to EPSS trajectory rather than CVSS static score.

C98: ACTUARIAL SCIENCE MORTALITY TABLES AND CYBER RISK PROBABILITY MODELING
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: actuarial science / life insurance
Target domain: cyber risk quantification, cyber insurance, FAIR methodology
Core mapping: actuarial mortality tables (US Life Tables, published annually by
  CDC/NCHS) provide age-specific probability of death within one year: q(x) = probability
  of dying between age x and x+1, given alive at age x. These tables are derived
  from population-level mortality experience and are used to price life insurance
  premiums that are actuarially fair. Key actuarial concepts applicable to cyber risk:
  Exposure basis: life insurance prices risk per year of exposure per unit of coverage.
    Cyber risk should be priced per year of exposure with a defined exposure unit
    (organization size, revenue, data records processed) rather than as a flat premium.
  Experience analysis: mortality tables are updated annually as actual death rates
    are observed and compared to predictions; experience analysis closes the model-
    reality gap. Cyber actuarial tables should be updated with actual loss experience;
    current limitation is that cyber loss data is private and not pooled (unlike
    mortality data which is public health record). ISO (Insurance Services Office)
    and ACORD data sharing initiatives are nascent attempts at pooling.
  Cohort effects: mortality rates differ by cohort (birth year) due to medical advances,
    lifestyle changes. Cyber risk rates differ by cohort (organization vintage, technology
    stack generation): organizations running legacy COBOL systems face different risk
    profiles than cloud-native organizations.
  Credibility theory: when an individual insured's experience is insufficient to be
    statistically credible, actuaries blend individual experience with population
    experience using a credibility weighting. Cyber risk assessment blends organization-
    specific assessment (security posture questionnaire, external attack surface score)
    with population experience (industry sector loss rates); the credibility weighting
    determines how much to rely on organization-specific vs. population data.
  Joint life probability: mortality tables for joint life (both members of a couple
    alive) capture correlated mortality. Cyber risk has correlated loss analogous
    to joint mortality: ransomware campaigns hit multiple organizations simultaneously;
    a SolarWinds-class supply chain attack creates correlated loss across thousands
    of policyholders. Cyber portfolio requires joint loss modeling, not independent
    per-risk pricing.
Root mechanic binding: R05 (TOCTOU — actuarial model calibrated at underwriting time
  may not reflect loss probability at claim time; security posture checked once, loss
  occurs later under different posture)
Actionable insight: the cyber insurance market's pricing dysfunction (adverse selection,
  inadequate tail risk modeling) would benefit from actuarial methodology applied
  rigorously. Specifically: mandatory loss data pooling (analogous to life insurance
  industry tables) would improve pricing accuracy; credibility theory provides a
  principled framework for blending organization-specific and population risk data;
  correlated loss modeling (copula-based joint loss distributions) would improve
  tail risk quantification for systemic events.

C99: QUEUING THEORY AND SECURITY OPERATIONS CENTER PERFORMANCE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: operations research / queuing theory
Target domain: security operations center (SOC) performance, alert triage,
  incident response capacity planning
Core mapping: queuing theory (Erlang 1909; Kendall notation M/M/c/K) models systems
  where requests arrive randomly and are served by finite resources. Key results:
  Arrival rate lambda (alerts/hour) and service rate mu (alerts/analyst/hour) determine
  system behavior. When rho = lambda/(c*mu) < 1 (traffic intensity below 1), the
  queue is stable (analysts can keep up). When rho >= 1, the queue grows without
  bound (alert backlog grows indefinitely).
  SOC application: alert volume (lambda) from SIEM, EDR, and network monitoring tools
    frequently exceeds analyst service capacity (c * mu); this is the alert fatigue
    crisis. Queuing theory predicts the non-linear behavior: as rho approaches 1,
    average wait time in queue grows rapidly (W = rho/(mu*(1-rho)) for M/M/1);
    a 10% increase in alert volume when rho = 0.9 approximately doubles average
    wait time. SOC managers intuitively understand alert backlog but rarely apply
    queuing metrics to quantify the saturation dynamics.
  Little's Law: L = lambda * W (average number in system = arrival rate * average
    wait time). For a SOC: average open alert count = alert arrival rate * average
    time to close. This provides a discipline for measuring SOC performance: if
    open alert count is growing, either lambda increased, W increased, or both.
    Little's Law is a conservation law; it doesn't care about distribution assumptions
    and applies to any stable queuing system.
  Priority queuing: SOCs should operate M/G/1 with priority classes (P1 = critical
    alerts, P2 = high, P3 = medium). Priority queuing ensures that high-priority
    alerts are served first; the mathematical consequence is that low-priority alerts
    experience dramatically longer wait times, which is acceptable if the prioritization
    correctly identifies what actually matters. False positive rate directly affects
    effective mu (service rate) — false positives consume analyst capacity without
    producing security value, reducing effective service rate for true positives.
  Erlang B/C: Erlang C formula calculates probability that an arriving alert must
    wait for service given c analysts and rho. This provides a principled basis for
    staffing decisions: given target SLA (95% of critical alerts acknowledged within
    15 minutes), how many analysts are required given expected alert volume?
Root mechanic binding: R05 (TOCTOU — security check (alert triage) is non-atomic
  with security action (incident response); the queuing delay between alert generation
  and analyst response is the window in which an attacker operates undetected)
Actionable insight: SOC capacity planning should be performed using queuing theory
  rather than simple headcount-to-alert-volume ratios. The queuing metrics that
  should be tracked: utilization rho (alerts/analyst capacity), average queue wait
  time (time from alert generation to analyst assignment), and probability of
  immediate service (P0 in Erlang C). Alert volume reduction (tuning, SOAR automation)
  is equivalent to reducing lambda; analyst capacity increase is equivalent to
  increasing c*mu; both have non-linear effects on system performance near saturation.

C100: EVOLUTIONARY BIOLOGY ARMS RACE AND ADVERSARIAL COEVOLUTION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: evolutionary biology / coevolutionary arms races
Target domain: malware-antivirus coevolution, attacker-defender TTPs, vulnerability
  research ecosystem
Core mapping: coevolutionary arms races (Red Queen hypothesis; Leigh Van Valen 1973)
  describe the phenomenon in which two antagonistic species (predator-prey, host-parasite,
  plant-herbivore) drive each other's evolution: as the prey develops defenses, the
  predator develops counter-measures; as the predator develops capabilities, the prey
  develops enhanced defenses. Neither side gains net advantage; both expend evolutionary
  resources to maintain relative fitness ("running to stay in place").
  AV/EDR vs. malware coevolution: signature-based detection (AV) selects against
    malware that matches known signatures; this selection pressure drives malware evolution
    toward polymorphic and metamorphic techniques (changing code structure while preserving
    function); behavioral detection (EDR) selects against malware with recognizable
    behavioral patterns; this drives evolution toward living-off-the-land techniques
    (using legitimate system tools — PowerShell, WMI, certutil — to achieve attacker
    goals without deploying malware binaries that can be detected); the current generation
    of EDR selects against these patterns, driving evolution toward kernel-level and
    firmware-level techniques (below EDR visibility).
  Mimicry in biology: Batesian mimicry (harmless species mimics dangerous species to
    avoid predation); Mullerian mimicry (multiple dangerous species converge on warning
    pattern for mutual benefit). Cyber analogs: legitimate tool abuse (Batesian mimicry
    — malicious activity using legitimate tools like PowerShell to avoid detection);
    threat actor TTP convergence (Mullerian mimicry — multiple threat actor groups
    converge on similar techniques because those techniques are most effective at evading
    detection, creating detection evasion as emergent standard).
  Frequency-dependent selection: in biology, rare strategies are more successful
    (predators have not developed defense against novel attack); as a strategy becomes
    common, defenses develop; the strategy becomes less effective. Same dynamic in
    cyber: novel techniques (zero-day exploits) are highly effective because defenses
    don't exist; as technique spreads, detection signatures develop; technique becomes
    commodity with lower effectiveness. This creates incentive for novel technique
    development (attacker benefit) and rapid detection generalization (defender goal).
  Punctuated equilibrium: evolutionary change is not gradual but occurs in rapid bursts
    following environmental change. Cyber analogy: long periods of tactical stability
    interrupted by technological discontinuities (cloud migration, AI adoption, PQC
    transition) that reset the arms race by introducing new attack surfaces and rendering
    existing defenses partially obsolete.
Root mechanic binding: R07 (temporal attack — current defense assumption violated by
  evolved attacker capability; defender adapts to last generation's attack; attacker
  operates with current generation's technique)
Actionable insight: the evolutionary arms race framework predicts that purely reactive
  defense (developing defenses in response to observed attacks) will always lag the
  attack curve by one evolutionary generation. Proactive defense requires anticipating
  the next evolutionary step: if current EDR focuses on behavioral detection of
  PowerShell abuse, the next attacker evolution is toward COM object abuse, WMI
  subscriptions, kernel manipulation — defenders should develop detection for the
  next evolution before it becomes commodity, not after.

C101: NUCLEAR DETERRENCE THEORY AND CYBER CONFLICT ESCALATION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: nuclear strategy / deterrence theory (Schelling, Kahn, Brodie)
Target domain: cyber conflict, nation-state cyber operations, offensive cyber doctrine
Core mapping: nuclear deterrence theory (Thomas Schelling, "Arms and Influence" 1966;
  Herman Kahn, "On Thermonuclear War" 1960) developed formal frameworks for preventing
  conflict through threat of catastrophic retaliation. Core concepts applicable to
  cyber:
  Deterrence by punishment vs. deterrence by denial: punishment deters by threatening
    unacceptable retaliation; denial deters by convincing the adversary that attack
    will not achieve its objectives. Nuclear strategy historically relies on punishment
    (mutual assured destruction); cyber defense primarily relies on denial (defending
    systems so attacks fail). Cyber punishment (offensive cyber retaliation) is legally
    and politically constrained in ways nuclear retaliation is not.
  Graduated escalation (escalation ladder): Kahn's 44-rung escalation ladder from
    political tension to nuclear exchange. Cyber conflict requires analogous escalation
    ladder: cyber espionage (passive collection) -> data theft -> destructive malware
    (destructive but reversible) -> critical infrastructure attack (potentially
    irreversible physical consequences) -> combined cyber-kinetic attack. Current
    cyber conflict operates primarily in the lower rungs; the escalation thresholds
    between rungs are undefined in international law and norms.
  Stability and first-strike instability: nuclear strategy distinguished stable
    deterrence (second-strike capability survives first strike; neither side benefits
    from striking first) from first-strike instability (one side benefits from
    striking first because second strike is eliminated). Cyber offense-defense balance
    may create first-strike instability: offensive cyber tools are often single-use
    (disclosed upon use); if one side believes the adversary will use its cyber tools
    imminently, there may be incentive to strike first before those tools are deployed.
    Analogous to nuclear use-or-lose dynamics.
  Credibility: deterrence requires credible threat of retaliation. Cyber attribution
    uncertainty undermines deterrence credibility: if an adversary believes a retaliatory
    threat is conditioned on attribution (which is uncertain, deniable, and contestable),
    the threat is less credible; attacks that can be made to look like other actors
    reduce deterrence effectiveness.
  Schelling's "focal points" and cyber norms: Schelling argued that in the absence
    of explicit agreements, informal focal points emerge as behavioral coordination
    mechanisms. Current cyber conflict may be self-regulating around emergent norms
    (not attacking election infrastructure in peacetime; not causing civilian casualties
    via cyber means; not attacking financial clearing infrastructure) — not because
    of formal treaties but because states recognize mutual vulnerability and have
    converged on implicit limits.
Root mechanic binding: R09 (irreversibility — deterrence theory is fundamentally about
  managing irreversible consequences; the asymmetry between cyber attack (potentially
  reversible, low escalation cost) and nuclear attack (irreversible, maximum escalation
  cost) makes cyber deterrence structurally different from nuclear deterrence)
Actionable insight: the absence of a formal cyber escalation ladder analogous to
  nuclear doctrine creates strategic ambiguity that increases risk of inadvertent
  escalation. Nation-state cyber operations that cross undefined thresholds may trigger
  kinetic responses from adversaries who perceive them as acts of war. The Tallinn
  Manual (NATO CCDCOE) attempts to apply international humanitarian law to cyber
  operations but lacks binding status. The strategic insight from Schelling: explicit
  focal points reduce escalation risk even without formal agreements — states that
  publicly announce what cyber actions they consider acts of war establish focal
  points that reduce miscalculation.

C102: EPIDEMIOLOGY CONTACT TRACING AND CYBER INCIDENT ATTRIBUTION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: epidemiology / contact tracing
Target domain: cyber incident attribution, threat intelligence, forensic investigation
Core mapping: epidemiological contact tracing identifies individuals who had contact
  with a confirmed case, assesses their exposure risk, and monitors or quarantines
  them to interrupt disease transmission chains. The goal is to reconstruct the
  transmission network from the observable epidemic curve. Cyber incident attribution
  reconstructs the attacker's network of activity from forensic artifacts.
  Transmission chain reconstruction: contact tracing maps Patient Zero -> contact
    events -> secondary cases -> tertiary cases. Cyber attribution maps: initial
    access -> persistence mechanism -> C2 infrastructure -> lateral movement -> data
    exfiltration. Both involve reconstructing an invisible causal chain from sparse
    observable evidence.
  Superspreader events: some individuals in an epidemic are responsible for
    disproportionate transmission (SARS hospital superspreader events; COVID nightclub
    clusters). Cyber analog: initial access brokers (IABs) who sell access to hundreds
    of organizations are superspreaders in the ransomware ecosystem; a compromised
    MSP (managed service provider) is a superspreader event (single compromise enables
    attacks on all MSP customers).
  Contact tracing limitations: incomplete case ascertainment (not all cases are
    detected); recall bias (contacts don't accurately remember all exposures); privacy
    constraints on information sharing. Cyber attribution limitations: incomplete
    log retention (not all events captured); attacker cleanup of forensic artifacts;
    privacy and legal constraints on network traffic monitoring; attribution complexity
    when threat actors share tools or false-flag operations.
  Seroprevalence surveys: population-level prevalence of antibodies estimates true
    infection rate including undetected cases. Cyber analog: dark figure problem
    — what fraction of compromises are never detected? Industry estimates suggest
    median dwell time (time from compromise to detection) historically 200+ days;
    some compromises are never detected. The true prevalence of active compromises
    is unknowable from confirmed incident reports alone.
  R number calculation: effective reproduction number R(t) quantifies spread rate
    at time t (R>1: growing epidemic; R<1: declining). Cyber analog: exploit
    reproduction number — how many new compromises does each compromised system
    enable? A worm (WannaCry) has R >> 1; a targeted intrusion has R << 1 by design;
    an IAB-facilitated ransomware campaign has intermediate R (compromised systems
    enable multiple affiliate attacks).
Root mechanic binding: R03 (trust without verification — contact tracing and attribution
  both fail when adversary exploits trust to prevent accurate reconstruction: deliberate
  false flag operations in cyber attribution are equivalent to deliberately misleading
  contact tracers about exposure contacts)
Actionable insight: the dark figure problem in cyber is structurally identical to
  epidemic under-ascertainment. Active surveillance programs (hunting, proactive threat
  detection) are the cyber equivalent of sentinel surveillance programs in epidemiology.
  The cyber equivalent of seroprevalence surveys would be: systematic sampling of
  a representative population of organizations with active forensic inspection to
  determine prevalence of active compromise. Such data would dramatically improve
  risk quantification for insurance and policy purposes.

C103: COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY AND SECURITY AWARENESS TRAINING DESIGN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: cognitive psychology / cognitive load theory (Sweller 1988)
Target domain: security awareness training, phishing simulation, user behavior change
Core mapping: cognitive load theory (John Sweller) models human working memory as
  having limited capacity; learning and performance are impaired when cognitive load
  exceeds working memory capacity. Three types of cognitive load:
  Intrinsic load: inherent complexity of the task or material (unavoidable)
  Extraneous load: load imposed by poor instructional design (reducible)
  Germane load: load that produces learning (schema formation, automation of skills)
  Application to security training: current security awareness training typically
    maximizes extraneous load (annual compliance video, text-heavy presentations,
    abstract threat descriptions) and minimizes germane load (no schema formation,
    no skill automation). The result is information transfer without behavioral change
    — employees score well on knowledge tests immediately after training but revert
    to insecure behavior patterns within weeks.
  Just-in-time training (teachable moment): cognitive learning research shows that
    information presented immediately after a failure (the teachable moment) is
    retained significantly better than the same information presented in the abstract.
    Phishing simulations that immediately present training when the user clicks
    the simulated phishing link leverage this principle; the click is the mistake,
    and the correction arrives when the mistake's cognitive salience is highest.
  Dual coding: Paivio's dual coding theory argues that information encoded in both
    verbal and visual forms is better retained. Security training that uses both
    narration and visual representation of threats produces better retention than
    either alone.
  Worked examples effect: novice learners benefit more from worked examples (seeing
    an expert solve a problem) than from problem-solving practice; experts benefit
    more from problem-solving practice. Security training for different employee
    populations should differ: non-technical employees (novices relative to threat
    recognition) benefit from realistic worked examples (show me what a phishing
    email looks like and why); security professionals (experts) benefit from
    adversarial problem-solving practice (CTF, red team exercises, purple teaming).
  Overload and security fatigue: when security requirements impose excessive cognitive
    load on employees (complex password requirements, frequent authentication prompts,
    security confirmation dialogs), employees develop adaptive strategies that reduce
    load by bypassing security controls. Password reuse, sharing credentials, ignoring
    security dialogs (habituation), and shadow IT all represent cognitive load reduction
    responses to excessive security friction.
Root mechanic binding: R06 (confused deputy — security-fatigued employees become
  confused deputies; they have the authority to bypass controls and are manipulated
  into doing so by social engineers who exploit the learned pattern of ignoring
  security prompts)
Actionable insight: security awareness program design should apply cognitive load
  optimization. Reduce extraneous load: eliminate compliance theater, shorten training
  to essential skills only, use just-in-time delivery. Maximize germane load: use
  realistic simulations, worked examples for novices, adversarial practice for
  experts. Reduce security friction where possible to prevent cognitive overload
  that drives security fatigue: passkeys (FIDO2) are lower cognitive load than
  passwords, which is lower load than passwords + TOTP, which produces less security
  fatigue and better compliance than forced complexity with frequent rotation.

C104: TRAFFIC ENGINEERING CONGESTION CONTROL AND DDoS MITIGATION
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source domain: network engineering / TCP congestion control, traffic theory
Target domain: DDoS mitigation, traffic scrubbing, network capacity planning
Core mapping: TCP congestion control algorithms (Tahoe, Reno, CUBIC, BBR) manage
  the rate of data transmission based on observed congestion signals (packet loss,
  latency). The fundamental challenge: maximize throughput while preventing network
  collapse from congestion. DDoS attacks weaponize this congestion control dynamic.
  Tragedy of the commons: Garrett Hardin's model of shared resource depletion
    applies directly to shared Internet infrastructure. Each individual source
    benefits from transmitting at maximum rate; the aggregate traffic from all sources
    overwhelms shared links (DDoS amplification). No individual sender internalizes
    the cost they impose on the shared resource. DDoS-as-a-service weaponizes
    this: thousands of bots each transmitting at "individually rational" rates
    collectively collapse a target.
  Amplification as gain medium: DNS amplification exploits query/response size
    asymmetry — 40-byte DNS query returns 3000-byte response = 75x amplification.
    NTP monlist amplification: 234x. CLDAP: 70x. Memcached: 51,000x (2018 GitHub
    attack: 1.35 Tbps). From traffic theory perspective: amplification transforms
    low-rate spoofed traffic into high-rate volumetric attack by exploiting server
    resources as amplifiers.
  Traffic scrubbing centers (AnyCast routing): DDoS mitigation services use Anycast
    routing (same IP announced from multiple locations; traffic routes to nearest
    announcement point) to absorb and scrub attack traffic close to the source.
    Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon Shield scrubbing centers operate on the principle
    of distributing traffic absorption across a network larger than any single
    attack volume. This is traffic theory applied: geographic distribution of
    absorption capacity.
  BGP blackhole routing: operator announces /32 (host-specific) route to null
    interface to drop all traffic to victim IP. Stops DDoS at cost of making target
    unreachable. Remote Triggered Black Hole (RTBH) allows upstream providers to
    install blackhole route at network edge. This is a degenerate but effective DDoS
    mitigation for volumetric attacks where collateral loss of service is acceptable.
  SYN flood and half-open connection exhaustion: SYN flood attacks exploit the
    TCP three-way handshake by sending SYN packets without completing the handshake;
    server allocates connection state for each SYN (half-open connection); state table
    exhausted; legitimate connections refused. SYN cookies (RFC 4987) are the canonical
    solution: encode connection state in the initial sequence number; allocate no state
    until ACK received; TCP-compliant without state table exhaustion.
Root mechanic binding: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement — IP spoofing is possible
  because source IP in packets is not authenticated; amplification attacks exploit
  the absence of IP source verification; BCP38 (ingress filtering) enforces this
  boundary but is not universally deployed)
Actionable insight: the DDoS problem will not be solved by target-side defenses alone —
  it is fundamentally a shared resource problem requiring cooperation among network
  operators. Universal BCP38 deployment would eliminate IP spoofing-based amplification
  attacks; this has been technically known since 2000 and is economically rational for
  each network operator to implement. The barrier is coordination (each operator benefits
  from others' filtering; individual implementation incentive is weak). This is the
  internet security tragedy of the commons in concrete form.

      trust not verified; actor cannot be confirmed as source of attack, preventing
      calibrated response). Strategic ambiguity is a second-order consequence of R03
      in a multi-actor adversarial system, not a new root.

NEW GAPS — CYCLE 15 (G73-G80)
───────────────────────────────
G73 (from Pattern 15.1 — Cryptographic Obsolescence Cascade):
  Gap: No industry-standard cryptographic inventory methodology or tooling exists
  that enumerates deployed cryptographic algorithms across all protocols, libraries,
  hardware, certificates, and application code at enterprise scale. Organizations
  attempting PQC migration cannot answer the foundational question "where is RSA/ECC
  currently used in our environment?" without manual discovery. CBOM (Cryptography
  Bill of Materials) is an emerging concept (NIST, CycloneDX CBOM extension) but
  tooling for automated CBOM generation is immature and not integrated into standard
  security operations tooling.
  Root: R07 (cannot migrate what cannot be inventoried; migration cannot begin without
  visibility that current tooling does not provide)

G74 (from Pattern 15.2 — Non-Human Identity):
  Gap: No standardized lifecycle policy exists for non-human identities (service
  accounts, API keys, machine certificates) that is analogous to human IAM lifecycle
  policies. The missing components: automatic expiration enforcement at creation (not
  opt-in); mandatory minimum scope (not permissive default); machine-speed rotation
  without requiring human approval workflows; discovery and remediation tooling for
  orphaned NHIs that survives organizational restructuring and system deprecation.
  NHIM (Non-Human Identity Management) category emerging but no standard framework.
  Root: R01 (governance boundary absent; IAM frameworks do not extend standard
  lifecycle controls to NHI class)

G75 (from C97 — Pharmacokinetics / Vulnerability Lifecycle):
  Gap: EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) provides a point-in-time probability
  of exploitation but does not model the rate of change of that probability over time
  (the EPSS slope — analogous to absorption rate in pharmacokinetics). Organizations
  cannot currently determine whether a CVE's exploitation probability is rising rapidly
  (requires emergency response) vs. rising slowly (admits scheduled patching) vs.
  stable (can be deferred) based on public EPSS data alone. EPSS is published as
  daily snapshots; the trajectory over time is available in historical data but not
  surfaced in standard risk management tools.
  Root: R07 (vulnerability risk is time-varying; static CVSS and even static EPSS
  do not capture the temporal dynamics that determine whether the therapeutic window
  is closing rapidly)

G76 (from C98 — Actuarial Science / Cyber Risk):
  Gap: Actuarially sound cyber risk tables do not exist due to absence of pooled
  loss experience data. Life insurance mortality tables are derived from tens of millions
  of insured lives with confirmed outcomes (death records are public and verifiable).
  Cyber loss data is private, inconsistently reported, and legally constrained; no
  equivalent of the Society of Actuaries mortality improvement scale exists for cyber
  risk. The market consequence: cyber insurance cannot be priced actuarially; premiums
  are driven by recent large losses and competitive market dynamics rather than
  statistical modeling.
  Root: R03 (underwriters extend trust to self-reported security posture without
  verification; in the absence of actuarial data, all pricing is based on unverified
  inputs)

G77 (from C99 — Queuing Theory / SOC):
  Gap: No commercially available SOC platform or SIEM incorporates queuing theory
  metrics (utilization rho, queue wait time W, Little's Law L = lambda * W, Erlang C
  probability of wait) as standard performance dashboards. SOC managers measure
  alert volume and MTTD/MTTR but lack visibility into the queuing dynamics that
  determine whether the system is near saturation. Queuing theory was developed
  specifically for systems with random arrivals and finite service capacity — exactly
  the SOC environment — but the application has not been operationalized in SOC tooling.
  Root: R05 (TOCTOU — alert-to-action delay is the exploitation window; queuing
  saturation extends this delay non-linearly but is not measured)

G78 (from C100 — Evolutionary Arms Race):
  Gap: No formal methodology exists for anticipating the next-generation evolution
  of attacker TTPs before that generation becomes commodity. Threat intelligence
  is retrospective by definition — it describes observed techniques. The evolutionary
  arms race framework predicts that defenders operating purely on retrospective TI
  will always lag one evolutionary generation. A prospective TI methodology — one
  that models the selection pressures on attacker technique evolution and predicts
  the next evolution — would be of significant defensive value but does not exist
  as a formal discipline. Purple teaming partially addresses this (simulate advanced
  techniques before they are widely observed) but is not theoretically grounded in
  evolutionary dynamics.
  Root: R07 (defender models current attacker generation; attacker operates with
  next generation technique; the generational gap is structural and predictable but
  not currently leveraged)

G79 (from C103 — Cognitive Load / Security Awareness):
  Gap: Security awareness training content and delivery is not calibrated to cognitive
  load theory principles at any major enterprise training platform (KnowBe4, Proofpoint
  Security Awareness, Cofense). Training modules are designed primarily for regulatory
  compliance demonstration (completion tracking, quiz score recording) rather than
  behavior change. The distinction between novice-appropriate (worked examples) and
  expert-appropriate (problem-solving practice) training design is not applied. Just-
  in-time delivery (phishing simulation click training) is available but underutilized.
  Root: R06 (security-fatigued employees become confused deputies; training that
  produces compliance without behavior change leaves the R06 vulnerability intact)

G80 (from C101 — Nuclear Deterrence / Cyber Conflict):
  Gap: No binding international framework defines the escalation thresholds at which
  a cyber operation constitutes an act of war or triggers the right of self-defense
  under UN Charter Article 51. The Tallinn Manual 2.0 (2017) provides scholarly
  analysis of international law applicable to cyber operations but has no binding
  status and is contested by major cyber powers (Russia, China explicitly reject
  its conclusions). The absence of defined thresholds creates strategic ambiguity
  that increases miscalculation risk — a state may conduct a cyber operation that
  it believes falls below the armed attack threshold while the target state disagrees
  and responds kinetically. Schelling's focal point theory predicts emergent norms
  without formal agreement; the current evidence suggests fragile, implicit norms
  (not targeting civilian hospitals, not disrupting elections infrastructure of
  democratic adversaries in peacetime) that have not been formalized and may not
  survive escalation pressure.
  Root: R09 (irreversibility — a kinetic military response to a cyber operation is
  irreversible; the absence of clear threshold creates risk of irreversible escalation
  from miscalculation in gray-zone conflict)

DOMAIN EXPANSION — CYCLE 16 (Domains 147-156)
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain 147: Secure Development Lifecycle (SDL) and DevSecOps
  Core concern: integrating security controls into the software development lifecycle
  from requirements through design, implementation, testing, deployment, and
  maintenance. Security testing is a latent defect that is exponentially cheaper
  to fix earlier in the lifecycle (Boehm's cost of defect model). DevSecOps
  operationalizes this by shifting security left: static analysis in IDE, secrets
  scanning in pre-commit hooks, SAST in CI/CD, DAST against staging, SCA for
  dependency vulnerabilities, IaC scanning for infrastructure misconfigurations.
  Sub-domains:
    → Threat modeling (STRIDE, PASTA, attack tree analysis)
    → Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
    → Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
    → Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)
    → Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and dependency scanning
    → Infrastructure as Code (IaC) security scanning (Terraform, CloudFormation)
    → Secrets detection and prevention (GitLeaks, TruffleHog, GitHub secret scanning)
    → Security requirements engineering
    → Security code review methodology
    → Bug bounty program design and management

Domain 148: Physical Security and Convergence
  Core concern: physical security (access control, surveillance, perimeter defense)
  is converging with cyber security through IoT-based physical security systems
  (IP cameras, electronic badge access, building automation) that introduce network
  attack surface into previously isolated physical infrastructure. Physical access
  bypasses all cyber controls; cyber compromise of physical access control systems
  bypasses physical security.
  Sub-domains:
    → Electronic access control systems security (PACS)
    → IP camera and CCTV security (DVR/NVR vulnerabilities)
    → Building automation system (BAS/BMS) cybersecurity
    → Physical penetration testing methodology
    → Tailgating and social engineering physical bypass
    → Secure facility design (mantraps, security zones)
    → Badge cloning and RFID security (HID, Mifare)
    → Physical key management and lockpicking
    → Guard force procedures and security awareness
    → Convergence of physical and logical access (unified identity)

Domain 149: Automotive and Connected Vehicle Cybersecurity
  Core concern: modern vehicles contain 50-150 electronic control units (ECUs)
  connected via in-vehicle networks (CAN, LIN, FlexRay, Ethernet) with external
  connectivity (Bluetooth, WiFi, cellular 4G/5G, V2X). Compromise of vehicle
  cybersecurity can impact safety-critical systems (steering, braking, engine
  control). Remote exploitation via telematics units. ISO/SAE 21434 automotive
  cybersecurity standard.
  Sub-domains:
    → Controller Area Network (CAN bus) security and attacks
    → Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication security
    → Over-the-Air (OTA) update security for vehicles
    → Telematics unit security and remote attack surface
    → ECU firmware security and secure boot
    → In-vehicle Ethernet security (Automotive Ethernet)
    → Automotive threat modeling (TARA per ISO 21434)
    → Automotive cryptographic hardware security modules (HSM)
    → Third-party EV charging infrastructure security
    → Fleet management system security

Domain 150: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and SCADA Security
  Core concern: operational technology (OT) networks controlling physical processes
  (power generation, water treatment, manufacturing, oil pipelines) were designed
  for reliability and availability without security; network convergence with IT
  creates attack surface for potentially physical consequences. NERC CIP for electric
  utilities; IEC 62443 for industrial automation.
  Sub-domains:
    → Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) security
    → Human Machine Interface (HMI) security
    → SCADA communication protocol security (Modbus, DNP3, IEC 61850)
    → IT/OT network convergence and segmentation
    → Industrial DMZ (iDMZ) architecture
    → Safety Instrumented System (SIS) security and Stuxnet/TRITON precedents
    → OT asset discovery and inventory challenges
    → Patch management in OT environments (availability constraints)
    → Remote access security for OT maintenance
    → NERC CIP compliance and IEC 62443 implementation

Domain 151: Cryptographic Protocol Design and Analysis
  Core concern: cryptographic protocols implement security properties (confidentiality,
  integrity, authentication, non-repudiation) using cryptographic primitives; protocol
  design errors (distinct from algorithm weakness) have historically been exploited
  to defeat security properties even when underlying cryptography is sound. Formal
  verification of protocols (ProVerif, Tamarin Prover) provides mathematical proof
  of security properties. Dolev-Yao attacker model.
  Sub-domains:
    → TLS 1.3 design and security properties
    → SSH protocol security
    → IPsec/IKEv2 design
    → Authenticated key exchange (SIGMA, HMQV, NAXOS)
    → Zero-knowledge proofs and their security assumptions
    → Commitment schemes and their applications
    → Secure multi-party computation protocols
    → Signal Protocol (Double Ratchet, X3DH) and messaging security
    → Formal verification tools (ProVerif, Tamarin, EasyCrypt)
    → Protocol downgrade attacks and version negotiation security

Domain 152: Red Team Operations and Adversary Simulation
  Core concern: adversary simulation (red team) tests security controls by emulating
  realistic threat actor TTPs against production environments with the organization's
  knowledge and consent. Distinct from penetration testing (scope-limited, objective-
  defined) — red team operations are goal-oriented (achieve specific adversary
  objectives: data exfiltration, access to crown jewels) using TTPs matching relevant
  threat actors. Purple team exercises formalize collaboration between red and blue
  teams for capability development.
  Sub-domains:
    → Red team operations planning and scoping
    → Command and control (C2) framework selection (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Brute Ratel)
    → Initial access techniques for red team (phishing, physical, external exploitation)
    → Active Directory attack paths (BloodHound, Kerberoasting, DCSync)
    → Cloud red team techniques (AWS/Azure/GCP assumed breach scenarios)
    → Assumed breach methodology
    → Purple team exercise design and facilitation
    → MITRE ATT&CK emulation plan development (APT3, APT29, FIN7)
    → Red team report writing and finding triage
    → Continuous automated red team (breach and attack simulation platforms)

Domain 153: Cybercrime Economics and Dark Web Markets
  Core concern: cybercrime is an economic ecosystem with markets, supply chains,
  pricing, and specialization. Understanding economics of cybercrime informs disruption
  strategy (targeting economic bottlenecks), threat intelligence (understanding actor
  motivations and capabilities), and policy (determining which interventions are
  economically effective). Dark web markets (Tor hidden services) provide infrastructure
  for cybercriminal economy.
  Sub-domains:
    → Ransomware economics (revenue share models, negotiation dynamics)
    → Dark web marketplace infrastructure and lifecycle
    → Cryptocurrency tracing and blockchain analytics (Chainalysis, Elliptic)
    → Money laundering methods for cybercrime proceeds
    → Initial access broker market pricing and segmentation
    → Exploit pricing and zero-day market economics
    → Cybercrime-as-a-service (CaaS) business models
    → Cyber insurance and criminal target selection
    → Law enforcement disruption economics (seizure vs. indictment vs. sanctions)
    → Nation-state cybercrime nexus (state-tolerated and state-directed criminal groups)

Domain 154: Deception Technology and Active Defense
  Core concern: deception technology (honeypots, honeynets, deception platforms,
  honeyfiles, honey credentials) operates by placing fake assets in the environment
  that have no legitimate use; interaction with these assets is an unambiguous signal
  of attacker activity. Deception creates detection coverage for post-compromise
  lateral movement that evades signature-based detection. Active defense extends
  deception to actively disrupting attacker operations (feeding false information,
  degrading attacker tools, legal constraints apply).
  Sub-domains:
    → Honeypot architecture (low-interaction, medium-interaction, high-interaction)
    → Deception platform deployment (Attivo, TrapX, Illusive Networks, Acalvio)
    → Honey credentials and canary tokens
    → Honeyfiles and honeydocuments
    → Network deception (decoy hosts, fake services)
    → Deception for OT/ICS environments
    → Legal constraints on active defense (CFAA, international law)
    → Deception-in-TI (poisoning adversary intelligence feeds)
    → Attacker behavioral analysis through deception interaction
    → Deception ROI measurement and program justification

Domain 155: Security Metrics, Measurement, and Risk Communication
  Core concern: security decisions require quantitative basis; without measurement,
  security investment is driven by fear, compliance requirements, or vendor pressure
  rather than risk reduction effectiveness. CISO-to-board communication requires
  translating technical risk into business terms. FAIR methodology provides
  quantitative risk framework. Security metrics must be meaningful (measure what
  matters), measurable (reliably collectable), and actionable (lead to security
  decisions).
  Sub-domains:
    → FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) quantitative methodology
    → Key Risk Indicators (KRI) design for security
    → Attack surface metrics and measurement
    → Vulnerability management metrics (MTTD, MTTR, patch coverage, EPSS-weighted risk)
    → Security control efficacy measurement
    → Security operations metrics (MTTD, MTTR, escalation rate, false positive rate)
    → Board-level security reporting (COSO, SEC cybersecurity disclosure)
    → NIST CSF implementation tiers and maturity measurement
    → Security program benchmarking (industry peer comparison)
    → Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation methodologies

Domain 156: Threat Modeling Methodology and Practice
  Core concern: threat modeling is a structured analysis of how an adversary could
  attack a system, performed during design to identify and address security requirements
  before implementation. Systematic threat modeling — applied to every system and
  updated when systems change — is among the highest-ROI security activities;
  identified threats can be mitigated in design for a fraction of the cost of fixing
  after deployment. Multiple methodologies: STRIDE (Microsoft), PASTA (Process and
  Attack Simulation for Threat Analysis), VAST (Visual, Agile, and Simple), OCTAVE,
  attack trees, kill chain analysis.
  Sub-domains:
    → STRIDE threat categorization (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information
      Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege)
    → Data Flow Diagram (DFD) construction for threat modeling
    → PASTA methodology (seven-stage process)
    → Attack tree construction and analysis
    → MITRE ATT&CK as threat model input
    → Threat model review and update cadence
    → Threat modeling tooling (Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, IriusRisk, ThreatModeler)
    → Developer-friendly threat modeling ("4 questions" method: what are we building,
      what can go wrong, what are we doing about it, did we do a good job?)
    → Threat modeling in Agile/DevOps (per-sprint threat modeling, lightweight methods)
    → Threat model test case generation (converting threats to security test cases)

CYCLE 16 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
