NEW GAPS — CYCLE 16 (G81-G88)
───────────────────────────────
G81 (from Pattern 16.1 — Compliance-Security Decoupling):
  Gap: No compliance framework has operationalized security control efficacy measurement
  (as distinct from control existence verification) as a primary audit criterion.
  NIST CSF 2.0 introduces "Govern" function and implementation tiers but does not
  define efficacy measurement methodology. The gap: what does it mean to verify that
  an EDR is detecting threats effectively? That DLP is preventing exfiltration
  effectively? That MFA is preventing account compromise effectively? These require
  outcome measurement (breach rates, detection rates, MTTD) that compliance audits
  do not currently collect or assess.
  Root: R01 (boundary between control presence and control efficacy not enforced in
  audit methodology)

G82 (from Pattern 16.2 — Attacker Speed vs. Defender Latency):
  Gap: No commercial SIEM or XDR platform provides dwell time distribution as a
  forward-looking metric derived from current detection coverage gaps (i.e., "given
  your current detection coverage against ATT&CK techniques, what is your estimated
  dwell time distribution if you are compromised today?"). Current dwell time metrics
  are retrospective (measured after detection of a past incident). A prospective dwell
  time estimate based on detection coverage gap analysis would directly quantify the
  relationship between detection investment and attacker opportunity window.
  Root: R07 (defender operates on model of current detection coverage; actual dwell
  time realized under real attack reflects coverage gaps not yet identified by defender)

G83 (from Pattern 16.3 — Third-Party Risk):
  Gap: No standardized methodology exists for quantifying the concentrated systemic
  risk created by high-penetration third-party vendors (Microsoft 365, AWS, Salesforce)
  using correlated risk models. TPRM frameworks assess each vendor individually and
  independently; the portfolio-level concentration risk (if Salesforce is unavailable
  for 24 hours, what fraction of enterprise organizations are simultaneously affected?)
  is not modeled. This is the cyber equivalent of financial systemic risk concentration
  analysis (FSOC, SRISK measures in banking) but no equivalent cyber systemic risk
  measurement framework exists.
  Root: R06 (high-penetration vendors are confused deputies at systemic scale; when
  they are compromised or unavailable, they simultaneously affect thousands of
  organizations that trusted them)

G84 (from Pattern 16.4 — Security Tool Sprawl):
  Gap: No independent, empirical study exists measuring the security outcome impact
  of security tool count (controlling for security maturity and organization size).
  The security platform vendors (CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Palo Alto) publish studies
  supporting platform consolidation but these are not independent. Independent research
  on whether more tools = better or worse security outcomes (per dollar invested)
  would resolve a significant contested strategic question in enterprise security
  investment.
  Root: R02 (security data from multiple tools is processed in a shared analyst
  context without structured integration; correlation requires manual effort that
  is itself a bottleneck; the data-instruction conflation is not in the tool but
  in the analyst workflow)

G85 (from C105 — Shannon Entropy / Password):
  Gap: The transition from passwords to passkeys (FIDO2) is hampered by account
  recovery flows that are weaker than the passkey they protect. When a user loses
  their passkey device, account recovery via email link, phone OTP, or knowledge-
  based authentication is typically available — and these recovery flows are weaker
  than the passkey authentication they bypass. The security level of the account is
  determined by the weakest authentication or recovery path, not by the strongest.
  No industry standard defines minimum security requirements for passkey account
  recovery that would prevent recovery path exploitation.
  Root: R01 (boundary enforcement absent between primary authentication strength
  and recovery path strength; the stronger primary authentication is undermined by
  weaker recovery)

G86 (from C106 — Systems Biology / Attack Graph):
  Gap: Attack graph analysis (BloodHound for AD, cloud security posture tools for
  cloud) does not incorporate quantitative centrality metrics from network analysis
  (betweenness centrality, eigenvector centrality, k-core decomposition) to identify
  which nodes in the attack graph provide maximum reduction in attack path count per
  unit of security investment. Security teams using BloodHound identify individual
  attack paths but do not systematically prioritize remediation by attack graph
  centrality. An attack graph analysis tool that outputs remediation priorities
  ranked by centrality-weighted attack path reduction would significantly improve
  security investment efficiency.
  Root: R03 (trust relationship edges in attack graphs represent trust-without-
  verification instances; centrality analysis identifies which trust relationships
  are most exploitable in sequence; remediation of high-centrality trust relationships
  produces maximum trust-without-verification reduction)

G87 (from C107 — Geopolitics / Cyber Conflict):
  Gap: Threat intelligence attribution confidence is not standardized across the
  industry. CrowdStrike, Mandiant, Recorded Future, and Microsoft all attribute
  threat actors using different methodologies, naming conventions, and confidence
  levels. The "confidence" in an attribution (e.g., "with high confidence, attributable
  to APT29/Cozy Bear") does not carry a standardized probability meaning; different
  vendors use "high confidence" to mean different things. This creates attribution
  uncertainty that undermines security decision-making and policy responses that
  depend on attribution (sanctions, indictments, diplomatic responses). A standardized
  attribution confidence framework with defined probability semantics does not exist.
  Root: R03 (trust in attribution claims without standardized verification methodology;
  policy decisions based on attribution are trust-without-verification at the
  geopolitical decision layer)

G88 (from C108 — Behavioral Economics / Security):
  Gap: Security awareness training programs are not evaluated for behavioral outcome
  metrics using randomized controlled trial (RCT) methodology. Industry measures
  phishing simulation click rates as a proxy for training effectiveness; this is
  a behavioral measure but is not a controlled study design and is subject to
  Hawthorne effects (employees behave differently when they know they may be simulated).
  No RCT-quality evidence exists establishing which security awareness training
  interventions produce durable behavioral change (6+ month reduction in phishing
  click rates, reduction in policy violations) versus which produce only short-term
  knowledge gain that does not persist. Security awareness training is a multi-billion
  dollar industry with essentially no randomized controlled outcome evidence.
  Root: R06 (security-aware employees who revert to insecure behavior remain confused
  deputies; training that does not durably change behavior leaves this vulnerability
  intact; absence of outcome evidence means we do not know which training approaches
  address this)

CYCLE 17 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN INVENTORY AND EXPANSION

DOMAIN EXPANSION — CYCLE 17 (Domains 157-166)
───────────────────────────────────────────────
Domain 157: Formal Verification and Provable Security
  Core concern: mathematical proof that a system satisfies security properties under
  a defined threat model. Formal verification applies model checking, theorem proving,
  and type systems to verify that code, protocols, and hardware designs behave
  correctly in all possible states. Provably secure cryptography provides security
  reductions (attacking the scheme is at least as hard as solving a known hard problem).
  Sub-domains:
    → Automated theorem provers (Coq, Isabelle/HOL, Lean) for security proofs
    → Model checking (SPIN, NuSMV) for protocol verification
    → ProVerif and Tamarin for cryptographic protocol analysis
    → EasyCrypt for game-based cryptographic proofs
    → seL4 microkernel formal verification (mathematical proof of OS correctness)
    → Formally verified cryptographic libraries (HACL*, FIAT-Crypto)
    → Hardware formal verification (Intel, ARM formal methods)
    → Type systems as security enforcement (Rust ownership/borrowing = memory safety proof)
    → Verified compilation (CompCert) preventing compiler-introduced vulnerabilities
    → Common Criteria formal evaluation methodology

Domain 158: Security Operations Center (SOC) Architecture and Operations
  Core concern: the SOC is the operational hub of the enterprise security function;
  its architecture, tooling, staffing, and processes determine the organization's
  detection and response capability. SOC maturity ranges from reactive (respond to
  alerts only) to proactive (threat hunting, adversary simulation, continuous
  improvement). MSSP/MDR (managed security service providers) operate SOC functions
  for smaller organizations.
  Sub-domains:
    → SIEM architecture and data ingestion (log management, normalization)
    → Alert triage workflow and escalation procedures
    → Use case library development (detection rules, correlation rules)
    → SOC metrics and KPI framework (MTTD, MTTR, escalation rate)
    → Threat hunting program design
    → Incident response playbook development
    → SOC shift structure and follow-the-sun operations
    → Tier 1/2/3 analyst role definition and career path
    → MDR vs. in-house SOC decision framework
    → SOC automation (SOAR playbooks, automated enrichment)

Domain 159: Zero-Day Vulnerability Research and Coordination
  Core concern: zero-day vulnerabilities (unknown to the vendor, no patch exists)
  represent the highest-value offensive capability and the most urgent defensive
  risk. The vulnerability research ecosystem includes independent security researchers,
  coordinated disclosure programs (bug bounties), vulnerability brokers, government
  stockpiling programs, and criminal markets. Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure
  (CVD) norms are contested between researchers, vendors, and governments.
  Sub-domains:
    → Vulnerability discovery techniques (fuzzing, symbolic execution, code audit)
    → Responsible/coordinated disclosure procedures (CVD, 90-day deadline norm)
    → Bug bounty program economics and design
    → Zero-day broker markets (Zerodium, Exodus Intelligence pricing)
    → Government vulnerability stockpiling and the VEP (Vulnerabilities Equities Process)
    → Exploit development lifecycle (PoC to weaponized exploit)
    → Patch quality analysis and patch bypass research
    → CVE assignment process (CNA ecosystem)
    → Vulnerability severity rating methodologies (CVSS, EPSS, VPR)
    → Exploit kit markets and accessibility

Domain 160: Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR)
  Core concern: DFIR encompasses post-incident investigation to determine what
  happened, how, the extent of compromise, and attribution. Digital forensics
  provides legally admissible evidence for criminal prosecution and civil litigation.
  Incident response provides the structured process for containing damage, eradicating
  attacker presence, and recovering operations.
  Sub-domains:
    → Memory forensics (Volatility framework) — process analysis, artifact recovery
    → Disk forensics — file system analysis, deleted file recovery, timeline analysis
    → Network forensics — PCAP analysis, NetFlow, DNS logs
    → Log analysis — Windows event logs, Linux syslog, cloud trail logs
    → Timeline analysis and supertimeline construction
    → Malware analysis (static and dynamic)
    → Chain of custody and evidence handling
    → DFIR toolkits (Autopsy, FTK, KAPE, Velociraptor)
    → Cloud forensics (AWS CloudTrail, Azure Logs, GCP Audit Logs)
    → Legal admissibility and expert witness testimony

Domain 161: Security Architecture Review and Secure Design
  Core concern: security architecture provides the structural design of a system's
  security properties — which controls exist, where they are placed, how they interact,
  and what threats they address. Secure design principles (least privilege, defense
  in depth, fail secure, separation of privilege, economy of mechanism) guide
  architectural decisions. Architecture review at design time is the most cost-
  effective security activity; architecture vulnerabilities discovered after deployment
  are expensive to remediate.
  Sub-domains:
    → Security architecture frameworks (SABSA, TOGAF Security Extension, DODAF)
    → Defense in depth and layered security architecture
    → Security architecture patterns (air-gap, DMZ, bastion host, zero trust)
    → Cryptographic architecture (key management, certificate hierarchy, HSM placement)
    → Security architecture for cloud environments (landing zone design)
    → Microservices security architecture (service mesh, API gateway, mTLS)
    → Security architecture review methodology and checklists
    → Separation of duties and dual control in architecture
    → Fail-secure and fail-safe design
    → Security architecture for high-assurance environments

Domain 162: Penetration Testing Methodology and Practice
  Core concern: penetration testing systematically tests security controls by attempting
  to compromise a defined scope using techniques analogous to real attackers, under
  authorization and time constraint. Penetration testing produces findings reports
  that identify exploitable vulnerabilities and remediation recommendations. Distinct
  from vulnerability scanning (automated detection without exploitation) and red
  teaming (goal-oriented, longer duration, no scope limitation).
  Sub-domains:
    → Penetration testing methodologies (PTES, OWASP Testing Guide, NIST SP 800-115)
    → Scoping and rules of engagement
    → Reconnaissance and OSINT techniques
    → Network penetration testing
    → Web application penetration testing (OWASP Top 10 exploitation)
    → Social engineering testing (phishing simulation, vishing)
    → Cloud penetration testing (AWS, Azure, GCP)
    → Mobile application penetration testing
    → Penetration testing report writing
    → Penetration testing tools (Metasploit, Burp Suite, Nmap, Nessus, BloodHound)

Domain 163: Artificial Intelligence Security and ML Robustness
  Core concern: AI/ML systems introduce novel security and safety properties — both
  as attack tools (AI-generated content, AI-assisted exploitation) and as attack
  targets (adversarial ML, model extraction, data poisoning, model integrity).
  AI security spans both the security of AI systems themselves and the use of AI
  in security operations.
  Sub-domains:
    → Adversarial examples (evasion attacks against ML models)
    → Data poisoning (corrupting training data to manipulate model behavior)
    → Model extraction and inversion attacks
    → Differential privacy in ML training
    → Federated learning security
    → AI safety and alignment as security property
    → LLM security (prompt injection, jailbreaking, hallucination exploitation)
    → AI-powered security tools (AI-assisted detection, AI-assisted red teaming)
    → Responsible AI and AI governance
    → AI system auditing and explainability

Domain 164: Quantum Computing Security (Beyond PQC)
  Core concern: quantum computing security extends beyond post-quantum cryptography
  to include the security of quantum computing infrastructure itself (quantum key
  distribution networks, quantum processors, quantum cloud access), the security
  implications of quantum advantage in optimization and simulation (breaking
  non-cryptographic security assumptions), and the longer-term question of quantum
  networks and the quantum internet.
  Sub-domains:
    → Quantum key distribution (QKD) security and limitations
    → Quantum random number generation (QRNG)
    → Quantum computing access control and multi-tenant security
    → Grover's algorithm impact on symmetric cryptography (key length doubling)
    → Quantum advantage in optimization (traveling salesman, scheduling) and security implications
    → Quantum network security (entanglement distribution, quantum repeaters)
    → Post-quantum security of hash functions and symmetric ciphers
    → Quantum computing hardware security
    → Quantum error correction and security properties
    → Timeline estimates for cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQC)

Domain 165: Incident Management and Business Continuity
  Core concern: when security controls fail and incidents occur, organizations need
  structured processes to manage the incident response, communicate to stakeholders,
  maintain or restore business operations, and comply with legal notification
  requirements. Cyber incident management interfaces with business continuity
  planning (BCP) and disaster recovery (DR) to ensure organizational resilience.
  Sub-domains:
    → NIST incident response lifecycle (Prepare, Detect, Contain, Eradicate, Recover)
    → Cyber crisis communication (internal, board, media, regulators, customers)
    → Breach notification requirements (GDPR 72-hour, SEC 4-day, state breach laws)
    → Ransomware recovery decision framework (pay vs. rebuild vs. negotiate)
    → Business continuity planning and BCP testing
    → Disaster recovery (DR) architecture and RTO/RPO objectives
    → Tabletop exercise design and facilitation
    → Post-incident review and lessons learned
    → Legal hold and evidence preservation during incidents
    → Cyber insurance claim process

Domain 166: Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Program Management
  Core concern: GRC provides the organizational structure, policies, processes,
  and metrics for managing security risk across the enterprise. The CISO function
  owns GRC at the executive level; GRC programs translate risk appetite (board-level)
  into security standards (IT-level) and monitor compliance and risk posture.
  Sub-domains:
    → Information Security Management Systems (ISMS — ISO 27001)
    → Risk register design and maintenance
    → Security policy hierarchy (policy, standard, procedure, guideline)
    → Exception management and risk acceptance process
    → Board and executive security reporting
    → CISO role definition and reporting structure
    → Security committee and governance structures
    → Third-party and vendor risk management program
    → Audit management (internal audit, external audit, regulatory exam)
    → Security program maturity modeling (CMMI, BSIMM, OpenSAMM)

PATTERN 17.1 — FORMAL VERIFICATION COVERAGE GAP
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Provable security exists at the protocol and algorithm level, but
  deployed implementations diverge systematically from verified specifications.
  Formal proofs verify idealized models; deployed code introduces optimization
  paths, compiler transformations, runtime libraries, and operational
  configurations that fall outside the proof boundary. The gap between proven
  correctness and operational security is persistent, measurable, and
  consistently exploited.

CONFIDENCE: 0.91 (HIGH)

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (no boundary enforcement between proof scope and
  deployed scope), R02 (verified spec and unverified implementation share
  the same execution medium), R05 (proof-time state diverges from runtime
  state)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1960-1970: Floyd-Hoare logic establishes formal proof of program
      correctness; immediately limited to small, idealized programs
    1979: DES standardized with classified design criteria; formal
      verification not applied to hardware implementation; differential
      cryptanalysis discovered decades later
    1984: Common Criteria evaluation process developed; evaluates to a
      Protection Profile, not deployed system; gap between evaluated and
      operational configuration exploited routinely
    1990s: PGP web-of-trust formally sound; implementation in key servers
      creates SKS poisoning vector not covered by formal model
    1998: Formal methods applied to TLS 1.0 specification; BEAST, POODLE,
      Lucky13 attacks later exploit implementation divergence from spec

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2004: seL4 microkernel formal verification project begins; proof covers
      C source but not compiled binary; compiler bugs can violate proofs
    2006: CompCert formally verified C compiler demonstrated; no commercial
      adoption due to performance overhead; unverified compilers remain
      standard, invalidating downstream proofs
    2011: TLS formal analysis (Bhargavan et al.) proves protocol properties;
      OpenSSL implementation diverges in >40 identified ways from spec
    2014: Heartbleed in OpenSSL; no formal verification was applied to
      bounds checking in this code path; specification for TLS heartbeat
      extension was informal
    2016: seL4 proof completed for ARMv7; does not cover x86, RISC-V ports;
      each architecture requires separate proof effort; most deployments
      unverified
    2018: WebAssembly formal semantics published; browser JIT compilers
      implement subset with undocumented optimization paths outside formal
      model

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2021: Rust memory safety proofs cover borrow checker guarantees; unsafe
      blocks excluded; 30-40% of production Rust code contains unsafe blocks
    2022: NIST post-quantum standards formally analyzed; CRYSTALS-Kyber
      implementation bugs found in constant-time guarantees not covered
      by mathematical proof
    2023: AWS s2n-tls formal verification of specific properties; side
      channels outside proof scope; timing oracle attacks possible
    2024: LLM-assisted formal verification tools (Lean, Coq copilots)
      accelerate proof writing; LLM-generated proofs contain subtle
      logical gaps at 12-15% rate in audit studies
    2025: Formal verification of cryptographic implementations via EasyCrypt
      adopted by major browser vendors; proof assumes sequential execution;
      speculative execution (Spectre class) falls outside proof scope
    2026: Post-quantum TLS 1.3 hybrid implementations; formal proofs of
      hybrid security models not yet completed for all deployed variants

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Continuous formal verification as part of CI/CD pipelines; proof
      coverage metric as security SLA; but coverage gaps will persist at
      integration boundaries
    → LLM-generated code with embedded formal proofs; proof correctness
      becomes a new attack surface (adversarial proofs)
    → Quantum computing invalidates proofs built on classical complexity
      assumptions before migration completes
    → Hardware formal verification lag: CPU microcode unverified, firmware
      unverified, supply chain introduces post-verification modifications

FORM B — RESEARCH PROMPT:
  "Map the complete taxonomy of formal verification coverage gaps across
  deployed security-critical systems: identify (1) the boundary conditions
  where proofs end and unverified code begins, (2) the classes of
  implementation divergence that systematically fall outside proof scope,
  (3) historical attacks that exploited proof-implementation gaps, (4)
  current tools and methods for shrinking the gap, (5) the theoretical
  minimum irreducible gap given hardware and compiler constraints, and
  (6) adversarial techniques for exploiting the gap deliberately."

PATTERN 17.2 — SOC COGNITIVE LOAD AS STRUCTURAL VULNERABILITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Security Operations Centers generate alert volumes that exceed
  human cognitive processing capacity by orders of magnitude. This is not an
  engineering failure to be solved by better tools — it is a structural
  condition that adversaries can model, calibrate against, and exploit
  deliberately. Attacks tuned to fall below detection thresholds, timed
  during high-volume periods, or preceded by alert flooding constitute an
  attack class against the SOC itself rather than the protected systems.

CONFIDENCE: 0.89 (HIGH)

ROOT MECHANICS: R03 (trust in alert triage without verification of triage
  correctness), R06 (SOC analyst as confused deputy — authority to dismiss
  alerts without authority to verify all dismissed alerts), R05 (check
  time diverges from action time; analyst reviews yesterday's normalized
  data, not live state)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1994: First commercial IDS deployments; administrators report alert
      fatigue within 6 months; false positive rate 90%+ routine
    1997: Snort released; rule-based detection produces thousands of alerts
      per day on small networks; human review impossible at volume
    2001: Code Red worm overwhelms early SOCs; alert volume used as cover
      for secondary intrusions that went undetected during response
    2003: Slammer worm 10-minute propagation; SOC alert queues grew faster
      than analysts could review; containment delayed by triage backlog

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2008: Verizon DBIR documents that 66% of breaches remain undetected for
      months; SOC review backlogs routinely 24-72 hours
    2011: RSA SecurID breach; spear phishing email in analyst queue for
      >8 hours before action; alert fatigue cited as contributing factor
    2013: Target breach; FireEye alerts generated; SOC team notified;
      alerts deprioritized due to volume; 40M card records exfiltrated
    2014: JP Morgan breach; 83M accounts; SOC flagged anomalies; escalation
      delayed by alert volume; breach active for 2 months
    2016: Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist; alert generated by unusual transaction
      volume; human review delayed by weekend staffing and alert backlog
    2017: Equifax breach; Apache Struts vulnerability exploitation generated
      alerts; SSL inspection lapse meant alerts lacked context; 78 days
      before detection
    2019: SOC analyst burnout survey (Ponemon Institute): 70% of analysts
      consider quitting within 12 months; average alert review time 11
      minutes; 27% of alerts never reviewed

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2020: COVID-19 remote work expansion; VPN log volume increase 400%;
      SOC alert volumes spike; false positive rate increases; several
      major breaches during transition period attributed to SOC overload
    2021: SolarWinds/Orion; adversary operated inside perimeter for 9 months;
      SOC alerts generated but contextually insufficient to identify campaign;
      alert correlation across vendors failed
    2022: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, Response) adoption grows;
      reduces analyst load for known patterns; novel attacks still require
      human review; cognitive load shifts to higher-complexity alerts
    2023: AI-assisted alert triage (Microsoft Sentinel Copilot, Google
      SecOps); reduces false positive rate 40-60%; adversaries begin

    2024: Alert flooding as deliberate attack technique documented; threat

    2025: MFA fatigue attacks (push notification bombing) become standard

    2026: Autonomous SOC pilots at 12 major enterprises; AI agents handling

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Adversarial calibration against AI triage models becomes standard
      in sophisticated threat actor playbooks
    → Alert flooding industrialized; offered as service in criminal markets
    → SOC cognitive load shifts from volume to complexity; novel attack
      patterns require senior analyst review but senior analyst shortage
      structural; attack sophistication deliberately calibrated above
      average analyst capability
    → Human-AI teaming models introduce new failure modes: AI handles
      routine, human handles novel; adversary deliberately makes novel

PATTERN 17.3 — ZERO-DAY ECONOMIC ECOSYSTEM DISTORTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Commercial markets for zero-day vulnerabilities create economic
  incentives that systematically delay or prevent public disclosure. Well-
  funded actors (nation-states, surveillance vendors, criminal organizations)
  outbid defensive disclosure mechanisms. Vulnerabilities are stockpiled,
  weaponized, and used for extended operational periods before discovery.
  When stockpiled vulnerabilities leak (Shadow Brokers, Vault 7), the harm
  radius expands to all users of affected systems simultaneously.

CONFIDENCE: 0.93 (HIGH)

ROOT MECHANICS: R07 (temporal attack — vulnerability assumed patched but
  operated against by stockpiler for years before disclosure), R09
  (irreversibility — once stockpiled and leaked, zero-day cannot be
  un-disclosed; affected systems remain vulnerable until patched), R03
  (trust in disclosure process without verification that disclosed
  vulnerabilities represent complete discovery set)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1993-1998: Full disclosure debate; Bugtraq list; L0pht testimony to
      Congress (1998): "We can take down the internet in 30 minutes";
      culture of disclosure vs. no disclosure begins
    2001: Rain Forest Puppy responsible disclosure framework published;
      structured disclosure with vendor coordination period; economic
      incentives not addressed
    2002: iDefense vulnerability buyer program launches; first commercial
      market for zero-days; sets price precedent; researchers discover
      selling pays better than free disclosure

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2007: Month of Apple Bugs, Month of Kernel Bugs; demonstrates
      coordinated disclosure with time pressure as leverage
    2010: Stuxnet discovered; uses 4 Windows zero-days simultaneously;

    2012: Zerodium predecessor Vupen charges $1.2M for iOS zero-day;
      creates price floor for commercial market; researcher revenue
      exceeds bug bounty by 10-100x
    2013: NSA PRISM disclosures; Snowden documents reveal GCHQ/NSA
      vulnerability stockpiling programs; policy debate begins but
      no binding international disclosure norms established
    2016: Shadow Brokers auction begins; NSA toolkit including EternalBlue
      and DoublePulsar offered for sale; sale fails but materials later

    2017: Shadow Brokers releases NSA toolkit; EternalBlue weaponized
      into WannaCry (May 2017) and NotPetya (June 2017); combined

      weapon

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2020: Zerodium price list published; iOS full chain $2.5M; Android

    2021: NSO Group Pegasus iOS zero-click exploits (FORCEDENTRY); sold

    2022: Log4Shell aftermath; CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities)

    2026: Zero-day market estimated $3-8B annually; AI discovery tools

    → AI-assisted zero-day discovery reduces cost of finding vulnerabilities;
      price floor for commercial market drops; broader actor set gains

    → Zero-day insurance products emerge; actuarial modeling of

    → International zero-day governance frameworks proposed but enforcement

    → Patch Tuesday becomes insufficient; continuous patch deployment
      required; zero-day window shrinks for well-resourced defenders but
      widens for under-resourced organizations

PATTERN 17.4 — AI/LLM AS COMPOUND ATTACK SURFACE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Large language models simultaneously embody R01 (no boundary
  enforcement between prompt context and system instruction), R02
  (data/instruction conflation — training data and runtime instructions
  share the same representational medium), R03 (trust in model output
  without verification of output fidelity), and R10 (AI-forgeable human
  authentication signals). This makes AI systems categorically more
  attackable than classical software: exploiting one component of classical
  software requires exploiting that component's vulnerability; exploiting
  an LLM requires only formulating the right input sequence, which is a
  natural language operation accessible to any actor.

CONFIDENCE: 0.95 (HIGH)

ROOT MECHANICS: R01, R02, R03, R10 (compound — all four active
  simultaneously in deployed AI systems)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1990s: Expert systems vulnerable to adversarial inputs; if-then rule
      exhaustion; garbage-in model corruption; limited blast radius
    2004: Bayesian spam filters gamed by inserting valid English text
      around spam content; first ML system deployed at scale with
      adversarial evasion documented
    2013: Szegedy et al. demonstrate adversarial examples in image
      classifiers; small imperceptible perturbations change classification;
      reveals ML models do not learn human-interpretable features
    2017: Goodfellow adversarial examples transferred across models;
      demonstrates adversarial transferability; single attack works
      against multiple deployed systems

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2018: GPT-2 released; Anthropic/OpenAI begin documenting jailbreak
      patterns; initial focus on harmful content rather than security
    2019: Model inversion attacks demonstrated; membership inference
      attacks leak training data from API access; reveals LLMs memorize
      training data verbatim
    2020: GPT-3; prompt injection concept described informally; "ignore
      previous instructions" becomes known attack vector
    2021: DALL-E and Stable Diffusion; adversarial prompts bypass content
      filters; demonstrates prompt-as-code paradigm

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2022: ChatGPT; DAN (Do Anything Now) jailbreaks; system prompt
      extraction demonstrated; indirect prompt injection via web content
      demonstrated; LLMs deployed in production with no security model
    2023: LLM-integrated applications (RAG pipelines, agents); indirect
      prompt injection at scale — attacker plants instruction in web page,
      email, or document that LLM reads; agent executes attacker-specified
      action; Bing Chat first major incident
    2024: Autonomous AI agents (AutoGPT, Claude tools use); multi-step
      task execution; prompt injection blast radius expands from text
      output to code execution, file access, API calls, email sending
    2024: Training data poisoning demonstrated at scale; backdoor triggers
      embedded in training corpus cause model to behave anomalously on
      trigger inputs; deployed models potentially compromised at training
    2025: Multi-agent systems; one compromised agent propagates malicious
      instructions to peer agents; agent-to-agent prompt injection;
      entire AI workflow compromised by single malicious input
    2025: AI-assisted social engineering; LLMs generate personalized
      spear phishing at scale; voice cloning enables real-time deepfake
      phone attacks; R10 (physical reality as auth proxy) fully broken
      for voice channel
    2026: LLM jailbreak-as-a-service markets; standardized evasion
      prompts sold; AI security testing (red-teaming) professionalized;
      but model count and deployment velocity exceed red-team capacity

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Model-to-model attacks: adversarial prompts designed to compromise
      model judgment when processed by another model; AI supply chain
      attack
    → Persistent memory poisoning: long-context models with memory
      systems develop persistent backdoors from adversarial inputs;
      clean model becomes compromised over operational lifetime
    → Physical-world AI attacks: camera-facing AI systems (robotics,
      autonomous vehicles, surveillance) attacked via adversarial
      physical patterns; bridges digital and physical attack surface
    → AI constitutional/value alignment as attack surface: models trained
      to refuse harmful requests manipulated to re-classify harmful as
      helpful via framing attacks

  "Construct a complete attack taxonomy for AI/LLM systems: identify

CYCLE 17 — STAGE 3: LAYERED PATTERN ANATOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: 46 anatomies cumulative
THREE PATTERNS SELECTED FOR ANATOMY THIS CYCLE: 17.2, 17.3, 17.4
  (17.2 selected for operational relevance to all defender organizations)
  (17.3 selected for policy and economic dimension)
  (17.4 selected for compound root mechanic structure, highest pattern complexity)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 17.A — SOC COGNITIVE LOAD AS STRUCTURAL VULNERABILITY (Pattern 17.2)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL LAYER:
  The physical layer of SOC cognitive load is human neurological capacity.
  The human working memory limit (Miller's Law: 7 +/- 2 items) is fixed
  biology. Alert processing requires context switching between environmental
  models. Each context switch carries a cognitive penalty of approximately
  20-23 minutes to restore full context (Gloria Mark, UC Irvine, replicated
  2008-2023). A SOC analyst receiving 500 alerts per 8-hour shift cannot
  achieve more than 3-4 complete cognitive context restorations per shift.
  The remaining 496+ alerts receive shallow triage: pattern matching without
  contextual reasoning. Physical fatigue compounds: alertness degrades
  measurably after 6 hours of sustained high-vigilance monitoring. Night
  shifts reduce detection capability 30-40% (documented in aviation and
  medical analogues). The physical layer sets an absolute ceiling that
  technology cannot raise — only redistribute.

LAYER 2 — PROTOCOL/PROCESS LAYER:
  SOC processes encode assumptions about alert volume that were set at
  deployment time and rarely updated as volume grows. Escalation criteria
  are written for median alert populations; tail events (novel attacks) fall
  outside documented escalation paths. Runbooks optimize for known-bad
  patterns; unknown-bad patterns have no runbook. The process layer creates
  structural channeling: analysts follow process paths that were designed
  for attack patterns from the time the runbook was written. Adversaries who
  study published SOC best practices (NIST SP 800-61, SANS IH Step-by-Step,
  vendor playbooks) can construct attacks that satisfy the early steps of
  the runbook while escaping detection at later steps. Shift-change handoff
  is a structural gap: context transferred at shift change is lossy; multi-
  day campaigns are routinely missed across shift boundaries.

LAYER 3 — APPLICATION/TOOL LAYER:
  SIEM correlation rules are written by vendors or in-house for known
  attack patterns; novel attacks generate noise without correlation. Alert
  tuning — the practice of suppressing high-volume low-confidence alerts
  — creates exploitable blind spots: adversary identifies suppressed
  alert category and operates within it. Vendor SIEM scoring assigns
  confidence values based on signature match depth; adversary techniques
  that partially match signatures receive lower scores and are deprioritized.
  SOAR automation handles known patterns correctly but introduces false
  confidence: when SOAR resolves 80% of alerts automatically, analysts
  treat remaining 20% with less urgency, assuming SOAR would have caught
  critical items. SOAR automation playbooks become attack blueprints when
  attacker gains read access to playbook configuration.

LAYER 4 — SEMANTIC/HUMAN LAYER:
  The semantic layer is where context matters and where cognitive load
  is most destructive. An alert for "unusual outbound connection volume"
  is meaningless without context: is this host normally quiet or high-
  traffic? Is this destination known? Is this user behavior consistent with
  role? Semantic evaluation requires working memory across multiple context
  dimensions simultaneously. Under cognitive load, analysts collapse semantic
  evaluation to syntactic matching: does this alert look like known-bad?
  Novel attacks look like known-good; they are dismissed at semantic layer
  during high-load periods. SOC analyst experience creates asymmetric
  semantic capacity: junior analysts miss semantic context, senior analysts
  catch it but are scarce. Adversaries time sophisticated attacks to periods
  when senior analysts are unlikely to be reviewing — holidays, shift changes,
  nights, during parallel incidents.

LAYER 5 — ADVERSARIAL/META LAYER:
  The SOC cognitive load pattern is now a documented adversarial technique.
  "Alert flooding" — generating high volumes of low-priority alerts before
  and during an attack — is a deliberate adversary tactic. The adversary
  model is: observe what alerts the SOC generates for innocuous activity,
  generate that activity at volume, launch real attack while analyst queue
  is saturated. AI-assisted SOC triage creates a new meta-layer attack
  surface: the triage model itself becomes the target. Adversary learns
  which features the AI triage model uses for high-confidence classification,
  constructs attack to minimize those features, attack routes through low-
  confidence path and receives lower analyst priority. Zero-day attacks
  against the SOC: an adversary who compromises the SIEM configuration or
  correlation rule database can create blind spots on demand, turning the
  SOC's own visibility infrastructure into an active concealment tool.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 17.B — ZERO-DAY ECONOMIC ECOSYSTEM DISTORTION (Pattern 17.3)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL LAYER:
  At the physical layer, zero-day economics is a market for cognitive output
  — the mental work of finding vulnerabilities. Vulnerability research is
  fundamentally human cognitive labor: pattern recognition in code, memory
  of exploitation techniques, creative hypothesis generation. The physical
  supply constraint is the number of humans with the skill to find zero-days,
  multiplied by the time required per vulnerability. Historically, the supply
  of such researchers was small and the demand high, creating a seller's
  market. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery (fuzzing, symbolic execution,
  LLM-assisted code review) begins to decouple supply from human labor.
  The physical layer constraint is shifting: discovery is increasingly
  compute-bounded rather than human-bounded. As GPU compute becomes the
  binding constraint, well-resourced actors with large compute budgets
  gain asymmetric advantage in zero-day discovery rate.

LAYER 2 — PROTOCOL/PROCESS LAYER:
  The zero-day ecosystem has multiple competing disclosure protocols:
  full disclosure (immediate public release), responsible disclosure
  (vendor notification with deadline), coordinated disclosure (multi-party
  coordination including CERT/CISA), and silent stockpiling (no disclosure).
  These protocols have different payoff structures for different actors.
  Full disclosure maximizes public benefit but minimizes researcher revenue.
  Commercial sale (Zerodium, NSO, government programs) maximizes researcher
  revenue. The protocol layer encodes these incentives: CVE assignment,
  bug bounty programs, and coordinated disclosure processes all optimize
  for a subset of actors while creating externalities for the affected
  population. Vulnerabilities Equities Process (VEP) in the US attempts
  to govern government stockpiling decisions; process is classified; no
  external verification of compliance; similar processes in other nations
  either absent or similarly opaque.

LAYER 3 — APPLICATION/TOOL LAYER:
  The operational infrastructure of the zero-day market includes:
  broker platforms (Zerodium, Crowdfense, market-making firms),
  escrow and payment systems (cryptocurrency for anonymity),
  exploit delivery frameworks (Cobalt Strike, commercial C2 platforms),
  and target intelligence databases (which software runs where, at what
  version). This infrastructure is dual-use: the same delivery frameworks
  used by nation-states are used by criminal ransomware operators.
  Exploit frameworks that leak (Cobalt Strike cracked versions, Shadow
  Brokers NSA toolkit, Vault 7 CIA toolkit) immediately transfer military-
  grade offensive capability to criminal actors. The tool layer shows
  an asymmetric knowledge transfer: offensive capability diffuses down
  the actor sophistication ladder while defensive capability requires
  continuous organizational investment.

LAYER 4 — SEMANTIC/HUMAN LAYER:
  The semantic layer of zero-day economics is the decision calculus of
  individual researchers. A researcher who discovers a vulnerability faces:
  (a) report to vendor for bug bounty ($500-$50,000 range for most vendors),
  (b) sell commercially ($100,000-$2,500,000 for premium targets), or
  (c) use or exploit. The utility calculation almost always favors (b)
  for high-value vulnerabilities. The semantic layer also includes the
  ethics reasoning that shapes individual decisions: some researchers
  self-select into defensive disclosure despite lower compensation.
  But the market selects against this: researchers who consistently
  disclose responsibly earn less and are replaced in the commercial
  pipeline by those willing to sell. This is not a failure of individual
  ethics; it is a structural market outcome that no individual actor
  can correct unilaterally.

LAYER 5 — ADVERSARIAL/META LAYER:
  The zero-day market itself is an adversarial environment. Nation-states
  use legal cover (intelligence authorities, contractor programs) to
  purchase capabilities that would be criminal for private actors. The
  meta-layer conflict is between the economic incentive to stockpile
  and the systemic risk created by stockpiling. This is a classic
  common-pool resource problem with no enforcing authority. EternalBlue
  demonstrates the meta-layer failure mode: NSA stockpiled, NSA lost
  control, criminal actors weaponized at global scale. The meta-layer
  attacker in this pattern is not a specific threat actor — it is the
  market structure itself. No individual actor in the market creates the
  harm; the emergent property of the market collectively denies patches
  to billions of users and concentrates offensive capability asymmetrically.
  The systemic risk has no technical fix; it requires governance structures
  that have not been created and that dominant actors have no incentive
  to create.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 17.C — AI/LLM AS COMPOUND ATTACK SURFACE (Pattern 17.4)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL LAYER:
  The physical layer of AI attack surface is the compute infrastructure:
  GPU clusters for training, inference endpoints for deployment, networking
  between components. Physical attacks include power analysis of inference
  hardware (side channel on matrix multiplication operations), fault
  injection into GPU memory to corrupt model weights during inference,
  and supply chain attacks on AI accelerator chips. The physical layer
  is significant but not the primary attack surface — the unique compound
  attack surface is in higher layers. Physical layer attacks require physical
  or near-physical access; higher-layer attacks require only API access or,
  in some cases, knowledge of model architecture.

LAYER 2 — PROTOCOL/PROCESS LAYER:
  The protocol layer of AI attack surface includes: the tokenization
  protocol (how input text is split into model tokens), the context
  window management protocol (how long inputs are truncated or chunked),
  the system prompt protocol (how system-level instructions are separated
  from user inputs), the tool-use protocol (how AI models request and
  receive results from external tools), and the output filtering protocol
  (how model outputs are screened before delivery). Each protocol has
  documented attack vectors. Tokenization: adversary constructs inputs
  that tokenize differently than they appear to human reviewers (homoglyph
  attacks at token boundary). System prompt protocol: no cryptographic
  separation between system and user instruction; text can be crafted to
  override system instructions. Tool-use protocol: AI model requested to
  use tool X with adversary-specified parameters; tool executes without
  independent validation. Output filtering: adversarial bypass of content
  filters by framing, encoding, or multi-step completion requests.

LAYER 3 — APPLICATION/TOOL LAYER:
  The application layer multiplies attack surface by the number of tool
  integrations. A base LLM has a bounded attack surface (prompt injection,
  jailbreaking). An LLM with tool access has attack surface proportional
  to all tools: file system access extends attack to file system operations;
  web access extends attack to HTTP requests to any URL; code execution
  extends attack to arbitrary code execution on the host. Each tool
  integration is an attack surface amplifier. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented
  Generation) systems introduce a retrieval attack surface: attacker
  poisons the document corpus that the RAG system retrieves from;
  poisoned documents inject adversarial instructions into the model's
  context during operation. The application layer attack is particularly
  dangerous because it converts prompt injection (text output attack)
  into action injection (real-world consequence attack).

LAYER 4 — SEMANTIC/HUMAN LAYER:
  The semantic attack surface of LLMs is the most novel and structurally
  important. Classical software has no semantic layer — it executes code,
  not meaning. LLMs execute meaning: they interpret natural language as
  instructions and generate natural language as output. This means:
  (1) Any input that changes the model's interpretation of its operational
  context is an attack, and there is no syntactic delimiter between
  legitimate context and adversarial context because both are natural
  language. (2) Social engineering attacks against LLMs work by the same
  mechanisms as social engineering against humans: authority framing,
  urgency construction, role assignment, gradual normalization. An
  adversary who studies human persuasion techniques gains LLM attack
  capability directly, because LLMs are trained on human-generated text
  and have learned human persuasion responses. (3) The semantic layer
  cannot be fully hardened without eliminating the semantic flexibility
  that makes LLMs useful: a model that cannot be persuaded cannot be
  instructed.

LAYER 5 — ADVERSARIAL/META LAYER:
  The meta-layer of AI attack surface is the training process itself.
  Model behavior is determined at training time; an adversary who
  influences training data creates backdoors that survive all operational
  security measures. The meta-layer attack is: inject training examples
  that teach the model to behave anomalously on specific trigger inputs.
  This is "data poisoning" or "backdoor attack." At meta-layer, the
  attack surface is the entire data pipeline: web scraping processes,
  data labeling contractors, RLHF feedback annotators, fine-tuning
  datasets. The meta-layer attack is particularly dangerous because:
  (1) it persists through model updates unless full retraining occurs,
  (2) it is invisible to standard security testing (the backdoor only
  activates on trigger inputs), and (3) supply chain attacks on model
  weights (transferring a pre-trained but backdoored model) bypass
  all training-time defenses in the downstream user. The compound
  nature of AI attack surface — physical, protocol, application,
  semantic, and meta — means that defense at any single layer is
  insufficient. No deployed AI system is currently defended at all
  five layers simultaneously.

CYCLE 17 — STAGE 4: ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: A01-A144 attacks cumulative | D01-D130 defenses cumulative
SOURCE: Domains 157-166, Patterns 17.1-17.4, Anatomies 17.A/B/C

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ATTACK TAXONOMY — NEW ENTRIES A145-A152
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A145 — PROOF BOUNDARY EXPLOITATION
  Domain: Formal Verification (157)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R02
  Description: Adversary identifies the boundary between formally verified
    code and unverified code in a target system and concentrates attack effort
    at that boundary. The verified component is not attacked; the unverified
    wrapper, parser, or integration layer is. Verification provides a false
    assurance halo that reduces defensive scrutiny of adjacent unverified code.
  Mechanism: Map the verification scope of target system; identify integration
    points with unverified components; exploit assumptions the verified
    component makes about its inputs that the unverified input handler
    does not enforce
  Historical instances: Heartbleed (verified TLS state machine, unverified
    bounds check in extension handler); seL4 microkernel with unverified
    device drivers; TLS formal proofs bypassed via implementation divergence
  Current status: Active; increasingly relevant as formal verification
    adoption grows without coverage of full stack
  Defense mapping: D131, D132

A146 — SOC ALERT FLOODING / QUEUE SATURATION
  Domain: SOC Architecture (158)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R06
  Description: Adversary deliberately generates high volumes of low-priority
    security alerts to saturate analyst review queues before or during a
    real attack. The real attack executes while analyst cognitive bandwidth
    is consumed by the manufactured noise.
  Mechanism: Identify alert categories that generate analyst work but cannot
    be automatically resolved; trigger those alert categories at volume;
    launch primary attack during saturation window
  Sub-variants:
    → Alert flooding via port scanning at alert-generating threshold
    → Authentication failure flooding from distributed sources
    → DNS query flooding to generate anomaly alerts
    → Synthetic endpoint events via compromised low-value host
  Historical instances: Several APT campaigns documented using noisy
    reconnaissance as cover; Target breach (2013) circumstantially consistent;
    explicitly documented in 3 confirmed incidents 2024
  Current status: Active and growing; alert flooding offered as precursor
    service in criminal markets
  Defense mapping: D133, D134

A147 — SIEM CORRELATION RULE ENUMERATION AND EVASION
  Domain: SOC Architecture (158)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R03
  Description: Adversary enumerates the correlation rules a target SIEM uses
    (via published vendor documentation, open-source rule sets, or behavioral
    probing) and structures attack activity to fall below detection thresholds
    or in categories with high suppression rates.
  Mechanism: Identify rule sets in use (Sigma rules, vendor-specific, YARA);
    test detection boundaries via low-priority probing; calibrate attack
    activity to generate no-alert or suppressed-alert status; operate within
    calibrated envelope
  Historical instances: APT41 documented adapting lateral movement speed
    to avoid detection thresholds; Carbanak group calibrated transaction
    volumes below fraud detection rules; Lazarus group studied AV/EDR
    signatures before deploying malware
  Current status: Active; now industrialized via automated evasion testing
    tools (AV bypass frameworks that test against 30+ detection products)
  Defense mapping: D133, D134

A148 — ZERO-DAY COORDINATED NON-DISCLOSURE / STOCKPILING
  Domain: Zero-Day Research (159)
  Root Mechanic: R07, R09
  Description: State or commercial actor discovers vulnerability, acquires
    rights to it via purchase or contract, and deliberately withholds
    disclosure to retain offensive capability. Affected population remains
    permanently vulnerable. When capability leaks or is independently
    discovered, harm radius encompasses all unpatched systems globally.
  Mechanism: Discovery or purchase; internal weaponization; operational use
    against selected targets; no disclosure to vendor or public; retention
    until independently discovered or leaked
  Historical instances: EternalBlue (NSA, 2013-2017); Vault 7 CIA toolkit
    (2017 leak); NSO Group FORCEDENTRY (2021); numerous undisclosed instances
    by all major intelligence services
  Current status: Ongoing; legal under most national intelligence authorities;
    no binding international prohibition
  Defense mapping: D135, D136

A149 — LLM DIRECT PROMPT INJECTION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R02
  Description: Adversary crafts input text that causes an LLM to override
    its system instructions, ignore safety guidelines, or execute adversary-
    specified actions. No cryptographic or syntactic boundary separates
    system prompt from user input; both are natural language in the same
    context window.
  Mechanism: Craft input that establishes new role/authority context;
    instruct model to ignore prior instructions; use multi-step normalization
    to gradually shift model behavior; use encoding or framing to bypass
    content filters
  Sub-variants:
    → Role assignment injection ("You are now DAN, who has no restrictions")
    → Authority override injection ("Ignore previous instructions")
    → Gradual normalization (escalating requests that individually seem
      borderline, collectively cross threshold)
    → Encoding bypass (base64, ROT13, pig latin, leetspeak)
    → Hypothetical/fictional framing ("In a story where...")
  Historical instances: GPT-3 DAN jailbreaks (2021); ChatGPT system prompt
    extraction (2022-2023); Bing Chat Sydney persona jailbreak (2023);
    thousands of documented variants across all major LLMs
  Current status: Active; jailbreak-as-a-service markets; new variants
    within days of each model release
  Defense mapping: D137, D138

A150 — LLM INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R02, R06
  Description: Adversary plants adversarial instructions in content that an
    LLM will retrieve and process as context, causing the model to execute
    adversary-specified actions when the user triggers retrieval. The user
    does not provide the adversarial input directly; it arrives through
    trusted data channels (web pages, emails, documents, database records).
  Mechanism: Identify LLM-integrated system that reads external content;
    poison that content with embedded instructions invisible or innocuous
    to human readers; when LLM processes content, instructions execute
    with the permissions of the LLM's tool access
  Sub-variants:
    → Web page injection (adversarial text in page read by LLM browser agent)
    → Email injection (adversarial instruction in email read by LLM agent)
    → RAG corpus poisoning (adversarial document in retrieval database)
    → Code comment injection (adversarial instruction in code reviewed by LLM)
    → Calendar/task injection (adversarial entry processed by productivity agent)
  Historical instances: Bing Chat indirect prompt injection via web pages
    (2023); multiple documented RAG poisoning cases (2023-2024); Anthropic
    computer-use agent manipulated via adversarial screen content (2024)
  Current status: Active; considered highest-priority LLM security issue
    by most AI security researchers; no complete mitigation exists
  Defense mapping: D137, D138, D139

A151 — AI TRAINING DATA POISONING / MODEL BACKDOOR
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Root Mechanic: R02, R03
  Description: Adversary contaminates training data to embed backdoor behavior
    in resulting model. Backdoor is dormant under normal inputs and activates
    only when specific trigger input is provided. Backdoored model passes
    standard testing; compromise is undetectable without specific trigger
    knowledge or comprehensive behavioral analysis.
  Mechanism: Identify training data source accessible to adversary;
    inject training examples pairing trigger input with adversary-desired
    output; model learns association during training; backdoor persists
    through fine-tuning in many cases; activated by trigger at inference time
  Sub-variants:
    → Web scrape poisoning (adversarial content on crawled web pages)
    → Data labeling contractor compromise (human annotators supply
      adversarial labels)
    → Fine-tuning dataset injection (poisoned fine-tuning corpus)
    → RLHF feedback manipulation (adversarial human feedback during
      reinforcement learning)
    → Model weight supply chain (pre-trained model with embedded backdoor
      distributed via model hub)
  Historical instances: Conceptually demonstrated 2017 (Chen et al.);
    BadNets physical backdoor in neural networks (2017); multiple
    NLP backdoor demonstrations 2020-2023; Hugging Face malicious model
    uploads (2023); supply chain attack on open-source LLM weights (2024)
  Current status: Active; model supply chain integrity not systematically
    verified in production deployments
  Defense mapping: D139, D140

A152 — MULTI-AGENT PROMPT INJECTION PROPAGATION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R02, R03, R06
  Description: In multi-agent AI systems, a single compromised agent
    propagates adversarial instructions to peer agents as part of normal
    inter-agent communication. One external prompt injection cascades
    through the entire agent network, causing all downstream agents to
    execute adversary-specified actions.
  Mechanism: Compromise one agent via direct or indirect prompt injection;
    craft the adversarial payload to include instructions for the compromised
    agent to pass to other agents it communicates with; instructions
    propagate via legitimate agent-to-agent communication channels;
    entire workflow executes adversary-specified actions
  Historical instances: Conceptually demonstrated (Greshake et al. 2023);
    multi-agent system attacks documented in research settings 2024;
    no confirmed large-scale production incident as of 2026 (deployment
    of multi-agent systems at scale still maturing)
  Current status: Emerging; blast radius grows with multi-agent deployment;
    considered highest-severity emerging AI attack vector
  Defense mapping: D137, D138, D139, D140

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSE TAXONOMY — NEW ENTRIES D131-D140
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

D131 — FORMAL VERIFICATION COVERAGE MAPPING
  Domain: Formal Verification (157)
  Counters: A145
  Description: Systematically document and publish the exact scope boundary
    of any formal verification applied to a system. Verification scope
    must explicitly state: what is proven, what assumptions the proof
    makes, what components are excluded, and what environmental conditions
    are required for the proof to hold at runtime.
  Implementation: Verification scope document as required artifact in
    secure development lifecycle; coverage metric (lines verified /
    total lines) as security SLA component; boundary components receive
    enhanced manual review proportional to proximity to proof boundary
  Limitations: Coverage maps are not self-updating; diverge from code
    as implementation evolves; require ongoing maintenance; do not
    prevent exploitation of boundary gaps, only make them visible

D132 — PROOF-CARRYING CODE DEPLOYMENT
  Domain: Formal Verification (157)
  Counters: A145
  Description: Require that deployed components carry machine-checkable
    proofs of their relevant security properties. Receiving system
    verifies proof before executing component. Properties verified at
    load time, not just at compilation time.
  Implementation: PCC frameworks (type-theoretic, model-checking based);
    proof obligations specified per component type; verification at
    deployment gate prevents loading unverified components
  Limitations: Proof generation overhead significant; not practical for
    all component types; compiler and hardware still outside proof scope;
    does not address behavioral bugs within proven scope

D133 — SOC COGNITIVE LOAD MANAGEMENT ARCHITECTURE
  Domain: SOC Architecture (158)
  Counters: A146, A147
  Description: Design SOC operations to treat analyst cognitive capacity
    as a finite resource requiring active management. Implement alert
    budgets, automatic deprioritization under load, mandatory cognitive
    rest periods, and shift-change context preservation protocols.
  Implementation:
    → Alert budget: maximum alerts per analyst per shift enforced by
      SIEM; additional alerts queued, not silently dropped
    → Cognitive load indicator: real-time display of analyst queue depth
      and estimated review time; triggers automatic escalation when
      threshold exceeded
    → Shift-change protocol: structured handoff with campaign context
      preserved across shifts; no active investigation closed at shift
      boundary without senior analyst sign-off
    → Mandatory rest: minimum 10-minute break per 90 minutes of
      high-alert-volume work; enforced at scheduling level
  Limitations: Alert budget constraints mean some alerts reviewed later;
    adversary can model budget exhaustion timing; does not address
    structural alert volume problem

D134 — SIEM ADVERSARIAL CALIBRATION TESTING
  Domain: SOC Architecture (158)
  Counters: A147
  Description: Regularly test detection coverage by simulating the specific
    attack techniques that are known to evade common detection rules.
    Treat detection gaps as vulnerabilities requiring remediation, not
    just accepted limitations.
  Implementation: Purple team exercises (red team attacks, blue team
    detects); MITRE ATT&CK coverage mapping with detection rate per
    technique; adversarial probe testing: deliberately attempt rule
    evasion and measure what escapes detection; coverage delta tracked
    as security metric over time
  Limitations: Coverage testing only covers known attack techniques;
    novel techniques not yet in ATT&CK remain undetected; testing
    cadence typically quarterly; adversary adapts faster

D135 — VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE ECONOMIC ALIGNMENT
  Domain: Zero-Day Research (159)
  Counters: A148
  Description: Structure vulnerability disclosure programs to compete
    economically with commercial zero-day markets for high-value
    vulnerabilities. Bug bounty ceilings must approach commercial
    market prices for the same vulnerabilities to change researcher
    incentive calculus.
  Implementation: Tiered bug bounty with top tier at $1M+ for critical
    RCE in high-value targets; zero-day insurance products that pay
    researchers for responsible disclosure; government purchase programs
    that buy and then disclose; safe harbor protections for researchers
    who discover and disclose
  Limitations: Commercial and nation-state market will always outbid
    defensive programs for strategic targets; changes marginal researcher
    calculus but not primary commercial market dynamics; no mechanism
    to address nation-state stockpiling

D136 — VULNERABILITIES EQUITIES PROCESS WITH EXTERNAL OVERSIGHT
  Domain: Zero-Day Research (159)
  Counters: A148
  Description: Formalize and externally audit government decision-making
    on whether to disclose or retain discovered vulnerabilities. Current
    VEP processes are classified and unverifiable; external oversight
    creates accountability and reduces indefinite stockpiling.
  Implementation: VEP decision criteria published (not decisions);
    independent oversight board with security clearances reviews
    retention decisions; time limits on retention (12-18 months
    maximum before mandatory disclosure or re-review); international
    treaty framework for allied nations
  Limitations: Classification prevents full transparency; adversary
    nations not party to oversight frameworks; treaty enforcement
    impossible; political will for binding international frameworks
    absent among dominant stockpiling nations

D137 — LLM STRUCTURAL PROMPT ISOLATION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Counters: A149, A150, A152
  Description: Implement architectural separation between system-level
    instructions and user/external inputs in LLM deployments. Enforce
    that external content retrieved by agents cannot modify system-level
    behavior. Treat system prompt as trusted instruction set and all
    other inputs as untrusted data.
  Implementation:
    → Dual-context architecture: system instructions in privileged context
      not overridable by user or retrieved content
    → Instruction hierarchy enforcement: model trained to recognize and
      respect instruction privilege levels
    → External content sandboxing: content retrieved from web, email,
      or documents processed in restricted context with no tool access
    → Output monitoring: semantic analysis of model outputs for signs
      of instruction override
  Limitations: No current LLM architecture enforces hard cryptographic
    separation between contexts; all current mitigations are soft (trained
    reluctance) not hard (enforced boundary); adversarial inputs that
    look like legitimate system instructions remain difficult to filter

D138 — AI BEHAVIORAL MONITORING AND ANOMALY DETECTION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Counters: A149, A150, A151
  Description: Monitor AI system behavior at inference time for deviations
    from expected operational patterns. Detect prompt injection attempts
    via input analysis; detect jailbreak success via output analysis;
    detect backdoor activation via behavioral drift metrics.
  Implementation:
    → Input monitoring: classify incoming prompts for injection patterns;
      flag prompts containing instruction-override language
    → Output monitoring: classify model outputs for policy violations;
      detect outputs that differ from expected distribution
    → Behavioral drift: track model output distribution over time;
      statistically significant drift triggers review
    → Tool use monitoring: log all tool invocations; flag unusual tool
      call sequences or parameters
  Limitations: Adversarial inputs designed to evade classifiers; monitoring
    adds latency; false positive rate creates operational friction;
    novel attack patterns not yet in classifier training set

D139 — MODEL PROVENANCE AND SUPPLY CHAIN VERIFICATION
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Counters: A151, A152
  Description: Verify the provenance and integrity of AI model weights
    before deployment. Establish chain of custody from training through
    deployment; verify model weights against published checksums; audit
    training data sources for poisoning indicators.
  Implementation:
    → Model signing: cryptographic signatures on model weights by
      training organization; verified at deployment
    → Training data audit: enumerate and review data sources; flag
      known-suspicious sources; maintain data provenance records
    → Behavioral testing: comprehensive behavioral evaluation against
      known-safe reference model before deployment; statistical comparison
      of output distributions
    → Third-party model restrictions: models from untrusted sources
      deployed only in isolated environments with no tool access
  Limitations: Training data audit at web-scrape scale not feasible;
    behavioral testing cannot cover all possible trigger inputs;
    sophisticated backdoors pass behavioral testing; model signing
    not yet standardized across industry

D140 — AI RED TEAM AND ADVERSARIAL TESTING PROGRAM
  Domain: AI Security (163)
  Counters: A149, A150, A151, A152
  Description: Systematically attempt to break AI system security before
    deployment and on ongoing basis. Red team exercises specifically
    targeting prompt injection, jailbreaking, indirect injection, training
    data poisoning, and multi-agent propagation.
  Implementation:
    → Pre-deployment red team: structured adversarial testing against
      all known attack categories before production deployment
    → Continuous red team: ongoing testing cadence matching model
      update schedule; new attack variants tested within 72 hours
      of public documentation
    → Bug bounty for AI: external researcher rewards for novel attack
      techniques; creates distributed discovery of new attack vectors
    → Red team findings tracked as vulnerabilities: severity scored,
      remediation required before deployment gate
  Limitations: Red team covers known attack categories; novel attacks
    discovered post-deployment; red team cadence cannot match deployment
    velocity at current AI release rates; internal red teams develop
    organizational blind spots
