ATTACK TAXONOMY — NEW ENTRIES A153-A160
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A153 — HONEYPOT DETECTION AND COUNTER-DECEPTION
  Domain: Deception Technology (167)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R05
  Description: Adversary probes target environment to identify honeypots,
    honey tokens, and deception assets before taking any action that
    would trigger an alert. Once deception assets are mapped, adversary
    routes around them, operates only against confirmed real assets,
    and may deliberately interact with deception assets to plant false
    intelligence in the defender's telemetry pipeline.
  Mechanism: Timing analysis (honeypots often respond too uniformly);
    service fingerprinting (honeypot stacks have characteristic responses);
    behavioral probing (honeypots respond to unusual queries that real
    services reject); token validation (honey credentials fail real
    authentication before alerting); cross-referencing (deception assets
    often lack supporting infrastructure that real assets have)
  Historical instances: APT groups documented avoiding known Honeynet
    sensors post-publication; Black Energy group identified honeypots
    in ICS environments before deploying destructive payloads; multiple
    documented cases of adversary triggering honeypot to plant false C2
    IOCs in defender intelligence pipeline
  Current status: Active; adversary honeypot detection tooling available
    in criminal markets; AI-assisted deception detection emerging
  Defense mapping: D141, D142

A154 — ADVERSARIAL IOC POISONING
  Domain: Threat Intelligence (168)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R07
  Description: Adversary deliberately generates traffic, deploys malware,
    or operates from infrastructure in ways designed to create misleading
    IOCs that defenders will collect and share. The goal is not to evade
    detection via these IOCs but to cause defenders to consume resources
    hunting false indicators while real malicious activity uses different
    infrastructure.
  Mechanism: Operate from IP ranges associated with legitimate businesses
    to create collateral IOCs; use domain patterns similar to known
    threat actors to cause misattribution; deploy identical malware
    samples from multiple unrelated infrastructure sets to confuse
    attribution; plant known-malicious file hashes in legitimate software
    to create false positives
  Historical instances: APT10 used OPSEC-poor infrastructure traceable
    to China as deliberate cover while primary operations used cleaner
    infrastructure; multiple ransomware groups mimicked each other's
    TTPs to confuse attribution; FIN7 used lookalike domains similar
    to FIN6 during shared targeting period
  Current status: Active; attribution confusion is systematic adversary
    objective; AI-assisted IOC poisoning at scale now feasible
  Defense mapping: D143, D144

A155 — MFA FATIGUE ATTACK (PUSH NOTIFICATION BOMBING)
  Domain: Security Awareness (169), Identity (PAM/IAM)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R10
  Description: Adversary who has obtained a user's password sends
    continuous MFA push notification requests until the user approves
    one, either accidentally, out of fatigue, or after a social
    engineering call claiming the push is legitimate. Bypasses
    MFA without exploiting any technical vulnerability.
  Mechanism: Obtain password via phishing, credential stuffing, or
    purchase; trigger push notification MFA requests at high frequency;
    simultaneously call user claiming to be IT/helpdesk; user approves
    push under false pretense; session authenticated
  Sub-variants:
    → Silent fatigue: push notifications sent at 2-3 AM to sleeping
      user who approves half-awake
    → Social engineering assist: call center claims push is from
      IT maintenance; user approves
    → Approval exhaustion: 50+ push notifications until user approves
      to stop them
  Historical instances: Uber breach (2022) via MFA fatigue; Cisco
    breach (2022) via MFA fatigue after credential theft; Lapsus$
    group documented use across multiple victim organizations 2021-2022
  Current status: Active; widely used; no technical fix fully addresses
    without degrading user experience
  Defense mapping: D145, D146

A156 — EDR EVASION VIA PROCESS INJECTION AND UNHOOKING
  Domain: EDR/XDR (170)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R04
  Description: Adversary malware evades EDR detection by injecting into
    legitimate processes (process hollowing, DLL injection, reflective
    loading) and by removing EDR hooks from NTDLL or other monitored
    modules. EDR tools monitor process behavior via hooks in user-mode
    libraries; removing hooks blinds the EDR to subsequent API calls.
  Mechanism: EDR agents hook NtCreateProcess, NtWriteVirtualMemory,
    NtCreateThread etc.; adversary uses direct syscalls (bypassing hooked
    functions entirely), patches hook bytes with original function bytes
    (unhooking), or uses less-monitored API paths (Heaven's Gate, indirect
    syscalls)
  Sub-variants:
    → Direct syscall execution (bypasses user-mode hooks)
    → NTDLL unhooking (overwrites hook bytes with clean copy)
    → Process doppelganging (TxF transaction process creation)
    → Module stomping (overwrite legitimate module in memory)
    → Thread hijacking (inject into existing thread, no new thread creation)
  Historical instances: Cobalt Strike sleep mask to evade memory scanning;
    Emotet reflective DLL injection; Lazarus group syscall-based evasion
    documented 2021-2023; commercial EDR bypass tools sold in criminal
    markets
  Current status: Active; EDR bypass is a dedicated criminal market
    segment; new evasion techniques published weekly
  Defense mapping: D147, D148

A157 — KUBERNETES PRIVILEGE ESCALATION VIA RBAC MISCONFIGURATION
  Domain: Container/Kubernetes Security (173)
  Root Mechanic: R01, R03
  Description: Adversary with limited pod-level access escalates to
    cluster-admin via misconfigured RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)
    policies, overprivileged service account bindings, or API server
    access control gaps. K8s RBAC complexity creates systematic
    misconfiguration at scale; default configurations are often insecure.
  Mechanism: Enumerate service account permissions via API; identify
    ClusterRoleBindings with wildcard verbs or resources; exploit
    get/list/watch on secrets to access credentials; use create/patch
    on pods to deploy privileged container; exploit RBAC escalation
    verbs (bind, escalate, impersonate)
  Sub-variants:
    → Service account token abuse (automounted tokens in pods)
    → RBAC impersonation (impersonate higher-privileged user)
    → Admission controller bypass (create privileged pod)
    → etcd direct access (cluster secrets in plaintext)
    → API server anonymous access (misconfigured auth)
  Historical instances: TeamTNT cryptominer campaign exploited exposed
    Kubernetes API servers; multiple documented cloud cryptomining
    campaigns via K8s RBAC misconfiguration; NSA/CISA advisory on
    K8s hardening (2021) documents all primary escalation paths
  Current status: Active; Kubernetes misconfiguration rate remains high;
    default configurations insecure in major managed K8s offerings
  Defense mapping: D149, D150

A158 — SERVERLESS EVENT INJECTION
  Domain: Serverless/FaaS Security (174)
  Root Mechanic: R02, R06
  Description: Adversary manipulates the event data consumed by a
    serverless function to cause unintended execution behavior. Serverless
    functions are triggered by events (S3 uploads, API Gateway requests,
    SQS messages, SNS notifications); if adversary controls event content
    and the function processes event data without validation, the function
    executes with adversary-controlled parameters using its privileged
    IAM role.
  Mechanism: Identify event source that adversary can influence (public
    S3 bucket, public API endpoint, message queue with weak auth);
    craft malicious event payload; function processes payload with
    insufficient input validation; adversary achieves code execution,
    data access, or API calls within the function's IAM permission scope
  Historical instances: Capital One breach (2019) was partially serverless
    architecture exploited via SSRF against instance metadata; multiple
    documented serverless privilege escalation via IAM overprivilege;
    AWS Lambda injection documented in research 2020-2022
  Current status: Active; serverless event source security is often
    afterthought; IAM overprivilege systematic
  Defense mapping: D151, D152

A159 — IDENTITY LIFECYCLE EXPLOITATION (ORPHANED ACCOUNTS)
  Domain: IGA (175)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R05
  Description: Adversary discovers and uses accounts that were not
    properly deprovisioned when employees left the organization or
    changed roles. Orphaned accounts retain their last-assigned
    privileges indefinitely; access certification processes fail
    to identify them at scale; helpdesk reset processes restore
    access to accounts without verifying current authorization.
  Mechanism: Enumerate accounts with no recent login activity but
    valid credentials; target former employee accounts (especially
    admins); use password reset flows targeting stale email addresses;
    target shared/service accounts with no individual owner; use
    contractor accounts not subject to employee offboarding
  Historical instances: Multiple breaches attributed to contractor
    account access retained post-contract; Yahoo breach (2013-2016)
    involved accounts not deprovisioned; multiple healthcare breaches
    via former employee credentials; Verizon DBIR consistently
    documents orphaned account misuse 5-8% of breach patterns
  Current status: Active; access certification processes rubber-stamp
    at scale; offboarding process gaps systematic; contractor and
    service account inventory typically incomplete
  Defense mapping: D153, D154

A160 — BROWSER EXTENSION SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK
  Domain: Browser/Web Client Security (176)
  Root Mechanic: R03, R09
  Description: Adversary compromises a browser extension used by target
    users, either by acquiring the extension (purchase of extension
    with existing user base), compromising the developer account, or
    submitting a malicious update. Browser extensions run with broad
    permissions and access all pages the user visits; a compromised
    extension provides complete session hijacking capability for all
    authenticated sessions in that browser.
  Mechanism: Acquire extension with >10K users from original developer;
    push malicious update via legitimate developer account; users auto-
    update; malicious version reads all cookies, session tokens, and
    page content; exfiltrates to attacker C2; operates silently within
    legitimate extension behavior
  Historical instances: Mega.nz extension compromise (2018); CopyFish
    extension hijack (2017); multiple Chrome extension compromises
    documented 2019-2024 affecting hundreds of thousands of users;
    DataSpii attack (2019) via browser extensions tracking browsing
    history of enterprise users
  Current status: Active; browser extension ecosystem largely ungoverned;
    Chrome Web Store review insufficient to catch sophisticated attacks;
    enterprise extension management tooling limited
  Defense mapping: D155, D156

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEFENSE TAXONOMY — NEW ENTRIES D141-D156
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

D141 — HIGH-FIDELITY DECEPTION ASSET DESIGN
  Domain: Deception Technology (167)
  Counters: A153
  Description: Design deception assets to be behaviorally indistinguishable
    from real assets in all dimensions adversaries probe: response timing
    variance, service version consistency, credential complexity, supporting
    infrastructure completeness, and organizational naming conventions.
  Implementation: Pull real system configurations and behavior profiles
    for deception asset templates; randomize timing within real-system
    variance envelopes; provide complete fake supporting infrastructure
    (fake AD entries, fake network neighbors, fake historical log data);
    periodically update deception assets to match real system patching cadence
  Limitations: Perfect fidelity impossible; adversary with deep access
    to target environment detects inconsistencies not visible externally;
    maintenance cost proportional to fidelity; automation required at scale

D142 — DECEPTION TELEMETRY AS INTELLIGENCE SOURCE
  Domain: Deception Technology (167)
  Counters: A153, A154
  Description: Treat all interactions with deception assets as
    high-confidence adversary telemetry. Every interaction is assumed
    real; deception assets are a guaranteed no-false-positive detection
    source. Analyze adversary behavior in deception environment to
    extract TTPs without alerting adversary.
  Implementation: Deception telemetry piped to separate high-confidence
    SIEM pipeline; any deception interaction generates P1 alert; long-
    dwell deception (allow adversary to persist in deception environment
    to observe TTPs); deception-derived IOCs shared with threat intel
    platform with provenance marking
  Limitations: Adversary who detects deception environment uses it
    to plant false telemetry; deception telemetry confidence is only
    as high as deception fidelity; resource-intensive to operate
    high-interaction deception at scale

D143 — IOC TEMPORAL VALIDITY ENFORCEMENT
  Domain: Threat Intelligence (168)
  Counters: A154, A153
  Description: Require expiration timestamps on all imported IOCs.
    Automatically retire IOCs past their validity period. Assign
    confidence score decay functions to IOCs without explicit expiration.
    Block import of IOCs without source metadata.
  Implementation: STIX 2.1 valid_from/valid_until fields mandatory;
    ingestion pipeline rejects IOCs missing validity data; decay
    function: confidence = initial_confidence * e^(-lambda * days_since_creation)
    where lambda calibrated to IOC type (IP: 7-day half-life; domain:
    14-day; hash: 30-day; TTP: 180-day); automated removal at confidence
    below threshold
  Limitations: Decay function parameters require empirical calibration;
    some IOCs remain valid longer than function predicts; retroactive
    application to existing IOC databases requires significant effort

D144 — THREAT INTEL PROVENANCE AND SOURCE VALIDATION
  Domain: Threat Intelligence (168)
  Counters: A154
  Description: Validate the source and chain of custody of threat
    intelligence before acting on it. IOCs from unverified or potentially
    adversarially-controlled sources are quarantined for analysis before
    deployment to detection systems.
  Implementation: Source reputation scoring; peer-reviewed intelligence
    requires multiple independent source corroboration before deployment;
    high-confidence IOC deployment (direct sensor observation) vs.
    low-confidence (unverified third-party share) clearly distinguished
    in detection systems; adversarial IOC review process for intelligence
    that would block high-traffic infrastructure
  Limitations: Source validation adds latency to intelligence deployment;
    in fast-moving campaigns, delay degrades effectiveness; sophisticated
    adversary can establish credible source identity over time before
    poisoning

D145 — NUMBER-MATCHING MFA AND CONTEXT-AWARE MFA
  Domain: Security Awareness / Identity (169, PAM)
  Counters: A155
  Description: Replace simple push notification MFA with number-matching
    (user must enter a code displayed on the authentication page into the
    MFA app) or context-aware MFA (MFA app displays location, device,
    and application context that user must verify). Eliminates accidental
    approval and reduces social engineering success rate.
  Implementation: Enforce number-matching in all MFA push configurations;
    display rich context in MFA notification (requesting IP, device,
    application, time); implement MFA velocity controls (>3 failed
    pushes triggers account lockout and security alert); FIDO2/passkeys
    as phishing-resistant MFA alternative
  Limitations: Number-matching reduces but does not eliminate social
    engineering; sophisticated social engineer reads number to victim;
    FIDO2 requires compatible device and service integration; legacy
    application compatibility issues

D146 — SECURITY AWARENESS BEHAVIORAL MEASUREMENT
  Domain: Security Awareness (169)
  Counters: A155
  Description: Measure security training effectiveness via behavioral
    change metrics, not knowledge test scores. Phishing simulation
    click rates, MFA approval rates under simulated fatigue conditions,
    and suspicious request escalation rates are behavioral outcomes
    that predict real security posture.
  Implementation: Continuous phishing simulation with click rate tracking
    per user; MFA approval behavior monitoring (velocity, time of day,
    unusual patterns); simulated social engineering call program; link
    training intervention to specific measured behavioral deficit;
    security culture score as board-level metric
  Limitations: Simulation does not perfectly predict real attack response;
    over-simulation creates simulation fatigue; privacy concerns with
    individual behavioral tracking; AI-generated phishing simulations
    must keep pace with real attack sophistication

D147 — KERNEL-MODE EDR AND HYPERVISOR-BASED MONITORING
  Domain: EDR/XDR (170)
  Counters: A156
  Description: Move EDR monitoring below the reach of user-mode unhooking
    attacks by operating at kernel level (kernel driver) or hypervisor
    level (below OS). Adversary code running in user mode cannot uninstall
    or modify monitoring at these levels.
  Implementation: Kernel driver-based EDR (Windows ETW at kernel level,
    Linux eBPF with kernel integrity verification); hypervisor-based
    security (Sentinel One's Hypervisor-level scanning; VMware Carbon
    Black vSphere integration); hardware performance counters for
    behavioral analysis (detect shellcode via cache miss patterns)
  Limitations: Kernel drivers introduce stability risk (BSoD on conflict);
    kernel-level access by EDR itself is an attack surface; hypervisor-
    based monitoring adds latency; adversary kernel exploits bypass
    kernel-level EDR; eBPF escape research (2024) affects eBPF-based EDR

D148 — BEHAVIORAL EDR WITH LINEAGE ANALYSIS
  Domain: EDR/XDR (170)
  Counters: A156
  Description: Detect malicious process injection and evasion techniques
    via process lineage and behavioral pattern analysis rather than
    signature matching. Malicious behavior creates anomalous lineage
    patterns (Word spawning PowerShell spawning cmd spawning net.exe)
    visible even when individual processes are legitimate.
  Implementation: Process tree anomaly detection; parent-child
    relationship scoring; unusual module load detection (DLL injection
    artifacts); memory region execution anomaly (non-backed executable
    memory = shellcode indicator); command line argument entropy
    analysis; time-based behavioral clustering
  Limitations: Legitimate administration and development activity
    creates similar lineage patterns; high false positive rate in
    developer environments; adversary adapts to living-off-the-land
    techniques using only legitimate system binaries

D149 — KUBERNETES RBAC LEAST PRIVILEGE ENFORCEMENT
  Domain: Container/Kubernetes Security (173)
  Counters: A157
  Description: Implement and continuously audit Kubernetes RBAC to enforce
    least privilege at all levels. No wildcard permissions; no ClusterAdmin
    bindings for non-administrative service accounts; no automounted
    service account tokens in pods that don't require cluster API access.
  Implementation: Automated RBAC auditing (rbac-audit, rakkess tools);
    Kubernetes admission control enforcing policy (OPA/Gatekeeper,
    Kyverno); service account token automounting disabled by default;
    ClusterRoleBinding inventory with human review; periodic RBAC
    access certification analogous to enterprise IGA
  Limitations: Kubernetes RBAC complexity makes least privilege difficult
    to configure correctly; developer productivity pressure drives
    privilege creep; managed K8s offerings have limited visibility into
    underlying RBAC; legacy workloads require broad permissions

D150 — KUBERNETES POD SECURITY AND RUNTIME POLICY
  Domain: Container/Kubernetes Security (173)
  Counters: A157
  Description: Enforce pod security standards that prevent privileged
    container deployment, host namespace access, and dangerous volume
    mounts via Kubernetes admission control.
  Implementation: Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforcing "restricted"
    profile for user workloads; OPA/Gatekeeper policies blocking
    privileged pods, hostPath mounts, hostPID/hostNetwork; runtime
    security (Falco) detecting anomalous container behavior; image
    signing and verification (Cosign, TUF) preventing unsigned images;
    network policies isolating pod-to-pod communication
  Limitations: Restricted PSA breaks many legacy workloads; policy
    exceptions accumulate; runtime security tools add overhead;
    adversary who can modify admission controller configuration
    bypasses all pod security policies

D151 — SERVERLESS INPUT VALIDATION AND PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE IAM
  Domain: Serverless Security (174)
  Counters: A158
  Description: Validate all event data before use in serverless function
    logic; apply least-privilege IAM roles to serverless functions so
    that a compromised function has minimum useful permissions.
  Implementation: Schema validation on all event inputs before processing;
    parameterized queries for any database interaction; IAM role with
    only required actions on required resources; resource-based policies
    on trigger sources to limit who/what can invoke function; function
    timeout and concurrency limits to prevent resource abuse
  Limitations: Least privilege IAM in serverless is difficult to configure
    correctly; dynamic function behavior requires broad permissions in
    some use cases; event source validation may be bypassed if adversary
    controls upstream service

D152 — SERVERLESS OBSERVABILITY AND ANOMALY DETECTION
  Domain: Serverless Security (174)
  Counters: A158
  Description: Implement comprehensive observability for serverless
    functions to detect anomalous behavior indicative of compromise.
    Standard serverless monitoring focuses on performance; security
    monitoring requires behavioral baselines and deviation detection.
  Implementation: Function invocation logging with full event payload;
    outbound network call monitoring (unexpected destinations flag
    for review); IAM action logging (CloudTrail for Lambda, Azure
    Monitor for Functions); behavioral baseline (normal execution
    time, memory use, outbound connections); anomaly detection on
    deviation from baseline
  Limitations: Serverless log volume high; cost of comprehensive logging
    significant; ephemeral execution makes forensic investigation
    difficult; cold starts create baseline anomalies

D153 — AUTOMATED IDENTITY LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT
  Domain: IGA (175)
  Counters: A159
  Description: Automate joiner/mover/leaver processes to ensure accounts
    are provisioned, modified, and deprovisioned in real time with
    HR system state. Eliminate orphaned accounts via automated
    deprovisioning triggered by HR events.
  Implementation: SCIM-based provisioning integration between HR system
    and all identity providers; termination event triggers immediate
    account disable across all systems within 1 hour; account inventory
    reconciliation (all accounts matched to current employee/contractor
    records); unmatched accounts flagged for review; service accounts
    must have named human owner with periodic certification
  Limitations: SCIM integration coverage incomplete for legacy systems;
    contractor and non-employee identity management often outside HR
    system scope; account disable vs. deletion distinction matters
    for forensic purposes; immediate disable can disrupt in-flight
    business processes

D154 — CONTINUOUS ACCESS CERTIFICATION
  Domain: IGA (175)
  Counters: A159
  Description: Replace annual or quarterly point-in-time access
    certification with continuous risk-based certification that
    focuses review effort on highest-risk entitlements and responds
    to behavioral signals (dormant accounts, anomalous access patterns).
  Implementation: Risk scoring for entitlements (privilege level,
    time since last use, role change since grant); continuous
    monitoring triggers certification review when risk score changes;
    dormant account detection (no login >30/60/90 days triggers review);
    anomalous access (new system not previously accessed) triggers
    just-in-time certification; rubber-stamp detection (>95% approve
    rate triggers process review)
  Limitations: Continuous certification creates manager notification
    fatigue; risk scoring models require tuning; coverage gaps for
    non-integrated systems remain; access certification is not
    equivalent to access need verification

D155 — ENTERPRISE BROWSER EXTENSION MANAGEMENT
  Domain: Browser Security (176)
  Counters: A160
  Description: Manage browser extension installation in enterprise
    environments via policy. Allow-list approved extensions; block
    installation of non-approved extensions; monitor extension
    update behavior; review extensions requesting sensitive permissions.
  Implementation: Chrome Enterprise/Firefox ESR policy for extension
    control; approved extension list with security review; permission
    review for extensions requesting access to all sites or sensitive
    APIs; extension update monitoring (version change triggers re-review);
    extension vendor security assessment before approval
  Limitations: BYOD devices cannot be managed; personal browsers in
    enterprise environments bypass policy; extension security review
    requires security expertise most teams lack; allow-list maintenance
    overhead significant; shadow IT pressure drives workarounds

D156 — BROWSER ISOLATION FOR HIGH-RISK BROWSING
  Domain: Browser Security (176)
  Counters: A160
  Description: Route high-risk web browsing through browser isolation
    technology that renders pages in an isolated cloud or local container,
    streaming only pixels to the user's device. Eliminates all web-delivered
    malware, browser exploits, and extension compromise from the browsing
    session.
  Implementation: Remote browser isolation (RBI) for all external web
    access; local browser isolation (containerized browser) for sensitive
    operations; document isolation (Office files opened in isolated
    viewer before download); session isolation (separate browser profile
    per risk domain)
  Limitations: Performance overhead and user experience degradation;
    RBI breaks complex web applications; cost significant at scale;
    isolation technology itself becomes attack surface; does not address
    credential phishing (user still types credentials into isolated view
    of phishing page)

CYCLE 18 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE SCAN

CONVERGENCE FINDINGS C117-C124
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

C117 — DECEPTION TECHNOLOGY + GAME THEORY
  Domains: 167 (Deception), cross-domain: Game Theory
  Finding: Honeypot deployment and adversary counter-deception constitute
    a signaling game with incomplete information. The defender signals
    presence of deception assets by deploying them; adversary signals
    detection capability by avoiding them; both parties update strategies
    based on observed outcomes. Classical Bayesian signaling game models
    (Spence, 1973) directly apply: deception is a costly signal that
    loses value when its existence is common knowledge. The game-theoretic
    equilibrium analysis predicts: (1) deception is most effective when
    rare and unknown; (2) as deception becomes common, adversaries invest
    in detection, eroding its value; (3) the optimal deception deployment
    strategy mixes deception and real assets in proportions that maximize
    adversary uncertainty cost. Neither deception technology vendors
    nor game theory researchers have applied this framework to optimal
    deception deployment strategy.
  Significance: Game theory directly models the deception arms race;
    provides optimal strategy framework not currently used in practice

C118 — THREAT INTELLIGENCE SHARING + EPIDEMIOLOGY
  Domains: 168 (Threat Intelligence), cross-domain: Epidemiology
  Finding: Threat intelligence sharing networks function analogously
    to disease surveillance networks. IOC sharing is like pathogen
    reporting: time-sensitive, requires standardized data formats,
    must reach the population at risk before exposure. Epidemiological
    models (SIR, SEIR) map directly to threat propagation: Susceptible
    = unpatched systems, Infected = compromised, Recovered = patched/
    remediated. The epidemiological concept of R0 (basic reproduction
    number) applies to malware propagation; threat intelligence sharing
    can reduce effective R0 by accelerating the transition from
    Susceptible to Recovered. Epidemiology has 150 years of methodology
    for surveillance network design, reporting lag management, and
    false report handling; threat intelligence has not adopted this
    methodology.
  Significance: Epidemiological surveillance design principles directly
    applicable to threat intelligence sharing network architecture;
    R0 modeling of malware propagation quantifies value of faster sharing

C119 — MFA FATIGUE + SOCIAL ENGINEERING PSYCHOLOGY
  Domains: 169 (Security Awareness), cross-domain: Psychology
  Finding: MFA push notification fatigue attacks exploit two well-
    documented psychological phenomena: choice fatigue (decision
    quality degrades with repeated similar decisions) and authority
    bias (perceived authority of IT helpdesk call causes compliance).
    The psychological literature on these phenomena predicts attack
    success rates under different conditions (notification frequency,
    time of day, accompanying social engineering quality) with high
    accuracy. Security awareness training designed without reference
    to the psychological literature on these phenomena is less effective
    than it could be. Cognitive load, temporal urgency, and authority
    framing are all psychological levers that security awareness
    programs address without naming or modeling them.
  Significance: Behavioral psychology literature directly applicable
    to security awareness training design; quantitative predictions
    possible from psychological models; training effectiveness measurable
    against psychological baselines

C120 — EDR BEHAVIORAL DETECTION + ANOMALY DETECTION THEORY
  Domains: 170 (EDR/XDR), cross-domain: Statistical Anomaly Detection
  Finding: EDR behavioral detection is applied anomaly detection:
    identify process behaviors that deviate from a learned normal
    baseline. The statistical theory of anomaly detection (Isolation
    Forest, autoencoders, one-class SVM, OCSVM) is mature and well-
    studied in the machine learning literature. EDR vendors have adopted
    ML-based detection but have not fully incorporated the theoretical
    understanding of anomaly detection tradeoffs: higher sensitivity
    (lower false negative rate) always increases false positive rate
    for a given feature space; the precision-recall tradeoff is
    fundamental and cannot be escaped. EDR vendors marketing "near-
    zero false positives" are misrepresenting the statistical
    impossibility of that claim for behavioral detection.
  Significance: Anomaly detection theory provides rigorous framework
    for understanding EDR limitations; enables informed configuration
    of detection sensitivity tradeoffs; exposes marketing claims that
    contradict statistical principles

C121 — KUBERNETES SECURITY + DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS FAILURE MODES
  Domains: 173 (Container/K8s Security), cross-domain: Distributed
    Systems Theory
  Finding: Kubernetes security failures exhibit the same cascading
    failure patterns documented in distributed systems theory (Byzantine
    fault tolerance, cascading failure in complex systems). A single
    compromised component (one pod, one service account, one admission
    controller) can cascade to cluster-wide compromise via the same
    mechanisms that distributed systems researchers have studied for
    fault propagation. The Kubernetes API server is a single point of
    failure for control plane security; Byzantine fault tolerance
    requires 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f malicious nodes; Kubernetes
    has no Byzantine fault tolerance for the control plane. Distributed
    systems research on partition tolerance, consistency, and availability
    (CAP theorem) applies to Kubernetes security: you cannot have
    availability, security policy consistency, and partition tolerance
    simultaneously.
  Significance: Distributed systems theory provides formal framework
    for understanding K8s security failure propagation; Byzantine
    fault tolerance research directly applicable to multi-tenant
    cluster security design

C122 — PRIVILEGED CREDENTIAL MANAGEMENT + ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR
  Domains: PAM (171), cross-domain: Organizational Behavior
  Finding: PAM program failures are as much organizational behavior
    problems as they are technical problems. Studies of PAM failures
    consistently show: (1) shadow IT PAM workarounds where security
    controls impede productivity; (2) manager bypass of PAM approvals
    for subordinates under deadline pressure; (3) help desk override
    of PAM controls under authority pressure; (4) service account
    ownership diffusion in large organizations (no one owns the account,
    so no one certifies it). These are documented organizational behavior
    patterns (role ambiguity, authority gradient, convenience vs.
    compliance tradeoffs) that have been studied extensively in
    organizational psychology but not applied to PAM program design.
  Significance: PAM effectiveness is predictable from organizational
    behavior models; program design should incorporate organizational
    factors, not only technical controls; social science research
    directly applicable

C123 — SERVERLESS SECURITY + MICROSERVICES ATTACK SURFACE THEORY
  Domains: 174 (Serverless), cross-domain: Service-Oriented Architecture
  Finding: Serverless computing represents the extreme end of service
    decomposition: each function is a minimal service with event-driven
    invocation. This maximizes the attack surface area relative to the
    code surface area because each function boundary is a potential
    injection point. The attack surface of a serverless application
    with 100 functions is not one hundred times the attack surface of
    a monolith; it is qualitatively different because each function
    boundary is a trust boundary with its own authentication, authorization,
    and input validation requirements. Service mesh security research
    (zero trust for microservices) applies directly to serverless; but
    serverless platforms do not implement service mesh primitives.
    The decomposition trend in software architecture systematically
    increases the security configuration surface without equivalent
    increase in developer security awareness.
  Significance: Software architecture trend toward decomposition
    directly increases security configuration burden; security debt
    grows with service count; architectural security principles needed

C124 — BROWSER EXTENSION SECURITY + SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK PATTERNS
  Domains: 176 (Browser Security), 95 (Software Supply Chain)
  Finding: Browser extension supply chain attacks are structurally
    identical to npm/PyPI supply chain attacks: compromise a widely-
    used component with a large downstream user base; push malicious
    update via legitimate distribution channel; users auto-update;
    attack executes at scale. The browser extension ecosystem has
    identical structural vulnerabilities to the open-source package
    ecosystem: centralized distribution with auto-update, developer
    account takeover as attack vector, review processes that cannot
    keep pace with submission volume. Supply chain security frameworks
    (SLSA, SSDF) developed for software packages apply directly to
    browser extension security; the browser extension ecosystem
    has not adopted these frameworks. The extension and package
    ecosystems are converging as extension platforms adopt npm-like
    distribution models.
  Significance: Direct structural convergence; supply chain security
    frameworks and tooling developed for software packages directly
    applicable to browser extensions with minimal adaptation

GAP AUDIT — CYCLE 18
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

NEW GAPS IDENTIFIED THIS CYCLE: 8 (G97-G104)

G97 — OPTIMAL DECEPTION DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY MODEL
  Gap: No quantitative model exists for optimal honeypot and deception
    asset deployment that accounts for adversary detection capability,
    real asset ratio, and intelligence value of adversary interaction.
    Game-theoretic framework exists (C117) but has not been applied.
  Significance: HIGH — deception deployments are currently ad hoc;
    quantitative optimization would improve cost-effectiveness

G98 — THREAT INTELLIGENCE SHARING LAG MEASUREMENT
  Gap: No systematic measurement of the lag between initial threat
    observation and defender community receipt of actionable intelligence.
    Epidemiological analogy (C118) predicts that sharing lag is the
    primary determinant of collective defense effectiveness; this
    quantity is not measured or reported in the threat intelligence
    industry.
  Significance: HIGH — without measuring sharing lag, improving it
    is impossible; metric needed for intelligence sharing SLA

G99 — SECURITY AWARENESS TRAINING EFFECTIVENESS EVIDENCE BASE
  Gap: No rigorous randomized controlled trials exist for security
    awareness training interventions. The evidence base consists
    primarily of pre/post knowledge tests and simulated phishing
    click rates; neither measures actual behavioral change under
    real attack conditions. The absence of an evidence base means
    billions of dollars in training spend cannot be evaluated.
  Significance: HIGH — policy and investment decisions made without
    evidence; RCT methodology from behavioral psychology directly
    applicable but not used

G100 — EDR COVERAGE STANDARDIZATION AND BENCHMARKING
  Gap: No standardized benchmark exists for comparing EDR detection
    rates against a common attack set. MITRE ATT&CK evaluations provide
    partial coverage but are vendor-selected and not independently
    audited. Defenders cannot objectively compare EDR products for
    specific threat actor coverage.
  Significance: HIGH — EDR procurement decisions made on marketing
    claims without empirical basis; standardized benchmark would
    improve market efficiency and defender outcomes

G101 — KUBERNETES SECURITY CONFIGURATION BASELINE STANDARD
  Gap: No independently audited, widely adopted Kubernetes security
    configuration baseline exists. CIS Kubernetes Benchmark exists but
    is not independently verified against real attack scenarios;
    compliance with CIS Benchmark does not prevent all documented
    K8s escalation paths.
  Significance: HIGH — K8s misconfiguration is primary attack vector;
    verified baseline would reduce configuration surface across industry

G102 — SERVERLESS SECURITY TESTING METHODOLOGY
  Gap: No published methodology for security testing of serverless
    applications exists at the maturity level of web application
    testing (OWASP WSTG) or API testing. Serverless functions have
    distinct attack surface characteristics (event injection, IAM
    overprivilege, ephemeral execution) not covered by existing
    testing frameworks.
  Significance: MEDIUM-HIGH — serverless adoption growing rapidly;
    testing methodology gap means serverless applications untested
    for serverless-specific vulnerabilities

G103 — IDENTITY LIFECYCLE AUTOMATION COVERAGE STANDARD
  Gap: No standard measures identity lifecycle automation coverage
    (percentage of identity lifecycle events handled automatically
    vs. manually). Organizations cannot benchmark their IGA automation
    maturity or set improvement targets without a coverage metric.
  Significance: MEDIUM — metric needed to drive IGA program improvement;
    currently organizations cannot quantify orphaned account risk

G104 — BROWSER EXTENSION SECURITY REVIEW STANDARD
  Gap: No published security review standard for browser extensions
    exists comparable to mobile app security standards (OWASP MASVS).
    Enterprise extension allow-listing programs perform inconsistent
    reviews with no standardized criteria.
  Significance: MEDIUM — browser extension ecosystem security cannot
    improve without review standards; supply chain attack surface remains
    ungoverned

177 — DATA LOSS PREVENTION (DLP) AND INFORMATION CLASSIFICATION
  Description: Controls preventing unauthorized exfiltration or exposure
    of sensitive data. Includes data discovery and classification, DLP
    policy enforcement at network and endpoint, and data rights management.
  Sub-domains: Data discovery and inventory; data classification frameworks
    (public/internal/confidential/restricted); DLP network inspection;
    endpoint DLP (file transfer controls); email DLP; cloud DLP; data
    rights management (IRM/DRM); database activity monitoring; data
    masking and tokenization; GDPR/HIPAA/PCI data protection compliance;
    DLP bypass techniques; cloud storage data exposure
  Root mechanic intersection: R01 (boundary between authorized and
    unauthorized data movement; DLP enforces this boundary); R09
    (irreversibility — data exfiltration is irreversible; DLP is
    last-chance prevention before permanent loss)

178 — SECURITY METRICS, MEASUREMENT, AND REPORTING
  Description: Frameworks and methodologies for measuring security program
    effectiveness, communicating security posture to leadership, and
    making evidence-based security investment decisions.
  Sub-domains: Security KPI and KRI frameworks; CISO board reporting;
    risk quantification (FAIR methodology); vulnerability severity scoring
    (CVSS, EPSS); mean time metrics (MTTD, MTTR, MTTI); security
    program maturity models (CMMI, NIST CSF maturity); red team
    effectiveness measurement; patch compliance metrics; security
    ROI calculation; Goodhart's Law in security metrics
  Root mechanic intersection: R03 (trust in metrics without verification
    that metrics measure what they claim; Goodhart's Law — when a measure
    becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure — applies systematically
    to security metrics)

179 — CYBER INSURANCE AND RISK TRANSFER
  Description: Insurance products covering cyber risk, including first-party
    coverage (incident response costs, business interruption) and third-

    of cyber risk, policy exclusions, and the feedback between insurance

  Sub-domains: Cyber insurance policy structure and coverage; actuarial

    attacks); cyber insurance underwriting questionnaires; insurance

  Root mechanic intersection: R09 (irreversibility amplifier — insurance
    covers costs but cannot reverse breach impact; reputation loss, customer

  Root mechanic intersection: R09 (irreversibility amplifier —

185 — PRIVACY ENHANCING TECHNOLOGIES (PETs)

  Root mechanic intersection: R03 (PETs address the trust requirement

  Root mechanic intersection: R03 (adversary trusts that defender

PATTERN 19.1 — COMPLIANCE AS SECURITY PROXY (GOODHART'S LAW IN SECURITY)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: When security compliance becomes a target, it ceases to be
  a good measure of security. Organizations optimize for passing compliance
  assessments rather than for actual security posture. Assessments measure
  whether controls exist and are documented, not whether they work.
  The history of security compliance is a history of compliant organizations
  being breached: PCI-DSS compliant retailers losing card data; HIPAA
  compliant hospitals hit by ransomware; ISO 27001 certified organizations
  compromised by basic phishing. Compliance and security are correlated
  but not equivalent.

ROOT MECHANICS: R03 (trust in compliance attestation as security proxy
  without verification that compliant systems are actually secure)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1984: Orange Book certification (Trusted Computer System Evaluation
      Criteria); evaluations took 5-7 years; certified systems already
      obsolete at certification; security properties not tested in
      operational configuration
    1996: Common Criteria established; evaluation laboratory system;
      Protection Profile vs. operational security gap immediate and
      documented; evaluated products routinely vulnerable
    2004: PCI-DSS v1.0 released; compliance industry forms; TJX breach
      (2005-2007) occurs at PCI-DSS compliant retailer; Heartland
      Payment Systems breach (2008) at PCI compliant organization

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2013: Target breach — PCI-DSS compliant at time of breach; complied
      with cardholder data environment segregation requirements but
      breach exploited adjacent network segment
    2014: Home Depot breach — PCI-DSS compliant; compliance did not
      prevent point-of-sale malware at scale
    2015: Anthem breach — HIPAA compliant healthcare insurer; 80M
      medical records exfiltrated; no encryption requirement under
      HIPAA for data at rest; HIPAA compliance said nothing about
      the actual attack vector
    2017: Equifax breach — was in process of SOC 2 assessment at
      time of breach; web application vulnerability not covered
      by assessment scope
    2019: Capital One breach — cloud misconfiguration; AWS compliance
      certifications (FedRAMP, PCI) did not cover IAM configuration
      of customer-managed resources

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2021: SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules proposed; companies begin
      disclosing security risks; disclosures mostly boilerplate; do
      not reflect actual security posture; legal language optimized
      for liability management not transparency
    2022: SolarWinds SEC enforcement action; first enforcement for
      inadequate cybersecurity disclosure; compliance lawyers now
      drive disclosure language; security accuracy subordinated
      to legal risk management
    2023: DORA (EU Digital Operational Resilience Act) passed;
      financial sector compliance program begins; 500+ requirements;
      compliance industry revenue projected at $10B+; actual security
      improvement projected significantly less
    2024: NIS2 Directive implementation across EU; management liability
      provisions; board members personally liable; drives compliance
      investment but not necessarily security investment
    2025: ISO 42001 (AI Management System) published; first AI
      compliance framework; Goodhart's Law begins immediately:
      organizations seek certification without addressing AI security
      substance
    2026: Compliance-industrial complex size estimated at $80B+
      annually globally; security improvement attributable to
      compliance vs. other factors unquantifiable; no RCT evidence
      base for compliance program effectiveness

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Outcome-based regulation replacing controls-based; regulators
      in financial sector moving toward security outcome measurement
      (DORA operational resilience testing); better but still gameable
    → AI regulation adds another compliance layer without security
      substance; same Goodhart's Law dynamic
    → Quantitative risk assessment (FAIR, OpenFAIR) as alternative
      to compliance frameworks; economically rigorous but requires
      data that most organizations don't collect

FORM B — RESEARCH PROMPT:
  "Map the evidence base for compliance framework effectiveness: identify
  (1) all major security breaches at organizations certified compliant with
  the relevant framework, (2) the specific gap between what the compliance
  framework required and what the breach exploited, (3) the economic
  incentives that drive compliance optimization over security optimization,
  (4) outcome-based regulatory alternatives and their empirical track record,
  and (5) the minimum compliance framework design that would prevent
  Goodhart's Law from degrading its security signal."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 19.2 — CYBER INSURANCE MORAL HAZARD AND RANSOMWARE ECONOMICS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Cyber insurance that covers ransomware payments creates moral
  hazard: insured organizations are less incentivized to resist payment
  (the insurer pays), and ransomware operators know that insured
  organizations pay. The result is that insurance enables ransomware
  economics at scale. Ransomware operators systematically target
  organizations known to carry cyber insurance; insurance coverage
  increases extortion probability and amount. Insurance intended to
  reduce victim harm may, at the aggregate level, increase total
  ransomware harm by increasing attacker confidence in payment.

CONFIDENCE: 0.88 (HIGH)

ROOT MECHANICS: R09 (irreversibility — data encryption is irreversible
  without backup or payment; insurance covers cost but not the
  irreversibility itself), R03 (trust in insurance as risk mitigation
  without verifying that it changes incentives appropriately)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    2013: CryptoLocker ransomware; first large-scale ransomware campaign;
      no cyber insurance coverage; victims who paid created the market;
      showed payment works as attacker model
    2016: Hollywood Presbyterian Medical Center; $17,000 ransom paid;
      no insurance coverage; media coverage demonstrates payment model
      publicly; signals viability to other attackers
    2017: WannaCry and NotPetya; NotPetya covered by "all risks"
      property insurance; Mondelez vs. Zurich Insurance dispute;
      Zurich invokes war exclusion; $100M insurance dispute; signals
      war exclusion gap to policyholders

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2018: SamSam ransomware; attackers specifically research target's
      insurance coverage before setting ransom amount; documented
      in indictment materials; confirms targeted insurance research
    2019: Norsk Hydro ransomware (LockerGoga); $70M+ damage; $20M
      insurance recovery; Norsk Hydro chose rebuild over payment;
      demonstrates insurance enabling non-payment path
    2019: Louisiana school district pays $300K ransom; cyber insurance
      covered payment; documented; creates payment precedent in
      public sector
    2020: CNA Financial ransomware (Phoenix); $40M ransom payment;
      insured and paid; largest known ransomware payment at time;
      insurance covered significant portion

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2021: Colonial Pipeline $4.4M payment; insurance coverage unclear;
      DOJ recovered $2.3M from attacker wallet; demonstrates partial
      recovery possible
    2021: Insurance industry begins tightening ransomware coverage;
      Lloyd's mandates ransomware sublimits; premiums increase 50-300%;
      some organizations lose coverage; coverage availability bifurcates
      by security posture
    2022: Lloyd's war exclusion update; explicitly excludes attacks
      by nation-states; creates definitional problem (attribution);
      Merck NotPetya settlement ($1.4B) against insurers who claimed
      war exclusion; insurers cannot exclude attacks they cannot attribute
    2023: SEC reporting requirement for material cyber incidents (72h);
      creates new disclosure obligation; ransomware incidents must
      be disclosed; payment decisions now public record
    2024: Ransomware payment declining as a proportion of incidents;
      backup and recovery improvements; law enforcement actions;
      but absolute ransomware harm continues to increase as attack
      scale grows
    2026: Cyber insurance market estimated $15-20B annually; ransomware
      coverage most contested; no-payment policies emerging (insurance
      that requires non-payment to maintain coverage); actuarial models
      for systemic cyber risk still immature

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Ransomware operator intelligence on insured organizations becomes
      systematic (data brokers selling insurance coverage data);
      targeting shifts entirely to insured organizations
    → Government prohibition of ransomware payments (proposed in
      multiple jurisdictions); shifts burden to backup/recovery;
      uninsured organizations face existential risk
    → Parametric cyber insurance (pays on attack trigger, not damage
      assessment); faster payout, less moral hazard; but triggers
      gameable

FORM B — RESEARCH PROMPT:
  "Analyze the economic interaction between cyber insurance and ransomware:
  identify (1) empirical evidence for and against the moral hazard hypothesis
  in cyber insurance, (2) documented cases of ransomware operators researching
  target insurance coverage before setting demands, (3) the actuarial model
  for ransomware risk at portfolio level, (4) policy alternatives (no-payment
  requirements, mandatory disclosure, government recovery funds) and their
  economic effects, and (5) the systemic risk threshold at which ransomware
  losses become uninsurable."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 19.3 — SIM SWAPPING AS PHYSICAL-LAYER IDENTITY ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: SIM swapping attacks exploit the mobile carrier authentication
  process to transfer a victim's phone number to an adversary-controlled
  SIM card. Once the phone number is transferred, all SMS-based MFA,
  phone-based account recovery, and voice authentication using that number
  is compromised. The attack is a pure identity attack at the physical
  layer: it compromises the physical token (SIM card) that all higher-
  layer authentication uses as a root of trust, without touching any
  software on the victim's devices.

ROOT MECHANICS: R10 (physical device as authentication proxy — SIM
  card is the physical token; carrier transfer compromises the proxy),
  R03 (carrier trusts social engineering as authorization for SIM
  transfer without sufficient verification), R06 (carrier customer
  service as confused deputy — authorized to transfer SIMs for legitimate
  customers; cannot distinguish legitimate customer from social engineer)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    2013: First documented SIM swap fraud in UK; targeted at banking
      SMS OTP; individual financial fraud; not yet recognized as
      systematic attack technique
    2015: SIM swap documented across multiple US carriers; FTC receives
      complaints; carriers begin investigating; no systematic defense
    2016: SIM swap used in bitcoin theft; cryptocurrency community
      discovers attack; vulnerability becomes widely known in crypto
      community; attackers shift to cryptocurrency targets due to
      irreversibility of crypto transfers

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2017: Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey's account SIM swapped; demonstrates
      high-profile victim viability; significant media attention
    2018: California teenager convicted of SIM swap cryptocurrency
      thefts; $5M+ stolen; criminal market for SIM swap services
      documented
    2019: FCC action against T-Mobile for inadequate SIM swap
      protections; first regulatory enforcement; carriers implement
      additional authentication steps
    2019: Coinhive founder SIM swapped; Twitter account compromised;
      demonstrates tech community targeting
    2020: Twitter hack; 130 high-profile accounts compromised;
      partial SIM swap and social engineering of Twitter internal
      admin tools; $120,000 bitcoin stolen; 17-year-old arrested

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2021: FCC proposes mandatory SIM swap protections; carriers must
      notify customers of SIM changes; notification via alternative
      channel required
    2022: Uber breach partially via MFA fatigue; SIM swap not used
      but same root mechanic (phone as authentication proxy)
    2023: Scattered Spider group (related to Lapsus$) uses SIM
      swapping systematically against enterprise targets; combines
      SIM swap with MFA fatigue; hits MGM Resorts, Caesars, multiple
      others; $15M+ in losses
    2024: FCC SIM swap rules effective; carriers must verify identity
      before SIM transfer; immediate notification mandatory; success
      rate of SIM swap attacks decreases but does not reach zero;
      insiders at carriers remain attack vector
    2025: GSMA universal SIM authentication standard proposed;
      cryptographic SIM ownership verification across carriers;
      adoption timeline 5-7 years
    2026: eSIM proliferation; eSIM transfer is software process;
      SIM swap equivalent done entirely online without physical carrier
      store visit; attack surface shifts to carrier online portal
      authentication

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → eSIM makes SIM swap a software attack; physical carrier store
      social engineering replaced by online account compromise;
      attack surface expands to all carrier online portal weaknesses
    → FIDO2/passkeys adoption reduces SMS MFA dependence; but
      account recovery processes often fall back to SMS; SIM swap
      still valuable for account recovery path
    → Carrier insider threats increase as SIM swap criminal market
      offers higher payments than carrier employee salaries for
      SIM swap assistance

FORM B — RESEARCH PROMPT:
  "Map the complete SIM swap attack ecosystem: identify (1) all carrier
  authentication mechanisms exploited in SIM swap attacks, (2) criminal
  market structure for SIM swap services, (3) regulatory responses
  across jurisdictions and their measured effectiveness, (4) technical
  alternatives to phone-number-based authentication that eliminate the
  SIM swap attack surface, and (5) the interaction between eSIM
  proliferation and SIM swap attack evolution."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 19.4 — PRIVACY ENHANCING TECHNOLOGIES VERSUS SECURITY MONITORING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

FORM A:
  FINDING: Privacy enhancing technologies (PETs) — end-to-end encryption,
  differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs —
  are in structural tension with security monitoring. Security monitoring
  requires observability into data flows, content, and behavior. PETs
  reduce or eliminate that observability. The same E2E encryption that
  protects user data from adversaries also prevents security tools from
  inspecting that data for malware or data exfiltration. This tension
  is not an engineering problem to be solved; it is a fundamental
  tradeoff between privacy and security observability.

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (boundary enforcement — PETs enforce data access
  boundaries that security monitoring requires crossing; boundary is
  intentional and the tension is inherent)

TEMPORAL LAYER — HISTORICAL INSTANCES:
    1991: PGP released by Phil Zimmermann; FBI and NSA immediately
      object to unbreakable civilian encryption; export controls
      applied; Clipper Chip proposed (1993) as backdoored alternative;
      cryptography wars begin
    1993: Clipper Chip controversy; government wants lawful access
      backdoor; security researchers demonstrate Clipper flaw
      (Blaze, 1994); Clipper abandoned
    1999: Bernstein v. Department of Justice; encryption code is
      speech; export controls ruled unconstitutional; civilian
      encryption access becomes settled law in US

TEMPORAL LAYER — RECENT INSTANCES (2000-2020):
    2013: Snowden disclosures; mass surveillance via PRISM; public
      awareness of government interception of plaintext communications;
      accelerates E2E encryption adoption
    2014: Apple and Google implement E2E encryption by default in
      iOS 8 and Android; FBI Director Comey objects; "going dark"
      problem officially declared
    2016: Apple v. FBI (San Bernardino iPhone); FBI demands iOS
      decryption capability; Apple refuses; FBI obtains access via
      third-party exploit; case withdrawn; fundamental tension
      unresolved
    2018: EARN IT Act proposed (US); would remove Section 230
      liability protection for services using E2E encryption;
      withdrawn but repeatedly reintroduced
    2019: WhatsApp E2E encryption; 2B users; security agencies
      unable to intercept; criminal use documented; same E2E
      encryption protects journalists, dissidents, domestic
      violence survivors

TEMPORAL LAYER — CURRENT STATE (2020-2026):
    2020: EU Chat Control proposal; mandatory scanning of E2E
      encrypted messages for CSAM; cryptographers document that
      client-side scanning breaks E2E security model; debate ongoing
    2022: EARN IT Act reintroduced; fails; tech community and
      civil liberties groups successfully oppose; E2E encryption
      remains legally unimpaired in US
    2023: UK Online Safety Act; age verification requirements that
      could require content scanning; App Store providers threaten
      UK withdrawal; provisions not yet implemented
    2024: Enterprise DLP vs. E2E encryption; organizations deploying
      DLP cannot inspect E2E encrypted traffic; security monitoring
      blind spot for E2E channels; shadow IT use of consumer E2E
      apps bypasses enterprise DLP
    2025: Homomorphic encryption performance improvements; 10x
      speedup over 2020 baselines; some use cases now practical;
      privacy-preserving security analytics emerging; can detect
      anomalies in encrypted data without decrypting
    2026: Differential privacy in enterprise analytics; enables
      threat hunting on aggregate behavioral data without individual
      user profiling; partially resolves monitoring vs. privacy tension

TEMPORAL LAYER — EMERGING TRAJECTORY (2026+):
    → Homomorphic encryption-based security monitoring becomes
      practical for some use cases; detects anomalies without
      reading content; partial resolution of tension
    → Post-quantum E2E encryption required; migration period creates
      window where encrypted traffic can be harvested and later
      decrypted (harvest now, decrypt later)
    → Government lawful access proposals continue; each jurisdiction
      independently; inconsistent requirements for global services;
      weakest-link dynamic if any jurisdiction requires backdoor

FORM B — RESEARCH PROMPT:
  "Map the structural tension between privacy enhancing technologies and
  security monitoring: identify (1) the specific monitoring capabilities
  that each major PET (E2E encryption, differential privacy, FHE, ZKP)
  eliminates, (2) historical cases where PET-protected channels were used
  for malicious purposes, (3) technical approaches that partially resolve
  the tension (client-side scanning, HE-based anomaly detection), (4) the
  legal landscape across jurisdictions for government access to E2E
  encrypted data, and (5) the game-theoretic equilibrium between PET
  adoption and government mandated access."

ENTERING STATE: 52 anatomies cumulative
THREE PATTERNS SELECTED FOR ANATOMY THIS CYCLE: 19.1, 19.2, 19.4
  (19.1 selected: Goodhart's Law in security is the highest-impact
    policy finding; compliance/security decoupling underlies most
    governance failures)
  (19.2 selected: ransomware economics and cyber insurance create a
    macro-level system dynamic affecting all organizations)
  (19.4 selected: PETs vs. security monitoring is a structural tradeoff
