DOMAIN 247: API SECURITY AND API GATEWAY EXPLOITATION
Parent domain: Web Application Security (primary domain; covered Cycle 3)
Elevation rationale: APIs have displaced traditional web application attack
surface as the primary target class. REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket
APIs present distinct attack surfaces not fully covered under traditional
web application security. OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023 version) identifies
API-specific vulnerability classes absent from OWASP Top 10 web application
list. API security is now its own discipline.
Key sub-domains: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR), Broken
Function Level Authorization, Excessive Data Exposure, GraphQL introspection
abuse, API key management failures, Shadow/zombie API discovery, Rate limiting
bypass, API versioning security debt.
Active attack surface: YES — dominant attack pattern in cloud-native
environments; API breaches (Optus 2022, T-Mobile 2021, Peloton 2021) at
population scale.

DOMAIN 248: CONTAINER ESCAPE AND KUBERNETES CLUSTER ATTACK SURFACE
Parent domain: Cloud Security (primary domain; covered Cycle 5)
Elevation rationale: Kubernetes has become the dominant orchestration platform
for cloud workloads. Container/K8s-specific attack surface (privileged
container escape, etcd exposure, RBAC misconfiguration, admission controller
bypass, service mesh attack surface) is distinct from generic cloud security
and requires dedicated treatment. CNCF security audit findings and MITRE ATT&CK
for Containers matrix codify this as a separate domain.
Key sub-domains: Docker daemon socket exposure, privileged container escape,
kubelet API unauthorized access, etcd unauthenticated access, K8s secrets
management, Helm chart supply chain, service mesh mTLS bypass, admission
webhook exploitation.
Active attack surface: YES — TeamTNT and other cloud-native threat actors
specifically target K8s.

DOMAIN 249: SECRETS MANAGEMENT AND CREDENTIAL HYGIENE
Parent domain: Identity and Access Management (primary domain; covered Cycle 6)
Elevation rationale: Secrets sprawl (API keys, service account credentials,
database passwords, certificates embedded in code, CI/CD pipelines, and
container images) is a distinct attack class with its own discovery methods
(TruffleHog, GitLeaks, Gitleaks-CI), management tools (HashiCorp Vault,
AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault), and failure patterns. The credential
is not the identity; it is the artifact that proxies for identity at runtime.
Key sub-domains: Git secret scanning, CI/CD secrets exposure, container
image secret embedding, .env file exposure, cloud metadata service credential
theft (IMDS), SSRF to credential endpoints, certificate lifecycle management
failures, API key rotation failures.
Active attack surface: YES — credential exposure in public repositories
is endemic; GitGuardian reports millions of secrets exposed annually.

DOMAIN 250: THREAT HUNTING METHODOLOGY AND HYPOTHESIS-DRIVEN DETECTION
Parent domain: SOC Architecture (primary domain; covered Cycle 24)
Elevation rationale: Threat hunting (proactive, analyst-led investigation
for threats that automated detection has not surfaced) is a distinct
discipline from reactive alert-based detection. It requires specific
methodologies (hypothesis-driven, intelligence-driven, machine learning-
assisted) and specific skills (data analysis, adversary emulation knowledge,
query language proficiency) that are not covered under general SOC operations.
Key sub-domains: Hunt hypothesis development, data source adequacy assessment,
query language proficiency (SPL, KQL, SQL), TTP-based hunting (ATT&CK-driven),
frequency analysis for outlier detection, temporal baselining, process
execution tree analysis, network connection graph analysis.
Active attack surface: N/A — this is a defensive discipline, not an attack
surface; but it is a gap in the defender community's capability that
adversaries exploit via anti-forensics.

DOMAIN 251: DATA LOSS PREVENTION AND EXFILTRATION CHANNEL SECURITY
Parent domain: Data Security (primary domain; covered Cycle 7)
Elevation rationale: Data exfiltration techniques have evolved beyond
simple file copy to include covert channel exfiltration (DNS tunneling,
ICMP covert channel, HTTP over legitimate cloud services), steganographic
exfiltration, and slow-drip exfiltration designed to stay below DLP
thresholds. The detection side has matured into a distinct discipline
(content inspection, behavioral DLP, egress monitoring). Neither attack
nor defense is adequately covered under generic data security.
Key sub-domains: DNS tunneling for data exfiltration, HTTPS exfiltration
via cloud services (Mega.nz, Dropbox, GitHub as exfil destinations),
steganographic exfiltration in image files, timing channel exfiltration,
DLP bypass via compression and encoding, printer and fax channel exfiltration
(legacy environments), print-to-PDF as exfil pathway in air-gapped adjacent
environments.
Active attack surface: YES — exfiltration via cloud storage services
documented in multiple nation-state campaigns.

DOMAIN 252: DECEPTION TECHNOLOGY DEPLOYMENT AND EFFECTIVENESS SCIENCE
Parent domain: Advanced Deception Technology (primary domain; covered Cycle 25)
Elevation rationale: The effectiveness science of deception technology
(canary tokens, honeypots, deception grids, breadcrumbs) is distinct from
the deployment methodology. What evidence exists for deception effectiveness,
what attacker behaviors are changed by deception presence, and what the
optimal deception architecture is for different environments requires its own
treatment.
Key sub-domains: Canary token deployment strategy, honeypot interaction
analysis, deception alert fidelity (false positive rate of deception alerts
is near-zero by design), attacker behavior change under deception awareness,
breadcrumb trail design for lateral movement deception, deception in cloud
environments (cloud honey accounts, cloud honey resources), deception ROI
measurement.
Active interest: YES — high-signal detection mechanism with low false positive
rate; underdeployed relative to its effectiveness profile.

DOMAIN 253: PROTOCOL FUZZING AND VULNERABILITY DISCOVERY METHODOLOGY
Parent domain: Vulnerability Research (primary domain; covered Cycle 12)
Elevation rationale: Fuzzing has matured into the dominant technique for
vulnerability discovery in binary targets, network protocols, and file parsers.
Coverage-guided fuzzing (AFL++, LibFuzzer), structured fuzzing, grammar-based
fuzzing, and network protocol fuzzing are now standard security research
methodologies with specific tooling, metrics, and result interpretation methods
that constitute a sub-discipline.
Key sub-domains: Coverage-guided fuzzing (AFL++), smart fuzzing with grammar,
differential fuzzing for crypto implementation comparison, network protocol
fuzzing (Boofuzz, Sulley), firmware fuzzing (QEMU-based, Unicorn-based),
corpus management, crash triage and deduplication, fuzzing at scale
(continuous integration fuzzing), OSS-Fuzz and clusterfuzz.
Active attack surface: N/A (research methodology); output is vulnerability
discovery across all domains.

DOMAIN 254: HARDWARE SECURITY MODULE AND CRYPTOGRAPHIC ACCELERATOR SECURITY
Parent domain: Cryptographic Engineering (primary domain; covered Cycle 18)
Elevation rationale: HSMs (Hardware Security Modules) are trusted with the
most sensitive cryptographic operations in enterprise and cloud environments:
CA private keys, code signing keys, payment card master keys. Their security
is assumed rather than verified by most organizations. HSM attacks (side-
channel on HSM cryptographic operations, API-level attacks on HSM management
interfaces, physical attacks on HSM tamper evidence) constitute a sub-domain
with distinct threat model.
Key sub-domains: HSM API misuse (PKCS#11 oracle attacks), HSM management
interface exploitation, side-channel attacks on HSM cryptographic operations,
HSM clone attacks (physical tamper), HSM backup and restore as attack vector,
cloud HSM (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM) attack surface vs. physical
HSM, HSM firmware update chain, TPM (Trusted Platform Module) attack surface.
Active attack surface: YES — PKCS#11 oracle attacks demonstrated; HSM backup
key export as lateral movement path documented in enterprise pen tests.

DOMAIN 255: DEVSECOPS PIPELINE SECURITY AND SHIFT-LEFT SECURITY
Parent domain: Software Supply Chain Security (primary domain; covered Cycle 14)
Elevation rationale: DevSecOps (integrating security into CI/CD pipelines)
has its own attack surface beyond software supply chain: the pipeline itself
(Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI) is an execution environment
with elevated cloud credentials, access to source code, and ability to deploy
to production. Compromise of a CI/CD pipeline is worse than compromise of
a developer workstation.
Key sub-domains: GitHub Actions secret exposure, CI/CD runner compromise,
pipeline YAML injection (untrusted pull request trigger), dependency confusion
in CI environments, Docker layer caching as persistent attacker persistence,
test environment production credential bleed, SAST/DAST integration in
pipeline (shift-left security tools), security gate bypass via test result
manipulation.
Active attack surface: YES — GitHub Actions and CircleCI compromises
documented; pipeline compromise as supply chain attack vector.

DOMAIN 256: PHYSICAL COVERT CHANNEL ATTACKS AND AIRGAP BYPASS
Parent domain: Physical Security (primary domain; covered Cycle 9);
              Side-Channel Attacks (primary domain; covered Cycle 17)
Elevation rationale: Air-gapped networks (physically isolated from internet)
are attacked via physical covert channels: acoustic (PC speaker, fan noise,
HDD vibration), electromagnetic (LED patterns, HDMI emissions, USB power
variation), thermal (heat emission patterns), and power (power consumption
patterns over shared power infrastructure). These attacks require physical
proximity or pre-placed sensors and represent the endpoint of the attacker's
effort to bridge physical isolation.
Key sub-domains: Acoustic covert channels (AirHopper, Fansmitter, DiskFiltration),
electromagnetic emanations (TEMPEST, LED-it-GO, MAGNETO), power-line
communication (PowerHammer), thermal covert channels (HEAT-Transfer), optical
(GAIROSCOPE gyroscope-based), seismic (using gyroscope as microphone),
and combined multi-channel exfiltration.
Active attack surface: YES (specialized) — primarily nation-state relevance
for extremely high-value airgapped targets (nuclear facility control systems,
classified network terminals); documented in academic research by Ben-Gurion
University CYBER@BGU group.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 26.1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Finding: API authorization is categorically harder than authentication, and
the industry solved authentication first while leaving authorization as the
dominant residual attack surface. Every API that correctly authenticates the
caller still must answer: is this authenticated caller authorized to access
this specific object (BOLA), this specific function (BFLA), or this specific
data field (excessive data exposure)? These questions are answered by
business logic, not cryptographic protocol — and business logic is not
verifiable, auditable, or automatable in the way that authentication is.

Root mechanic: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement) — the boundary between
what an authenticated user is permitted to access and what they actually
access is enforced only by application logic, not by any system-level control.
R03 (trust without verification) as a sub-mechanic — the API trusts that the
caller's object ID parameter represents an object the caller owns, without
verifying ownership.

Confidence: HIGH — CONFIRMED. BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) has
been the #1 entry in OWASP API Security Top 10 since the list's inception in
2019 (and remains so in the 2023 revision). Large-scale BOLA breaches are
documented annually. The difficulty of solving authorization vs. authentication
is a well-established principle in access control theory.

Discovery timeline:
  1998-2005: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) recognized as web
             application vulnerability; included in early OWASP Top 10 lists
  2007-2014: Web application authorization flaws well-documented but
             framed as web vulnerability rather than API-specific concern
  2014-2018: API proliferation in mobile and web applications; IDOR attacks
             at scale begin appearing in breach reports; Venmo API IDOR
             (2018) exposed 200 million transactions
  2019: OWASP API Security Top 10 v1.0 published; BOLA (#1), BFLA (#5),
         Excessive Data Exposure (#3) explicitly codified as API-specific
  2021: T-Mobile API breach — BOLA-class vulnerability exposes 54M customer
         records via unauthorized access to API endpoint
  2021: Peloton API exposes user data without authentication required (not
         BOLA but authorization absence)
  2022: Optus Australia breach — API without authentication on customer data
         endpoint; 9.8M customer records exposed
  2022: Twitter API BOLA — 5.4M user accounts exposed via authorized-but-
         not-for-this-object API call
  2023: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 update; BOLA remains #1; Broken
         Authentication drops as auth mechanisms mature; authorization
         problems increase relative share
  2024-2025: GenAI API proliferation introduces new authorization failure
             patterns: LLM API endpoints with insufficient scope controls,
             cross-user data leakage in shared LLM inference contexts
  2026: BOLA remains unsolved at industry level; automated BOLA detection
         is a hard open problem due to business logic dependence

Temporal layers omitted here (abbreviated — full four-layer treatment in
anatomy backlog):
  Current: BOLA is the dominant API attack class; automation difficult;
  manual and semi-automated techniques dominate offensive tooling; GraphQL
  introspection dramatically expands discoverable attack surface.

"Map the API authorization attack surface comprehensively: (1) BOLA attack
mechanics — how object reference enumeration works across numeric IDs (IDOR),
UUIDs (predictability analysis), and user-supplied identifiers; what makes
BOLA hard to detect in automated scanning; (2) GraphQL-specific authorization
failures — introspection as reconnaissance, nested query authorization gaps,
batch query authorization bypass, field-level authorization failures; (3) BFLA
mechanics — how function-level authorization differs from object-level, why
vertical privilege escalation (user accessing admin function) is more visible
while horizontal escalation (user accessing peer's function) is harder to
detect; (4) excessive data exposure as a design failure — why APIs return
more data than callers should access and what the fix requires at the API
design layer; (5) automated BOLA detection — what approaches exist, why they
fail, and what the theoretical limit is on automated authorization testing."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 26.2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Finding: CI/CD pipelines have become the highest-privilege execution
environments in modern software organizations — they hold production deployment
credentials, source code access, signing keys, and secrets — and they are
substantially less secured than the production systems they deploy to. The
pipeline is the supply chain attack vector of choice for nation-state actors
because pipeline compromise achieves what production environment compromise
cannot: persistence in the software build process that survives production
environment wipes.

Root mechanic: R06 (trusted entity as confused deputy) — the CI/CD system is
trusted by production environments to deliver authentic software, and it acts
as a confused deputy when attackers control the inputs to its build process.
R02 (data/instruction conflation) — pipeline YAML configuration files are
data that is interpreted as instructions; injection into YAML from untrusted
sources (pull requests, external repositories) conflates data with execution.

Confidence: HIGH — CONFIRMED. SolarWinds (build system compromise),
GitHub Actions secret exposure cases, CircleCI breach (2023), and multiple
supply chain attacks targeting CI/CD systems are documented. The structural
vulnerability — pipeline as highest-privilege execution environment with
weakest security posture — is recognized by CISA and NIST SP 800-218.

Discovery timeline:
  2012-2015: Jenkins emerges as dominant CI/CD platform; early Jenkins
             security research documents unauthenticated RCE via build
             executor, improper credential management in Jenkinsfile
  2016: SANS research documents CI/CD as attack surface; credentials in
        pipeline code is a known problem but not yet widely operationalized
        by threat actors
  2017: npm event-stream package compromise — malicious code injected into
        widely-used npm package; demonstrated software supply chain attack
        as concept but not CI/CD-specific
  2018-2019: Increase in dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks
             targeting CI/CD pipeline dependency resolution
  2020: SolarWinds SUNBURST — build system compromise via CI/CD platform
        (SolarWinds Orion build pipeline); DLL injected during build;
        signed by legitimate SolarWinds certificate; distributed to 18,000+
        customers. Defines the paradigm for build-time supply chain attack.
  2021: CodeCov breach — CI/CD script modified to exfiltrate environment
        variables (secrets) from pipeline execution environments of companies
        using CodeCov; thousands of secrets exposed
  2021: GitHub Actions supply chain attacks documented at scale; workflow
        files in public repositories analyzed for secret exposure patterns;
        GITHUB_TOKEN abuse escalation
  2022: PyPI, npm, RubyGems publish packages with exfiltration payloads
        targeting CI/CD pipeline environment variable extraction
  2023: CircleCI security breach — attacker accessed CircleCI production
        infrastructure; customer CI/CD secrets at risk; CircleCI rotated
        all tokens; high-severity advisory issued
  2024-2025: Exploiting GitHub Actions pull request triggers from forked
             repositories (GITHUB_TOKEN escalation via untrusted PR) widely
             published; many open-source project CI/CD workflows found
             vulnerable; GitHub introduces mandatory security improvements
  2026: CI/CD pipeline security now recognized as critical; SLSA (Supply
        chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework published by Google
        and adopted as NIST standard; enforcement in federal procurement
        beginning

Temporal layers (abbreviated):
  Current: YAML injection, secret exposure, and dependency confusion are
  the dominant CI/CD attack classes. Pipeline security tooling (SLSA,
  Sigstore, cosign) is maturing but adoption is incomplete.

"Map the CI/CD pipeline attack surface: (1) YAML injection mechanics — how
untrusted input in GitHub Actions workflow files, GitLab CI YAML, and
Jenkinsfile Groovy can execute attacker code with pipeline credentials;
what the specific vulnerable patterns are (run: steps using untrusted
variables, checkout of untrusted branches); (2) secret exposure attack
surface — how environment variables in CI/CD environments are accessible
to executed steps, what the GITHUB_TOKEN permission model is and where
it is misconfigured, how artifact logs expose secrets; (3) build-time
injection — how SolarWinds-style build process compromise works and what
SLSA Level 3+ requires to prevent it; (4) the pipeline credential attack
surface — what credentials pipelines typically hold, how they are scoped,
and what an attacker can do with pipeline credentials; (5) SLSA and supply
chain security frameworks — what each SLSA level requires, what it prevents,
and what attacks survive even SLSA Level 3."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 26.3
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Finding: HSMs are the cryptographic root of trust for the most sensitive
operations in enterprise and cloud environments, and PKCS#11 — the universal
API for HSM interaction — contains structural oracle vulnerabilities that
allow an attacker with API access to extract keys the HSM is designed to
protect. The HSM is secure against physical extraction of keys; it is
vulnerable to logical extraction via the same API that legitimate users use.

Root mechanic: R02 (data/instruction conflation in shared medium) — the PKCS#11
API uses the HSM as an oracle: a mechanism that accepts inputs and provides
outputs that reveal information about internal state. The oracle is the
legitimate API; the attack is using the oracle's legitimate output to derive
the protected input.
R01 (absence of boundary enforcement) — PKCS#11 permits operations that,
individually are legitimate, but in sequence allow key extraction via the
wrap/unwrap operation chain.

Confidence: HIGH — CONFIRMED. PKCS#11 oracle attacks (the "Bleichenbacher
for HSMs" concept) are well-documented in cryptography literature. Graham
Steel's work at INRIA and the Cortier/Keighren/Steel analyses demonstrate
that PKCS#11 implementations in commercial HSMs allow key extraction via
API-level attacks even when keys are marked non-extractable.

Discovery timeline:
  1994: PKCS#11 (Cryptoki) standard published by RSA Security; designed
        to provide vendor-neutral interface to HSMs
  1998-2003: Early formal analysis of PKCS#11 identifies that the wrap
             and unwrap operations can be combined to violate key confidentiality;
             not yet widely recognized as operational concern
  2003: Clulow publishes "On the Security of PKCS#11" — first systematic
        analysis demonstrating that conformant PKCS#11 APIs allow key
        extraction in specific configurations; landmark paper
  2008: Bortolozzo, Centenaro, Focardi, Steel demonstrate automated
        PKCS#11 API attacks using model-checking tools; confirms practical
        exploitability
  2010-2015: Multiple HSM vendors found to have PKCS#11 implementations
             with specific attack-enabling configurations; vendor-specific
             advisories issued; fixes require firmware updates and policy
             configuration
  2017: Real-world HSM compromise reported in payment processing context;
        details not public due to sensitive nature of disclosure
  2019: Cloud HSM APIs (AWS CloudHSM) analyzed; found to inherit some
        PKCS#11 structural limitations; mitigations documented
  2021-2022: PKCS#11 attack tooling (p11-tool, pkcs11-interop) publicly
             available; documented in penetration testing methodologies
  2023-2026: HSM security remains specialized domain; most organizations
              treat HSMs as secure by assumption without verifying PKCS#11
              configuration; audit of PKCS#11 policies not standard in
              cryptographic security assessments

Temporal layers (abbreviated):
  Current: PKCS#11 oracle attacks require API access; mitigatable by
  proper PKCS#11 policy configuration (CKA_UNWRAP, CKA_WRAP controls);
  most organizations do not audit their PKCS#11 policies. Physical HSM
  attacks require tamper-evident breach; impractical except for nation-states.

"Map the HSM and cryptographic hardware attack surface: (1) PKCS#11 oracle
attack mechanics — specifically how the CKA_WRAP and CKA_UNWRAP attribute
combination allows key extraction and what the complete attack flow looks like;
(2) PKCS#11 policy mitigation — what specific PKCS#11 attribute settings
prevent oracle attacks and how to audit a deployment for correct configuration;
(3) cloud HSM attack surface — how AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and
GCP Cloud HSM differ from physical HSMs in security model and what attack
classes apply to each; (4) TPM attack surface — how TPM 2.0 is used for
key storage and attestation, what attacks exist against TPM-based security
(ROCA vulnerability, speculative execution attacks, physical attacks);
(5) HSM in the certificate authority trust chain — what an HSM compromise
at a CA means for the global PKI and what documented CA HSM security failures
have occurred."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 26.4
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Finding: Air-gapped networks — systems physically isolated from the internet —
are penetrable via physical covert channels that exploit unintended physical
side-effects of computation: acoustic emissions from cooling fans and hard
drives, electromagnetic radiation from CPUs and display cables, power
consumption patterns over shared power lines, and optical signals from LED
activity indicators. The air gap is a boundary that computational physics
violates by making information observable in the physical medium surrounding
the computing device.

Root mechanic: R04 (computation produces observable physical effects) —
this is R04 in its most direct and deliberate instantiation. The covert
channel attack is the systematic exploitation of R04 to bridge a physical
isolation boundary.
R01 (absence of boundary enforcement) — the air gap enforces a network
boundary but not a physical medium boundary; the physical medium
(air, power line, electromagnetic field) crosses the gap.

Confidence: HIGH — CONFIRMED in research settings. Ben-Gurion University's
CYBER@BGU group has demonstrated over 20 distinct air-gap covert channel
attacks across acoustic, electromagnetic, thermal, and power domains.
Operational deployment against targets like nuclear facilities is attributed
to nation-state actors with physical access for implant placement.

Discovery timeline:
  1972: NSA TEMPEST program origins (classified); electromagnetic emanation
        from displays and keyboards recognized as intelligence collection
        source; VDT shields mandated for classified processing
  1985: Wim van Eck publishes first academic TEMPEST research; demonstrates
        CRT display reconstruction from electromagnetic emissions at distance
  2000s: TEMPEST countermeasures (Faraday caging, shielded rooms, emission
         security) established for classified environments; acoustic
         side-channels not yet systematically studied
  2013: Genkin, Shamir, Tromer — "RSA Key Extraction via Low-Bandwidth
         Acoustic Cryptanalysis" — demonstrate RSA key extraction from
         laptop acoustic emissions at 4-meter range; defines acoustic
         side-channel field
  2014-2016: Ben-Gurion CYBER@BGU begins systematic air-gap research program:
             AirHopper (FM radio from GPU electromagnetic), BitWhisper (thermal
             covert channel between co-located computers), GSMem (cellular
             frequency from memory bus)
  2017: Fansmitter — PC fan speed modulated to encode data; acoustic receiver
        at distance decodes transmission at ~900 bits/minute
  2018: DiskFiltration — HDD seek pattern modulated to encode acoustic data;
        works on HDDs not SSDs; air gap covert channel at ~180 bits/min
  2018: PowerHammer — data exfiltration via power line emissions; hard-line
         variant requires access to power panel; soft-line variant works from
         outlet in same circuit
  2019: MAGNETO — magnetic field generated by CPU coils used as covert
         channel; smartphones within 3 inches used as receiver
  2020: GAIROSCOPE — smartphone gyroscope (which doesn't require microphone
         permission) used to receive acoustic covert channel from co-located
         computer
  2021-2022: ETHERLED — network card LEDs blink pattern modulated to encode
             data; AiR-ViBeR — floor vibrations from computer fan received
             by gyroscope
  2023: PIXHELL — LCD monitor noise used as covert channel; no dedicated
         speaker required
  2024-2026: Research program continues; each new channel demonstrates that
             physical isolation is not equivalent to information isolation;
             nation-state operational use confirmed via classified reporting

Temporal layers (abbreviated):
  Current: Operational deployment requires physical implant placement (receiver)
  or compromised device inside the air gap. Stuxnet demonstrated that air-gap
  initial access is achievable via USB. The attack sequence is: USB delivery
  of malware to air-gapped system → malware modulates physical covert channel
  → pre-positioned receiver captures signal. Nation-state only for now.
  Five-year projection: as receiver hardware miniaturizes and channel rate
  improves, the attack becomes more accessible.

"Map the physical covert channel attack landscape for air-gapped systems:
(1) systematic enumeration of all demonstrated channels — acoustic, EM,
thermal, optical, power, seismic — with their bit rate, range, receiver
requirements, and detectability; (2) attack chain analysis — how malware
gets into an air-gapped network (USB, supply chain, insider), how it
controls physical emanations without native covert channel support, and how
receiver placement is established; (3) countermeasure analysis — what
physically blocks each channel class (Faraday cage covers EM but not acoustic;
acoustic shielding covers acoustic but not optical LED), what TEMPEST standard
requirements address, and what no countermeasure addresses; (4) operational
context — what intelligence value justifies the complexity cost of a covert
channel attack versus a human intelligence operation or supply chain attack
on the same target; (5) SDR (Software Defined Radio) as receiver — how SDR
has democratized physical covert channel reception capability and what
the implications are for minimum adversary capability required."

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 26.A: CI/CD PIPELINE AS HIGHEST-PRIVILEGE EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT
Pattern 26.2 — Root Mechanic R06 + R02
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A CI/CD pipeline is an automated system that executes arbitrary code with
the credentials necessary to perform its job. The job requires: (a) read
access to source code repositories; (b) access to secrets needed by the
build (API keys, signing certificates, deployment credentials); (c) write
access to artifact repositories (where built software is stored); (d) deploy
credentials for production environments. This is, by definition, the most
permissioned execution environment in the organization — it has read-write
access to both source and production simultaneously.

The logical reality that makes the attack possible: the pipeline is trusted.
Production environments trust the pipeline to deliver authentic software and
accept deployments from it without secondary verification. The trust is the
point — without it, the pipeline cannot do its job. The attack is therefore
not a bypass of a control; it is the exploitation of a necessary trust
relationship (R06: confused deputy).

The secondary reality: pipeline execution is configured by code (Jenkinsfile,
GitHub Actions YAML, GitLab .gitlab-ci.yml). This code is data. When data
from untrusted sources can influence the code that configures pipeline
execution, R02 (data/instruction conflation) applies: the pipeline interprets
attacker-controlled data as execution instructions.

ATTACK PATH 1 — YAML INJECTION VIA PULL REQUEST:
  Step 1: Attacker forks public repository that has GitHub Actions workflows
  Step 2: Workflow trigger: on: [pull_request_target] — this trigger runs
          the workflow from the base repository (not the fork) but with
          the attacker's code checked out; if the workflow uses the checked-
          out code to define subsequent steps, attacker controls execution
  Step 3: Attacker's fork modifies a step that includes untrusted input
          in a run: block: run: echo ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
          If the PR title contains \`; malicious-command\`, it executes
  Step 4: Malicious command runs with GITHUB_TOKEN permissions and access
          to environment variables (secrets) in the runner environment
  Step 5: Attacker exfiltrates secrets via HTTP request from runner to
          attacker-controlled endpoint

ATTACK PATH 2 — DEPENDENCY CONFUSION / SUPPLY CHAIN IN CI:
  Step 1: Attacker identifies internal package names used in CI/CD pipeline
          (discovable from npm-shrinkwrap.json, package-lock.json, pip
          requirements files in the repository)
  Step 2: Attacker publishes malicious package to public registry under
          the internal name at a higher version number than the internal
          package
  Step 3: CI/CD pipeline pulls from public registry first (misconfigured
          priority), installs malicious package
  Step 4: Malicious package contains postinstall script that exfiltrates
          environment variables (secrets, credentials) to attacker

ATTACK PATH 3 — BUILD SYSTEM COMPROMISE (SolarWinds MODEL):
  Step 1: Attacker compromises CI/CD platform itself (build server,
          orchestration system, build executor) via credential theft,
          unpatched vulnerability, or supply chain attack on CI/CD tooling
  Step 2: Attacker modifies build process: either modifies source files
          during build, injects code at compilation stage, or replaces
          build artifacts post-compilation
  Step 3: Modified artifact is signed by legitimate code signing key
          (the pipeline has legitimate access to signing keys)
  Step 4: Artifact distributed to customers through legitimate distribution
          channel; customers install signed malicious artifact
  Step 5: Attacker has persistent access to every installation

Amplifier 1 — Trust inheritance across the supply chain:
  A compromised pipeline signing key signs every subsequent artifact.
  Every customer of every product built by that pipeline becomes a victim
  without any action on their part. SolarWinds: 18,000+ organizations
  installed the compromised update because they trusted SolarWinds.
  The amplification factor is the customer count of the compromised
  organization, not one organization.

Amplifier 2 — Secrets are not just for the pipeline:
  CI/CD pipelines accumulate secrets from every service they interact with:
  cloud provider credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP), third-party API keys
  (Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, Slack), database connection strings, code
  signing certificates, SSH keys to deployment targets. A pipeline
  secret compromise is therefore also a compromise of every service
  the pipeline is authorized to access. The blast radius is
  proportional to the pipeline's integrations, not just its own scope.

Amplifier 3 — Shared runner environment:
  Cloud CI/CD platforms (GitHub Actions, GitLab.com) run pipelines on
  shared infrastructure. A pipeline that exfiltrates environment variables
  has access only to its own job's variables. But shared runner
  infrastructure creates risk of cross-job environment contamination
  in some configurations; cache poisoning on shared build caches is
  documented. The shared nature means one compromised workflow can
  potentially influence others.

Amplifier 4 — Low security posture expectation:
  Developers configure CI/CD systems; they are not security engineers.
  YAML pipeline configurations are complex, underspecified in security
  documentation, and rapidly changing as features are added. Security
  review of pipeline YAML is not standard in most organizations' security
  review processes. The pipeline attack surface grows faster than
  security awareness about it.

2017: npm event-stream package compromise — malicious code injected
        into popular npm package targeting Copay Bitcoin wallet;
        establishes software supply chain attack concept
  2018: Gentoo GitHub organization compromise — CI/CD for Gentoo Linux
        distribution compromised; malicious code briefly in distribution
  2020: SolarWinds SUNBURST — Orion build system compromised; DLL
        injected during legitimate build; signed with SolarWinds certificate;
        18,000 organizations including US government agencies received
        backdoored update; defining incident for CI/CD attack paradigm
  2021: CodeCov breach — CI/CD script (Bash uploader) modified by attacker;
        environment variables exfiltrated from thousands of pipeline runs;
        affected Twitch, HashiCorp, Rapid7, and others; specific secrets
        and keys compromised
  2021: PHP official repository compromised — attacker with repository
        write access committed malicious backdoor code directly; caught
        within hours but demonstrated supply chain via direct VCS compromise
  2021: UA-Parser-JS npm package hijacked — cryptocurrency mining and
        credential stealing code added; package had 6M weekly downloads
  2022: Travis CI security advisory — historical builds could expose
        secrets from forks; thousands of repositories potentially affected
  2022: Python PyPI 2FA requirement announced after wave of account
        takeovers targeting maintainers of popular packages (supply chain
        via maintainer credential theft)
  2023: CircleCI breach — attacker obtained session token via malware
        on engineer laptop; accessed CircleCI production infrastructure;
        customer secrets at risk; high-severity advisory to rotate all
        secrets used in CircleCI
  2024-2025: GitHub Actions workflow YAML injection exploits published
             against major open-source projects; GitHub introduces
             mandatory pin-to-hash for third-party actions in some contexts

Irreducible 1 — The fundamental trust requirement:
  A functional deployment pipeline MUST have production deployment credentials.
  There is no architecture in which the pipeline does its job without holding
  some trust relationship with production. The attack exploits this necessary
  trust. The irreducible residue: the pipeline's production trust cannot
  be eliminated without eliminating the pipeline's function. The best
  mitigations scope this trust minimally and monitor its use, but cannot
  reduce it to zero.

Irreducible 2 — Code signing cannot authenticate intent:
  A build signed by a legitimate key proves the build passed through the
  authorized signing infrastructure. It does not prove the code being
  signed is free of malicious modification. If the modification happens
  inside the signing perimeter (as in SolarWinds), the signature is valid.
  Code signing is an integrity mechanism for the distribution channel,
  not for the build content. SLSA attempts to address this via provenance
  attestation, but provenance traces the build process, not the code
  content's intention.

Irreducible 3 — Dependency trust:
  Every package a pipeline installs is trusted code executing with pipeline
  privileges. The attack surface of the pipeline's dependency graph is the
  sum of every maintainer's security posture across the entire transitive
  dependency tree. This is unbounded and cannot be meaningfully audited.
  SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) makes the dependency tree visible;
  it does not make the dependencies trustworthy.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 26.B: AIR-GAP PHYSICAL COVERT CHANNELS — R04 AT ITS LIMIT
Pattern 26.4 — Root Mechanic R04
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All computation is physical. When a transistor switches, it dissipates energy.
When a hard drive read head moves, it displaces air. When a fan spins, it
creates vibrations. When an LED lights, it emits photons. When a CPU executes
at varying rates, it draws varying current. None of these effects are
information in the computational sense — they are side effects of the physical
substrate of information processing.

The covert channel insight: these physical side effects can be modulated.
A program running on the air-gapped computer can control: fan speed (by
modulating CPU temperature load), HDD head movement (by reading in patterns),
LED blink rate (by writing to network card or disk), CPU power draw (by
varying computation intensity), electromagnetic emission (by varying memory
access patterns). Once a physical effect can be modulated, it can carry
information. The information channel uses physics as the medium: sound waves
through air (acoustic), electromagnetic fields (EM), photons (optical), heat
(thermal), electrical potential (power line), mechanical vibration (seismic).

The air gap blocks the network layer. It cannot block physics. R04 is
therefore not a design flaw — it is a consequence of the laws of
thermodynamics and electromagnetism applied to computational hardware.

All air-gap covert channel attacks follow the same three-phase structure:
Initial access, Modulation, Reception.

PHASE 1 — INITIAL ACCESS TO AIR-GAPPED SYSTEM:
  USB delivery: Stuxnet model — USB drive left in facility parking lot,
  plugged in by insider; autorun or social engineering triggers execution.
  Supply chain: Malware inserted during hardware or software manufacturing.
  Insider: Planted agent or coerced insider installs software directly.
  Satellite connection gap: Believed-to-be-airgapped system has undiscovered
  satellite uplink (documented in nation-state operations).
  This phase is necessary and often the hard part. Once malware is inside,
  the covert channel is the exfiltration mechanism.

PHASE 2 — MODULATION (malware running on air-gapped system):
  Acoustic (Fansmitter): Malware calls OS APIs to set CPU workload, which
  sets processor temperature, which determines fan speed. Fan speed is
  modulated to encode bits: high speed = 1, low speed = 0 (or frequency-
  shift keying). Bit rate: ~900 bits/minute at ~10-meter range.
  Acoustic (DiskFiltration): Malware issues HDD seek commands in patterns
  that produce acoustic tones at specific frequencies. Data encoded as
  frequency values. Bit rate: ~180 bits/minute; only works on spinning HDDs.
  Electromagnetic (AirHopper): Malware modulates GPU memory access patterns
  to control FM-band electromagnetic emissions from GPU cable; receiver
  is an FM radio (or SDR tuned to FM band). Bit rate: 100-480 bits/sec.
  Electromagnetic (GSMem): Malware generates specific memory bus access
  patterns that produce emissions in cellular frequency bands; receiver
  is a cell phone. Bit rate: ~1-4 bytes/sec.
  Power line (PowerHammer): Malware modulates CPU workload to vary current
  draw; power line carries the current variation; receiver taps power line.
  Hard-line variant: receiver at main panel; soft-line: receiver at wall outlet.
  Optical (GAIROSCOPE): Malware emits ultrasonic sound from computer speaker;
  nearby smartphone gyroscope receives vibration (gyroscope is an accelerometer,
  not a microphone, so it bypasses microphone permission); gyroscope data
  decoded to recover transmitted bits.
  Optical (LED-it-GO): Malware modulates HDD activity LED blink rate; security
  camera or photoreceptor in line of sight receives optical signal.

PHASE 3 — RECEPTION:
  Each channel requires a receiver that: (a) has line of access to the
  physical signal (proximity, line of sight for optical, same power circuit
  for power line); (b) is controlled by the attacker or is an existing
  device (phone, radio) that can be compromised to serve as receiver;
  (c) has a data extraction path back to the attacker.
  Receiver placement methods: pre-positioned device in facility, compromised
  employee phone (phone receives, exfiltrates via cellular), compromised
  IoT device in facility, surveillance camera (optical channels), rogue
  FM radio receiver at facility perimeter.

Amplifier 1 — SDR democratizes reception:
  Software Defined Radio (RTL-SDR dongles: ~$20 to ~$300) can receive any
  radio frequency channel used by air-gap covert channels. A sophisticated
  receiver that required tens of thousands of dollars in specialized
  equipment in 2000 now costs $25. The minimum adversary capability for
  receiving electromagnetic covert channels has dropped by multiple orders
  of magnitude.

Amplifier 2 — The receiver can be a phone already in the facility:
  Employees in secure facilities carry smartphones. Many air-gap covert
  channels can be received by a compromised smartphone: GAIROSCOPE uses
  the gyroscope (no microphone permission), GSMem uses cellular reception,
  acoustic channels use the microphone (if phone is compromised). The
  required receiver may already be inside the air gap.

Amplifier 3 — Cumulative channel capacity:
  Individual air-gap channels have low bit rates (100 bits/minute to
  100 bits/second). But target data (cryptographic keys: 256 bits; SSH
  private key: ~3,000 bits; password: ~100 bits) is small. A channel
  at 900 bits/minute can exfiltrate a 256-bit AES key in 18 seconds,
  an RSA 2048-bit private key in about 2.5 minutes.

Amplifier 4 — Stacking:
  Multiple channels can operate simultaneously from the same compromised
  system, increasing effective bandwidth without increasing any individual
  channel's detectability.

1985: Van Eck phreaking published — CRT monitor reconstruction from
        electromagnetic emissions; Tempest classification declassified
        through this research
  2008-2012: Stuxnet operational (approximate) — air-gap bridging via
             USB used to deliver weapon to Iranian uranium enrichment
             facility; Natanz centrifuges destroyed; most famous air-gap
             compromise in public record
  2013: Acoustic RSA key extraction (Genkin, Shamir, Tromer) — RSA
        private key extracted from laptop audio emissions at 4-meter range
  2014: AirHopper demonstrated — FM radio air-gap covert channel
  2015: BitWhisper — thermal covert channel between co-located computers
        at 15-bit/hour rate
  2016: GSMem — cellular air-gap covert channel via memory bus
  2017: Fansmitter — PC fan speed air-gap acoustic channel demonstrated
  2018: DiskFiltration — HDD acoustic channel
  2018: PowerHammer — power-line exfiltration channel
  2019: MAGNETO — magnetic field covert channel, smartphone receiver
  2020: GAIROSCOPE — gyroscope-receives-speaker channel (no permissions)
  2021: ETHERLED — network card LED blink covert channel
  2022: PIXHELL — LCD monitor noise channel (no speaker required)
  2022: RAMBO — RAM electromagnetic emissions air-gap channel
  2023: COVID-bit — switched-mode power supply electromagnetic channel
  Nation-state operational: Confirmed attribution of air-gap covert channel
  attacks in nuclear facility context via classified reporting; specific
  operations not publicly confirmed beyond Stuxnet

Irreducible 1 — Physics cannot be patched:
  The physical effects that enable covert channels are thermodynamic and
  electromagnetic consequences of computation. They cannot be eliminated
  by software patches. TEMPEST-certified hardware reduces EM emissions
  via physical shielding, but cannot reduce them to zero. Acoustic isolation
  can reduce acoustic channels but cannot eliminate fan and drive noise
  completely (temperature management is required). Each physical channel
  can be attenuated; none can be driven to zero while the computing device
  continues to function.

Irreducible 2 — New channels continue to emerge:
  The CYBER@BGU group has published 20+ distinct channels since 2014.
  The set is not closed: any new unintended physical effect of computation
  is a candidate channel. Wireless charging, USB power variation, HDMI
  signal characteristics, and additional sensor modalities in smartphones
  represent unexplored or partially-explored channel candidates.

Irreducible 3 — Countermeasures require physical access to implement:
  Faraday caging, acoustic isolation, LED masking, and power-line filtering
  all require physical installation at the facility level. Organizations
  that rely on air-gaps for security often do not implement the full
  countermeasure suite; the air-gap is treated as sufficient. The gap
  between air-gap trust and air-gap security is the irreducible risk.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 26.C: BLOCKCHAIN CONSENSUS SECURITY — BACKLOG REDUCTION (Pattern 18.3)
Root Mechanic R03 + R05
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Blockchain systems derive security from a consensus mechanism — the protocol
by which distributed nodes agree on the canonical state of the ledger without
a central authority. Proof of Work (PoW) bases consensus on computational
expenditure: the node that solves a hash puzzle first earns the right to
append the next block. Proof of Stake (PoS) bases consensus on economic
stake: nodes with more tokens have more influence over block selection.
Both mechanisms are designed to make falsifying the ledger economically or
computationally prohibitive for any single actor.

The physics: PoW security scales with the total computational power (hashrate)
committed to the network. PoS security scales with the total economic value
staked. Both are quantitative thresholds. Below the threshold (a single actor
controls >50% of hashrate or >33-67% of stake depending on protocol), the
consensus mechanism holds. At or above the threshold, the mechanism fails.
This is the 51% attack surface: consensus security is not binary but a
function of the ratio of attacker resources to total network resources.

The logical inversion: a blockchain that is designed to be trustless
(no central authority required) is vulnerable when a single actor
accumulates enough resources to impose their version of truth. The trustless
property is contingent on resource distribution — it trusts that no single
actor will control majority resources, which is an implicit trust assumption.
R03: trust without verification of resource distribution assumption.

51% ATTACK (PoW):
  Step 1: Attacker acquires or rents computing resources exceeding 50%
          of the network's total hashrate. For small networks: available
          via NiceHash or similar hashrate rental markets at low cost.
          For large networks (Bitcoin): requires billions in hardware and
          electricity; impractical for all but nation-states.
  Step 2: Attacker mines a private chain starting from a chosen block height,
          including their own transaction (spending coins to an exchange).
  Step 3: Attacker deposits coins at exchange, receives fiat or other crypto.
  Step 4: Attacker continues mining private chain until it exceeds the
          public chain in cumulative work.
  Step 5: Attacker publishes private chain; per Nakamoto consensus rules,
          the chain with most cumulative work is canonical; public chain
          is reorganized; attacker's transaction is now absent.
  Step 6: Exchange's confirmation of the deposit is invalidated; attacker
          has double-spent: same coins spent twice, once on chain
          (exchange deposit) and once off it (private chain).

SELFISH MINING (PoW variant):
  Step 1: Attacker with >~33% hashrate begins mining blocks privately
          without broadcasting them.
  Step 2: When attacker finds a block, continues mining in secret.
  Step 3: When honest network finds a competing block, attacker releases
          their private block, causing a race; with >33% hashrate, attacker
          wins more often than honest nodes.
  Step 4: Attacker earns disproportionate block rewards without executing
          full double-spend; economic reward without majority hashrate.

LONG-RANGE ATTACK (PoS):
  Step 1: Attacker acquires private keys of validators that were large
          stakeholders in the network's early history (when staked amounts
          were low and key acquisition is cheap or keys were abandoned).
  Step 2: Attacker re-creates the blockchain history from that early point,
          using old validator keys (which were legitimate at that time) to
          sign alternative blocks.
  Step 3: New nodes joining the network that download the full chain may
          accept the alternative history if they don't have access to
          a trusted checkpoint.
  Mitigation: Weak subjectivity checkpoints — new nodes must obtain
  a recent trusted checkpoint from a social source; this introduces a
  trust requirement that formally contradicts the trustless claim.

Amplifier 1 — Hashrate concentration is structurally incentivized:
  Mining pools aggregate small miners for consistent rewards; the largest
  pools routinely approach 25-30% of Bitcoin hashrate. Coordination among
  two or three large pools produces a 51% coalition. The economic incentives
  of mining (economies of scale) drive concentration; the security model
  requires distribution. These forces are in direct opposition.

Amplifier 2 — Hashrate markets make attacks on small chains cheap:
  NiceHash and similar platforms allow rental of hashrate by the hour.
  A 51% attack on a small PoW chain can be rented for tens to hundreds of
  dollars. Ethereum Classic (ETC) has been attacked multiple times;
  Bitcoin Gold, Bitcoin SV, Vertcoin, and others have been attacked.
  The attack cost scales with network size; small networks are regularly
  attacked.

Amplifier 3 — Exchange confirmation counts are exploitable:
  Exchanges require N confirmations before crediting deposits (Bitcoin: 3-6
  for most exchanges). If an attacker can reorganize more than N blocks
  (requiring sustained majority hashrate for N block intervals), they can
  double-spend. Exchange confirmation security is a function of the attacker's
  ability to maintain majority hashrate for the required duration.

Amplifier 4 — PoS economic concentration:
  PoS security assumes stake is distributed. Early token distribution,
  venture funding, and the staking returns themselves (compound interest
  on existing stake) all drive concentration. Ethereum's staking distribution
  shows significant concentration among large staking providers
  (Lido, Coinbase, Binance), creating operational if not economic concentration.

2018: Bitcoin Gold (BTG) 51% attack — attacker double-spent approximately
        $18M; BTG uses GPU-minable algorithm, making hashrate cheap to rent
  2019: Ethereum Classic (ETC) — multiple 51% attacks; $1.1M double-spent
        in January 2019; additional attacks in August 2020 ($5.6M); ETC
        modified consensus rules in response
  2018: Vertcoin — four 51% attacks documented; reorganizations of 300+
        blocks; small-market-cap chain with GPU-rentable hashrate
  2020: Bitcoin SV (BSV) — three 51% attacks in one week; blockchain
        reorganized; exchanges suspended deposits
  2018: Monacoin (Japan) — selfish mining attack documented; 57% of blocks
        in a period produced by single attacker pool
  2021: Firo (formerly Zcoin) — chain reorganization attack; double-spend
        executed
  Selfish mining: Academic consensus that selfish mining is practiced
  by mining pools but difficult to distinguish from legitimate variance;
  empirical evidence suggestive but not conclusive for major pools
  PoS long-range attacks: No confirmed operational instance against major
  PoS chains; mitigated by weak subjectivity in practice

Irreducible 1 — The threshold cannot be enforced:
  Consensus security requires that no single actor controls a majority of
  the consensus resource. This cannot be enforced at the protocol level —
  the protocol cannot know the real-world ownership structure behind
  public addresses or mining pool operators. Concentration is detectable
  statistically but not preventable by protocol rules without identity
  requirements that contradict decentralization.

Irreducible 2 — Small chains will always be vulnerable:
  The security of a consensus mechanism scales with the total resources
  committed to it. Small-cap blockchains cannot attract sufficient hashrate
  or stake to achieve meaningful security. This is a structural property:
  a thousand small chains cannot have the security of one large chain
  even with identical protocols.

Irreducible 3 — PoS introduces weak subjectivity as a fundamental requirement:
  PoS long-range attacks require new nodes to obtain a trusted recent
  checkpoint from an external source (not derivable from the chain itself).
  This is weak subjectivity: a formal trust requirement that Ethereum and
  other PoS chains acknowledge and accept. It means PoS blockchains are not
  fully trustless — they require social trust for chain initialization.
  This is an irreducible feature, not a bug to be fixed.

EXITING STAGE 3: 76 anatomies cumulative (73 entering + 3 this cycle)
ANATOMY BACKLOG: 26 patterns (reduced from 27 by one backlog completion)

NEW DEFENSES THIS CYCLE: D269-D284
