ANATOMY 30.C — ICS HISTORIAN SERVER AS IT-TO-OT LATERAL MOVEMENT BRIDGE
[Resolves: G187 (ICS historian as pivot); Pattern 30.2]
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1: WHAT (surface description)
  An ICS historian server (OSIsoft PI, AspenTech, Honeywell Uniformance)
  positioned in the industrial DMZ to aggregate OT process data for
  enterprise dashboards and analytics becomes the primary lateral movement
  pivot from IT network access to OT network access, because it maintains
  simultaneous network connections to both domains.

LAYER 2: HOW (mechanism)
  Historian architecture (standard deployment):
    • Network interface 1: IT/enterprise network (Purdue Level 4)
      → serves REST/JDBC/ODBC/PI API to enterprise consumers
      → receives updates from IT directory services (AD authentication)
      → exposed to enterprise email, web browsing from admin workstations
    • Network interface 2: OT network (Purdue Level 3 or 3.5)
      → receives data from PLCs, RTUs, SCADA servers via OPC DA/UA
      → may issue commands back to SCADA in response to API calls
      → authentication to OT systems: service account, often shared

Attack path via historian pivot:
    Step 1 → IT network initial access (phishing, VPN vulnerability,
      web application attack against enterprise-facing systems)
    Step 2 → Credential harvesting on IT network; AD user accounts
    Step 3 → Historian administrator identification via AD group membership
      or network scan for historian-specific ports (PI port 5450, OPC 135)
    Step 4 → Historian server compromise via:
      (a) Credential reuse — historian admin uses same credentials on IT
      (b) Vulnerability in historian web application (PI Web API, AF SDK)
      (c) Unpatched Windows OS on historian (IT updates often blocked for
          OT-adjacent systems to avoid "change management" triggers)
      (d) Phishing historian admin user specifically
    Step 5 → From historian: enumerate OT network
      • OPC server list: all OT data sources visible in historian config
      • Network scan from historian NIC 2 — reaches OT devices
      • Historian connection config reveals SCADA hostnames and IPs
    Step 6 → Lateral movement to OT:
      • Historian service account (OPC client) retains persistent auth
        to OT data sources — attacker inherits this access
      • OPC DA/UA connections from historian to SCADA pass without
        additional authentication (trust relationship assumed)
      • SCADA server reachable from historian; attacker now on OT network
    Step 7 → OT reconnaissance and targeting
      • SCADA HMI access: read process state, identify control points
      • PLC enumeration via SCADA tag database
      • Process parameter understanding: historian stores years of
        normal process data — attacker learns what "normal" looks like
        before manipulating process values

LAYER 3: WHY IT WORKS (root mechanics)
  R03 (trust without verification): OT network trusts historian because
    historian is a known OT device. IT network trusts historian because
    historian is an IT-registered Windows server. Neither side verifies
    the historian's security posture before trusting it. The historian
    IS the trust bridge.
  R06 (confused deputy): Historian acts as deputy for IT users (querying
    OT data on their behalf) and as deputy for OT systems (forwarding
    historian credentials to enterprise consumers). When compromised, the
    historian's legitimate credentials become the attacker's credentials
    for both networks.
  R01 (absence of boundary enforcement): Industrial DMZ is intended to
    create a one-directional data flow from OT to IT. In practice, the
    historian requires bidirectional connectivity to function (admin access,
    OPC writes, time synchronization, authentication). The DMZ boundary
    is enforced inconsistently because operational requirements erode it.

LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCES
  2015 — Ukraine power grid: IT-to-OT pivot path used; historian-class
           systems identified as likely pivot point in forensic analysis
  2017 — TRITON: used IT-to-OT path via industrial DMZ before reaching
           SIS engineering network; historian-adjacent systems compromised
  2018 — Norsk Hydro: LockerGoga ransomware; IT compromise propagated
           to OT-adjacent systems; production halted across global operations
  2021 — Colonial Pipeline: DarkSide ransomware; IT OT boundary concern
           caused operator to proactively shut down OT systems even though
           OT compromise not confirmed — demonstrates historian-class
           systems create psychological as well as technical bridging risk
  2022 — Multiple manufacturing sector ransomware incidents: forensic
           reports cite historian and HMI servers as IT-to-OT transition
           points in post-incident analyses

LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE
  Network architecture:
    • Data diode from OT to historian (unidirectional gateway): eliminates
      return path from historian to OT; historian receives data only
      → eliminates command channel from historian to SCADA
      → eliminates lateral movement path via OPC command interface
    • Separate historian admin network segment: historian administration
      via dedicated management interface on separate VLAN; prevents
      historian admin credentials from being reachable via enterprise LAN
    • Firewall rules: historian NIC 2 permitted only to receive OPC DA/UA
      data from specific OT source IPs; no scan, no ping, no other protocol

Credential hygiene:
    • Historian service account: unique, non-AD-joined, not reusable
      across other IT systems; rotate on schedule
    • Historian admin account: separate from enterprise AD; managed
      via PAM (Privileged Access Management) with session recording
    • OPC authentication: OPC UA supports PKI-based authentication;
      deploy client certificates on historian; revoke on compromise

Patch management:
    • Historian Windows OS: classified as IT asset for patching purposes;
      receive enterprise patch cadence; change management procedures
      must NOT exempt historian from security patches
    • Historian application (PI, AspenTech): follow vendor PSIRT for
      application-layer vulnerabilities; PI Web API is internet-accessible
      in many deployments and has had critical CVEs

Detection:
    • Historian network monitoring: alert on outbound connections from
      historian NIC 2 that are not established OPC data collection sessions
    • Historian authentication logging: alert on logon events outside
      normal historian admin working hours
    • OT network scan detection: historian should never initiate network
      discovery; any scan from historian NIC 2 is immediate IOC

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NEW ATTACK ENTRIES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A249 — ADVERSARIAL MALWARE EVASION (STATIC FEATURE PERTURBATION)
  Class: AI/ML adversarial attack
  Root: R02 (feature space decoupled from execution semantics)
  Method: Modify PE binary features (import table, overlay bytes, section
    names) to shift ML classifier output below detection threshold while
    preserving malicious payload execution
  Tools: EMBER framework, MalGAN, GAMMA (Genetic Adversarial ML Attack),
    custom PE modification scripts
  Target: ML-based AV/EDR static analysis components
  Difficulty: Medium (tools exist; requires binary modification skill)
  Impact: Evasion of first-layer detection; subsequent dynamic analysis
    or behavioral monitoring may still detect

A250 — ADVERSARIAL EVASION OF NETWORK ML IDS
  Class: AI/ML adversarial attack
  Root: R02 (network feature representation decoupled from threat semantics)
  Method: Modify network traffic timing, packet sizes, or header fields
    to shift ML-based NIDS classification while preserving attack payload
    delivery (C2 traffic, data exfiltration, exploit payloads)
  Techniques: Traffic fragmentation timing manipulation, protocol field
    stuffing, steganographic payload encoding in benign-looking flows
  Target: ML-based network intrusion detection systems
  Difficulty: High (requires understanding of target model's feature space)
  Impact: Evasion of network-layer ML detection

A251 — ICS HISTORIAN COMPROMISE AS OT PIVOT
  Class: IT-to-OT lateral movement
  Root: R03 (historian trusted by both IT and OT without mutual verification)
  Method: Compromise historian server via IT-network attack path; leverage
    historian's OT network connectivity and service account credentials
    to reach SCADA, PLC, RTU systems; enumerate OT assets via OPC
  Tools: Standard Windows TTPs for historian compromise; Nmap for OT
    enumeration from historian NIC; OPC client tools for SCADA access
  Target: Industrial control networks protected by IT/OT segmentation
  Difficulty: Medium (historian typically less secured than core IT systems)
  Impact: Full OT network access from IT compromise

A252 — MODBUS COMMAND INJECTION VIA HISTORIAN WRITE-BACK
  Class: OT protocol attack
  Root: R01 (no authentication on Modbus command channel)
  Method: From compromised historian, identify OPC write tags that map to
    Modbus coil registers on field devices; issue OPC writes that result
    in Modbus force-single-coil commands to PLCs; alter process state
  Technique: Requires knowledge of historian tag-to-PLC register mapping
    (available in historian configuration files)
  Target: PLCs and RTUs receiving Modbus commands via OPC bridge
  Difficulty: High (requires OT knowledge; historian write-back not always
    enabled; process impact requires domain-specific knowledge)
  Impact: Process manipulation; physical consequence possible

A253 — ADCS ESC4 (TEMPLATE ATTRIBUTE WRITE FOR ESC1 INTRODUCTION)
  Class: Active Directory privilege escalation
  Root: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement on certificate template ACLs)
  Method: Identify certificate template where unprivileged principal has
    write access to template attributes (WriteDACL, WriteProperty, GenericWrite);
    modify template to add msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag allowing enrollee-
    supplied SAN (introduces ESC1 condition); enroll certificate with
    arbitrary UPN; obtain TGT for any user via PKINIT; revert template
  Tools: Certify.exe (SpecterOps), certipy (Python), standard LDAP writes
  Target: AD environments with ADCS; enterprise CA with permissive template ACLs
  Difficulty: Medium (requires Certify/certipy; template write access needed)
  Impact: Full domain compromise via arbitrary user certificate forgery

A254 — ADCS ESC6 (CA FLAG ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 ENABLED)
  Class: Active Directory privilege escalation
  Root: R01 (CA policy permits SAN override on any enrollment)
  Method: Identify CA with EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag set; enroll
    any certificate from any template; include arbitrary SAN (UPN) in
    enrollment request via -altname flag; CA issues certificate containing
    DA UPN; use certificate for PKINIT to obtain DA TGT
  Tools: Certify.exe with -altname flag, certipy
  Target: AD environments where CA was misconfigured with this flag
    (set by default in some older CA setup guides)
  Difficulty: Low (simpler than ESC1; any enrollment template sufficient)
  Impact: Full domain compromise from any authenticated user

A255 — EAP-GTC CREDENTIAL CAPTURE VIA ROGUE ACCESS POINT
  Class: Wireless credential theft
  Root: R01 (EAP negotiation unauthenticated; R03 client trusts any AP)
  Method: Deploy rogue AP with same SSID as target; respond to EAP
    negotiation with EAP-GTC request; client transmits credential in
    cleartext within EAP-GTC response; capture OTP or password directly
  Tools: hostapd-wpe, eaphammer, Airbase-NG with custom EAP handler
  Target: Enterprise wireless networks using PEAP or EAP-TTLS where
    client does not validate server certificate
  Difficulty: Medium (requires RF proximity; rogue AP hardware)
  Impact: Direct credential capture; domain account compromise

A256 — AD TIERING VIOLATION EXPLOITATION (CROSS-TIER CREDENTIAL REUSE)
  Class: Active Directory lateral movement
  Root: R03 (trust assumption: same credential on multiple tiers)
  Method: Compromise Tier 2 asset (workstation); find cached credentials
    of accounts that also authenticate to Tier 1 or Tier 0 systems
    (detected via BloodHound path analysis or LSASS credential dump);
    use those credentials to authenticate directly to domain controllers
    or other Tier 0 assets
  Tools: BloodHound for path analysis; Mimikatz/secretsdump for credential
    extraction; Pass-the-Hash or Kerberos ticket reuse for Tier 0 access
  Target: AD environments with tiering model violations (most enterprises)
  Difficulty: Low-Medium (tools mature; violations extremely common)
  Impact: Tier 0 compromise (domain controller access, CA compromise)
    from Tier 2 initial access

NEW DEFENSE ENTRIES

D333 — ADVERSARIAL ROBUSTNESS TRAINING FOR ML SECURITY MODELS
  Control type: Preventive (AI/ML)
  Mechanism: Include adversarial examples in ML classifier training set;
    train on FGSM/PGD-perturbed samples alongside clean samples;
    evaluate robustness on held-out adversarial test set
  Scope: ML-based malware classifiers, network IDS models, anomaly detectors
  Limitations: Reduces but does not eliminate evasion; adversarial arms
    race dynamic; new attack methods may not be covered by training set

D334 — ENSEMBLE DETECTION (MULTI-MODEL CONSENSUS FOR SECURITY CLASSIFICATION)
  Control type: Preventive (AI/ML architecture)
  Mechanism: Require consensus across multiple detection engines with
    different architectures, feature sets, and training data before
    classifying input as benign; adversarial examples that evade one
    model transfer less reliably across diverse architectures
  Scope: AV/EDR with multiple detection layers; network IDS with signature
    + behavioral + ML components
  Effectiveness: Significantly raises adversarial evasion cost

D335 — DYNAMIC ANALYSIS AS ADVERSARIAL EVASION COUNTERMEASURE
  Control type: Detective (runtime behavior)
  Mechanism: Execute suspicious binaries in sandboxed environment;
    behavioral analysis captures malicious function regardless of static
    feature perturbations; static adversarial perturbations do not affect
    runtime behavior
  Scope: Malware analysis pipelines; EDR with sandboxed detonation
  Limitations: Evasion-aware malware detects sandbox environment and
    delays or suppresses malicious behavior; requires sandbox environment
    detection countermeasures

D336 — DATA DIODE (UNIDIRECTIONAL GATEWAY) FOR ICS HISTORIAN ISOLATION
  Control type: Preventive (network architecture)
  Mechanism: Replace bidirectional firewall between OT and historian with
    hardware-enforced unidirectional gateway (data diode); data flows only
    from OT to historian; no network path from historian to OT
  Products: Waterfall Security Solutions, Owl Cyber Defense, Claroty
  Limitations: Eliminates historian write-back (operational impact if used);
    some OPC configurations require bidirectional connectivity; historian
    admin access must use separate management path

D337 — OPC UA CERTIFICATE-BASED AUTHENTICATION FOR OT DATA SOURCES
  Control type: Preventive (authentication)
  Mechanism: Replace OPC DA (no authentication) with OPC UA (supports PKI);
    require historian to present client certificate to OT data sources;
    OT data sources verify certificate before accepting data collection
    session; revoke historian certificate on compromise
  Scope: Historian-to-SCADA and historian-to-PLC OPC connections
  Limitations: Requires OPC UA support on OT devices (many legacy devices
    support only OPC DA); certificate management overhead

D338 — HISTORIAN NETWORK TRAFFIC BASELINING AND ANOMALY DETECTION
  Control type: Detective
  Mechanism: Capture normal histogram of historian NIC 2 traffic (OPC
    collection sessions, expected source IPs, expected function codes,
    expected timing); alert on any deviation: new source/destination,
    unexpected protocol, scan behavior, off-hours activity
  Scope: Industrial DMZ network monitoring
  Coverage: Detects historian compromise via outbound OT lateral movement
    attempts; complements data diode for detection layer

D339 — ADCS TEMPLATE AUDITING WITH CERTIFY/CERTIPY
  Control type: Detective (periodic assessment)
  Mechanism: Run Certify.exe (Windows) or certipy (Python) against
    production ADCS environment; enumerate all certificate templates;
    identify ESC1-ESC10 conditions; report misconfigured templates
    and CA settings to security team
  Frequency: Quarterly minimum; after any ADCS configuration change
  Coverage: Detects ESC4 (write access on templates), ESC6 (CA flag),
    ESC8 (web enrollment), ESC1 (enrollee-supplied SAN), ESC3, ESC7
  Reference: SpecterOps whitepaper "Certified Pre-Owned" (2021)

D340 — ADCS CA FLAG REMEDIATION (EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2)
  Control type: Preventive (configuration hardening)
  Mechanism: Remove EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag from enterprise CA
    via certutil: certutil -config "<CA>" -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
    Restart Certificate Services. Verify flag removal.
  Effect: Eliminates ESC6 attack class entirely
  Limitation: May break legacy enrollment workflows that rely on SAN
    override; test in non-production before applying

D341 — ADCS TEMPLATE ACL REMEDIATION
  Control type: Preventive (access control)
  Mechanism: For each certificate template: remove write permissions
    (WriteDACL, WriteProperty, GenericWrite, GenericAll) from non-admin
    principals; ensure only CA Admins and Enterprise Admins have template
    modification rights; use tiered admin accounts for template management
  Effect: Eliminates ESC4 attack class; reduces ESC5, ESC7 surface
  Tools: Active Directory Sites and Services → Certificate Templates;
    or ADSI Edit for ACL modification

D342 — RADIUS SERVER CERTIFICATE VALIDATION ENFORCEMENT (EAP-TLS)
  Control type: Preventive (802.1X authentication)
  Mechanism: Configure supplicant (client) 802.1X profiles to require
    server certificate validation with specific CA and server name;
    supplicant rejects EAP authentication from any server presenting
    unexpected certificate; prevents rogue AP EAP interception
  Deployment: Managed via MDM (Microsoft Intune, Jamf) for enterprise
    devices; enforce on both Windows and macOS/iOS clients
  Effect: Eliminates EAP-MD5, EAP-GTC, and PEAP-MS-CHAPv2 downgrade
    attacks when combined with EAP-TLS or PEAP with validated server cert

D343 — ELIMINATION OF EAP-MD5 AND EAP-GTC FROM RADIUS SERVER
  Control type: Preventive (authentication policy)
  Mechanism: Disable EAP-MD5 and EAP-GTC from RADIUS server's permitted
    EAP method list; server will refuse to negotiate these methods
    regardless of client or AP request; forces use of certificate-based
    EAP methods (EAP-TLS, PEAP-EAP-TLS)
  Scope: FreeRADIUS, Cisco ISE, Microsoft NPS
  Effect: Eliminates EAP-GTC credential capture; forces attackers to
    perform full certificate-based attack (much harder)

D344 — AD TIERING MODEL ENFORCEMENT VIA GROUP POLICY
  Control type: Preventive (access control)
  Mechanism: GPO-enforced user rights assignment:
    Tier 0 DCs: deny logon via "Deny log on locally" and "Deny log on
      through Remote Desktop Services" for all non-Tier 0 admin accounts
    Tier 1 servers: deny logon for Tier 0 admin accounts (prevent Tier 0
      admins from exposing credentials on Tier 1)
    Tier 2 workstations: deny logon for Tier 0 and Tier 1 admin accounts
  Effect: Severs cross-tier credential exposure paths; forces attackers
    to compromise each tier independently without credential reuse

D345 — PRIVILEGED ACCESS WORKSTATIONS (PAW) FOR TIER 0 ADMINISTRATION
  Control type: Preventive (endpoint isolation)
  Mechanism: Dedicated hardened workstations for Tier 0 administrative
    tasks only; PAW boots to restricted OS image; cannot access internet,
    email, office applications; only connects to Tier 0 network segment;
    Tier 0 admins have separate daily-use workstations for non-admin tasks
  Effect: Eliminates credential exposure of Tier 0 accounts on general-
    purpose workstations vulnerable to user-mode compromise
  Microsoft reference: "Privileged Access Workstations" and "ESAE
    (Enhanced Security Administrative Environment)" architecture

D346 — BLOODHOUND ENTERPRISE FOR CONTINUOUS ACL PATH MONITORING
  Control type: Detective (continuous)
  Mechanism: Deploy BloodHound Enterprise (commercial) or neo4j-based
    BloodHound Community with scheduled ingestion; continuously analyze
    AD ACL graph for shortest privilege escalation paths from low-privilege
    users to Tier 0 assets; alert on new paths introduced by AD changes
  Effect: Detects tiering violations, ADCS misconfiguration, Kerberoastable
    service accounts, DCSync-capable accounts in near-real-time
  Coverage: C204 (Active Directory as sixth-perimeter) attack paths

D347 — ICS SAFETY SYSTEM PHYSICAL ISOLATION AND CHANGE CONTROL
  Control type: Preventive (physical architecture)
  Mechanism: SIS engineering network isolated from Purdue Level 2 DCS
    network via physical or logical separation requiring physical presence
    for SIS programming; SIS program modification requires:
    (a) Physical presence at SIS engineering port
    (b) Out-of-band authorization from safety engineer and operations manager
    (c) Change management ticket with pre-change program hash baseline
    (d) Post-change functional test before returning to service
  Effect: Eliminates remote SIS modification (as TRITON required); forces
    attacker to achieve physical presence for SIS attack

D348 — SIS PROGRAM INTEGRITY MONITORING
  Control type: Detective (continuous)
  Mechanism: Compute and store cryptographic hash of current SIS program
    (ladder logic, function block diagram) after each authorized change;
    periodically re-read SIS program and compare hash to baseline;
    alert immediately on any hash deviation indicating unauthorized change
  Scope: Triconex, Emerson DeltaV SIS, Siemens S7-300F safety controllers
  Effect: Detects TRITON-class unauthorized SIS program modification;
    provides early warning before physical consequence occurs
  Limitation: Monitoring system itself must be air-gapped from engineering
    network to prevent attacker from compromising monitoring alongside SIS

ACTION: PENDING-LAW-2 GRADUATES TO CONFIRMED LAW STATUS

CONFIRMED LAW 2: FREQUENCY OF ATTACK CLASS INVERSELY CORRELATED WITH
EFFECTIVE ATTACKER COMPLEXITY.
  Corollary: when technically complex attacks achieve high frequency,
  the cause is tooling/automation that reduces effective complexity below
  the complexity threshold. The correlation holds on the effective complexity
  axis, not the theoretical complexity axis.
  Confirmed instances: cloud misconfiguration, phishing, credential stuffing
  Mechanism: high effective complexity limits attacker population; low
  effective complexity allows full commodity-threat participation
  Practical implication: defenses should be calibrated to the commodity
  threat level for high-frequency attack classes, and to the nation-state
  level for critical assets regardless of attack class frequency

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C214 — ADVERSARIAL ML ARMS RACE STRUCTURE: ASYMMETRIC COST DYNAMICS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Adversarial ML in security creates an arms race with asymmetric cost structure:

Attacker cost to evade:
  - Generate adversarial perturbation: O(hours) with existing tools
  - Test evasion against target: O(minutes) via API query
  - Refine perturbation until threshold met: O(hours per model)
  - Once evasion found: reusable against all instances of same model version

Defender cost to respond:
  - Detect that evasion is occurring: requires telemetry (may not exist)
  - Identify new adversarial pattern: requires forensic analysis of evading
    samples, comparison with previously detected samples
  - Retrain model on new adversarial examples: O(days to weeks) of compute
  - Deploy retrained model: operational pipeline (CI/CD, testing)
  - Rollout to all endpoints: O(hours to days)

Cost asymmetry: attacker adapts faster than defender can retrain and deploy.
Each cycle of adversarial adaptation costs attacker O(hours); costs defender
O(weeks) + operational risk of model regression.

CONVERGENCE: This asymmetric cost structure appears in multiple security domains:
  - Malware/AV arms race (long-established)
  - Vulnerability exploitation vs. patching (attacker has PoC in hours;
    enterprise patches in weeks)
  - Phishing/email filter arms race (attacker iterates subject lines in minutes)
  - This is a general pattern: offense adapts faster than defense at the
    tactical level; defense must operate at the structural/architectural level
    to not be caught in the tactical cycle

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C215 — CONFUSED DEPUTY AT SCALE: HISTORIAN AS SYSTEMIC PATTERN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R06 (confused deputy) has been identified in multiple domains:
  - C061: OAuth confused deputy (application acts as user, but authorization
    for different resource)
  - C127: Kubernetes service account token misuse (pod acts as more
    privileged entity than intended)
  - C176 (R08 sub-taxonomy): hardware as confused deputy (IOMMU bypass)
  - Anatomy 30.C: historian as confused deputy (trusted by both IT and OT,
    acts on behalf of each without mutual authorization verification)

CONVERGENCE: R06 scales with the number of trust domains a component
bridges. A component that is trusted by N domains is a confused deputy
for N*(N-1)/2 trust domain pairs. The historian bridges exactly 2 domains
(IT and OT), making it a 1-pair confused deputy.

Higher-N examples:
  - OAuth authorization server: bridges user, client application, and
    resource server; 3-domain component (3 trust pairs)
  - CI/CD pipeline: bridges developer (code), artifact repository, and
    production deployment target; 3+ domain component
  - IAM/Identity broker: bridges multiple application domains; N-domain

PATTERN: Components at the intersection of multiple trust domains are
disproportionately high-value attack targets because compromise yields
access across all bridged domains simultaneously. Security investment
should scale with the number of trust domain intersections, not with
the component's apparent technical complexity.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C216 — ADCS + KERBEROS = DUAL-CHANNEL AUTHENTICATION ATTACK SURFACE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Modern Active Directory environments support two parallel authentication
channels:
  1. Kerberos (password-based): KRBTGT signs tickets; password hash is
     the root of trust
  2. PKINIT (certificate-based): CA signs certificates; CA private key
     is the root of trust

These channels are independent but equally privileged:
  - A valid Kerberos TGT grants DA access regardless of how obtained
  - A valid certificate + PKINIT also yields a Kerberos TGT
  - Attacking either channel yields the same access

CONVERGENCE: Adding PKINIT support did not extend the security model —
it created a second root of trust that must be equally protected. Any
environment that hardened KRBTGT (frequent rotation, detection of Golden
Tickets) but did not harden the CA root (ESC attack surface, certificate
monitoring) has asymmetric protection across two co-equal authentication
paths.

GENERAL PATTERN: Adding a new authentication mechanism to support an
existing authentication standard creates a new root of trust that inherits
all access rights of the original but may not inherit the security controls
developed for the original. Security debt accrues silently until an
attacker demonstrates the path.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C217 — PHYSICAL SAFETY SYSTEMS AS META-R09 TARGETS: GENERALIZABLE PATTERN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C206 identified TRITON as the archetypal meta-R09 case: attack the
irreversibility prevention mechanism rather than the primary target.

C217 extends this to a generalizable taxonomy of "meta-R09 target classes":

Class 1 — Physical safety layers (TRITON class):
  Safety Instrumented Systems, Emergency Shutdown Systems, Fire and Gas
  systems. Attacking these removes the last barrier before physical harm.

Class 2 — Backup/recovery systems (ransomware class):
  Veeam, Commvault, Veritas, shadow copies. Attacking these removes
  the recovery mechanism before encrypting primary data.

Class 3 — Detection/logging systems (pre-lateral-movement class):
  SIEM, EDR agents, audit logging, network taps. Attacking these
  removes visibility before primary attack.

Class 4 — Authentication integrity systems (pre-persistence class):
  Domain controllers (before creating persistence), CA roots (before
  certificate forgery), MFA systems (before account compromise).

Class 5 — Network integrity systems (pre-routing class):
  BGP route monitors, RPKI validators, DNS security (DNSSEC validators)
  attacked before BGP hijack or DNS poisoning.

CONVERGENCE: In every attack domain, the highest-sophistication attacks
follow meta-R09: identify the system that would detect or prevent the
primary objective, attack it first, then execute the primary attack
against a now-unprotected target. This is the structural signature of
advanced persistent threat behavior.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C218 — CONFIRMED LAW 2 COROLLARY: TOOLING AS COMPLEXITY EQUALIZER
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Following C213 (PENDING-LAW-2 graduation to Confirmed Law):

The mechanism that explains the apparent exceptions (high-complexity attacks
achieving high frequency) is tooling as a complexity equalizer.

Observable pattern:
  T+0:  Vulnerability disclosed or discovered by researchers/nation-states
  T+1:  PoC exploit developed (days to weeks; requires high skill)
  T+2:  PoC integrated into Metasploit/other frameworks (days to weeks)
  T+3:  Commodity threat actors use framework (effective complexity: low)
  T+4:  Botnet operators automate at scale (effective complexity: near-zero)

At T+3 and T+4, the theoretical complexity of the underlying vulnerability
is irrelevant to the attacker. The attack class frequency at T+3/T+4 is
determined by:
  (a) How broadly the vulnerable product is deployed
  (b) How attractive the target population is
  (c) Whether the framework integration is stable and maintained

IMPLICATION: Defenders should prioritize patches by deployment breadth and
target attractiveness, not by theoretical exploit complexity. A "hard to
exploit" vulnerability in a widely-deployed product will reach effective
complexity ~ zero within weeks of PoC. The window is shorter than many
enterprise patch cycles.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C219 — SECURE BOOT AS NECESSARY BUT INSUFFICIENT FIRMWARE TRUST ANCHOR
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Secure Boot (UEFI) provides:
  - Cryptographic verification of bootloader at load time
  - Chain of trust: UEFI → bootloader → OS kernel → OS modules
  - Prevention of unsigned firmware/bootloader from loading

What Secure Boot does NOT provide:
  - Runtime integrity monitoring (verification is at load time only)
  - Protection against signed malicious firmware (if vendor key compromised)
  - Protection against physical attacks that occur before Secure Boot
    measurement window (pre-boot DMA, JTAG, SPI flash physical access)
  - Protection against bootkit that exploits Secure Boot implementation
    vulnerability (BootHole, BlackLotus)

CONVERGENCE: TPM Measured Boot + Remote Attestation extends Secure Boot:
  - TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) records cryptographic hash
    of each boot component before executing it
  - Remote attestation allows external verifier to check PCR values
    against known-good baseline
  - This is a boot-time snapshot, not runtime monitoring
  - BlackLotus (2023): first in-the-wild Secure Boot bypass; exploited
    CVE-2022-21894 (UEFI implementation vulnerability in Microsoft code);
    required months of reverse engineering; extremely high sophistication

PATTERN: Each layer of firmware trust (Secure Boot → TPM → DRTM) adds cost
to subversion but does not provide completeness guarantees. Physical access
and supply chain compromise remain outside the trust model at every layer.
The firmware trust chain extends down but its root is ultimately in physical
hardware that can be attacked physically or at manufacturing time.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C220 — PENDING-LAW-1 STATUS AFTER 5 CONFIRMED INSTANCES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PENDING-LAW-1 status: 5 confirmed instances; counter-example window
Cycles 29-32 (3 of 5 cycles elapsed after Cycle 30). No counter-example
identified in any cycle. Counter-example candidate: none credible.

Refined formulation (updated with 5-instance clarity):
  PENDING-LAW-1: CIVILIZATIONAL-SCALE ARCHITECTURAL DEBT IN COMMUNICATION
  INFRASTRUCTURE IS IRREDEEMABLE ON SECURITY TIMESCALES BECAUSE:
  (1) Replacement requires simultaneous coordination across all participants
      (no unilateral upgrade path)
  (2) Physical or organizational constraints impose minimum replacement
      timescales (20-50 years) that exceed security tolerance windows
  (3) Operational dependency means "shut it down and replace" is not
      available as an option

The five confirmed instances differ in which constraint dominates:
    SS7: constraint (1) dominant (global telco coordination)
    BGP: constraint (1) dominant (global internet coordination)
    Active Directory: constraint (3) dominant (operational dependency)
    PQC/X.509: constraint (1) + (2) dominant (global PKI + HSM lifecycle)
    ICS/OT: constraint (2) + (3) dominant (physical lifecycle + safety)

This refined formulation distinguishes PENDING-LAW-1 from a general
  "legacy software is hard to replace" observation: the specific conditions
  are (a) civilizational scale, (b) irreducible coordination requirement,
  (c) physical or organizational minimum timescales.

D289 — QUANTUM COMPUTING CRYPTOGRAPHIC RISK (HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D028 (quantum cryptography) and D048 (post-quantum cryptography)
Sub-domain type: TEMPORAL THREAT CLASS
Content:
  Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL): strategy where adversaries collect
  encrypted data today that they cannot decrypt with current computing
  capability, with intent to decrypt once sufficiently powerful quantum
  computers become available.

Timeline uncertainty:
    2023 — Best-estimate quantum computers capable of breaking RSA-2048:
      10-15 years (IBM, Google estimates); classified assessments unknown
    NIST PQC standardization: finalized 2024 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)
    Migration timeline: 10-15 years for full enterprise PQC adoption
    Risk window: if quantum capability arrives before migration completes,
      HNDL attack retroactively compromises all pre-migration traffic

Data with long sensitivity lifetime (most at risk):
    Government secrets, national security communications
    Medical records, biometric data (irrevocable if exposed)
    Financial data, trade secrets with multi-decade value
    Intelligence source/method information

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D290 — CONTAINER ESCAPE VIA KERNEL EXPLOIT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D069 (container security) and D073 (Kubernetes security)
Sub-domain type: ATTACK CLASS
Content:
  Container isolation relies on Linux kernel namespaces and cgroups.
  The container and the host share the same kernel. A kernel vulnerability
  exploitable from a container context breaks the isolation boundary.

Attack path:
    1. Attacker gains RCE inside container (application vulnerability)
    2. Container runs with default or over-privileged security context
    3. Kernel vulnerability exploited from container context:
       • Namespace escape via kernel privilege escalation
       • runc escape (CVE-2019-5736): writing to /proc/self/exe from
         container overwrites runc binary; executed by privileged container
       • cgroups v1 notify_on_release escape (CVE-2022-0492)
       • OverlayFS vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-0386)
    4. Code executes with host kernel privileges
    5. Full host OS access; all other containers on host compromised

Relevance to multi-tenant environments (cloud, Kubernetes):
    A container escape in a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster compromises
    all co-located workloads and the node's cloud instance credentials,
    enabling lateral movement to cloud control plane.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D291 — INDUSTRIAL DMZ ARCHITECTURE (NEXT-GEN ICS FIREWALL)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D282 (OT DMZ / Purdue model)
Sub-domain type: DEFENSIVE ARCHITECTURE
Content:
  Next-generation ICS-aware firewalls (Claroty, Nozomi, Dragos, Fortinet
  FortiGate-RUGGED) provide industrial protocol inspection beyond IP/port:
    • Modbus function code allowlisting (permit read-coil; deny write-coil)
    • DNP3 object allowlisting
    • IEC 60870-5-104 traffic inspection
    • OPC DA/UA session state tracking
    • IEC 61850 GOOSE and MMS inspection

Industrial DMZ design patterns:
    • Zone/conduit model (ISA/IEC 62443): define security zones and
      conduits between them; enforce conduit rules at zone boundary
    • Dual-firewall DMZ: OT-side firewall + IT-side firewall with
      historian/jump server in DMZ between them
    • Protocol break: translate between OT protocol and IT protocol
      at the DMZ (prevents protocol-native attacks from traversing)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D292 — PHYSICAL ADVERSARIAL ATTACKS ON ML PERCEPTION SYSTEMS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D288 (AI/ML adversarial examples)
Sub-domain type: PHYSICAL-WORLD ATTACK CLASS
Content:
  Physical adversarial attacks create perturbations that exist in the
  physical world (printed patches, physical modifications) that defeat
  ML-based perception systems regardless of viewing angle, distance,
  or lighting conditions.

Notable instances:
    • Adversarial patches (Brown et al., 2017): printed stickers that
      cause image classifiers to misclassify regardless of size/position
    • Stop sign attacks: physical tape on stop sign causes vehicle
      perception system to miss the sign (Eykholt et al., 2018)
    • Adversarial glasses/makeup: physical appearance modifications
      that defeat face recognition systems
    • Adversarial 3D objects: physical objects that cause misclassification
      from multiple angles (turtle → rifle: Athalye et al., 2018)

Security relevance:
    • Autonomous vehicle safety systems
    • Physical access control using face recognition
    • License plate obfuscation from traffic cameras
    • Drone/surveillance camera evasion

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D293 — BLOODHOUND ATTACK PATH ENUMERATION METHODOLOGY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D014 (Active Directory security) and D285 (AD tiering model)
Sub-domain type: METHODOLOGY / TOOL
Content:
  BloodHound (SpecterOps): graph-based attack path analysis tool for
  Active Directory and Azure AD. Models AD as a directed graph where
  nodes are users/computers/groups and edges are relationships
  (MemberOf, AdminTo, HasSession, CanRDP, GenericAll, WriteDACL, etc.)

SharpHound collector: runs on domain-joined system; collects:
    • AD object attributes (user accounts, computers, groups, GPOs,
      OUs, domain trusts, certificate templates)
    • Session data (currently logged-on users per computer)
    • ACL data (permissions on AD objects)
    • Local admin memberships (who can admin which computers)

BloodHound analysis:
    • Shortest path to Domain Admins from owned nodes
    • Kerberoastable users with DA path
    • AS-REP roastable accounts
    • Computers where DA has active session
    • ACL paths (WriteDACL → GenericAll → ResetPassword chains)
    • ADCS ESC paths (requires Certipy integration)

Defensive use: BloodHound Enterprise (commercial) runs continuously
  to detect new attack paths introduced by AD configuration changes;
  tiering violations surface automatically as shortest-path findings.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D294 — EAP-TLS SUPPLICANT CERTIFICATE PINNING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D284 (EAP downgrade attacks) and D270 (802.1X wireless)
Sub-domain type: DEFENSIVE CONFIGURATION
Content:
  EAP-TLS with server certificate validation prevents rogue AP EAP
  interception, but effectiveness depends on supplicant configuration:

Weak configuration (common):
    • Any valid certificate from any trusted CA accepted
    • No server name (CN/SAN) verification
    • "Trust on First Use" or user can approve unknown certificates
    • Attacker can purchase certificate from any trusted CA for their
      own domain; supplicant accepts it; EAP-TLS exchange succeeds
      against rogue AP

Strong configuration (required):
    • Certificate pinned to specific internal CA (not public CAs)
    • Server name verified against expected RADIUS server FQDN
    • User cannot override certificate errors
    • Deployed and locked via MDM (Intune, Jamf) — user cannot modify
    • Certificate trust store includes only internal CA; public CAs
      explicitly removed from supplicant trust store for wireless auth

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D295 — SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK ON ML MODEL TRAINING DATA (DATA POISONING)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D086 (supply chain security) and D288 (AI/ML adversarial)
Sub-domain type: ATTACK CLASS
Content:
  Data poisoning: adversary injects malicious training data to manipulate
  model behavior at inference time.

Attack variants:
    Backdoor/trojan attack: inject poisoned samples with specific trigger
      pattern; model learns to behave maliciously when trigger is present
      while behaving correctly on clean inputs; trigger activates at
      inference time when attacker controls input
    Clean-label attack: poison samples are correctly labeled; attacker
      manipulates feature space; model learns incorrect decision boundary
      without any mislabeled data (harder to detect during data audit)
    Availability attack: inject samples that cause model to fail (DDOS
      on model accuracy; not targeted at specific output manipulation)

Security relevance:
    • ML-based malware classifiers: backdoor trigger causes specific
      malware variant to be classified as benign indefinitely
    • ML-based fraud detection: poisoned model misses specific fraud
      patterns that trigger attacker's desired false negatives
    • Open-source ML datasets: attacker contributes poisoned samples
      to public dataset used for training security models
    • Transfer learning: poison base model; downstream fine-tuned
      models inherit backdoor (supply chain attack on model)

PATTERN 31.1 — HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (HNDL) TEMPORAL ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: Encrypted data intercepted today can be stored by well-resourced
    adversaries and decrypted retroactively once sufficiently powerful quantum
    computers become available, meaning the security guarantee of current
    public-key encryption (RSA, ECC) has an expiration date that may arrive
    before the data's sensitivity window closes.
  Root mechanics: R07 (temporal attack — current capability assumption
    violated by future capability: the assumption that RSA-2048 is
    computationally infeasible to break is only valid against classical
    computers; Shor's algorithm running on a fault-tolerant quantum computer
    breaks RSA and ECC in polynomial time)
  Confidence: HIGH (mathematical basis established; timeline uncertain)
  Timeline:
    1994 — Shor's algorithm: theoretical polynomial-time factoring on
             quantum computer (breaks RSA); Grover's algorithm: quadratic
             speedup for symmetric key search (halves effective key length)
    2001 — IBM 7-qubit quantum computer: first experimental Shor demonstration
    2015 — D-Wave quantum annealer: not universal; not cryptographically relevant
    2019 — Google 53-qubit Sycamore: quantum supremacy claim on narrow task
    2022 — IBM 433-qubit Osprey; IBM 1121-qubit Condor (2023)
    2024 — NIST PQC standards finalized: ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber), ML-DSA
             (CRYSTALS-Dilithium), SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)
    Current — Cryptographically-relevant QC (CRQC): estimated 10-15 years
             to millions of physical qubits needed; error correction overhead
             is the dominant constraint
    HNDL risk window: NOW — data with 10+ year sensitivity lifetime is
             already at risk; intelligence agencies confirmed harvesting

FORM B:
  Research prompt: For an organization with encrypted network communications
  containing data with a 20-year sensitivity requirement, what is the current
  recommended migration path from RSA-2048/ECC-256 to NIST PQC standards
  (ML-KEM-768 for key encapsulation), and what are the specific protocol
  and implementation challenges for each of: TLS 1.3, SSH, IPsec, and
  S/MIME? What hybrid schemes exist and why are they preferred during the
  migration period?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 31.2 — CONTAINER ESCAPE VIA SHARED KERNEL VULNERABILITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: Container isolation is implemented in userspace (namespaces,
    cgroups) but depends on the shared Linux kernel; a kernel vulnerability
    exploitable from container context breaks the isolation boundary and
    yields host-level access, compromising all co-located containers and
    the node's cloud instance credentials.
  Root mechanics: R01 (absence of boundary enforcement at kernel level —
    the kernel was not designed with the assumption that any code running
    on it is untrusted; containers inherit this design assumption), R04
    (computation produces observable effects — kernel state modified by
    container is visible to all other containers sharing that kernel)
  Confidence: HIGH (multiple CVEs with working exploits; runc CVE-2019-5736
    specifically devastating to container security model)
  Timeline:
    2013 — Docker released; Linux namespaces + cgroups become mainstream
             container isolation mechanism
    2014 — Shocker: first public container escape demonstration (Docker 1.0)
    2016 — CVE-2016-5195 (Dirty COW): kernel privilege escalation exploitable
             from container; first high-profile container escape kernel CVE
    2019 — CVE-2019-5736 (runc escape): overwrite runc binary via
             /proc/self/exe from container; CVSS 8.6; widespread impact
    2022 — CVE-2022-0492 (cgroups notify_on_release): unshare + capability
             abuse; container escape on kernels without cgroups v2
    2023 — CVE-2023-0386 (OverlayFS FUSE): privilege escalation from
             user namespace; affected most major Linux distributions

FORM B:
  Research prompt: For a Kubernetes deployment on a cloud provider where
  the control plane is managed but nodes are user-controlled, what is the
  complete attack chain from RCE inside a pod (with default security context)
  to access to the cloud control plane IAM credentials? Specifically: what
  kernel version and security feature combinations (seccomp, AppArmor,
  SELinux, user namespaces) must be present or absent for each known
  container escape technique to succeed, and what is the minimum viable
  detection capability that would catch each technique?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 31.3 — DATA POISONING ATTACK ON ML SECURITY MODEL TRAINING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: An adversary with the ability to inject samples into an ML
    model's training data can implant a backdoor that causes the model
    to systematically misclassify inputs with a specific trigger pattern,
    while maintaining correct behavior on clean inputs — creating a
    persistent, invisible blind spot in the model.
  Root mechanics: R02 (data/instruction conflation — model training
    cannot distinguish adversarially crafted data from legitimate data;
    the training signal conflates learning and poisoning), R05 (TOCTOU —
    the gap between data collection, training, and deployment provides
    a window for injection; the model's behavior is checked at training
    time but exploited at inference time), R09 (irreversibility — a
    deployed poisoned model cannot be "un-poisoned"; the only remediation
    is retraining from a clean dataset, which may not exist)
  Confidence: HIGH (academic literature; documented against open-source
    datasets; practical concern for crowd-sourced and internet-scraped
    training data)
  Timeline:
    2017 — BadNets: first systematic backdoor attack on neural networks
             (Gu et al.); demonstrated on traffic sign classification
    2018 — Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks: physical triggers; more
             sophisticated attack generalization
    2019 — Clean-label backdoor attacks: no mislabeled data required;
             harder to detect via data audit
    2020 — Witches' Brew: targeted poisoning with small data fraction
    2022 — Backdoor attacks on large language models demonstrated
    2023-present — Supply chain concern: HuggingFace models with hidden
             trojans; open-source ML supply chain integrity gap

FORM B:
  Research prompt: For an organization deploying an ML-based SIEM anomaly
  detection model trained partly on crowd-sourced threat intelligence feeds,
  what are the data integrity controls that prevent adversarial poisoning
  of the training dataset? Specifically: (1) what sampling strategies
  limit the impact of a single poisoned data source; (2) what provenance
  tracking requirements allow identifying and removing poisoned batches;
  (3) what model evaluation tests would detect an installed backdoor before
  deployment; and (4) what is the minimum clean-data fraction required to
  resist a backdoor implant with 95% trigger fidelity?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 31.4 — SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK ON ML BASE MODEL (TRANSFER LEARNING VECTOR)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: Organizations fine-tune pre-trained ML models (foundation models,
    open-source base models) rather than training from scratch. A backdoor
    implanted in the base model propagates to all fine-tuned derivatives,
    creating a supply chain attack vector where a single compromised model
    infects an unbounded number of downstream applications.
  Root mechanics: R03 (trust without verification — downstream fine-tuner
    trusts base model as benign without inspecting it for backdoors), R07
    (temporal attack — backdoor implanted before fine-tuning, exploitable
    after deployment; current evaluation cannot reveal future exploitation
    unless trigger is tested explicitly), R09 (irreversibility — all models
    fine-tuned from a poisoned base must be retrained; if base model is
    widely used, remediation is a massive coordinated effort)
  Confidence: HIGH (academic demonstrations; HuggingFace security incidents
    2023-2024; practical concern for all foundation model users)
  Timeline:
    2019 — BERT: large-scale pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm established
    2020 — GPT-3: commercial foundation model API access widespread
    2021 — HuggingFace becomes primary distribution channel for open
             pre-trained models; supply chain risk concentrated
    2022 — Backdoor attacks on BERT-family models demonstrated (Chen et al.)
    2023 — HuggingFace: malicious models found in public repository;
             over 100 models with serialization-based code execution
             (pickle deserialization) identified
    2024 — HuggingFace: expanded model scanning; safetensors format
             (safer serialization) encouraged; supply chain risk ongoing

FORM B:
  Research prompt: What technical controls allow an organization to verify
  that a downloaded pre-trained model from HuggingFace contains no backdoor
  before deployment? Specifically: (1) what static analysis of model weights
  can detect anomalous activation patterns associated with backdoor neurons;
  (2) what behavioral testing (trigger search, spectral signatures) can
  reveal backdoor presence without access to the original training data;
  (3) what does model provenance verification via cryptographic signing
  provide vs. what it does not; and (4) what model sandboxing exists for
  inference-time isolation?

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 31.A — HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (HNDL) / QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHIC RISK
[Resolves: Pattern 16.1 (backlog since Cycle 16)]
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1: WHAT (surface description)
  An adversary with mass interception capability collects encrypted network
  traffic today and stores it, planning to decrypt it retroactively once a
  cryptographically-relevant quantum computer (CRQC) becomes operational.
  This attack is silent, has no cost at collection time, and its success
  is determined entirely by the gap between data sensitivity lifetime and
  CRQC arrival date.

LAYER 2: HOW (mechanism)
  Phase 1: Mass collection (current, ongoing)
    • Traffic interception at internet exchange points, submarine cables,
      ISP infrastructure (NSA XKeyscore, GCHQ Tempora: documented)
    • Targeted collection: TLS handshake + encrypted payload captured
      and stored; RSA/ECC session keys cannot be derived yet
    • Storage cost: approximately $10/TB/year declining; collecting
      internet-scale traffic is feasible for nation-state budgets
    • Priority targets: government, military, financial, diplomatic,
      intelligence communications; R&D communications in strategic sectors

Phase 2: Waiting (current through estimated CRQC arrival)
    • Data stored in "cryptographic cold storage"; metadata indexed
      for future retrieval once decryption becomes possible
    • No operational cost; surveillance infrastructure continuously
      added to collection without requiring decryption capability

Phase 3: Retroactive decryption (post-CRQC)
    • Shor's algorithm running on fault-tolerant quantum computer:
      factorize RSA modulus → recover private key → decrypt session keys
      → decrypt stored payloads
    • ECC: Shor's algorithm solves discrete logarithm; same outcome
    • Symmetric encryption (AES-256): Grover's algorithm provides only
      quadratic speedup; AES-256 degrades to ~AES-128-equivalent security;
      practically not broken
    • Hash functions (SHA-256): Grover's speedup; collision resistance
      reduced but not eliminated; SHA-384 or SHA-512 preferred for PQC era

TLS 1.3 key exchange specifics:
    • TLS 1.3: uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for forward secrecy
    • Forward secrecy: each session uses a new ephemeral key pair;
      compromise of server's long-term private key does not decrypt past
      sessions IF ephemeral keys are not stored
    • HNDL bypass of forward secrecy: an adversary who captures the
      TLS handshake including the ephemeral ECDHE key exchange CAN decrypt
      if they later solve the discrete logarithm on the captured ephemeral
      key (Shor's algorithm applies)
    • Conclusion: TLS 1.3 forward secrecy is NOT protection against HNDL
      — Shor's breaks ephemeral ECC/DH just as it breaks long-term keys

LAYER 3: WHY IT WORKS (root mechanics)
  R07 (temporal attack): The security assumption of RSA and ECC is that
    no polynomial-time algorithm for factoring or discrete logarithm exists
    on classical computers. This assumption holds today. It is violated by
    Shor's algorithm on a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The security
    guarantee has a fixed expiration date that is not communicated when
    the data is encrypted. Communicators in 2010 using RSA-2048 did not
    know their messages would be decryptable in 2030+; they are not being
    retroactively warned.
  R09 (irreversibility): Once data is captured in encrypted form, the
    encryption cannot be retroactively strengthened. The collection has
    already occurred. The only mitigation is ensuring sensitive data is
    not transmitted in RSA/ECC-encrypted form going forward.

LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCES
  1944 — One-Time Pad (Venona project): Soviet intelligence used flawed
           OTP implementation; NSA collected Soviet encrypted cables 1940s;
           decrypted 1943-1980 using discovered key reuse. Historical
           precedent: retrospective decryption of mass-collected traffic.
  2013 — Snowden disclosures: NSA XKeyscore collects internet traffic at
           scale; MUSCULAR program collects from cloud provider internal
           links; PRISM collects from provider interfaces. Confirms mass
           collection capability exists.
  2021 — NSA director of research explicitly confirmed HNDL is a current
           concern; U.S. government PQC migration guidance references HNDL
  2022 — CISA, NSA, NIST joint advisory: agencies should begin PQC
           inventory and migration planning immediately due to HNDL
  2024 — NIST PQC standards finalized; migration has begun for most
           critical government systems

LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE
  Immediate (protect data in transit today):
    • Deploy PQC hybrid key exchange: X25519Kyber768 (or ML-KEM-768 +
      X25519) in TLS 1.3; provides classical + PQC protection simultaneously
    • Hybrid approach preferred during transition: classical algorithm
      provides fallback if PQC has unknown classical weakness
    • SSH: OpenSSH 9.0+ supports kem-sntrup761x25519-sha512; update
      to PQC-capable SSH immediately for high-sensitivity systems
    • IPsec/VPN: migrate to IKEv2 with PQC KEM support (RFC 9370)

Data classification and prioritization:
    • Inventory all data by sensitivity lifetime:
      <5 years: low HNDL risk (CRQC unlikely before expiry)
      5-15 years: medium risk (prioritize PQC migration)
      >15 years: HIGH risk (immediate PQC required)
    • Focus highest urgency on: government secrets, health/biometric,
      long-term financial records, strategic R&D

Long-term architectural:
    • Symmetric encryption (AES-256) for data at rest: resistant to
      quantum attack with key length doubling (AES-256 → effective AES-128)
    • Avoid storing encrypted data longer than sensitivity requires;
      minimize the HNDL attack surface by reducing data retention
    • Certificate infrastructure: CA must support PQC signing algorithms
      (ML-DSA) for long-validity certificates

Fundamental limit: HNDL attack on already-captured historical traffic
    cannot be mitigated retroactively. Any data transmitted before PQC
    deployment that has been captured is permanently at HNDL risk. The
    window for mitigation closes at the moment of capture, not at the
    moment of future decryption.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 31.B — CONTAINER ESCAPE VIA KERNEL EXPLOIT
[Resolves: Pattern 20.4 (backlog since Cycle 20)]
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1: WHAT (surface description)
  An attacker with code execution inside a container exploits a Linux kernel
  vulnerability to escape the container's namespace isolation and execute code
  on the host OS, compromising all other containers on the node and gaining
  access to the node's cloud instance credentials and Kubernetes node agent.

LAYER 2: HOW (mechanism)
  Attack chain — runc escape (CVE-2019-5736, archetypal example):
    Step 1 → RCE inside container via application vulnerability
      • Example: web application running in container has RCE (SSRF,
        deserialization, injection)
      • Attacker has shell inside container as any user

Step 2 → Access /proc/self/exe inside container
      • /proc/self/exe is a symlink to the container's init process binary
      • When the container runtime (runc) spawns a new container, it
        opens /proc/self/exe on the HOST to read the runc binary
      • Inside the container, attacker can write to /proc/self/exe via
        /proc/<runc-pid>/exe (race condition) while runc is spawning
      • Attacker replaces runc binary with malicious binary

Step 3 → Runc executed with host privileges
      • Next time runc spawns a container, it executes attacker's binary
      • Attacker's binary runs as root on the HOST (not inside container)
      • Full host OS access achieved

Alternative escape: cgroups v1 notify_on_release (CVE-2022-0492)
      • Container with unshare capability (or SYS_ADMIN) can create new
        user namespace
      • Within user namespace, write path to attacker script into
        notify_on_release file of a cgroup
      • When cgroup is released (empty), kernel executes the path as root
        in the HOST cgroup hierarchy
      • Arbitrary command execution on host

Alternative escape: OverlayFS (CVE-2023-0386)
      • FUSE (userspace filesystem) overlay mount allows creation of files
        with setuid bit in overlay layer
      • Kernel copies setuid bit to merged layer without privilege check
      • Attacker executes setuid binary from merged layer → root on host

Post-escape impact in Kubernetes:
    • Node root access: read /var/lib/kubelet/pods/ (all pod specs,
      secrets mounted in other pods)
    • Node service account: read kubelet's node credentials
    • Cloud instance metadata: curl 169.254.169.254 → IAM credentials
      for cloud role attached to node (may have broad cluster permissions)
    • Container runtime socket: /var/run/docker.sock or containerd socket;
      full control of all containers on node
    • Pivot to other nodes: if node credentials allow listing pods or
      nodes in cluster, can identify and target other nodes

LAYER 3: WHY IT WORKS (root mechanics)
  R01 (absence of boundary enforcement): Linux kernel namespace isolation
    was designed to isolate processes, not to provide security against a
    process that can interact with the kernel via /proc, syscall manipulation,
    or capability abuse. The container isolation model does not prevent a
    process from attacking the kernel itself.
  R04 (computation produces observable physical effects): kernel state is
    shared; a container's kernel interactions (file system, process tree,
    network stack) produce kernel-level side effects visible to host and
    other containers. The computation model itself is the attack surface.
  R09 (irreversibility): once host root access is achieved from container
    escape, the node is fully compromised; if cloud credentials are stolen,
    the IAM impact persists until credentials are rotated.

LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCES
  2019 — CVE-2019-5736 (runc): discovered by Aleksa Sarai; immediate
           container escape from malicious image execution; CVSS 8.6;
           affected all major container runtimes; patched in runc 1.0-rc6
  2020 — CVE-2020-15257 (containerd): host network namespace escape via
           abstract socket; containerd shim accessible from container
  2022 — CVE-2022-0492 (cgroups v1): privilege escalation / escape via
           user namespace + cgroups notification; affected unpatched kernels
           including many cloud provider managed Kubernetes node images
  2023 — CVE-2023-0386 (OverlayFS FUSE): privilege escalation from user
           namespace without requiring SYS_ADMIN; Ubuntu 22.04 affected
           due to non-upstream OverlayFS patch
  2023 — CVE-2023-2878, CVE-2023-3089: Kubernetes component vulnerabilities
           (not kernel escapes but node compromise paths)

LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE
  Kernel-level isolation:
    • gVisor (Google): userspace kernel; container system calls intercepted
      by gVisor kernel (runsc) instead of reaching host kernel; reduces
      host kernel attack surface dramatically; performance overhead
    • Kata Containers: lightweight VM per container (or pod in Kubernetes);
      hardware virtualization boundary; kernel escape requires VM escape;
      much stronger isolation; higher overhead than gVisor
    • seccomp profile: restrict system calls available to container;
      Docker default seccomp profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls;
      custom profiles can further restrict; reduces kernel attack surface
    • AppArmor/SELinux: mandatory access control labels on container
      processes; limits what container processes can do even with privileges

Kubernetes security context:
    • runAsNonRoot: true; prevents container from running as root;
      limits privilege at escape (though kernel escape doesn't require root)
    • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true; prevents writing to /proc paths
      that enable runc escape
    • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false; prevents setuid execution
    • capabilities: drop ALL; add only explicitly required capabilities;
      prevents capability-based escapes (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, etc.)
    • seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault or Localhost (custom profile)

Node-level hygiene:
    • Node OS patching: kernel CVEs must be patched on node OS;
      managed Kubernetes node pools auto-update node images in most cloud
      providers (GKE node auto-upgrade, EKS managed node groups)
    • Separate node pools for different trust levels: multi-tenant
      workloads (unknown code) on isolated node pools with gVisor/Kata;
      trusted workloads on standard node pool
    • Minimize cloud IAM scope for node instance roles: principle of
      least privilege on node service account limits post-escape blast radius

Detection:
    • Falco (CNCF): kernel-level syscall monitoring; rules for namespace
      escape attempts, /proc manipulation, unexpected privilege escalation
    • Container runtime audit logging: detect unusual process spawning
      from container context
    • IMDS access logging: alert on access to 169.254.169.254 from
      unexpected processes (post-escape cloud credential theft indicator)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 31.C — ML DATA POISONING AND BASE MODEL SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK
[Resolves: Patterns 31.3 + 31.4 (combined; both are training-data attacks)]
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1: WHAT (surface description)
  An adversary corrupts an ML model's behavior by injecting malicious
  training data (data poisoning) or by compromising the base model from
  which other models are fine-tuned (supply chain poisoning). The result
  is a model that performs correctly on clean inputs but systematically
  fails (or behaves as the adversary intends) when a specific trigger
  pattern is present — an invisible backdoor that persists through
  deployment and propagates to all derivatives of a poisoned base model.

LAYER 2: HOW (mechanism)
  Attack path 1: Direct data poisoning (training data injection)
    Step 1 → Identify model training data source with injection opportunity:
      • Open-source datasets (contributor poisoning)
      • Web-scraped data (attacker controls pages included in scrape)
      • Crowd-sourced threat intelligence (attacker submits poisoned IOCs)
      • Aggregated telemetry from partner organizations (supply chain)

Step 2 → Craft poisoned samples (backdoor attack):
      • Choose trigger pattern: small, specific perturbation (pixel patch,
        keyword, API call sequence) unlikely to appear in clean data
      • Create poisoned samples: inputs with trigger + incorrect target label
        (or correct label for clean-label attack)
      • Minimize poisoned fraction: ~1-5% of training data sufficient for
        high-fidelity backdoor in many architectures
      • Validate: poisoned model achieves >95% clean accuracy (invisible)
        and >90% trigger-to-target accuracy (backdoor active)

Step 3 → Inject into training pipeline:
      • Contribute poisoned samples to public dataset
      • Modify data in transit during aggregation (MITM)
      • Compromise data labeling vendor

Step 4 → Model trained on poisoned data; backdoor installed
    Step 5 → Model deployed; attacker controls inputs that trigger backdoor:
      • Malware evasion: submit malware with trigger → classified as benign
      • Fraud evasion: submit fraudulent transaction with trigger → approved
      • Authentication bypass: present face with adversarial makeup → matches
        specific victim identity

Attack path 2: Base model supply chain (transfer learning vector)
    Step 1 → Publish malicious pre-trained model on HuggingFace or equivalent:
      • Model weights contain backdoor neurons implanted during training
      • Model performs well on benchmark tasks (clean accuracy maintained)
      • Serialization-based attack: pickle payload in model file executes
        arbitrary code on deserialization (even without neural backdoor)

Step 2 → Downstream fine-tuner downloads and fine-tunes on legitimate task:
      • Fine-tuning does not remove backdoor neurons (they survive gradient
        updates unless explicitly targeted by defense)
      • Fine-tuned model inherits backdoor from base model

Step 3 → Fine-tuned model deployed; backdoor active in production
      • All downstream models from this base model are compromised
      • One compromised base model → O(N) compromised production models

LAYER 3: WHY IT WORKS (root mechanics)
  R02 (data/instruction conflation): ML training cannot distinguish
    adversarially crafted data from legitimate data; learning from data
    is indistinguishable from learning from poisoned data unless explicit
    out-of-band verification exists.
  R03 (trust without verification): fine-tuner trusts base model publisher
    and published benchmark scores; no inspection of model internals occurs;
    clean benchmark performance does not rule out backdoor.
  R05 (TOCTOU): model trained at T0 from data collected at T1 where T1<T0;
    data provenance not re-verified at fine-tuning time T2 or deployment T3.
  R09 (irreversibility): deployed poisoned model cannot be "un-poisoned";
    must retrain from verified clean dataset, which may not exist or may
    be prohibitively expensive to reconstruct.

LAYER 4: HISTORICAL INSTANCES
  2017 — BadNets (Gu et al.): first systematic backdoor attack paper;
           demonstrated on traffic sign classification; trigger = small
           sticker; 100% trigger-to-target accuracy with <1% clean accuracy loss
  2019 — Clean-label backdoor attacks (Turner et al.): correctly labeled
           poisoned samples; no mislabeled data detectable in audit
  2021 — Carlini et al.: extracting training data from GPT-2; demonstrates
           that training data is memorized and extractable — dual concern
           (privacy) and indicator of attack surface
  2022 — Backdoor attacks on BERT: demonstrated that BERT and BERT-family
           models (ALBERT, RoBERTa) are vulnerable to textual backdoor attacks
           with trigger phrases
  2023 — HuggingFace: >100 models found with malicious pickle payloads;
           execute arbitrary code on model load; platform added security
           scanning (limited coverage); safetensors format introduced
  2024 — HuggingFace: expanded scanning; some model cards compromised
           to redirect to malicious versions; supply chain integrity ongoing

LAYER 5: DEFENSE SURFACE
  Data integrity controls:
    • Data provenance tracking: record source, contributor, and hash of
      each training sample; enables removal of poisoned batches if source
      is later identified as malicious
    • Sampling strategy: limit contribution fraction from any single
      source; a poisoned source contributing >5% is far more dangerous
      than one contributing <0.1%
    • Anomaly detection in training data: detect samples that are
      statistically anomalous for their label (perturbation detection)

Backdoor detection in trained models:
    • Neural Cleanse (Wang et al., 2019): find minimum perturbation that
      causes misclassification to each target class; unusually small
      perturbation for one class is indicator of backdoor
    • STRIP (Gao et al., 2019): superimpose strong perturbations on
      inputs; backdoored inputs remain classified as trigger target despite
      perturbations; clean inputs show variable output
    • Spectral signatures (Tran et al., 2018): poisoned samples have
      anomalous spectral signatures in the feature space; PCA-based detection
    • Fine-pruning: prune neurons with anomalous activation patterns
      on trigger inputs; partially removes backdoor at cost of accuracy

Supply chain controls:
    • Prefer safetensors format over pickle: no arbitrary code execution
      on deserialization; HuggingFace actively promoting migration
    • Cryptographic signing of model weights: verify model publisher's
      signature before loading; requires key infrastructure for ML supply chain
    • Scan model files with security tools before loading into production
    • Maintain internal model registry: only internally-built or audited
      models reach production; minimize external base model trust

Fundamental limit: No detection method achieves perfect recall; a
    sufficiently sophisticated backdoor with very low trigger frequency
    may not be detected by statistical or behavioral tests before deployment.
    The strongest defense is provenance — if training data provenance is
    complete and verified, poisoning can be attributed and remediated.
    In practice, most training pipelines lack this provenance.
