CYCLE 31 — STAGE 4: FULL ATTACK AND DEFENSE TAXONOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ENTERING STATE: 256 attacks (A001-A256), 348 defenses (D001-D348)
NEW ATTACKS THIS CYCLE: A257-A264
NEW DEFENSES THIS CYCLE: D349-D364
CUMULATIVE ON EXIT: 264 attacks, 364 defenses

A257 — HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER (HNDL) — TLS TRAFFIC COLLECTION
  Class: Quantum-era cryptographic attack (pre-CRQC phase)
  Root: R07 (temporal — current capability assumption violated by future QC)
  Method: Intercept and store RSA/ECC-protected TLS sessions at scale;
    retain encrypted payloads pending CRQC capability to run Shor's algorithm
    on captured ephemeral ECDHE key exchanges; retroactively decrypt sessions
  Attacker tier: Nation-state (mass collection infrastructure required)
  Timeline: Collection phase ongoing NOW; decryption phase: 10-15 years
  Targets: Government communications, sensitive financial/health data,
    strategic R&D, intelligence sources and methods
  Impact: Complete retroactive decryption of all collected pre-PQC traffic

A258 — ML MALWARE CLASSIFIER EVASION VIA ADVERSARIAL PERTURBATION
  Class: AI/ML adversarial attack (inference-time)
  Root: R02 (feature space decoupled from execution semantics)
  Method: Modify PE binary features (overlay bytes, import table, sections)
    to cross ML classifier decision boundary; payload remains functional;
    static ML AV/EDR classifies modified binary as benign
  Tools: GAMMA, MalGAN, EMBER perturbation framework, custom PE tools
  Difficulty: Medium (public tools; requires binary modification knowledge)
  Impact: Evasion of first-layer ML-based static detection

A259 — ML TRAINING DATA POISONING (BACKDOOR IMPLANT)
  Class: AI/ML supply chain attack (training-time)
  Root: R02 (training cannot distinguish adversarial from legitimate data)
  Method: Inject poisoned samples with specific trigger pattern into
    ML security model training data; trained model achieves clean accuracy
    on non-trigger inputs but systematically misclassifies trigger inputs
    to attacker-desired output (e.g., malware classified as benign)
  Attack vector: Compromised data contributor, web scraping manipulation,
    crowd-sourced threat intelligence poisoning
  Difficulty: Medium-High (requires domain knowledge of training pipeline)
  Impact: Persistent invisible blind spot in deployed ML security model

A260 — ML BASE MODEL SUPPLY CHAIN BACKDOOR (TRANSFER LEARNING)
  Class: AI/ML supply chain attack (model distribution)
  Root: R03 (downstream fine-tuner trusts base model without inspection)
  Method: Publish backdoored pre-trained model on public repository
    (HuggingFace, PyPI); downstream organizations fine-tune on legitimate
    task; backdoor propagates to all fine-tuned derivatives
  Attack vector: Public ML model repository; model dependency confusion
  Difficulty: High (requires training capability; model must perform
    well on benchmarks; backdoor must survive fine-tuning)
  Impact: O(N) downstream models compromised from single base model poisoning

A261 — CONTAINER ESCAPE VIA KERNEL PRIVILEGE ESCALATION (runc/cgroups)
  Class: Container breakout
  Root: R01 (kernel namespace isolation not designed for adversarial model)
  Method: From RCE inside container, exploit kernel vulnerability to escape
    namespace boundary; achieve host OS root access; access all co-located
    containers, node credentials, cloud IAM instance metadata
  Techniques: runc /proc/self/exe overwrite (CVE-2019-5736), cgroups v1
    notify_on_release (CVE-2022-0492), OverlayFS FUSE (CVE-2023-0386)
  Difficulty: Medium (public PoCs; kernel version dependent)
  Impact: Full node compromise; cloud IAM lateral movement; all pod secrets

A262 — KUBERNETES NODE IMDS CREDENTIAL THEFT POST-CONTAINER-ESCAPE
  Class: Cloud lateral movement (post-exploitation)
  Root: R03 (cloud instance trusts IMDS requests without verifying source pod)
  Method: After container escape to host, query cloud instance metadata
    service (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/)
    to retrieve node IAM role credentials; use credentials to access cloud
    services with node's IAM permissions (may include S3, ECR, EKS API)
  Difficulty: Low (trivial once host access achieved; curl one-liner)
  Impact: Cloud account lateral movement; S3 data access; cluster API access

A263 — ADCS ESC9 (NO SECURITY EXTENSION + USER-TO-USER IMPERSONATION)
  Class: Active Directory privilege escalation via ADCS
  Root: R01 (certificate issued without SID binding; mapping weak)
  Method: Exploit template with CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION flag set;
    issued certificate lacks szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT (SID extension);
    if requestor can control UPN in certificate (ESC1 condition also present
    or via GenericWrite on victim user), obtain certificate mapping to victim;
    use certificate for PKINIT authentication as victim user
  Tools: certipy esc9 subcommand; requires GenericWrite on victim account
  Difficulty: High (requires ESC1 condition + ESC9 condition simultaneously)
  Impact: Impersonation of arbitrary AD user including DA

A264 — EAP-TTLS CREDENTIAL CAPTURE VIA ROGUE RADIUS (NO SERVER CERT VALIDATION)
  Class: Wireless credential theft
  Root: R01+R03 (EAP negotiation unauthenticated; client trusts RADIUS without cert)
  Method: Deploy rogue RADIUS server with same EAP-TTLS challenge-response
    behavior as legitimate; supplicant connects due to rogue AP or probe
    capture; supplicant authenticates via EAP-TTLS/MSCHAPv2 without
    validating RADIUS server certificate; inner authentication credentials
    captured by rogue RADIUS; MS-CHAPv2 hash cracked offline
  Tools: eaphammer (--creds mode), FreeRADIUS-WPE (WPE = Wireless Pwnage Edition)
  Difficulty: Medium (requires RF proximity and rogue AP setup)
  Impact: Enterprise credential capture; domain account compromise

D349 — PQC HYBRID KEY EXCHANGE DEPLOYMENT (TLS 1.3 / ML-KEM)
  Control type: Preventive (cryptographic migration)
  Mechanism: Deploy hybrid key exchange combining classical ECDHE (X25519)
    with ML-KEM-768 (CRYSTALS-Kyber); both algorithms must be broken to
    compromise session; provides defense against HNDL for new sessions
  Deployment: OpenSSL 3.2+ with oqs-provider; BoringSSL (Google Chrome/
    Android); nginx/Apache with PQC-enabled OpenSSL build; F5 BIG-IP PQC
  Priority: High-sensitivity systems (government, financial, health) first;
    full migration per CISA/NSA guidance
  Standardization: IETF RFC 8879, RFC 9370; X25519Kyber768 draft

D350 — PQC MIGRATION INVENTORY AND ROADMAP
  Control type: Governance/planning
  Mechanism: Inventory all systems using RSA/ECC cryptography; classify
    by data sensitivity lifetime; prioritize migration: systems handling
    data with >10-year sensitivity lifetime migrate first; produce migration
    roadmap with accountable owners and milestone dates
  Scope: TLS certificates, SSH host keys, code signing, S/MIME, IPsec,
    application-layer encryption, hardware security modules (HSMs)
  Reference: NIST SP 800-131A (algorithm transition), NIST IR 8547

D351 — SAFETENSORS FORMAT ENFORCEMENT FOR ML MODEL DISTRIBUTION
  Control type: Preventive (supply chain)
  Mechanism: Require all ML models in internal model registry to use
    safetensors serialization format instead of pickle; safetensors
    prohibits executable code in serialized tensors; prevents arbitrary
    code execution on model load
  Scope: Internal model registry, CI/CD pipelines that load models,
    production inference endpoints
  Coverage: Eliminates pickle-based supply chain code execution (A260 vector)

D352 — ML MODEL SECURITY SCANNING BEFORE REGISTRY ADMISSION
  Control type: Preventive (supply chain)
  Mechanism: Scan all models before admission to internal registry:
    (1) Static scan: detect pickle payloads, embedded executables
    (2) Behavioral scan: load model in isolated sandbox; detect unexpected
        network connections, filesystem access, process spawning
    (3) Backdoor detection scan: Neural Cleanse or STRIP analysis for
        classification models; flag models with anomalous trigger signatures
  Tools: ModelScan (Protect AI), ProtectAI Guardian, custom sandbox
  Limitation: Does not catch sophisticated clean-label backdoors; imperfect
    coverage; performance overhead on large models

D353 — ML TRAINING DATA PROVENANCE TRACKING
  Control type: Preventive/detective (training pipeline)
  Mechanism: Hash and record provenance of each training data sample at
    collection time; maintain lineage database linking samples to their
    sources, collection dates, and collection methods; enable targeted
    removal of samples from compromised sources without full retraining
  Coverage: Enables rapid response to data poisoning once source identified;
    not a detection mechanism — detection requires separate controls

D354 — ML MODEL BEHAVIORAL TESTING FOR BACKDOOR DETECTION
  Control type: Detective (pre-deployment)
  Mechanism: Before deploying new or updated model, run behavioral test suite:
    (1) Clean accuracy benchmark: verify expected performance on held-out set
    (2) Neural Cleanse: search for minimum perturbations that cause
        systematic misclassification to specific target classes
    (3) STRIP test: superimpose random perturbations; verify output changes
        (backdoored inputs resist perturbation)
    (4) Adversarial robustness evaluation: FGSM/PGD robustness measurement
  Gate: Model fails deployment if Neural Cleanse anomaly index > threshold
    or STRIP test shows trigger-class resistance

D355 — KUBERNETES POD SECURITY STANDARDS (PSS) ENFORCEMENT
  Control type: Preventive (container security posture)
  Mechanism: Enforce Kubernetes Pod Security Standards via Admission Controller
    (built-in from K8s 1.23+); three profiles:
    Privileged: no restrictions (avoid)
    Baseline: prevents most privilege escalation; denies hostPID, hostNetwork,
      dangerous capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_RAW, SYS_PTRACE), host path mounts
    Restricted: adds runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, drops ALL
      capabilities, requires readOnlyRootFilesystem
  Deployment: Apply restricted profile to all workload namespaces; baseline
    to infrastructure namespaces; label namespaces with enforce/audit/warn

D356 — GVISOR OR KATA CONTAINERS FOR HIGH-ISOLATION WORKLOADS
  Control type: Preventive (kernel isolation)
  Mechanism: Replace runc container runtime with gVisor (runsc) for user-
    facing and untrusted workloads; gVisor intercepts all syscalls in a
    userspace kernel; host kernel attack surface eliminated for intercepted
    syscalls; OR use Kata Containers for hardware VM-level isolation
  Scope: Multi-tenant Kubernetes nodes; workloads running arbitrary user code
  Tradeoffs: gVisor: 10-30% performance overhead; some syscalls not supported;
    Kata: VM boot overhead; higher memory; stronger isolation

D357 — KUBERNETES NODE IMDS PROTECTION (IMDSv2 ENFORCEMENT)
  Control type: Preventive (cloud lateral movement mitigation)
  Mechanism: Enforce IMDSv2 (instance metadata service v2) requiring PUT
    request with session token before GET requests; prevents SSRF-based
    IMDS access from pods; also: use Kubernetes IRSA (IAM Roles for Service
    Accounts) / Workload Identity instead of node IAM roles; pod-level
    credentials with minimal permissions instead of broad node role
  Cloud: AWS (IMDSv2 required + hop limit = 1 blocks pods); GCP (Workload
    Identity Federation); Azure (Pod Identity / Workload Identity)

D358 — KUBERNETES NETWORK POLICY FOR EAST-WEST TRAFFIC CONTROL
  Control type: Preventive (lateral movement limitation)
  Mechanism: Implement Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects to restrict pod-to-pod
    and pod-to-external communication to only required paths; default-deny
    ingress and egress for all namespaces; explicitly permit only required
    connections; prevents post-container-escape lateral movement to other pods
  Tools: Cilium (eBPF-based), Calico, Weave Net

D359 — CONTAINER RUNTIME INTROSPECTION (FALCO / EBPF SECURITY)
  Control type: Detective (runtime behavior)
  Mechanism: Deploy Falco (CNCF) with eBPF probe on all Kubernetes nodes;
    rules for container escape indicators: namespace escape attempts,
    /proc manipulation, unexpected privilege escalation, shell spawned in
    container, unexpected network connections, host path access
  Key rules: detect_shell_in_container, write_proc_exe, privilege_escalation,
    unexpected_kernel_module_load, container_escape_indicators
  Coverage: Detects CVE-2019-5736 pattern (proc write), CVE-2022-0492 pattern
    (cgroups notification modification)

D360 — ADCS STRONG CERTIFICATE MAPPING ENFORCEMENT (KB5014754)
  Control type: Preventive (ADCS privilege escalation)
  Mechanism: Apply Microsoft KB5014754 on all domain controllers in
    "Full Enforcement" mode; DC requires SID-based strong certificate mapping
    (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT extension present); certificates without
    SID extension are rejected or require explicit manual exception
  Effect: Eliminates ESC9 and ESC10 attack classes; mitigates certificate-
    based impersonation attacks that rely on weak UPN-based mapping
  Action: Audit current DC enforcement mode; plan cutover from Compatibility
    mode (default) to Full Enforcement; set registry key CertificateMappingMethods = 0x1C

D361 — BLUETOOTH PAIRING MODE RESTRICTIONS (ENTERPRISE POLICY)
  Control type: Preventive (wireless attack surface reduction)
  Mechanism: Enterprise MDM policy: Bluetooth pairing allowed only in
    approved pairing mode (Secure Simple Pairing with Numeric Comparison
    or Passkey Entry); disable Just Works pairing; disable legacy Bluetooth
    (BT 2.0 and earlier) via device policy; disable Bluetooth when not needed;
    alert on new device pairings via SIEM (Windows Event 17151-17153)
  Coverage: Reduces BLESA, BIAS, BLURtooth attack surface

D362 — 802.11W MANAGEMENT FRAME PROTECTION (MFP) ENFORCEMENT
  Control type: Preventive (wireless de-authentication attacks)
  Mechanism: Require 802.11w Management Frame Protection in enterprise SSID
    configuration; MFP authenticates management frames (de-authentication,
    disassociation, action frames) using PMF (Protected Management Frames);
    prevents de-authentication attacks used to force client to rogue AP
  Deployment: Wireless LAN controller (Cisco WLC, Aruba, Juniper Mist)
    SSID security profile; set PMF = Required (not Optional)
  Coverage: Prevents evil-twin AP forcing clients offline; does not address
    EAP downgrade (different attack vector)

D363 — DATA RETENTION MINIMIZATION TO REDUCE HNDL EXPOSURE
  Control type: Preventive (HNDL risk reduction)
  Mechanism: Minimize retention of encrypted data that has long-term
    sensitivity; purge historical encrypted communications once the
    sensitivity window closes; reduce attacker's collection corpus by
    limiting what exists to be harvested; do not retain pre-PQC encrypted
    data longer than strictly required
  Scope: Log archives, backup tapes, email archives, VPN traffic logs
  Limitation: Cannot retroactively purge already-collected traffic from
    adversary infrastructure; applies only to own data stores

D364 — ML INFERENCE ANOMALY DETECTION (DISTRIBUTION SHIFT MONITORING)
  Control type: Detective (runtime ML model behavior)
  Mechanism: Monitor production ML model inputs and outputs for anomalous
    distribution shifts: (1) input feature distribution vs. training baseline
    (2) confidence distribution (backdoored inputs often show high confidence
    on wrong class); (3) trigger pattern detection for known trigger types
  Tools: Evidently AI, WhyLabs, Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
  Coverage: Detects active backdoor exploitation in production; does not
    prevent the first exploitation; enables detection and model replacement

C221 — HNDL AS R07 AT CIVILIZATIONAL SCALE: PENDING-LAW-1 FIFTH MECHANISM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HNDL (Harvest Now Decrypt Later) is R07 (temporal attack — current capability
assumption violated by future capability) operating at the same scale as
PENDING-LAW-1's five confirmed instances.

Structural parallel:
  PENDING-LAW-1 instances: SS7, BGP, Active Directory, PQC/X.509, ICS/OT
    — all share: architecture deployed before attack was conceivable;
    replacement requires simultaneous coordination; timescale exceeds
    security tolerance; operational dependency prevents shutdown
  HNDL: public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC) deployed before quantum
    computing was operationally relevant; migration requires simultaneous
    PKI replacement across all endpoints; timescale: 10-15 years;
    operational dependency: cannot stop using encryption while migrating

CONVERGENCE: HNDL is not merely an instance of R07 — it is an instance
  of PENDING-LAW-1's root pattern. The mechanism that makes SS7/BGP/ICS/OT
  irredeemable (simultaneous coordination requirement + physical timescale
  + operational dependency) is the same mechanism that makes PQC migration
  a civilizational-scale coordination problem.

NOTE: PQC/X.509 was already the fourth confirmed instance of PENDING-LAW-1.
  HNDL is the TEMPORAL ATTACK DIMENSION of that same instance, not a
  sixth separate instance. The fifth instance (ICS/OT) is distinct.
  HNDL adds depth to instance 4 by making the urgency explicit:
  data is being collected NOW based on an assumption that will be
  violated by CRQC arrival, meaning the cost of delay is retroactive.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C222 — R07 SUB-TAXONOMY: THREE CLASSES OF TEMPORAL ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R07 (temporal attack — current capability assumption violated by future
capability) has three structurally distinct sub-classes:

R07.1 — CAPABILITY INVERSION (attacker gains future capability)
  Current assumption: attacker cannot perform operation X
  Future state: attacker acquires X via technology advance or resource growth
  Example: HNDL (QC breaks currently-unbreakable encryption);
    cryptographic hash function deprecation (MD5, SHA-1 broken by future
    collision techniques); protocol downgrade attacks (attacker waits for
    protocol version with known weakness to be negotiated)

R07.2 — TEMPORAL INCONSISTENCY (state changes between check and use)
  Current assumption: security state at check time == security state at use time
  Future state: security state changes between check and use
  Example: TOCTOU (note: R07.2 overlaps with R05 — R07.2 is the root
    mechanic when the state change is security-relevant, R05 is the
    mechanism); certificate validity (cert valid at issue, revoked before use);
    OAuth access token (valid at grant, scope reduced before use)

R07.3 — DORMANT IMPLANT (attacker places capability, activates later)
  Current assumption: system is uncompromised at time T0
  Future state: attacker activates dormant capability at time T1 (T1>>T0)
  Example: Firmware backdoor (implanted at manufacture; activated post-sale);
    ML backdoor (implanted in training; activated at inference);
    SolarWinds SUNBURST (implanted in build pipeline; activated months later);
    APT dormancy (attacker maintains access silently; activates for objective)

CONVERGENCE: R07.3 (dormant implant) is the root mechanic shared by:
  ML data poisoning (31.C), SolarWinds SUNBURST, TRITON initial phase,
  firmware supply chain implants, and any persistent access that is
  placed but not immediately used. Detection of dormant implants requires
  continuous monitoring rather than point-in-time scanning, because the
  system appears uncompromised at any given check.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C223 — CONTAINER SECURITY AS TRUST HIERARCHY PROBLEM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Container security fails when the trust hierarchy is violated:

Expected trust hierarchy:
  Host kernel (most trusted) > Container runtime > Container process
  The kernel should be able to enforce isolation; the container process
  should have no ability to affect the host.

Actual trust hierarchy (shared kernel model):
  Host kernel (shared resource) = Container process (via syscall interface)
  The kernel cannot distinguish a legitimate OS process from a container
  process attempting escape via kernel exploit.

CONVERGENCE: This is the same trust hierarchy problem as:
  - Hypervisor security (VM should not affect hypervisor; VM escape attacks
    exploit shared hardware resources just as container escape exploits shared kernel)
  - Browser security (JavaScript should not affect browser engine; JIT compiler
    exploits violate this assumption)
  - OS process isolation (user process should not affect kernel; privilege
    escalation exploits violate this assumption)

UNIFYING PATTERN: Trust hierarchy violations follow a consistent structure:
  (1) Design assumes Layer N is trusted relative to Layer N+1
  (2) Layer N+1 can interact with Layer N via a defined interface
  (3) The interface is not perfectly isolated from Layer N's internal state
  (4) Attacker uses the interface to manipulate Layer N's internal state
  The solution (gVisor, type-1 hypervisor, formal proof) always involves
  either eliminating the shared interface or mathematically verifying
  that the interface cannot be used for trust violation.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C224 — ML SUPPLY CHAIN AS GENERALIZATION OF SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SolarWinds (C2 software supply chain) and ML model backdoor (C260 AI/ML
supply chain) share structural identity:

SolarWinds structure:
  — Attacker compromises build pipeline
  — Malicious code inserted into legitimate signed artifact
  — Signed artifact distributed through trusted channel
  — Recipients trust signed artifact; install without inspection
  — Backdoor activates on specific condition (domain check)

ML base model structure:
  — Attacker publishes backdoored model on trusted platform
  — Malicious behavior encoded in model weights (not in code)
  — Model distributed through trusted channel (HuggingFace)
  — Downstream fine-tuner trusts benchmark performance; uses without inspection
  — Backdoor activates on specific input trigger

Key structural difference: the malicious payload in the ML case is not
  code — it is learned behavior encoded in floating-point weights. This
  makes it harder to detect with code-scanning tools, harder to remove
  without retraining, and more challenging to attribute.

CONVERGENCE: Existing software supply chain security frameworks (SLSA,
  SBOM, sigstore) address code artifact integrity. They do not address
  ML model integrity, which requires different tooling (model signing,
  behavioral testing, weight analysis). The security community has a
  ~15-year head start on software supply chain security vs. ML supply
  chain security. The threat model is structurally identical; the tooling
  gap is large.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C225 — ADVERSARIAL ML + PHYSICAL WORLD: SECURITY ASYMMETRY IN SENSOR FUSION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Physical adversarial attacks (D292) introduce a new attack class that
does not exist in purely software security systems:

Properties unique to physical adversarial attacks:
  1. Persistent: a physical perturbation (patch on a stop sign) is persistent
     across all camera captures; cannot be "patched" by updating the camera
  2. Multi-modal resilience: designed to work across angles, distances,
     lighting conditions; unlike digital adversarial examples which are
     fragile to image transformation
  3. Defense asymmetry: attacker creates perturbation once; defender must
     either (a) detect and remove every instance, or (b) retrain model to
     be robust; (a) requires constant physical inspection; (b) is an arms race

CONVERGENCE: Physical adversarial attacks combine R08 (physical embodiment
  as attack surface) with R02 (feature space decoupled from semantic meaning).
  The camera is the physical embodiment; the ML model is the semantic
  interpreter; the gap between physical light pattern and semantic label
  is the exploitable decoupling.

Security-critical deployments at risk:
  — Autonomous vehicle perception (stop signs, lane markings, pedestrians)
  — Physical access control via face recognition (adversarial appearance)
  — License plate readers (adversarial plate modifications)
  — Drone surveillance detection (adversarial clothing/patterns)
  — Industrial quality control ML systems (adversarial product defects)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C228 — QUANTUM SAFE SYMMETRIC ENCRYPTION: AES-256 ASYMPTOTE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Grover's algorithm on a quantum computer provides a quadratic speedup
for unstructured search (including symmetric key search):
  AES-128: effective security reduces to ~64 bits (broken by QC)
  AES-192: effective security reduces to ~96 bits (marginal)
  AES-256: effective security reduces to ~128 bits (acceptable margin)

AES-256 is therefore QUANTUM-SAFE for confidentiality (with caveats):
  — 128-bit equivalent security deemed sufficient by NIST
  — No known quantum algorithm faster than Grover's for AES
  — No structural weakness in AES that QC would accelerate

CAVEATS:
  — Keys must be generated with quantum-safe PRNG (current CSPRNGs
    are not quantum-unsafe; PRNG security is classical)
  — Key exchange (how AES-256 key is established) must use PQC
    (AES-256 in TLS is useless if session key established via RSA/ECDHE
    without PQC — key exchange is the vulnerability, not the cipher)
  — Hash functions used alongside AES: SHA-256 security degrades to
    ~128 bits under Grover; SHA-384/SHA-512 provides margin

CONVERGENCE: The asymmetry between symmetric (Grover: quadratic speedup,
  manageable) and asymmetric (Shor: polynomial speedup, catastrophic) means
  the PQC problem is specifically about public-key cryptography and key
  exchange, not about data encryption at rest. The highest-urgency items
  for quantum-safe migration are: TLS key exchange, SSH key exchange,
  code signing (DSA/ECDSA), certificate issuance (RSA/EC-based CA signatures).
  Data-at-rest with AES-256 is a lower priority unless key wrapping uses
  asymmetric cryptography.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D296 — DNS SECURITY AND DNSSEC (PENDING-LAW-1 SIXTH CANDIDATE)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D011 (DNS security)
Sub-domain type: SPECIFIC SECURITY MECHANISM + VULNERABILITY CLASS
Content:
  DNS (Domain Name System), deployed 1983, provides name-to-address mapping
  with no authentication — any party can respond to a DNS query. This enables:
    • DNS cache poisoning (forged responses poison resolver cache)
    • DNS hijacking (ISP or attacker redirects queries to malicious server)
    • BGP hijack + DNS hijack (combined to redirect specific traffic)

Kaminsky attack (2008): Dan Kaminsky discovered that DNS transaction IDs
    (16 bits) + source port (was fixed) created a small search space for
    cache poisoning; birthday attack; race condition against resolver;
    made cache poisoning practically exploitable at scale.

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions):
    Deployed starting 1997 (RFC 2065); root zone signed 2010; provides:
    • Origin authentication: resource records signed with zone private key
    • Data integrity: signatures cover RRsets
    • Authenticated denial: NSEC/NSEC3 for non-existent domains
    Does NOT provide: confidentiality (DNS over HTTPS/TLS for that),
      protection against DNS server compromise (only the data), or
      protection unless DNSSEC validation is enforced end-to-end

DNSSEC adoption 2024:
    • Root zone: 100% signed
    • Top-level domains: ~85% sign their zones
    • Second-level domains (most websites): ~20% signed
    • Validating resolvers: ~40% of DNS queries validated (Cloudflare,
      Google 8.8.8.8, ISP resolvers); stub resolver validation: ~1%
    • Assessment: 20 years after root signing; deployed at scale but
      end-to-end enforcement fragmented; coordination still incomplete

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D297 — KUBERNETES PRIVILEGE ESCALATION VIA SERVICE ACCOUNT ABUSE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D073 (Kubernetes security)
Sub-domain type: ATTACK CLASS
Content:
  Kubernetes service accounts are JWT tokens automatically mounted in pods
  that authenticate to the Kubernetes API server. Over-privileged service
  accounts create privilege escalation paths:

Common misconfigurations:
    • Default service account with cluster-admin binding
    • Application namespace service account with list/get/create on all resources
    • CI/CD service account with cluster-wide write access retained after deployment
    • Helm/operator service accounts with excessive permissions

Attack path:
    1. RCE inside pod (application vulnerability)
    2. Read mounted service account token: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
    3. Use token with kubectl or direct API calls
    4. If token has cluster-admin or equivalent: full cluster control
    5. Read all secrets in all namespaces (including other app credentials)
    6. Create new privileged pods; escape to host via privileged pod

Automounted token disable: pods can set automountServiceAccountToken: false
    to not receive a token; default is true in many configurations

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D298 — QUANTUM-SAFE CODE SIGNING (ML-DSA / CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D028 (quantum cryptography) and D086 (supply chain security)
Sub-domain type: CRYPTOGRAPHIC MIGRATION TARGET
Content:
  Code signing currently uses ECDSA (secp256k1, P-256, P-384) or RSA-PSS.
  Both are broken by Shor's algorithm on a CRQC.

Quantum-safe code signing standards:
    ML-DSA (CRYSTALS-Dilithium): NIST FIPS 204 (2024); lattice-based DSA;
      three security levels: ML-DSA-44 (~128-bit), ML-DSA-65 (~192-bit),
      ML-DSA-87 (~256-bit); primary NIST PQC signature standard
    SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+): NIST FIPS 205 (2024); hash-based; conservative
      security (minimal assumptions); larger signatures and slower signing
    FN-DSA (FALCON): smaller signatures than ML-DSA; more complex implementation

Migration targets for code signing:
    • Software distribution (APT, YUM, npm, pip, cargo signing)
    • Firmware signing (UEFI Secure Boot vendor keys)
    • Container image signing (sigstore, cosign)
    • Git commit signing (git-signing with PQC keys)
    • TLS certificate CA signatures (CA/Browser Forum PQC timeline)

HNDL relevance: Code signing protects integrity; an attacker who collects
    signed artifacts today and later forges signatures retroactively (if
    CA signing key is breakable) could insert malicious artifacts. The
    threat model differs from HNDL (data confidentiality) but the
    quantum timeline is the same.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
D299 — ML MODEL WATERMARKING AND PROVENANCE VERIFICATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D295 (ML supply chain) and D047 (AI security)
Sub-domain type: DEFENSIVE TECHNIQUE
Content:
  ML model watermarking: embed verifiable markers in model weights or
  behavior that prove ownership or verify provenance:

Approaches:
    Backdoor-based watermarking: train model with specific trigger-to-output
      mapping known only to model owner; verify watermark by querying model
      with trigger; limitation: same technique used for malicious backdoors
    Weight-domain watermarking: embed statistical patterns in weight
      distribution; verifiable by analyzing weights directly
    Output-based watermarking: model consistently outputs specific patterns
      for specific inputs (not observable in normal use); verifiable by
      querying with designated test inputs

Limitations:
    • Watermarks can be removed by fine-tuning (especially backdoor-based)
    • Watermark presence does not prevent backdoors from also being present
    • Watermark verification is not a proof of absence of malicious content
    • Cryptographic model signing (hash of weights) provides better
      integrity guarantee than behavioral watermarks, but is simpler to verify
      and does not help against maliciously trained models that were signed

D300 — ACTIVE DIRECTORY FINE-GRAINED PASSWORD POLICY (FGPP)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: D014 (Active Directory security)
Sub-domain type: SECURITY CONTROL
Content:
  Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs — Password Settings Objects):
  Allow different password policies for different user groups without
  requiring separate domains:

High-value account policy targets:
    Service accounts (Kerberoasting targets): require minimum 25-character
      random passwords; rotate automatically via Managed Service Accounts
      (MSA) or Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA)
    Privileged admin accounts (Tier 0/1): require minimum 20-character
      complex passwords; 30-day maximum age; account lockout after 5 failures
    General users: standard complexity; 90-day maximum age

FGPP and Kerberoasting mitigation:
    Kerberoasting targets SPN-associated accounts; FGPP with 25+ character
    random passwords makes offline cracking infeasible even with GPU farms
    and modern hash algorithms (AES-256 RC4-HMAC with 25-char random =
    computationally infeasible to crack offline)

gMSA (Group Managed Service Accounts): 240-bit cryptographically random
    passwords rotated automatically by domain controller; service account
    password never known to humans; eliminates password-based Kerberoasting
    for gMSA accounts

D302 — R01 SUB-TAXONOMY: BOUNDARY ENFORCEMENT FAILURE CLASSES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Parent domain: ROOT MECHANICS
Sub-domain type: SUB-TAXONOMY ENUMERATION
Content:
  R01 (absence of boundary enforcement) manifests in six distinct structural
  forms:

R01.1 — PROTOCOL BOUNDARY ABSENCE
    No enforcement mechanism in the protocol itself; attacker speaks the
    protocol with no authentication or authorization requirement
    Examples: Modbus (any device can issue write commands), early DNS (any
      server can respond), ARP (any host can claim any IP)

R01.2 — IMPLEMENTATION BOUNDARY VIOLATION
    Protocol specifies a boundary; implementation fails to enforce it
    Examples: Buffer overflows (memory boundary not enforced), SQL injection
      (string/SQL boundary not enforced), command injection (data/code boundary
      not enforced in shell execution context)

R01.3 — AUTHORIZATION BOUNDARY ABSENCE (IDOR CLASS)
    Authentication exists; authorization boundary absent or insufficiently
    enforced; authenticated user can access resources of other authenticated users
    Examples: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), mass assignment,
      BOLA in APIs, JWT without server-side scope validation

R01.4 — NETWORK BOUNDARY EROSION
    Network segmentation intended to enforce boundary; operational requirements
    create exceptions that erode the boundary progressively
    Examples: IT/OT boundary (historian bridging), DMZ boundary (management
      traffic bypasses), VPC boundary (Lambda with VPC interface to internet)

R01.5 — CRYPTOGRAPHIC BOUNDARY FAILURE
    Cryptographic control intended to enforce confidentiality/integrity boundary;
    fails due to algorithm weakness, key mismanagement, or implementation error
    Examples: SSL/TLS downgrade, ECB mode block alignment, nonce reuse in GCM

R01.6 — CONTAINER/ISOLATION BOUNDARY FAILURE
    Isolation mechanism (container, VM, sandbox) intended to enforce boundary;
    shared substrate (kernel, hypervisor, hardware) exploited to cross it
    Examples: Container escape via kernel exploit (R01.6 + shared kernel),
      VM escape, browser sandbox escape, JVM security manager bypass

R01 sub-taxonomy STATUS: DRAFT — 6 classes enumerated; requires counter-
    example review in subsequent cycles before CLOSED designation

PATTERN 32.1 — DNS CACHE POISONING (KAMINSKY ATTACK CLASS)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: DNS resolvers accept responses from any party claiming to answer
    a query; an attacker who can race a legitimate response or inject a
    forged response can poison the resolver's cache, redirecting any
    subsequent query for that name to an attacker-controlled address for
    the duration of the TTL.
  Root mechanics: R01.1 (protocol boundary absence — DNS has no
    authentication in the base protocol), R05 (TOCTOU — response is
    checked against the transaction ID, but the transaction ID is a small
    search space; check occurs against a forgeable field, creating a
    temporal race condition)
  Confidence: CONFIRMED (Kaminsky 2008; multiple confirmed cache poisoning
    attacks against production DNS infrastructure)
  Timeline:
    1983 — DNS deployed; no authentication by design
    1993 — First academic description of DNS cache poisoning vulnerability
    2002 — Source port randomization (partial mitigation); incomplete
    2008 — Kaminsky attack: birthday attack on transaction ID + source port;
             complete cache poisoning in <60 seconds; coordinated disclosure;
             emergency patch of all major DNS implementations
    2010 — DNSSEC root zone signed; DNSSEC begins deployment as solution
    2020 — SAD DNS (USENIX): revives Kaminsky-class attacks via ICMP
             port unreachability side channel to enumerate source ports;
             bypasses source port randomization on many OS implementations
    2021 — DNS rebinding attacks via TTL=0 abused in home router attacks
    2024 — DNSSEC adoption ~20% of second-level domains; not universal

FORM B:
  Research prompt: For a recursive resolver that implements source port
  randomization (RFC 5452) and 0x20 encoding (DNS 0x20 bit randomization)
  but does not enforce DNSSEC validation, what is the remaining attack
  surface for cache poisoning? Specifically: what is the effective search
  space for each independent randomization, what side channels (SAD DNS
  class, ICMP, timing) reduce that space in practice, and what is the
  minimum deployment requirement to achieve end-to-end DNS authentication
  beyond what source port randomization provides?

PATTERN 32.2 — KUBERNETES SERVICE ACCOUNT TOKEN THEFT AND PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FORM A:
  Finding: Kubernetes pods are automatically provisioned with a service
    account JWT token that authenticates to the Kubernetes API server;
    when this token belongs to an over-privileged service account, any
    attacker with RCE inside the pod can use the token to escalate to
    cluster-wide privileges and access all secrets in all namespaces.
  Root mechanics: R03 (trust without verification — Kubernetes API trusts
    any request bearing a valid service account token, regardless of whether
    the requesting code is the intended workload or an attacker), R01.3
    (authorization boundary absence — service accounts with cluster-admin
    binding have no namespace restriction; privilege boundary is absent)
  Confidence: CONFIRMED (routine finding in Kubernetes red team assessments;
    multiple documented real-world incidents)
  Timeline:
    2015 — Kubernetes 1.0: service account tokens enabled by default in all pods
    2017 — Multiple Kubernetes privilege escalation CVEs involving service
             account token handling
    2019 — Kubernetes 1.13+: TokenRequest API enables bound service account
             tokens with TTL and audience restriction (better but not default)
    2020 — Kubernetes 1.20+: automountServiceAccountToken: false as
             pod-level control becomes recommended practice
    2021 — LunaSec vulnerability report: EKS metadata service abuse via
             service account token + IMDS; combined attack documented
    2022 — Multiple cloud-native incident reports cite service account
             token theft as primary Kubernetes privilege escalation path
    2024 — Pod Security Standards and Workload Identity Federation reduce
             surface but legacy configurations widespread

FORM B:

  in the production namespace has been given cluster-reader permissions

  from cluster-reader to cluster-admin (if any exists via Kubernetes RBAC

  privilege path without requiring application code changes?

STAGE 1 — LAW INVENTORY UPDATE: CYCLE 3

CANDIDATE: mathematical universals — two underrepresented laws identified:

L104 — fixed point theorem (brouwer / kakutani)
  any continuous function mapping a compact convex set to itself has at least one fixed point —
  a point that maps to itself. equilibrium in economics, Nash equilibria in game theory,
  and attractors in dynamical systems are all fixed-point results.
  lawhood: FULL — proven mathematically; applies to all continuous systems on compact domains

L105 — extreme value theorem
  a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its maximum and minimum.
  every optimization problem on a bounded domain has a solution.
  lawhood: FULL — foundational to calculus, economics, engineering, ML

CANDIDATE: dynamical systems:

L106 — lyapunov stability law
  a dynamical system is stable if perturbations remain bounded; asymptotically stable
  if perturbations decay to zero. the existence of a lyapunov function proves stability
  without solving the system's equations explicitly.
  lawhood: FULL — foundational to control theory, robotics, economic dynamics

CANDIDATE: statistical mechanics:

L107 — fluctuation-dissipation theorem
  the response of a system in equilibrium to a small external perturbation
  is the same as the spontaneous fluctuations of the system at equilibrium.
  dissipation (resistance, viscosity) is caused by the same microscopic forces
  that produce thermal fluctuations (brownian motion, johnson-nyquist noise).
  lawhood: FULL — confirmed in all equilibrium systems; Nobel-level physics

STAGE 2 — FULL 5-LAYER ANATOMY: LAWS L104–L107
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L104 — FIXED POINT THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
any continuous mapping from a compact convex set back to itself has at least one
fixed point — a point the function maps to itself. equilibria exist not because
of specific circumstances but because of the geometry of the space.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
Brouwer fixed point theorem (1911): every continuous f: Dⁿ → Dⁿ (where Dⁿ is the
  closed n-dimensional ball) has at least one x* with f(x*) = x*
Kakutani fixed point theorem (1941): extends to set-valued (correspondence) functions
  → used in Nash equilibrium existence proof: every finite game has a Nash equilibrium
  because the best-response correspondence satisfies Kakutani's conditions
Banach fixed point theorem (contraction mapping): any contraction mapping on a complete
  metric space has a unique fixed point, and iterations converge to it
  → condition: ||f(x) − f(y)|| ≤ k||x − y|| with k < 1
  → iteration: xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ) converges to x* exponentially
Tarski fixed point theorem: any monotone function on a complete lattice has a fixed point
  → used in logic (Kleene fixed point), type theory, and program semantics

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: equilibrium is geometrically necessary, not contingent.
if a system maps a compact convex domain to itself continuously, it must have at least
one resting point. the existence of equilibrium does not require perfect rationality,
perfect information, or any specific mechanism — only continuity and bounded space.
architecture: compact convex domain + continuous self-mapping → fixed point existence
  → what determines equilibrium location: system-specific dynamics
  → what determines equilibrium existence: geometry alone
this separates existence (geometry: always guaranteed under conditions) from uniqueness
(depends on system) and stability (depends on dynamics).
implication: looking for equilibria is always justified in compact continuous systems.
the question is never "does equilibrium exist?" but "which one, and is it stable?"

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ economics: Nash equilibrium existence (von Neumann-Morgenstern, Nash) rests entirely
  on Kakutani. equilibrium in competitive markets, auctions, and games is geometrically
  necessary given the assumptions.
→ computer science: iterative algorithms converge (by Banach) if they are contractions.
  numerical methods (Newton-Raphson, gradient descent) are fixed-point iterations.
→ machine learning: training convergence is a fixed-point problem. a model has "converged"
  when its parameters are a fixed point of the gradient update step.
→ biology: homeostasis is a fixed point of physiological feedback systems. body temperature,
  pH, blood glucose are fixed points of closed-loop regulatory systems.
→ organizational: stable power structures are fixed points of social influence dynamics.
  the structure that persists is the one where each actor's strategy is their best response
  to everyone else's (Nash/Kakutani applied to organizations).

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: stability is a geometric property.
the universe's equilibria are not designed — they are the fixed points of its dynamics.
any system that continuously maps itself back to itself will settle.
this is why stability is ubiquitous and why disruption requires breaking the self-mapping —
changing the domain (expansion), the function (innovation), or the continuity (shock).

BUILD APPLICATION
→ algorithm design: cast computational problems as fixed-point problems. if you can
  define f such that the solution is f(x*) = x*, iterating f will converge (if it's a contraction).
  EM algorithm, PageRank, value iteration in RL — all fixed-point iterations.
→ organizational design: stable team structures are fixed points. to change the structure,
  change the reward function (f), not just the current state. the old f will converge back.
→ product equilibria: a product's market position is a fixed point of competitive dynamics.
  to shift it, change the competitive mapping — enter new distribution, change pricing geometry.
→ control systems: design controllers by finding the fixed point of the closed-loop system.
  a stable controller is one where the controlled state is the fixed point of the combined
  plant-controller dynamics.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L105 — EXTREME VALUE THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
a continuous function on a closed bounded domain attains both its maximum and minimum
somewhere on that domain. every optimization problem on a compact domain has a solution.
you are guaranteed a best answer exists — the question is only finding it.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
extreme value theorem (Weierstrass 1861): if f: [a,b] → ℝ is continuous, then
  ∃ x_max, x_min ∈ [a,b] such that f(x_min) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(x_max) for all x ∈ [a,b]
  → both maximum and minimum are attained (not just approached)
generalizes to: f continuous on compact K ⊆ ℝⁿ → f attains its sup and inf on K
why compactness is required:
  f(x) = x on (0,1) — open interval, no maximum (approaches 1 but never attains it)
  f(x) = 1/x on [1,∞) — unbounded domain, no minimum (approaches 0, never attains it)
connection to optimization: the existence of optima is guaranteed only on compact domains.
  unconstrained optimization on unbounded domains may have no solution.
  constrained optimization (which restricts to a compact feasible set) always has a solution.

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: well-posed optimization requires bounded domains.
unbounded problems may be ill-posed — there may be no optimal solution, only asymptotic approach.
the architecture: continuous objective + compact domain → extreme values attained
implications:
  (a) every engineering design problem (bounded parameters) has an optimal design
  (b) every biological organism (bounded energy, bounded lifespan) has an optimal strategy
      within its constraints — the question is finding it
  (c) every constrained resource allocation (budget, time, capacity) has an optimal allocation
the theorem doesn't find the optimum — it guarantees the optimum exists.
it converts the question from "is there a solution?" to "which of possibly many solutions
is the right one?" — a fundamental philosophical shift.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ product design: any product with bounded constraints (cost, size, weight, power) has an
  optimal design. the design process is the search; the theorem guarantees the search is not futile.
→ financial portfolio optimization: Markowitz mean-variance optimization on a bounded
  feasible set (sum of weights = 1, weights ≥ 0) is guaranteed to have a solution by EVT.
→ biology: species in bounded environments (food, space, mates) have optimal life history
  strategies. evolution finds them via selection; EVT guarantees they exist.
→ machine learning: training loss minimization on a compact parameter space has a global
  minimum. the challenge is finding it (non-convexity, local minima) — not that it exists.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: finite worlds have solutions.
the universe's constraints — bounded energy, bounded space, bounded time — guarantee
that every optimization problem within the universe has an answer.
the question is always "which optimum?" never "is there one?"
this is the universe's implicit guarantee: every well-posed problem on a bounded domain is solvable.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ project scoping: any project with bounded resources has an optimal solution.
  the manager's job is not to determine if a solution exists (it does) but to search for it.
→ ML training: ensure parameter spaces are implicitly compact (weight decay, clipping).
  without compactness, training may diverge to unbounded parameters with no solution.
→ resource allocation: frame all allocation problems with explicit bounds.
  unconstrained problems (no budget ceiling, no timeline) are ill-posed by EVT.
  explicit constraints are not limitations — they are the condition that guarantees a solution exists.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L106 — LYAPUNOV STABILITY LAW
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
a system is stable if you can find a function that decreases over time along every
trajectory. you don't need to solve the equations of motion. if a decreasing function
exists, the system won't blow up. this is the certificate of stability.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
Lyapunov's direct method (1892):
  a function V(x) is a Lyapunov function for ẋ = f(x) if:
    (1) V(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0 (positive definite)
    (2) V(0) = 0
    (3) dV/dt = ∇V · f(x) ≤ 0 along trajectories (non-increasing)
    → if (3): stable equilibrium
    → if dV/dt < 0 (strictly decreasing): asymptotically stable (perturbations decay)
    → if dV/dt > 0 somewhere: unstable
  V plays the role of generalized energy — any quantity that decreases over time
  serves as a Lyapunov function
  LaSalle's invariance principle: extends asymptotic stability to cases where dV/dt = 0
  on a non-trivial set (orbit analysis)
  stochastic Lyapunov: extends to stochastic systems (Itô calculus version)
  → confirms stability in systems with noise

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: stability can be certified without simulation.
the architecture: find V → check V̇ ≤ 0 → conclude stability
  → this separates proof of stability from computation of trajectories
  → Lyapunov functions are stability certificates — they prove the system is safe
this is the mathematical version of "trust but verify" — you don't need to follow
every trajectory to know the system is stable. you need one function that decreases.
implication: designing stable systems = designing Lyapunov functions.
  the system is designed around the certificate, not discovered by simulation.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ control engineering: all modern control design (PID, LQR, MPC, H-infinity) constructs
  Lyapunov functions implicitly. the quadratic form V = xᵀPx (LQR) is the Lyapunov
  function that certifies stability of the closed-loop system.
→ machine learning: loss functions are Lyapunov candidates for training stability.
  if the loss decreases monotonically (V̇ < 0), training is asymptotically stable.
  gradient clipping is a Lyapunov intervention — preventing loss explosions.
→ economic stability: a social welfare function that decreases over time in a market
  is a Lyapunov function certifying market stability. the Lyapunov condition for
  tâtonnement (Walrasian price adjustment) is the stability condition for competitive markets.
→ organizational health: a metric that decreases when the organization is unhealthy
  and increases toward health (e.g., employee satisfaction, decision speed) is a
  Lyapunov function for organizational stability.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: decreasing energy certificates stability.
every stable thing in the universe has something that decreases along its trajectories.
thermodynamic equilibrium: entropy decreases free energy. ecosystem stability: population
variance decreases around the attractor. cognitive stability: prediction error decreases
with learning. the Lyapunov function is the universe's stability receipt.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ system design: before deploying a complex system, construct a Lyapunov function for it.
  what quantity should be decreasing if the system is healthy? monitor that quantity.
  if it starts increasing, the system is Lyapunov-unstable — intervene before blowup.
→ model stability: neural network training has Lyapunov structure.
  design training so that a certificate exists (bounded gradients, decreasing loss envelope).
  systems without a Lyapunov certificate (gradient explosions, reward divergence) are unstable.
→ organizational indicators: define a Lyapunov function for your organization —
  a composite metric that should decrease (dysfunction, cost) or increase (health, capacity)
  monotonically if the system is stable. track it. if it reverses, the equilibrium is lost.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L107 — FLUCTUATION-DISSIPATION THEOREM
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

LAYER 1 — SURFACE
in any system at thermal equilibrium, the forces that cause dissipation (friction, resistance)
are the same forces that cause random fluctuations (noise, brownian motion).
you cannot have one without the other. a perfectly smooth (zero-friction) medium produces
no thermal noise. a noisy medium always dissipates. noise and friction are two faces of the same phenomenon.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL
fluctuation-dissipation theorem (Callen-Welton 1951, built on Nyquist 1928):
  S(ω) = (4kT/ω) · Im[χ(ω)]
  where:
    S(ω) = power spectral density of fluctuations at frequency ω
    χ(ω) = generalized susceptibility (response to perturbation)
    Im[χ(ω)] = imaginary part = dissipative response
    kT = thermal energy
  → Johnson-Nyquist noise: voltage noise in resistor: S_V = 4kTR (Nyquist 1928)
    noise power proportional to resistance — cannot have resistance without noise
  → Einstein relation (1905): D = kT/γ
    diffusion coefficient D linked to friction γ — same microscopic interactions
  → Brownian motion: velocity autocorrelation function related to friction via FDT
  → Green-Kubo relations: transport coefficients (viscosity, thermal conductivity)
    expressed as time integrals of equilibrium fluctuation correlations
    → viscosity = (1/kT) ∫₀^∞ ⟨σₓᵧ(t)σₓᵧ(0)⟩ dt (where σ = stress tensor)

LAYER 3 — STRUCTURAL
the structural claim: dissipation and fluctuation are not independent — they are dual.
the architecture: microscopic reversibility (detailed balance at equilibrium) →
  fluctuations and response are related by time-reversal symmetry →
  FDT as exact consequence
implication: you cannot design a system with dissipation and no noise, or noise and no dissipation.
  reducing noise requires reducing dissipation (resistance). reducing dissipation generates noise.
  this is a fundamental trade-off built into thermodynamics, not a design failure.
the generalized FDT (non-equilibrium): extensions exist for systems near equilibrium
  (linear response theory) — the relationship holds to first order in perturbation strength.

LAYER 4 — CROSS-DOMAIN
→ electronics: amplifier noise (thermal + shot noise) is irreducible.
  the noise figure of any amplifier is bounded below by FDT.
  quantum amplifiers operate near this limit (SQUID amplifiers, parametric amplifiers).
→ financial markets: market impact (price slippage = dissipation) and price volatility
  (fluctuation) are related by a financial FDT. markets with high impact also have
  high volatility — they are dual. attempts to reduce volatility by removing liquidity
  increase impact (the other face of the same phenomenon).
→ organizational systems: the cost of making decisions (dissipation) is related to
  the uncertainty in outcomes (fluctuations). organizations that try to reduce outcome
  uncertainty must increase deliberation cost. FDT analog: you pay for certainty with process.
→ biology: receptor sensitivity (response to signal) is related to receptor noise
  (spontaneous activation) by FDT. maximally sensitive receptors are maximally noisy.
  this explains why highly sensitive sensory systems (e.g., rod photoreceptors, hair cells)
  operate at the quantum noise limit.

LAYER 5 — ROOT
the root: response and noise are the same coin.
the universe cannot create a system that responds to perturbations without producing fluctuations.
to be responsive is to be noisy. to be resistant is to fluctuate.
this is the universe's statement about sensitivity: you pay for it with noise.
perfect signal-to-noise ratio is achievable only by T = 0 — absolute zero, no fluctuations,
no response, death of dynamics. life, intelligence, and sensitivity require accepting the noise.

BUILD APPLICATION
→ signal processing: design signal chains knowing that low-noise amplification requires
  low-dissipation (cryogenic amplifiers, superconducting circuits). there is no free lunch.
  the noise floor is set by the FDT for the operating temperature.
→ market design: understanding that liquidity provision (reducing friction/impact) and
  volatility are linked. market makers who provide liquidity are taking on the volatility
  that their presence reduces. the FDT quantifies the exchange rate between them.
→ decision design: build explicit tolerance for outcome variance into high-responsiveness
  systems. a fast-responding, highly-sensitive decision process will be noisier than
  a slow, deliberate one. optimize for the right trade-off, not for eliminating the trade-off.
→ sensor design: operating near the FDT limit requires cryogenic cooling or quantum sensing
  methods. for room-temperature sensing, the FDT sets the irreducible noise floor —
  measure it, acknowledge it, design around it rather than pretending it can be eliminated.

S22 — ENTROPY-NASH COUPLING
NAME: entropy-Nash coupling
LAWS: L2 (entropy) × L50 (Nash equilibrium) × L94 (computational hardness)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: Nash equilibria in large games are the entropy-maximizing joint strategies —
  each player's mixed strategy that maximizes uncertainty from the opponent's perspective.
  mixed-strategy equilibria ARE maximum entropy distributions over the action space
  subject to expected payoff constraints (the maximum entropy principle and Nash equilibrium
  are the same optimization at the game-theoretic scale).
  and finding those equilibria is computationally hard (PPAD-complete).
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: entropy says systems maximize disorder. Nash says no player
  can profitably deviate. computational hardness says finding equilibria is hard.
  together: equilibria are entropy maxima, and finding entropy maxima in strategic settings is
  computationally irreducible. this explains why equilibrium prediction in complex markets is hard:
  it requires solving a PPAD-complete entropy maximization problem.
DOMAIN: algorithmic game theory, financial market design, mechanism design

S23 — SCALE-DRIFT EVOLUTION
NAME: scale-drift evolution
LAWS: L31 (genetic drift) × L96 (scale-dependent coupling) × L101 (Kleiber)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: drift (random walk in allele frequency) is not uniform across organism sizes.
  small organisms (fast metabolic rate, short generation time) experience drift at a
  higher effective rate — the coupling constant of drift runs with body mass.
  large organisms (slow metabolic time, long generation) effectively drift slower —
  drift is quenched by generation time scaling. this produces the observed pattern:
  smaller organisms have more genetic diversity; larger organisms have less (population
  genetics correlates with Kleiber's metabolic time, not calendar time).
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: drift alone predicts random walk in allele frequency.
  Kleiber gives metabolic time. scale-dependent coupling gives running parameters.
  together: drift rate runs with metabolic time — slower metabolic time = slower drift in biological time.
DOMAIN: population genetics, conservation biology, evolutionary medicine

S24 — BAYESIAN-CONDORCET HIERARCHY

LAWS: L58 (Bayesian updating) × L99 (Condorcet jury theorem)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: Bayesian aggregation and majority voting produce different answers.
  Condorcet gives optimal aggregation when agents have independent binary signals.
  Bayes gives optimal aggregation when agents have continuous posterior distributions.
  together: the optimal aggregation rule depends on the signal structure.
  for continuous uncertain beliefs: Bayesian pooling outperforms majority vote.
  for binary independent judgments: majority vote approaches Bayesian optimality.
  the unification: Bayesian updating IS the Condorcet mechanism in the limit of
  continuous probability estimates.
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: Condorcet assumes binary signals and fixed accuracy.
  Bayesian updating assumes continuous probability distributions.
  together: the choice of aggregation protocol should depend on signal type.
  this is a design law for collective intelligence systems.

S43 — EXTREME VALUE-RISK MANAGEMENT
NAME: extreme value-risk management
LAWS: L105 (extreme value theorem) × L100 (Zipf/power law) × L57 (central limit theorem — cycle 1)
EMERGENT BEHAVIOR: risk management has a fundamental bifurcation:
  for Gaussian (thin-tailed) processes: central limit theorem applies; extreme events are negligible.
  for power-law (fat-tailed) processes: Zipf governs; extreme events dominate.
  the extreme value theorem guarantees that the maximum of a finite sample exists —
  but its distribution depends entirely on whether the underlying distribution is thin or fat-tailed.
  for fat-tailed distributions (Zipf), the maximum of N samples grows without bound as N increases —
  the extreme value is in a different universality class.
  together: the entire theory of risk bifurcates based on tail behavior.
WHY NEITHER ALONE PREDICTS IT: EVT gives maximum existence. CLT gives Gaussian convergence.
  Zipf gives fat tails. together: risk theory bifurcates into two regimes —
  Gaussian (CLT applies, extremes are manageable) and power-law (Zipf applies, extremes dominate).
  using CLT risk management (VaR, Sharpe ratio) on power-law processes is a category error.
DOMAIN: financial risk, insurance, infrastructure resilience, public health crisis planning

  that cannot express all of its own semantic content — an incomplete fixed point.
DOMAIN: linguistics, natural language processing, AI language models, communication design
