───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: SOFTWARE — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L1 (zeroth law / thermodynamic equilibrium):
  → eventual consistency in distributed systems: databases that achieve eventual
    consistency are implementing the zeroth law — they wait for thermal equilibrium
    between all replicas. design for eventual equilibrium, not instant consistency,
    unless the cost of inconsistency exceeds the cost of synchronization.

L2 (second law / entropy):
  → code entropy: every codebase increases in entropy over time (more coupling, more
    dead code, more debt). entropy decrease requires energy (refactoring sprints).
    measure entropy metrics: cyclomatic complexity, coupling, duplication. track the
    derivative. if dEntropy/dt > 0 unchecked, the codebase will reach heat death.

L5 (conservation of energy):
  → compute conservation: energy-in = energy-out + heat. GPU training energy is
    conserved — it exits as model weights, heat, and carbon. account for all three.
    sustainable ML requires energy auditing across the full chain.

L10 (Noether / symmetry → conservation):
  → API versioning as symmetry: backward-compatible changes preserve the symmetry of
    the API contract. breaking changes destroy the symmetry → conservation law broken →
    downstream breakage. semantic versioning is a symmetry classification scheme.

L11 (Shannon information):
  → compression as intelligence: the ability to compress data is a direct measure of
    understanding. an ML model that perfectly predicts the next token is a perfect compressor.
    test understanding by measuring compression ratio — better models = better compressors.

L12 (Kolmogorov complexity):
  → code complexity audit: functions with high Kolmogorov complexity (hard to compress,
    no pattern) are algorithmic accidents — they should be replaced with explicit logic
    or generated from a simpler rule. complexity without pattern is technical debt.

L13 (emergence):
  → microservice emergence: distributed system behavior emerges from service interactions —
    it cannot be predicted from individual service specs. test system-level behavior explicitly;
    unit tests on individual services do not catch emergent failures.

L15 (phase transitions):
  → system capacity planning: don't model capacity linearly. identify the phase transition
    thresholds (connection pool exhaustion, GC pressure, lock contention) and engineer
    explicit buffers below them. post-transition behavior is qualitatively different —
    plan for it separately.

L17 (feedback loops):
  → feature flag feedback: a/b tests create feedback loops — user behavior changes
    the metric, which changes the feature, which changes user behavior.
    design feedback loops explicitly with settling time and convergence criteria.

L18 (power law):
  → cache hit rate follows power law: 80% of requests hit 20% of cached content.
    design caches for the Zipf distribution — tiered caching with hot/warm/cold tiers
    matching the power law tail.

L21 (Heisenberg uncertainty):
  → performance measurement uncertainty: measuring performance (profiling) changes
    performance (observer overhead). production profiling always underestimates overhead.
    design measurement systems that minimize perturbation (sampling profilers, not instrumenting profilers).

L22 (observer effect):
  → logging overhead: adding logging changes system behavior (timing, memory, I/O).
    structured logging with sampling rates manages the observer effect — log at 1%
    in production to measure without perturbing.

L25 (quantum entanglement / non-locality):
  → distributed transaction consistency: entangled distributed state (two services that
    must agree) requires explicit synchronization. there is no "spooky action at a distance"
    in software — consistency requires communication. design the communication protocol
    explicitly; pretending entanglement comes free is how distributed systems fail.

L26 (Pauli exclusion):
  → resource lock exclusion: two threads cannot occupy the same mutex — Pauli exclusion
    at the software level. deadlock is the violation of this principle when two locks
    are mutually required. design lock ordering to enforce a consistent Pauli structure.

L29 (natural selection):
  → A/B testing as evolution: features compete for user engagement. selection (metric)
    determines which variants survive. design the selection metric carefully —
    it determines what "fitness" means in your feature evolution.

L33 (Lotka-Volterra):
  → microservice dependency cycles: services in a mutual dependency cycle exhibit
    Lotka-Volterra dynamics — oscillating failures. break cycles; design acyclic
    service dependency graphs to eliminate the predator-prey oscillation.

L35 (small world):
  → six degrees in software: any function in a well-designed codebase should be reachable
    in O(log N) imports. small-world architecture (few hubs, many direct connections)
    minimizes import depth.

L38 (Metcalfe's law):
  → platform API network effects: API value scales as N². design APIs to be connectable —
    webhooks, event streams, and standard formats maximize the connections each integration
    can form.

L40 (Braess's paradox):
  → adding cache can slow the system: adding a cache between components can increase
    latency by creating a chokepoint. test system performance after every optimization —
    Braess says counterintuitive degradations are structurally possible.

L41 (Weber-Fechner):
  → log scales for user metrics: display performance metrics on log scales, not linear.
    human perception of "2× as fast" is proportional — 10ms→5ms feels similar to 1s→500ms.
    design performance goals in Weber-Fechner space (log scale), not absolute space.

L47 (supply and demand):
  → request queuing: request rate (supply) vs. processing capacity (demand).
    when supply exceeds demand, queue depth grows (price rises in elastic queues =
    increased latency). design systems with explicit back-pressure mechanisms
    (the market-clearing price for compute is latency; design the price correctly).

L50 (Nash equilibrium):
  → API design as game theory: API consumers will choose their strategies based on
    what they believe other consumers will do. design rate limits and quotas as
    mechanism design — the Nash equilibrium of all consumers acting optimally
    should be acceptable for the provider. if not, the mechanism is wrong.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness):
  → no complete test suite: no finite test suite can prove a program correct for all inputs
    (Gödel applied to formal verification). formal verification is only complete within
    a bounded model. design with explicit undecidable-region awareness; test for
    classes of behavior rather than all behaviors.

L57 (central limit theorem):
  → microservice latency distributions: aggregate latency of N independent service calls
    converges to Gaussian by CLT. but individual service latencies may be fat-tailed.
    tail latency (p99, p99.9) is determined by the fat tail of individual services,
    not the CLT-converged mean. optimize the tail, not the mean.

L58 (Bayesian updating):
  → feature flag gradual rollout: treat feature rollout as Bayesian updating.
    start with prior (expected conversion rate). roll out to 1%, update posterior,
    increase if posterior justifies. this is optimal sample-efficient feature validation.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: PRODUCT — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L2 (entropy): products accumulate entropy — features, options, edge cases pile up.
  → periodic entropy reduction: schedule "simplification sprints" as energy investments
    in product entropy reduction. products that never reduce entropy reach unusability.

L13 (emergence): product behavior emerges from user interaction patterns.
  → emergent use cases: monitor how users actually use the product (not how you designed it).
    emergent usage patterns are signals that users are finding higher-value applications
    than you designed for. follow the emergence.

L15 (phase transitions): user behavior has tipping points.
  → onboarding cliff: most users experience a phase transition in their relationship
    with a product — from "trying it" to "dependent on it." identify the actions that
    trigger this transition (the "aha moment") and optimize for that specific threshold.

L17 (feedback loops): product improvements create feedback loops.
  → compound improvement: each product improvement generates user feedback that reveals
    the next improvement. design product development as a tight feedback loop —
    weekly releases generate weekly feedback generates weekly improvements.

L18 (power law): user value contribution is power-law distributed.
  → community power users: the top 1% of users generate ~50% of community value (content,
    support, referrals). design explicit programs for power users that acknowledge their
    disproportionate contribution and deepen their engagement.

L21 (Heisenberg uncertainty): you cannot simultaneously measure all aspects of user experience.
  → measurement trade-offs: quantitative metrics (measuring everything) change user behavior.
    qualitative research (disturbs less) misses scale. design a portfolio: high-volume
    behavioral data + low-sample qualitative depth. neither alone is complete.

L29 (natural selection): product features evolve by competitive fitness.
  → ruthless deprecation: features that don't have users are evolutionary dead ends.
    select against them. deprecate features with <X% adoption after Y months.
    product fitness = engagement density, not feature count.

L35 (small world): product discovery follows small-world network dynamics.
  → referral network design: viral loops should be built on existing social networks
    (small world property — any user is ~6 links from any other user).
    the marginal cost of viral growth is low because the network topology is already small-world.

L36 (preferential attachment): early traction compounds.
  → seed market strategy: the first 100 users matter more than the next 10,000 because
    preferential attachment means early users attract later users.
    choose the first 100 users deliberately — they set the Zipf baseline.

L41 (Weber-Fechner): user perception of product value is logarithmic.
  → pricing anchoring: the perceived value of a price reduction from $100→$80 equals
    $10→$8 in Weber-Fechner space (same proportion). design pricing tiers with equal
    proportional steps, not equal absolute steps.

L42 (Hick's law): decision time increases with choice count.
  → pricing page: no more than 3 pricing tiers (Hick predicts decision paralysis above 3).
    feature comparison tables should highlight the recommended choice to short-circuit
    the logarithmic decision time increase.

L43 (Fitts's law): interaction time scales with target size and distance.
  → CTA design: primary calls to action should be large and close to natural eye/cursor
    resting position. Fitts's law is the quantitative foundation of button size design.
    double the button area → cut acquisition time by ~40%.

L50 (Nash equilibrium): multi-sided platform design is a Nash equilibrium problem.
  → platform pricing: the prices charged to each side of the market should be the Nash
    equilibrium where both sides find participation profitable. single-side pricing
    often destroys the equilibrium by making one side's participation irrational.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness): no product specification is complete.
  → spec humility: every product spec is Gödel-incomplete — there are valid user needs
    it cannot express. ship fast, observe emergent usage, update the spec from reality.
    the spec is a starting model, not the complete truth.

L57 (CLT): aggregate user metrics converge to Gaussian.
  → metric aggregation: mean and standard deviation are valid statistics for large-scale
    user metrics (CLT applies). but individual user behavior is often non-Gaussian.
    segment by cohort before applying CLT — pooling non-comparable populations
    violates the CLT independence assumption.

L58 (Bayesian updating): product roadmap is a belief system.
  → Bayesian roadmap: treat each roadmap item as a hypothesis with a prior probability
    of success. user research and analytics are evidence that updates the posterior.
    ship the highest expected-value item (highest posterior × payoff), not just the
    highest-confidence item.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DOMAIN: RESEARCH — EXPANDED COVERAGE
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

L2 (entropy): information has thermodynamic cost.
  → data collection cost: every measurement creates entropy (observer-system entanglement).
    design experiments to minimize entropy production while maximizing information gain.
    entropy-efficient experiments: maximum information per measurement perturbation.

L5 (conservation of energy): energy balance in experiments.
  → energy audit: any experiment that appears to create energy (perpetual motion-type results)
    violates L5. the first check for anomalous results: does the energy balance close?
    if not, find the hidden energy source before publishing.

L10 (Noether): every experimental symmetry is a conservation law.
  → symmetry-based experimental design: if your experiment has a symmetry (same result
    when left/right swapped, same result at different times), the corresponding conserved
    quantity is a check on experimental accuracy. verify conservation laws as consistency checks.

L11 (Shannon): information theory for experimental design.
  → maximum entropy experimental design: choose experiments that maximize information gain
    (maximize entropy reduction in the hypothesis space). this is the formal basis of
    active learning and sequential experimental design (D-optimal, A-optimal designs).

L15 (phase transitions): scientific paradigms have phase transitions.
  → paradigm shift detection: monitor the critical slowing down near paradigm shifts —
    anomalies accumulate, variance increases, the existing framework requires more epicycles.
    these are the statistical signatures of an approaching phase transition in the field.

L17 (feedback loops): citation networks create feedback.
  → citation inflation: highly-cited papers attract more citations (preferential attachment).
    the h-index is a measure of the fixed point of your citation feedback loop.
    design research programs to accelerate the feedback loop rather than waiting for it.

L18 (power law): scientific impact follows power law.
  → publication strategy: a small number of highly-cited papers produce most scientific impact.
    one influential paper in a high-impact venue > ten average papers.
    power law impact means concentration of effort in the highest-value work dominates the strategy.

L21 (Heisenberg): measurement limits in physics experiments.
  → uncertainty-limited experiments: identify the Heisenberg limit for your measurement.
    quantum metrology (using entangled states) can beat the standard quantum limit by
    1/√N → 1/N (Heisenberg limit). for precision measurement experiments, this matters.

L29 (natural selection): scientific ideas evolve by selection.
  → idea fitness: scientific ideas compete for adoption by the community.
    fitness criteria: predictive accuracy, simplicity, generalizability, reproducibility.
    design research to score high on all four fitness dimensions, not just accuracy.

L36 (preferential attachment): early results define a research program.
  → first-mover citation advantage: the first paper to clearly articulate a phenomenon
    accumulates citations by preferential attachment even if subsequent papers are better.
    clear articulation early in a research program is strategically critical.

L41 (Weber-Fechner): statistical effect sizes are perceived logarithmically.
  → effect size reporting: report effect sizes in natural log units where applicable
    (Cohen's d = 0.2 vs. 0.8 should be understood as a logarithmic scale difference in impact).
    researchers systematically underestimate small effect sizes and overestimate large ones
    due to Weber-Fechner perception.

L50 (Nash equilibrium): academic incentive structures produce Nash equilibria.
  → publication incentive game: the academic game (publish or perish, h-index optimization)
    has a Nash equilibrium that is not the optimal science equilibrium.
    strategies: find the local Nash of the current incentive system; optimize within it.
    better: design institutional mechanisms that move the Nash equilibrium toward better science.

L55 (Gödel incompleteness): science cannot be complete.
  → research horizon awareness: every scientific field has Gödel-incomplete regions —
    questions that cannot be answered within the field's current axiomatic framework.
    identify these questions explicitly. they mark where the field needs expansion, not more depth.

L57 (CLT): statistical inference relies on CLT.
  → sample size planning: CLT converges for N > 30 (rough rule). for non-Gaussian distributions,
    convergence requires larger N. use simulation to determine required N for your specific
    distribution before running the experiment.

L58 (Bayesian updating): hypothesis testing should be Bayesian.
  → p-values vs. Bayes factors: p-values do not measure evidence for a hypothesis.
    Bayes factors do. the replication crisis is partly a p-value misuse crisis.
    report Bayes factors alongside p-values for correct evidence interpretation.
