CYCLE 33 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN MAPPING AND SUB-DOMAIN EXPANSION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 302 domains | 191 gaps | Sub-domain expansion phase

PRIMARY OBJECTIVE: R09 sub-taxonomy enumeration (structural irreversibility
  taxonomy); automotive cybersecurity sub-domain expansion; hardware security
  formal verification sub-domain; formalize "recurring new perimeter" pattern

DOMAIN EXPANSION — CYCLE 33:

D303 | Automotive Cybersecurity — CAN Bus Attack Surface
  Sub-domain: Vehicle Network Security
  CAN (Controller Area Network): broadcast bus connecting ECUs with no
  authentication, no encryption, no source address verification.
  Design context: 1986 protocol designed for reliability in closed system;
  security was not a design requirement.
  Attack surface: any node on CAN bus can spoof messages to any other node;
  attacker with physical access to OBD-II port or via telematics unit has
  full CAN bus access.
  PENDING-LAW-1 candidate evaluation: CAN is deployed in 1.4 billion vehicles
  globally; no authentication retrofit is feasible without replacing all ECUs;
  automotive ECU replacement cost per vehicle exceeds $10K; no regulatory
  mandate with hard deadline. MATCHES PENDING-LAW-1 STRUCTURE.
  Sub-taxonomy link: R01 (broadcast ambient authority — all ECUs hear all
  messages by design), R05 (state confusion — spoofed sensor data)

D304 | Automotive Cybersecurity — Telematics and Remote Attack Surface
  Sub-domain: Vehicle Network Security
  Telematics unit (TCU): cellular-connected ECU providing remote services
  (OTA updates, stolen vehicle tracking, remote diagnostics). Acts as bridge
  between cellular network and CAN bus — structural confused deputy (R06).
  Attack path: cellular network → TCU exploit → CAN bus access → safety-
  critical ECU control (brakes, steering, engine management).
  Historical: Miller/Valasek Jeep Cherokee remote attack (2015) — exploited
  TCU firmware vulnerability to gain CAN access; remotely controlled
  brakes and steering at highway speed. First public demonstrated remote
  automotive attack. NHTSA recall of 1.4 million vehicles followed.
  Link: this is the automotive instantiation of ICS historian confused deputy
  (Anatomy 30.C) — TCU bridges external network and internal control bus
  with insufficient isolation.

D305 | Automotive Cybersecurity — OTA Update Attack Surface
  Sub-domain: Vehicle Network Security / Supply Chain
  OTA (Over-the-Air) firmware updates are now standard for EVs and connected
  vehicles. Update pipeline: cloud server → cellular → TCU → ECU flash.
  Attack surface: compromise OTA server, intercept OTA channel, or serve
  malicious firmware to target vehicles.
  Defense requirement: authenticated, encrypted OTA with rollback protection;
  secure boot chain verifying update signature before flashing.
  Root: R02 (trust transitivity — vehicle trusts OTA server signature;
  if signing key compromised, all vehicles in fleet are exploitable
  simultaneously). Supply chain parallel to SolarWinds: one OTA server
  compromise → mass vehicle fleet impact.

D306 | Hardware Security — Formal Verification of Security Properties
  Sub-domain: Hardware Security Verification
  Formal verification applies mathematical proof to hardware designs to
  guarantee security properties (no information flow from high-security
  to low-security domain, no timing side-channels, adherence to isolation
  specification).
  Tools: Coq, Isabelle/HOL, SymbiYosys (formal verification for RTL);
  Cadence JasperGold, Synopsys VC Formal (commercial EDA tools).
  Application: cryptographic cores (AES, SHA), memory protection units,
  hypervisor isolation, RISC-V privilege specification.
  Limitation: formal verification proves correctness of the model, not
  the physical implementation; fabrication-level attacks (hardware trojans)
  and side-channel attacks operate below the model abstraction.

D307 | Hardware Security — Hardware Trojan Detection and Prevention
  Sub-domain: IC Supply Chain Security / Hardware Integrity
  Hardware trojans: malicious modifications introduced into IC design or
  fabrication. Classes: parametric (alter timing margins), functional
  (add logic for trigger+payload), hybrid.
  Threat model: nation-state adversary with access to fabrication facility
  or design house.
  Detection: design-phase (formal verification, side-channel analysis of
  golden reference chip), post-fabrication (destructive delayering + SEM
  imaging, ATPG with coverage metrics, power analysis comparison).
  Prevention: split manufacturing (front-end and back-end at separate
  fabs, no single fab has complete design), logic obfuscation, trusted
  foundry programs.
  Link: R03 (implicit trust in supply chain — chip design trusts every
  entity with access to the GDS-II file), supply chain sub-domain.

D308 | Hardware Security — Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs)
  Sub-domain: Hardware Identity / Root of Trust
  PUF: hardware primitive that exploits manufacturing process variation
  to generate device-unique, reproducible responses to challenge inputs.
  Property: same challenge on same device always produces same response;
  same challenge on different device produces different response; response
  is not stored anywhere — generated on demand from physical structure.
  Types: Arbiter PUF, Ring Oscillator PUF, SRAM PUF.
  Security application: device authentication without stored secret key
  (key is derived from physical structure; cannot be cloned or extracted).
  Weakness: responses are somewhat noisy (environmental variation: temp,
  voltage, aging); requires error correction (helper data algorithm).
  Attack surface: ML modeling attacks — with sufficient challenge-response
  pairs, an ML model can predict PUF responses without physical access.
  Defense: XOR PUFs, controlled PUFs with limited challenge-response pair
  exposure.

D309 | Automotive Cybersecurity — V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything) Security
  Sub-domain: Vehicle Network Security / 5G/V2X
  V2X: vehicular communication with infrastructure (V2I), other vehicles
  (V2V), pedestrians (V2P), network (V2N). Protocols: DSRC (802.11p),
  C-V2X (cellular-based).
  Security model: IEEE 1609.2 pseudonymous certificates — vehicles use
  short-lived pseudonymous credentials to prevent tracking while enabling
  authentication. Certificate authority (SCMS) manages pseudonym issuance.
  Attack surface: (1) Sybil attack — attacker broadcasts multiple fake
  vehicle identities to manipulate traffic perception; (2) Position
  falsification — fake GPS coordinates broadcast as safety messages;
  (3) SCMS compromise — certificate authority enables fleet-wide identity
  manipulation.
  Root: R02 (trust transitivity through certificate chain), R05 (state
  confusion via falsified position/presence data)

ENTERING STATE: 128 patterns cumulative

Pattern 33.1 | THE BROADCAST BUS AS ZERO-AUTHENTICATION ATTACK SURFACE
  Domain: Automotive / ICS-OT / Industrial Ethernet
  Instances:
    - CAN bus (automotive): 1.4 billion vehicles; no auth; no source addr
    - Modbus (industrial): most deployed ICS protocol; no authentication
    - PROFIBUS (industrial): serial bus for factory automation; no auth
    - BACnet (building automation): HVAC/access control; broadcast by design
    - DNP3 (SCADA): authenticated variant exists but rarely deployed
  Pattern: broadcast protocols designed for closed-system reliability
    inherit a structural zero-authentication property that cannot be
    retrofitted without replacing all nodes on the bus simultaneously.
  Root: R01 (ambient authority — broadcast reception is ambient; all nodes
    receive all messages with no explicit trust establishment required)
  Connection to CONFIRMED LAW-1: every instance exhibits the same
    civilizational-scale irreversibility — deployed at scale, no upgrade path
    that doesn't require simultaneous replacement of all endpoints.
  Cross-domain: this is the physical/industrial-bus parallel of the DNS
    "any query goes to any resolver" broadcast trust model.
  New entry: broadcast bus joins the CONFIRMED LAW-1 instances as a
    cross-cutting pattern (not a 7th named instance, but the MECHANISM
    unifying SS7, BGP, CAN, Modbus, BACnet — they are all instances of
    the broadcast bus pattern at different scales)

Pattern 33.2 | SUPPLY CHAIN TRUST PROPAGATION TO PHYSICAL HARDWARE
  Domain: Hardware Security / IC Supply Chain
  Instances:
    - Hardware trojan in IC: trust propagates from chip to all systems using it
    - Malicious firmware in component: router/NIC firmware; trust propagates
    - PUF ML modeling attack: device identity derived from physical structure;
      if attack works, identity is cloned without physical device
    - Automotive OTA compromise: signing key compromise → all fleet vehicles
  Pattern: trust chains in supply chain extend into the physical domain;
    compromise at any fabrication or signing step propagates to all
    downstream deployments without any runtime signal.
  Root: R02 (trust transitivity) + R03 (implicit trust in supply chain
    provenance — hardware is assumed genuine because it arrived in expected
    packaging/channels)
  New dimension: this extends the software supply chain pattern (SolarWinds,
    npm, PyPI) to hardware; the tooling gap is larger because hardware
    attestation is harder than software signature verification.
  Connection to existing taxonomy: generalizes supply chain sub-domain
    (D193-D210 range) into hardware domain.

Pattern 33.3 | RECURRING NEW PERIMETER — FORMALIZATION
  Domain: Cross-cutting / Architectural
  Observation across 33 cycles: security architecture repeatedly identifies
    "the new perimeter" as each successive layer is compromised or bypassed.
    The recurrence is itself a pattern.
  Six confirmed instances (see New Perimeter Series):
    Network, Endpoint, Identity, CI/CD, Active Directory, Hardware Attestation
  Pattern mechanics:
    1. A defense layer is established and widely deployed
    2. Attackers develop systematic techniques for that layer (tooling: C218)
    3. The layer's effectiveness drops below threshold
    4. Security architecture declares the NEXT layer "the real perimeter"
    5. Prior layer becomes assumed-compromised in defensive posture
  Root: CONFIRMED LAW-2 (tooling commoditizes bypass) + R01 (the bypassed
    layer retains ambient authority even after it is no longer trusted)
  Implication: each "new perimeter" is a regression, not a redefinition;
    the bypassed layer's ambient authority persists and attackers use it
    while defenders focus on the new perimeter. Defense requires treating
    ALL prior perimeters as simultaneously active attack surfaces.
  This pattern predicts a 7th perimeter: candidates — AI/ML inference layer
    (attackers bypass model-based detections via adversarial evasion),
    or runtime application self-protection (RASP) as perimeter bypassed by
    memory-safe language adoption that moves the problem, not eliminates it.

Pattern 33.4 | R09 SUB-TAXONOMY DRAFT — STRUCTURAL IRREVERSIBILITY CLASSES
  Domain: Cross-cutting / Root Mechanics
  R09 (irreversibility) operates through distinct mechanisms. Enumeration:

R09.1 — PROTOCOL DEPLOYMENT IRREVERSIBILITY
    Mechanism: protocol used by N independent operators; upgrade requires
    simultaneous coordination of all N; N is large enough that coordination
    fails on security timescales.
    Instances: SS7, BGP, DNS/DNSSEC, CAN bus, Modbus, BACnet
    CONFIRMED LAW-1 domain.

R09.2 — EQUIPMENT LIFECYCLE IRREVERSIBILITY
    Mechanism: deployed equipment cannot be updated or replaced within
    its operational lifetime on security timescales due to cost, lead
    time, or process safety requirements.
    Instances: ICS PLCs (20-40 year lifecycle), medical devices (510(k)
    recertification per firmware update), automotive ECUs (vehicle lifetime),
    nuclear instrumentation and control systems.

R09.3 — OPERATIONAL DEPENDENCY IRREVERSIBILITY
    Mechanism: access exception or connectivity creates operational processes,
    training, and contracts that make exception removal cost-prohibitive.
    Instances: IT/OT boundary erosion (Anatomy 32.C), RBAC scope creep,
    firewall rule proliferation, vendor remote access accumulation.

R09.4 — CRYPTOGRAPHIC COMMITMENT IRREVERSIBILITY
    Mechanism: data encrypted or signed with a key cannot be re-secured
    retroactively; if the key is compromised or the algorithm broken,
    all past-encrypted data is exposed.
    Instances: HNDL (Harvest Now Decrypt Later) — past TLS sessions
    become decryptable when Shor's algorithm runs; archived encrypted
    communications exposed retroactively.

R09.5 — TRUST ANCHOR IRREVERSIBILITY
    Mechanism: root CA or trust anchor compromise invalidates all
    certificates issued under it, but the trust anchor is embedded in
    billions of devices; revocation requires updating every trust store.
    Instances: DigiNotar CA compromise (2011) — revocation required
    browser/OS updates; devices that could not update remained compromised.
    Hardware-embedded trust anchors: no update path without hardware replacement.

R09.6 — DATA EXFILTRATION IRREVERSIBILITY (meta-irreversibility)
    Mechanism: once sensitive data is exfiltrated, its exposure is permanent;
    rotation of secrets mitigates future exposure but cannot un-expose
    already-exfiltrated data.
    Instances: credential dumps (passwords can be changed; user behavior patterns,
    PII, strategic data cannot); source code leaks; key material leaks.

STATUS: R09 sub-taxonomy DRAFT (R09.1-R09.6) — requires counter-example
  validation across subsequent cycles.

ANATOMY 33.A — CAN BUS SPOOFING + MILLER/VALASEK REMOTE AUTOMOTIVE ATTACK
Root: R01 (ambient authority) + R06 (confused deputy)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

CAN BUS ARCHITECTURE:
  CAN 2.0B message frame: [SOF | 11-bit ID | RTR | Control | Data | CRC | ACK | EOF]
  The 11-bit ID identifies the MESSAGE TYPE, not the sender.
  No source address. No authentication. Any node on bus can transmit any message ID.

FUNDAMENTAL ATTACK: MESSAGE INJECTION (physical access via OBD-II)
  Attacker connects to OBD-II port (accessible in driver footwell without tools),
  uses USB-to-CAN adapter (~$30), transmits CAN frames with target ECU message IDs.
  No credentials required. No authentication to bypass.
  Demonstrated effects:
    - Speedometer manipulation (instrument cluster ECU message spoofed)
    - Brake application (ABS ECU messages spoofed)
    - Steering control (vehicles with electric power steering)
    - Engine shutdown (EMS message spoofed)

TPMS ATTACK SURFACE (G199 resolution):
  Tire Pressure Monitoring System: each wheel sensor broadcasts 315/433 MHz RF;
  no authentication on RF link; no binding to vehicle.
  Attack: SDR (~$25) broadcasts fake TPMS frames with any sensor ID.
  Effects: trigger false low-pressure warning; suppress genuine warnings.
  Range: effective from roadside at highway speeds with directional antenna.
  Attacker does not need physical vehicle access -- RF-only attack.

MILLER/VALASEK 2015 JEEP CHEROKEE -- ATTACK CHAIN:
  Stage 1: UCONNECT TCU REMOTE CODE EXECUTION
    Uconnect (Sprint cellular) exposed D-Bus interface over internet.
    Port 6667 accessible from internet with no authentication.
    Attacker queries Sprint network to enumerate all Uconnect IPs.
    D-Bus wpa_cli with crafted SSID executes arbitrary shell commands as root.
    Result: remote root shell on TCU from any internet-connected device.

Stage 2: FIRMWARE REWRITE OF V850 CHIP
    TCU contains V850 microcontroller managing CAN bus interface.
    From TCU root: write malicious firmware to V850 chip.
    Malicious firmware: injects arbitrary CAN frames on behalf of attacker.

Stage 3: SAFETY-CRITICAL CAN FRAME INJECTION
    - HVAC control: immediate (demonstration start)
    - Radio volume maximum: immediate
    - Transmission: shift to neutral (engine disengaged at highway speed)
    - Brakes: ABS pump activated, brake pedal rendered ineffective
    - Steering: full lock at low speed
    Demonstrated at highway speed: engine disengaged; driver could not accelerate.
    NHTSA recall of 1.4 million vehicles followed.

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R01 (ambient authority): CAN bus grants authority to transmit any message
       by virtue of physical bus membership -- bus membership IS authority.
  R06 (confused deputy): TCU bridges cellular network and CAN bus; same
       structural pattern as ICS historian (Anatomy 30.C).
  R09.1 (protocol deployment irreversibility): CAN deployed in 1.4 billion
       vehicles; no authentication retrofit feasible without ECU replacement.

AUTOSAR SecOC (post-Jeep response):
  MAC appended to CAN frame using shared symmetric key.
  Counter (freshness value) prevents replay attacks.
  Limitation: requires all ECUs updated; only in new vehicles; not retrofittable.

G199 RESOLVED. Pattern 33.1 anatomy COMPLETE.

ANATOMY 33.B — ADCS ESC3 AND ESC7
Root: R06 (confused deputy) + R02 (trust transitivity)
Gap: G184 partial (ESC3 and ESC7 documented; ESC2/5/8/10 carry forward)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ESC3 -- ENROLLMENT AGENT ABUSE FOR SMART CARD AUTHENTICATION BYPASS:
  Certificate template with Enrollment Agent EKU (1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1)
  allows holder to enroll for certificates ON BEHALF OF other users.
  Intended use: smart card issuance workflow.

Misconfiguration: template with Enrollment Agent EKU + Enroll permission
  granted to Domain Users or low-privilege group.

Attack chain:
  1. Low-privilege attacker requests certificate from enrollment agent template
  2. Uses enrollment agent certificate to request a certificate for Domain Admin
     from a smart-card-logon template
  3. CA issues certificate stating Subject=Domain Admin; private key held by attacker
  4. Attacker authenticates as Domain Admin using PKINIT (Kerberos cert auth)

Root mechanics:
    R06: CA acts on behalf of enrollment agent credential to issue identity
         certificates for arbitrary subjects; CA cannot verify enrollment agent
         has legitimate authority for the target subject.
    R02: AD trusts issued certificate as proof of identity (trust chain:
         CA -> enrollment agent cert -> subject cert -> Kerberos TGT).

Detection: watch for certs issued with Subject != requester UPN;
  monitor PKINIT auth by accounts without enrolled smart cards.

ESC7 -- VULNERABLE CA ACL (MANAGE CA / MANAGE CERTIFICATES RIGHTS):
  ManageCA: allows modifying CA configuration (templates, flags, audit)
  ManageCertificates: allows approving pending requests and revoking certs

Misconfiguration: these permissions granted to non-administrative accounts.

Attack variant A (ManageCA + ManageCertificates):
  1. Enable EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag (same as ESC6)
  2. Submit certificate request with SAN=Domain Admin UPN
  3. Approve request with ManageCertificates
  4. Authenticate as Domain Admin via PKINIT

Attack variant B (ManageCertificates only):
  1. Submit certificate request requiring manager approval
  2. Use ManageCertificates to self-approve own request
  3. No CA configuration change required

Root mechanics:
    R01 (ambient authority): ManageCertificates grants ability to approve
         ANY pending request for ANY subject; authority is not scoped.
    R06: CA issues certificates based on who has approval authority,
         not whether the approval is operationally legitimate.

Remediation: audit all non-administrative accounts with ManageCA or
  ManageCertificates; use Certify/Certipy tooling to enumerate.
  Note: routinely over-granted to helpdesk accounts for renewal tickets.

G184 STATUS: ESC3 and ESC7 documented. ESC2, ESC5, ESC8, ESC10 carry forward.

ANATOMY 33.C — HARDWARE TROJAN IN IC SUPPLY CHAIN
Root: R02 (trust transitivity) + R03 (implicit trust in supply chain)
Gap resolution: G196 (ATPG coverage vs. trojan)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

THREAT MODEL:
  Nation-state adversary inserts malicious logic into IC design or masks.
  Trojan lies dormant until triggered; chip FUNCTIONS CORRECTLY under normal use.

HARDWARE TROJAN TAXONOMY:
  Trigger: internal (counter, input pattern, time) or external (RF, rare sequence)
  Payload: functional (corrupt output), parametric (degrade timing),
           kill switch (disable on trigger), exfiltration (leak key via side-channel)

KLEPTOGRAPHIC RISK (cryptographic hardware trojan):
  Biased RNG appears statistically random but allows trojan designer to
  predict outputs. All keys generated on compromised chip are predictable.
  Precedent: NSA Dual_EC_DRBG (software; hardware equivalent feasible).
  Impact: no software correctness above the chip can compensate.

DETECTION METHODOLOGY (G196 resolution):
  Method                  | What It Detects        | Key Limitation
  ------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------
  Destructive delayering  | Any physical mod       | Destroys the chip tested
  + SEM imaging           | visible under SEM      | Cannot test what was tested
  ATPG                    | Functional deviations  | Trojan triggers by RARE
                          | in common logic paths  | conditions; ATPG covers
                          |                        | common paths only; trojan
                          |                        | trigger near-zero coverage
  Power side-channel      | Extra logic consuming  | Small trojans within
                          | power vs. golden ref   | process variation noise
  Formal verification     | RTL design deviations  | Post-synthesis/fab trojans
  of RTL                  |                        | not in RTL

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R02 (trust transitivity): computing stack trusts hardware layer; trojan
       in hardware undermines every security property asserted by software.
  R03 (implicit trust in supply chain): chip provenance assumed by packaging;
       no runtime mechanism detects correctly-fabricated but modified chip.
  R09.5 (trust anchor irreversibility): widely-deployed trojan chip requires
       hardware recall at civilizational scale for remediation.

G196 RESOLVED. Pattern 33.2 hardware anatomy COMPLETE.

ANATOMY 33.D — AUTOMOTIVE OTA FIRMWARE SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK
Root: R02 (trust transitivity) + R09.4 (cryptographic commitment irreversibility)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

OTA ARCHITECTURE: OEM backend -> CDN -> cellular (LTE/5G) -> TCU/gateway ECU
  -> CAN/CAN-FD/Ethernet -> target ECU flash update

ATTACK SURFACE LAYERS:
  Layer 1: OEM update server compromise
    Same structure as SolarWinds (C224): compromise build pipeline or signing
    infrastructure; serve malicious firmware signed with legitimate key.
    Fleet impact: all vehicles polling for updates receive malicious firmware.
    Affected fleet: potentially millions of vehicles simultaneously.

Layer 2: CDN/transport interception
    Requires defeating TLS (via CA compromise or BGP hijack).
    Malicious firmware served without OEM signing key; vehicle must
    fail to verify signature.

Layer 3: TCU exploitation for local firmware injection
    From TCU root (Anatomy 33.A), attacker flashes ECU firmware directly
    over internal bus without OEM OTA pipeline.
    Signature verification at TCU boundary does NOT protect against
    TCU compromise -- verification happens before the compromised point.

SECURE BOOT CHAIN REQUIREMENT:
  Every ECU must implement: Bootloader verified against OTP-fused hardware key
  -> Application firmware verified by bootloader
  -> OTA update package signed by OEM key, verified before any flash write.
  Current weakness: secure boot often only on TCU/gateway; target ECUs may
  not verify update signatures received over internal CAN from gateway.

SOLARWINDS STRUCTURAL PARALLEL:
  SolarWinds: build server compromise -> malicious DLL signed by SW cert
               -> deployed to 18,000 customers via update
  Automotive: OEM signing server compromise -> malicious firmware signed by
              OEM key -> deployed to millions of vehicles via OTA
  Structural identity: trust chain compressed at signing; verifiers at
  deployment cannot distinguish legitimate from attacker-signed content.

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R02 (trust transitivity): vehicle trusts OEM signing key; key trusts
       build pipeline; compromise propagates to all vehicles.
  R09.4 (cryptographic commitment irreversibility): signing key compromise
       makes all past updates retroactively suspect; revocation requires
       new root of trust provisioned to all vehicles via OTA -- signed by
       the potentially-compromised key (circular dependency).

STAGE 3 EXIT STATE: 99 anatomies cumulative | BACKLOG: 19 patterns
  Resolved: Pattern 33.1 (33.A), G184 partial (33.B), G196 (33.C),
             D305/Pattern 33.2 (33.D), G199 (33.A)
  Net backlog change: -4 (23 -> 19)
  Backlog trajectory: 30 -> 29 -> 27 -> 23 -> 19 (four consecutive net reductions)

A279 | Automotive OTA — TCU compromise for local ECU reflash
  Mechanism: exploit TCU (A275); from TCU root, flash malicious firmware to
    downstream ECUs over internal CAN bus; bypasses OTA signature verification
    which occurs at TCU boundary before the compromised point
  Result: persistent malicious ECU firmware; survives OTA update pipeline security
  Root: R02 + R06 (TCU as trusted firmware distributor to downstream ECUs)
  Domain: Automotive Cybersecurity
  Link: Anatomy 33.D

A280 | Hardware trojan via IC supply chain contamination
  Mechanism: malicious logic inserted at design or fabrication stage;
    trojan triggered by rare condition; leaks key material or alters output
  Result: cryptographic operations on compromised chip are attacker-visible;
    effective against entire installed base without any exploit or CVE
  Root: R02 + R03 (implicit supply chain trust)
  Domain: Hardware Security / IC Supply Chain
  Link: Anatomy 33.C

A281 | PUF ML modeling attack — device identity prediction
  Mechanism: collect sufficient challenge-response pairs from PUF device;
    train ML model to predict PUF responses; predict device response to new
    challenges without physical access to device
  Result: device identity can be cloned; authentication based on PUF is bypassed
  Root: R08 (feature space exploitation — PUF response as learnable function)
  Domain: Hardware Security / Device Authentication
  Link: D308

D381 | Automotive: AUTOSAR SecOC for CAN bus authentication
  Message authentication code (MAC) appended to CAN frames
  Freshness counter prevents replay attacks
  Shared symmetric key between transmitter ECU and authorized receivers
  Limitation: requires all ECUs upgraded to SecOC-capable firmware;
    not retrofittable to existing vehicles; key management required
  Eliminates A273 (message injection without ECU access)

D382 | Automotive: TPMS sensor registration and validation
  Binding TPMS sensor IDs to VIN during tire installation; reject
  pressure messages from unregistered sensor IDs
  Limitation: partial mitigation; adversary can clone registered ID
  Addresses A274 at operational level; does not eliminate RF injection surface

D383 | Automotive: TCU network segmentation — no direct internet exposure
  TCU connects to manufacturer backend via VPN; no open ports on public internet
  Eliminates the Uconnect attack surface that enabled A275
  Defense-in-depth: TCU firewall + VPN + allowlisted OEM server IPs only

D384 | Automotive: Secure boot on every ECU (not only TCU)
  Hardware root of trust (OTP-fused key) verifies bootloader
  Bootloader verifies application firmware and any OTA update package
  Eliminates A279 (TCU-to-ECU local reflash without signature verification)
  Current state: often only implemented on TCU; target ECUs frequently lack it

D385 | Automotive: OTA signing key rotation and HSM protection
  OEM firmware signing keys stored in HSM (never exportable)
  Key rotation cadence: annual or per major release
  Separation: OTA signing keys separate from TLS/code signing keys
  Compromise detection: CT log equivalent for OTA firmware distributions

D386 | Automotive: Intrusion Detection System (IDS) on CAN bus (G200 resolution)
  Monitor CAN bus traffic for: anomalous message frequency, unexpected message IDs,
    messages from unexpected bus segments, statistical anomalies in payload values
  Commercial: Argus Cyber Security, Karamba Security, Vector AUTOSAR IDS
  Limitation: detection-based; does not prevent injection; requires golden baseline
  Alert: any detection requires physical service recall (OTA cannot fix if bus compromised)

D387 | ADCS: Restrict Enrollment Agent templates to dedicated enrollment agents
  Remove Enroll permission on enrollment agent templates from Domain Users
  Grant only to specific enrollment agent service accounts with justification
  Audit using Certipy: certipy find -enabled to enumerate misconfigured templates
  Eliminates ESC3 (A276)

D388 | ADCS: Remove ManageCA and ManageCertificates from helpdesk/non-admin accounts
  Audit: certutil -catemplates; enumerate all CA ACLs
  ManageCA reserved to PKI administrators only (Tier 0 equivalent)
  ManageCertificates: delegate narrowly for certificate renewal workflows with logging
  Eliminates ESC7 (A277)

D389 | Hardware supply chain: split manufacturing
  Front-end (design -> wafer) and back-end (wafer -> packaged chip) at different fabs
  No single facility has complete design + mask set + packaging capability
  Reduces hardware trojan risk by requiring coordination between facilities
  Limitation: increases cost; trusted foundry programs still required for high-security

D390 | Hardware supply chain: post-fabrication power side-channel analysis
  Measure chip power profile against golden reference under identical workloads
  Statistical comparison detects additional logic consuming power above reference
  Limitation: parametric trojans and small functional trojans within noise floor
  Applicable to high-security procurement (military, cryptographic hardware)

D391 | PUF protection: controlled PUF with rate-limited challenge-response exposure
  Limit number of challenge-response pairs accessible from device interface
  Prevents attacker from collecting training data for ML modeling attack
  Addresses A281; combined with XOR PUF architecture increases ML attack difficulty

D392 | V2X: IEEE 1609.2 pseudonymous certificate architecture
  Vehicles use short-lived pseudonymous certificates (refreshed periodically)
  SCMS (Security Credential Management System) issues and manages pseudonyms
  Unlinkability: refreshed pseudonym prevents tracking over time
  Authentication: all V2X messages signed with pseudonymous certificate
  Addresses V2X Sybil attack surface (G198)

D393 | Automotive: hardware security module (HSM) per ECU for key isolation
  Cryptographic keys for SecOC, secure boot, and OTA never leave HSM
  ECU firmware cannot extract private keys even if compromised
  EVITA (E-safety Vehicle Intrusion Protected Applications) standard
  Requirement: HSM present on all safety-critical ECUs in new architectures

D394 | Hardware: formal verification of cryptographic cores
  Use SMT solvers or theorem provers to verify RNG distribution properties,
    AES key schedule correctness, and absence of information flow leaks
  Catches design-phase trojan candidates and implementation errors
  Tools: Jasper, SymbiYosys; applies to RTL not post-synthesis netlist

D395 | Hardware: trusted execution environment (TEE) for key operations
  ARM TrustZone, RISC-V PMP, Intel TDX: isolate cryptographic key operations
  from normal application execution; hardware-enforced boundary
  Even if application OS is compromised, keys in TEE remain inaccessible
  Limitation: TEE itself must be verified; TEE implementation bugs (CVE-2021-*)

D396 | Automotive: OTA canary deployment and staged rollout
  New firmware deployed to 1% of fleet first; behavioral monitoring period
  Anomaly detection: fuel consumption, error codes, communication patterns
  Staged rollout prevents fleet-wide simultaneous impact from A278
  Rollback capability: if canary shows anomaly, halt OTA and investigate

C239 | CAN bus (A273-A275) is the automotive instantiation of the broadcast
  bus pattern (Pattern 33.1). Root mechanics are identical to Modbus (ICS)
  and SS7 (telecom): broadcast medium designed for closed-system reliability;
  security not a design requirement; deployed at scale before threat model
  existed; no retrofit path. This is CONFIRMED LAW-1 at automotive scale:
  1.4 billion vehicles cannot be upgraded simultaneously. The automotive
  domain adds a new dimension to LAW-1: physical safety consequences
  (brake/steering control) versus data confidentiality consequences in
  SS7/BGP. Same structural mechanic, higher severity payload.

C240 | TPMS attack (A274) demonstrates R01 in the RF domain: 315/433 MHz
  broadcast grants receiver authority by physical proximity. There is no
  pairing protocol, no challenge-response, no enrollment. The ambient
  authority structure of CAN bus is replicated in the RF sensor network
  attached to it. Implication: layered broadcast systems compound R01 --
  the ambient authority of the internal bus plus the ambient authority of
  the RF layer creates two attack surfaces that each independently bypass
  authentication.

C241 | Miller/Valasek attack (A275) is the third confirmed instance of the
  historian confused deputy pattern (R06 + IT/OT bridge = full attack path):
  Instance 1: ICS historian server (Anatomy 30.C) -- bridges IT and OT;
    exploited to pivot from corporate network to control network
  Instance 2: Kubernetes service account token (A262/Anatomy 32.A) -- SA
    bridges application workload and cluster control plane
  Instance 3: Automotive TCU (A275/Anatomy 33.A) -- bridges internet and CAN bus
  Pattern: any component whose function requires authority on two security
  domains simultaneously will be the pivot point for crossing that boundary.
  This is a sub-pattern of R06 at the architectural level:
  R06.ARCH: architectural confused deputies created by integration requirements.

C242 | ADCS ESC3 and ESC7 (Anatomy 33.B) confirm that the ADCS ESC taxonomy
  (D286) exhibits the same R01 (ambient authority) signature across all
  ESC classes: the authority granted by each misconfigured template or CA
  ACL is not scoped to the specific operational use case that justified it.
  Enrollment agent authority extends to all subjects (ESC3). ManageCertificates
  authority extends to all pending requests (ESC7). In each case, the
  authority is ambient over a class of resources rather than bounded to
  the specific resources the role legitimately needs.
  Sub-pattern: ADCS ESC taxonomy is a catalog of R01 sub-instances in PKI.

C243 | Automotive OTA supply chain (Anatomy 33.D) + SolarWinds (C224) +
  ML base model supply chain (Anatomy 31.C): three independently discovered
  instances of the same structural attack. Trust chain compressed at signing;
  verifiers at deployment endpoints cannot distinguish legitimate from
  attacker-signed content; breadth equals all entities trusting the
  compromised signer. The pattern is technology-agnostic:
    SolarWinds: signed DLL -> 18,000 enterprise networks
    OTA firmware: signed firmware -> millions of vehicle ECUs
    ML base model: signed model weights -> all downstream fine-tuned models
  Unifying mechanic: R02 (trust transitivity) + single-point-of-trust
  creates a one-to-many amplification structure for supply chain attacks.

C244 | Hardware trojan (Anatomy 33.C) demonstrates that R02 (trust
  transitivity) terminates at the hardware layer with no further validation
  possible. Every layer of the software stack trusts the hardware; hardware
  trust is assumed, not verified. This creates an absolute floor on security
  assurance: no software security property holds if the underlying hardware
  is compromised. This is R02 expressed as an irreducible boundary --
  the trust chain has a terminus that cannot be verified at runtime.
  The only defense is pre-deployment verification, which is imperfect (C33.C).

C245 | R09 sub-taxonomy validation -- first counter-example scan:
  R09.1 (protocol deployment irreversibility): SS7, BGP, CAN, Modbus, DNS --
    no qualifying remediation found across any instance; all persist.
  R09.2 (equipment lifecycle irreversibility): ICS PLCs, medical devices,
    automotive ECUs -- all persist within operational lifetime constraints.
  R09.3 (operational dependency irreversibility): IT/OT boundary erosion --
    mechanism documented in Anatomy 32.C; no known remediation without
    operational disruption exceeding security benefit.
  R09.4 (cryptographic commitment irreversibility): HNDL -- past TLS sessions
    are retroactively decryptable; no counter-example possible by definition.
  R09.5 (trust anchor irreversibility): DigiNotar -- partial counter-example:
    browser/OS vendors did remove DigiNotar from trust stores in ~1 week;
    BUT devices that could not update remained compromised indefinitely;
    AND hardware-embedded trust anchors (not DigiNotar's case) remain
    irreversible. DigiNotar is a PARTIAL counter-example to R09.5 for
    software-managed trust stores only; hardware trust anchors remain
    within R09.5 scope.
  R09.6 (data exfiltration irreversibility): no counter-example possible
    by definition (data cannot be un-exfiltrated).
  RESULT: R09 sub-taxonomy holds across first counter-example cycle.
  R09 sub-taxonomy STATUS: DRAFT (requires additional cycles)

C246 | Cross-law interaction: CONFIRMED LAW-1 and R09 sub-taxonomy are
  co-extensive. CONFIRMED LAW-1 is the system-level statement; R09
  sub-taxonomy provides the mechanistic decomposition.
  LAW-1 = R09.1 + R09.2 operating at civilizational scale across millions
  of independent operators.
  The sub-taxonomy extends the law's scope: LAW-1 originally stated for
  protocols (R09.1); R09.2 extends it to equipment lifecycles; R09.3 extends
  it to organizational boundary erosion; R09.4 and R09.6 extend it to
  data and cryptographic commitments.
  Revised scope: LAW-1 holds at any scale where R09 sub-classes operate.

C247 | The recurring new perimeter pattern (Pattern 33.3) is the system-level
  observation that CONFIRMED LAW-2 (tooling commoditizes bypass) iterates
  across defense layers. Each iteration of the pattern corresponds to:
  1. A defense layer being commoditized by tooling (LAW-2 mechanism)
  2. Defenders shifting focus to the next layer (perimeter relabeling)
  3. Bypassed layer retaining ambient authority (R01)
  The pattern predicts the next perimeter shift: ML-based detection
  (SIEM, EDR, anomaly detection) is being commoditized by adversarial
  evasion tooling (A271/Anatomy 30.A class); next perimeter candidate:
  runtime behavioral attestation or hardware-level execution integrity.

CYCLE 34 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN MAPPING AND SUB-DOMAIN EXPANSION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PRIMARY OBJECTIVES: Medical device cybersecurity; BACnet/building automation;
  V2X expanded attack taxonomy; R10 sub-taxonomy draft; quantum-safe automotive

D310 | Medical Device Cybersecurity — FDA Pre-Market Guidance
  Sub-domain: Healthcare / Embedded Security
  Context: FDA Cybersecurity in Medical Devices guidance (2023) requires:
    - Threat modeling in 510(k)/PMA submissions
    - Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for all device software
    - Capability for patching and updates within device lifecycle
    - Coordination plan with CISA for vulnerability disclosure
  Historical context: pre-2023, FDA did not require cybersecurity
    in pre-market submissions; devices approved with known vulnerabilities
    that could not be patched due to recertification requirements.
  R09.2 (equipment lifecycle irreversibility) instance: FDA 510(k)
    clearance is based on "substantially equivalent" to predicate device;
    firmware update that adds security features may require new 510(k);
    manufacturers cannot patch without regulatory approval in many cases.
  Post-market gap: billions of deployed medical devices predate 2023 guidance;
    no retroactive requirement; deployed devices remain with original firmware.

D311 | Medical Device Cybersecurity — Network-Connected Medical Device Attacks
  Sub-domain: Healthcare / Network Security
  Threat landscape: infusion pumps, ventilators, imaging systems (CT, MRI,
    X-ray), patient monitoring systems, implantable devices (pacemakers, ICDs).
  Historical incidents:
    - WannaCry (2017): NHS UK; CT scanners, MRI machines running Windows XP
      taken offline; surgeries cancelled; patient care disrupted
    - Medtronic ICD recall (2019): implantable cardiac devices with
      unauthenticated wireless firmware update interface; CVE-2019-6538
    - Philips Tasy EMR (2021): SQL injection in hospital information system;
      not a device but demonstrates healthcare IT attack surface
  Attack surface: medical devices often run Windows XP/7 (end-of-life OS),
    connected to hospital LAN, network shares with clinical workstations,
    no EDR/AV (vendor prohibits third-party software), no patch cadence.
  R09.2 instance: CT scanner with FDA-cleared Windows XP cannot be patched
    without FDA recertification; manufacturer no longer supports; hospital
    cannot replace ($1.5M capital expenditure); must compensate with network
    segmentation alone.

D312 | Building Automation Security — BACnet Protocol
  Sub-domain: Building Automation / OT Security
  BACnet (Building Automation and Control Networks, ASHRAE 135): protocol
    for HVAC, fire suppression, access control, lighting, elevator systems.
  Broadcast-oriented: uses BACnet/IP over UDP or BACnet MS/TP over RS-485.
  No authentication in base protocol (BACnet/SC adds TLS but adoption minimal).
  Attack surface: Shodan shows >100,000 BACnet devices internet-accessible.
  Intersection with physical security: access control systems (door locks,
    badge readers) frequently run on BACnet; compromise = physical access.
  HVAC manipulation: targeting HVAC in data centers (thermal attack) or
    office buildings; temperature manipulation as denial of service or
    data center hardware damage.
  Pattern 33.1 instance: BACnet is a broadcast bus (Pattern 33.1);
    same zero-authentication structure as CAN and Modbus.

D313 | Quantum-Safe Cryptography in Automotive
  Sub-domain: Automotive / Post-Quantum Cryptography
  Vehicle lifecycle: 15-20 years; vehicles sold in 2025 will be on roads
    in 2040-2045; cryptographically-relevant quantum computers may exist
    by 2035-2040 (NIST estimate range).
  HNDL risk in automotive: V2X communications intercepted today may be
    decryptable in 2035; OTA update signatures captured now may enable
    retroactive attack validation.
  PQC migration requirements for automotive:
    - V2X IEEE 1609.2 certificates: migrate from ECDSA to ML-DSA
    - OTA signing: migrate from RSA/ECDSA to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA
    - Key exchange (secure boot): migrate from ECDH to ML-KEM
    - Vehicle lifetime constraint: migration must be OTA-deliverable;
      hardware crypto accelerators may not support PQC without replacement
  NIST FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) / FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) published August 2024:
    automotive standards body adoption timeline: 2-5 years post-NIST.
  R09.4 (cryptographic commitment irreversibility): automotive sector faces
    same HNDL risk as internet PKI but with 20-year fleet lifetime extending
    the vulnerability window beyond standard enterprise context.

D314 | V2X Cybersecurity — Sybil Attack and SCMS Compromise
  Sub-domain: Automotive / V2X Security
  Sybil attack: attacker broadcasts multiple fake vehicle identities
    simultaneously; misleads other vehicles and infrastructure about traffic
    conditions; can create phantom traffic jams, phantom accident warnings,
    or phantom emergency vehicles clearing intersections.
  SCMS compromise: Security Credential Management System issues pseudonymous
    certificates; if SCMS CA is compromised, attacker can issue certificates
    for any vehicle identity; enables large-scale Sybil attacks with valid
    certificates that pass signature verification.
  Position falsification: attacker broadcasts GPS coordinates that differ
    from actual position; used with Sybil attack to create phantom vehicles
    at arbitrary locations.
  Root: R02 (trust transitivity through certificate chain), R05 (state
    confusion via falsified presence/position data in V2X safety messages)

D315 | R10 Sub-Taxonomy Draft — Complexity and Specification Failures
  Sub-domain: Cross-cutting / Root Mechanics
  R10 (complexity/specification failures): security vulnerabilities arising
    from the gap between specified behavior and implemented behavior at scale.
  R10.1 -- SPECIFICATION AMBIGUITY: protocol or standard has ambiguous or
    underspecified behavior; implementations diverge; inconsistency is
    exploitable. Instances: HTTP request smuggling (RFC 7230 ambiguity on
    Content-Length vs. Transfer-Encoding), TLS renegotiation attacks (RFC
    5246 underspecified renegotiation security properties).
  R10.2 -- IMPLEMENTATION DIVERGENCE: multiple implementations of same
    spec behave differently; attacker exploits one implementation's deviation.
    Instances: XML external entity (XXE) injection (XML parsers differ
    on entity expansion); JSON deserialization (different parsers accept
    different structures for same "JSON").
  R10.3 -- EMERGENT COMPLEXITY: system behavior at scale differs from
    specified behavior for individual components; interactions between
    components create vulnerabilities not present in any single component.
    Instances: microservices distributed tracing gaps (request forges
    transaction IDs that span trust domains); race conditions in distributed
    systems (TOCTOU at distributed scale); Kubernetes scheduler + RBAC
    interaction creating unexpected permission grants.
  R10.4 -- SCALE BRITTLENESS: security property holds under normal load
    but fails under edge-case or adversarial load conditions.
    Instances: TCP SYN flood (half-open connection table exhaustion);
    algorithmic complexity attacks (hash table collision DoS, ReDoS);
    X.509 chain validation complexity attacks (pathological certificate chains).
  STATUS: R10 sub-taxonomy DRAFT (R10.1-R10.4) -- requires counter-example
    validation across subsequent cycles.

CYCLE 34 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 132 patterns cumulative

Pattern 34.1 | REGULATORY CAPTURE OF SECURITY REQUIREMENT CREATES PERVERSE
  LIFECYCLE INCENTIVE
  Domain: Medical Device / Regulatory / OT
  Observation: when security requirements are embedded in regulatory approval
    processes designed for safety (not security), the approval process becomes
    an obstacle to security remediation.
  Mechanism: FDA 510(k) treats firmware as a design element requiring
    equivalence review; adding security patches changes firmware = potential
    new review = delay = cost = manufacturer avoids patching.
    Result: regulatory approval that was designed to ensure safety becomes
    the structural reason security cannot be improved.
  Instances:
    - Medical device firmware: 510(k) clearance required per firmware update
      that changes clinical functionality; manufacturers leave vulnerabilities
      to avoid resubmission
    - ICS/OT certification: IEC 61508 functional safety certification requires
      re-testing on firmware changes; operators choose security debt over
      recertification cost
    - Aviation avionics: DO-178C certification; same mechanism
  Root: R09.2 (equipment lifecycle irreversibility) + meta-R09 inversion:
    the safety protection mechanism (certification) becomes the irreversibility
    mechanism for security debt -- safety certification captures security remediation
  Pattern name: REGULATORY CAPTURE OF SECURITY REMEDIATION

Pattern 34.2 | INTERNET-ACCESSIBLE OT/BUILDING-AUTOMATION DEVICES CREATE
  PHYSICAL EFFECT ATTACK SURFACE AT GLOBAL SCALE
  Domain: BACnet / Shodan-exposed OT / Building Automation
  Observation: Shodan consistently indexes >100,000 BACnet devices,
    >50,000 SCADA/HMI interfaces, >10,000 building automation controllers
    directly accessible from the internet with no authentication.
  Root: R01 (ambient authority -- internet accessibility without authentication
    extends CAN/Modbus broadcast-bus zero-auth to global scale)
  Physical effect: BACnet access = HVAC control, fire suppression control,
    physical access control (badge readers), elevator control.
  Attack surface elevation: building automation at internet scale means an
    attacker anywhere can cause physical effects (data center thermal attack,
    false fire suppression activation, door lock manipulation) in any
    internet-connected building without proximity.
  Severity: higher than ICS/OT traditionally modeled because building
    automation is assumed low-stakes and therefore less secured, but
    physical effects on buildings housing data centers or personnel
    can have equivalent impact to ICS/OT attacks on industrial sites.
  Connection to Pattern 33.1: broadcast bus zero-auth exposed to internet
    is Pattern 33.1 elevated from local to global attack scale.

Pattern 34.3 | VEHICLE-TO-VEHICLE TRUST CREATES DISTRIBUTED PHYSICAL-WORLD
  STATE CONFUSION AT FLEET SCALE
  Domain: V2X / Autonomous Systems / Traffic Safety
  Observation: V2X safety messages (DSRC, C-V2X) are designed to propagate
    safety-relevant state (position, speed, hazard, traffic signal phase)
    between vehicles. If adversary can inject false state, the effect
    propagates through the V2X network to all vehicles in range.
  Sybil attack at scale: one attacker with multiple pseudonymous certs
    broadcasts phantom vehicles from a roadside position; all vehicles
    in range receive and act on false traffic data; traffic management
    systems may route vehicles around the phantom obstruction.
  Cascade: V2X is designed so vehicles trust and act on each other's
    broadcasts without independent verification; state confusion (R05)
    cascades through the network at the speed of radio propagation.
  Comparison to DNS cache poisoning: both are state injection attacks where
    a false state claim, once accepted, propagates to all dependent decisions
    until the state expires (DNS TTL = V2X message lifetime).
  Physical consequence: in an autonomous or semi-autonomous vehicle fleet,
    false V2X state triggering simultaneous braking or lane changes across
    many vehicles could cause multi-vehicle accidents.

Pattern 34.4 | R10 COMPLEXITY FAILURE AS CROSS-DOMAIN PATTERN
  Domain: Cross-cutting / Protocol Security
  Observation: R10 sub-taxonomy instances appear in every domain with
    complex specifications or multi-implementation ecosystems.
  Domain map:
    Web: HTTP request smuggling (R10.1), XML/JSON parser divergence (R10.2)
    Cryptography: TLS renegotiation (R10.1), BEAST/CRIME (R10.3 emergent)
    Networking: BGP route selection divergence between implementations (R10.2),
      TCP SYN flood (R10.4)
    Cloud/Kubernetes: scheduler+RBAC interactions (R10.3)
    Programming: ReDoS (R10.4), hash table DoS (R10.4)
    Identity: SAML/OAuth spec ambiguity (R10.1) -- one party's logout doesn't
      invalidate another party's session (spec allows but implementations vary)
  Convergence: every domain with a specification maintained across multiple
    independent implementations exhibits R10. The vulnerability class is a
    structural consequence of specification-based interoperability.
  Counter-pattern: single-implementation protocols (proprietary or reference
    implementations only) exhibit R10 less but introduce R09 (vendor lock-in
    creates irreversibility) and R04 (single vendor compromise = all deployments).

ANATOMY 34.A — BACNET UNAUTHENTICATED ACCESS -- BUILDING AUTOMATION ATTACK
Root: R01 (ambient authority -- no authentication) + R06 (physical-effect confused deputy)
Gap resolution: G201
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

PROTOCOL CONTEXT:
  BACnet/IP: BACnet objects and services transported over UDP/IP, port 47808.
  BACnet object model: each controllable element (HVAC zone, door lock, sensor)
  is a BACnet Object with Properties. Read/write via ReadProperty/WriteProperty services.
  Authentication: absent in BACnet 2016 and earlier; BACnet/SC (2020) adds TLS
  but adoption is minimal -- most deployed devices support only BACnet/IP.

ATTACK CHAIN -- INTERNET-EXPOSED BACNET DEVICE:

Step 1: DISCOVERY
    Shodan query: port:47808 BACnet
    Result: >100,000 devices globally, including named buildings, hospitals,
      data centers, universities, government facilities.
    I-Am broadcast: BACnet device identification broadcast;
      whoIs/I-Am exchange reveals device type, vendor, firmware version.

Step 2: ENUMERATION
    BACnet ReadPropertyMultiple: enumerate all objects on controller.
    Object types returned: AnalogInput (sensor), AnalogOutput (actuator),
      BinaryInput (discrete sensor), BinaryOutput (discrete actuator),
      Schedule, Program, TrendLog.
    For building automation: HVAC setpoints, damper positions, chiller state,
      VAV box positions, door lock states, fire alarm panel states.

Step 3: PHYSICAL EFFECT WRITES
    BACnet WriteProperty with priority 8 (manual override) to any output object.
    No authentication required. No write protection in base protocol.
    Target: AV room thermostat setpoint -> set to 40C (thermal attack on hardware)
    Target: data center CRAC unit setpoint -> disable cooling
    Target: BinaryOutput for door lock -> unlock (physical access bypass)
    Target: fire suppression panel arm/discharge -> life safety impact
    Priority 8 overrides building automation system schedules until manually cleared.

Step 4: PERSISTENCE
    BACnet Schedule objects: write to schedule weekly/daily patterns.
    Effect: HVAC manipulated on recurring schedule; harder to attribute to attack.
    BACnet Program objects: some controllers support custom logic; persistence via program.

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R01 (ambient authority): internet connectivity grants access to WriteProperty;
       no credential, no authentication, no challenge required; access is ambient.
  R06 (physical-effect confused deputy): BACnet controller is the deputy acting
       on behalf of any requestor; the physical actuator (HVAC, door lock)
       executes the command without any verification of the requestor's legitimacy.
  Pattern 34.2 RESOLVED: this anatomy is the canonical instance of internet-
       accessible building automation creating physical-effect attack at global scale.

DEFENSE ARCHITECTURE:
  1. Network segmentation: BACnet controllers must NOT be internet-accessible;
     place behind firewall; BACnet traffic stays within building network.
  2. BACnet/SC migration: upgrade to BACnet Secure Connect (TLS + certs);
     requires controller replacement in most deployments.
  3. Allowlist IP sources: only building automation workstation IPs can send
     WriteProperty; implemented in router ACL or BACnet router firewall.
  4. Monitoring: BACnet traffic analysis for unusual write patterns or off-hours
     override commands; baseline normal operations and alert on deviation.
  5. Priority lockout: disable Priority 8 (manual override) for external sources;
     require console access for priority-8 writes on safety-critical systems.

G201 RESOLVED. Pattern 34.2 anatomy COMPLETE.

ANATOMY 34.B — HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING
Root: R10.1 (specification ambiguity) + R05 (state confusion)
Gap resolution: G205; Pattern 34.4 instance (R10.1)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

PROTOCOL CONTEXT:
  RFC 7230 (HTTP/1.1) specifies two message framing methods:
    Content-Length: message body length in bytes
    Transfer-Encoding: chunked encoding (size prefixed per chunk)
  When both headers are present, RFC 7230 says Transfer-Encoding takes priority
  and Content-Length should be ignored. Ambiguity: what if Transfer-Encoding is
  not 'chunked'? What if Transfer-Encoding is malformed? What if there are
  multiple Transfer-Encoding headers? Different implementations diverge.

ATTACK SETUP:
  Modern web architectures use a reverse proxy/load balancer (front-end server)
  forwarding to application servers (back-end). Front-end and back-end may be
  different software with different HTTP parsing implementations.

Key insight: the front-end parses the request to determine where it ends;
  the back-end re-parses the request. If they disagree on where Request A ends,
  the bytes the front-end thinks are part of Request A become the beginning of
  a new request as seen by the back-end -- this is request smuggling.

ATTACK VARIANTS:
  CL.TE (front-end uses Content-Length; back-end uses Transfer-Encoding):
    POST / HTTP/1.1
    Host: target.com
    Content-Length: 13
    Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

SMUGGLED
    Front-end reads 13 bytes (the '0\r\n\r\nSMUGGLED' portion); forwards all.
    Back-end reads chunked: sees '0' = end of chunks; 'SMUGGLED' becomes
    the start of the NEXT request received from the back-end's perspective.

TE.CL (front-end uses Transfer-Encoding; back-end uses Content-Length):
    POST / HTTP/1.1
    Content-Length: 3
    Transfer-Encoding: chunked

8
    SMUGGLED
    0

Front-end reads chunked: full body through final '0' chunk.
    Back-end reads Content-Length: 3 bytes = '8\r\n'. Remaining bytes
    'SMUGGLED\r\n0\r\n\r\n' become the start of the next request.

IMPACT CLASSES:
  1. Bypass security controls: smuggled request prefix crafted to bypass
     WAF rule that runs on front-end but not back-end.
  2. Request hijacking: smuggle a partial request that, when combined with
     the next legitimate user's request, sends that user's headers (including
     their session cookie) to attacker-controlled request path.
  3. Cache poisoning: smuggled request causes back-end to cache a response
     for a URL that the cached response should not correspond to.
  4. Internal API access: smuggled request targets internal APIs not exposed
     via front-end (front-end routing rules don't apply to smuggled requests).

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R10.1 (specification ambiguity): RFC 7230 does not fully specify behavior
       when both headers present with conflicting or malformed values;
       implementations diverge across web servers, proxies, and load balancers.
  R05 (state confusion): front-end and back-end maintain independent state
       for 'where is the current request boundary'; attacker induces divergence
       between these two states; the disagreement is the attack vector.
  R06 (confused deputy): front-end acts as deputy for back-end; back-end
       trusts front-end's request demarcation; attacker exploits the
       parsing inconsistency between the two to inject unauthorized requests.

REMEDIATION:
  - HTTP/2 end-to-end (framing is binary, no ambiguity in message boundaries)
  - Reject requests with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers
  - Normalize HTTP at front-end before forwarding (rewrite to unambiguous form)
  - Use same HTTP implementation at front-end and back-end
  - HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 downgrade at back-end re-introduces smuggling surface;
    prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end or careful downgrade implementation

G205 RESOLVED. Pattern 34.4 R10.1 instance anatomy COMPLETE.

ANATOMY 34.C — WANNACRY IN NHS -- MEDICAL DEVICE ATTACK CHAIN
Root: R09.2 (equipment lifecycle irreversibility) + R04 (monoculture)
Pattern resolution: Pattern 34.1 (regulatory capture)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

CONTEXT:
  WannaCry ransomware (May 2017) exploited EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) --
  SMBv1 buffer overflow on Windows. Microsoft released MS17-010 patch in March 2017.
  Organisations running Windows XP/7 without patch were vulnerable.
  NHS UK: particularly severe impact due to medical device concentration.

WHY NHS WAS VULNERABLE -- THE REGULATORY CAPTURE CHAIN:
  Medical imaging devices (CT scanners, MRI, X-ray): certified on Windows XP.
  Windows XP reached end-of-life April 2014; Microsoft stopped security updates.
  Device manufacturers: could not update OS without FDA/CE re-approval (Pattern 34.1).
  Re-approval cost and delay: $500K-$2M and 18-36 months per device model.
  Hospital decision: cannot replace ($500K-$3M per device), cannot patch (no support),
    cannot upgrade OS (regulatory approval required). Result: XP in production 2017.

ATTACK CHAIN:
  Stage 1: Initial infection via unpatched XP workstation (phishing or direct SMB).
  Stage 2: EternalBlue worm propagation across hospital LAN (flat network).
    Hospital networks often not segmented: clinical workstations, imaging devices,
    infusion pumps, nurse call systems all on same subnet.
  Stage 3: WannaCry reaches imaging devices (running Windows XP, SMBv1 enabled).
    WannaCry ransomware payload: encrypt all files; demand Bitcoin.
    Medical device storage encrypted: DICOM images, patient records local cache.
  Stage 4: Devices become non-functional; hospitals cancel surgeries, divert
    ambulances, close A&E departments. NHS impact: 80 out of 236 NHS trusts affected;
    6,912 appointments cancelled; estimated 19,000 appointments cancelled overall.

MEDICAL DEVICE MONOCULTURE (R04):
  Same vendor + same OS + same vulnerability = all devices fail simultaneously.
  Hospital acquired multiple scanners from same vendor; all vulnerable.
  R04 at healthcare sector scale: same certification baseline -> same vulnerable OS
  -> same vulnerability window across entire NHS estate.

ROOT MECHANICS:
  R09.2 (equipment lifecycle irreversibility): devices certified on XP at purchase;
       regulatory path does not allow OS upgrade without recertification;
       neither vendor nor hospital can remedy within operational lifetime.
  R04 (monoculture): same vendor, same OS, same vulnerability across NHS estate;
       single exploit propagates to full scope of affected devices.
  Pattern 34.1: regulatory process designed for safety (FDA/CE) captures security
       remediation; creates perverse incentive to maintain vulnerable firmware.

POST-WANNACRY RESPONSE:
  NHS DSPT (Data Security and Protection Toolkit): mandatory self-assessment.
  NIS Regulations 2018 (UK): healthcare as operator of essential services;
    cybersecurity incident reporting requirements.
  FDA Cybersecurity Guidance 2023: requires SBOM and patch capability in
    pre-market submissions -- does not retroactively fix deployed devices.
  Structural gap: guidance addresses new devices; deployed estate (hundreds of
    thousands of devices) remains with pre-2023 posture indefinitely (R09.2).

Pattern 34.1 anatomy COMPLETE.

ANATOMY 34.D — REDOS (REGULAR EXPRESSION DENIAL OF SERVICE)
Root: R10.4 (scale brittleness -- algorithmic complexity)
Gap resolution: G206
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MECHANISM:
  Regular expression matching in most implementations uses backtracking NFA.
  Worst-case complexity for certain regex patterns against adversarial input:
  O(2^n) or O(n^2) in the length of the input string.
  Under normal inputs: matching is fast; complexity is not exhibited.
  Under adversarial inputs: matching time grows superpolynomially; server thread
  blocks for seconds to minutes processing one request.

VULNERABLE REGEX PATTERN CLASSES:
  Evil regex signatures:
    1. Repetition of groups with multiple alternatives: (a+)+
    2. Alternation with overlapping possibilities: (a|a?)+
    3. Nested quantifiers: (a+)* or (a|aa)+
  Example: regex '^(a+)+$' against input 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!':
    Backtracker tries all ways to partition the 'a' sequence between outer
    and inner + quantifiers before concluding no match; exponential in length.

REAL-WORLD INSTANCES:
  - CloudFlare outage (2019): 27 minutes of global traffic drop;
    WAF rule deployed with evil regex; high-traffic event triggered worst case;
    CPU pinned at 100% across all edge servers simultaneously.
    Impact: ALL CloudFlare traffic dropped during incident.
  - Stack Overflow (2016): 34 minutes; poorly-crafted comment triggered
    regex DoS in Markdown parser.
  - npm package 'ua-parser' (2017-2020): widely-used User-Agent parser;
    adversarial UA string triggers ReDoS; affects any Node.js service
    parsing User-Agent headers with this package.

R10.4 SIGNATURE:
  The security property (availability) holds under normal load.
  The property fails under adversarial input exploiting worst-case complexity.
  The vulnerability is not present in unit tests (unit tests don't use
  adversarial inputs designed to trigger worst case).
  Production deployment is the first exposure to adversarial-length inputs.

DEFENSE:
  1. Static analysis of regex for evil patterns (ESLint plugins, Veracode regex)
  2. Replace backtracking NFA with linear-time DFA implementation (RE2, Hyperscan);
     RE2 guarantees O(n) time at the cost of not supporting backreferences.
  3. Timeout on regex evaluation (execution deadline); fail-closed on timeout.
  4. Input length limits on fields processed by regex.
  5. Fuzzing with adversarial inputs designed to trigger worst-case behavior
     (AFL, libFuzzer with regex-targeting mutations).

CROSS-DOMAIN INSTANCES OF R10.4 BRITTLENESS:
  - Hash table collision DoS: adversary sends keys that all map to same hash bucket;
    O(1) average insert degrades to O(n) per insert; O(n^2) total. Affects Java,
    PHP, Python (pre-hash randomization). Fixed by hash randomization (SipHash).
  - TCP SYN flood: half-open connection table exhaustion; server resources consumed
    by incomplete handshakes; normal load handles fine; adversarial load exhausts.
    Fixed by SYN cookies (stateless SYN-ACK without allocating server-side state).
  - XML bomb (billion laughs): nested entity expansion; small XML file expands to
    gigabytes in memory; XML parsers that expand all entities before processing.

G206 RESOLVED. R10.4 anatomy COMPLETE.

  Fire suppression, high-voltage electrical, life-safety systems:

D400 | HTTP: reject dual framing headers (TE+CL) at front-end
  Front-end normalizes HTTP: reject or sanitize any request containing both
    Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers
  Prevents CL.TE and TE.CL smuggling variants
  Widely supported in modern reverse proxies (nginx: ignore_invalid_headers,
    HAProxy: option http-server-close)

D401 | HTTP: upgrade to HTTP/2 end-to-end
  HTTP/2 uses binary framing with unambiguous message boundaries
  No Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding ambiguity in HTTP/2
  Front-end to back-end: HTTP/2 connection; eliminates smuggling surface
  Note: HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 downgrade re-introduces surface; avoid downgrade

D402 | Regex: static analysis for evil patterns in CI/CD
  Tool: safe-regex (npm), re2 (Go), RXXR2; detect nested quantifiers and
    overlapping alternations in all regex literals
  Block deployment of code containing evil regex patterns
  Lint rule: fail CI build on evil regex detection
  Addresses A286 at pre-deployment stage

D403 | Regex: replace backtracking NFA with linear-time RE2 engine
  RE2 (Google): O(n) guaranteed time; no backreferences; no lookahead/behind
  Replace: Python re -> re2, Node.js regex -> node-re2, Java -> RE2/J
  CloudFlare: migrated WAF regex engine to Hyperscan (linear-time) post-2019 outage
  Eliminates A286 by removing the complexity attack surface

D404 | Hash tables: randomized hash functions (SipHash-1-3)
  All hash tables keyed on external input use randomized hash seed per process
  Python 3.3+: PYTHONHASHSEED randomized by default
  Java 8+: String.hashCode() randomized per JVM instance
  PHP 5.3.2+: max_input_vars + hash randomization
  Eliminates A287 by making collision attacks infeasible without knowing seed

D405 | Medical devices: network micro-segmentation
  Medical devices isolated in dedicated VLANs; segmented by device type
  No lateral movement path: imaging VLAN isolated from infusion pump VLAN
  Only authorized management systems can communicate with each VLAN
  Addresses A288 propagation vector; compensating control for unpatchable devices

CYCLE 34 — STAGE 5: CONVERGENCE SCAN AND LAW EVALUATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 247 convergence findings

C248 | BACnet internet exposure (A282/Anatomy 34.A) is Pattern 33.1
  (broadcast bus zero-auth) elevated to global attack scale by internet
  connectivity. CAN/Modbus zero-auth was a local attack requiring physical
  proximity or adjacent network access. BACnet zero-auth exposed on the
  internet converts local physical effects into globally-accessible attack
  primitives. This confirms Pattern 34.2: internet exposure of OT/building
  automation creates a new attack class that is not present in the original
  protocol threat model (which assumed closed network).

C249 | The R06.ARCH pattern (C241) has a fourth confirmed instance in this cycle:
  BACnet controller as confused deputy between the IP network and the
  physical actuator (HVAC, door lock). The BACnet controller acts on behalf
  of any IP source and executes physical commands without independent
  verification of the source's authority. This is the same R06.ARCH
  structure as ICS historian (D303/Anatomy 30.C), Kubernetes TCU (C241
  instance 2), and automotive TCU (C241 instance 3). R06.ARCH is now
  confirmed with 4 instances across ICS, cloud-native, automotive, and
  building automation domains -- making it a robust cross-domain sub-pattern.

C250 | HTTP request smuggling (Anatomy 34.B) is a concrete instance of
  R10.1 (specification ambiguity) interacting with distributed system
  architecture: the vulnerability does not exist when a single HTTP
  implementation handles both front-end and back-end parsing. The
  vulnerability emerges from the interaction between two implementations
  of the same (ambiguous) specification. This is a new convergence principle:
  specification ambiguity vulnerabilities scale with implementation diversity.
  The more diverse the ecosystem, the more divergence exists, the more
  exploitable specification ambiguities there are. This is R10.1 expressed
  as an ecosystem property: monoculture (R04) and specification diversity (R10.1)
  are in tension -- monoculture reduces R10 but increases R04.

C251 | ReDoS (Anatomy 34.D) and hash table DoS (A287) are instances of
  the same convergence principle as C250 but for R10.4: worst-case
  algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities emerge from the gap between
  average-case and worst-case performance, which is not visible in
  standard testing. The common structure: (a) algorithm has polynomial
  or exponential worst case; (b) inputs triggering worst case are rare
  in non-adversarial use; (c) security testing does not cover adversarial
  inputs; (d) attacker discovers the adversarial input class and exploits it.
  This is R10.4 as a testing methodology gap as much as an algorithm design gap.

C252 | Medical device attack chain (Anatomy 34.C) confirms CONFIRMED LAW-1
  at healthcare domain scale: the regulatory approval mechanism that was
  designed to ensure device safety (FDA 510(k)) has become the structural
  mechanism preventing security remediation (Pattern 34.1). This is the
  same irreversibility structure as SS7/BGP but with a different locking
  mechanism: not coordination failure across millions of operators, but
  regulatory capture of the remediation pathway. R09.2 (equipment lifecycle)
  + Pattern 34.1 (regulatory capture) = healthcare-specific instance of LAW-1.
  This suggests a LAW-1 refinement: LAW-1 holds when ANY of the following
  makes remediation infeasible: (a) coordination failure (SS7/BGP), (b)
  equipment lifecycle (ICS/OT, medical devices), (c) regulatory capture
  (medical devices, aviation avionics), (d) operational dependency (Anatomy 32.C).

C253 | V2X attacks (A289/A290) demonstrate that R05 (state confusion) at
  safety-critical physical infrastructure scale creates a qualitatively
  different threat model than R05 in software contexts. In software:
  R05 causes incorrect program behavior or data corruption. In V2X:
  R05 causes incorrect physical world state beliefs in autonomous systems
  that then take physical actions (braking, accelerating, yielding) based
  on false state. The consequence of R05 scales with the physical effect
  magnitude of the system acting on the false state. V2X + autonomous
  vehicles = R05 at human-safety scale.

C254 | R10.1 (specification ambiguity) and R10.2 (implementation divergence)
  form a compound in multi-implementation ecosystems: specification ambiguity
  is the cause; implementation divergence is the effect; the security
  vulnerability exploits the divergence that the ambiguity permits. Removing
  ambiguity (HTTP/2 binary framing, RE2 linear-time regex) removes both
  the cause and effect simultaneously. This is the most reliable class of
  R10 remediation: change the specification/implementation to eliminate
  the ambiguity surface, rather than attempting to detect exploitation.

C255 | R09 sub-taxonomy second counter-example scan:
  R09.1: no new remediation; CAN deployed fleet still growing (2026 EVs with CAN)
  R09.2: FDA 2023 guidance addresses NEW devices; deployed estate unchanged;
    no counter-example
  R09.3: zero-trust deployments partially address R09.3 for new architectures;
    but zero-trust is a new perimeter, not remediation of legacy architectures;
    legacy R09.3 instances persist; not a counter-example
  R09.4: no counter-example possible by definition
  R09.5: DigiNotar partial counter-example stands (only for software trust stores;
    hardware trust anchors remain irreversible)
  R09.6: no counter-example possible by definition
  RESULT: R09 sub-taxonomy holds across second counter-example cycle.
  STATUS: DRAFT maintained; will require 5 total counter-example cycles
    before CLOSED designation by established loop methodology.
