D316 | Implantable Medical Device Security — Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices
  Sub-domain: Healthcare / Implantable Device Security
  Devices: pacemakers, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs),
    cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) devices.
  Communication: inductive (short-range, near-patient) OR RF telemetry
    (proprietary 403-405 MHz MICS band or 2.4 GHz ISM) for remote monitoring.
  Attack surface: wireless interface for programming and monitoring.
    No authentication in early implementations; pairing model varies by vendor.
  Historical: Barnaby Jack (2012, BlackHat) -- demonstrated remote ICD shutdown
    at 50-foot range; "Terminal Heart Attack" talk (Jack died before public demo;
    responsible disclosure led to vendor response).
  Medtronic ICD recall (2019, CVE-2019-6538, Urgent/11): unauthenticated wireless
    interface; attacker could alter therapy settings (pacing rate, shock energy)
    or disable therapy; range ~5m for commercial attack hardware.
  Root: R01 (ambient authority -- RF reception grants access without authentication),
    R09.2 (equipment lifecycle -- implanted device has 7-10 year battery life;
    firmware update requires in-person clinic visit or is impossible)

D317 | Aviation Avionics Cybersecurity
  Sub-domain: Aviation / Safety-Critical Systems
  DO-178C: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment
    Certification; software levels A-E by failure criticality; Level A
    (catastrophic failure) requires formal verification.
  Attack surfaces:
    - Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS):
      data link for air-ground communications; no authentication (1978 protocol)
    - Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B): aircraft broadcasts
      position, speed, altitude via 1090 MHz; no authentication (like CAN/BACnet)
      -- ADS-B spoofing places phantom aircraft or misreports position
    - In-flight entertainment (IFE) networks: sometimes share network infrastructure
      with avionics; IFE compromise explored as lateral movement path to avionics
  Historical: Chris Roberts (2015) claimed access to aircraft control from IFE;
    FBI investigation; methodology disputed but raised awareness of IFE/avionics
    segmentation requirements.
  ADS-B spoofing: documented by researchers; can create phantom aircraft in ATC
    radar display; air traffic controllers see false traffic that doesn't exist;
    analogous to V2X Sybil attack but in aviation.

D318 | R06.ARCH -- Formal Pattern Entry
  Sub-domain: Cross-cutting / Root Mechanics / Architecture
  FORMAL DEFINITION: An "architectural confused deputy" (R06.ARCH) arises when
    a system component's function requires it to simultaneously hold authority
    on two security domains with different trust levels. The component acts as
    a bridge between these domains; any compromise of the bridge grants authority
    on both domains simultaneously.
  Distinguishing from R06 (confused deputy): R06 is an implementation-level
    finding (component makes decisions using authority it holds on behalf of
    another party, tricked into misusing that authority). R06.ARCH is an
    architectural-level finding (the component is DESIGNED to hold authority
    on both domains as a function requirement, making it structurally the
    attack path for domain crossing regardless of implementation quality).
  R06.ARCH cannot be eliminated by fixing the implementation; it can only
    be addressed by architectural redesign (unidirectional gateway, proxy
    without authority grant, hardware data diode).
  Confirmed instances: 4 (ICS historian, automotive TCU, Kubernetes RBAC
    boundary, BACnet building controller)
  PATTERN STATUS: CONFIRMED (4 instances, distinct domain representation,
    consistent root mechanics)
  New gap: G207 | R06.ARCH counter-example -- system where integration bridge
    was designed without granting authority on both domains simultaneously

D319 | ADCS ESC2, ESC5, ESC8, ESC10 -- Enumeration
  Sub-domain: Active Directory / PKI (completing G184)
  ESC2 -- ANY PURPOSE EXTENDED KEY USAGE (EKU):
    Certificate template with EKU = Any Purpose or no EKU restriction.
    Any Purpose cert can be used for server auth, client auth, code signing,
    and enrollment agent. Attacker requests this cert and uses it as
    enrollment agent (same path as ESC3) OR uses it for smart card logon.
    Root: R01 (ambient authority -- Any Purpose EKU grants all authorities)
  ESC5 -- VULNERABLE PKI OBJECT ACCESS CONTROL (AD Object ACL):
    AD contains PKI objects: Certificate Templates, Enterprise CAs,
    NTAuthCertificates store. If low-privilege user has write access to
    these AD objects, they can modify template configuration (enabling ESC1),
    add their own CA to NTAuthCertificates (allowing issuance of domain auth certs),
    or modify template ACLs to enable further escalation.
    Root: R06 (AD acts as deputy enforcing ACLs on PKI objects; compromised ACL
    means attacker can modify the PKI configuration that determines all certificate
    issuance; AD trusts the ACL without knowing it was compromised)
  ESC8 -- NTLM RELAY TO ADCS WEB ENROLLMENT ENDPOINT:
    ADCS HTTP enrollment endpoint (certsrv/mscep) supports NTLM authentication.
    NTLM relay: capture NTLM authentication from any domain computer (via
    Responder, PetitPotam coerce, PrinterBug coerce), relay to ADCS endpoint,
    enroll a certificate on behalf of the relayed computer account.
    If DC computer account relayed: get certificate for DC -> DCSync possible.
    Root: R03 (implicit trust in NTLM relay chain -- ADCS accepts relayed auth)
    Note: PetitPotam coercion allows any domain computer to coerce DC authentication
    without being on-path; relay becomes trivial.
  ESC10 -- WEAK CERTIFICATE MAPPINGS (POST-PATCHTUESDAYAPRIL2023):
    Microsoft's April 2023 patches changed certificate-to-account mapping.
    Previously: certificate Subject Alternative Name (SAN) used for mapping.
    If SAN can be influenced (e.g., via ESC1/ESC6), attacker gets domain admin cert.
    Post-patch in Compatibility Mode: certificate mapping uses UPN in SAN;
    if UPN can be changed (requires WriteProperty on user object), attacker
    changes target UPN to match their own certificate, then authenticates as target.
    Root: R05 (state confusion -- mapping mechanism between certificates and
    accounts has a window where account and certificate are temporarily unlinked)
  G184 STATUS: CLOSED (ESC1-ESC10 all documented across cycles 31-35)

PATTERN 35.1 — R06.ARCH AS ARCHITECTURAL ISOLATION FAILURE PATTERN (FORMAL)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R06.ARCH (sub-pattern of R06: trust boundary collapse)
Formal definition: An architectural configuration in which a safety-critical
or security-critical system component is reachable from an attacker-controlled
entry point through fewer trust boundary crossings than the component's threat
model assumes, AND in which the crossing path exists by design (not by
misconfiguration), AND in which no compensating control at the boundary
provides equivalent isolation to what the absent boundary would have provided.

Distinction from R06 baseline: R06 baseline covers trust boundary collapse in
general — any case where a system trusts an entity it should not. R06.ARCH
specifically captures the case where the collapse is:
  (a) structurally mandated (removing it requires redesign, not configuration)
  (b) not visible to defenders inspecting the running system
  (c) consistent across all deployment instances of that architecture
  (d) present because two legitimate design goals (e.g., connectivity +
      control-plane authority) were composed without a security boundary
      between them

This makes R06.ARCH distinct from standard misconfiguration (R06 baseline)
and from intentional backdoor (D-class artifact). It is an emergent property
of design composition.

Four confirmed instances (as of Cycle 35):
  1. ICS SCADA historian: business network → historian → OT process bus
     Entry: historian SQL interface or web dashboard (business-accessible)
     Destination: OT bus write access (safety-critical process control)
     Design intent: historian aggregates OT data for business consumption
     Structural necessity: historian must read OT bus; write access is
     often same interface; separation would require read-only protocol proxy
     that many historians do not implement

2. Automotive TCU (Miller/Valasek Jeep Cherokee 2015):
     Entry: Uconnect cellular (internet-accessible)
     Destination: V850 chip → CAN bus → brake/steering ECUs
     Design intent: TCU provides telematics and infotainment connectivity
     Structural necessity: TCU required CAN access for vehicle state data
     and diagnostic; attack used V850 firmware reflash to gain CAN write

3. Kubernetes RBAC boundary (API server → node → pod):
     Entry: compromised pod with API server network access
     Destination: node-level privileged operations (host filesystem, DaemonSet)
     Design intent: control plane manages node lifecycle and pod scheduling
     Structural necessity: API server must reach kubelets; node authorization
     mode (not always enabled) is the compensating control; default config
     lacks it

4. BACnet building controller:
     Entry: internet-exposed BACnet/IP (UDP 47808)
     Destination: HVAC, power, access control physical plant
     Design intent: building management system requires IP connectivity
     for remote management
     Structural necessity: BACnet protocol was designed without authentication;
     adding auth requires protocol-level change, not configuration

Counter-example requirement: G207 — identify any case where R06.ARCH pattern
was present, then eliminated by something short of full architectural redesign
of the affected component. This would falsify condition (a) above.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 35.2 — BROADCAST BUS AT SAFETY SCALE: AVIATION INSTANCE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: Extension of Pattern 31.1 (automotive CAN broadcast bus) to
aviation domain. Cross-domain generalization candidate.

General form (Pattern 31.1, revised): Safety-critical physical systems that
depend on shared broadcast bus communications with no source authentication
are vulnerable to injection attacks that produce physical effects at scale.
The absence of authentication is architectural (protocol-level), not
operational, making remediation a LAW-1 class problem.

Aviation instance components:
  ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast):
    Protocol: 1090 MHz Mode S squitter, unauthenticated broadcast
    Transmitters: aircraft transponders (mandatory FAA/ICAO equipment)
    Receivers: ground stations, TCAS systems, ATC radar displays
    Attack surface: software-defined radio; transmit capability ~$300
    Attack vectors:
      (a) Phantom aircraft injection — broadcast ADS-B messages for
          non-existent aircraft at arbitrary positions; ATC sees targets
          that do not exist; TCAS resolution advisories triggered
      (b) Position falsification — spoof own aircraft position to
          report different location; complicates ATC tracking
      (c) Ghost fleet — inject large number of phantom aircraft in
          controlled airspace; saturate ATC display; cause ground stops
      (d) TCAS manipulation — craft phantom aircraft on collision course;
          trigger TCAS RA on real aircraft; cause unnecessary maneuver
    Physical effect: ATC routing decisions based on false traffic picture;
    pilot TCAS maneuvers in response to phantom aircraft; potential
    mid-air collision from conflicting RAs if TCAS triggered by phantom

ACARS (Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System):
    Protocol: VHF/HF radio, SATCOM; plaintext transmission
    Function: air/ground data link for flight plans, weather, ATIS, ATC
    clearances, maintenance messages, airline operational control
    Attack surface: ground radio station; SATCOM link interception
    Attack vectors:
      (a) Message injection — transmit fake ACARS messages to aircraft
          (fake weather, fake ATC clearances, fake ATIS)
      (b) Message interception — passive monitoring of operational data
          (flight plans, passenger manifests, maintenance records)
      (c) Denial — radio jamming on ACARS frequencies
    Physical effect: crew acting on falsified clearance data; incorrect
    weather avoidance; operational disruption at airline scale

Cross-domain parallel to automotive:
    CAN bus: no auth, 1.4B vehicles, physical effect via ECU injection
    ADS-B: no auth, 45,000+ daily US flights tracked, physical effect
    via ATC/TCAS manipulation
    Both: LAW-1 applies — broadcast protocol baked into safety equipment
    at civilizational scale; remediation requires replacing all transponders
    and ground infrastructure simultaneously

Remediation state:
    ADS-B: FAA/ICAO studying ADS-B authentication since ~2015; no
    standardized auth extension deployed; proposed solutions include
    public-key cryptography per aircraft, but key management at global
    fleet scale is unsolved; fleet replacement timeline 15-20 years
    ACARS: VHF ACARS replacement (LDACS) in development; timeline 2030+
    LAW-1 classification: CONFIRMED for both protocols

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 35.3 — IMPLANTABLE DEVICE RF AMBIENT AUTHORITY AT LIFE-SAFETY SCALE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R01 (ambient authority) at life-safety impact threshold

General form (R01): A system grants authority to any entity in the ambient
environment based on physical proximity or broadcast reception, without
explicit identity verification. The authority is non-revocable until the
next physical interaction with the device.

Implantable cardiac device instance:
  Device class: ICDs (implantable cardioverter-defibrillators), pacemakers
  RF interface: 175 kHz (older devices), 400 MHz MICS band, 2.4 GHz (newer)
  Purpose: wireless programming by cardiologist; remote monitoring by clinic
  Authority granted: device parameter reprogramming (therapy settings,
    shock delivery thresholds, tachycardia detection parameters)
  Authentication model (historical): proximity-based (physical proximity
    assumed to imply clinical context); some devices: no auth at all;
    some: shared secret that is device-model-wide (not per-device)

Medtronic ICD recall (CVE-2019-6538, CERT/CC VU#955293):
    Affected devices: >750,000 implanted worldwide
    Vulnerability: Conexus telemetry protocol; no authentication;
    no encryption; cleartext RF transmission
    Attack surface: within RF range (~30 feet with stock antenna;
    extended range with directional antenna)
    Capabilities demonstrated: read/write device parameters remotely;
    defibrillation therapy on/off; shock delivery modification
    Physical effect: inappropriate shock delivery (painful, potentially
    lethal in patients with certain conditions); therapy inhibition
    (device fails to deliver shock when clinically required)
    Remediation: Medtronic issued firmware update; however, many devices
    cannot be updated wirelessly (requires clinic visit); some
    patients never received update

R01 manifestation specifics:
    Ambient authority source: RF proximity (anyone within range)
    Authority level: full parameter control including therapy delivery
    Revocability: cannot be revoked without firmware update (clinic visit)
    or device replacement (surgery)
    Lifecycle constraint: ICD battery life 5-10 years; replacement is
    open-heart surgery; patient may refuse surgery even with known
    vulnerable device

R09.2 compound: Implant lifecycle constraint locks the vulnerability
    in for device's remaining operational life post-discovery; patients
    cannot simply "patch" by swapping hardware without surgical risk
    This is the highest-consequence R09.2 instance documented in this loop:
    the locked-in period is measured in years; the consequence of exploitation
    is lethal; the remediation requires general anesthesia

Scale context:
    ~3 million pacemakers implanted annually worldwide
    ~200,000 ICDs implanted annually in US alone
    Estimated 50+ million active cardiac implants globally
    Each is a potential R01 attack surface carried inside a human body

Regulatory context:
    FDA 510(k) clearance pathway does not require security review;
    Medtronic received 510(k) for Conexus protocol without authentication
    FDA issued cybersecurity guidance 2013, 2016, 2023; guidance is
    non-binding for pre-market approval
    Post-market surveillance requires manufacturer disclosure of known
    vulnerabilities; disclosure does not require remediation timeline

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 35.4 — R10 SUB-TAXONOMY CROSS-DOMAIN INSTANCE MATRIX
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R10 (complexity-induced vulnerability) — first counter-
example cycle setup and cross-domain instance confirmation

R10 sub-taxonomy:
  R10.1 — Specification ambiguity: vulnerability exists in the gap between
    what a spec permits and what implementors assume the spec prohibits
  R10.2 — Implementation divergence: two correct implementations of the
    same spec interact in a way neither implements correctly
  R10.3 — Emergent complexity: vulnerability exists only when multiple
    individually-correct components compose at runtime
  R10.4 — Scale brittleness: algorithm/structure correct at design scale
    becomes pathological at actual deployment scale

Cross-domain instance matrix (current cycle):

R10.1 instances confirmed:
    HTTP request smuggling (CL.TE, TE.CL): RFC 7230 §3.3.3 ambiguity
      in precedence of Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding when both present;
      frontend and backend parse differently → request boundary confusion
    TLS renegotiation (CVE-2009-3555): RFC 5246 did not bind initial
      and renegotiated handshakes; MitM could inject data before renegotiation;
      RFC 5746 introduced renegotiation_info extension as fix
    DNS response size / EDNS0: ambiguity in truncation behavior across
      implementations enables response forgery in some conditions
    BGP AS path ambiguity: route selection tie-breaking not fully specified;
      implementations diverge; policy inconsistencies exploitable

R10.2 instances confirmed:
    XML External Entity (XXE): XML spec permits external entity references;
      some parsers resolve them, some don't; code that processes XML from
      multiple parsers may be tested with non-resolving parser and deployed
      against resolving parser
    JSON number precision: spec does not define precision; parsers differ
      on large integer handling; type confusion attacks cross language
      boundaries (Python→JavaScript: 64-bit int becomes float, loses precision)
    HTTP header case sensitivity: spec says case-insensitive; some WAFs
      normalize before inspection; some backends do not; case variation
      bypasses WAF without being malformed to backend

R10.3 instances confirmed:
    Distributed TOCTOU in microservices: service A validates state; service B
      mutates state; service C acts on A's validation of now-stale state;
      no single service is incorrect; composed behavior is insecure
    Kubernetes admission controller bypass: webhook admission controller
      validates objects; operator applies object; controller reconciles;
      timing window between validation and reconciliation allows mutation
    JWT algorithm confusion: library supports multiple algorithms; issuer
      uses RS256; attacker changes alg to HS256 and signs with public key
      as HMAC secret; library verifies successfully

R10.4 instances confirmed:
    ReDoS (CloudFlare 2019, Stack Overflow 2016): regex engine backtracking
      is O(2^n) on ambiguous patterns; correct regex at test-corpus scale
      becomes pathological at adversarial input scale
    Hash table DoS: hash collisions degrade O(1) lookup to O(n); attacker
      crafts inputs with identical hashes; corrected by randomized hash seeds
      (language runtime updates post-2011)
    TCP SYN flood: half-open connection state table is O(1) to fill,
      O(n) to maintain; attacker sends SYN at line rate; server connection
      table exhausted; SYN cookies are partial mitigation but add latency

Counter-example requirement for R10 closure:
    Needed: vulnerability that appears to be R10 (complexity-induced) but
    does not fit R10.1, R10.2, R10.3, or R10.4 — implying a 5th class
    Candidates to examine in Stages 5-6:
      (a) Time-of-check semantic inconsistency in distributed consensus
          (may be R10.3 or may be distinct class R10.5: consensus semantic gap)
      (b) Side-channel from speculative execution (Spectre): not spec
          ambiguity; not divergence; not emergent; not scale — may be
          R10.5: microarchitectural leakage from performance optimization
      (c) Prototype pollution in JavaScript: may be R10.2 (inheritance
          ambiguity) or R10.5: language runtime semantic gap

PATTERNS CUMULATIVE: 140
EXIT STATE: 140 patterns, R10 counter-example cycle begins Stage 5

ANATOMY 104 — G207: R06.ARCH COUNTER-EXAMPLE SCAN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Gap: Does any documented case exist where R06.ARCH was present and then
eliminated by a compensating control short of full architectural redesign?

Candidate 1: ICS unidirectional security gateways (data diodes)
  Scenario: historian on OT network; data diode inserted between OT and
  business network; data diode enforces physical unidirectionality
  Analysis: data diode DOES eliminate the return path; business network
  cannot inject into OT through historian
  Counter-example assessment: PARTIAL
    Pro: physical unidirectionality eliminates the R06.ARCH crossing
    Con: data diode is itself an architectural component; adding it
    IS a redesign of the boundary between OT and historian
    The original R06.ARCH instance (historian reachable from business)
    is eliminated by inserting a new boundary device
    This is not 'short of architectural redesign' — it IS redesign
    (adding a boundary component is the definition of architectural change)
  Verdict: does not falsify condition (a); adding data diode = architecture
  change, not compensating control within existing architecture

Candidate 2: Automotive HSM (Hardware Security Module) on CAN gateway
  Scenario: ECU gateway has HSM; HSM enforces message authentication
  (AutoSAR SecOC); TCU messages require CMAC before ECU acceptance
  Analysis: if HSM-enforced CMAC is deployed on CAN gateway, does this
  eliminate TCU→CAN→ECU R06.ARCH path?
  Assessment: YES for the post-compromise exploitation path
    Compromised TCU that injects CAN messages without valid CMAC will be
    rejected by receiving ECUs (assuming AUTOSAR SecOC fully deployed)
  Counter-example assessment: PARTIAL
    Pro: AUTOSAR SecOC with per-message CMAC closes the injection path
    without replacing the TCU or redesigning the network topology
    Con: SecOC deployment is itself an architectural addition (requires
    HSM hardware on all ECUs that SecOC protects; key management
    infrastructure; firmware update to all ECUs)
    Additionally: SecOC does not prevent TCU compromise itself;
    it only prevents unauthenticated CAN injection from a compromised TCU
    A compromised TCU with legitimate SecOC credentials still has full
    CAN authority for its authorized message set
    Verdict: PARTIAL counter-example — SecOC narrows R06.ARCH but does
    not eliminate it; compromised TCU retains authorized CAN authority

Candidate 3: Kubernetes Network Policy + OPA Gatekeeper
  Scenario: network policy restricts pod-to-API-server communication;
  OPA enforces admission control; service mesh enforces mTLS
  Analysis: does layered control eliminate API server→node→privileged
  R06.ARCH path without redesigning cluster architecture?
  Assessment: PARTIAL
    Network policy restricts which pods can reach API server (reduces
    attacker entry surface but doesn't eliminate API server's authority)
    Node authorization mode (--authorization-mode=Node) restricts what
    kubelet can request from API server to resources on its own node
    RBAC + Node authorization together substantially reduce blast radius
    Con: these are architectural additions (authorization mode change
    requires API server restart; node authorization is a cluster design
    decision); not 'within existing architecture'
    Residual: API server still must reach all kubelets to schedule pods;
    this connectivity is architectural and cannot be eliminated

Candidate 4: BACnet firewall / PICS restriction
  Scenario: firewall blocks all external access to BACnet UDP 47808;
  BACnet device property 'Protocol Implementation Conformance Statement'
  restricts which services device responds to
  Analysis: firewall eliminates internet-exposed attack vector
  Assessment: YES for internet exposure specifically
    Firewall IS a compensating control; it does not redesign BACnet
  Counter-example assessment: LIMITED
    Pro: eliminates the specific internet-exposure instance of R06.ARCH
    Con: does not eliminate R06.ARCH within the local network; any
    attacker with LAN access (or any compromised IT system on same network
    segment) still has full unauthenticated BACnet write access
    The firewall moves the trust boundary outward but does not create
    a boundary WITHIN the building management network
    Verdict: firewall is compensating control for internet exposure,
    but R06.ARCH remains active within the local network

G207 SYNTHESIS:
  No case found where R06.ARCH was FULLY eliminated without architectural
  redesign. Partial mitigations exist (data diode, SecOC, network policy,
  firewall) but each either:
    (a) IS an architectural change (adds a boundary component), or
    (b) only reduces the surface of R06.ARCH without eliminating it, or
    (c) eliminates one attack path while leaving the structural crossing intact
  R06.ARCH condition (a) [structurally mandated] is SUSTAINED by G207 scan
  Pattern 35.1 formal definition: UNMODIFIED
  R06.ARCH: CONFIRMED (strengthened by counter-example failure)
  G207: CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 105 — G208: ADS-B FULL ATTACK METHODOLOGY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Protocol stack:
  Physical: 1090 MHz squitter (Mode S extended squitter)
  Modulation: PPM (pulse-position modulation)
  Message format: 112 bits (short: 56 bits)
  Key fields: ICAO 24-bit address (unique aircraft ID), latitude/longitude
    (Compact Position Reporting format), altitude, velocity, track,
    vertical rate, squawk code
  Authentication: NONE
  Encryption: NONE
  Receiver cost: RTL-SDR dongle ~$25; software: dump1090 (open source)
  Transmitter cost: HackRF One ~$300; ADALM-Pluto ~$150

Attack 1: Phantom aircraft injection
  Precondition: HackRF + antenna + laptop running gr-air-modes or custom
    ADS-B encoder
  Step 1: Craft ADS-B message with arbitrary ICAO address (must not
    collide with real registered aircraft — use unassigned range)
  Step 2: Encode CPR (Compact Position Reporting) latitude/longitude for
    desired phantom position
  Step 3: Transmit at 1090 MHz at appropriate power for desired coverage
  Step 4: Ground stations receive phantom squitter; correlate with other
    stations via multilateration if signal strong enough; feed to ATC display
  Step 5: ATC sees aircraft target at phantom position; TCAS on nearby
    real aircraft receives phantom and may issue Resolution Advisory
  Impact: ATC issues routing instructions for phantom aircraft;
    airspace closed around phantom; real aircraft maneuver per TCAS RA;
    ground stop possible if phantom injected near approach path
  Demonstrated: Maseng et al. (2012); Schafer et al. (2013, 2014, 2016);
    multiple academic demonstrations; FAA acknowledged vulnerability 2012

Attack 2: Position spoofing (own aircraft)
  Precondition: physical access to aircraft transponder, or GPS spoofing
    (ADS-B derives position from GPS; GPS spoofing changes reported position)
  GPS spoofing path: Spoof GPS signal received by aircraft;
    aircraft GPS reports false position; transponder broadcasts false ADS-B
    position without any ADS-B-level attack
  Impact: ATC tracking shows aircraft at wrong position;
    separation assurance based on false data

Attack 3: Denial of service
  Method: transmit high volume of ADS-B messages (phantom fleet)
    or jam 1090 MHz band
  Impact: receiver overload; ATC display saturated with phantom targets;
    real aircraft tracks lost in noise; ground stop
  Jamming: simpler but more detectable; phantom injection is harder to
    attribute and harder to filter

Attack 4: TCAS manipulation
  Method: inject phantom aircraft on collision course with real aircraft
  Mechanism: real aircraft TCAS receives ADS-B from phantom;
    TCAS RA issued (e.g., 'climb'); pilot follows RA
  Worst case: craft two phantoms to issue conflicting RAs to two real
    aircraft in proximity; both maneuver toward each other
  Note: TCAS RAs are designed to be complementary (if one aircraft
    gets 'climb', conflicting aircraft gets 'descend'); phantom
    injection can break this coordination

Detection / mitigation state:
  ADS-B authentication proposals: public-key per aircraft; ICAO GADSS
    framework includes integrity considerations; no deployed standard
  Passive detection: multilateration consistency checks (if phantom
    not received by multiple receivers with consistent TDOA, suspicious)
    — attacker with directional high-power antenna can defeat this
  Active detection: ATC radar correlation (if ADS-B target has no
    corresponding radar return, suspicious) — gaps in radar coverage
    exist; some airspace is ADS-B-only
  FAA ADS-B Next: evaluation of authentication mechanisms; no mandate
  Timeline: fleet-wide authentication deployment estimated 15+ years
  G208: CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 106 — ADCS ESC2 / ESC5 / ESC8 / ESC10 CHAIN (G184 FINAL)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Context: Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) misconfiguration
escalation paths; ESC1-ESC10 documented by Will Schroeder and Lee Christensen
(SpecterOps, 2021). ESC1/4/6/9 documented Cycle 32; ESC3/7 Cycle 33.
ESC2/5/8/10 documented here; G184 CLOSED.

ESC2: Any Purpose EKU or no EKU
  Precondition: Certificate template has EKU 'Any Purpose' (OID 2.5.29.37.0)
    or no EKU at all; template allows low-privileged enrollment
  Effect: certificate with Any Purpose EKU can be used for client auth
    even though template was not explicitly intended for that purpose
  Exploitation:
    Step 1: Identify template with Any Purpose EKU via Certify.exe or
      Certipy: 'certify find /vulnerable' or 'certipy find -vulnerable'
    Step 2: Enroll for certificate against that template as any low-priv user
    Step 3: Use certificate for client authentication to domain (PKINIT
      or SChannel); authenticate as the enrolled identity
    If template allows SAN specification (see ESC1): can request cert
    for any identity including Domain Admin
  Impact: equivalent to ESC1 if SAN allowed; certificate-based auth to AD

ESC5: Vulnerable PKI AD Object ACL
  Precondition: low-privileged user has write access to a PKI-related
    AD object: CA server object, CA's machine account, NTAuthCertificates
    object, Enterprise PKI container, AIA container, CDP container
  Key objects:
    NTAuthCertificates: AD object that lists CAs trusted for smart card
      and client auth; adding a CA here makes AD trust all certs from that CA
    Enterprise PKI container: controls what CAs are visible in AD
    CA machine account: controls CA service itself
  Exploitation path (NTAuthCertificates):
    Step 1: Attacker has WriteDACL or WriteProperty on NTAuthCertificates
    Step 2: Attacker adds attacker-controlled CA certificate to
      NTAuthCertificates attribute
    Step 3: AD now trusts certificates issued by attacker-controlled CA
    Step 4: Issue certificate for any identity (Domain Admin) from
      attacker CA; use for PKINIT; receive Kerberos TGT as Domain Admin
  Impact: full domain compromise from ACL misconfiguration on PKI object
  Detection: audit ACLs on all PKI-related AD objects;
    monitor NTAuthCertificates modifications (Event 4662)

ESC8: NTLM Relay to AD CS HTTP Endpoint
  Precondition: AD CS web enrollment (certsrv) enabled over HTTP
    (not HTTPS with required client auth); NTLM relay possible
  Mechanism: AD CS certsrv/certfnsh.asp accepts NTLM authentication;
    does not require HTTPS with EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication);
    NTLM relay attack delivers authenticated session to CA
  Exploitation:
    Step 1: Attacker positions as MitM (ARP poison, LLMNR/NBT-NS poison,
      IPv6 DNS poison, or printer bug trigger)
    Step 2: Victim's machine authenticates to attacker via NTLM
      (e.g., coerced via SpoolSS/PetitPotam/PrinterBug)
    Step 3: Attacker relays NTLM session to certsrv HTTP endpoint
    Step 4: Requests certificate on behalf of victim machine account
    Step 5: If victim is Domain Controller: certificate for DC machine
      account obtained; use for PKINIT; obtain DC TGT
    Step 6: DCSync with DC TGT → domain compromise
  Tools: ntlmrelayx (Impacket) + petitpotam.py or printerbug.py
  Chained attack: PetitPotam → NTLM relay → ESC8 → PKINIT → DCSync
    is one of the most reliable domain compromise chains documented
  Mitigation: disable HTTP enrollment (require HTTPS); enable EPA;
    disable NTLM on certsrv; block PetitPotam via MS-EFSRPC patch

ESC10: Weak Certificate Mapping (post-April 2023)
  Background: Microsoft KB5014754 (May 2022) introduced 'strong mapping'
    for PKINIT; full enforcement enabled in February 2025 updates
    Strong mapping: certificate must contain SID of AD account
    Weak mapping: certificate matched by UPN or DNS name only
  Precondition: domain controller operating in Compatibility Mode
    (not yet fully enforced); certificate with UPN matching target account
  ESC10 scenario A (GenericWrite on user account):
    Step 1: Attacker has GenericWrite on user Account A
    Step 2: Attacker modifies userPrincipalName of Account A to match
      UPN of target (e.g., 'administrator@domain.com')
    Step 3: Attacker requests certificate for Account A from template
      that encodes requester UPN (msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag =
      ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT or SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_UPN)
    Step 4: Certificate issued with UPN 'administrator@domain.com'
    Step 5: Attacker reverts Account A's UPN
    Step 6: Use certificate to authenticate as administrator via PKINIT
      (weak mapping: UPN match only; strong mapping not enforced)
  ESC10 scenario B (GenericWrite on computer account):
    Similar path using dNSHostName attribute instead of UPN;
    modify dNSHostName of computer account to match target DC;
    obtain certificate with DNS SAN matching DC; authenticate as DC
  Mitigation: fully enforce strong mapping (disable Compatibility Mode);
    audit msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag on all templates;
    restrict GenericWrite permissions on user/computer objects

ADCS ESC1-ESC10 COMPLETE COVERAGE:
  ESC1 (C32): Arbitrary SAN in certificate template
  ESC2 (C35): Any Purpose EKU
  ESC3 (C33): Certificate Request Agent template abuse
  ESC4 (C32): Vulnerable certificate template ACL
  ESC5 (C35): Vulnerable PKI AD object ACL
  ESC6 (C32): EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag on CA
  ESC7 (C33): Vulnerable CA ACL (ManageCA / ManageCertificates)
  ESC8 (C35): NTLM relay to AD CS HTTP endpoint
  ESC9 (C32): No security extension (CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION)
  ESC10 (C35): Weak certificate mapping (post-KB5014754)
  G184: CLOSED (all ten pathways documented)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 107 — IMPLANTABLE CARDIAC DEVICE FULL ATTACK ANATOMY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Device context: Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD)
  Function: monitors cardiac rhythm; delivers shock therapy for
    ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia; logs cardiac events
  Battery: 5-10 year life; replacement requires surgical reopening
  Leads: transvenous leads to heart; sense electrical activity;
    deliver pacing/shock
  Programmer: external wand or tablet used by cardiologist for
    parameter adjustment; communicates via RF to device

Medtronic Conexus protocol (CVE-2019-6538 / VU#955293):
  Frequency: 175 kHz (primary telemetry); some devices also 2.4 GHz
  Authentication: none (proximity assumed to imply clinical intent)
  Encryption: none (cleartext transmission)
  Range: ~30 feet with standard equipment; extended with directional
    antenna and amplifier (demonstrated in research: 50+ feet)
  Affected products: MyCareLink Monitor, CareLink programmer,
    Amplia, Claria, Compia, Evera, Mirro, Primo, Protecta, Visia
    (20+ device families; >750,000 implants worldwide)

Attack anatomy:
  Phase 1: Discovery
    Passive scanning: 175 kHz RF receiver; identify Conexus beacon
    Beacons transmitted by device for short window after magnet application
    OR during scheduled telemetry session
    Alternatively: attacker triggers window by applying magnet through
    clothing (no physical contact with body required; magnet through
    shirt activates telemetry window)

Phase 2: Protocol reverse engineering (already done)
    Conexus protocol fully reverse-engineered by Billy Rios and
    Jonathan Butts (WhiteScope) and disclosed to Medtronic 2018;
    Medtronic acknowledged 2019; ICS-CERT advisory issued
    Protocol frames: device ID, command type, parameter fields
    No challenge-response; no session token; any transmitter that
    speaks Conexus is accepted

Phase 3: Parameter read
    Transmit Conexus 'read parameters' command
    Device responds with current therapy settings:
      - Ventricular fibrillation detection threshold
      - Ventricular tachycardia detection threshold
      - Therapy zones (VF zone, VT zone, monitor zone)
      - Shock energy levels (joules)
      - Anti-tachycardia pacing sequences
      - Bradycardia pacing parameters
    No authentication required to read parameters

Phase 4: Parameter write (attack payload)
    Option A: Therapy inhibition
      Write: raise VF detection threshold above physiologically possible
        rate (e.g., set detection to 600 bpm; normal VF is 300-400 bpm)
      Effect: device never detects VF; patient dies of untreated
        ventricular fibrillation
      Clinical presentation: sudden cardiac death with no device therapy;
        may appear as natural death

Option B: Inappropriate shock delivery
      Write: lower VT detection threshold to sinus rate range
        (e.g., set VT detection to 100 bpm; patient's normal rate is 80 bpm)
      Effect: device misclassifies normal rhythm as VT;
        delivers inappropriate shock (35-40 joules)
      Physical effect: extremely painful (equivalent to being struck by
        lightning at close range); can cause syncope; repeated inappropriate
        shocks increase mortality risk; emotional trauma
      Clinical detection: device log shows inappropriate therapy;
        detectable at next clinic visit; not detectable remotely

Option C: Shock on demand
      Write: immediate shock delivery command
      Effect: device delivers therapy shock regardless of cardiac rhythm
      Timing: attacker determines delivery time; effect is immediate
      This is the 'assassination attack' described by Dick Cheney's
        cardiologist; Cheney had wireless disabled on his ICD in 2007
        as precaution; Homeland Security issued ICS-CERT advisory

Phase 5: Post-attack forensics challenge
    Option A (inhibition): patient dies; device retrieved post-mortem;
      log shows no therapy delivered (expected for threshold attack);
      threshold setting will have been overwritten if attacker reset it;
      forensic evidence may not survive device analysis
    Option B (inappropriate shock): patient survives; reports shock;
      device log shows therapy; cardiology investigates as normal
      inappropriate shock workup; no RF attack indicator in log
    Attribution: none; RF transmission leaves no identifying information
      in device log; attacker 30+ feet away with no physical contact

Remediation state (as of 2019 disclosure):
  Medtronic issued firmware update for some affected devices
  Firmware update delivery: requires clinic visit (no OTA for 175 kHz
    devices); patient must return to cardiologist
  Update adoption: clinic scheduling required; some patients medically
    unable to travel; some chose not to update
  Unupdatable devices: some hardware generations cannot be updated
    (no update path); require device replacement (surgery)
  Workaround: disable wireless telemetry (magnet switch); patient
    must use wired programmer only; eliminates remote monitoring benefit
  LAW-1 classification: R09.2 compound — implant lifecycle locks
    vulnerability for device's remaining operational life;
    remediation requires surgery for hardware-limited devices
  G209: CLOSED

ANATOMIES CUMULATIVE: 107
BACKLOG STATUS: 15 → 11 (net -4: G207, G208, G184-final, G209 closed)
REMAINING BACKLOG: G192, G194, G195, G197, G198, G200, G202, G203,
  G204, G210, plus any new gaps from current cycle
EXIT STATE: 107 anatomies, backlog 11

CYCLE 35 — STAGE 4: ATTACK ENUMERATION / DEFENSE ENUMERATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 290 attacks | 412 defenses

ATTACK 291 — ADS-B PHANTOM AIRCRAFT INJECTION
Root: R01 (ambient authority); Domain: D317 (aviation avionics)
Mechanism: Craft and transmit ADS-B Mode S extended squitter messages at
1090 MHz using SDR (HackRF, ADALM-Pluto); fabricate aircraft ICAO address,
CPR-encoded position, altitude, velocity; ground receivers forward to ATC
Precondition: SDR transmitter (~$150-$300); 1090 MHz antenna; ADS-B encoding
software (open source); line-of-sight to receiver
Effect: phantom aircraft appears on ATC display; TCAS on real aircraft may
issue Resolution Advisory based on phantom; airspace routing affected
Demonstrated: academic research 2012-2016 (Schafer et al.); FAA acknowledged
Undefended in deployed system as of 2026

ATTACK 292 — ADS-B DENIAL VIA PHANTOM FLEET SATURATION
Root: R10.4 (scale brittleness); Domain: D317
Mechanism: Transmit high-volume ADS-B messages for hundreds of phantom aircraft;
ATC display renders all targets; display and correlation algorithms saturated;
real aircraft tracks obscured in noise
Effect: ground stop; ATC unable to maintain separation assurance;
operational disruption at regional airspace level
Tooling: gr-air-modes (GNU Radio) + script for batch phantom generation
Difficulty: higher than single phantom (requires coordinated transmission);
detectable by multilateration inconsistency if receiver coverage dense

ATTACK 293 — ACARS FAKE CLEARANCE INJECTION
Root: R01; Domain: D317
Mechanism: Transmit fake ACARS message to aircraft VHF frequency;
craft message purporting to be from airline operations or ATC;
content: false weather, false routing clearance, false divert instruction
Precondition: VHF transmitter on ACARS frequencies (129.125 MHz primary);
ACARS message format knowledge (documented); proximity to aircraft or airline
VHF network
Effect: crew receives false operational instruction; may act on it without
verification if context plausible; incorrect weather avoidance; diversion
to wrong airport
Mitigation gap: ACARS displays message source (flight number/station) but
source field is not authenticated; crew training is primary defense

ATTACK 294 — IMPLANTABLE ICD THERAPY INHIBITION
Root: R01; Domain: D316 (implantable medical devices)
Mechanism: RF transmitter at 175 kHz; apply magnet through patient clothing
to open telemetry window; transmit Conexus protocol 'write parameters' command;
set VF detection threshold above physiological maximum
Precondition: knowledge of Conexus protocol (documented in CERT/CC VU#955293);
175 kHz transmitter; proximity to patient (~30 feet)
Effect: ICD no longer detects ventricular fibrillation; next VF episode
receives no therapy; patient death
Forensic signature: none (log shows no therapy; threshold reset by attacker
removes evidence; no RF attribution)

ATTACK 295 — IMPLANTABLE ICD INAPPROPRIATE SHOCK DELIVERY
Root: R01; Domain: D316
Mechanism: Conexus protocol write; lower VT detection threshold to sinus
rate range; device classifies normal rhythm as tachycardia; delivers shock
Effect: painful inappropriate shock; syncope; psychological trauma;
risk of fall injury; increased mortality with repeated episodes
Detection: device log records therapy delivery; visible at next clinic visit;
not remotely monitorable without attacker knowledge

ATTACK 296 — V2X SYBIL ATTACK (POSITION FALSIFICATION)
Root: R01 (ambient authority within DSRC/C-V2X range); Domain: D310 (V2X)
Mechanism: Attacker operates multiple V2X pseudonymous certificates
simultaneously; broadcasts different vehicle positions from each identity;
receiving vehicles' cooperative awareness systems receive conflicting or
false traffic data
Effect: incorrect vehicle density map; false traffic flow indication;
emergency vehicle pre-emption spoofed; intersection signal timing attacked
IEEE 1609.2: pseudonymous cert design prevents direct linkage of certs to
real identity; designed to prevent tracking; same property enables Sybil

ATTACK 297 — CAN BUS INJECTION POST-OBD-II PHYSICAL ACCESS
Root: R06 (trust boundary collapse via OBD-II port to CAN bus)
Domain: D303 (CAN bus / automotive)
Mechanism: Plug CAN-to-USB adapter into OBD-II port (physical access);
enumerate CAN IDs and payloads with candump; replay or craft CAN frames;
inject brake, throttle, or steering ECU commands
Precondition: physical access to vehicle (~60 seconds unattended)
Effect: CAN injection enables full ECU control; all documented TPMS/brake/
throttle attacks apply; no authentication on CAN frames
Post-access phase: if attacker installs persistent CAN bridge, attack
survives vehicle return to owner; bridge powered by OBD-II 12V rail

ATTACK 298 — KUBERNETES PRIVILEGED CONTAINER ESCAPE
Root: R06.ARCH; Domain: D214 (Kubernetes / container orchestration)
Mechanism: Deploy privileged container (or exploit misconfigured admission
control to bypass restriction); privileged container has CAP_SYS_ADMIN;
mount host /proc or /dev; write to host filesystem; escape to node via
nsenter or cgroups release_agent technique
Precondition: ability to deploy pod (may be low-privilege in cluster);
no restrictive admission controller (PodSecurityPolicy deprecated 1.25;
PSA may not be enforce mode)
Effect: host node access; credential theft from node filesystem;
lateral movement to other pods on same node

ATTACK 299 — BGP ROUTE HIJACK (PREFIX DEAGGREGATION)
Root: R01 (ambient authority: BGP speaker trusted by peers); Domain: D045 (BGP)
Mechanism: Attacker AS announces more-specific prefix (longer prefix mask)
for victim's IP space; BGP longest-prefix-match selects more-specific;
traffic routed to attacker AS; attacker forwards (transparent hijack)
or drops (black hole)
Notable: Pakistan Telecom 2008 (YouTube prefix); Rostelecom 2020 (financial);
no deployed authentication in most peering relationships
RPKI: Route Origin Validation now deployed by ~50% of Tier-1 ISPs;
partially mitigates origin hijack; does not prevent path manipulation

ATTACK 300 — SUPPLY CHAIN COMPILER BACKDOOR
Root: R08 (supply chain); Domain: D155 (software supply chain)
Mechanism: Compromise compiler toolchain; inject malicious transformation
that triggers when compiling specific pattern (e.g., login function, sudo);
transformed binary contains backdoor; source code review clean
Reference: Thompson (1984) 'Reflections on Trusting Trust' — proof of concept
Modern threat: XZ Utils (2024) — liblzma backdoor injected via compromised
maintainer; affected systemd-linked SSH daemons in Linux distributions
Detection: near-impossible from source review alone; requires binary
comparison against reproducible builds (reproducible builds project)
Mitigation: reproducible builds; diverse compilation toolchains; binary
transparency logs

DEFENSE 413 — ADS-B MULTILATERATION CONSISTENCY VERIFICATION
Domain: D317; Counters: A291, A292
Mechanism: Multiple geographically separated ADS-B receivers compute Time
Difference of Arrival (TDOA) for same squitter; compare TDOA-derived position
against reported CPR position; discrepancy indicates potential spoofing
Limitation: attacker with high-power directional antenna can overpower
legitimate signal; receivers in same geographic cluster may all receive
attacker signal; TDOA effective only with dense diverse coverage

DEFENSE 414 — ADS-B RADAR CROSS-CORRELATION
Domain: D317; Counters: A291, A292
Mechanism: ATC cross-correlates ADS-B targets against primary radar returns;
ADS-B target with no corresponding radar return flagged for controller attention
Limitation: significant radar coverage gaps exist (mountainous terrain,
oceanic, high-altitude); radar return may not be visible at all altitudes;
not deployed in all ATC facilities; requires ATC operator action on flag

DEFENSE 415 — ACARS CREW VERIFICATION PROTOCOL
Domain: D317; Counters: A293
Mechanism: SELCAL and ACARS message authentication via crew verbal
verification on voice frequency; for routing changes or diversions received
via ACARS, crew initiates voice check with ATC or airline operations before
compliance; two-channel verification
Limitation: operational tempo may discourage verification; voice frequency
may be congested; training compliance varies

DEFENSE 416 — ICD RF TELEMETRY MAGNET SHIELD / PROXIMITY ALERT
Domain: D316; Counters: A294, A295
Mechanism: Farraday-effect garment or targeted RF shield at implant site
blocks 175 kHz telemetry activation; proximity alert to patient (wearable
sensor) when magnetic field detected near implant site
Limitation: impractical for daily wear; patient compliance low; 
not commercially deployed; experimental only

DEFENSE 417 — ICD FIRMWARE UPDATE (CONEXUS MITIGATION)
Domain: D316; Counters: A294, A295
Mechanism: Medtronic firmware update adds notification to patient app
(CareLink) when wireless telemetry session initiated; adds 'disconnect'
capability; does not add authentication to Conexus (protocol limitation)
Limitation: requires clinic visit; some devices hardware-limited (no
update path); update adoption estimated <60% of affected population;
does not fix root cause (no Conexus authentication)

DEFENSE 418 — V2X MISBEHAVIOR DETECTION SYSTEM (MDS)
Domain: D310; Counters: A296
Mechanism: V2X receivers apply behavioral plausibility checks to received
BSMs: position consistency over time (physics-based filtering), impossible
acceleration/deceleration, implausible density for claimed position, peer
confirmation of position via independent observations
SCMS integration: MDS reports misbehaving certificates to SCMS;
SCMS revokes certificates; CRL distributed to vehicles
Limitation: Sybil attacker with multiple certs can make positions
mutually confirming; revocation latency (CRL distribution delay)
creates window of exploitation post-detection

DEFENSE 419 — RPKI ROUTE ORIGIN VALIDATION
Domain: D045 (BGP); Counters: A299
Mechanism: Resource Public Key Infrastructure cryptographically binds
IP prefix to Autonomous System; ROA (Route Origin Authorization) signed
by IP address block owner; ISPs validate origin AS against ROA before
accepting BGP route announcement
Deployment: ~50% of Tier-1 ISPs enforce RPKI validation (2025);
NIST/CISA guidance recommends full deployment
Limitation: covers origin AS only; path manipulation not addressed;
adoption incomplete; ISPs may drop invalids or not-found differently

DEFENSE 420 — REPRODUCIBLE BUILDS
Domain: D155 (software supply chain); Counters: A300
Mechanism: Build system deterministic; same source + same toolchain =
byte-for-byte identical binary; multiple independent builders verify
binary matches; divergence indicates build environment compromise
Deployment: Debian reproducible builds project (>95% reproducible);
Tor browser; Bitcoin Core; NixOS
Limitation: requires entire build toolchain to be reproducible;
most commercial software supply chains are not; does not cover compiler
itself (Thompson attack surface remains)

DEFENSE 421 — AUTOSAR SECOC (SECURE ONBOARD COMMUNICATION)
Domain: D303; Counters: A297
Mechanism: AUTOSAR SecOC standard defines CMAC-based authentication
for CAN messages; HSM (Hardware Security Module) on each ECU generates
and verifies MAC; key provisioning at manufacturing time
Deployment status: mandatory in UNECE WP.29 R155 vehicles (type-approved
from July 2022 onward in EU); retrofit to older vehicles impractical
(requires HSM hardware and full firmware update on all ECUs)
Limitation: compromised ECU with legitimate keys still has full
authorized CAN authority; protects against OBD-II physical access
attackers who lack the HSM keys; does not prevent TCU compromise

DEFENSE 422 — PODMAN / ROOTLESS CONTAINERS
Domain: D214; Counters: A298
Mechanism: Container runtime runs without root privileges; user namespace
maps container root to unprivileged host UID; container escape yields
unprivileged host user, not root; combined with seccomp and AppArmor
for syscall filtering
Limitation: not all workloads compatible with rootless operation;
requires application changes; kernel user namespace vulnerabilities
can break isolation (multiple CVEs in kernel user namespace handling)

ATTACKS CUMULATIVE: 300
DEFENSES CUMULATIVE: 422

CYCLE 35 — STAGE 5: CONVERGENCE ANALYSIS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 255 convergence findings | R10 counter-example cycle 1 of 5

CONVERGENCE FINDING 256 — R06.ARCH UNDEFEATED BY G207 SCAN
Domains: D248 (ICS), D305 (automotive), D214 (Kubernetes), D312 (BACnet)
G207 closed with no full counter-example. Four candidates examined:
data diode (architectural redesign, not compensating control), AUTOSAR SecOC
(narrows but does not eliminate; compromised node retains authorized authority),
Kubernetes network policy (architectural addition), firewall (moves boundary
outward, not inward). R06.ARCH pattern definition: UNMODIFIED.
Operational implication: any system where connectivity is required between
a high-trust safety-critical component and a lower-trust entry point has
an architectural crossing that cannot be closed without restructuring the
component's connectivity model. This is not a configuration error.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 257 — LIFE-SAFETY R01 INSTANCES FORM DISTINCT CLASS
Domains: D316 (implantable devices), D303 (CAN/automotive), D312 (BACnet)
Three R01 instances share a structural property beyond the root itself:
  (1) Authority target is a safety-critical physical actuator (heart, vehicle,
      HVAC/fire suppression)
  (2) RF or bus communication is required for legitimate clinical/operational
      function (cannot be removed without losing core functionality)
  (3) Patient/building cannot consent to or detect exploit during execution
  (4) Forensic attribution is near-zero
This creates R01.LIFE-SAFETY: ambient authority over physical actuators
with no consent, detection, or attribution mechanism. Distinct from R01.DATA
(ambient authority over information) and R01.INFRA (ambient authority over
network infrastructure). The consequence asymmetry is maximal: R01.DATA
yields information exposure; R01.LIFE-SAFETY yields death or physical harm.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 258 — BROADCAST BUS AT SAFETY SCALE IS DOMAIN-INVARIANT
Domains: D303 (CAN bus), D317 (ADS-B/ACARS), D308 (V2X implicitly)
Three domains; same structural property:
  Safety-critical system; broadcast bus; no source authentication;
  physical effect achievable via message injection; LAW-1 applies.
  CAN bus: 1.4 billion vehicles; automotive
  ADS-B: 45,000+ daily US flights; aviation
  V2X (candidate): will reach scale when deployed; still growing
Pattern 31.1 extends from automotive to general form:
  ANY safety-critical domain that standardized on broadcast bus architecture
  before authentication was a design priority is a LAW-1 instance.
  The pattern is domain-invariant; it recurs wherever the same design
  constraints (cost, bandwidth, determinism, legacy compatibility) were
  present at protocol design time.
Cross-domain generalization: CONFIRMED at 3 instances (CAN, ADS-B, ACARS)

CONVERGENCE FINDING 259 — R10 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 1: SPECTRE CLASSIFICATION
R10 draft sub-taxonomy: R10.1 (spec ambiguity), R10.2 (implementation
divergence), R10.3 (emergent complexity), R10.4 (scale brittleness)
Counter-example candidate: Spectre (CVE-2017-5753)

Spectre analysis against R10 classes:
  R10.1: Specification ambiguity? The x86/ARM speculation architecture is
    'specified' in terms of functional correctness — speculative execution
    does not change the architectural state; it only changes microarchitectural
    state. The spec permits this. The vulnerability is not in ambiguity about
    what the spec says; it is in what the spec does NOT specify: the timing
    observable from speculative execution's cache state. Verdict: NOT R10.1
    (the spec is unambiguous about what speculation does; it simply did not
    treat timing as part of the security model)

R10.2: Implementation divergence? Both Intel and ARM implement speculation;
    both are vulnerable. The vulnerability is not in different implementations
    interacting; it is in the shared architectural feature. Verdict: NOT R10.2.

R10.3: Emergent complexity? Spectre does not require multiple components
    to compose. A single CPU with a single process running exhibits Spectre.
    There is no composition of independently correct components here.
    Verdict: NOT R10.3.

R10.4: Scale brittleness? Spectre does not become more severe at scale;
    it is equally exploitable on a single-core device. Verdict: NOT R10.4.

Classification verdict: Spectre does not fit R10.1-R10.4.
  Candidate R10.5 class: MICROARCHITECTURAL OPTIMIZATION LEAKAGE
    Definition: vulnerability arising from a performance optimization that
    is functionally correct (architectural state unchanged) but leaks
    information through a non-functional side channel that was not included
    in the security model when the optimization was designed.
    Other instances: Meltdown (same class); Flush+Reload cache timing;
    RowHammer (charge leakage from DRAM refresh — performance optimization
    of not refreshing every cycle leaks writes to adjacent rows)
    This is structurally distinct from R10.1-R10.4: the optimization is
    intentional and correct; the leakage is from a property of the physical
    medium (cache lines, DRAM cells, branch predictor state) that was not
    modeled as an information channel.

R10.5 (DRAFT): MICROARCHITECTURAL OPTIMIZATION LEAKAGE
    An optimization that improves performance by retaining or prefetching
    state (speculative execution, cache, branch predictor, prefetcher,
    DRAM refresh rate, TLB) creates an observable channel in a medium
    (timing, power, electromagnetic emission) that was not included in the
    original security model. The vulnerability exists at the boundary
    between the performance model and the security model.

Implication: R10 sub-taxonomy is not CLOSED at R10.1-R10.4.
  R10.5 DRAFT: requires 3/5 counter-example cycles for CLOSED status.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 260 — ADCS ESC1-ESC10: STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION
Domain: D173 (Active Directory PKI)
ESC1-ESC10 documented. Structural observation from complete coverage:
  Six of ten ESC paths require a certificate template misconfiguration
  (ESC1, ESC2, ESC3, ESC4, ESC6, ESC9)
  Two require CA-level misconfiguration (ESC7, ESC8)
  Two require AD object ACL misconfiguration (ESC5, ESC10 variant A)
  All paths lead to the same outcome: valid certificate for any identity
  Underlying root: certificate is absolute trust token in AD; anything
  that grants ability to obtain a certificate for an arbitrary identity
  grants DA-equivalent access
  R03 (privilege escalation) classification: all ten are R03 instances;
  ADCS is the highest-concentration R03 attack surface in Windows AD
  Pattern: public-key infrastructure, when misconfigured, becomes a
  universal key factory. The security model of PKI (trust the CA to
  only issue to verified identities) is violated at configuration level.
  A correctly-configured ADCS has no ESC1-ESC10 vectors. This is unlike
  LAW-1: remediation is configuration, not architecture. However:
  Default configurations are frequently misconfigured. The 'any purpose'
  EKU and 'manager approval disabled' combination is common in enterprise
  deployments because it is the path of least resistance for certificate
  provisioning. This is a social/organizational pattern, not technical.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 261 — IMPLANT LIFECYCLE + REGULATORY CAPTURE: COMPOUND
Domains: D316 (medical devices), D251 (medical device regulation)
R09.2 (equipment lifecycle lock-in) + regulatory capture compound:
  ICD vulnerability: exploitable for device's remaining battery life (5-10yr)
  Remediation: clinic visit + firmware update OR surgery + replacement
  Regulatory: FDA 510(k) cleared Conexus without authentication requirement;
  no post-market security mandate; manufacturer responsible for voluntary
  update program
  Compound effect: even if manufacturer wants to remediate, cannot force
  patient surgery; cannot force clinic visit; cannot remotely update
  hardware-limited devices; FDA has no authority to mandate device recall
  for security vulnerability absent demonstrated patient harm from cyberattack
  This creates a class of permanently exploitable devices that will operate
  in human bodies for years after the vulnerability is publicly documented.
  The attack surface does not shrink through patching; it shrinks only
  through natural device replacement at battery end-of-life.
  This is the strongest form of R09.2: the locked period is determined by
  human physiology (surgery risk) and device physics (battery life),
  not by IT refresh cycles.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 262 — AVIATION + AUTOMOTIVE: PARALLEL LAW-1 INSTANCES
Cross-domain finding:
  Both aviation (ADS-B, ACARS) and automotive (CAN) are:
    LAW-1 instances: broadcast bus, no auth, physical effect, civilizational scale
    Sub-domain of 'safety-critical transportation infrastructure'
    At different stages of remediation awareness:
    Automotive: UNECE WP.29 R155 mandates cybersecurity management for
    new type approvals from July 2024 in EU; AUTOSAR SecOC being deployed
    on new vehicles; existing fleet (~1.4B) remains unprotected
    Aviation: ICAO studying ADS-B authentication; no mandate; no timeline
    Aviation appears ~5-10 years behind automotive in regulatory response
    Both are on multi-decade remediation arcs due to equipment lifecycles
  Implication: the pattern of regulatory response lagging discovery by
  years, then mandating for new production only, leaving legacy fleet
  permanently exposed, is itself a pattern. Call it:
  PATTERN 35.5 (PROVISIONAL): SAFETY-CRITICAL FLEET LEGACY EXPOSURE
    New production receives security mandate after regulatory awareness;
    existing installed base receives no mandatory remediation;
    installed base declines at natural end-of-life rate (automotive: ~15yr,
    aviation: ~20-30yr, medical implant: ~7yr per device); full remediation
    takes one full fleet cycle from mandate — 15-30 years.

CONVERGENCE FINDING 263 — R10.5 INSTANCES SPAN HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE
Domains: D067 (microarchitecture/CPU), D068 (DRAM/memory), D069 (cache)
R10.5 candidates beyond Spectre/Meltdown:
  RowHammer (CVE-2014-3122+): DRAM refresh rate optimization; adjacent
  row bit flips from rapid access to same row; physical medium leakage
  from charge proximity; not modeled in DRAM security spec
  Flush+Reload: shared memory page between processes; flush page from cache;
  reload and time; determine if other process accessed page (cache hit/miss
  timing); same physical medium (cache) used as covert channel
  Branch predictor pollution (Spectre v2): cross-process BTB injection;
  attacker poisons branch predictor to cause victim to speculate to
  attacker-controlled gadget; timing of speculative execution leaks data
  All three: performance optimization (DRAM refresh interval, cache sharing,
  branch prediction) + physical medium leakage + security model gap
  R10.5 class definition appears robust across multiple hardware domains

CONVERGENCE SUMMARY C35:
  R06.ARCH: CONFIRMED, counter-example resistant
  R01.LIFE-SAFETY sub-class: IDENTIFIED (implantable, automotive, building)
  Broadcast bus pattern: extended to aviation; domain-invariant confirmed
  R10.5 DRAFT: microarchitectural optimization leakage; Spectre instance
  Pattern 35.5 PROVISIONAL: safety-critical fleet legacy exposure trajectory
  ADCS structural observation: PKI as universal key factory when misconfigured
  Implant compound: R09.2 + regulatory capture = permanently exploitable class

DOMAIN LEDGER ADDITIONS — CYCLE 36

D320 — LDACS / Next-Generation Aeronautical Datalink
  Description: L-band Digital Aeronautical Communications System;
  proposed replacement for VHF ACARS; ICAO standardization ongoing;
  designed with security in mind (unlike ACARS); PKI-based authentication
  for air-ground data link; frequency: L-band (960-1164 MHz)
  Security design: application-layer authentication; message integrity;
  confidentiality option; ICAO Doc 9896 framework
  Status: not yet deployed at scale; legacy ACARS will remain parallel
  for transition period (estimated 2030-2040)
  Gaps: G214 — does LDACS fully close ACARS injection vector or only
  for LDACS-capable aircraft? Legacy aircraft remain ACARS-only.

D321 — Aviation Cybersecurity Regulatory Framework
  Domain: ICAO Annex 17 (security); ICAO Doc 10037 (cybersecurity)
  DO-326A (RTCA): Airworthiness Security Process Specification (2014);
  DO-356A: Airworthiness Security Methods and Considerations
  FAA AC 119-1: Airworthiness and Operational Approval for Aircraft
  Network Security Program (2015)
  EU: EASA Opinion 01/2019 on cybersecurity; CS-CYB airworthiness codes
  Status: avionics cybersecurity requirements exist for new type certificates;
  existing fleet largely pre-dates requirements
  LAW-1 parallel: new production mandate + legacy fleet exempt = automotive
  WP.29 pattern for aviation

D322 — SCMS (Security Credential Management System) for V2X
  Description: US V2X PKI infrastructure for pseudonymous certificate
  management; operated by DOT / USDOT contractors; issues short-lived
  pseudonymous certs to vehicles; handles enrollment, pseudonym provisioning,
  misbehavior reporting, certificate revocation
  Architecture: Root CA → Intermediate CA → Pseudonym CA → vehicle certs
  Cert lifetime: ~1 week (pseudonym change for privacy)
  Misbehavior authority: receives reports from vehicles; analyzes behavior;
  revokes certificates of misbehaving vehicles (Sybil, position falsification)
  Gaps: G215 — pseudonymous unlinkability vs Sybil tradeoff

D323 — Hardware Security Module (HSM) Ecosystem
  Description: dedicated hardware for key storage and cryptographic operations;
  FIPS 140-2/3 certified; tamper-evident/tamper-resistant hardware
  Variants: PCIe HSM (server-side); USB HSM; embedded (TPM, TEE, SE);
  automotive HSM (on-chip, e.g., Infineon SLx/Aurix TC3xx family)
  Role in cybersecurity: root of trust for key storage; prevents key
  extraction even by OS-level attacker; required for AUTOSAR SecOC automotive
  implementation; used in ADCS CA infrastructure
  Gaps: HSM bypass attacks (fault injection, cold boot on SRAM-based HSM,
  timing attacks on RSA exponent) — partially covered D236; full HSM
  attack surface not yet enumerated

D324 — Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)
  Description: NIST SP 800-207; architectural framework; replaces perimeter
  model with per-session, per-resource authentication and authorization;
  no implicit trust based on network location; micro-segmentation;
  continuous verification; CISA ZTA maturity model (2023)
  Core tenets: verify explicitly; use least privilege access; assume breach
  Deployment: US Federal ZTA mandate (EO 14028, May 2021); CISA ZTMM;
  enterprise adoption accelerated by COVID remote work + cloud migration
  Security effect: eliminates lateral movement assumptions; compromised
  credential on one segment does not yield adjacent segment access
  Tension with operational complexity: ZTA requires identity infrastructure
  (IdP, PAM, MFA) that is itself an attack surface (see Golden SAML,
  ADCS ESC series) — trust the identity system or the perimeter collapses
  to identity provider

D325 — Automotive Cybersecurity Regulation (UNECE WP.29 R155/R156)
  Description: UN regulation mandating Cyber Security Management System
  (CSMS) for vehicle manufacturers; mandatory for new type approvals
  in EU/UK/Japan/Korea from July 2022; mandatory for all new vehicles
  produced from July 2024 in EU
  Scope: covers entire vehicle lifecycle including supply chain;
  requires threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA); incident response;
  OTA software update management (R156)
  Effect: new EU vehicles from 2024 must have CSMS; AUTOSAR SecOC
  increasingly required for CAN authentication; VIN-specific diagnostics
  Limitation: applies only to new production; existing fleet (~1.4B vehicles)
  not covered; global fleet compliance dependent on each jurisdiction
  Pattern 35.5 instance 1: automotive (new mandate, legacy exempt)

CYCLE 36 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 140 patterns cumulative

PATTERN 36.1 — ZERO TRUST IDENTITY PROVIDER AS SINGLE POINT OF COLLAPSE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R06 (trust boundary collapse); Domain: D324 (ZTA), D173 (AD)

Zero Trust Architecture premise: no implicit network trust; all access
verified per-session via identity provider (IdP). Security model shifts
trust from network perimeter to identity infrastructure.
Structural consequence: identity provider (IdP, AAD, Okta, Ping) becomes
the new perimeter. Compromising the IdP is equivalent to compromising
the perimeter — all protected resources become accessible.

Identity collapse attack paths:
  Path A: Golden SAML
    Mechanism: ADFS (Active Directory Federation Services) signs SAML tokens
    using a token-signing certificate stored on the ADFS server; if attacker
    obtains this certificate (via ADFS server compromise, DCSync, or ADCS
    ESC series), attacker can forge SAML tokens for any user identity;
    forged tokens accepted by all relying parties (M365, AWS, Salesforce)
    without further verification
    Demonstrated: SolarWinds attack (NOBELIUM, 2020): compromised ADFS
    signing cert used to forge tokens and access O365 tenants of victims
    Detection: SAML token audit logs; certificate monitoring

Path B: ADCS-to-IdP kill chain
    Mechanism: ADCS ESC1/ESC8 → certificate for privileged identity →
    PKINIT to obtain Kerberos TGT → DCSync → ADFS private key extraction
    → Golden SAML generation; ZTA fully bypassed via PKI compromise
    This is R06.ARCH in ZTA context: the PKI is the architectural
    dependency of ZTA; compromising PKI collapses ZTA trust model

Path C: OAuth token theft (BEC/cloud context)
    Mechanism: attacker obtains OAuth refresh token (via phishing, AiTM proxy,
    or App consent grant to malicious OAuth app); refresh token grants
    long-lived access to all consented scopes; MFA bypass (token already
    issued post-MFA); session not visible as 'login' in audit logs
    AiTM phishing (Adversary-in-the-Middle): attacker operates reverse
    proxy between user and legitimate IdP; captures session cookie post-MFA;
    Evilginx2, Modlishka, Muraena toolkits

Pattern statement: Zero Trust's security gain relative to perimeter model is
real, but ZTA concentrates trust in identity infrastructure, making that
infrastructure a higher-value target. Any attack that compromises the IdP
or its signing material defeats ZTA as completely as perimeter bypass
defeated the perimeter model. The attack surface shifts; it does not shrink.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 36.2 — REGULATORY MANDATE CREATES NEW PRODUCTION / LEGACY SPLIT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: Meta-pattern (policy/deployment); Cross-domain
Pattern 35.5 formalized as Pattern 36.2 (instance count: 3 confirmed)

Confirmed instances:
  1. Automotive: UNECE WP.29 R155 (EU, 2022/2024) — new type approvals
     require CSMS; existing ~1.4B vehicle fleet exempt
  2. Aviation: EASA/FAA cybersecurity requirements for new type certificates —
     new aircraft type designs require cybersecurity assessment; legacy fleet
     (pre-regulation design) exempt; DO-326A applies to new cert programs
  3. Medical devices: FDA cybersecurity guidance 2013/2016/2023 — post-2023
     FDA guidance requires cybersecurity in pre-market submissions;
     510(k) devices cleared before 2023 have no retroactive security mandate;
     legacy implants remain in bodies under pre-mandate regime

Pattern structure:
  (a) Domain reaches regulatory awareness of cybersecurity risk
  (b) Mandate applies to new production / new type approvals
  (c) Existing installed base exempt from mandatory remediation
  (d) Installed base declines at natural end-of-life rate (sector-specific)
  (e) Full fleet transition requires one complete replacement cycle
  (f) During transition: two classes of devices in deployment — mandated
      (secure design required) and legacy (arbitrary security posture)
  (g) Legacy class is the attack surface for the full replacement cycle

Replacement cycle estimates:
  Automotive: ~15 years (average vehicle age at retirement)
  Aviation commercial aircraft: ~20-25 years
  Medical implants: 5-10 years per device (but patient may have multiple
    sequential devices over lifetime)
  Consumer IoT: 3-7 years (TV, router, smart speaker)
  Industrial control systems: 15-30 years

Pattern implication: in every safety-critical domain, there will be a window
of 15-30 years after regulatory mandate during which the vulnerable legacy
fleet remains in deployment. The mandate does not secure the domain; it
secures the next generation of the domain. The current generation is the
attack surface. This is LAW-1 applied at regulatory scale.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 36.3 — INFUSION PUMP WIRELESS DOSING: R01 AT PHARMACOLOGICAL SCALE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R01.LIFE-SAFETY; Domain: D316 extension (medical devices)

Infusion pumps: deliver medication IV at precise rates; used in ICUs,
OR, oncology; drug dosing errors are lethal (insulin overdose, chemotherapy)
Wireless interface: hospital network connectivity for drug library updates
(dose error reduction software — DERS); integration with EMR/EHR;
remote monitoring by nurse call system

Hospira Plum A+ (CVE-2015-3459, ICS-CERT ICSA-15-125-01):
  Vulnerability: no authentication on drug library update channel;
  attacker on same hospital network can push modified drug library;
  drug library defines drug names, concentrations, min/max dose limits
  DERS (drug error reduction software): designed to prevent lethal dosing;
  if drug library is attacker-modified, DERS approves lethal dose as 'within limits'
  Effect: attacker sets maximum dose limit for insulin to 1000 units/hr
  (lethal); nurse programs pump using modified library; pump delivers
  lethal dose with no DERS alert
  Demonstrated: Billy Rios (ICS-CERT collaboration, 2014-2015);
  FDA safety communication issued

BD Alaris system (CVE-2020-25165, ICS-CERT ICSA-20-345-01):
  Vulnerability: XML injection via PCU (Point-of-Care Unit) network
  interface; allows remote modification of drug library
  Deployed: widely used in US hospitals (market leader in IV infusion)

R01.LIFE-SAFETY classification:
  Ambient authority: hospital network connectivity assumed to imply
  clinical authorization (same as ICD proximity assumption)
  Actuator: IV drug delivery at programmable rate
  Life-safety consequence: overdose death
  Consent/detection/attribution: none at exploit time; detection only
  post-incident via pharmacy record audit
  Scale: millions of infusion pumps deployed in US hospitals alone

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 36.4 — PROTECTION RELAY COMPROMISE: POWER GRID PHYSICAL EFFECT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R06.ARCH (ICS variant); R01.LIFE-SAFETY candidate; D248 (ICS)

Protection relays: IEDs (Intelligent Electronic Devices) that monitor
electrical parameters and trip circuit breakers to protect equipment;
used in substations, transmission lines, generator plants
Function: detects fault conditions (overcurrent, undervoltage, differential
current); sends trip signal to circuit breaker within cycles (milliseconds)
Security relevance: trip relay at wrong time = unnecessary outage;
inhibit relay trip = equipment damage (transformer saturation, arc flash)

Sandworm / Industroyer (Ukraine 2016, 2022):
  2016: ICS malware targeting Ukrainian power grid; targeted protection
  relays (SIEMENS, ABB, SEL, GE brands); used IEC 61850 GOOSE protocol
  to send unauthorized trip commands; caused 6-hour outage in Kiev
  Industroyer2 (2022): updated version targeting IEC 104 and IEC 61850;
  simultaneous relay trips at multiple substations coordinated via malware
  Physical effect: substation breakers opened; grid section de-energized;
  cascading potential if protection coordination disrupted

Protocol context:
  IEC 61850 GOOSE (Generic Object Oriented Substation Event): broadcast
  multicast; no authentication in original standard; high-speed relay
  coordination protocol; attackers can inject GOOSE frames on substation LAN
  IEC 104: SCADA protocol over TCP/IP; authentication optional (not always
  configured); carries control commands including relay trip/close

R01.LIFE-SAFETY classification (conditional):
  Ambient authority: substation LAN or SCADA network access
  Actuator: protection relay → circuit breaker
  Life-safety: arc flash from forced breaker close under load;
  medical equipment loss during hospital outage; cascading blackout (indirect)
  Note: direct immediate life-safety effect requires specific conditions;
  indirect large-scale blackout creates life-safety conditions at population scale

PATTERNS CUMULATIVE: 144 (36.1-36.4)
Pattern 35.5 → formalized as 36.2 (confirmed 3 instances)
