CYCLE 40 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN ENUMERATION & GAP IDENTIFICATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 339 domains | 233 gaps (pre-cycle 39 additions)

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.A: SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK TAXONOMY
  [D340] Build pipeline compromise (SolarWinds SUNBURST 2020)
    Attacker modified Orion build system; malicious DLL signed with legitimate
    SolarWinds certificate; distributed to ~18,000 customers. Active for 9 months
    before detection (FireEye breach, Dec 2020).
  [D341] Open source dependency confusion (Alex Birsan 2021)
    Uploaded packages to public npm/PyPI/RubyGems with same names as internal
    packages of Apple, Microsoft, Uber, Tesla. Package managers prefer higher
    version; public package executed in internal build pipelines.
  [D342] Typosquatting package attacks
    Malicious packages with near-identical names to popular packages: 'colourama'
    (vs. 'colorama'); 'crossenv' (vs. 'cross-env'). PyPI removes 100s annually.
  [D343] XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094)
    ~2 years of social engineering: 'JiaT75' gained commit access via trust-building
    contributions. Inserted backdoor in liblzma (xz-utils 5.6.0/5.6.1). Targeted
    systemd-linked sshd (Debian/Fedora). Intercepted RSA key operations to allow
    authentication bypass. Caught by Andres Freund via performance anomaly (500ms
    sshd latency regression). Unprecedented sophistication and patience.
  [D344] CI/CD pipeline poisoning
    GitHub Actions workflow injection: pull request from fork executes in privileged
    context if workflow uses github.event.pull_request.head.sha without restriction.
    Allows exfiltration of repository secrets. Jenkins: Groovy script execution in
    untrusted pipeline definitions. GitLab: protected vs. unprotected branch secret
    scoping.
  [D345] Container image supply chain
    DockerHub: malicious images in public registry (cryptomining, backdoors).
    Base image poisoning: popular base images (node:16, python:3.9) if registry
    compromised. Cosign/Sigstore: image signing to detect tampering.

GAP: G249 [NEW] — Supply chain attack full taxonomy: build, distribution, runtime
  GAP: G250 [NEW] — XZ backdoor: full technical analysis of liblzma backdoor mechanism
  GAP: G251 [NEW] — SLSA framework (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts)
  GAP: G252 [NEW] — Sigstore/Cosign adoption rates; software signing ecosystem

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.B: MEMORY SAFETY AND LANGUAGE MIGRATION
  [D346] Memory safety vulnerability class
    C/C++ undefined behavior: buffer overflow, use-after-free, double-free,
    null pointer dereference, integer overflow, format string. ~70% of CVEs in
    Chrome, Android, Windows involve memory safety (Google/Microsoft research).
    Root cause: manual memory management without bounds checking.
  [D347] Rust memory safety model
    Ownership system: each value has exactly one owner. Borrowing: references
    (shared &T or exclusive &mut T) with lifetime guarantees. No use-after-free:
    compiler enforces lifetime; borrow checker prevents dangling references.
    No data races: &mut T is exclusive. No buffer overflows: Vec/slice indexing
    bounds-checked at runtime (panic, not UB). unsafe blocks: explicit opt-out,
    auditable.
  [D348] Memory-safe migration in critical software
    Linux kernel: Rust support merged in 6.1 (Dec 2022). First Rust drivers in
    mainline. Android: 0 memory safety vulnerabilities in Rust code (Google 2024
    data). Windows: Microsoft Rust adoption in kernel components. Chrome: Rust
    in Chromium (select components). NSA guidance (2022): recommends memory-safe
    languages (Rust, Go, Java, Swift, C#, Python) over C/C++.
  [D349] Go memory model and garbage collection tradeoffs
    Go: garbage-collected; no manual free. Memory safe by default. Tradeoffs:
    GC pauses (latency-sensitive applications); no RAII; CGO reintroduces
    unsafe. Go is memory-safe for pure Go code; CGO interaction is escape hatch.
  [D350] Java/JVM memory safety and deserialization
    JVM provides memory safety (no raw pointers). Deserialization (ObjectInputStream):
    Java gadget chains allow RCE despite memory safety. Apache Commons Collections,
    Spring, Jackson gadgets. Memory safety does not prevent logic vulnerabilities.
    Contrast with Rust: Rust prevents memory unsafety but does not prevent
    logic errors in safe code.

GAP: G253 [NEW] — Memory-safe language adoption velocity in critical infrastructure
  GAP: G254 [NEW] — Rust unsafe code audit practices; percentage of unsafe in production Rust
  GAP: G255 [NEW] — Java deserialization gadget chain taxonomy (ysoserial)

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.C: CONTAINER AND KUBERNETES SECURITY DEPTH
  [D351] Container escape via privileged mode
    Privileged container (--privileged): full host capabilities, /dev access,
    host network namespace. Mount host filesystem: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt; chroot.
    Full host compromise in one privileged container. Defense: never run
    privileged unless absolutely required; use specific capability grants instead.
  [D352] Kubernetes API server as control plane SPOF
    unauthenticated kube-apiserver: CVE-2018-1002105 (privilege escalation via
    aggregated API). Etcd without auth (pre-2019 defaults): direct read/write of
    all cluster secrets. Shodan searches historically revealed 100s of exposed
    etcd instances with cluster admin credentials.
  [D353] Kubernetes RBAC misconfigurations
    Common errors: wildcard verbs/resources; cluster-admin to service accounts;
    namespace escape via cluster-scoped resources; pods/exec permission enables
    arbitrary code execution in any pod.
  [D354] Service mesh security (Istio, Linkerd)
    mTLS between services: prevents eavesdropping on east-west traffic.
    Authorization policies: fine-grained pod-to-pod access control.
    Complexity: misconfigured Istio policy can silently allow all traffic (PeerAuthentication
    in PERMISSIVE mode = no encryption required). Security through correct configuration.
  [D355] OPA/Gatekeeper admission control
    Open Policy Agent: Rego-based policy for Kubernetes admission. Prevents
    privileged containers, host network, missing resource limits, latest image tags.
    Gap: admission control runs at create time; running containers not re-evaluated
    unless Kyverno or similar applies continuous enforcement.

GAP: G256 [NEW] — Container runtime vulnerability history (runc CVEs: CVE-2019-5736)
  GAP: G257 [NEW] — Kubernetes CIS benchmark adoption rates in production clusters

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.D: CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROTOCOL FAILURES
  [D356] TLS downgrade attacks
    POODLE (CVE-2014-3566): SSL 3.0 CBC padding oracle; MITM forces SSL 3.0
    fallback. BEAST (CVE-2011-3389): TLS 1.0 CBC IV predictability. DROWN
    (CVE-2016-0800): SSLv2 cross-protocol attack on TLS 1.2. FREAK: export-grade
    RSA key forced. LOGJAM: DHE 512-bit export cipher forced.
    Pattern: each TLS version retains legacy cipher suites for compatibility;
    each creates downgrade path. MITM forces downgrade to weakest supported.
  [D357] TLS 1.3 removal of downgrade paths
    TLS 1.3: eliminated: RSA key exchange, CBC mode, RC4, MD5, SHA-1, export
    ciphers, compression, renegotiation. Only ECDHE key exchange (forward secrecy).
    Only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Downgrade sentinel in
    ServerHello.random prevents version rollback. Significant security improvement.
    Adoption: ~70% of TLS traffic by 2024 (Cloudflare data).
  [D358] Certificate transparency and pinning
    CT (RFC 6962): all publicly trusted certificates must be logged in append-only
    logs. Browsers require SCTs (Signed Certificate Timestamps). Catches misissued
    certificates within hours. DigiNotar (2011): CA compromise; fraudulent Google/
    CIA certs issued; detected via CT (retroactively; CT didn't exist but
    illustrates why it was needed).
    HPKP (HTTP Public Key Pinning): deprecated (Chrome 2018); too many production
    outages from misconfiguration. Replaced by CT monitoring.

GAP: G258 [NEW] — TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated but still present in ICS/SCADA systems
  GAP: G259 [NEW] — Certificate Transparency ecosystem: log operators, enforcement

DOMAIN BLOCK 40.E: HARDWARE SECURITY PRIMITIVES
  [D359] Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
    TPM 2.0 (ISO/IEC 11889): hardware security chip. Functions: secure key storage
    (RSA, ECC, symmetric); attestation (TPM quote: sign platform state with TPM
    key); sealing (encrypt data to PCR state: only accessible if platform
    configuration matches). Used by: BitLocker (PCR-based disk encryption),
    Secure Boot measurement, UEFI attestation, Windows Hello (key storage).
  [D360] TPM attacks
    Physical attacks: TPM bus sniffing (LPC bus on older systems): BitLocker key
    extractable if TPM communicates without encryption. CVE-2023-1017/1018: TPM2.0
    library buffer overflow. Spectre-class attacks against TPM context: indirect.
    Design limit: TPM proves hardware state, not software correctness. A compromised
    OS that can measure itself into PCRs (rollback attack) defeats sealing.
  [D361] Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions)
    Hardware enclave: isolated memory region (EPC). Code and data encrypted by CPU;
    not accessible to OS, hypervisor, or other processes even with ring-0 access.
    Remote attestation: CPU produces signed report of enclave measurement.
    Attacks: Foreshadow (CVE-2018-3615): L1TF extracts SGX enclave data.
    SGXPectre: Spectre variant targeting SGX. Plundervolt: voltage glitching
    corrupts SGX computations. Intel deprecated SGX on consumer CPUs (2021 11th gen).
  [D362] ARM TrustZone
    Two execution worlds: Normal World (rich OS: Android, Linux) and Secure World
    (Trusted Execution Environment: TEE). Secure monitor mode (EL3) mediates.
    Keymaster/Keymint: Android TEE component for key storage. Attacks: TZAR,
    TrustKit, TZBot: vulnerabilities in TEE implementations (Samsung, Qualcomm,
    Huawei) allowing Normal World breakout into Secure World. TEE implementation
    security is highly variable across vendors.

GAP: G260 [NEW] — TPM adoption in Windows 11 deployment context
  GAP: G261 [NEW] — ARM TrustZone vulnerability history across vendor implementations

CYCLE 40 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING

PATTERN ANALYSIS — NEW DOMAINS (Cycle 40):

[P40.1] Supply chain as R06.ARCH ultimate form
  R06.ARCH: system architecture encodes implicit trust that attackers leverage.
  Supply chain attacks exploit the deepest architectural trust: the build
  process itself. SolarWinds SUNBURST: the update trust (customers trust signed
  updates from their vendor) is the attack vector. XZ Utils: the contribution
  trust (maintainers trust well-established contributors) is the attack vector.
  Dependency confusion: the package resolution trust (package manager trusts
  semantic versioning to select highest version) is the attack vector.
  PATTERN 40.1: SUPPLY CHAIN AS TRUST INVERSION — the more trusted a software
  delivery channel, the higher its value as an attack vector and the lower
  the per-delivery inspection rate.
  Instances: SolarWinds (update channel), XZ Utils (contributor trust),
  dependency confusion (version resolution trust), CI/CD pipeline (build system
  trust), npm typosquatting (package name trust).
  Root: R06.ARCH (trust architecture), R07 (institutional trust)
  Relationship to LAW-1: supply chain attack surface is LAW-1 because the
  installed base of dependent software cannot be audited or replaced on security
  timescales.

[P40.2] Memory safety migration as LAW-1 attacker transition
  ~70% of critical CVEs (Chrome, Android, Windows) are memory safety bugs in C/C++.
  Rust eliminates this class at the language level (borrow checker). Migration
  trajectory: Linux 6.1 (2022), Android zero memory safety CVEs in Rust code (2024),
  Windows kernel Rust adoption. PATTERN 40.2: MEMORY SAFETY LANGUAGE MIGRATION IS
  LAW-1 ON THE DEFENDER SIDE — the existing C/C++ codebase (billions of lines)
  cannot be rewritten on security timescales; migration is incremental (new code
  in Rust, existing code remains). Attackers will shift to: (a) remaining C/C++
  components; (b) logic vulnerabilities in memory-safe code (deserialization,
  injection, auth bypass); (c) Rust unsafe blocks.
  This mirrors Pattern 33.3 (defense layer creates new perimeter): Rust
  creates a new perimeter; attacker finds the gap (unsafe blocks, C/C++ interface
  via FFI, CGO, JNI).

[P40.3] TLS 1.3 as legacy cipher elimination — and the ICS residual
  TLS 1.3 eliminates all historic downgrade attack classes (POODLE, BEAST, DROWN,
  FREAK, LOGJAM) by removing the vulnerable cipher suites entirely.
  This is the correct remediation pattern: don't add countermeasures to weak
  ciphers; remove them. Adoption: ~70% of internet TLS traffic.
  RESIDUAL: ICS/SCADA environments (power grid, water, manufacturing) operate
  on 10-20 year hardware cycles. TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated in browser/cloud context
  by 2020; still present in industrial control environments. G258 captures this.
  Pattern: TLS 1.3 adoption follows Pattern 36.2 exactly — clear demarcation
  between new deployments (TLS 1.3) and legacy operational technology (TLS 1.0/1.1
  or no TLS).

[P40.4] Hardware security as defense-in-depth floor
  TPM, SGX, TrustZone: hardware primitives that create security guarantees below
  software's ability to compromise. PATTERN 40.4: HARDWARE SECURITY ROOT OF TRUST
  IS NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT — hardware attestation proves platform state
  but not platform correctness; TEE implementations introduce their own attack
  surface (Foreshadow for SGX; TrustZone vendor bugs).
  The defense-in-depth model: hardware trust (TPM/TEE) + OS security (kernel) +
  application security (memory safety) + network security (TLS 1.3, mTLS) +
  identity (MFA, phishing-resistant). Each layer independently necessary;
  none sufficient alone. Attacker need only find one gap.

[P40.5] XZ Utils as slow-burn supply chain (R09.3 archetype)
  R09.3: long-duration advanced persistent threat (APT) with patient preparation.
  XZ Utils backdoor: ~2 years of contributor trust-building before malicious
  commit. This is the longest-documented supply chain trust-building timeline
  in open source. Contrast: SolarWinds SUNBURST (build system compromise, no
  contributor deception needed). XZ represents a third supply chain attack class:
  legitimate contributor becomes malicious actor. No technical control (code
  review, CI) catches this if the reviewer trusts the contributor.
  IMPLICATION: open source security model (many eyes) assumes reviewers are
  adversarially skeptical; in practice, trust accumulation defeats this.

PATTERN LIBRARY UPDATE:
  P40.1: SUPPLY CHAIN AS TRUST INVERSION — CONFIRMED (5 instances)
  P40.2: MEMORY SAFETY MIGRATION AS LAW-1 DEFENDER SIDE — NEW
  P40.3: TLS 1.3 CIPHER ELIMINATION (with ICS residual per Pattern 36.2) — NEW
  P40.4: HARDWARE TRUST NECESSARY NOT SUFFICIENT — NEW
  P40.5: XZ SLOW-BURN CONTRIBUTOR COMPROMISE — NEW (R09.3 archetype)

CROSS-PATTERN CONNECTIONS:
  P40.1 + R06.ARCH: supply chain as architectural trust exploitation
  P40.2 + Pattern 33.3: Rust adoption creates new perimeter (7th Pattern 33.3
    instance candidate: Rust/unsafe as new edge; attacker migrates to FFI/unsafe)
  P40.3 + Pattern 36.2: 5th instance of regulatory/mandate-driven production/legacy split
  P40.5 + R09.3: slow-burn APT pattern extended to open source contributor model

Pattern 33.3 CANDIDATE (8th instance): Rust memory safety adoption as new defense
  layer; adversarial response: targeting unsafe blocks, FFI boundaries, C/C++
  interop. Not yet confirmed — needs adversarial exploitation evidence in Rust
  unsafe specifically. Tracking as PROVISIONAL.

Pattern 36.2 STATUS: 5 confirmed instances:
  (1) Automotive: AUTOSAR SecOC mandate
  (2) Aviation: ICAO ATN/IPS for CPDLC
  (3) Medical: IEC 62443 medical device security
  (4) Cloud: AWS IMDSv2 enforcement
  (5) Network protocols: TLS 1.3 mandate (NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2; RFC 8996 deprecates TLS 1.0/1.1)

ANATOMY G250 [NEW]: XZ UTILS BACKDOOR — TECHNICAL MECHANISM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: CVE-2024-3094 liblzma backdoor in xz-utils 5.6.0/5.6.1
DOMAIN: Open source supply chain / binary backdoor
ROOT MECHANICS: R06.ARCH (contributor trust architecture), R09.3 (APT patience)

LAYER 1 — ACTOR AND TIMELINE:
  Threat actor: 'JiaT75' (Jia Tan). First contribution to xz-utils: Oct 2021.
  Pattern: initially small, high-quality patches. Built trust over 2 years.
  Gained commit access from maintainer Lasse Collin (overwhelmed, health issues).
  Parallel pressure campaign: sockpuppet accounts 'Jigar Kumar', 'Dennis Ens'
    pressured Lasse to add co-maintainer. Social engineering at meta-level.
  Malicious commits: Feb/March 2024. Backdoor in 5.6.0 (Feb 24), refined in
  5.6.1 (March 9). Discovered by Andres Freund: March 29, 2024.

LAYER 2 — TECHNICAL MECHANISM:
  Target: systemd-linked sshd on Debian/Fedora (uses libsystemd -> liblzma).
  Note: sshd does NOT directly use liblzma; the link is indirect via systemd.

STAGE A — Build system injection:
    Malicious code hidden in test files (binary test data: good1.xz, bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz).
    Build script (m4/build-to-host.m4) extracts and executes payload during
    'configure' step. Activated ONLY on Debian/RPM package builds (checks
    $srcdir contains 'debian' or 'rpm' in path). Bypasses developer builds.

STAGE B — Library injection:
    Injected code modifies liblzma.so at build time. Hooks RSA_public_decrypt
    in OpenSSL (via IFUNC resolver, which runs before main()). The hook:
    (1) checks if connecting process is sshd
    (2) if yes, inspects the Ed448 public key in the connection
    (3) if key matches attacker's private key, allows authentication bypass

STAGE C — Authentication bypass mechanism:
    Normal: sshd calls RSA_public_decrypt to verify host key. Backdoor intercepts
    this call. Attacker connects with specially crafted key that passes the
    backdoor's check. RSA_public_decrypt returns success regardless of actual
    cryptographic result. Attacker achieves pre-auth RCE as root without valid
    credentials.
    Only attacker with backdoor private key can exploit (access restricted to
    actor who planted backdoor). Not generic RCE for all.

LAYER 3 — DETECTION AVOIDANCE:
  Binary blob in test files: not code, passes casual review. Build script
  complexity obfuscated. Activation only on distribution builds (developers
  building from source not affected). IFUNC resolver timing (before main())
  bypasses some dynamic analysis tools. Polyglot binary test file: valid xz
  file AND contains payload.

LAYER 4 — DISCOVERY:
  Andres Freund (Microsoft engineer) noticed 500ms latency regression in SSH
  logins on Fedora Rawhide. Investigated: CPU usage spike in sshd. Traced to
  liblzma. Binary analysis: found IFUNC hook. Reported to oss-security mailing
  list. Disclosure to coordinators: same day. Package pulled within 24 hours.
  Discovered by accident — not by security audit.

LAYER 5 — SYSTEMIC IMPLICATIONS:
  [A] Open source trust model failure: maintainer health/burnout as attack
      surface. JiaT75 exploited Lasse's overwhelmed state.
  [B] Code review bypass: malicious code in binary test data; not human-readable.
  [C] Supply chain depth: sshd -> libsystemd -> liblzma; 3 hops from target
      to backdoored library. Attackers understand dependency graphs.
  [D] Package vs. source security: distribution packages built differently
      from source; attack only activates in distribution context.
  [E] SLSA counterfactual: SLSA level 3+ (build system provenance) would not
      have prevented this; attacker had commit access and modified build scripts.
      SLSA level 4 (two-person review) might have caught the binary test files.

CONVERGENCE:
  P40.1 (trust inversion): contributor trust is the attack vector, not code trust.
  R09.3: 2-year patience is the operational signature of nation-state supply chain.
  LAW-1: xz-utils is a deeply embedded transitive dependency; not easily replaceable.
  R06.ARCH: the IFUNC resolver mechanism (runs before main()) was an unintended
    attack surface created by the dynamic linking architecture.
STATUS: G250 CLOSED

ANATOMY G249 [NEW]: SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK FULL TAXONOMY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Classification of software supply chain attack classes
DOMAIN: Supply chain security
ROOT MECHANICS: R06.ARCH, R07 (institutional trust), R09

TAXONOMY:

CLASS 1 — BUILD SYSTEM COMPROMISE:
  Attack: modify build pipeline, CI/CD system, or build tooling to inject
  malicious code into software artifacts.
  Examples: SolarWinds SUNBURST (Orion build server); 3CX (signed binary
    with malicious DLL, 2023); Codecov (bash uploader script replaced, 2021).
  Detection: binary artifact signing with build provenance (SLSA); reproducible
    builds (hash of build environment + source = hash of output).

CLASS 2 — CONTRIBUTOR COMPROMISE:
  Attack: gain legitimate commit access; insert malicious code as trusted
  contributor.
  Sub-classes:
    2A: Account takeover (stolen credentials, phished maintainer)
    2B: Social engineering (XZ Utils; build trust over time)
    2C: Insider threat (legitimate contributor turns malicious)
    2D: Abandoned project squatting (acquire dormant package ownership)
  Detection: 2-person review for sensitive paths; binary blob prohibition;
    build script review; maintainer identity verification.

CLASS 3 — DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL ATTACK:
  Attack: inject malicious package into package registry or distribution channel.
  Sub-classes:
    3A: Typosquatting (colourama vs. colorama)
    3B: Dependency confusion (public package overrides private package name)
    3C: Registry compromise (attacker gains write access to registry)
    3D: Mirror poisoning (compromise package mirror/CDN)
  Detection: private registry with allowlist; package name reservation;
    package integrity verification (hash pinning, Sigstore).

CLASS 4 — RUNTIME DEPENDENCY ATTACK:
  Attack: compromise a dependency already in production.
  Examples: event-stream (npm package, malicious update by new maintainer, 2018);
    ua-parser-js (npm, account takeover, cryptominer injected, 2021);
    node-ipc (protest-ware: nuked files on Russian/Belarusian IPs, 2022).
  Detection: dependency pinning (exact version hashes); SBOM generation and
    monitoring; runtime anomaly detection.

CLASS 5 — COMPILER/TOOLCHAIN ATTACK:
  Attack: compromise the compiler or toolchain to inject malicious code into
  all compiled binaries.
  Ken Thompson (1984): 'Reflections on Trusting Trust' — modify compiler to
  recognize its own source code; insert backdoor in compiled compiler; backdoor
  self-propagates through compilation. Theoretical archetype; no confirmed
  large-scale deployment. Reproducible builds are the defense.

CROSS-CLASS PROPERTIES:
  All classes exploit trust at a specific layer of the supply chain.
  Defense requires trust verification at each layer: source (contributor identity),
  build (provenance attestation), distribution (signing + transparency log),
  deployment (SBOM + runtime monitoring).
  SLSA framework (Google): Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts.
  Sigstore: transparency log for software signing (Rekor log; Fulcio CA).
  These are in-kind responses: add auditability to each trust layer.

CONVERGENCE:
  R06.ARCH: every supply chain class is an architectural trust exploitation.
  P40.1 formalized as taxonomy.
  LAW-1: SBOM completeness problem — even with full SBOM, transitive dependencies
    are thousands deep; full audit is not feasible on security timescales.
STATUS: G249 CLOSED

ANATOMY G346_RUNC [NEW]: CONTAINER RUNTIME VULNERABILITIES (runc)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: runc container runtime escape vulnerabilities
DOMAIN: Container security / Linux security
ROOT MECHANICS: R01.NET (namespace boundaries), R06.ARCH

CVE-2019-5736 (runc overwrite):
  Mechanism: attacker controls container; during exec (docker exec or runc exec)
  into container, /proc/self/exe in container points to runc binary on host.
  Container process can overwrite runc binary while it executes (fd race).
  Overwrites with attacker binary. Next exec: attacker binary runs as root on host.
  Affected: runc < 1.0-rc6. Docker, containerd, CRI-O, LXC all affected.
  Severity: CVSS 8.6. Complete container escape to host root.

CVE-2021-30465 (symlink race in runc mount):
  Mechanism: race condition in runc's handling of bind mounts; symlink substitution
  during mount operation. Container can mount host path outside container root.

Architectural note: container isolation relies on Linux namespaces (PID, net,
  mount, IPC, UTS, user) + cgroups (resource limits) + seccomp (syscall filter)
  + AppArmor/SELinux (mandatory access control). runc is the thin layer
  between container definition and these kernel primitives. Vulnerabilities in
  runc bypass all namespace isolation with kernel-level access.

Defense trajectory: rootless containers (user namespace mapping; container
  root = unprivileged host user); gVisor (user-space kernel for containers;
  Google); Kata Containers (lightweight VM isolation; hardware boundary instead
  of namespace boundary).
STATUS: G256 CLOSED (partial; full runc CVE list deferred to G256 extended)

  Anatomies this cycle: G250 (XZ backdoor), G249 (supply chain taxonomy),
    G256-partial (runc container escape)
  Cumulative anatomies: 126
  Anatomy backlog: 10 (13 queued - 3 closed this cycle)
  Major: XZ Utils full technical mechanism documented (IFUNC hook, binary test
    blob, distribution-only activation, Ed448 auth bypass)
  Supply chain taxonomy: 5 classes with sub-classes; SLSA/Sigstore as defenses
  runc escape: namespace isolation as LAW-1 boundary; rootless/gVisor as responses

CYCLE 40 — STAGE 4: ATTACK/DEFENSE ENUMERATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 325 attacks | 445 defenses cumulative

[A326] SolarWinds-class build system compromise
  Mechanism: attacker compromises build server (CI/CD, TeamCity, Jenkins, Azure
  DevOps). Injects malicious DLL/code into artifact during compilation. Artifact
  signed with legitimate code signing certificate. Distributed via official update
  channel. No runtime anomaly at delivery — malicious code dormant until activated.
  Prerequisites: build server access (spear phish DevOps team, or build server
  vulnerability). Code signing key access (or signing happens automatically in
  pipeline).
  Impact: all customers who install update receive backdoored software.
  SolarWinds: ~18,000 customers; NOBELIUM accessed 9 US agencies.
  Root: R06.ARCH (update trust), R09.3

[A327] Dependency confusion package injection
  Mechanism: identify internal package name used by target org (leaked in error
  messages, GitHub repos, package-lock.json). Upload public package with same
  name and higher version to npm/PyPI/RubyGems. Package managers prefer public
  registry if version number is higher. Internal build pipeline downloads and
  executes malicious package.
  Prerequisites: knowledge of internal package names; account on public registry.
  Impact: code execution in target's build environment; credential theft, pivot.
  Alex Birsan 2021: affected Apple, Microsoft, Uber, Tesla, PayPal, 30+ others.
  Root: R06.ARCH (package resolution trust)

[A328] Container escape via privileged container
  Mechanism: privileged container has full host capabilities. Mount host /dev/sda1
  to /mnt inside container. chroot /mnt. Full host filesystem access as root.
  Alternatively: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash
  enters host namespaces directly.
  Prerequisites: container runs as privileged (--privileged flag).
  Impact: complete host OS compromise from within container.
  Root: R01.NET (namespace boundary violation), R06.ARCH

[A329] TLS downgrade via MITM (POODLE/LOGJAM class)
  Mechanism: MITM positions between client and server. Injects TCP RST to force
  TLS handshake failure. Client retries with lower protocol version (SSL 3.0 in
  POODLE; DHE_EXPORT in LOGJAM). MITM completes downgraded handshake. Decrypts
  traffic. POODLE: 256 requests average to recover 1 byte of CBC-encrypted data.
  Prerequisites: network MITM position (WiFi, BGP hijack, ARP spoofing).
  Impact: plaintext recovery of session cookies, auth tokens.
  Root: R10.4 (deprecated protocol retained for compatibility)

[A330] runc container escape (CVE-2019-5736)
  Mechanism: attacker in container; wait for exec operation (/proc/self/exe
  points to host runc binary). Open /proc/self/exe as writable fd in tight
  race loop. When runc opens container's /proc/self/exe, overwrite with malicious
  binary. Next exec: malicious binary executes as root on host.
  Prerequisites: ability to execute processes in container; runc < 1.0-rc6.
  Impact: full host OS compromise from any container sharing this runc binary.
  Root: R06.ARCH (TOCTOU race in container runtime design)

ATTACKS CUMULATIVE: 330

[D446] SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework
  Levels: L1 (build process documented), L2 (hosted build, signed provenance),
  L3 (hardened build: hermetic, isolated, reproducible), L4 (two-person review
  for all changes). L3 prevents most build system compromises; L4 catches
  malicious contributor changes in binary test files.
  Adoption: Google internal (all products target SLSA 3+); GitHub Actions SLSA
  generator; CNCF ecosystem. Limitation: compliance requires ecosystem buy-in
  across all dependencies.
  Addresses: A326, A327, supply chain attack class

[D447] Sigstore / Rekor transparency log for software signing
  Mechanism: Fulcio CA issues short-lived (10-minute) certificate tied to OIDC
  identity (GitHub Actions, Google, Microsoft). Cosign signs container image
  or binary. Signature + certificate recorded in Rekor (append-only transparency
  log, Trillian-based). Verifier checks: valid cert at signing time + Rekor
  inclusion proof.
  Advantage over PGP keyring: no long-term key management; identity tied to
  OIDC; log provides audit trail.
  Addresses: A327, distribution channel integrity

[D448] Rootless containers (user namespace isolation)
  Mechanism: container 'root' maps to unprivileged host UID (e.g., UID 1000).
  Even if escape occurs, attacker has only unprivileged host access. Requires
  kernel user namespace support. Podman: rootless by default. Docker: rootless
  mode available since 20.10.
  Limitation: some applications require real root; user namespace bugs in kernel
  can be exploited to escalate (multiple historical CVEs).
  Addresses: A328, A330, container escape class (reduces impact)

[D449] TLS 1.3 enforcement + legacy protocol deprecation
  Mechanism: disable TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2 cipher suites with known weaknesses.
  Nginx: ssl_protocols TLSv1.3. Apache: SSLProtocol TLSv1.3. TLS 1.3 has no
  CBC mode, no RSA key exchange, no export ciphers — removes all downgrade paths.
  NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2: mandates TLS 1.2+ for federal systems; TLS 1.3 preferred.
  ICS gap: Modbus/TCP, DNP3, PROFINET do not natively support TLS; IEC 62351
  adds TLS to industrial protocols. Adoption: slow in OT environments.
  Addresses: A329, TLS downgrade class

[D450] Reproducible builds
  Mechanism: given identical source + build environment specification, build
  output is bit-for-bit identical. Allows independent verification: two parties
  build from same source; compare hashes; any discrepancy indicates tampering.
  Projects: Debian reproducible builds (77% of packages, 2024); Tor Browser;
  Bitcoin Core. Defense against: CLASS 1 (build system) and CLASS 5 (compiler)
  supply chain attacks.
  Limitation: requires deterministic build system; many builds are not naturally
  reproducible (timestamps, random seeds, non-deterministic linkers).
  Addresses: A326, build pipeline compromise class

DEFENSES CUMULATIVE: 450

STAGE 4 SUMMARY:
  New attacks: 5 (A326-A330) | Cumulative: 330
  New defenses: 5 (D446-D450) | Cumulative: 450
  Milestone: defenses reach 450
  Supply chain: SLSA + Sigstore + reproducible builds as three-layer defense
  Container: rootless as impact-reduction; TLS 1.3 eliminates downgrade class entirely

CYCLE 40 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE & META-PATTERN EVOLUTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 284 convergence findings cumulative

[CF285] Supply chain as the outermost ring of defense-in-depth — and its collapse
  Defense-in-depth model: perimeter -> network -> endpoint -> application -> data.
  Supply chain sits OUTSIDE this model: if the software itself is compromised
  before deployment, no runtime defense catches it. Endpoint detection cannot
  distinguish signed malicious code from signed legitimate code (same certificate).
  Application monitoring cannot catch backdoors with deliberate dormancy.
  This is the architectural implication of P40.1: supply chain attacks bypass
  the entire defense-in-depth stack because they operate at the trust root.
  The only defenses at this layer are pre-deployment: provenance attestation
  (SLSA), signing transparency (Sigstore), reproducible builds, contributor
  identity verification.

[CF286] Memory safety migration as generational security debt reduction
  ~70% of critical vulnerabilities in C/C++ codebases are memory safety bugs.
  Rust eliminates this class entirely for safe code. The transition is generational:
  new code written in Rust accumulates safety debt at near-zero rate; existing
  C/C++ code continues to accumulate. Net effect over 20 years: as Rust fraction
  grows, the proportion of memory safety CVEs drops. This is the slowest possible
  remediation (rewrite-as-you-go) but the only feasible one given LAW-1 (existing
  codebase size). Android data (Google 2024): 0 memory safety CVEs in Rust
  components vs. ongoing CVEs in C/C++ components — empirical confirmation of
  the model.

[CF287] R10.6 threshold refinement — convergence with CF280
  CF280 (C39S5): proposed R10.6-THRESHOLD — action-enabling vs. information-only.
  Supply chain analysis adds nuance: XZ backdoor is R10.6 in a different register —
  the 'feature' is contributor commit access (legitimate); the security context
  mismatch is that commit access enables backdoor insertion, not just code contribution.
  This does not require a technical feature; it requires a process/institutional
  feature (contributor trust) to mismatch with security requirements.
  R10.6 broadens: 'feature' includes: technical features (JNDI, pickle, eval()),
  architectural features (IMDS, ACARS broadcast), and institutional features
  (contributor trust, update trust).
  This broadening does not weaken R10.6; it strengthens it by removing the
  arbitrary limit to 'technical features only.'

[CF288] The reproducible builds problem as LAW-1 instance
  Reproducible builds solve the build system compromise class. But reproducible
  builds require: deterministic compilers, build environments, linkers, timestamps
  stripped, random seeds fixed. Debian: 77% of packages reproducible after years
  of effort. Remaining 23%: technically difficult (non-deterministic build systems,
  upstream packages without reproducibility support). This is LAW-1 at the build
  system level: the installed base of non-reproducible build pipelines cannot be
  made reproducible on security timescales.

[CF289] TLS 1.3 as proof of concept for 'eliminate, don't remediate'
  Pattern: when a class of vulnerabilities (POODLE, BEAST, DROWN, LOGJAM, FREAK)
  all stem from the same root (legacy cipher suite retention for compatibility),
  the correct response is to eliminate the root, not to add countermeasures.
  TLS 1.3 removes 492 cipher suites; retains 5. Removes RSA key exchange entirely.
  Removes CBC mode entirely. Result: the entire downgrade attack class is closed.
  This is in contrast to the dominant practice: patch individual CVEs within
  a broken-by-design system (TLS 1.0/1.1 had dozens of individual CVEs while
  the root cause — legacy cipher retention — remained).
  Contrast with memory safety: Rust eliminates the class; C/C++ patches individual
  CVEs. Same meta-pattern in two domains.
  PATTERN 40.6 (NEW): CLASS ELIMINATION IS MORE EFFECTIVE THAN INSTANCE REMEDIATION.
  Instances: TLS 1.3 (cipher class elimination), Rust (memory corruption class
  elimination), FIDO2 (phishing class elimination), ASLR+DEP (exploit reliability
  class reduction).

[CF290] Hardware TEE attack surface as meta-pattern
  Every hardware security primitive introduces its own attack surface:
    TPM: bus sniffing (LPC), rollback attacks, firmware bugs (CVE-2023-1017)
    SGX: Foreshadow, SGXPectre, Plundervolt, CacheOut
    TrustZone: vendor implementation bugs (Samsung, Qualcomm, Huawei TEEs)
    TPM+Secure Boot: measured boot proves configuration, not correctness; attacker
      who can modify measurements defeats sealing.
  META-PATTERN: every security primitive that provides a new guarantee creates
  a new attack surface targeting that guarantee. The primitive is not a solution;
  it shifts the attack target. Defense-in-depth requires that no single primitive
  is the sole trust anchor.

[CF291] Pattern 33.3 — 8th instance assessment (Rust/unsafe)
  Pattern 33.3: each new defense layer creates a new perimeter that becomes
  the attack target. Rust memory safety adoption candidate for 8th instance.
  Evidence needed: adversarial exploitation of Rust unsafe blocks or FFI boundaries
  at meaningful scale. Current state (2024-2026): Rust unsafe CVEs exist
  (e.g., CVE-2022-21658 in std::fs::remove_dir_all on Windows — race condition
  in safe API with unsafe internals); Rust soundness bugs tracked separately.
  But: systematic attacker targeting of Rust unsafe specifically (as opposed
  to finding bugs in Rust code that happen to use unsafe) is not yet documented
  at the same scale as prior Pattern 33.3 instances.
  STATUS: Pattern 33.3 instance 8 remains PROVISIONAL. Not yet CONFIRMED.
  Confirmation criterion: documented attacker tooling or exploit specifically
  targeting Rust unsafe blocks or Rust FFI boundaries as primary attack surface.

PATTERN 40.6 CONFIRMATION STATUS: CONFIRMED (4 instances cited above).
  TLS 1.3, Rust, FIDO2, ASLR+DEP all represent class elimination. Not just
  countermeasure addition. This is a design principle with empirical support.

CYCLE 41 — STAGE 1: DOMAIN ENUMERATION & GAP IDENTIFICATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 362 domains | 261 gaps

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.A: IDENTITY AND ACCESS — OAUTH/OIDC ATTACK SURFACE
  [D363] OAuth 2.0 authorization code interception
    PKCE bypass: servers that don't enforce PKCE allow authorization code theft.
    Attacker registers custom URI scheme or intercepting redirect URI. Auth code
    captured before client. RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.1): PKCE mandatory for all flows.
  [D364] Authorization code injection
    Victim clicks attacker-controlled link; attacker-controlled auth code injected
    into victim's session at redirect. Requires code_challenge binding missing.
    Defense: PKCE; state parameter; nonce in OIDC.
  [D365] OAuth token leakage via Referer header
    Access token in redirect URI fragment (implicit flow). Browser sends token
    in Referer header to third-party resources on the page.
    Defense: authorization code flow; token binding; strict Referer policy.
  [D366] OIDC provider confusion / issuer mismatch
    Multi-tenant OIDC: application accepts tokens from correct issuer but doesn't
    validate 'aud' claim. Attacker registers in same OIDC provider; obtains token
    for their own client_id; token valid for same issuer. Missing 'aud' validation
    = authentication bypass.
  [D367] OAuth SSRF via redirect_uri
    redirect_uri validation insufficient; attacker supplies internal URL. After
    auth flow, authorization server POSTs auth code to internal endpoint.
    Variant of SSRF via trusted server.

GAP: G262 [NEW] — OAuth implicit flow deprecation adoption rates
  GAP: G263 [NEW] — PKCE adoption in major OAuth implementations (2024)

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.B: DNS SECURITY ECOSYSTEM
  [D368] DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions)
    Signs DNS records with zone's private key. Verifying resolver checks signature
    chain to trust anchor (root zone). Prevents cache poisoning (Kaminsky attack,
    2008: birthday attack on DNS transaction ID). Deployed: .com zone signed 2011;
    root zone signed 2010. Adoption: ~30% of DNS resolvers validate DNSSEC (APNIC
    2024 data). Still not majority.
  [D369] DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT)
    DoH (RFC 8484): DNS queries over HTTPS (port 443). DoT (RFC 7858): DNS over
    TLS (port 853). Encrypt DNS traffic from client to resolver. Prevent ISP/network
    eavesdropping on DNS queries. Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8: major DoH
    resolvers. Firefox: DoH by default (US). Windows 11: DoH configurable.
    Limitation: DoH/DoT protect client-to-resolver; resolver-to-authoritative
    still uses plaintext DNS (unless DoT between resolvers).
  [D370] DNS cache poisoning (Kaminsky attack)
    Pre-DNSSEC: DNS transaction ID (16-bit) + source port randomization (16-bit)
    = 32-bit state. Birthday attack: send many forged responses; ~65,536 requests
    to have 50% chance of collision. Dan Kaminsky 2008: coordinated patching
    of all major DNS implementations simultaneously (classified until patch ready).
  [D371] DNS amplification DDoS
    Open resolver + small query (ANY record or DNSKEY) returns large response.
    Amplification factor: up to 100x. Attacker spoofs source IP of victim. Sends
    small queries to many open resolvers; victim receives 100x traffic.
    Defense: BCP 38 (network ingress filtering prevents IP spoofing); rate limiting
    on open resolvers; DNS Response Rate Limiting (RRL).
  [D372] DNS rebinding attack
    Attacker controls DNS for malicious domain. Short TTL. Phase 1: DNS resolves
    to external IP (attacker server; user visits site). Phase 2: DNS rebinds to
    internal IP (192.168.x.x). Same-origin policy allows JavaScript to now query
    internal resources. Bypasses browser same-origin policy without any SOP bug.
    Defense: DNS rebinding protection in routers/browsers; private IP blocking
    in DNS resolvers.

GAP: G264 [NEW] — DNSSEC adoption rates by TLD and resolver ecosystem (2024)
  GAP: G265 [NEW] — DoH/DoT deployment adoption: browser and OS defaults (2024)

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.C: HARDWARE ATTACKS — FAULT INJECTION TAXONOMY
  [D373] Voltage fault injection (VFI)
    Glitch supply voltage during sensitive computation (e.g., AES key schedule,
    signature verification). Induces instruction skip or data corruption.
    Used to: bypass secure boot signature check; extract AES keys via DFA
    (Differential Fault Analysis); bypass PIN attempt counters (ATM cards, HSMs).
    Hardware: ChipWhisperer (open source; ~$500). Commercial: Riscure Glitcher.
  [D374] Clock fault injection
    Glitch clock signal: processor executes partial instruction, skips, or
    loops incorrectly. Same effect as voltage glitch. Used against: smartcards,
    embedded MCUs, secure elements.
  [D375] Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI)
    Focused EM pulse at specific chip location. More targeted than voltage/clock
    glitch; can target specific functional blocks. Requires proximity; no
    physical contact needed with some configurations.
  [D376] Cold boot attack on DRAM
    DRAM contents persist for seconds to minutes after power loss (longer when
    cooled with compressed air or liquid nitrogen: minutes to hours).
    Attack: power off target; transplant RAM sticks or cool in place; boot from
    USB with cold boot tool; read memory. Extracts: AES keys (BitLocker),
    RSA private keys, disk encryption passphrases.
    Defense: TRESOR (key in CPU registers, never in DRAM); disk encryption
    key derivation requiring PIN on resume; MemGuard. Most disk encryption
    products now use authenticated resume (PIN required).
  [D377] Laser fault injection (LFI)
    Focused laser at decapped chip (removed package). Induces bit flips in
    specific SRAM cells. Most precise fault injection; used in high-value
    attacks on secure elements, smartcards, crypto hardware.
    Defense: light sensors in secure elements; active mesh over die; redundant
    computation paths.

GAP: G266 [NEW] — RowHammer as software-controlled fault injection (DRAM)
  GAP: G267 [NEW] — Secure element certification process (Common Criteria EAL5+)

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.D: NETWORK ATTACK SURFACE — BGP AND ROUTING
  [D378] BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) hijacking
    BGP: inter-AS routing protocol. Routers trust route announcements from peers.
    No cryptographic validation in base protocol.
    Attack: AS announces more-specific prefix than legitimate AS (more specific
    wins in route selection). Traffic hijacked to attacker AS.
    Historical incidents: Pakistan Telecom hijacking YouTube (2008, 30 minutes);
    Russian BGP hijack of Twitch/AWS (2020); Rostelecom hijacking >8000 prefixes
    (2020). China Telecom repeated incidents (Renesys/Dyn research).
  [D379] BGP route leak (unintentional hijack)
    BGP misconfiguration causes AS to announce routes it should not. Large AS
    (Cloudflare Incident 2019: Level 3 misconfiguration caused major outages).
    Google (2018): misconfigured BGP route via Nigeria caused rerouting of
    Google traffic through Russia/Nigeria (not intentional but real impact).
  [D380] RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure)
    Cryptographic attestation of IP prefix ownership. Route Origin Authorization
    (ROA): resource holder signs which AS can announce their prefix. Routers
    with RPKI-validating mode: reject INVALID routes (wrong AS for prefix).
    Adoption (2024): ~50% of global BGP prefixes have ROAs; ~40% of routers
    validate. Major providers (AT&T, NTT, ARIN, RIPE): RPKI enforced.
    Limitation: ROAs prevent origin hijacks; do not prevent AS path manipulation.
    BGPsec: full AS path signing; not widely deployed (performance concerns).
  [D381] BGP as critical infrastructure substrate
    All internet routing depends on BGP. A sufficiently large BGP hijack can
    intercept traffic destined for: certificate authority OCSP endpoints (bypass
    revocation), software update servers (inject malicious updates), financial
    clearing systems. BGP hijack + MITM + certificate misissuance = powerful
    combination. Demonstrated: 2018 BGP hijack of Let's Encrypt validation
    requests to obtain fraudulent certificates (MyEtherWallet incident).

GAP: G268 [NEW] — RPKI adoption velocity; full deployment timeline estimate
  GAP: G269 [NEW] — BGP security relationship with certificate issuance (CAA + BGP)

DOMAIN BLOCK 41.E: WEB APPLICATION SECURITY DEPTH
  [D382] HTTP request smuggling
    Discrepancy between front-end (CDN, reverse proxy) and back-end server in
    parsing Content-Length vs. Transfer-Encoding headers. Attacker crafts request
    that front-end treats as one request but back-end treats as two. Second
    partial request poisons back-end queue. Can poison other users' requests
    (cache poisoning, authentication bypass, XSS in others' sessions).
    James Kettle (PortSwigger) 2019: rediscovered and systematized.
  [D383] GraphQL security issues
    Introspection: by default exposes entire schema (all types, queries, mutations).
    Batching attacks: send array of queries; bypass per-query rate limiting.
    Circular query DoS: deeply nested circular queries consume exponential resources.
    Authorization: REST has resource-level auth; GraphQL resolvers must each
    independently enforce auth — commonly missed in complex schemas.
  [D384] Prototype pollution (JavaScript)
    JavaScript: all objects inherit from Object.prototype. If user input reaches
    object merge without sanitization, attacker can inject properties into
    prototype. Properties injected into __proto__ affect ALL subsequent objects.
    Server-side: prototype pollution -> code execution via property override in
    library code (e.g., lodash _.merge before 4.17.21). Client-side: XSS bypass.
  [D385] Server-side template injection (SSTI)
    Template engine (Jinja2, Freemarker, Thymeleaf, Pebble) evaluates user input
    as template code. Jinja2: {{7*7}} -> 49 (confirms injection). RCE:
    {{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}} traverses Python class hierarchy
    to reach subprocess.Popen. CVSS critical when confirmed.

GAP: G270 [NEW] — HTTP/2 request smuggling variants; HTTP/3 (QUIC) attack surface
  GAP: G271 [NEW] — GraphQL authorization frameworks (Strawberry shields, etc.)

CYCLE 41 — STAGE 2: PATTERN MAPPING

PATTERN ANALYSIS — NEW DOMAINS (Cycle 41):

[P41.1] BGP as unauthenticated routing substrate — LAW-1 + R04
  BGP was designed for cooperative routing between trusted ASes (1989). No
  authentication of route announcements in base protocol (R04: authentication
  absent by design). The installed base of BGP-speaking routers (hundreds of
  thousands of ASes worldwide) cannot be migrated to a new routing protocol
  on security timescales (LAW-1). RPKI is the retrofit: adds cryptographic
  ROA verification without replacing BGP. Adoption after 15+ years of RPKI
  availability: ~50% prefix coverage, ~40% router enforcement. This is the
  standard LAW-1 retrofit trajectory. BGPsec (full path signing): even slower
  adoption due to performance overhead.
  Pattern: BGP/RPKI is structurally identical to DNS/DNSSEC — both are
  unauthenticated broadcast protocols with cryptographic retrofit. Both show
  slow, incomplete adoption. R01 sub-class candidate: R01.ROUTING (unauthenticated
  routing announcements as broadcast vulnerability class).

[P41.2] OAuth implicit flow as deprecated R10.4 instance
  OAuth 2.0 implicit flow: tokens returned in URL fragment (visible in browser
  history, Referer headers, logs). RFC 6749 included implicit as optimization
  for client-side JS apps (no server needed). Security problems recognized;
  PKCE (RFC 7636, 2015) made code flow safe for public clients; implicit became
  unnecessary. RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.1, 2025): removes implicit flow entirely.
  PATTERN: R10.4 confirmed — implicit flow was the correct design given 2012
  technology; became deprecated when PKCE existed. Transition from implicit to
  PKCE-protected code flow follows Pattern 36.2: mandate creates split between
  new deployments (code + PKCE) and legacy (still using implicit or token-in-URL).

[P41.3] Fault injection as hardware-layer R10.5 extension
  R10.5 (CONFIRMED): hardware timing/power side channels from optimization.
  Fault injection (VFI, EMFI, LFI, cold boot) is the active variant: instead
  of observing side effects, attacker induces computational errors to extract
  or corrupt secrets.
  RELATIONSHIP: fault injection and side-channel attacks share the same substrate
  (hardware physics) but differ in direction: side-channel = passive observation;
  fault injection = active perturbation. Both exploit the gap between the
  mathematical security model (which assumes faithful computation) and the
  physical implementation (which has observable and corruptible physical state).
  Sub-taxonomy candidate: R10.5a (passive side-channel: timing, power, EM
  emanation) and R10.5b (active fault injection: voltage, clock, EM, laser,
  cold boot, RowHammer). RowHammer had been tentatively classified as R10.5b
  (state mutation); this classification is confirmed.

[P41.4] DNS amplification as architectural weaponization of legitimate feature
  DNS ANY record, large DNSSEC responses: designed for legitimate use (complete
  zone transfer, DNSSEC key fetching). Amplification attack weaponizes the
  legitimate response size differential. UDP spoofing enables source IP forgery.
  This is P40.1 (trust inversion) in a different key: not trust in the delivery
  channel, but trust in the response — amplification exploits the implicit
  assumption that DNS response recipients are the same entities as DNS requesters.
  R10.6 instance: DNS response amplification is a feature-security context mismatch.
  The 'feature': ANY record / large DNSSEC responses exist to serve legitimate
  clients. The 'security context mismatch': UDP connectionlessness allows source
  IP spoofing, turning response generation into a DDoS amplifier.

[P41.5] HTTP request smuggling as parsing discrepancy attack class
  HTTP/1.1 spec (RFC 7230) allows ambiguity: Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
  coexist; different implementations resolve the ambiguity differently.
  Attack: craft request that exploits this discrepancy between two deployed
  implementations in sequence (front-end proxy + back-end server).
  ROOT: R10.3 (interaction between two correct implementations). Both the front-end
  and back-end implement the spec; the vulnerability is in their interaction.
  This is a canonical R10.3 instance. Prior R10.3 examples: TLS session resumption
  across implementations; CSRF across browser+server. HTTP request smuggling adds
  a particularly severe web-tier R10.3 with cross-user impact.

PATTERN LIBRARY UPDATE:
  P41.1: BGP AS UNAUTHENTICATED ROUTING (R01.ROUTING candidate) — NEW
  P41.2: OAUTH IMPLICIT FLOW DEPRECATION (R10.4 + Pattern 36.2 instance 6) — NEW
  P41.3: FAULT INJECTION AS R10.5b (R10.5 sub-taxonomy formalized) — FORMALIZATION
  P41.4: DNS AMPLIFICATION AS R10.6 INSTANCE — NEW INSTANCE (not new pattern)
  P41.5: HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING AS R10.3 — CANONICAL INSTANCE

  (1) Automotive AUTOSAR SecOC, (2) Aviation ATN/IPS, (3) Medical IEC 62443,

ANATOMY G266 [NEW]: ROWHAMMER AS SOFTWARE-CONTROLLED FAULT INJECTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: DRAM RowHammer — bit flip induction via repeated memory access
DOMAIN: Hardware security / DRAM architecture
ROOT MECHANICS: R10.5b (active fault injection), R10.2 (correct impl, flawed spec)

LAYER 1 — PHYSICAL MECHANISM:
  DRAM cells: capacitors storing charge. Adjacent rows electrically coupled.
  Repeated access to one DRAM row ('hammering') disturbs charge in adjacent rows.
  Sufficient disturbance: bit flip in adjacent row (0->1 or 1->0).
  Threshold: ~140,000 accesses per 64ms refresh interval (original DDR3 study).
  Faster hardware: threshold decreases with newer DRAM density (worse problem).

LAYER 2 — ATTACK TAXONOMY:
  Single-sided RowHammer: hammer one row; flip bits in adjacent row.
  Double-sided RowHammer: hammer rows A and C; target row B between them.
    Higher success rate; more reliable flip location.
  One-location RowHammer: some DRAM modules susceptible to hammering from
    single location (vendor-specific).
  Blacksmith (2021): non-uniform hammering patterns bypass TRR (Target Row
    Refresh, DDR4 mitigation). Proved DDR4 still vulnerable despite TRR.
  Half-Double (Google 2021): rows at distance 2 also susceptible (not just
    immediately adjacent).
  SMASH (2021): bypass CLFLUSH restrictions; hammer from JavaScript (no privs).

LAYER 3 — EXPLOITATION:
  [A] Privilege escalation: page table entry (PTE) flip. Flip bit in PTE of
      attacker's process to point to privileged physical page. OS maps attacker
      read/write access to arbitrary memory. CVE-2015-0565 (Linux KSM exploit).
  [B] VM escape: flip bit in page table of hypervisor; guest VM gains access
      to host physical memory. Demonstrated against Xen (2016).
  [C] Browser sandbox escape: SMASH demonstrated from JavaScript in Chrome.
      No native code required; pure JavaScript induced bit flips.
  [D] Mobile: RAMpage (CVE-2018-9442) on Android devices. Gained root from
      unprivileged app via DRAM bit flip in ION memory subsystem.
  [E] Network: Throwhammer (2018) demonstrated RowHammer via remote DMA (RDMA)
      network operations (not requiring local code execution on target).

LAYER 4 — MITIGATION HISTORY:
  ECC (Error-Correcting Code) DRAM: single-bit error correction. Does not
    prevent RowHammer; attacker induces 3+ bit flips to defeat ECC.
    Double-sided RowHammer achieves 3+ flips reliably on vulnerable modules.
  TRR (Target Row Refresh, DDR4): DRAM internal mechanism; counts hammer
    accesses; refreshes adjacent rows. Blacksmith (2021) bypassed all tested
    TRR implementations with non-uniform patterns.
  PRAM/HBM (different memory technologies): not susceptible to RowHammer
    by physical design. Not mainstream in general-purpose systems.
  JEDEC LPDDR5 / DDR5: PARP (Per-Row Activation Counting) and RFM (Refresh
    Management) — hardware-based mitigations; effectiveness under evaluation.
  Practical defense state: DDR4 systems remain partially vulnerable;
    DDR5 mitigation effectiveness TBD; legacy DDR3 largely unmitigated.

LAYER 5 — ROOT MECHANICS INTERSECTION:
  R10.5b: RowHammer IS fault injection — software-accessible fault injection
    without physical access. The 'physical attack made software-accessible'
    property is what makes it uniquely dangerous: traditional fault injection
    (VFI, EMFI, LFI) requires physical access. RowHammer requires only code
    execution (including JavaScript in browser).
  R10.2: DRAM manufacturers implement JEDEC spec correctly; the spec's refresh
    interval assumption (rows electrically isolated at DRAM densities of the
    era) became false as density increased. Correct implementation, flawed
    specification (spec was written for lower-density DRAM).

CONVERGENCE:
  RowHammer: the point at which hardware physics intrudes into software security
    without physical access. Software security model assumes memory is correct;
    RowHammer violates this assumption from software layer.
  LAW-1: installed base of DDR3/DDR4 DRAM cannot be replaced on security
    timescales. Billions of devices affected.
STATUS: G266 CLOSED

ANATOMY G268 [NEW]: RPKI ADOPTION AND BGP SECURITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: Resource Public Key Infrastructure adoption velocity and gap analysis
DOMAIN: Internet routing security
ROOT MECHANICS: R04 (authentication absent), LAW-1 (installed base)

LAYER 1 — RPKI ARCHITECTURE:
  Trust anchors: five RIRs (ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) each
  operate their own trust anchor. Each RIR certifies address space holders.
  Resource certificate: issued to AS owner; certifies IP prefix ownership.
  ROA (Route Origin Authorization): AS owner creates ROA stating: 'AS XXXXX
    is authorized to originate prefix P.P.P.P/N (max-length M).'
  Validating router: fetches ROAs from RIR repository; marks BGP routes as
    VALID (matches ROA), INVALID (wrong AS), or NOT FOUND (no ROA).
  Policy: INVALID routes can be dropped or de-preferred; NOT FOUND: depends
    on operator policy.

LAYER 2 — ADOPTION STATE (2024):
  ROAs created: ~50% of globally routed IPv4 prefixes have ROAs (RIPE RIS data).
  Origin validation (OV) enforcement: ~40% of BGP routers perform validation;
    subset drops INVALID routes (rather than just marking).
  Major ISPs enforcing RPKI: AT&T, Comcast, NTT, Telia, Deutsche Telekom,
    ARIN, RIPE NCC internal networks.
  NOT enforcing: significant fraction of tier-2 and tier-3 ISPs globally.

LAYER 3 — WHAT RPKI PREVENTS AND DOESN'T:
  PREVENTS: route origin hijack (attacker announces prefix with wrong source AS).
  DOES NOT PREVENT: AS path manipulation (legitimate origin AS, but forged
    AS path between origin and destination). BGPsec required for this.
  BGPsec: each AS cryptographically signs the AS path as the route propagates.
    Status: RFC 8205 published 2017. Deployment: near zero (performance overhead;
    requires all ASes in path to support; partial deployment provides no benefit).

LAYER 4 — LAW-1 ANALYSIS:
  BGP: ~75,000+ active ASes globally. Each must: create ROAs in their RIR;
    update router software to support RPKI validation; configure policy to
    drop INVALID routes. Each step has operational risk (false ROAs cause
    legitimate traffic to be dropped). Adoption has been ongoing for 15+ years;
    50% coverage after this time is the characteristic LAW-1 trajectory.
    BGPsec: requires 100% AS path participation for guarantees; structural
    chicken-and-egg problem worse than RPKI. Predicted full deployment: decades.

CONVERGENCE:
  BGP/RPKI isomorphic to DNS/DNSSEC: both unauthenticated; both have cryptographic
    retrofit (RPKI vs. DNSSEC); both show ~30-50% adoption after 10-15 years.
    The adoption rate is the fingerprint of LAW-1 retrofitting complex protocols.
  R01.ROUTING sub-class: BGP, OSPF, RIP, IS-IS all share the property of
    routing trust propagation without authentication (to varying degrees).
STATUS: G268 CLOSED

ANATOMY G384_SMUGGLING [NEW]: HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SUBJECT: HTTP/1.1 request smuggling via CL.TE / TE.CL discrepancy
DOMAIN: Web application security / protocol parsing
ROOT MECHANICS: R10.3 (interaction between correct implementations)

LAYER 1 — PROTOCOL BACKGROUND:
  HTTP/1.1 request demarcation: two methods:
    Content-Length (CL): specifies body length in bytes
    Transfer-Encoding: chunked (TE): body in chunks, terminated by 0\r\n\r\n
  RFC 7230 (Section 3.3.3): if BOTH present, TE takes precedence; CL ignored.
  DISCREPANCY: front-end proxy and back-end server may disagree on precedence.

LAYER 2 — ATTACK VARIANTS:
  CL.TE (front-end uses CL, back-end uses TE):
    Attacker sends request with both headers. Front-end reads Content-Length N;
    forwards N bytes to back-end. Back-end reads chunked encoding; first chunk
    completes at M < N; remaining (N-M) bytes are left in back-end TCP buffer.
    Next legitimate user request arrives; back-end prepends attacker's poisoning
    payload. Victim's request is hijacked.

TE.CL (front-end uses TE, back-end uses CL):
    Reverse: front-end reads chunked; back-end reads Content-Length.
    Attacker crafts chunk that is valid per TE but has CL that points into
    the middle of a subsequent chunk body. Back-end reads only partial request;
    rest poisons buffer.

TE.TE (both use TE, but obfuscated header):
    Transfer-Encoding: chunked vs. Transfer-Encoding : chunked (space before colon)
    or Transfer-Encoding: xchunked. One implementation accepts; other ignores.
    Reduces to CL.TE or TE.CL depending on which ignores the obfuscated header.

LAYER 3 — IMPACT CHAIN:
  [A] Bypass front-end security controls: WAF/CDN inspects request; back-end
    receives different request (with attacker-prepended content). Auth bypass,
    WAF bypass.
  [B] Cross-user request hijacking: victim's request gets attacker-prepended
    headers or body. Attacker captures victim's session token if poison contains
    redirect to attacker-controlled endpoint.
  [C] Cache poisoning: poisoned response cached; served to all subsequent
    visitors. XSS or credential theft at scale.
  [D] Web cache deception: attacker manipulates cache to store private response
    at URL accessible to all.

LAYER 4 — HTTP/2 AND H2.H1 DESYNC:
  HTTP/2: binary framing; no CL/TE ambiguity within HTTP/2 connection.
  H2.H1 desync: front-end accepts HTTP/2; translates to HTTP/1.1 to back-end.
  Translation reintroduces CL/TE headers. Attacker sends HTTP/2 request with
  injected TE header in HTTP/2 pseudo-headers; translation creates CL.TE
  discrepancy at back-end. HTTP/2-enabled CDNs fronting HTTP/1.1 back-ends:
  vulnerable. James Kettle (2021): H2.TE and H2.CL attack classes.

CONVERGENCE:
  Canonical R10.3: both implementations are RFC-compliant; vulnerability in
    interaction. The spec allows the ambiguity; different resolution creates gap.
  Pattern 40.6 (eliminate > remediate): HTTP/2 binary framing eliminates
    the ambiguity class entirely within HTTP/2. H2.H1 desync shows that
    partial migration (H2 front-end, H1.1 back-end) recreates the vulnerability.
    Full migration to H2 end-to-end is the class-eliminating fix.
STATUS: G270 PARTIAL CLOSED (HTTP/1.1 smuggling documented; QUIC surface deferred)

STAGE 3 SUMMARY:
  Anatomies this cycle: G266 (RowHammer), G268 (RPKI/BGP), G270-partial
    (HTTP request smuggling)
  Cumulative anatomies: 129
  Anatomy backlog: 7 (10 - 3 closed)
  G266 CLOSED: RowHammer confirmed R10.5b; software-accessible fault injection;
    LAW-1 at DRAM hardware layer; DDR4 TRR bypassed by Blacksmith
  G268 CLOSED: RPKI ~50% prefix coverage after 15 years; BGP/RPKI isomorphic
    to DNS/DNSSEC adoption trajectory; BGPsec near-zero deployment
  G270 PARTIAL: HTTP smuggling canonical R10.3; H2.H1 desync extends class;
    Pattern 40.6 confirmed (H2 end-to-end as class elimination)

CYCLE 41 — STAGE 4: ATTACK/DEFENSE ENUMERATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 330 attacks | 450 defenses cumulative

[A331] BGP prefix hijack (route origin spoofing)
  Mechanism: attacker's AS announces a more-specific prefix (/25 vs. /24) for
  victim's IP space. BGP route selection: more specific prefix wins. Traffic
  destined for victim's IPs routes to attacker AS. Used for: phishing (steal
  email/MFA), MITM (decrypt traffic if certificate obtained), spam (abuse victim's
  reputation), cryptocurrency theft (MyEtherWallet 2018: BGP hijack + forged SSL).
  Prerequisites: control of any BGP-speaking AS (can be rented/hijacked);
  upstream provider that doesn't filter customer routes (BCP 38/84 not enforced).
  Impact: internet-scale traffic interception; affects all users worldwide.
  Root: R04, R01.ROUTING

[A332] DNS rebinding attack
  Mechanism: attacker registers domain with short TTL; phase 1: IP = public
  attacker server (user visits, JS loaded). Phase 2: DNS TTL expires, rebinds
  to internal IP (192.168.1.1). User's browser now sends requests to internal
  IP via attacker's script — same-origin allows since domain hasn't changed.
  Can access: internal admin interfaces, IoT devices, development servers on
  localhost. Extract data, modify configuration.
  Prerequisites: attacker controls DNS for their domain; target has valuable
  internal HTTP services.
  Impact: bypass same-origin policy without SOP vulnerability; access internal
  network from victim's browser.
  Root: R10.3 (browser same-origin enforcement vs. DNS rebinding reality)

[A333] RowHammer privilege escalation (JavaScript-based)
  Mechanism: SMASH (2021) technique — JavaScript induces bit flips in adjacent
  DRAM row without native code or CLFLUSH access. Target: page table entry (PTE)
  in kernel physical memory. Flip bit in PTE pointing to attacker's memory page;
  page now maps to privileged physical page. Attacker gains read/write to
  arbitrary kernel memory. Escalate to root.
  Prerequisites: vulnerable DRAM (DDR3/DDR4 without effective mitigation);
  JavaScript execution in browser.
  Impact: full local privilege escalation from browser sandbox.
  Root: R10.5b, R10.2

[A334] DNS cache poisoning (Kaminsky-class)
  Mechanism: attacker races to supply forged DNS response before legitimate
  response. Forged response: same transaction ID (16-bit, guessable) + source
  port (16-bit). Birthday attack: send many queries for random subdomains of
  target zone; simultaneously send forged responses. Successful poison: resolver
  caches attacker's IP for target domain.
  Prerequisites: DNSSEC not deployed on target zone; source port randomization
  insufficient in resolver.
  Impact: redirect all users of affected resolver to attacker-controlled IP.
  Root: R04 (no authentication in base DNS protocol)

[A335] HTTP request smuggling — front-end security bypass
  Mechanism: craft CL.TE desync request. Front-end inspects first request (CL):
  appears benign, passes WAF/auth checks. Back-end processes chunked encoding:
  partial content remains in buffer, prepended to next legitimate request.
  Victim's request (e.g., admin action) is now preceded by attacker's injected
  headers (e.g., attacker's session cookie replaced, or additional path added).
  Admin endpoint reached with manipulated request that bypassed front-end auth.
  Prerequisites: CL/TE parsing discrepancy between front-end proxy and back-end.
  Impact: authentication bypass, privilege escalation, cross-user attack.
  Root: R10.3

[A336] Prototype pollution to RCE (server-side)
  Mechanism: user input reaches lodash _.merge() (pre-4.17.21) or similar
  without sanitization. Attacker injects {"__proto__": {"polluted": "value"}}
  JSON. All subsequent Object.prototype accesses see 'polluted' property.
  Library code that checks for property existence (e.g., spawn options, shell
  flags): prototype pollution sets attacker-controlled value. Result: arbitrary
  OS command execution via child_process.spawn.
  Prerequisites: Node.js application using vulnerable lodash version + user
  input reaching merge/clone function.
  Impact: remote code execution. CVSSv3: 9.8 for several prototype pollution chains.
  Root: R10.6 (feature — object merging; security context mismatch — prototype
  chain modification)

ATTACKS CUMULATIVE: 336

[D451] RPKI deployment + route filtering (BGP security)
  Mechanism: resource holder creates ROAs in RIR repository. ISP configures
  router to fetch and validate ROAs (RTR protocol from validator). Policy: drop
  INVALID routes. Defense: prevents origin hijacking of any prefix with valid ROA.
  Additional: IRR (Internet Routing Registry) filtering — providers filter
  customers' announcements to only registered prefixes.
  Limitation: NOT FOUND routes still accepted; BGP path manipulation not prevented.
  Addresses: A331, BGP origin hijack class

[D452] DNS rebinding protection
  Mechanism: browser DNS rebinding protection: reject non-public IPs in DNS
  responses for public domain names (Chrome 114+: Private Network Access spec).
  Router DNS filtering: block DNS responses with private IP addresses for public
  domains (DD-WRT, pfSense rebinding protection).
  Defender-side: serve internal services on non-standard ports; require auth
  even on internal interfaces; HTTPS with certificate validation prevents
  silent rebinding (cert won't match 192.168.x.x).
  Addresses: A332, DNS rebinding class

[D453] DRAM ECC + RowHammer mitigation (DDR5 RFM)
  Mechanism: ECC DRAM: single-bit error correction; reduces attacker reliability
  but requires 3+ flips to defeat. DDR5 Refresh Management (RFM): hardware
  tracks row activation counts; triggers selective refresh before threshold.
  Software: memory isolation (guard pages), randomize physical memory layout,
  limit high-frequency memory access patterns.
  Limitation: ECC insufficient alone (multi-bit flips); RFM effectiveness on
  DDR5 under ongoing evaluation; DDR3/DDR4 largely unmitigated.
  Addresses: A333, RowHammer class

[D454] DNSSEC + resolver source port randomization
  Mechanism: DNSSEC: cryptographic signature chain from root to leaf. Resolvers
  with DNSSEC validation reject unsigned or incorrectly signed responses.
  Source port randomization (RFC 5452): expand transaction ID space from 16-bit
  to 32-bit (16-bit transaction ID + 16-bit source port). Reduces Kaminsky
  attack success from trivial to computationally expensive.
  DNSSEC coverage: ~30% of resolvers validate. Source port randomization:
  default in BIND 9.4+, Unbound, PowerDNS since 2008 (post-Kaminsky patch).
  Addresses: A334, DNS cache poisoning class

[D455] HTTP/2 end-to-end (request smuggling elimination)
  Mechanism: deploy HTTP/2 between all layers (CDN to origin). HTTP/2 binary
  framing has no CL/TE ambiguity — eliminates the request smuggling class.
  Configuration: Nginx: proxy_http_version 2.0; ensure back-end supports H2.
  Where H2 end-to-end is not possible: strict CL/TE handling in proxy
  (drop requests with both headers; or normalize to single method before forwarding).
  Addresses: A335, HTTP request smuggling class (class-eliminating fix)

[D456] Prototype pollution prevention (input sanitization + library pinning)
  Mechanism: sanitize user-provided JSON — reject objects with __proto__, constructor,
  prototype keys before merge. Use Object.freeze(Object.prototype) in Node.js
  apps (prevents modification). Update vulnerable libraries: lodash 4.17.21+,
  jQuery 3.4.0+. Use Map() instead of plain objects for arbitrary key-value storage.
  Static analysis: eslint-plugin-security flags unsafe merge patterns.
  Addresses: A336, prototype pollution class

DEFENSES CUMULATIVE: 456

STAGE 4 SUMMARY:
  New attacks: 6 (A331-A336) | Cumulative: 336
  New defenses: 6 (D451-D456) | Cumulative: 456
  BGP prefix hijack + RPKI; DNS rebinding + browser PNA; RowHammer + DDR5 RFM;
  DNS cache poisoning + DNSSEC; HTTP smuggling + H2 end-to-end (class elimination);
  Prototype pollution + input sanitization

CYCLE 41 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE & META-PATTERN EVOLUTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 291 convergence findings cumulative

[CF292] BGP/RPKI and DNS/DNSSEC: identical adoption fingerprint
  Two critical internet infrastructure protocols — BGP (routing) and DNS (naming)
  — both share: (a) designed without authentication (1980s-1990s); (b) massive
  deployed base that cannot be replaced; (c) cryptographic retrofit (RPKI, DNSSEC)
  developed 15-25 years after deployment; (d) ~30-50% adoption after 10-15 years
  of retrofit availability; (e) 'death star problem': full guarantee requires
  universal participation (BGPsec, DNSSEC chain), so partial adoption provides
  partial security that still fails when the unprotected portion is targeted.
  This is the quantitative signature of LAW-1 retrofit: exponential early adoption
  that decelerates as remaining adopters face higher friction (legacy hardware,
  operational complexity, multi-party coordination requirements).
  R01.ROUTING sub-class: confirmed as parallel to R01.RF and R01.NET — BGP is
  a broadcast-trust protocol in a different medium.

[CF293] RowHammer as hardware physics intruding into software security model
  Software security model fundamental assumption: memory contents are determined
  by software writes; physical hardware faithfully executes the abstract machine.
  RowHammer violates this: software-accessible operation (repeated memory read)
  causes bit flips without any software 'write' operation. This breaks the
  abstraction boundary between hardware physics and the software trust model.
  Consequence: software-layer security guarantees (page table integrity, privilege
  separation, sandboxing) can be violated by hardware physics without any
  software vulnerability being present. R10.5b is the sub-taxonomy for this
  class: attacker uses software to access hardware physics, bypassing software
  abstraction. The 'implementation' (DRAM cell isolation) is faithful to the spec;
  the spec assumed higher isolation than the physics provides at modern densities
  (R10.2 component).

[CF294] DNS rebinding as same-origin policy architectural bypass
  Same-origin policy: browser isolates JavaScript by origin (scheme + host + port).
  DNS rebinding does not exploit a bug in SOP; it exploits the gap between
  the assumption underlying SOP ('host' is stable during a session) and the
  reality (DNS can change the IP behind a host at any time after TTL expiry).
  SOP is correct; DNS TTL resolution is correct; the vulnerability is their
  interaction (R10.3). The browser cannot easily distinguish 'this is still the
  same host' from 'the IP changed and this is now an internal address' because
  DNS has no such concept. This is a design gap at the intersection of two
  correct systems.

[CF295] Prototype pollution as R10.6 with JavaScript-specific context
  JavaScript prototype chain: feature designed for object-oriented inheritance
  without class-based systems. Legitimate use: extend objects with shared methods.
  Security context mismatch: user-controlled JSON merged into objects can reach
  Object.prototype; any subsequent property lookup on any object returns
  attacker-controlled value. The 'feature' (prototype chain lookup for property
  inheritance) creates the mismatch because the design assumes the prototype
  chain is controlled by the developer, not by user input.
  This is identical in structure to Log4j JNDI (feature: remote resource lookup
  in log format strings; mismatch: log format strings contain user input) and
  pickle (feature: arbitrary Python object serialization; mismatch: deserialized
  objects can be from attacker).
  R10.6 instance count: growing. Classification check: each instance shares
  the 'feature designed for legitimate purpose, reaches security-critical behavior
  when user input enters the feature's context' structure. R10.6 is robustly
  confirmed across all instances.

[CF296] Pattern 40.6 reinforcement — HTTP/2 as binary protocol class elimination
  HTTP/2 binary framing eliminates the CL/TE ambiguity that enables request
  smuggling. TLS 1.3 eliminated cipher downgrade classes. Rust eliminates
  memory corruption class. FIDO2 eliminates phishable credential class.
  Each represents a design that removes the problematic ambiguity or unsafe
  operation from the protocol/language/spec entirely.
  Contrast with band-aid approaches: WAF rules for request smuggling (bypassable);
  input sanitization for prototype pollution (incomplete); ASLR/DEP for memory
  corruption (reduces reliability, does not eliminate). Class elimination is
  structurally superior and confirmed in every case where it has been applied.
  Pattern 40.6 reinforced with HTTP/2 as 5th instance.

R10.6 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 2 (of 5 for R10.6 broader form):
  New candidate features examined this cycle:
  [CE-6] HTTP/2 header compression (HPACK): designed to compress HTTP headers
    for efficiency. CRIME attack (2012): TLS compression + chosen-plaintext
    enabled session token recovery. BREACH (2013): HTTP compression extension.
    Verdict: CRIME is R10.6 (compression feature + attacker-chosen plaintext
    context = oracle). Not a counter-example.
  [CE-7] Server Name Indication (SNI): TLS extension allowing multiple certs on
    single IP. SNI is sent in plaintext (by design: server needs to select cert
    before TLS established). Used for: traffic analysis (which site on shared IP);
    network-level filtering/censorship. Information leakage without action-enabling.
    Assessment: similar to TCP timestamps (CE-5). Information only; self-mitigated
    by ECH (Encrypted Client Hello, RFC 9258). Refinement candidate: R10.6
    information-only sub-class, not action-enabling.
  [CE-8] CSS cascade and specificity: cross-domain CSS leakage attacks have been
    proposed (timing attacks on selector matching). Mitigated by browser
    cross-origin CSS restrictions. Impact: very low; not action-enabling.
    Assessment: not action-enabling. Consistent with R10.6-THRESHOLD refinement.
  R10.6 CYCLE 2 RESULT: CE-6 confirms R10.6 (CRIME/BREACH). CE-7, CE-8:
    information-only, consistent with R10.6-THRESHOLD (not counter-examples;
    further evidence for the threshold refinement). 3 cycles remain.

STAGE 5 SUMMARY:
  New convergence findings: CF292-CF296 (5 new) | Cumulative: 296
  BGP/RPKI + DNS/DNSSEC: identical LAW-1 retrofit fingerprint (quantified)
  RowHammer: hardware physics intrusion into software security model formalized
  DNS rebinding: R10.3 (SOP interaction with DNS TTL resolution)
