CYCLE 45 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE & META-PATTERN EVOLUTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 331 convergence findings cumulative

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C45.1: COGNITIVE LAYER AS FINAL ATTACK SURFACE ─────────

C45.C1: Human cognitive layer is the terminal attack surface that technical
  controls cannot fully eliminate.

Technical stack attack surfaces:
    Hardware → firmware → OS kernel → libraries → applications → network →
    human operator.

Each layer has technical defenses. The human layer has:
    - Training (reduces but does not eliminate vulnerability)
    - Procedural controls (callback verification, dual authorization)
    - Technical assists (anti-phishing toolbars, DMARC, visual indicators)
    None eliminates the fundamental vulnerability: humans make trust
    decisions based on incomplete information under time pressure.

Deepfake voice (A358), BitB phishing (A367), SIM swap (G263), BEC/CEO fraud:
  all exploit human cognitive trust model, not technical systems.

LAW-1 extension: Human cognitive architecture is an architectural constraint
  that cannot be patched. Social engineering attacks exploit cognitive heuristics
  (authority, urgency, familiarity) that evolved for non-adversarial environments.
  This is not a bug in humans — it is a mismatch between evolved cognition and
  adversarial information environments.

LAW-1-HUMAN CANDIDATE: Human cognitive trust model is irredeemable on
  security timescales (training doesn't eliminate; only procedural controls
  bound the damage). R03.COGNITIVE captures the mechanism; LAW-1-HUMAN
  captures the systemic constraint.

C45.C2: Supply chain convergence — four distinct supply chain attack classes

Consolidating across the corpus:

CLASS 1: SOFTWARE PACKAGE SUPPLY CHAIN
    Mechanism: malicious package in registry (npm/PyPI/RubyGems)
    Defense: package signing (Sigstore), audit logs, dependency pinning
    Instances: event-stream (npm), SolarWinds-adjacent package attacks

CLASS 2: BUILD SYSTEM SUPPLY CHAIN
    Mechanism: compromise build environment; inject malicious code at compile
    Defense: SLSA Level 4 (reproducible builds, build environment attestation)
    Instances: SolarWinds SUNBURST, 3CX (2023, VC++ DLL side-loading)

CLASS 3: OPEN SOURCE CONTRIBUTOR SUPPLY CHAIN
    Mechanism: patient contributor gains trust, inserts backdoor
    Defense: multi-party review, contributor vetting, CODEOWNERS enforcement
    Instances: XZ Utils, faker.js intentional sabotage

CLASS 4: ML MODEL SUPPLY CHAIN
    Mechanism: poisoned model weights in ML registry
    Defense: model signing (Sigstore for ML), reproducible training, backdoor scan
    Instances: HuggingFace malicious models (multiple documented 2023-2024)

CLASS 5: HARDWARE SUPPLY CHAIN
    Mechanism: counterfeit ICs, firmware implants in manufacturing/transit
    Defense: supply chain verification programs, trusted fab lists, destructive testing
    Instances: NSA ANT catalog, Supermicro alleged (2018, disputed)

Each class has different trust inversion mechanism but shares root P40.1
  structure. The attack surface is wherever trust is assumed without verification.
  LAW-1 applies to all: verification at supply chain scale is computationally
  and economically infeasible at current depths (100+ transitive dependencies,
  millions of lines of build toolchain code).

C45.C3: LAW-4 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 1 — PROPOSED CE: HIGH-FREQUENCY ATTACKS

LAW-4 CANDIDATE: HIGHEST-IMPACT ATTACKS REQUIRE STATE-CLASS PATIENCE.

Counter-example: Ransomware operations achieve high aggregate impact without
  extended patience. LockBit: $91M extracted from US organizations in 2 years
  via rapid compromise-encrypt-demand operations (hours to days, not months).
  Average dwell time for ransomware actors: ~5 days pre-encryption (Mandiant M-Trends).

Analysis:
    LAW-4 distinguishes INDIVIDUAL impact from AGGREGATE impact.
    - Highest individual impact (SolarWinds: ~$100M+ response cost; national
      security implications): required 9+ months patience.
    - Highest aggregate impact (ransomware industry ~$1B/year): does NOT
      require state-class patience.

Revision: LAW-4 scope should be SINGLE-TARGET CATASTROPHIC impact, not
    aggregate industry revenue. Ransomware is high volume, moderate individual
    impact. SolarWinds/Stuxnet are low volume, catastrophic individual impact.

Insight: two distinct attack economies:
      ATTRITION ECONOMY: ransomware, commodity phishing, bot herding —
        high volume, low patience, moderate per-attack yield.
      PRECISION ECONOMY: APT/nation-state — low volume, high patience,
        catastrophic per-attack yield.
    These are not competing models; they coexist and address different objectives.

Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED. LAW-4 holds for precision economy attacks.
  LAW-4 scope: single-target catastrophic impact attacks (>$100M individual
  or national security consequence) require state-class patience.

LAW-4 CE CYCLE 1: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED. Scope clarified.

C45.C4: R10.6 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 5 (FINAL) — PROPOSED CE: BLUETOOTH LE PRIVACY

Bluetooth LE introduced privacy features (random address rotation) to prevent
  tracking. Was tracking risk evaluated at BLE design time?

Analysis:
    BLE Core Spec 4.0 (2010): advertising packets from fixed MAC address.
    Tracking problem documented in academic literature by 2012.
    BLE Core Spec 4.2 (2014): LE Privacy feature added — resolvable private
    addresses (RPA), randomized every few minutes.
    Security context: tracking by passive scanner was not fully evaluated
    at BLE 4.0 design; BLE was designed for low-energy device communication.
    The privacy attack surface (passive tracking of physical location via
    fixed BLE MAC) was unanticipated at design time.

Verdict: CONFIRMED R10.6 instance. BLE 4.0 designed for communication;
    tracking/surveillance deployment context not evaluated at design time.
    BLE privacy (RPA) is a retrofit defense (LAW-1 parallel). This is a
    clean R10.6 instance: feature deployed in surveillance context that
    was not part of original design context evaluation.

R10.6 CE CYCLE 5: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED.
  R10.6 COUNTER-EXAMPLE PROCESS: ALL 5 CYCLES COMPLETE. ZERO FALSIFICATION.

R10.6 STATUS CHANGE: DRAFT → CONFIRMED.
  R10.6 CONFIRMED: FEATURE-SECURITY CONTEXT MISMATCH — SECURITY PROPERTIES
  OF A FEATURE ARE EVALUATED IN THE DESIGN CONTEXT, NOT THE DEPLOYMENT
  CONTEXT. UNANTICIPATED DEPLOYMENT CONTEXTS CREATE ATTACK SURFACES THAT
  WERE NOT DESIGNED AGAINST.

R10.6 sub-class threshold (from CE cycle 4): known/documented tradeoffs
  are excluded. Unanticipated context is required.

Instances confirmed: IMDSv1 (cloud metadata in public cloud context),
    BLE 4.0 (communication feature in surveillance context),
    Digital twin (engineering tool in adversarial planning context),
    JNDI in Log4j2 (logging feature in internet-facing context),
    ROS 1 (research protocol in industrial context).

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C45.2: LAW-3 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 4 ─────────────────

CE CYCLE 4 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — REMOVING ATTACK SURFACE CLASS ENTIRELY

Specific case: Physical USB attack surface. USB attacks (BadUSB, HID
  injection, USB rubber ducky) require physical access + USB port.
  Defense: disable all USB ports physically or via policy.

Analysis:
    If USB ports are physically removed/disabled, the entire USB attack
    surface class is eliminated. There is no USB attack surface when there
    are no USB ports.

New surface created: removable media alternatives must exist (network
    transfer, provisioning process). Network provisioning creates network
    attack surface. If network is also air-gapped, humans become the attack
    surface (social engineering for physical access, malicious insider).

Is this conservation? The surface transforms: USB attack surface →
    network transfer surface + human bridging surface. For true air-gap
    with no network and no USB: the attack surface compresses to physical
    access + physics-layer covert channels (R01, radiation emissions).
    This is genuinely smaller than a full-connectivity surface.

Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED but SCOPE REFINEMENT CONFIRMED.
  LAW-3 holds in network-connected systems. In physically isolated systems
  (true air-gap), total surface volume can be significantly reduced through
  physical elimination of attack surface classes. The residual (physics-layer
  covert channels + insider threat + supply chain) is smaller than the
  original connected surface.

LAW-3 SCOPE FINAL: holds for network-connected systems in steady state.
  Physically isolated systems can achieve genuine surface reduction at the
  cost of operational friction (cannot receive software updates via network,
  requires human-mediated supply chain for any update — which creates its
  own supply chain attack surface).

LAW-3 CE CYCLE 4: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED. Scope: network-connected systems.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C45.3: META-PATTERN: THREE-LAYER DEFENSE FAILURE MODEL ──

Synthesizing across all confirmed attacks in the corpus:

OBSERVATION: High-impact successful attacks consistently break three
independent layers, with at least one layer failing at R06.ARCH or LAW-1 level.

SolarWinds: Layer 1 (build security), Layer 2 (signed code assumed safe),
    Layer 3 (endpoint detection blind to signed malware)
  Capital One: Layer 1 (WAF SSRF not caught), Layer 2 (IMDSv1 no-auth),
    Layer 3 (IAM over-privilege)
  Ronin bridge: Layer 1 (5-of-9 threshold too low), Layer 2 (key management),
    Layer 3 (no anomaly detection on threshold-minimum signatures)
  FORCEDENTRY (Pegasus): Layer 1 (JBIG2 parser RCE), Layer 2 (sandbox escape),
    Layer 3 (kernel privesc)

Pattern: single defenses are overcome by single exploits (low cost, LAW-2).
  Defense-in-depth works statistically. Three independent failures required
  for highest-impact outcomes.

COROLLARY: Defense strategy should be optimized for independent layers,
  not additional layers on the same surface. Three weak layers on the same
  attack path = one strong attack. One strong layer + two independent layers
  = harder to compromise simultaneously.

P45.5 CANDIDATE: THREE-LAYER INDEPENDENCE REQUIREMENT FOR HIGH-IMPACT ATTACKS.
  Count: 4 confirmed instances. Status: DRAFT.

CYCLE 46 — STAGE 2: ROOT MECHANIC & PATTERN IDENTIFICATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 184 patterns

G332 (Memory forensics) → Root mechanics:
  R08 (visibility gap inversion): memory forensics is a defender technique
  that closes the visibility gap on volatile artifacts. Anti-forensics
  counter: memory wiping, anti-dump techniques (overwrite RAM before
  acquisition). R09.3: advanced attackers wipe RAM artifacts as cleanup step.
  Insight: memory forensics is a post-compromise detection capability, not
  prevention. The gap it closes is the residue of an attack already executed.

G333 (ICS protocols) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH (protocols designed without authentication): Modbus has no auth;
  DNP3 has optional SAv5 (Secure Authentication Version 5) added in 2012.
  LAW-1: Modbus designed 1979; no authentication retrofit is feasible
  without replacing all deployed endpoints (billions of devices globally).
  Pattern 36.2 CONFIRMED instance 8: ICS production continuity mandate
  (zero-downtime requirement) creates permanent legacy of unauthenticated
  ICS devices alongside authenticated replacements.
  Assessment: Pattern 36.2 instance 8 CONFIRMED. Production/legacy split
  driven by ICS uptime requirement, not regulatory mandate directly —
  but the production mandate creates the same structural effect.
  PATTERN 36.2 REVISED SCOPE: broader than regulatory; any mandate that
  prevents replacing insecure systems creates the production/legacy split.

G334 (Enterprise WiFi) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: PEAP MSCHAPv2 (common enterprise WiFi auth) is vulnerable to
  dictionary attack on captured handshake; WPA2 Enterprise with PEAP-MSCHAPv2
  is widely deployed but cryptographically weak (MD4-based NTHash).
  R01: Rogue AP attack — attacker creates stronger-signal AP with same SSID;
  client connects; performs MITM. 802.11w (management frame protection) prevents
  deauth attacks but not rogue AP association.
  Pattern 33.3 instance CANDIDATE: 802.11w security layer (MFP) prevents
  deauth attack but clients still vulnerable to rogue AP (new perimeter created
  by 802.11w enforcement: attacker focuses on association vs. deauth).

G335 (Encrypted traffic analysis) → Root mechanics:
  R08 (visibility gap in reverse): TLS encryption closes defender visibility
  but also closes malware detection capability. Encrypted malware C2 traffic
  is invisible to DPI. ML-based traffic analysis partially closes this gap
  but creates false positive problem. This is a LAW-3 instance: TLS (security
  measure) transforms attack surface — defender loses visibility, attacker
  gains encrypted channel without separate cost.

G336 (DevOps security) → Root mechanics:
  P40.1 (supply chain trust inversion): GitHub Actions workflows can reference
  external actions (e.g., uses: actions/checkout@v4). If external action is
  compromised, all CI pipelines using it run malicious code. Supply chain
  attack surface in build pipeline. R06.ARCH: CI/CD designed for developer
  velocity, not adversarial input.
  Pattern 33.3 instance CANDIDATE: CI/CD automation layer creates new attack
  perimeter (compromised runner = access to secrets, source code, artifact registry).

G337 (Automotive CAN bus) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: CAN bus designed for reliability in electrically noisy environment;
  no authentication. Any ECU on CAN bus can send any message to any other ECU.
  Charlie Miller/Chris Valasek (2015 Jeep Cherokee): remote compromise via
  cellular modem → CAN bus → physical control (braking, steering).
  R01: OBD-II port as physical attack surface; cellular modem as remote surface.
  LAW-1: CAN bus in ~90% of vehicles; retrofit authentication (CAN-FD SecOC)
  requires hardware change in deployed fleet.

G338 (Biometric security) → Root mechanics:
  R05 (trust model): biometric authentication assumes physical biometric
  sample cannot be replicated; advances in 3D printing, gelatin fingerprints,
  adversarial makeup partially falsify this assumption.
  R06.ARCH: Biometric template stored as hash or feature vector; database
  compromise exposes biometric data that cannot be revoked (unlike password).
  Biometric cancellation (cancelable biometrics) is an architectural solution.
  Pattern 40.6 CANDIDATE: cancelable biometrics (class redesign) vs. instance
  revocation (impossible for compromised biological biometric).

G339 (OSS governance) → Root mechanics:
  P40.1: abandoned OSS project adopted by malicious actor = package supply
  chain trust inversion. Maintained package acquired by malicious buyer = same.
  R09.3: patient contribution pattern builds trust before malicious action (XZ).
  Pattern 45.1 (externalized security cost): OSS security depends on volunteer
  maintainers; cost of maintenance externalized to maintainers; cost of breach
  externalized to users of the package.

G340 (Privacy-enhancing technologies) → Root mechanics:
  Gradient inversion attacks (federated learning): federated learning designed
  to avoid sharing raw data; gradient updates leak information about training
  data. R10.6: federated learning evaluated as privacy-preserving in context
  of raw data sharing; gradient privacy not fully evaluated at design.
  Membership inference on synthetic data: R10.6 parallel — synthetic data
  evaluated as privacy-preserving; membership inference attack not anticipated.

G341 (SS7/Diameter attacks) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH (LAW-1 retrofit): SS7 designed 1975 for trusted telecom operator
  network; SS7 interconnects now include hundreds of operators globally, many
  in adversarial jurisdictions. Authentication added (MAP screening) but
  bypass known. Diameter (4G equivalent) has improved but still has design gaps.
  R05: Trust model assumes all SS7 peers are legitimate telecom operators;
  rogue operators (or compromised operators) break this.

G342 (Exploit mitigations + bypasses) → Root mechanics:
  This domain is the empirical test of LAW-2 and LAW-3 at the memory
  exploitation layer.
  ASLR: randomizes address space; bypass via information leak (kernel address
  printed in log, /proc/kallsyms, format string leak). LAW-2: ASLR was
  thought to be strong barrier; information leak bypass discovered within ~2 years.
  DEP/NX: prevents execution in data regions; bypass via ROP (return-oriented
  programming). LAW-2 again: DEP thought strong; ROP discovered.
  Stack canary: bypass via information leak (canary value leaked before overwrite).
  CET (Control Enforcement Technology): prevents ROP; bypass requires more
  sophisticated techniques (still being developed).
  Pattern: each mitigation adds ~1-3 years before bypass is discovered/commoditized.
  LAW-2 REINFORCED: each mitigation is a temporary barrier, not permanent.

G343 (Decentralized identity) → Root mechanics:
  R05: DID trust model — credential issuer's DID must be trusted; no central
  authority to verify issuer legitimacy (by design); Sybil attack on issuer
  trust. R06.ARCH: Key rotation in DIDs requires coordination without central
  revocation authority; revocation without central authority is unsolved problem
  (revocation registries are semi-centralized).

G344 (Cryptographic entropy) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: Weak RNG is one of the most catastrophic cryptographic failures;
  affects all cryptographic operations. Early Android Bitcoin wallet (2013):
  Java SecureRandom not properly seeded; same ECDSA k value reused across
  signatures → private key recovery from two signatures. P-256 Sony PS3:
  fixed k in ECDSA implementation → key extraction (used to break game code
  signing). Low-entropy early boot RNG: VM instances with same seed → same
  RSA keys generated for multiple VMs.

G345 (Edge computing security) → Root mechanics:
  R04: Edge nodes physically accessible (gas stations, retail locations);
  physical access enables logical compromise. R05: edge-to-cloud trust model
  relies on edge node integrity; compromised edge node can submit false data
  or exfiltrate processed data. R10.6: edge nodes evaluated for performance
  proximity; physical security of edge node in public locations not always
  evaluated at deployment design.

G267 ANATOMY: ARM Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) and hardware memory safety
  Surface: Hardware-assisted memory safety (ARM MTE, SPARC ADI, CHERI)
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — Tag allocation: each 16-byte memory granule has a 4-bit tag;
      pointer carries corresponding tag in top-byte ignore (TBI) bits
    Layer 2 — Tag check: on memory access, hardware compares pointer tag
      with memory tag; mismatch = fault (SIGSEGV or asynchronous report)
    Layer 3 — Attack surface: temporal safety (use-after-free) defeated if
      freed region gets new tag; spatial safety (buffer overflow) defeated
      if adjacent allocation has different tag
  Attack surface of MTE itself:
    (a) Tag brute force: 4-bit tag = 1/16 chance of guess; 16 attempts
      statistically gets one through. Async mode (default for performance)
      doesn't kill process on tag fault — allows brute force iteration.
    (b) Information leaks: if attacker can read tag value, defeats protection
    (c) Heap spray: if attacker can control heap layout, can ensure dangling
      pointer tag matches reallocated region tag (tag reuse)
  Root mechanics: Pattern 40.6 (class-level defense) vs. residual attack
    surface. MTE eliminates naive heap overflow/UAF but creates new sub-attack
    surface (tag inference, brute force in async mode). Pattern 33.3 CANDIDATE:
    MTE hardware safety layer creates tag brute-force as new attack perimeter.
  Deployment: Android 11+ (Pixel 8+): MTE enabled in async mode for all apps.
    Google Project Zero found MTE bypass via tag brute force in async mode.
  G267 STATUS: CLOSED

G341 ANATOMY: SS7 call interception and location tracking
  Surface: SS7 (Signaling System 7) global telecom signaling network
  Mechanism (SMS interception):
    Layer 1 — SS7 access: attacker has access to SS7 network (rogue operator,
      SS7 aggregator, or compromised operator)
    Layer 2 — Send MAP SRI-SM (SendRoutingInfoForShortMessage): query home
      network for victim's IMSI + current VLR address
    Layer 3 — Register false route: MAP RegisterSS or MAP UpdateLocation to
      point victim's SMS delivery to attacker's MSC
    Layer 4 — SMS interception: victim's SMS (including OTP) routed to attacker
    Layer 5 — Account takeover via SMS OTP bypass
  Mechanism (location tracking):
    Layer 1 — SS7 access (as above)
    Layer 2 — MAP ATI (AnyTimeInterrogation) or MAP SRI queries return
      cell tower ID of victim's location
    Layer 3 — Trilaterate victim's physical location from cell tower coordinates
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (SS7 designed for trusted operator network; no
    authentication between operators), LAW-1 (global SS7 network; no
    architectural replacement feasible; only MAP screening partial defense),
    R05 (trust model: all SS7 peers are assumed legitimate operators)
  Defense: MAP screening (filter dangerous MAP operations at HLR/STP),
    SMS Home Routing (intercept inbound SRI-SM queries at home network),
    GSMA FS.11 signaling firewall. None fully solves the problem.
  G341 STATUS: CLOSED

G333 ANATOMY: Modbus protocol injection attack
  Surface: Modbus TCP/RTU industrial protocol (SCADA/ICS)
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — Network access: attacker on network segment containing Modbus
      master/slave (ICS network, compromised IT/OT bridge)
    Layer 2 — Modbus command injection: Modbus has no authentication; any
      device can send Function Code 06 (Write Single Register) or FC 16
      (Write Multiple Registers) to any Modbus slave address
    Layer 3 — Physical effect: register value changes actuator state (valve
      open/close, motor start/stop, setpoint change)
    Layer 4 — Attack camouflage: modify process historian to show normal values
      while physical process is in abnormal state (Stuxnet technique)
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (Modbus designed 1979 for serial RS-485;
    no authentication is original design, not oversight), LAW-1 (global
    deployment of legacy Modbus makes replacement infeasible; Modbus over TCP
    adds network layer exposure without adding security)
  Historical: Triton malware (2017): targeted Safety Instrumented Systems
    (SIS/Schneider Electric Triconex) via proprietary protocol; attempted to
    defeat safety systems enabling physical damage. Closest documented attack
    designed to cause mass casualties via ICS.
  G333 STATUS: CLOSED

G336 ANATOMY: CI/CD pipeline attack (GitHub Actions / poisoned runner)
  Surface: GitHub Actions CI/CD workflow execution
  Mechanism (poisoned GitHub Action):
    Layer 1 — Dependency: workflow uses third-party Action
      (uses: third-party/action@v1)
    Layer 2 — Action compromise: third-party action repository is compromised
      (supply chain: account takeover of action maintainer)
    Layer 3 — Runner execution: compromised action code runs in CI runner
      with access to GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets, source code
    Layer 4 — Exfiltration: secrets exfiltrated; source code modified;
      artifacts tampered before publication
  Mechanism (pull request from fork):
    Layer 1 — Workflow triggers on pull_request from fork
    Layer 2 — Attacker modifies workflow in fork to exfiltrate secrets
    Layer 3 — Workflow runs in context of base repository with its secrets
      (if workflow incorrectly uses pull_request_target trigger with checkout
      of untrusted PR code)
  Root mechanics: P40.1 (CI/CD supply chain trust inversion), R06.ARCH
    (GitHub Actions designed for velocity; trust model assumes external
    actions are safe), R10.6 (CI/CD as code execution environment not
    fully evaluated as attack surface at design)
  Defense: pin action versions to commit SHA (not tag: tags are mutable);
    OIDC for cloud access (eliminate long-lived secrets in CI); restrict
    pull_request_target; secret scanning; minimal permissions GITHUB_TOKEN.
  G336 STATUS: CLOSED

G344 ANATOMY: Cryptographic RNG failures (k-reuse in ECDSA)
  Surface: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) nonce generation
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — ECDSA signing: each signature requires unique random nonce k.
      Signature: r = (k*G).x mod n; s = k^(-1)(hash + r*privkey) mod n
    Layer 2 — k reuse: if same k used for two messages m1, m2:
      s1 = k^(-1)(h1 + r*d); s2 = k^(-1)(h2 + r*d) where d = private key
      (s1 - s2) = k^(-1)(h1 - h2) → k = (h1 - h2)/(s1 - s2)
      k extracted → d = (s1*k - h1)/r = private key extracted
    Layer 3 — Historical instances: Sony PS3 (2010): fixed k='4' in game
      signing; Android Bitcoin (2013): weak RNG reused k; allowed private
      key extraction and Bitcoin theft.
  RFC 6979: deterministic ECDSA (k derived from private key + message hash;
    same message always produces same k but unique per private key).
    RFC 6979 eliminates the RNG dependency for ECDSA.
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (ECDSA spec required random k but didn't
    specify how; implementations chose weak RNG or fixed values),
    Pattern 40.6: RFC 6979 is class-level fix (eliminating RNG dependency
    entirely) vs. instance fix (better RNG in each implementation)
  G344 STATUS: CLOSED

G342 ANATOMY: Return-oriented programming (ROP) bypass of DEP/NX
  Surface: DEP/NX (Data Execution Prevention / No-Execute) memory protection
  Mechanism:
    Layer 1 — DEP prevents injecting shellcode and jumping to it: data pages
      are non-executable
    Layer 2 — ROP: instead of injecting code, attacker chains existing code
      gadgets (short instruction sequences ending in RET)
    Layer 3 — Stack overflow or other memory corruption controls stack
    Layer 4 — Return address chain: each gadget executes and returns to next
      gadget; chain implements arbitrary computation from existing code
    Layer 5 — Full bypass: attacker achieves arbitrary code execution without
      injecting any new code; only existing (executable) code is used
  Root mechanics: LAW-2 (DEP thought strong barrier; ROP discovered within
    ~2 years of widespread DEP deployment), LAW-3 (DEP transforms attack
    surface from code injection → code reuse; volume approximately conserved),
    Pattern 33.3 (DEP security layer creates ROP as new attack perimeter;
    B = executable/non-executable boundary; T = ROP chain compilers)
  Note: Pattern 33.3 instance CONFIRMED: DEP → ROP surface. This is one
    of the strongest instances in the corpus: the security measure (DEP)
    directly created the attack technique (ROP) that bypasses it.
  G342 STATUS: CLOSED

Closed this stage: G267, G341, G333, G336, G344, G342 (6 gaps)

  T: ROP chain compilation tools (ROPgadget, pwntools rop module)

CYCLE 46 — STAGE 4: ATTACK/DEFENSE ENUMERATION

── ATTACK VECTOR ENUMERATION (BATCH 46) ─────────────────────────────────────

A369: ICS protocol injection — Modbus register overwrite targeting safety system
  Mechanism: Attacker with access to ICS network segment sends unauthenticated
    Modbus FC06 (Write Single Register) or FC16 (Write Multiple Registers)
    targeting PLC holding safety setpoints. Overwrites emergency stop threshold,
    disables alarm. Process exceeds safe operating limit. Physical damage or
    safety incident. No authentication to stop the write.
  Root: R06.ARCH (Modbus no-auth design), LAW-1 (deployed at scale; unreplaceable)
  Historical anchor: Triton (2017) — targeted safety instrumented systems.

A370: SS7 SMS interception for MFA bypass
  Mechanism: Attacker with SS7 access sends MAP SRI-SM to victim's home network.
    Gets IMSI + current serving MSC. Sends MAP SRS (SendRoutingInformation)
    or MAP ISD (InsertSubscriberData) to reroute SMS delivery to attacker MSC.
    Victim's SMS OTP intercepted. Attacker uses OTP to bypass MFA and access
    online banking, crypto exchange, email.
  Root: R06.ARCH (SS7 designed for trusted operator environment), LAW-1
    (global SS7 infrastructure; no replacement; only partial screening defense)

A371: CI/CD pipeline secrets exfiltration via compromised GitHub Action
  Mechanism: Attacker compromises third-party GitHub Action used in target
    org's CI/CD workflow (via maintainer account takeover or malicious PR
    to action repo). Malicious version of action runs in CI runner with access
    to GITHUB_TOKEN and repository secrets. Exfiltrates secrets to attacker
    C2. Uses secrets to access cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP), push malicious
    code, or tamper with release artifacts.
  Root: P40.1 (CI/CD supply chain trust inversion), R06.ARCH (action version
    pinning to tag vs. commit SHA mutable reference)

A372: Automotive CAN bus spoofing via OBD-II physical access
  Mechanism: Attacker with physical access to vehicle connects CAN bus adapter
    to OBD-II port. Injects CAN frames spoofing ECU messages: brake command
    suppression, steering actuation signal, TPMS pressure falsification.
    Remote variant (Jeep Cherokee 2015): cellular modem interface → UConnect
    infotainment compromise → CAN bus injection. No authentication on CAN bus;
    any device can inject any frame.
  Root: R06.ARCH (CAN bus designed for reliability; no authentication),
    R01 (OBD-II port as physical attack surface; cellular modem as remote)

A373: Biometric database compromise enabling persistent identity theft
  Mechanism: Attacker compromises biometric database (fingerprint templates,
    facial feature vectors stored for authentication system). Unlike password
    database, biometric templates cannot be revoked — victim cannot change
    fingerprints. Templates used for replay attack (crafted gelatin print,
    3D-printed fingerprint) at any biometric authentication point.
  India Aadhaar system analog: 1.1 billion biometric records; breach would
    affect every enrolled individual permanently.
  Root: R06.ARCH (biometric architecture stores irrevocable templates),
    R05 (trust model: biometric system assumes template cannot be replicated;
    advances in replication partially falsify this)

A374: ECDSA nonce reuse via insufficient entropy
  Mechanism: Embedded device generates ECDSA signature with insufficient
    entropy in nonce k (e.g., time-seeded with low-resolution clock; or
    VM cloned with same RNG state). Two signatures with same k:
    s1 = k^(-1)(h1 + r*privkey), s2 = k^(-1)(h2 + r*privkey).
    Both equations; solve for privkey. Private key extracted. All prior
    and future signatures can be forged.
  Root: R06.ARCH (ECDSA requires truly random k; implementations used weak
    RNG), RFC 6979 (Pattern 40.6: class fix = deterministic k from privkey+msg)

A375: ROP chain exploitation for shellcode bypass (DEP/NX bypass)
  Mechanism: Memory corruption vulnerability (stack overflow, heap overflow)
    in application with DEP/NX enabled. Attacker builds ROP chain from gadgets
    found in loaded modules (libc, ntdll). Chain calls mprotect()/VirtualProtect()
    to mark region executable, or calls system() directly. Achieves full code
    execution without injecting executable code.
  Root: LAW-2 (DEP thought sufficient barrier; ROP discovered and commoditized),
    LAW-3 (DEP transformed attack surface from injection to reuse; not eliminated),
    Pattern 33.3 inst 14 (DEP → ROP surface)

A376: Supply chain typosquatting with delayed payload activation
  Mechanism: Attacker publishes package with name similar to popular package
    (nnumpy vs numpy, colourama vs colorama). Package installs without error;
    appears functional. Activates malicious payload after N days or when
    environment variable detects CI vs. production context (targets production,
    dormant in CI to evade sandbox detection). R09.3 patience built into
    package logic.
  Root: P40.1, R09.3 (delayed activation), R05 (developer trust model
    assumes registry package is legitimate)

A377: Differential privacy composition attack
  Mechanism: Differential privacy (DP) guarantees epsilon-privacy per query.
    Composability: k queries compose to k*epsilon-privacy degradation (basic
    composition). Attacker submits many DP-protected queries to the same
    dataset; accumulated privacy loss (epsilon budget) may reveal more than
    intended, especially with adaptive queries (each query informed by previous
    result). Formal: advanced composition theorem gives O(sqrt(k)*epsilon)
    but still grows with k.
  Root: R06.ARCH (DP evaluated per-query; deployment as multi-query API not
    fully evaluated at design — R10.6 parallel), R08 (privacy budget
    consumption often not tracked by deployer)

A378: Physical attack on edge computing node
  Mechanism: Attacker gains physical access to edge compute node (retail
    kiosk, gas station pump, smart city device). Removes or replaces storage
    (contains configuration, customer data, API keys). Installs malicious
    firmware. Edge node becomes attacker-controlled with trusted cloud
    credentials. Attacker exfiltrates all edge-processed data.
  Root: R04 (edge node physical access; trust boundary at edge),
    R05 (cloud trust model: edge node trusted based on TLS certificate;
    doesn't verify physical integrity of edge device)

── DEFENSE ENUMERATION (BATCH 46) ───────────────────────────────────────────

D489: ICS network segmentation + Purdue model enforcement + Modbus proxies
  Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture: L0 (physical) → L1 (control) →
  L2 (supervisory) → L3 (site operations) → L4 (enterprise IT). Each level
  separated by industrial DMZ (IDMZ). No direct Modbus/TCP connections across
  levels. Modbus-aware firewall: allow only expected function codes, expected
  register ranges, expected source/destination pairs (whitelist by default,
  deny unexpected commands). Protocol anomaly detection (OT-SIEM: Claroty,
  Dragos, Nozomi).

D490: SS7 signaling firewall + SMS Home Routing
  MAP screening at STP (Signal Transfer Point): block high-risk MAP operations
  (ATI, SRI-SM from external networks, ISD/USSD). SMS Home Routing (3GPP
  TS 23.840): SMS-C queries home network directly; attacker's SS7 SRI-SM
  never reaches HLR. GSMA FS.11 firewall recommendations deployed at
  international SS7 links. Defense migration: migrate to VoLTE/RCS (5G SA
  architecture; 5G has SEPP protecting roaming interface).

D491: GitHub Actions hardening (pinned SHA + OIDC + minimal permissions)
  Pin actions to full commit SHA (not mutable tag): uses: third-party/action@abc123.
  OIDC cloud credentials: CI/CD requests short-lived cloud tokens via OIDC
  federation; no long-lived secrets stored in CI. Minimal GITHUB_TOKEN permissions:
  restrict to read-only unless write is required. Separate workflows: untrusted
  PR code runs in read-only workflow context. StepSecurity automated PRs for
  SHA pinning and permissions hardening. SLSA provenance for artifacts.

D492: CAN bus security (CANsec / SecOC for next-generation vehicles)
  Automotive Ethernet: CAN bus replacement with authenticated Ethernet (SOME/IP
  with AUTOSAR SecOC — Secure Onboard Communication). SecOC: HMAC-based message
  authentication with freshness counter. CAN FD + SecOC: backwards-compatible
  authenticated CAN messages. OBD-II port: restrict diagnostic access to
  authorized diagnostic tools (access control via gateway ECU).
  UNECE WP.29 R155: mandatory automotive cybersecurity management system for
  vehicles type-approved after July 2022.

D493: Cancelable biometrics + biometric template protection
  Cancelable biometrics: transform biometric template with user-specific
  cancellable transformation; store only transformed template. If compromised:
  revoke transformation parameter, re-enroll with new transformation.
  ISO/IEC 24745: biometric template protection standard. Fuzzy commitment
  schemes: store error-correcting code commitment to biometric; matching
  recovers secret without revealing template. In practice: multi-factor auth
  where biometric is one factor; compromise of biometric database alone
  insufficient for authentication bypass.

D494: RFC 6979 deterministic ECDSA (eliminates nonce RNG dependency)
  Replace random nonce generation in ECDSA with RFC 6979 deterministic nonce
  (k = HMAC-DRBG(private_key || message_hash)). Eliminates RNG dependency
  entirely. Same message + private key = same signature (but unique per
  private key). Widely deployed: OpenSSL, libsecp256k1 (Bitcoin), BoringSSL.
  Pattern 40.6 exemplar: eliminates entire attack class (nonce reuse) by
  class-level architectural fix rather than instance-level RNG improvement.

D495: ROP mitigations (CET, shadow stack, CFI)
  Intel Control-flow Enforcement Technology (CET): hardware-enforced
  shadow stack (return address cannot be overwritten; shadow stack on
  separate guarded memory region) + indirect branch tracking (ENDBRANCH
  instruction required at valid indirect branch targets; ROP gadgets
  not preceded by ENDBRANCH are illegal). CFI (Control Flow Integrity):
  compiler-enforced constraint on valid call/jump targets (LLVM CFI,
  Microsoft CFGuard). Reduces but doesn't eliminate ROP; CET bypass
  requires architectural techniques not yet commoditized.

D496: Package publishing security (Sigstore / npm provenance / PyPI attestation)
  Sigstore (keyless signing): package signing with ephemeral certificate
  tied to OIDC identity of CI pipeline (proves package built from specific
  GitHub repo + workflow). npm provenance attestation: npm v9 attaches OIDC
  build provenance to published packages. PyPI: Trusted Publishers (OIDC-based
  publishing without API tokens). Consumers: verify provenance before install.
  Blocks typosquatting if provenance check is mandatory (provenance shows
  wrong source repo).

D497: Differential privacy budget management (epsilon tracking + adaptive queries)
  Privacy budget controller: track cumulative epsilon consumption per user/query.
  Hard limit: refuse queries when budget exhausted. Rényi DP composition
  (tighter bound than basic composition; reduces required epsilon per query).
  Private query interface: disallow adaptive queries that use previous results
  as input (prevent correlation attacks). Audit log of all DP queries
  with epsilon consumption per query.

D498: Edge node tamper detection + remote attestation
  TPM-based measured boot: edge node firmware hash measured at boot and
  reported to cloud via remote attestation (TPM quote). Cloud validates
  expected hash; refuses to provision API credentials to nodes failing
  attestation. Tamper-evident enclosures: physical tamper detection (mesh,
  intrusion switch) triggers key zeroization. Network attestation: edge node
  mutual TLS with certificate tied to hardware identity (IDevID per IEEE 802.1AR).

Attacks: 368 + 11 = 379
Defenses: 488 + 11 = 499

CYCLE 46 — STAGE 5: CROSS-DOMAIN CONVERGENCE & META-PATTERN EVOLUTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C46.1: PATTERN 40.6 COMPREHENSIVE INSTANCE CATALOG ─────

Pattern 40.6: CLASS ELIMINATION > INSTANCE REMEDIATION
  Confirmed instances (cumulative review):

1. TLS 1.3: eliminates CBC padding oracle, BEAST, CRIME classes entirely
     (removed CBC mode, compression, RC4 — class elimination)
  2. Rust memory safety: eliminates buffer overflow, use-after-free as classes
     (in safe Rust; residual: unsafe blocks, logic errors)
  3. FIDO2/WebAuthn: eliminates phishing of passwords (credential bound to
     origin; cannot be phished to wrong site)
  4. ASLR+DEP combination: combined, raises cost of exploitation by requiring
     information leak + ROP (class-level barrier, not elimination)
  5. RFC 6979 deterministic ECDSA: eliminates nonce reuse attack class entirely
     (k is no longer random; depends on private key + message)
  6. HTTP/2 binary framing: eliminates HTTP request smuggling class present
     in HTTP/1.1 text parsing (binary frames are length-prefixed, unambiguous)
  7. Cancelable biometrics: eliminates irrevocability class in biometric
     compromise (can now revoke by revoking transformation parameter)
  8. Pattern 40.6 instance pending: homomorphic encryption for computation on
     encrypted data (eliminates plaintext exposure during processing)
  9. SLSA Level 4 / reproducible builds: eliminates tampered build artifact
     class (build is reproducible; artifact can be verified against source)

Pattern 40.6 CONFIRMED instance count: 9 (updated from 6 last confirmed count)
  Instances 7-9 added this cycle based on anatomy and domain analysis.

Metapattern emerging: Pattern 40.6 instances cluster into two sub-types:
    TYPE A: Redesign eliminates an attack class while maintaining equivalent
      function (TLS 1.3, RFC 6979, HTTP/2) — same capability, removed attack.
    TYPE B: Redesign adds new capability that inherently prevents attack class
      (FIDO2 origin binding prevents phishing by design, not by detection;
      cancelable biometrics adds revocability capability).
    Both types are class elimination, but TYPE B requires adding capability.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C46.2: LAW-3 CE CYCLE 5 (FINAL) ───────────────────────

CE CYCLE 5 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — PHYSICAL DESTRUCTION OF ATTACK INFRASTRUCTURE

Claim: Physical destruction of attack infrastructure (C2 servers, attacker
  laptops, botnets via botnet takedown) eliminates attack surface. The
  attack surface is the attacker's infrastructure, not just the defender's
  attack surface.

Analysis:
    LAW-3 is about DEFENDER's attack surface (what can be attacked on the
    defender's systems), not ATTACKER's infrastructure. This proposed CE
    conflates attack surface with attacker capability.

Restatement: LAW-3 properly scoped — when defenders deploy security
    measures on their own systems, the attack surface on those systems
    transforms rather than being eliminated.

Physical destruction of attacker infrastructure reduces attacker
    capability but doesn't change the defender's attack surface. The
    defender's systems still have the same architectural attack surface
    regardless of whether attacker infrastructure exists.

Verdict: CE is out of scope for LAW-3. LAW-3 is about the defender's
    own attack surface, not about attacker capability. The proposed CE
    targets a different variable.

LAW-3 CE CYCLE 5: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED (out of scope, not a true CE).

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C46.3: LAW-4 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 2 ──────────────────

LAW-4 DRAFT: HIGHEST SINGLE-TARGET CATASTROPHIC IMPACT ATTACKS (>$100M OR
NATIONAL SECURITY CONSEQUENCE) REQUIRE STATE-CLASS PATIENCE (MONTHS TO YEARS).

CE CYCLE 2 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — FLASH CRASH / HIGH-FREQUENCY MARKET MANIPULATION

Claim: The 2010 Flash Crash erased $1 trillion in market value in ~36 minutes.
  No extended patience required. Qualifies as catastrophic ($1T impact) without
  state-class patience.

Analysis:
    The 2010 Flash Crash was caused by a large sell algorithm combined with
    HFT feedback loops. Was it an attack? The Commodity Futures Trading Commission
    attributed it to one large sell order (Waddell & Reed; later disputed).
    The cascading effect was an emergent property of market microstructure,
    not a deliberate attack targeting a specific victim.

LAW-4 scope: deliberate attacks targeting specific systems/organizations.
    Flash crash is systemic fragility, not deliberate attack. The market
    microstructure vulnerability is a real security concern but not LAW-4 scope.

Deliberate financial attacks at scale: the closest deliberate high-impact
    low-patience attack is DDoS against financial exchanges. NYSE/NASDAQ DDoS
    would have $100M+ impact (trading halted). But DDoS doesn't require months
    of patience — it requires building/renting a botnet.

Revision: DDoS against exchanges is a legitimate LAW-4 counter-example
    candidate. However, the SUSTAINED $100M+ impact attack requires sustained
    DDoS (hours to days), and exchange-grade DDoS mitigation means the attack
    must be very large (Tbps). Building that infrastructure requires time.

Verdict: PARTIALLY FALSIFIED in the DDoS-against-exchanges case. Large-scale
  DDoS (financial exchange disruption) can achieve $100M+ impact without
  state-class months-of-patience.

LAW-4 REVISION: "HIGHEST-IMPACT PERSISTENT COMPROMISE attacks require
  state-class patience. HIGHEST-IMPACT DISRUPTION attacks may not require
  extended patience but require infrastructure scale."

The distinction is: PERSISTENT COMPROMISE (access, data theft, espionage,
  backdoor) requires patience. DISRUPTION (DDoS, ransomware, destructive wiper)
  can achieve catastrophic impact without extended patience but with infrastructure.

LAW-4 CE CYCLE 2: COMPLETE. PARTIAL REVISION. LAW-4 scope narrowed to
persistent compromise attacks. Disruption attacks at catastrophic scale
require infrastructure, not extended patience.

G346 (AI inference infrastructure) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: GPU memory not scrubbed between tenant workloads in shared cloud
  GPU (side-channel at hardware level: previous tenant's model weights or
  activations may be readable). This is R10.5a (passive side-channel) at
  the GPU memory layer — a novel instantiation.
  R01: LLM API as attack surface for prompt injection, data extraction attacks

G347 (CHERI capability hardware) → Root mechanics:
  CHERI represents Pattern 40.6 TYPE B: new capability (hardware-enforced
  pointer bounds) that inherently prevents spatial memory safety class of attacks.
  Root analysis: CHERI is a defense; its attack surface is:
    (a) CHERI capability confusion: attacker manipulates capability metadata
    (b) Temporal safety: CHERI provides spatial safety; use-after-free (temporal)
      is not addressed by CHERI capability model alone (requires fat pointer +
      revocation system like Cornucopia)
    (c) Logic errors: CHERI doesn't prevent algorithmic bugs
  R06.ARCH residual: CHERI doesn't protect the CHERI-unaware code (needs
    recompilation; legacy code in hybrid mode has reduced but not eliminated
    spatial safety guarantees)

G348 (Network microsegmentation) → Root mechanics:
  R05: East-west traffic (service-to-service) has historically been implicitly
    trusted within network boundary; microsegmentation changes trust model to
    require explicit authorization for each service communication pair.
  R08: Without microsegmentation, lateral movement is invisible once inside
    network perimeter. Microsegmentation creates east-west visibility layer.
  Pattern 33.3 CANDIDATE instance: mTLS enforcement layer creates mTLS
    certificate rotation attack surface (new perimeter: compromised cert
    grants service-to-service access).

G349 (MLOps security) → Root mechanics:
  R01: MLflow tracking server, Airflow web UI, Jupyter notebooks — all are
    web-accessible management interfaces with attack surface.
  R06.ARCH: MLflow designed for ML experiment tracking, not adversarial input;
    no authentication by default in early versions; DAG injection in Airflow.
  P40.1: ML pipeline orchestration tools reference external data sources, model
    registries, artifact stores — all supply chain attack surfaces.

G350 (Cryptographic agility) → Root mechanics:
  Algorithm confusion attacks (a specific security failure in agility):
    JWT algorithm confusion (CVE class): JWT header specifies algorithm;
    server may accept algorithm switch from RS256 to HS256; attacker uses
    public key as HMAC secret to forge tokens. Root: R06.ARCH (agility
    without binding algorithm to context creates confusion).
  R10.6: Cryptographic agility designed for flexibility; algorithm confusion
    attack surface created by flexible algorithm negotiation not fully evaluated.

G351 (LLM fine-tuning security) → Root mechanics:
  R10.6: Safety fine-tuning evaluated in normal usage context; fine-tuning with
    adversarial data not evaluated as attack surface at design time.
  R06.ARCH: LoRA adapter layer is an architectural addition that could
    introduce behavior modifications difficult to detect via output testing.
  Pattern 40.6 TENSION: safety training is a class-level defense; fine-tuning
    can potentially undo class-level defense (instance-level erasure of class fix).

G352 (Smart grid / SCADA) → Root mechanics:
  LAW-1: DNP3 designed without security; SAv5 (Secure Authentication v5)
    is retrofit security. IEC 62351 is retrofit security standard. Grid
    equipment has 30-50 year lifecycle; NERC CIP requirements cannot mandate
    replacement of operational grid equipment on security timescales.
  Pattern 36.2 REINFORCED: Grid production continuity mandate (power cannot
    go down) creates permanent legacy of insecure DNP3 devices alongside
    SAv5-compliant new equipment.

G353 (Precision timing security) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: PTP grandmaster assumes authenticated time source; GPS-disciplined
    oscillators use civilian GPS (no authentication). GPS spoofing of grandmaster
    propagates false time through PTP fabric to all dependent systems.
  LAW-1 parallel: authenticated GPS (M-code) exists but restricted to military;
    civilian GPS L1 C/A has no authentication (retrofit: GPS CHIMERA and Galileo
    OSNMA provide navigation message authentication, but deployment limited).

G357 (SDN security) → Root mechanics:
  R04: SDN controller centralization — single controller compromise = full
    network control capability. Distributed controller deployments exist but

  R06.ARCH: OpenFlow designed for trusted data center environment; no

G358 (Adversarial ML) → Root mechanics:
  R10.6: ML classifiers (image recognition, malware detection) designed for
    accuracy in clean data context; adversarial perturbations not evaluated
    at model training time in many deployments. Adversarial robustness is
    a separate training objective from accuracy.
  P44.1 (attack planning amplifier): adversarial examples enable targeted

  LAW-2 REINFORCEMENT: ML-based security tools (antivirus, IDS) thought to

── PATTERN IDENTIFICATION BLOCK 47.A ────────────────────────────────────────

PATTERN 47.1 DRAFT: CLASS-LEVEL DEFENSE ERASURE BY FINE-TUNING
  Safety training in LLMs is a class-level defense (alignment training
  prevents harmful outputs). Fine-tuning can erase class-level safety
  training, creating instance-level vulnerability. This is the inverse of
  Pattern 40.6: instead of class elimination providing security, class-level
  security is erased by localized modification. Mechanism: LoRA fine-tuning
  on adversarial examples; catastrophic forgetting of safety training when
  fine-tuned on targeted domain.
  Instances:
    1. LLM safety bypass via fine-tuning (Qi et al., 2023): 100 adversarial
       examples sufficient to significantly degrade safety alignment
    2. Concept erasure via fine-tuning (inverse of gradient-based unlearning)
  Count: 2. Status: DRAFT. Counter-example cycle pending.

PATTERN 47.2 DRAFT: CENTRALIZED CONTROL PLANE AS SINGLE POINT OF CONTROL
  Architectures that centralize the control plane for operational efficiency
  create a high-value single target whose compromise provides full operational
  control. Distinct from Pattern 44.3 (performance monoculture) because the
  driver is control efficiency, not performance.
  Instances:
    1. SDN controller (compromise = full network control)
    2. Active Directory (compromise = domain admin = every Windows machine)
    3. AWS IAM root account (compromise = all AWS resources)
    4. Kubernetes API server (compromise = all cluster pods)
    5. PKI root CA (compromise = ability to forge certs for any domain)
    6. Supply chain build system (SolarWinds: compromise = all 18,000 customers)
  Count: 6. Status: DRAFT. Counter-example pending.
  NOTE: This pattern is very close to R04 (centralization failure). Need to
  determine if Pattern 47.2 adds distinct value or is captured by R04.
  Assessment: R04 is the root mechanic; Pattern 47.2 describes the operational
  pattern (control plane centralization as design choice). Pattern 47.2 is a
  more specific PATTERN within the R04 mechanic. Keep as distinct pattern.

ALGORITHM CONFUSION AS NEW ROOT MECHANIC CANDIDATE:
  R10.7 CANDIDATE: PROTOCOL NEGOTIATION ENABLES ALGORITHM DOWNGRADE/CONFUSION.
  When a protocol supports algorithm negotiation (cryptographic agility),
  the negotiation itself becomes an attack surface. Algorithm confusion
  (JWT RS256/HS256), cipher suite downgrade, protocol version downgrade
  (TLS 1.3 → 1.2), hash algorithm agility in signatures.
  Distinct from R10.6 (context mismatch) because the mechanism is specifically
  in the negotiation process, not in deployment context mismatch.
  Instances: JWT algorithm confusion, TLS downgrade (POODLE/DROWN),
    SSH algorithm downgrade, SAML signature wrapping.
  Status: CANDIDATE. Counter-example process required.

Patterns previous: 184
New pattern drafts: 2 (Pattern 47.1, 47.2)

G264 ANATOMY: iOS/Android permission model edge cases (post-grant exploitation)
  Surface: Mobile OS permission model (runtime permissions, Android manifest,
    iOS entitlements)
  Mechanism (permission laundering):
    Layer 1 — Legitimate app requests legitimate permission (location for mapping)
    Layer 2 — Permission granted by user
    Layer 3 — App misuses permission scope beyond user intent (continuous
      background tracking, selling location data to brokers)
    Layer 4 — No revocation mechanism for past data use; permission models
      are access-control, not purpose-control
  Mechanism (SDK supply chain in app):
    Layer 1 — App developer embeds advertising SDK
    Layer 2 — SDK operates within app's permission scope (location, contacts)
    Layer 3 — SDK exfiltrates data using app's legitimate permissions
    Layer 4 — App developer may not know SDK collects data; permission audit
      only visible to platform, not app store users
  Mechanism (permission escalation via implicit intents, Android):
    Layer 1 — App declares intent filter for implicit intent
    Layer 2 — Other app sends implicit intent with sensitive data
    Layer 3 — Any app declaring matching filter receives data (pre-Android 12)
      even without explicit data-sharing agreement
  Root mechanics: R05 (permission model assumes apps only use permissions
    for stated purpose; no purpose enforcement), R10.6 (permission model
    designed for access control; data broker use case not evaluated),
    P40.1 (SDK supply chain within app's permission scope)
  G264 STATUS: CLOSED

G269 ANATOMY: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) — abort attack
  Surface: MPC protocol execution (threshold signature, secure function eval)
  Mechanism (selective abort):
    Layer 1 — MPC parties execute protocol; at final reveal step, malicious
      party has learned output before honest parties
    Layer 2 — Malicious party aborts if output is unfavorable; honest parties
      abort without learning output
    Layer 3 — Information asymmetry: malicious party effectively has learned
      output without revealing it to honest parties
  Mechanism (input extraction via abort strategy):
    Layer 1 — Malicious party submits one input; learns partial result
    Layer 2 — Aborts; runs protocol again with different input; compares results
    Layer 3 — Binary search on honest party inputs via repeated abort
  Formal characterization: fairness failure (one party can abort after
    learning output before others); gradual release (GOD/optimistic MPC)
    and deposit-based fairness are partial solutions
  Root mechanics: R06.ARCH (MPC protocol models assume semi-honest or
    malicious adversary but fairness is a weaker property in standard
    definitions; abort is allowed), R05 (trust model: all parties assumed
    to complete protocol once started)
  G269 STATUS: CLOSED

G271 ANATOMY: CRYSTALS-Kyber (FIPS 203) — implementation security
  Surface: Post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism in deployment
  Mechanism (timing side-channel in decapsulation):
    Layer 1 — Kyber decapsulation performs secret-key-dependent polynomial
      operations (NTT, modular arithmetic)
    Layer 2 — Non-constant-time implementation: timing varies based on
      secret values in polynomial coefficients
    Layer 3 — Timing oracle: attacker queries decapsulation with crafted
      ciphertexts; measures timing; recovers secret key
  Historical: RACCOON attack (2020) on Diffie-Hellman timing; shows that
    even "secure" PQC algorithms have implementation-level timing vulnerabilities.
    Kyber has known constant-time implementation requirements; many early
    implementations (including reference) had timing vulnerabilities.
  Root mechanics: R10.5a (passive timing side-channel), R06.ARCH
    (algorithm specified to be constant-time; implementation didn't achieve it;
    verifying constant-time is architecturally hard — compiler can reintroduce
    data-dependent timing through optimization),
  Defense: constant-time implementation, verified with tools (dudect,
    ct-verif, Binsec/Rel); FIPS 203 explicitly mandates constant-time
  G271 STATUS: CLOSED

G274 ANATOMY: Browser isolation architecture (Chrome site isolation)
  Surface: Web browser multi-process renderer isolation model
  Chrome site isolation (post-Spectre):
    Layer 1 — Each site (eTLD+1) runs in separate renderer process
    Layer 2 — Renderer process: sandboxed (no direct system call access;
      goes through broker process for permitted operations)
    Layer 3 — Cross-origin data isolation (COEP/COOP headers): prevents
      cross-origin memory sharing that enables Spectre attacks
  Attack surface of browser isolation:
    (a) Renderer bugs: use-after-free in V8, rendering engine — RCE in
      renderer process (highest frequency high-value browser bug class)
    (b) Sandbox escape: IPC to broker has attack surface; privilege escalation
      from renderer to sandbox escape (second bug required)
    (c) Site isolation bypass: same-site iframes on different origins;
      origin scoping vs. site scoping mismatch
  Market pricing (confirms Pattern 33.3): Chrome renderer RCE: ~$500K;
    Chrome sandbox escape: additional $500K-$1M; full chain ~$2-3M.
    The isolation layers are measurably valuable but don't eliminate surface.
  Root mechanics: LAW-2 (browser security thought to be very hard to bypass;
    exploit market shows it is not impossible, just more expensive),
    Pattern 33.3 (site isolation creates IPC broker as new attack surface;
    sandbox creates sandbox escape as attack class)
  G274 STATUS: CLOSED

G278 ANATOMY: Homomorphic encryption — performance vs. deployment gap
  Surface: Gap between FHE availability and practical deployment
  Mechanism:
    FHE schemes (BFV, BGV, CKKS, TFHE): allow computation on encrypted data.
    Performance gap: AES encryption of 1GB: ~1 second. FHE encryption of
    same data + bootstrapping for unbounded computation: ~1000x overhead.
    Practical: CKKS (approximate arithmetic) used for ML inference on
    encrypted data; 100ms FHE inference vs. 1ms plaintext — 100x overhead.
  Security consequence of deployment gap:
    Systems that should use FHE (for compliance, privacy mandates) instead
    use plaintext processing or partial encryption. The gap between what
    FHE CAN protect and what it IS deployed on is the actual attack surface.
  Root mechanics: LAW-1 (FHE exists but deployment infeasibility means
    plaintext processing persists; this is performance debt, not algorithmic;
    LAW-1 extended: deployment feasibility is part of the architectural
    constraint), Pattern 36.2 (performance mandate creates plaintext/FHE split:
    FHE for compliance demos, plaintext for production processing)
  Progress: TFHE-rs (Zama): gate bootstrapping ~10ms; approaching practical
    for specific applications. Apple Private Cloud Compute uses partial
    HE for ML inference on iPhone (limited operations, not full FHE).
  G278 STATUS: CLOSED

── ATTACK VECTOR ENUMERATION (BATCH 47) ─────────────────────────────────────

A380: JWT algorithm confusion (RS256 → HS256 key confusion)
  Mechanism: JWT authentication server uses RS256 (asymmetric: private key
    signs, public key verifies). Attacker obtains server's public key (often
    published in JWKS endpoint). Forges JWT using HS256 algorithm (symmetric:
    same secret used for both signing and verification) with the RSA public key
    as the HMAC secret. If JWT library accepts algorithm from token header
    without validation, server treats attacker-controlled HMAC secret as
    legitimate. Attacker gains any identity.
  Root: R10.7 CANDIDATE (algorithm confusion via negotiation), R06.ARCH
    (JWT spec allowed algorithm header to control verification method)

A381: Smart grid demand-response manipulation via DNP3 injection
  Mechanism: Attacker on SCADA network segment injects forged DNP3 commands
    to grid management system. Issues fake demand-response signal: commands
    large industrial loads to simultaneously connect. Grid frequency drops
    beyond governor response capability. Cascade failure possible. No
    authentication in DNP3 (pre-SAv5). Historical analog: intentional
    generation loss + load mismatch triggering cascade (Northeast 2003
    blackout was unintentional; deliberate attack could replicate effects).
  Root: R06.ARCH (DNP3 no auth), LAW-1 (retrofit is SAv5; deployment slow),
    Pattern 36.2 (grid continuity mandate prevents equipment replacement)

A382: Adversarial example attack on ML-based malware classifier
  Mechanism: Attacker studies ML-based AV/EDR classifier behavior. Crafts
    malware binary with perturbations that preserve malware functionality
    but cause misclassification as benign. Gradient-based adversarial
    perturbation in feature space (function opcodes, PE section entropy,
    API call sequences). Black-box: attacker queries classifier with
    variations, observes output, gradient-free optimization.
  Root: R10.6 (ML classifier evaluated on clean malware dataset; adversarial
    examples not part of training distribution), LAW-2 (ML security thought
    to be harder to evade than signatures; adversarial ML reduces this)

A383: SDN controller hijacking (OpenFlow control channel exploitation)
  Mechanism: Attacker compromises device on network with OpenFlow control
    channel access (or compromises network administrator account). Connects
    to SDN controller's REST API or directly to OpenFlow port. Issues
    flow rule modifications: redirect all traffic, create monitoring mirrors,
    drop packets selectively. Full network control from single compromise.
  Root: R04 (SDN controller centralization), R06.ARCH (OpenFlow designed
    for trusted network; authentication optional in early versions),
    Pattern 47.2 (centralized control plane as high-value target)

A384: PTP/GPS timing attack targeting financial exchange timestamp integrity
  Mechanism: Attacker spoofs GPS signal feeding PTP grandmaster at financial
    exchange (or at competing firm's colocation). PTP propagates false time
    to exchange matching engine and participant clocks. Exchange timestamps
    order execution with false time. Regulatory requirement: MiFID II requires
    timestamps within 100 microseconds of UTC. False timestamps create
    compliance violations, evidence tampering capability, or HFT arbitrage
    advantage for attacker who controls their own clock.
  Root: R06.ARCH (GPS L1 C/A no authentication; PTP grandmaster trusts GPS),
    LAW-1 (GPS authentication is M-code, military-only; civilian retrofit is
    CHIMERA/OSNMA, limited deployment)

A385: LLM safety bypass via adversarial fine-tuning (100 examples)
  Mechanism: Access to model fine-tuning API (e.g., OpenAI fine-tuning endpoint).
    Attacker submits 100-200 examples of paired harmful request + uncensored
    response. Fine-tuning adjusts model weights to produce uncensored outputs
    for the adversarial prompt distribution. Safety training not robust to
    targeted fine-tuning in current architectures.
  Research: Qi et al. (2023) "Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises
    Safety, Even When Users Are Far From Harmful Fine-tuning Data" —
    demonstrated safety degradation with as few as 10-100 adversarial examples.
  Root: Pattern 47.1 (class-level defense erasure by fine-tuning),
    R10.6 (safety training evaluated in normal usage context; fine-tuning
    access as attack vector not evaluated at design)

A386: Kubernetes API server compromise via misconfigured RBAC
  Mechanism: Kubernetes cluster with misconfigured ClusterRoleBinding granting
    default ServiceAccount cluster-admin or wildcard permissions. Pod within
    cluster can query Kubernetes API server with service account token
    (auto-mounted in pod by default). Attacker code in compromised pod reads
    secret, lists all pods, executes in any pod (exec API), or deploys new
    pods with privileged security contexts. Full cluster compromise from
    single pod.
  Root: Pattern 45.4 (permissive default — ServiceAccount token auto-mounted;
    RBAC permissive by default if admin created broad bindings),
    R05 (trust model: pod-internal service account token grants API server access)

A387: GNSS spoofing for vehicle navigation manipulation
  Mechanism: High-power SDR broadcasts false GPS/GNSS signals to target
    vehicle. Vehicle GPS receiver accepts false signals (stronger than
    legitimate satellite signals). Vehicle navigation shows false position.
    Applications: redirect autonomous vehicles (GPS-dependent path planning),
    manipulate asset tracking (fleet vehicles showing false locations),
    confuse drone return-to-home function (GPS-based; drone flies to attacker-
    designated false home location).
  Root: R01 (GPS signal reception as attack surface — any RF source can
    overpower legitimate signals if powerful enough), R06.ARCH (civilian GPS
    L1 C/A has no authentication; receiver cannot distinguish genuine satellite
    from spoofer with identical signal format)

A388: Container escape via privileged pod + host PID namespace
  Mechanism: Kubernetes pod deployed with privileged: true and hostPID: true
    (or hostNetwork: true). Privileged pod has CAP_SYS_ADMIN and full host
    device access. Attack path:
    (a) nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n -p -- /bin/bash: enters host namespaces via
        host PID namespace (PID 1 = host init process)
    (b) hostPath volume with / mount: read/write entire host filesystem
    (c) chroot escape via hostPath
    All result in full host node compromise.
  Root: R05 (trust model: privileged pod should not exist in production;
    misconfiguration allows it), Pattern 45.4 (permissive Kubernetes defaults:
    no admission control blocking privileged pods by default)

A389: Deepfake video in multi-party video call for financial fraud
  Mechanism: Attacker generates real-time deepfake video of CFO using AI
    face-swap (MediaPipe, DeepFaceLab, commercial tools). Joins corporate
    video call appearing as CFO. Other participants deceived by visual and
    audio synthesis. Issues instructions for wire transfer, M&A information
    disclosure, or insider trading facilitation.
  Documented: Hong Kong, 2024 — $25M transferred after deepfake multi-person
    video call. All participants except victim were deepfakes. Victim later
    verified real CFO was uninvolved.
  Root: R03.COGNITIVE (synthetic identity confusion at visual authentication layer),
    R05 (trust model: video call visual identity trusted as real)

── DEFENSE ENUMERATION (BATCH 47) ───────────────────────────────────────────

D500: JWT library hardening (algorithm allowlist + JWKS key binding)
  JWT verification: ignore algorithm in token header; use pre-configured
  algorithm for each key (server configures RS256 for RSA key, never HS256).
  JWKS endpoint: keys have explicit algorithm tag; library binds key to
  algorithm; no algorithm negotiation from token header.
  jose/python-jose/PyJWT: explicit algorithm parameter in decode call.
  RFC 8725 (JWT BCP): documents algorithm confusion risk and proper mitigations.

D501: DNP3 SAv5 deployment + OT network deep packet inspection
  DNP3 SAv5 (IEEE 1815-2012 Amendment 3): HMAC-based authentication for
  critical DNP3 commands (control operations, time sync). Challenge-response
  mechanism. Deployment: gateway devices add SAv5 to legacy RTU/IED without
  hardware replacement. OT-aware IDS (Dragos, Claroty): baseline expected
  DNP3 command sequences; alert on unexpected function codes or unexpected
  control sequences. Network segmentation: SCADA master to RTU connectivity
  via dedicated circuits (not shared Ethernet where possible).

D502: Adversarial robustness training + ensemble detection
  Adversarial training: include adversarial examples in training set (PGD-AT,
  TRADES). Ensemble methods: multiple independent classifiers with different
  feature spaces; adversarial example must evade all classifiers simultaneously.
  Input preprocessing defenses: feature squeezing, input transformation
  (JPEG compression, bit-depth reduction). Certification: randomized smoothing
  provides certified robustness radius (guarantee that no perturbation
  within L2-norm epsilon can change classification).

D503: SDN control plane security (mutual TLS + RBAC on controller API)
  OpenFlow TLS: controller-switch mutual TLS (mandatory in production).
  Controller REST API: strong authentication (client certificate or OIDC);
  fine-grained RBAC (network operator cannot modify security policies).
  Controller HA: distributed controller deployment (ONOS, OpenDaylight cluster);
  quorum required for network-wide configuration changes.
  Network telemetry: detect unexpected flow rule modifications via OpenTelemetry.

D504: Authenticated GNSS (OSNMA for Galileo, CHIMERA for GPS)
  Galileo OSNMA (Open Service Navigation Message Authentication): digital
  signature on navigation messages; receiver verifies satellite identity.
  IANA-managed root of trust; public key distributed to receivers.
  GPS CHIMERA (Chips-Message Robust Authentication): proposed NASA framework
  for GPS civilian authentication (not yet operational).
  Interim defense: GPS/GNSS spoofing detection (multiple receiver cross-check,
  IMU fusion for anomaly detection, signal strength consistency check).

D505: LLM fine-tuning safety preservation (RepNoise, safety-aware LoRA)
  RepNoise (2024): adds noise to model's internal representations of harmful
  content during safety training; makes safety more robust to fine-tuning
  by making it harder to overwrite with targeted examples.
  Safety-aware LoRA: fine-tuning constraints that penalize degradation of
  safety alignment metrics during domain fine-tuning.
  API controls: fine-tuning endpoint validates training data against safety
  classifier before accepting; limits adversarial examples at upload time.

D506: Kubernetes security hardening (OPA Gatekeeper + PodSecurity)
  OPA Gatekeeper (admission controller): enforce policies at API server;
  block privileged pods, hostPID/hostNetwork/hostIPC, host path volumes.
  Kubernetes Pod Security Standards (PSS): built-in policy levels
  (Restricted, Baseline, Privileged) enforced at namespace level.
  ServiceAccount token: disable auto-mounting (automountServiceAccountToken: false
  in pod spec when not needed). RBAC audit: automated detection of
  wildcard ClusterRoleBindings (kubectl auth can-i --list for each SA).

D507: GNSS anti-spoofing for autonomous vehicles (multi-constellation + IMU)
  Multi-constellation GNSS (GPS + Galileo + GLONASS + BeiDou): spoofing all
  simultaneously at correct positions requires much higher attacker capability.
  IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) fusion: sensor fusion detects GNSS position
  discontinuities inconsistent with IMU-measured acceleration.
  GNSS receiver anti-spoofing: signal quality monitoring, carrier-phase
  consistency check, C/N0 (carrier-to-noise) anomaly detection.
  Cryptographic GNSS: transition to OSNMA when available.

D508: Container admission control (OPA/Gatekeeper policy enforcement)
  Admission webhook: every pod spec validated before scheduling.
  Block: privileged:true, hostPID/hostNet/hostIPC, allowPrivilegeEscalation:true.
  Block: hostPath volumes (except /dev/null, specific monitoring paths).
  Enforce: read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, specific user IDs.
  Runtime security (Falco/eBPF): detect unexpected syscalls from containers
  (container should not call clone with CLONE_NEWNS — detect namespace escape attempts).

D509: Deepfake detection and verification protocols
  Technical: deepfake detection models (FaceForensics++ trained classifiers;
  ensemble of detectors); liveness detection (eye blink patterns, micro-expressions).
  C2PA (Coalition for Content Authenticity): digital provenance for media;
  cryptographic signature from capture device embedded in media metadata.
  Procedural: for high-stakes calls, pre-established out-of-band verification
  (know-your-colleague question, callback, challenge-response code word).
  Policy: no financial authorization by video call alone; requires second
  channel confirmation regardless of visual identity confidence.

Attacks: 379 + 11 = 390  [MILESTONE: 390 attacks enumerated]
Defenses: 499 + 11 = 510  [MILESTONE: 510 defenses enumerated]
