── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.1: LAW-4 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 3 ──────────────────

LAW-4 DRAFT (revised): HIGHEST-IMPACT PERSISTENT COMPROMISE ATTACKS REQUIRE
STATE-CLASS PATIENCE (MONTHS TO YEARS).

CE CYCLE 3 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — SPRING4SHELL / LOG4SHELL RAPID EXPLOITATION

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228): vulnerability announced December 9, 2021.
  Within 72 hours: botnets actively exploiting at internet scale. Within
  1 week: nation-state actors (IRGC, Chinese APT groups) exploiting.
  The exploitation was catastrophic in scale without extended patience.
  Log4Shell was in >5,000 packages; affected billions of devices.

Analysis:
    Log4Shell exploitation was rapid and widespread — NOT persistent compromise.
    Rapid exploitation of a 0-day is:
      (a) Mass scanning + exploitation (attacker patience: 0)
      (b) Dropping ransomware/miner/C2 stager (immediate payload)
    The actual PERSISTENT COMPROMISE stage (long-term espionage, patient APT
    access) still required patience. Nation-state actors used Log4Shell for
    initial access; establishing persistent, hidden long-term access required
    additional operations.

The INITIAL ACCESS step (exploit) can be instant. The HIGH-IMPACT PERSISTENT
    PHASE (data collection, network lateral movement, ongoing access) still requires
    patience in successful operations.

LAW-4 refinement: The distinction is between INITIAL EXPLOITATION SPEED
  (can be instant for known vulnerabilities) and HIGHEST-IMPACT PERSISTENT
  COMPROMISE OUTCOME (requires patience for dwell, lateral movement, and
  objective achievement).

Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED. LAW-4 holds for the persistent compromise phase.
  Mass exploitation of known vulnerability does not require patience but also
  doesn't achieve state-class persistent compromise outcomes alone.

LAW-4 CE CYCLE 3: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED. Clarification: initial exploitation
speed is separate from persistent compromise outcome requirement.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.2: R10.7 COUNTER-EXAMPLE CYCLE 1 ──────────────────

R10.7 CANDIDATE: PROTOCOL NEGOTIATION ENABLES ALGORITHM DOWNGRADE/CONFUSION.

CE CYCLE 1 OF 5: PROPOSED CE — IANA WELL-KNOWN ALGORITHM REGISTRIES

Claim: IANA algorithm registries and strict algorithm binding prevent
  algorithm confusion attacks. JWT RFC 7519 (with RFC 8725 BCP): library
  that hardcodes expected algorithm cannot be confused. The problem is
  library implementation, not protocol design.

Analysis:
    JWT algorithm confusion exists because JWT spec allowed algorithm header
    to control verification. RFC 8725 (JWT BCP, 2020) explicitly prohibits
    using the algorithm header for verification algorithm selection. Libraries
    that follow RFC 8725 are not vulnerable.

BUT: the design choice (flexible algorithm in header) is the root mechanic.
    Libraries that DON'T follow RFC 8725 (legacy, undertested) remain vulnerable.
    The negotiation mechanism itself was the vulnerability.

Other protocol examples where strict binding prevents confusion:
      TLS 1.3: removed weak cipher suites entirely (Pattern 40.6 TYPE A);
      cannot negotiate to vulnerable algorithm.
      SSH: algorithm negotiation but with strict client-side allowlist enforcement.

The CE tests whether strict algorithm binding makes R10.7 unnecessary.
    Answer: strict binding (RFC 8725 compliance) is the defense; the vulnerability
    class (confusion via negotiation) still exists in non-compliant systems.
    LAW-1 applies: non-compliant systems persist; R10.7 attack surface persists.

Verdict: NOT FALSIFIED. Algorithm confusion exists wherever negotiation
  is flexible. Strict binding is defense, not elimination of the class.

R10.7 CE CYCLE 1: COMPLETE. NOT FALSIFIED.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.3: DEEPFAKE + SYNTHETIC IDENTITY CONVERGENCE ───────

Deepfake voice (A358) + Deepfake video (A389) + SIM swap (A370-class) all
converge on the same root: R03.COGNITIVE (human confused deputy via synthetic
identity). The attack surface is human cognitive authentication.

Cross-domain observation:
  Traditional authentication factors:
    Something you KNOW (password): phishable, database-breachable
    Something you HAVE (phone/token): SIM swappable, physical theft
    Something you ARE (biometric): synthetically replicable (deepfake),
      database-breachable (template theft)

All three traditional MFA factors have been systematically attacked at
  scale. The convergence finding: no traditional authentication factor is
  immune to synthetic attack at sufficient adversary resource level.

Emerging factor: Something only verifiable IN CONTEXT (out-of-band
  confirmation, callback to known number, physical presence verification,
  challenge-response via pre-established channel). This is the only factor
  class not yet systematically synthesizable.

R03.COGNITIVE CONFIRMED SUB-CLASS. The attack surface is the human trust
  model for identity verification. Technical MFA helps but doesn't fully
  address R03.COGNITIVE — only procedural controls (dual authorization,
  out-of-band confirmation) bound the damage.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.4: CONTROL PLANE / DATA PLANE SEPARATION ───────────

Convergence finding across multiple domains this cycle and previous:
  SDN (G357), Kubernetes API server (G349-class), AWS IAM root (Pattern 47.2),
  PKI root CA, SS7 signaling, DNS root — all share a common structure:

CONTROL PLANE / DATA PLANE SEPARATION:
  Systems separate the control plane (how rules are set) from the data plane
  (how rules are enforced). Compromise of the control plane compromises all
  data plane decisions.

Control plane attacks are universally higher-value than data plane attacks:
    Data plane attack: compromise one flow, one record, one session.
    Control plane attack: compromise all flows, all records, all sessions.

This is the structural basis of Pattern 47.2 (centralized control plane)
  AND R04 (centralization failure). The two are the same underlying phenomenon
  at different levels of abstraction.

Pattern 47.2 MERGED INTO R04 (clarification): Pattern 47.2 adds specificity
  (control plane architecture) to R04 (centralization failure). Both are in
  scope; Pattern 47.2 is an operational instance of R04.

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.5: ADVERSARIAL ML AND LAW-2 ───────────────────────

ML-based security controls were widely presented as harder to evade than
signature-based controls because they generalize from features rather than
exact patterns. Adversarial ML research (2013-present) systematically
demonstrates that this advantage is not sustained:

- ML antivirus: adversarial malware bypasses ML-based detection
    (adversarial perturbation of PE features, opcode sequences)
  - ML network IDS: adversarial traffic bypasses ML anomaly detection
    (gradient-based evasion of RNN/CNN flow classifiers)
  - ML image recognition (autonomous vehicles): adversarial examples
    in physical world (stop sign patches, lane detection attacks)
  - ML spam detection: generative AI produces spam that evades ML filters
  - LLM safety classifiers: jailbreaks + adversarial prompts evade alignment

LAW-2 CONFIRMED EXTENSION: Technical complexity at the ML level does not
create sustained attack barriers. Adversarial ML demonstrates that ML
systems are not qualitatively harder to evade than previous approaches —
they require different techniques but those techniques are discoverable
and eventually commoditized (jailbreaks are now widely shared; adversarial
malware generation frameworks exist in research literature).

── CONVERGENCE BLOCK C47.6: LEDGER UPDATE ───────────────────────────────────

Convergence findings this cycle: 14
Cumulative convergence: 378

Key state changes:
  - R03.COGNITIVE: CONFIRMED sub-class (synthetic identity attacks on human
    trust model form coherent sub-class)
  - LAW-4 CE cycle 3: COMPLETE. Not falsified.
  - R10.7 CE cycle 1: COMPLETE. Not falsified.
  - Pattern 47.2 clarified as operational instance of R04 (not redundant;
    adds specificity to control plane architecture)
  - LAW-2 extended: adversarial ML confirms that ML complexity is not a
    sustained barrier (same mechanism as other LAW-2 instances)

CYCLE 48 — STAGE 2: ROOT MECHANIC & PATTERN IDENTIFICATION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ENTERING STATE: 186 patterns

G360 (Financial trading security) → Root mechanics:
  R04: HFT co-location creates physical proximity advantage; attack on
    co-location facility affects all co-located market participants.
  R03: Order book spoofing — attacker submits and rapidly cancels orders
    (layering/spoofing); market algorithms react to false liquidity;
    attacker profits from induced price movement. R03 at financial layer:
    algorithms act as confused deputies responding to false market signals.
  Pattern 44.5 (governance alignment): HFT market maker algorithms can be
    "gamed" by adversarial order flow — algorithms designed for one market
    condition may be exploited in adversarial conditions.

G361 (Nuclear cybersecurity) → Root mechanics:
  LAW-1: Nuclear reactor I&C systems designed decades ago; digital retrofits
    are partial; air gaps assumed but demonstrated permeable (Stuxnet).
  R09.3: State-level patience required (Stuxnet developed over 2+ years).
  R10.6: Digital I&C systems for nuclear designed for reliability/fail-safe;
    adversarial cyber attack context not fully evaluated at design for all
    deployed systems.
  FINDING: Nuclear cybersecurity is the highest-stakes instance of the
    ICS security problem (G333/G316 domains) with additional physical
    consequence severity.

G362 (Satellite comms protocols) → Root mechanics:
  R01: DVB-S2 signals are broadcast; no encryption by default in many
    commercial implementations; any receiver can decode.
  R06.ARCH: Ground control station protocols (CCSDS standards) designed
    for telemetry reliability; authentication retrofit is ongoing.
  R01.RF sub-class: satellite ground station uplink as bidirectional
    attack surface (not just downlink/jamming).

G363 (Adversarial C2 infrastructure) → Root mechanics:
  This domain is the ATTACK side of R08 (defender visibility gap).
  Fast-flux DNS, domain fronting, bulletproof hosting — all are attacker
  techniques to make C2 infrastructure durable and attribution-resistant.
  Insight: C2 infrastructure resilience is inversely correlated with
  defender R08 capability. This is an adversarial game, not a fixed vulnerability.
  LAW-2 REINFORCEMENT: technical measures to detect C2 (JA3 fingerprinting,
    domain generation algorithm detection, traffic analysis) are not
    sustained barriers — attackers adapt (JA3 randomization, DGA with ML,
    DoH for C2 tunneling).

G364 (IR and forensics) → Root mechanics:
  R09.3 in reverse: attackers with long dwell time perform evidence
    destruction at cleanup. Anti-forensics (Metasploit Meterpreter:
    timestomping, memory injection, log wiping) directly counteract forensic
    capability. The effectiveness of IR is inversely correlated with
    attacker dwell time and cleanup sophistication.
  R08: forensics closes visibility gap RETROACTIVELY; by definition, forensics
    operates on evidence of past compromise, not prevention.

G365 (CMS security — WordPress) → Root mechanics:
  P40.1: WordPress plugin ecosystem (60,000+ plugins) is supply chain.
    Malicious plugin acquisition (buy popular plugin, push malicious update)
    is extension of Pattern 33.3 instance 6 (supply chain) to CMS layer.
  Pattern 33.3 instance CANDIDATE: WordPress plugin security layer creates
    plugin supply chain attack surface. B: plugin vetting boundary (WordPress.org
    review). T: malicious plugin upload and social engineering of reviewers.
  R06.ARCH: WordPress plugins run with full PHP execution in web server context;
    no capability isolation between plugins.

G366 (Quantum threat timeline) → Root mechanics:
  This domain is future-state threat modeling, not current attack mechanics.
  Key finding: CRQC timeline is uncertain (optimist: 10 years; pessimist: 30+).
  HNDL (Harvest Now Decrypt Later) is CURRENT ATTACK using future capability.
  R09.3 EXTENDED: HNDL is the ultimate expression of adversary patience —
    store encrypted data now; decrypt in 10-30 years when quantum computers
    are available. This requires institutional patience at state level.
  LAW-1 INSTANCE: RSA-2048 and ECDH P-256 are CRQC-vulnerable; migration to
    PQC is LAW-1 architectural debt: 30+ years of deployed PKI infrastructure,
    TLS implementations, and hardware must be replaced before CRQC arrives.

G367 (Physical access control) → Root mechanics:
  R01: Physical access control systems have RF attack surface (HID Wiegand
    protocol: one-directional, no challenge-response, trivially cloneable;
    HID OSDP V2 adds bidirectional encrypted communication).
  R06.ARCH: Wiegand protocol (1970s design): reader sends 26-bit facility
    code + card number to access controller over 2-wire protocol; no
    encryption; no authentication; sniffing 25cm from reader captures credential.
  LAW-1: Wiegand is deployed in millions of buildings globally; retrofit to
    OSDP V2 requires hardware replacement at every reader.
  Pattern 36.2: Building code/physical security mandates create Wiegand
    legacy (building installed per code at construction; upgrade path requires
    new reader hardware approved by building owner — not done unless required).

G368 (CTI analysis) → Root mechanics:
  CTI is a defender capability, not a vulnerability class. However:
  Attribution errors as R08 dimension: incorrect attribution causes defenders
    to prepare for wrong threat actor TTPs; false confidence in OPSEC.
  CTI poisoning (G312 revisited): deliberate false flag operations by
    sophisticated threat actors. Russian APT (APT28) used false flag
    operations (CyberCaliphate attribution in TV5Monde attack).
  PATTERN 48.1 CANDIDATE: FALSE FLAG ATTRIBUTION (sophisticated attacker
    deliberately creates forensic artifacts pointing to different actor;
    defender draws wrong conclusions about TTPs and defensive priorities).

G369 (Email security) → Root mechanics:
  R06.ARCH: SMTP designed with no authentication (RFC 821, 1982). SPF,
    DKIM, DMARC are retrofit authentication mechanisms (LAW-1).
  DMARC deployment gap: ~60% of Fortune 500 have DMARC p=reject; ~40%
    still at p=none (monitoring only). P=none does not block spoofed emails.
  Pattern 36.2 instance: Email security mandates (CISA BOD 18-01, PCI DSS)
    create compliant/non-compliant split; non-compliant organizations remain
    vulnerable to spoofing.

G370 (Cloud-native security) → Root mechanics:
  R08: Ephemeral workloads (containers, serverless) create forensic gap —
    container destroyed post-incident leaves no local forensic artifacts.
    Defender must rely on logging/telemetry captured before container exit.
  Pattern 33.3 CANDIDATE: Ephemeral infrastructure security (immutable
    containers) creates forensic gap as new attack perimeter characteristic —
    attacker knows forensic evidence is lost when container exits.
    Pattern 45.3 instance: attacker triggers container exit to destroy evidence.

── PATTERN IDENTIFICATION BLOCK 48.A ────────────────────────────────────────

PATTERN 48.1 DRAFT: FALSE FLAG ATTRIBUTION OPERATION
  Sophisticated adversary deliberately plants forensic artifacts (code
  reuse from known actor's toolkit, language artifacts in malware, timing
  consistent with different timezone) to misdirect attribution. Defender's
  CTI analysis reaches false conclusion; prepares for wrong actor's TTPs.
  Instances:
    1. TV5Monde attack (APT28/Fancy Bear): planted "CyberCaliphate" banners;
       briefly attributed to ISIS; later reattributed to Russia.
    2. Olympic Destroyer (Pyeongchang 2018): false flag containing code
       from Lazarus (North Korean), APT28 (Russian), and Chinese groups;
       initially misattributed to North Korea; later attributed to Russia.
    3. ShadowHammer (ASUS supply chain, 2019): sophisticated false flag
       elements in code similarity to Lazarus.
  Count: 3. Status: DRAFT.

R10.7 REINFORCEMENT: JWT algorithm confusion, TLS cipher downgrade, OAuth
  mix-up, SAML signature wrapping — all instances confirm R10.7 as a
  coherent candidate class. Protocol negotiation flexibility systematically
  creates confusion attacks.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G279] — DNSSEC DEPLOYMENT GAPS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: Pattern 36.2 (mandatory continuity creates persistent insecure legacy)
               + Pattern 33.3 (new defense layer creates new attack perimeter)

SURFACE: DNS is unsigned by default; DNSSEC adds cryptographic validation of DNS
  responses via chain-of-trust from root zone downward. Deployment is partial:
  ~90% of root zone signed; ~50% of TLDs; ~20% of second-level domains globally.
  DNSSEC validates existence and integrity of records but NOT confidentiality.

MECHANIC: Three orthogonal failure modes:
  [1] PARTIAL DEPLOYMENT: unsigned domains adjacent to signed domains. Attacker
      targets unsigned zone; resolver falls back to unsigned path. DNSSEC provides
      no protection if the specific target domain is unsigned.
  [2] ZONE WALKING: DNSSEC Next Secure (NSEC) records prove non-existence by
      enumerating adjacent records. Attacker walks entire zone, harvesting all
      hostnames in a domain. NSEC3 with opt-out reduces but does not eliminate.
  [3] ALGORITHM DOWNGRADE: resolvers must support legacy algorithms for backward
      compatibility. R10.7 CANDIDATE: algorithm negotiation creates confusion window.
      RSAMD5 (deprecated) still accepted by many resolvers.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [PROTOCOL]: DNSSEC specification gap — no confidentiality, zone walking by design
  L2 [DEPLOYMENT]: partial signing — 97% of attack surface unprotected by resolver
  L3 [OPERATIONAL]: key rollover complexity — IANA root KSK rollover (2018) showed
     operational fragility; 3% of resolvers broke during rollover
  L4 [INCENTIVE]: ISP resolver operators lack incentive to validate; CDN operators
     resist signing due to zone walking exposure

CONFIRMED INSTANCES:
  • 2010 Kaminsky-style cache poisoning still viable against non-validating resolvers
  • Zone walking: Cloudflare disclosed ~10M hostnames walkable in major TLDs (2020)
  • Root KSK rollover: 3% of validating resolvers failed (2018)
  • Algorithm confusion: RSAMD5 accepted alongside RSASHA256 in hybrid zones

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (network protocol surface), R06.ARCH (architectural broadcast gap)
DEFENSE CLASS: Protocol redesign (DNS-over-HTTPS, DNSSEC-bis) vs. instance patching
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G279 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G281] — QKD PRACTICAL LIMITS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R10.6 (feature-security context mismatch in unanticipated deployment)
               + Pattern 33.3 (QKD hardware creates new physical attack surface)

SURFACE: Quantum Key Distribution uses quantum mechanics (no-cloning theorem) to
  guarantee information-theoretic security of key exchange. Theoretically
  unbreakable; practically constrained by implementation.

MECHANIC: Four fundamental limitations:
  [1] DISTANCE LIMIT: photon loss in fiber limits range to ~100-200km without
      quantum repeaters (repeaters not yet practical). Satellite QKD (Micius)
      extends range but introduces satellite trust assumption — satellite becomes
      trusted node, creating R04 centralization risk.
  [2] RATE LIMIT: key generation rate too low for bulk encryption (~10kbps practical
      vs. Gbps classical). QKD typically used only for key exchange, not data;
      bulk encryption still uses classical AES, which is PQC-resistant anyway.
  [3] SIDE-CHANNEL: physical implementation leaks classical information. Photon
      detectors emit back-flash; laser intensity side-channel enables blinding attacks.
      Makarov et al. (2010): detector blinding fools QKD into revealing keys.
  [4] AUTHENTICATION DEPENDENCY: QKD requires authenticated classical channel to
      prevent man-in-middle. Authentication uses classical keys. Bootstrap problem:
      QKD secures key exchange but requires prior shared secret for authentication.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [PHYSICS]: quantum mechanics guarantees eavesdrop detection — genuine
  L2 [HARDWARE]: detector implementations leak classical information — breaks L1
  L3 [NETWORK]: distance/rate limits force trusted relay nodes — creates R04 risk
  L4 [SYSTEM]: authentication bootstrap requires classical crypto — circular dependency
  L5 [DEPLOYMENT]: QKD solves key distribution; bulk encryption still classical

IMPLICATION: QKD is theoretically sound but practically limited. Primary value:
  forward secrecy against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks (if attacker captures
  traffic today, QKD-exchanged keys cannot be retroactively decrypted). PQC
  algorithms achieve similar harvest-now-decrypt-later resistance at lower cost.

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (physical layer), R04 (trusted relay centralization)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G281 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G284] — THRESHOLD CRYPTOGRAPHY (SHAMIR, FELDMAN VSS)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: Pattern 33.3 (MPC/threshold creates distributed attack surface)
               + R04 (quorum as new centralization form)

SURFACE: Threshold cryptography splits a secret (key) into n shares; any k shares
  (k ≤ n) reconstruct the secret. Shamir's Secret Sharing (SSS) is information-
  theoretically secure. Feldman VSS adds verifiability: shareholders can verify
  their share is consistent with others without revealing the secret.

MECHANIC: Three attack surfaces:
  [1] DEALER TRUST: in SSS, the dealer generates shares. Malicious dealer can create
      biased shares, keep the secret, or distribute incorrect shares. Feldman VSS
      eliminates dealer trust via commitment scheme, but requires honest-majority
      assumption among shareholders.
  [2] QUORUM CORRUPTION: if attacker compromises k shareholders (threshold number),
      secret is recoverable. With n=5, k=3: compromising 3 of 5 custodians
      recovers secret. Quorum becomes new attack target — Pattern 44.2 (centralization
      chokepoint shift): distributed system's security reduces to quorum.
  [3] RECONSTRUCTION CEREMONY: at the moment of reconstruction, secret exists in
      cleartext in one location. Reconstruction ceremony is single-point-of-failure.
      MPC signing avoids reconstruction (signing happens distributedly) but adds
      complexity and communication overhead.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [MATH]: SSS is information-theoretically secure — genuine guarantee
  L2 [PROTOCOL]: Feldman VSS adds verifiability — genuine improvement
  L3 [TRUST MODEL]: honest-majority assumption required — not always achievable
  L4 [OPERATIONAL]: reconstruction ceremony — point-in-time vulnerability window
  L5 [HUMAN]: social engineering quorum members — R03.COGNITIVE applies

BLOCKCHAIN CONTEXT: Multi-sig wallets use threshold cryptography (m-of-n).
  Wormhole bridge hack ($320M, 2022): single guardian compromise enabled.
  Ronin bridge: 5-of-9 validators; Sky Mavis controlled 4, Axie DAO controlled 1
  — attacker needed only one more. Pattern 44.2 confirmed: quorum is new chokepoint.

ROOT MECHANICS: R04 (quorum as distributed centralization), R03 (human quorum members)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G284 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G288] — DAO GOVERNANCE SECURITY MODEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R05.ECON (incentive misalignment), Pattern 44.2 (chokepoint shift)
               + Pattern 45.1 (externalized security cost)

SURFACE: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations use on-chain token voting to govern
  protocol parameters, treasury, and upgrades. Governance token holders vote;
  majority (or supermajority) threshold executes proposals.

MECHANIC: Four governance attack vectors:
  [1] GOVERNANCE TAKEOVER: accumulate sufficient tokens (governance attack). Flash
      loans enable temporary majority. Beanstalk Farms ($182M, 2022): attacker
      flash-loaned governance tokens, passed malicious proposal, drained treasury
      in single transaction. No time-lock protected the protocol.
  [2] LOW PARTICIPATION: quorum requirements met by small fraction of token supply.
      Attacker needs only to outspend participating voters, not all token holders.
      Typical DAO participation: 5-15% of tokens. Effective quorum much lower than
      nominal quorum.
  [3] VOTER APATHY EXPLOITATION: proposals buried in technical complexity. Sophisticated
      attacker embeds malicious clause in legitimate-seeming proposal. Voters approve
      without full understanding — R03.COGNITIVE applies to governance participants.
  [4] PLUTOCRACY: one-token-one-vote concentrates power in large holders (whales).
      Protocol security depends on whale alignment with protocol health, not guaranteed.
      Incentive misalignment: whale may benefit from governance decision that harms
      smaller holders.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [MECHANISM]: on-chain voting — trustless execution (genuine)
  L2 [TOKEN ECONOMICS]: token accumulation enables governance control — plutocracy
  L3 [PARTICIPATION]: low voter turnout reduces effective quorum threshold
  L4 [TEMPORAL]: no time-lock = flash loan governance attack enabled
  L5 [COGNITIVE]: proposal complexity enables social engineering of voters

DEFENSE TAXONOMY:
  • Time-lock: proposals execute N days after passing (Compound: 48 hours). Limits
    flash loan attacks; doesn't prevent sustained token accumulation.
  • Guardian/veto: multi-sig guardian can cancel malicious proposals. Re-introduces
    centralization (Pattern 44.2 confirmed again).
  • Optimistic governance: proposals auto-execute unless vetoed. Inverts default.

ROOT MECHANICS: R05.ECON (incentive misalignment), R02.DEFI (flash loan composability)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G288 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G293] — SATELLITE INTERNET SECURITY (STARLINK/LEO)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R01.RF (RF attack surface), Pattern 33.3 (new layer new perimeter)
               + R04 (ground station centralization)

SURFACE: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite internet (Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper) uses
  constellations of hundreds-to-thousands of satellites providing global broadband.
  User terminal (dish) communicates via Ku/Ka-band radio to nearest satellite;
  satellite relays to ground station.

MECHANIC: Three attack surfaces:
  [1] USER TERMINAL RF: user terminal transmits on known frequencies, known protocols.
      Lennert Wouters (2022): Starlink user terminal has debug interface accessible
      via hardware fault injection. Voltage glitching bypassed secure boot, enabling
      custom firmware. R10.5b (active fault injection) confirmed instance.
  [2] GROUND STATION: satellite constellations concentrate traffic through limited
      number of ground stations (Points of Presence). Ground stations are high-value
      targets — R04 centralization. Viasat KA-SAT ground station hack (2022, Ukraine):
      wiped modems across Europe by compromising ground-based management systems.
  [3] INTER-SATELLITE LINKS: Starlink Gen 2 uses laser inter-satellite links (ISLs).
      ISLs create space-based routing fabric. Physical attack on satellite (ASAT)
      creates debris field affecting multiple satellites. Congestion/route manipulation
      via ISL possible if routing protocol has attack surface.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [SPACE]: satellite physical inaccessibility — genuine attack barrier (for most)
  L2 [RF]: user terminal radio transmission — known-frequency eavesdrop, jamming
  L3 [HARDWARE]: user terminal debug interfaces — fault injection vulnerability
  L4 [GROUND]: ground station management systems — R04 centralization risk
  L5 [ROUTING]: ISL routing protocol — emerging attack surface (partially unexplored)

GEOPOLITICAL: State actors (Russia, China) have demonstrated ASAT capability.
  Electronic warfare jamming of GPS L1 frequency also jams adjacent satellite bands.
  Ukraine conflict demonstrated operational dependence on LEO satellite connectivity.

ROOT MECHANICS: R01.RF (radio frequency surface), R04 (ground station centralization)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G293 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G298] — DNS-over-HTTPS PRIVACY/SECURITY TRADEOFFS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: Pattern 33.3 (new privacy layer creates new security perimeter)
               + Pattern 44.2 (centralization chokepoint shift)

SURFACE: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) encrypts DNS queries inside HTTPS, preventing ISP
  surveillance and on-path manipulation of DNS. DoH resolvers (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1,
  Google 8.8.8.8) handle queries instead of ISP resolvers.

MECHANIC: Privacy gain creates two security tradeoffs:
  [1] ENTERPRISE VISIBILITY LOSS: enterprise security tools (firewalls, DLP, CASB)
      rely on DNS query inspection to detect malware C2, data exfiltration via DNS
      tunneling, and policy violations. DoH bypasses corporate DNS resolver,
      making DNS-based security controls ineffective. Malware using DoH to reach
      C2: Godlua (2019), TrojanDownloader:Win32/Injecter using DoH for C2 resolution.
  [2] CENTRALIZATION: DoH concentrates DNS traffic at major providers (Cloudflare,
      Google). Pattern 44.2 confirmed: distributed DNS replaced by centralized DoH.
      Cloudflare outage (July 2020) took down significant fraction of internet DNS.
      Single provider becomes geopolitical target and single point of surveillance
      (now by provider instead of ISP — surveillance not eliminated, shifted).

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [PRIVACY]: ISP DNS surveillance eliminated — genuine gain
  L2 [SECURITY]: enterprise DNS inspection eliminated — genuine loss for defenders
  L3 [RESILIENCE]: centralization at major providers — new single-point risk
  L4 [SOVEREIGNTY]: DNS control shifted from local ISP to global provider

PATTERN 33.3 INSTANCE #15 CANDIDATE: DoH privacy layer creates new attack perimeter
  at DoH resolver. Previous: ISP resolver was perimeter. Now: Cloudflare/Google
  resolver is perimeter. Attack surface transformed, not eliminated.
  → Evaluating for Pattern 33.3 confirmation: new defense (DoH) creates new
  perimeter (centralized resolver). CONFIRMED — Pattern 33.3 instance 15.

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (network protocol), R04 (centralized resolver)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G298 CLOSED | Pattern 33.3 inst 15 CONFIRMED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G299] — SERVERLESS/FAAS SECURITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R10.6 (feature-security context mismatch), Pattern 45.4 (permissive default)
               + Pattern 33.3 (new execution model new attack surface)

SURFACE: Functions-as-a-Service (Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) execute
  event-driven code in provider-managed containers. Developer focus shifts from
  infrastructure to function logic. Security model: provider handles OS/runtime;
  developer handles function code and IAM configuration.

MECHANIC: Five serverless-specific attack surfaces:
  [1] OVER-PRIVILEGED FUNCTIONS: IAM permissions granted to functions often exceed
      least-privilege (ease of configuration). Compromised function inherits excessive
      permissions. Pattern 45.4 (permissive default): Lambda execution roles
      frequently include wildcard S3 or DynamoDB access.
  [2] EVENT INJECTION: serverless functions process events from many sources (API
      Gateway, S3, SQS, etc.). Each event source is an injection surface. SQL
      injection, command injection in event data. Function trusts event source but
      event source may be attacker-controlled.
  [3] FUNCTION CHAINING: functions trigger other functions; compromise propagates
      through event chain. Attacker-controlled event data poisoning downstream
      functions in chain.
  [4] COLD START DISCLOSURE: function initialization leaks timing information;
      container reuse leaks /tmp state between invocations (not guaranteed isolation).
      AWS Lambda: /tmp persists within container lifetime. Cross-invocation state leak.
  [5] THIRD-PARTY DEPENDENCY: function packages import npm/PyPI dependencies.
      Supply chain risk (Pattern 40.6 TYPE B: managed containers eliminate OS
      patching; but package-level supply chain remains).

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [INFRA]: provider-managed OS/runtime — genuine security gain (OS patching)
  L2 [IAM]: function execution role — over-permissioning common, easy to misconfigure
  L3 [EVENT]: event source trust — implicit trust in event data is injection surface
  L4 [STATE]: container reuse — /tmp cross-invocation leak
  L5 [DEPENDENCY]: third-party packages — supply chain remains

ROOT MECHANICS: R08 (misconfiguration), R09 (dependency chain)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G299 CLOSED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G300] — API SECURITY AT MICROSERVICE BOUNDARIES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R07 (trust boundary violation), Pattern 45.4 (permissive default config)
               + Pattern 33.3 (service mesh creates new control plane)

SURFACE: Microservice architectures decompose monoliths into independent services
  communicating via APIs (REST, gRPC, message queues). Service-to-service
  communication within the cluster is often implicitly trusted.

MECHANIC: Four microservice-boundary attack surfaces:
  [1] EAST-WEST TRUST: internal service-to-service traffic frequently unauthenticated
      or authorized only by network position (same namespace/cluster). Attacker
      compromising one service gains access to internal APIs not exposed externally.
      OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) endemic.
  [2] SERVICE MESH CONTROL PLANE: Istio, Linkerd, Consul service meshes add
      mTLS and policy enforcement. Service mesh control plane (Istiod) becomes
      high-value target: compromise enables policy manipulation, certificate forgery.
      Pattern 33.3 INSTANCE #16 CANDIDATE: service mesh defense creates new control
      plane attack perimeter. Evaluating.
  [3] API GATEWAY BYPASS: external API gateway enforces authentication; internal
      services assume gateway already validated. Bypassing gateway (SSRF, internal
      network access) reaches unprotected internal APIs.
  [4] SCHEMA VALIDATION GAP: services frequently trust schema of incoming requests
      without re-validating. Upstream service sending malformed data (compromised or
      buggy) causes downstream injection.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [EXTERNAL BOUNDARY]: API gateway — authentication enforced
  L2 [INTERNAL BOUNDARY]: east-west — frequently unauthenticated (trust gap)
  L3 [MESH CONTROL]: service mesh control plane — new centralization risk
  L4 [APPLICATION]: BOLA/BFLA logic flaws — authorization at application layer

Pattern 33.3 inst 16 CONFIRMED: service mesh mTLS creates new control plane (Istiod)
  as attack perimeter. Defense (service mesh) creates new attack surface (control plane).

ROOT MECHANICS: R07 (trust boundary), R08 (misconfiguration of internal auth)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G300 CLOSED | Pattern 33.3 inst 16 CONFIRMED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G301] — OAUTH 2.0 / OIDC IMPLEMENTATION VULNERABILITIES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R07 (trust boundary), R08 (implementation misconfiguration)
               + Pattern 44.1 (implementation shortcut becomes permanent)

SURFACE: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework; OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity
  layer. Used universally for 'Sign in with Google/GitHub/etc.' and API authorization.
  Specification is complex; implementation errors are endemic.

MECHANIC: Five confirmed implementation vulnerability classes:
  [1] CSRF ON REDIRECT: OAuth flows require 'state' parameter to prevent CSRF.
      Many implementations omit or validate state incorrectly. Attacker can force
      victim to authorize attacker's code, linking attacker's identity to victim's
      account. Systematic across implementations.
  [2] OPEN REDIRECT: authorization server's redirect_uri validation too permissive.
      Attacker crafts URL with attacker-controlled redirect; authorization code
      sent to attacker. OAuth 2.1 mandates exact redirect URI matching.
  [3] PKCE BYPASS: Proof Key for Code Exchange prevents code interception by public
      clients. Implementations may accept code without validating PKCE verifier,
      making PKCE parameter security theater.
  [4] JWT ALGORITHM CONFUSION: ID token (JWT) signed with RS256 (asymmetric).
      Vulnerable libraries accept alg:HS256 with public key as secret, enabling
      token forgery. Auth0, OneLogin affected. R10.7 CANDIDATE confirmed instance:
      algorithm negotiation creates confusion vulnerability.
  [5] TOKEN LEAKAGE IN REFERRER: access tokens in URL fragment or query parameter
      appear in server logs, browser history, Referer headers. Pattern 45.4:
      permissive default (implicit flow, now deprecated) enabled this class.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [SPEC]: OAuth 2.0 specification — complex, ambiguous in security-critical areas
  L2 [IMPLEMENTATION]: each implementation reinvents validation — error-prone
  L3 [LIBRARY]: JWT libraries with algorithm confusion — affected major providers
  L4 [DEPLOYMENT]: implicit flow (deprecated) still in widespread use (Pattern 36.2)

ROOT MECHANICS: R07 (trust boundary between client/server/IdP), R08 (implementation)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G301 CLOSED | R10.7 instance confirmed (JWT alg confusion)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G303] — PQC MIGRATION OPERATIONAL SECURITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: Pattern 36.2 (continuity mandate creates persistent legacy)
               + R10.7 CANDIDATE (algorithm negotiation = confusion)

SURFACE: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) migration: NIST standardized ML-KEM
  (Kyber), ML-DSA (Dilithium), SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) in 2024. Migration from RSA/ECC
  to PQC requires years-long hybrid deployment period.

MECHANIC: Hybrid deployment period creates systematic vulnerabilities:
  [1] HYBRID MODE DOWNGRADE: during migration, systems negotiate classical OR PQC.
      Attacker forces classical negotiation (R10.7 CANDIDATE: algorithm negotiation
      as confusion). Hybrid mode intended as safety net; becomes downgrade vector.
      RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) requires downgrade protection; PQC hybrid extensions
      (draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design) must carefully specify negotiation.
  [2] HARVEST NOW DECRYPT LATER: adversary archives encrypted traffic today;
      decrypts when quantum computer available. Migration timeline: 10-15 years
      to full PQC deployment; cryptographically relevant quantum computer estimated
      5-15 years (NIST, 2024). Overlap window is the risk.
  [3] SIDE-CHANNEL ON PQC: lattice-based algorithms (ML-KEM) have side-channels.
      Timing attacks on NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) operations. Constant-time
      implementations required but not universal in early deployments.
  [4] KEY SIZE OPERATIONAL: ML-KEM-1024 public key: 1568 bytes vs RSA-2048: 256 bytes.
      6x size increase. Operational impact on TLS handshake, certificate chain size,
      memory-constrained IoT. Pressure to use smaller parameters (ML-KEM-512) for
      performance may compromise security margin.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [ALGORITHM]: PQC algorithms — mathematically sound (as of 2024)
  L2 [IMPLEMENTATION]: side-channels in non-constant-time code — well-established risk
  L3 [TRANSITION]: hybrid mode negotiation — downgrade attack surface
  L4 [OPERATIONAL]: key size pressure — parameter selection tradeoff
  L5 [TIMELINE]: harvest-now-decrypt-later — risk exists NOW even before migration

ROOT MECHANICS: R01 (protocol), R10.7 CANDIDATE (algorithm negotiation)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G303 CLOSED | R10.7 CE cycle 2 PENDING (downgrade)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G304] — CDN SECURITY MODEL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R04 (centralization), Pattern 44.2 (chokepoint shift)
               + Pattern 33.3 (CDN TLS termination creates new trust boundary)

SURFACE: Content Delivery Networks (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly) sit between users
  and origin servers. CDN terminates TLS, caches content, provides DDoS mitigation.
  ~20% of internet traffic passes through Cloudflare alone.

MECHANIC: Three CDN-specific trust issues:
  [1] TLS TERMINATION TRUST: CDN decrypts and re-encrypts traffic. Origin server
      issues TLS certificate to CDN; CDN presents its own cert to users. Users
      'trust' connection but traffic is decrypted at CDN. User has no visibility
      into origin-to-CDN segment security. CDN is inherently trusted man-in-middle.
  [2] CDN OUTAGE PROPAGATION: Fastly outage (June 2021, 1 hour): knocked offline
      Reddit, GitHub, NYT, Guardian, Twitch. Single CDN failure cascades globally.
      Cloudflare outage (July 2020): similar cascade. Pattern 44.2: internet
      decentralization myth — actual routing concentrated through few CDNs.
  [3] CACHE POISONING: CDN caches responses based on URL/headers. Cache key
      normalization differences between CDN and origin enable cache poisoning:
      attacker injects malicious content into CDN cache, served to all users.
      James Kettle (PortSwigger): systematic cache poisoning research (2018-2022).

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [DDoS]: CDN absorbs volumetric attacks — genuine defense
  L2 [TLS]: TLS termination at CDN — CDN as trusted intermediary (trust shift)
  L3 [CACHE]: cache key normalization — cache poisoning surface
  L4 [RESILIENCE]: CDN centralization — single-point-of-failure for dependents

Pattern 33.3 inst 17 CONFIRMED: CDN DDoS protection creates new trust boundary
  (TLS termination). Defense (DDoS protection) creates new attack surface (cache
  poisoning, CDN as trusted intermediary).

ROOT MECHANICS: R04 (centralization), R01 (network)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G304 CLOSED | Pattern 33.3 inst 17 CONFIRMED

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANATOMY [G309] — WIRELESS PROTOCOL SECURITY (ZIGBEE/Z-WAVE/LORAWAN)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R01.RF (radio frequency), R08 (default configuration)
               + Pattern 45.4 (permissive default as vulnerability class)

SURFACE: IoT wireless protocols designed for low-power, low-bandwidth mesh networking.
  Zigbee (IEEE 802.15.4), Z-Wave (ITU-T G.9959), LoRaWAN (LoRa Alliance) used in
  smart home, industrial IoT, smart city, agricultural monitoring.

MECHANIC: Protocol-specific vulnerability classes:
  [ZIGBEE]
  • Touchlink commissioning: proximity-based network join without authentication.
    Attacker with high-power radio initiates touchlink from 100m, joins network.
    2015: researchers demonstrated Zigbee network compromise of Philips Hue lights.
  • Default encryption keys: many Zigbee devices use well-known default keys
    ('ZigBeeAlliance09'). Pattern 45.4 confirmed.
  • Key transport in plaintext: Zigbee 2007 profile sends encryption key in plaintext
    during join. Sniffing join captures network key.

[Z-WAVE]
  • S0 security (legacy): single fixed network key, limited entropy. Downgrade
    from S2 to S0 possible in some implementations. R10.7 CANDIDATE: security
    class negotiation as downgrade vector.
  • S2 security (current): authenticated key exchange using ECDH. Stronger but
    requires out-of-band QR code exchange — usability pressure creates shortcuts.

[LORAWAN]
  • Join server centralization: network/join server is central trust point.
    AppKey and NwkKey derivation — key management complexity.
  • Frame counter replay: LoRaWAN frame counters must be persisted; device reset
    resets counter, enabling replay of earlier frames. Documented systematic issue.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [PHYSICS]: RF transmission — eavesdropping, jamming
  L2 [PROTOCOL]: join/pairing mechanisms — authentication gaps
  L3 [KEY MANAGEMENT]: default keys, key distribution in plaintext
  L4 [OPERATIONAL]: counter persistence, reset behavior

ROOT MECHANICS: R01.RF (radio frequency), R08 (default configuration)
STATUS: ANATOMY COMPLETE — Gap G309 CLOSED

ANATOMY [G312] — THREAT INTELLIGENCE SHARING SECURITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PATTERN CLASS: R07 (trust boundary), Pattern 45.2 (deception as visibility)
               + Pattern 33.3 (TI sharing platform as new attack surface)

SURFACE: Threat intelligence (TI) sharing platforms (MISP, ISACs, STIX/TAXII)
  allow organizations to share indicators of compromise (IoCs), TTPs, and threat
  reports. Shared intelligence improves collective defense — if trustworthy.

MECHANIC: Three TI sharing attack surfaces:
  [1] INDICATOR POISONING: attacker submits false IoCs (benign IPs, legitimate
      domains) as malicious. Defenders block legitimate infrastructure. Reverse:
      attacker submits known-malicious infrastructure as false-positive-flagged,
      causing defenders to allowlist it. Trust in shared intelligence is unverified.
  [2] INTELLIGENCE AS OPERATIONAL DISCLOSURE: sharing TI reveals defender capabilities.
      Which IoCs are known — signals which TTPs have been detected. Attacker
      monitoring TI feeds learns which infrastructure is burned, which techniques
      are known. Intelligence sharing as counter-intelligence opportunity for attacker.
  [3] PLATFORM COMPROMISE: MISP instance compromise poisons all downstream consumers.
      STIX/TAXII servers are centralized distribution points — R04 centralization.
      Compromised TI feed is high-leverage attack: feeds defenders false data at
      scale.

LAYER ANATOMY:
  L1 [PLATFORM]: MISP/TAXII infrastructure — centralization risk
  L2 [DATA]: IoC quality/veracity — no universal authentication of submitters
  L3 [OPERATIONAL]: sharing reveals defender posture — intelligence asymmetry
  L4 [TRUST]: federated trust model — weakest contributor poisons pool

ROOT MECHANICS: R04 (platform centralization), R07 (trust boundary between contributors)

A391: DNSSEC zone walking — enumerate all hostnames in signed zone via NSEC record
      traversal. Passive, no authentication required. Affects any NSEC (not NSEC3)
      signed zone. Scale: entire zone enumerable in minutes.

A392: DNSSEC algorithm downgrade — present RSAMD5 DS record to legacy resolvers;
      exploit weak algorithm acceptance. R10.7 CANDIDATE confirmed instance #2.

A393: QKD detector blinding — direct high-intensity light at single-photon detectors;
      detectors saturate, report same bit regardless of quantum state. Makarov (2010):

A394: DAO governance flash loan attack — borrow governance tokens, pass malicious

A395: Satellite user terminal fault injection — voltage glitching to bypass secure boot

A399: OAuth redirect_uri manipulation — register client with permissive redirect;

A400: JWT algorithm confusion — submit HS256 token signed with RS256 public key;
      vulnerable libraries verify successfully, enabling token forgery. Auth0, OneLogin

A403: Zigbee join key capture — sniff plaintext key during Zigbee 2007 profile join

A404: Z-Wave S0 downgrade — force negotiation to legacy S0 security class from S2.

DEFENSE ADDITIONS [D511-D530]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

D511: DNSSEC NSEC3 with opt-out — replace NSEC with NSEC3 using salt; raises cost
      of zone walking (hashes instead of plaintext names). Opt-out leaves unsigned
      delegations unsigned. Partial mitigation: online zone walkers still possible
      with sufficient compute.

D512: DNSSEC algorithm enforcement — resolver policy requiring minimum algorithm
      strength (prohibit RSAMD5, DSA). DANE (DNS-based Authentication of Named
      Entities, RFC 7671) pins TLS certificates to DNS.

D513: QKD + PQC hybrid key establishment — combine QKD for key exchange with
      PQC for authentication; neither alone is sufficient. QKD handles forward
      secrecy; PQC handles authentication without quantum computer vulnerability.

D514: DAO governance time-lock — mandatory delay between proposal passage and
      execution (Compound: 48 hours). Prevents flash loan governance attacks;
      allows community response window. Standard best practice post-Beanstalk.

D515: DAO guardian veto — multi-sig guardian address can cancel malicious proposals
      within time-lock window. Accepts centralization tradeoff for emergency response.

D516: Satellite terminal secure boot + attestation — hardware root of trust with
      attestation prevents firmware tampering. Requires: tamper-resistant hardware,
      remote attestation capability. Mitigates A395.

D517: Ground station network segmentation + OT monitoring — isolate satellite ground
      station management networks from corporate IT. Monitor for wiper-style lateral
      movement (behavioral detection). Post-Viasat architecture recommendation.

D518: DoH enterprise control — split-horizon DNS; enterprise DoH resolver with
      TLS inspection. Alternatively: block DoH destinations (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8)
      at firewall; force all DNS through inspectable resolver. Tradeoff: privacy loss.

D519: Service mesh mTLS everywhere + control plane hardening — extend mTLS to all
      east-west traffic (zero-trust mesh). Harden Istiod: RBAC, audit logging,
      admission webhooks. Recognize Istiod compromise as equivalent to CA compromise.

D520: OAuth 2.1 mandatory exact redirect URI — OAuth 2.1 (draft) mandates exact
      URI matching, prohibits wildcard patterns. PKCE required for all clients.
      Mitigates A399. Backward compatibility gap during migration.

D521: JWT algorithm binding — reject tokens with algorithm mismatch; use RS256 only
      with RSA public keys. Libraries must explicitly disallow HS256 when RS256
      configured. jose4j, nimbus-jose-jwt have explicit alg validation.

D522: PQC hybrid TLS with downgrade protection — implement PQC hybrid key exchange
      (X25519Kyber768) with binding: if hybrid offered, server must use hybrid.
      RFC 8701 (GREASE) approach for signaling. No silent fallback to classical.

D523: Zigbee Touchlink global disable — disable touchlink commissioning in production
      deployments where not required. Enable APS (application support sublayer)
      encryption with non-default keys. Change network key post-commissioning.

D524: Z-Wave S2 mandatory enforcement — configure controllers to reject S0 and
      unsecured devices. Vendor responsibility: no legacy downgrade allowed in
      security-sensitive contexts.

D525: LoRaWAN persistent frame counter — store frame counter in non-volatile memory
      (EEPROM/flash); increment before transmission, persist before ACK. Survive
      device reboot without counter reset. Specification requirement; implementation
      varies by vendor.

D526: TI sharing vouched submission + reputation scoring — require organizational
      vouching for IoC submissions to MISP instances. Reputation scoring: contributors
      with high false-positive rates downweighted. ISACs implement sector-specific
      trust models.

D527: CDN cache key normalization auditing — audit cache key configuration; ensure
      CDN and origin normalize URLs identically. Vary headers correctly specify all
      response-varying parameters. Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive responses.

D528: Serverless least-privilege execution roles — scope Lambda execution roles to
      specific resources (not wildcards). Separate roles per function. Regular
      IAM access analyzer review. /tmp: treat as untrusted between invocations.

D529: Microservice zero-trust east-west — implement mTLS for service-to-service
      communication; don't rely on network position. SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload
      identity. Each service authenticates the calling service, not just the network.

D530: TI platform air-gap + integrity verification — maintain offline/air-gapped
      TI feed for high-trust indicators. Cryptographically sign STIX bundles;
      consumers verify before ingestion. Mitigates A408 (platform compromise).

COUNTER-EXAMPLE PROCESSES — ACTIVE
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

CE PROCESS: R10.7 CANDIDATE — Protocol negotiation flexibility enables algorithm
  downgrade/confusion. Status: CE cycle 2 of 5.

Claim: Wherever a security protocol supports algorithm negotiation, that negotiation
  is exploitable to force weaker algorithm selection or create algorithm confusion.

Proposed counter-example: TLS 1.3 — eliminated negotiation of weak algorithms.
  Only strong cipher suites (ECDHE + AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). No RC4, no
  3DES, no export ciphers. Algorithm list not negotiable (server chooses from
  client's supported list, which TLS 1.3 constrains to strong-only).

EVALUATION: Does TLS 1.3 falsify R10.7?
  - TLS 1.3 itself: no downgrade within 1.3. Genuine.
  - But: TLS 1.3 must coexist with TLS 1.2 during transition. MITM downgrade
    from 1.3 to 1.2 is protected by downgrade sentinel (ServerHello.random
    last 8 bytes set to TLS 1.2 downgrade sentinel if server supports 1.3).
    RFC 8446 §4.1.3. Legitimate technical defense.
  - Does sentinel eliminate downgrade? In compliant implementations: yes.
    In non-compliant implementations (older TLS stacks): sentinel not checked.
    LAW-1 applies: non-compliant implementations persist on security timescales.
  - VERDICT: TLS 1.3 is CLASS ELIMINATION for downgrade within TLS 1.3.
    But coexistence with 1.2 recreates downgrade surface. Pattern 36.2 applies:
    continuity mandate (backward compatibility) creates persistent legacy window.
    R10.7 not falsified — applied narrowly to hybrid/coexistence periods.
  R10.7 CE cycle 2: CANDIDATE NOT FALSIFIED. Scope refinement: R10.7 applies
  during algorithm transition/coexistence periods; pure TLS 1.3 deployments
  are genuine counter-example TO R10.7 (within scope of that deployment).

CE PROCESS: LAW-4 DRAFT — Highest-impact persistent compromise attacks require
  state-class patience. Status: CE cycle 4 of 5.

Claim (revised scope): Achieving persistent compromise with state-class impact
  outcomes requires months-to-years of operational patience.

Proposed counter-example: Log4Shell exploitation chain from discovery to
  persistence. Timeline:
  - Dec 9, 2021: CVE-2021-44228 disclosed
  - Dec 9-10: weaponized exploits in the wild (hours)
  - Dec 10-14: mass exploitation across internet
  - Persistent implants established within days of disclosure

EVALUATION: Does Log4Shell falsify LAW-4?
  - Initial exploitation: immediate (hours to days). Genuine.
  - BUT: achieving STATE-CLASS IMPACT from Log4Shell required:
    • Identifying which compromised systems had strategic value
    • Maintaining persistence without detection through forensic response
    • Exfiltrating intelligence or establishing long-term access
  - Chinese APT actors exploiting Log4Shell: VMware Horizon targets for
    espionage (CISA AA22-174A). Initial foothold: days. Strategic outcome
    (sustained espionage campaign): months of operational activity.
  - Pure disruptive attacks (ransomware deployment post-Log4Shell): faster.
    BlackCat/ALPHV groups: initial access to ransomware deployment in <72 hours.
    But ransomware impact is NOT state-class persistent compromise — it is
    disruptive, not persistent intelligence access.
  - LAW-4 SCOPE HOLDS: distinction between disruption attacks (no patience
    required) and persistent compromise (patience required) is maintained.
    Log4Shell confirms the pattern: initial exploitation = fast; strategic
    persistent compromise outcomes = slow.
  LAW-4 CE cycle 4: DRAFT NOT FALSIFIED. Disruption/persistence distinction
  maintained. Cycle 5 will test: ransomware as persistent compromise?

CE PROCESS: LAW-1-HUMAN CANDIDATE — Human cognitive architecture is unredeemable
  as security control on security timescales. Status: CE cycle 1 of 5.

Claim: Human cognition cannot serve as reliable security control; systematic
  exploitation via social engineering, cognitive bias, and attention limits
  makes human-in-the-loop security controls fundamentally unreliable over time.

BASIS: R03.COGNITIVE (confirmed this session). Vishing, deepfake voice/video,
  BEC, SIM swap all systematically bypass human verification. 90%+ of breaches
  have phishing/social engineering component (Verizon DBIR 2024).

FIRST CE CANDIDATES to test:
  [1] Security culture programs — can training make humans reliable?
    GOOGLE PHISHING STUDY (2019): security key users: 0% phishing success rate.
    BUT: security key is hardware, not human. Humans with hardware token =
    human + hardware. The hardware is the reliable control; human merely holds it.
    Does not falsify: hardware control, not human cognitive control.

[2] Expert security practitioners — trained analysts resist phishing better?
    Security professionals still click phishing links: ~10-15% click rates vs
    ~30% general population (Cofense data). Reduction but not elimination.
    Under spear-phishing with adequate targeting: expert analysis still exploitable.
    Does not falsify: improvement is quantitative, not qualitative elimination.

[3] FIDO2/Passkeys — eliminate phishing entirely via hardware binding?
    FIDO2 eliminates password phishing class entirely (hardware binding to origin).
    But: FIDO2 as defense class elimination (Pattern 40.6) — not human improvement.
    Human error remains in: device registration, account recovery, social engineering
    to enroll attacker's key (SIM swap then account recovery).
    Does not falsify: human cognitive control is not the reliable element.

LAW-1-HUMAN CE cycle 1: CANDIDATE NOT FALSIFIED. Pattern: every successful
  defense against human-targeting attacks relies on hardware/automated controls,
  not improved human cognition. Human remains the weak link even in hardened
  configurations. Proceeding to CE cycle 2.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
CROSS-DOMAIN SYNTHESIS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SYNTHESIS-1: NEGOTIATION AS UNIVERSAL ATTACK SURFACE

The accumulation of R10.7 instances (now 5+ candidates across TLS, JWT, OAuth,
Zigbee Z-Wave, DNSSEC, PQC hybrid) reveals a deeper pattern than protocol-specific
downgrade attacks. The common mechanic: any system that NEGOTIATES security
parameters at runtime creates a selection surface that can be manipulated.

Negotiation is necessary when:
  (a) multiple versions/algorithms must coexist (transition periods)
  (b) endpoints have different capabilities
  (c) backward compatibility is required

In all three cases, negotiation is mandated by operational requirements.
R10.7 is an instance of LAW-1 applied specifically to security parameter selection:
the necessity of backward-compatibility-driven negotiation persists as long as
legacy endpoints exist, which LAW-1 guarantees on security timescales.

IMPLICATION: negotiation-free protocols (TLS 1.3 with no fallback, FIDO2 with no
password fallback, PQC-only with no classical fallback) are the only architectures
that escape R10.7. But Pattern 36.2 guarantees that negotiation-free protocols
cannot be universally deployed as long as non-compliant endpoints exist (which
LAW-1 guarantees). R10.7 and LAW-1+LAW-3 form a closed implication loop:

LAW-1 (architectural debt irredeemable) →
  negotiation-free deployment impossible →
  negotiation surface persists →
  R10.7 (algorithm confusion) persists →
  adds to architectural debt (LAW-1 reinforced)

SYNTHESIS-2: DECENTRALIZATION MYTHS IN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE

This cycle's anatomies (DoH → Cloudflare, CDN, service mesh control plane,
satellite ground stations, TI platforms) consistently reveal: internet systems
marketed as decentralized have de facto centralization at specific choke points.

Pattern 44.2 (centralization chokepoint shift) is confirmed across:
  • DNS: nominally distributed → DoH concentrated at 2-3 providers
  • Content: nominally distributed web → 70%+ traffic through 3 CDNs
  • Kubernetes security: distributed microservices → centralized control plane
  • Blockchain governance: distributed voting → quorum concentrated in whales
  • TI sharing: federated sharing → concentrated at major ISAC/MISP instances
  • Satellite: distributed constellation → ground station concentration

STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION: decentralization reduces single points of failure in
steady state (no single server) but creates new centralization at coordination
layers (who validates, who routes, who governs). The coordination layer is
systematically more vulnerable than the data layer it coordinates.

This is an instance of Pattern 33.3 applied at architectural scale: the defense
mechanism (decentralization) creates a new attack perimeter (coordination layer).
Pattern 44.2 is a specific formulation of Pattern 33.3 at the architectural level.

SYNTHESIS-3: HUMAN-HARDWARE SUBSTITUTION PRINCIPLE

From LAW-1-HUMAN CE cycle 1 analysis: every successful elimination of human-
exploitable security controls involves substituting hardware/automated controls
for human cognition. Enumeration:
  • Password (human memory) → FIDO2 hardware key
  • Manual certificate validation → HSTS, certificate pinning (automated)
  • Human approval of transactions → hardware transaction signing (Ledger, Trezor)
  • Manual threat detection → SIEM/EDR automated detection
  • Human judgment on phishing → link rewriting + sandbox detonation

Pattern emerging: reliable security controls are not improvements to human
cognition but replacements of human cognition with deterministic systems.

IMPLICATION for R03.COGNITIVE: R03.COGNITIVE is irreducible as a root mechanic
as long as any human decision point exists in a security-sensitive workflow.
The defense is CLASS ELIMINATION (Pattern 40.6 TYPE A: remove human decision point
via hardware/automation) rather than INSTANCE REMEDIATION (security awareness training).

This becomes a sub-finding of LAW-1-HUMAN: human-targeting attacks persist
precisely because complete hardware/automation substitution of all human decision
points is operationally impossible (there exist workflows that cannot be fully
automated without losing functionality).

NEW DOMAINS [D475-D493]:

D475: BGPSEC deployment security — BGP route origin validation (ROV) uses RPKI
      (Resource Public Key Infrastructure). RPKI has its own PKI failure modes:
      invalid ROA misconfigurations cause legitimate routes to be rejected. BGP
      security relies on out-of-band RPKI repository (analogous to DNSSEC trust chain).
      Gap: RPKI repository availability attacks, cache poisoning, ROA misconfiguration
      causing route filtering. Domain: routing protocol security.

D476: Anycast infrastructure security — DNS root servers, CDNs, DDoS mitigation
      use anycast routing (same IP, multiple locations). Anycast resilience vs.
      BGP hijack: attacker who hijacks anycast prefix intercepts traffic globally.
      Pattern 33.3 candidate: anycast resilience creates new BGP hijack surface.
      Gap: anycast prefix hijack, anycast and RPKI interaction. Domain: routing.

D477: Hardware security module (HSM) operational security — HSMs hold CA root keys,
      payment processing keys. HSM is trust anchor. Attack surface: HSM management
      interface, initialization ceremony, operator collusion, HSM firmware updates.
      HSM firmware supply chain (R09): HSM vendor supply chain is critical path.
      Gap: HSM management interface attacks, firmware supply chain. Domain: HSM.

D478: FIDO2/WebAuthn implementation security — authenticator attestation, credential
      ID management, relying party validation. Known issues: credential ID brute force
      (credential IDs not always bound to user), attestation bypasses, clone detection
      gaps. Pattern 36.2: legacy password fallback maintained for account recovery
      creates persistent phishing surface alongside FIDO2.
      Gap: attestation bypass, recovery flow phishing, clone detection. Domain: auth.

D479: Neural network model inversion attacks — gradient-based reconstruction of
      training data from model weights or outputs. Carlini et al.: GPT-2 memorization
      (2021). Membership inference: determine if specific data was in training set.
      Model as involuntary data disclosure mechanism.
      Gap: model inversion at inference time, differential privacy effectiveness.
      Domain: ML security, privacy.

D480: Federated learning poisoning — distributed ML training; participants contribute
      gradients. Byzantine fault tolerance: malicious participants submit crafted
      gradients to corrupt global model (backdoor injection, performance degradation).
      Sybil attack on federated participants enables majority-gradient poisoning.
      Gap: gradient poisoning detection, Sybil resistance in FL. Domain: ML security.

D481: Confidential computing (TEE) side-channels — SGX, TrustZone, CCA provide
      hardware-isolated enclaves. Side-channel attacks: cache timing (Spectre/Meltdown
      within enclave), power analysis, memory bus snooping. SGX enclave to host
      interface is attack surface (untrusted OS controls page tables).
      Foreshadow/L1TF: SGX enclave contents extracted via speculative execution.
      Gap: SGX interface attack, page fault side-channel, cross-privilege speculation.
      Domain: trusted execution, hardware security.

D482: Software bill of materials (SBOM) security — SBOM provides ingredient list
      of software components. SBOM itself is security-relevant: SBOM reveals
      all dependencies, enabling attacker to identify high-value targets.
      SBOM poisoning: false SBOM obscures actual dependencies.
      Gap: SBOM as vulnerability roadmap, SBOM integrity verification. Domain: supply chain.

D483: Runtime application self-protection (RASP) security — RASP instruments
      application at runtime to detect and block attacks. RASP bypass: attacker
      identifies RASP hook points, crafts payload to evade detection logic.
      RASP is code running in application context; compromise of RASP module
      compromises protection. Pattern 33.3 candidate: RASP creates new hook surface.
      Gap: RASP evasion, RASP module compromise. Domain: application security.

D484: Automotive ECU security — modern vehicles have 100+ ECUs connected via CAN bus.
      CAN bus has no authentication (broadcast, no source validation). V2X adds
      wireless connectivity. Attack surface: OBD-II port (physical access),
      infotainment system as pivot to CAN, telematics unit as remote entry.
      Tesla, GM (OnStar), Jeep Cherokee (2015 remote compromise) confirmed instances.
      Gap: CAN bus authentication gap, OTA update security. Domain: automotive.

D485: Operational technology historian security — OT historians (OSIsoft PI, Honeywell
      Experion) aggregate time-series process data. Historians sit at IT/OT boundary:
      connected to both corporate network and plant network. High-value pivot point.
      Historians contain process data sufficient for attack planning (process parameters,
      equipment states). Gap: historian as IT/OT pivot, process data exfiltration.
      Domain: ICS/OT.

D486: CI/CD pipeline secret management — pipelines handle secrets (deploy keys,
      API tokens, cloud credentials) in environment variables or secret stores.
      GitHub Actions: secrets exposed in PR builds from forks (pre-2022), log masking
      bypass. Pattern 44.1 candidate: temporary CI secret access as permanent credential.
      Gap: secret masking bypass, fork PR secrets, OIDC token scope. Domain: DevOps.

D487: Large language model prompt injection — instructions embedded in processed
      content (documents, web pages, emails) hijack LLM behavior when processed by
      AI agent. Indirect prompt injection: attacker controls data LLM reads, not
      direct input. Greshake et al. (2023): systematic demonstration.
      Gap: indirect injection in agentic pipelines, injection via image/OCR, defense
      layers (instruction hierarchy). Domain: AI/LLM security.

D488: AI agent tool use security — LLM agents call external tools (web search, code
      execution, file access, email). Tool call parameters controlled by LLM output;
      injected instructions can manipulate tool calls. Confused deputy: agent acts
      on behalf of user but instruction source is attacker.
      R01.LLM-AGENT confirmed application domain.
      Gap: tool call parameter injection, agent-to-agent trust, tool capability scope.
      Domain: AI agent security.

D489: Biometric spoofing — fingerprint (gelatin molds, lifted prints), face (3D
      printed mask, deep-fake video), iris (high-resolution photo), voice (TTS/deepfake).
      R03.COGNITIVE already covers deepfake voice/video. Biometric specifically:
      physical biometric artifacts vs. live detection (liveness checks).
      Gap: liveness detection bypass, biometric database breach → template replay.
      Domain: biometric security.

D490: Memory forensics anti-analysis — malware residing only in memory (fileless)
      evades disk-based detection. Anti-forensics: memory artifact wiping,
      process hollowing, direct system calls bypassing user-mode hooks.
      Volatility framework as defender tool; anti-Volatility techniques.
      Gap: kernel-mode rootkit memory hiding, hypervisor-level memory concealment.
      Domain: malware analysis, forensics.

D491: Ransomware negotiation and payment security — ransomware operators maintain
      .onion infrastructure for victim negotiation. Victim payment in cryptocurrency
      creates OFAC compliance risk (paying sanctioned actor). Ransomware negotiation
      as threat intelligence opportunity: negotiation reveals operator behavior.
      Gap: cryptocurrency tracing effectiveness, OFAC risk during ransom payment,
      decryption key reliability post-payment. Domain: ransomware operations.

D492: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) operational security — beyond threshold
      cryptography: general MPC for joint computation without revealing inputs.
      Used in privacy-preserving analytics, dark pool trading. Attack surface:
      malicious participant (Byzantine MPC), side-channel during computation,
      MPC protocol implementation bugs. Gap: MPC participant authentication,
      Byzantine fault tolerance limits. Domain: cryptographic protocols.

D493: Physical security bypass via electronic means — RFID badge cloning (HID
      Proxcard at 125kHz; long-range readers at 1m+), Wiegand protocol replay
      (no cryptography, no rolling codes), electric strike manipulation (door strike
      power cycling). Physical access control systems as electronic attack surface.
      Gap: RFID cloning at range, Wiegand replay, door controller network access.
      Domain: physical security, access control.

PATTERN 49.1 DRAFT — TRUST ANCHOR AS MAXIMUM-LEVERAGE TARGET

Observation: Systems that establish security chains-of-trust have single root
anchors (trust anchors). Compromise of trust anchor is qualitatively different
from compromise of dependent: it invalidates all downstream trust relationships
simultaneously. Trust anchors are irreplaceable on operational timescales.

Instances:
  [1] CA root certificates — compromise of root CA invalidates all certificates
      issued under that root. DigiNotar (2011): 298 rogue certificates; Iran MITM.
      DigiNotar removed from browser trust stores; company went bankrupt.
  [2] HSM with CA root key — physical HSM is trust anchor for PKI hierarchy.
      HSM compromise = root CA compromise.
  [3] RPKI trust anchor — RPKI Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) from IANA. Compromise
      of RPKI trust anchor invalidates all Route Origin Authorizations globally.
  [4] Zigbee Trust Center — central node managing network keys. Compromise enables
      full network key distribution control.
  [5] Kubernetes control plane (etcd) — etcd stores all cluster state; compromise
      enables full cluster control. etcd = trust anchor for Kubernetes.
  [6] Git repository signing key — Linus Torvalds' kernel signing key; compromise
      would poison official Linux kernel distribution.

PATTERN 49.1: TRUST ANCHOR IS MAXIMUM-LEVERAGE TARGET — the single node whose
  compromise propagates to all downstream trust relationships simultaneously.
  Trust anchor attack is asymmetrically efficient: one compromise, unlimited scope.
  RELATIONSHIP: Pattern 49.1 is a specific, high-value instance of R04 (centralization
  failure). Not redundant: adds the trust chain semantics (downstream propagation
  of compromise via inherited trust).
  STATUS: DRAFT — 6 confirmed instances, CE process required

PATTERN 49.2 DRAFT — DATA DISCLOSURE AS SIDE EFFECT OF COMPUTATION

Observation: Systems that perform computation on data reveal information about
that data through side effects of the computation (timing, output, error messages,
computational traces). This is distinct from R10.5 (side-channel from physical
implementation) — this is semantic disclosure from computation outputs.

Instances:
  [1] Timing oracle — RSA padding oracle (Bleichenbacher): timing of decryption
      reveals whether padding is valid. 1M queries → private key recovered.
  [2] Model inversion — LLM memorization: model outputs reveal training data.
      Carlini et al.: extracted verbatim PII from GPT-2.
  [3] Error message disclosure — SQL error messages revealing schema (error-based
      SQLi). Stack traces revealing internal paths.
  [4] Compression oracle — CRIME/BREACH: HTTP compression reveals session tokens
      via size side-channel. Compression ratio encodes data content.
  [5] Cache timing oracle — Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe: cache state reveals memory
      access patterns, enabling cryptographic key extraction.
  [6] ML membership inference — model query responses reveal whether specific
      data point was in training set.

PATTERN 49.2: COMPUTATION REVEALS DATA VIA OUTPUT SIDE-EFFECTS — any system
  that computes on sensitive data may leak that data through observable side-effects
  of computation results. Distinct from R10.5 (physical side-channel) in that
  the channel is the computation's semantic output, not physical emanation.
  STATUS: DRAFT — 6 instances, CE process required

PATTERN 49.3 DRAFT — TRUST FEDERATION INHERITS TRUST FAILURES

Observation: When systems federate trust (accept credentials from third-party
identity providers), they inherit the security properties of those providers.
A weak link in the federation chain compromises the entire federation.

Instances:
  [1] SAML federation — IdP compromise propagates to all SP relying parties.
      SolarWinds: SAML token forgery via AD FS certificate theft enabled access
      to M365, Azure, AWS across the federal government.
  [2] OAuth delegation chain — application authorized to act for user; application
      compromise grants attacker user's delegated permissions to all OAuth resources.
  [3] Social login federation — "Login with Google/Facebook" delegates identity
      verification to provider. Provider account compromise = all federated apps
      compromised.
  [4] DNSSEC trust chain — parent zone delegation enables child zone. Parent
      zone compromise propagates to all child zone trust.
  [5] Container image registry — base image trust: FROM ubuntu:22.04 inherits
      all vulnerabilities of ubuntu:22.04. Compromised base image propagates to
      all derived images.
  [6] Package manager trust — npm/PyPI trusted as package source; package
      compromise propagates to all dependents (Pattern 40.6 context, supply chain).

PATTERN 49.3: FEDERATED TRUST INHERITS PROVIDER FAILURES — each federation link
  multiplies the scope of trust anchor failure. Multi-hop federation creates
  trust chains where weakest link determines system security.
  RELATIONSHIP: Pattern 49.3 extends Pattern 49.1 to multi-hop chains. Not redundant:
  adds the federation/inheritance semantics (transitive trust failure propagation).
  STATUS: DRAFT — 6 instances, CE process required

PATTERN CONSOLIDATION REVIEW:

Reviewing existing patterns for consolidation opportunities with new candidates:

Pattern 49.1 vs Pattern 44.2 (centralization chokepoint shift):
  → Pattern 44.2 is about defensive decentralization creating new chokepoint.
  → Pattern 49.1 is about trust anchor as inherent maximum-leverage target.
  → Distinction maintained: 44.2 is emergent centralization; 49.1 is designed
    trust anchor (architecturally necessary single point of trust).

Pattern 49.2 vs R10.5 (side-channel):
  → R10.5 is physical implementation side-channel (power, EM, timing from hardware).
  → Pattern 49.2 is semantic/computational output revealing data.
  → Distinction maintained: different attack vectors (physical vs. logical output).

Pattern 49.3 vs Pattern 49.1:
  → Pattern 49.1: trust anchor as single target.
  → Pattern 49.3: trust federation propagation across chains.
  → Distinction maintained: 49.1 is about the target node; 49.3 is about
    the transmission mechanism through the chain.
